The pratijñā made was that by the knowledge of the cause everything is known: "Hast thou asked for that instruction by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought thought, the unknown known? — How, venerable sir, is that instruction?" (Chāndogya 6.1.3); "As, my dear, by one lump of clay everything made of clay is known; the modification is a mere word, a name; the clay alone is real" (Chāndogya 6.1.4); "Even so, my dear, is that instruction" (Chāndogya 6.1.6) — these are heard at the very opening of the section.

Now if pradhāna, being only the cause of the class of objects of enjoyment (bhogya-varga), were known by the word 'sat,' whether as fit to be discarded or not, the class of enjoyers (bhoktṛ-varga) would not thereby be known, since the bhoktṛ-varga is not a modification of pradhāna. Hence pradhāna is not the thing denoted by the word 'sat.'
BS_C01_S01_V09: Because of merging into one's own self (in deep sleep). (9)
BS_C01_S01_V09::block-0: And on what further ground is pradhāna not denoted by the word 'sat'? —
BS_C01_S01_V09::block-1:
Concerning that very 'sat' which has been taken up as the cause, the śruti says: "That, my dear, by which a man is said to be 'sleeping' (svapiti) — at that time, my dear, he is gone unto sat; he has gone unto his own (svam apīto bhavati); therefore men say of him 'svapiti'; for he has gone unto his own" (Chāndogya 6.8.1).

This śruti gives the etymology (nirvacana) of the word 'svapiti,' which is a name well known in common usage for 'sleeping.' Here the word 'sva' denotes the Ātman. He has gone (apīta), that is, become merged into, that very 'sat' which has been taken up as the topic. The verb 'i' preceded by 'api' is well attested in the sense of laya (dissolution); for in the compound 'prabhavāpyayau' it is seen used to mean 'origin and dissolution.'

When the jīva, through the special association with the upādhi of mental activity, perceives sense-objects through the differentiating particularity of those upādhis, he is awake (jāgarti). Possessed of the impressions of those experiences, when he sees dreams, he is denoted by the word 'manas.' At the cessation of both upādhis, in the state of deep sleep (suṣupti), since the particularities effected by upādhis are absent, he is as it were dissolved into his own self — therefore it is said "sva-aṃ hi apīto bhavati."

Just as the śruti shows the etymology of the word 'hṛdaya' — "This Self, verily, is in the heart; its etymology is this — 'He is in the heart' (hṛdi ayam); therefore it is called 'hṛdaya'" (Chāndogya 8.3.3); just as the śruti shows the source of the words 'aśanā' (hunger) and 'udanyā' (thirst) — "The waters lead away that which is eaten" (Chāndogya 6.8.3), "The fire leads away that which is drunk" (Chāndogya 6.8.5) — even so does the śruti, by giving the etymology of the name 'svapiti,' show this meaning, namely, that he goes back to his own Ātman, denoted by the word 'sat.'

Now a sentient (cetana) Ātman cannot accept an insentient (acetana) pradhāna as its own essential nature. If, on the other hand, pradhāna alone, being one's own (ātmīya), were denoted by the word 'sva,' even then it would be a contradiction that a sentient one merges into the insentient. Another śruti also — "Embraced by the prājña Ātman, he knows nothing whatsoever, neither external nor internal" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.3.21) — shows the apyaya (merging) into a sentient principle in the suṣupti state. Hence, that into which all sentient beings go is itself sentient, denoted by 'sat,' and is the cause of the world — not pradhāna.
BS_C01_S01_V10: Because of the uniformity of view (in all Vedānta texts). (10)
BS_C01_S01_V10::block-0: And on what further ground is pradhāna not the cause of the world? —
BS_C01_S01_V10::block-1:
If, as among the tārkikas (logicians), there had been in the Vedānta texts also a divergent apprehension of the cause — somewhere a sentient Brahman as the cause of the world, somewhere insentient pradhāna, somewhere yet another — then perhaps, in conformity with the doctrine of pradhāna as cause, one might somehow have construed the textual passages such as 'īkṣati' (Chāndogya 6.2.3) and the rest. But this is not the case. The apprehension of a sentient cause is uniform in all the Vedānta texts.

"As from a blazing fire sparks fly forth in all directions, even so from this Ātman issue forth all the prāṇas to their respective seats; from the prāṇas, the gods; from the gods, the worlds" (Kauṣītaki 3.3); "From this very Ātman ākāśa was born" (Taittirīya 2.1.1); "All this is from the Ātman alone" (Chāndogya 7.26.1); "From the Ātman this prāṇa is born" (Praśna 3.3) — thus all the Vedānta texts show the causality of the Ātman. And we have already said that the word 'ātman' denotes a sentient principle.

Moreover, this is itself a great ground of authority — namely, that the Vedānta sentences are uniform in their sense (samāna-gatitva) regarding a sentient cause, just as the eye and the other senses are uniform in their respective objects, form and the rest. Therefore, by reason of this uniformity of import (gati-sāmānya), the all-knowing Brahman is the cause of the world.
BS_C01_S01_V11: And because (it is so) revealed (in śruti). (11)
BS_C01_S01_V11::block-0: And on what further ground is the all-knowing Brahman the cause of the world? —
BS_C01_S01_V11::block-1: By the very own word (of śruti) is the all-knowing Īśvara declared to be the cause of the world. In the mantropaniṣad of the Śvetāśvataras, with reference to the all-knowing Īśvara, it is said: "He is the cause, the lord of the lords of the senses; for him there is no begetter, nor any lord above him" (Śvetāśvatara 6.9). Therefore it is established that the all-knowing Brahman is the cause of the world, and not insentient pradhāna or anything else.
BS_C01_S01_V12: (Brahman is) the Self consisting of bliss (ānandamaya), because of repetition. (12)
BS_C01_S01_V12::block-0:
Beginning with the sūtra "That from which arise the origin and so on of this (world)" (1.1.2) and ending with "Because it is heard so" (1.1.11), the Vedānta passages cited in the sūtras have been shown by reasoning to convey this meaning — that the all-knowing, all-powerful Īśvara is the cause of the origin, sustenance, and dissolution of the world. By the argument of uniformity of import (gati-sāmānya) it has been explained that all the Vedānta texts uphold a sentient cause. Now what is the occasion (utthāna) for the further portion of the work? It is replied —

Brahman, indeed, is apprehended in two forms: as qualified by the upādhis of the differences of name, form, and modification (nāma-rūpa-vikāra-bheda), and on the other hand as devoid of all upādhis. "Where there is duality as it were, then one sees another" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 2.4.14); "But where for him everything has become the very Self, then by what should one see whom?" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.5.15); "Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, knows nothing else, that is the Bhūman; where one sees something else, hears something else, knows something else, that is the small. The Bhūman alone is immortal; what is small is mortal" (Chāndogya 7.24.1); "Having created all forms, the wise one, having given them names, sits naming them" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.12.7); "Without parts, without action, tranquil, faultless, untainted, the highest bridge to the immortal — like a fire whose fuel is consumed" (Śvetāśvatara 6.19); "Not this, not this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 2.3.6); "Not gross, not subtle, not short, not long" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 3.8.8); "One station is deficient, another is full" — by such passages, in their thousands, the texts show the two-fold form of Brahman in accordance with the difference of vidyā and avidyā as their respective sphere.

There, in the state of avidyā, occurs all the empirical activity of Brahman characterised as worshipper, worshipped, and so forth. Of these, some upāsanās of Brahman are aimed at worldly elevation (abhyudaya), some at gradual liberation (krama-mukti), some at the prosperity of rites (karma-samṛddhi). Their distinction lies in the difference of the upādhis of specific qualities. The one supreme Ātman, Īśvara, though qualified by such-and-such specific qualities is what is meditated upon — yet the fruits differ according to the upāsanā, by virtue of the śruti, "As one meditates upon Him, so verily does he become," and "As is one's resolve in this world, so does one become hereafter on departing" (Chāndogya 3.14.1). The smṛti also says: "Whatever state of being one remembers when he leaves the body at the end, that alone he attains, O son of Kuntī, ever absorbed in that state" (Bhagavadgītā 8.6).

Though one Ātman is hidden in all beings, movable and immovable, still, by reason of the gradation of citta-upādhi, of the Ātman — though kūṭastha-nitya and of one form — when manifested progressively more and more, gradation through specific powers of lordship is heard: "Of the one who knows the Ātman as more manifest..." (Aitareya Āraṇyaka 2.3.2.1). The smṛti also: "Whatever being is endowed with vibhūti, with grace, with vigour — know that to be born of a portion of My splendour" (Bhagavadgītā 10.41) — wherever there is excess of vibhūti and the like, that is enjoined as Īśvara to be meditated upon.

Thus here too the puruṣa of golden hue in the orb of the sun, by the mark of being free from all sin (sarva-pāpma-udaya-liṅga), is none other than the Supreme — so it will be said. So too in "Ākāśa, by its mark" (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.22) and the rest. Even so, the knowledge of the Ātman which is the cause of immediate liberation (sadyo-mukti), though taught through the door of a particular upādhi, where the connection with upādhi is not intended — when there is doubt whether it pertains to the lower or to the higher — must be settled by analysis of the import of the passages, as for instance, "The ānandamaya, on account of repetition."
BS_C01_S01_V12::block-1:
Thus, in the Taittirīyaka, after enumerating in succession the annamaya, prāṇamaya, manomaya, and vijñānamaya, it is stated: "Other and inner than this vijñānamaya is the ānanda-maya Self" (Taittirīya 2.5.1). There the doubt arises — does the word ānandamaya here denote the supreme Brahman itself, that very thing taken up earlier as "Brahman is satya, jñāna, ananta" (Taittirīya 2.1.1), or does it denote something other than Brahman, like annamaya and the rest?

What then is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa)? — Ānandamaya as not the principal (mukhya) Ātman, must be other than Brahman. Why? Because it falls within the stream of non-principal selves like annamaya. — But it might be replied that, being the innermost of all (sarvāntara), ānandamaya is itself the mukhya Ātman. — That cannot be, because of the connection with parts such as 'priya' (the dear) and the rest, and because of the hearing of his being embodied (śārīratva). For the principal Ātman, were he ānandamaya, would have no contact with priya and the rest. But here it is said: "Of him priya is the head" (Taittirīya 2.5.1) and so forth. Embodiment (śārīratva) too is heard: "The śārīra Self of the former is this very one." The meaning is: of the former, the vijñānamaya, this ānandamaya is the very śārīra Ātman. And being embodied, contact with priya and a-priya cannot be excluded. Therefore the ānandamaya is none other than the saṃsārī Ātman. — Such being the prima facie view, this is now said —
BS_C01_S01_V12::block-2:
"Ānandamayaḥ abhyāsāt." The ānandamaya must be the Supreme Ātman alone. Why? On account of repetition (abhyāsa). For the word 'ānanda' is repeated many times in the supreme Ātman alone. Having taken up the ānandamaya, having said "He, verily, is rasa" (Taittirīya 2.7.1) and thus declared his being rasa, it is said: "Having obtained this rasa, one becomes blissful. Who indeed could exhale, who inhale, were not this ākāśa bliss? He alone causes bliss" (Taittirīya 2.7.1); "This is the inquiry into bliss" (Taittirīya 2.8.1); "He attains this Self consisting of bliss" (Taittirīya 2.8.5); "Knowing the bliss of Brahman one fears nothing whatsoever" (Taittirīya 2.9.1); "He knew bliss to be Brahman" (Taittirīya 3.6.1). And in another śruti — "Brahman is vijñāna and ānanda" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 3.9.28) — the word 'ānanda' is seen used of Brahman alone. Thus, by the repetition of the word 'ānanda' many times in respect of Brahman, it is understood that the ānandamaya Ātman is Brahman.

As to the objection that ānandamaya, being in the stream of non-principal selves like annamaya, is also non-principal — it is not a defect, since ānandamaya is the innermost of all. The śāstra, intending to teach the principal Ātman, follows worldly understanding: it takes up the annamaya, the body, which is no Ātman but is well known as the Ātman among the utterly deluded, and then, like images of molten copper poured into successive moulds, presents an inner, then a still inner — making the more outward each time appear as the Ātman in comparison with the next, in order to facilitate the disciple's apprehension; so most coherently does it teach as the Ātman the innermost ānandamaya which is the principal one.

Just as in the Arundhatī example, when many non-principal stars are pointed out as Arundhatī, the last one pointed out is the principal Arundhatī herself — even so here, the ānandamaya, being innermost of all, has principal Ātman-hood. As to your saying that the imagined head-hood and the rest of priya and the others are not consistent with the principal Ātman — that is brought about by the upādhi belonging immediately to the previous one, not natural; hence no defect. The śārīratva of the ānandamaya too is shown only by way of the succession of bodies beginning with annamaya — not directly śārīratva like that of the saṃsārin. Therefore the ānandamaya is the supreme Ātman alone.
BS_C01_S01_V13: If it be objected that (Brahman is not ānandamaya) because of the word denoting modification — no; on account of (the suffix denoting) abundance. (13)
BS_C01_S01_V13::block-0:
Here it is said: ānandamaya cannot be the supreme Ātman. Why? On account of the word denoting modification (vikāra-śabda). For from the word that was the topic, this other word 'ānandamaya' has been arrived at, denoting modification, since the suffix 'mayaṭ' carries the sense of vikāra. Therefore, like the words annamaya and the rest, the word ānandamaya too has only modifications as its sphere — so if it be urged, no; for the suffix mayaṭ is also remembered (in Pāṇini) in the sense of abundance.

"Tat-prakṛta-vacane mayaṭ" (Pāṇini 5.4.21) — the suffix mayaṭ is also recorded in the sense of abundance: just as 'annamayaḥ yajñaḥ' is said of a sacrifice in which annam is abundant, so 'ānanda-prakṛrṇa' Brahman is called ānandamaya. The abundance of bliss in Brahman is also established, since after saying that the bliss at each successive station, beginning from the human, is hundredfold, the bliss of Brahman has been ascertained as without any further excess (niratiśaya). Therefore the suffix mayaṭ is in the sense of abundance.
BS_C01_S01_V14: And because (Brahman) is mentioned as the cause of that (bliss). (14)
BS_C01_S01_V14::block-0: On this further ground also is mayaṭ in the sense of abundance: that the śruti speaks of Brahman as the cause of bliss — "He alone causes bliss" (eṣa hi eva ānandayāti) — meaning he gladdens others. He who gladdens others is well known to be one of abundant bliss; just as in worldly usage, he who confers wealth on others is understood to be of abundant wealth. Therefore, since mayaṭ is possible in the sense of abundance also, the ānandamaya is the supreme Ātman alone.
BS_C01_S01_V15: And the same (Brahman of the mantra) is sung. (15)
BS_C01_S01_V15::block-0:
And on this further ground also is the ānandamaya the supreme Ātman: from the fact that, beginning with "The knower of Brahman attains the Highest" (Taittirīya 2.1.1), the Brahman taken up in the mantra "Brahman is satya, jñāna, ananta" (Taittirīya 2.1.1) — the Brahman determined by the qualifications satya, jñāna, ananta, from which by the order of ākāśa and the rest the movable and immovable beings were born, which, having created the elements and entered into them, abides in the cave (guhā), innermost of all, for the cognition of which it is begun, "another inner Self," "another inner Self" — that very Brahman of the mantra (māntra-varṇika) is here sung as "another inner Self, the ānandamaya" (Taittirīya 2.5.1).

The oneness of import between mantra and brāhmaṇa is reasonable, since there is no contradiction; otherwise the topic taken up would be abandoned and an unrelated topic introduced (prakṛta-hāna and aprakṛta-prakriyā). Nor is, as in the case of the annamaya and others, another inner Self spoken of beyond the ānandamaya. And firmly resting upon this is the bhārgavī vāruṇī vidyā: "He knew bliss to be Brahman" (ānando brahmeti vyajānāt — Taittirīya 3.6.1). Therefore the ānandamaya is the supreme Ātman alone.
BS_C01_S01_V16: Not the other, on account of impossibility (anupapatti). (16)
BS_C01_S01_V16::block-0:
For this further reason the ānandamaya is the supreme Self alone, and not the other; the meaning is that the 'other'—that is, anything different from the Lord, namely the transmigrating jīva—is not denoted by the word ānandamaya. Why? Because of impossibility (anupapatti).

For with reference to the ānandamaya, scripture declares: 'He desired: May I be many, may I propagate myself. He performed tapas. Having performed tapas, He created all this, whatever there is' (Tai. Up. 2.6.1).

In that passage, there is meditative ideation prior to the production of bodies and the rest; the modifications which are being created are non-different from their creator; and the creation of all modifications is not possible from anything other than the supreme Self. (16)
BS_C01_S01_V17: And on account of the declaration of difference. (17)
BS_C01_S01_V17::block-0:
Further, for this reason the ānandamaya is not the transmigrating jīva: because in the section dealing with the ānandamaya, scripture declares, 'He alone is the essence (rasa); only by attaining this essence does one become blissful' (Tai. Up. 2.7.1), thereby designating the jīva and the ānandamaya as different. For the very same one cannot be both the attainer and that which is to be attained.

Objection (pūrvapakṣa): How then are the śruti and smṛti, 'The Self should be sought,' and 'There is nothing higher than the attainment of the Self' (Āp. Dh. Sū. 1.8.1.2), to be reconciled, since it has been said that the very attainer cannot be that which is to be attained?

Reply (siddhānta): Granted; nevertheless, even though the Self never falls away from its own Self-nature, due to non-comprehension of its true nature, there is observed in worldly experience a mithyā ascertainment of Self-hood in the body and other non-Self entities. Hence, with respect to that very Self that has come to be of the nature of the body and the rest, the Self is spoken of as 'unsought, to be sought,' 'unattained, to be attained,' 'unheard, to be heard,' 'unthought, to be thought,' 'uncomprehended, to be comprehended'—and so the declaration of difference is justified.

But from the standpoint of paramārtha, any seer, hearer, or the like other than the omniscient supreme Lord is altogether negated by passages such as, 'There is no other seer than this' (Bṛ. Up. 3.7.23). The supreme Lord, however, is other than the embodied agent and enjoyer—the so-called vijñānātman—who is fashioned by avidyā.

Just as the magician who, holding hide and sword, climbs up by a thread into the sky, is one with the magician of true form who stands on the ground; even so, just as the ākāśa enclosed in a pot, conditioned by adjuncts, is other than the ākāśa unconditioned by adjuncts; on the basis of such a difference between the vijñānātman and the paramātman, it is said, 'Not the other, on account of impossibility,' and 'on account of the declaration of difference.' (17)
BS_C01_S01_V18: And on account of desire, no inferred (entity) is to be considered. (18)
BS_C01_S01_V18::block-0:
And in the section on the ānandamaya, since 'desirership' is indicated by the words, 'He desired: May I be many, may I propagate myself' (Tai. Up. 2.6.1), the unconscious pradhāna postulated by the Sāṅkhyas, which is established only through inference, need not be considered as the ānandamaya or as the cause.

Though pradhāna has already been refuted under the sūtra 'On account of seeing, the non-scriptural is not (the cause)' (Br. Sū. 1.1.5), it is again incidentally refuted here, with reference to the śruti of desirership cited in the previous sūtra, in order to establish the general consistency (gati-sāmānya) of all Vedānta passages. (18)
BS_C01_S01_V19: And (scripture) teaches the (jīva's) union with this (Self). (19)
BS_C01_S01_V19::block-0:
Further, the word ānandamaya does not refer to pradhāna or to the jīva: because, with respect to this ānandamaya which is here under discussion as the Self, scripture teaches the union with that (tad-yoga) of this awakened jīva — tad-yoga means union with that as one's own Self, the attainment of that very being, that is, mokṣa.

Scripture teaches such union: 'When indeed this one finds fearless ground in this Invisible, Bodiless, Indefinable, Non-abode, then he attains fearlessness. But when he makes even the smallest interval (separation) in this, then there is fear for him' (Tai. Up. 2.7.1).

The purport is this: when one sees in this ānandamaya even the slightest interval in the form of non-identity, then one does not turn back from the fear of saṁsāra. But when one is established without break in this ānandamaya through identity, then one turns back from the fear of saṁsāra. And this is consistent only when the supreme Self is taken to be the ānandamaya, not when pradhāna or the jīva is taken. Hence, it stands established that ānandamaya is the supreme Self. (19)
BS_C01_S01_V19::block-1:
But here the following must be addressed: since there is a sequence in the use of the affix 'mayaṭ' in the sense of modification (vikāra) — 'Verily, this puruṣa is made of the essence of food (annarasamaya)' (Tai. Up. 2.1.1); 'Other than and inner to that one made of the food-essence is the Self made of prāṇa' (Tai. Up. 2.2.1); other than that, 'inner Self made of mind (manomaya)' (Tai. Up. 2.3.1); other than that, 'inner Self made of vijñāna' (Tai. Up. 2.4.1) — how, in the case of ānandamaya alone, by the half-hen reasoning (ardhajaratīya-nyāya), can one suddenly assume that 'mayaṭ' means abundance (prācurya) and that the term has Brahman as its referent?

If it be said that this is so on account of the topic being Brahman as introduced in the mantra portion — no; for then even annamaya etc. would have to be Brahman.

Objection: It is fitting that annamaya etc. are not Brahman, because in each case another, more inward Self is spoken of in succession. But beyond ānandamaya no further inner Self is spoken of. Hence ānandamaya is Brahman; otherwise there would be the contingency of abandoning the proposed topic and introducing a topic not under consideration.

Reply (siddhānta): Even though, unlike annamaya etc., it is not heard with respect to ānandamaya that 'there is another, inner Self,' yet ānandamaya is not Brahman. For with respect to ānandamaya scripture declares: 'Of that, the head is preference (priya); the right side is delight (moda); the left side is great delight (pramoda); the trunk-Self is bliss (ānanda); Brahman is the tail, the foundation' (Tai. Up. 2.5.1).

There, the Brahman which has been introduced in the mantra portion, 'Brahman is truth, knowledge, infinite' (Tai. Up. 2.1.1) — that very Brahman is here spoken of as 'Brahman is the tail, the foundation.' Indeed, it is for the very purpose of imparting knowledge of that Brahman that the five sheaths beginning with annamaya and culminating in ānandamaya are postulated. Where then is the contingency of abandoning the proposed topic?

Objection: But surely 'Brahman is the tail, the foundation' refers to Brahman as a limb of ānandamaya, just as in the case of annamaya etc. it is said, 'this is the tail, the foundation' (referring to a limb). On that view, how can Brahman's standing as primary in its own right be ascertained?

Reply: We say: because it is the topic under discussion (prakṛta). 

Objection: Even if Brahman is understood as a limb of ānandamaya, it does not lose its status as the topic, since ānandamaya itself is Brahman.

Reply: On that view, the same Brahman would be the ānandamaya Self as the whole (avayavin), and the same Brahman would be the tail, the foundation, as a part (avayava) — which would be incoherent. If only one is to be accepted, it is fitting to take the express designation of Brahman in the very passage 'Brahman is the tail, the foundation,' where the word 'brahman' is conjoined; but not in the passage about ānandamaya, where the word 'brahman' is not conjoined.

Further, after saying 'Brahman is the tail, the foundation,' it is said: 'On this point there is also this verse: He becomes as if non-existent, if he knows Brahman as non-existent. But if he knows that Brahman is, then they know him as one who is' (Tai. Up. 2.6.1). In this verse, without continuing the topic of ānandamaya, the merit and fault of knowing the existence and non-existence of Brahman alone are spoken of. From this it is understood that in 'Brahman is the tail, the foundation,' Brahman alone has primacy in its own right. The doubt of the existence or non-existence of the ānandamaya Self is not even apt, since the ānandamaya, characterized by priya, moda etc., is well-known to all the world.

Objection: But how can Brahman, while being primary in its own right, be designated as the tail of ānandamaya in 'Brahman is the tail, the foundation'? 

Reply: This is no fault. 'Tail' here means tail-like, that is, the foundation, the supreme resort, the one nest of all bliss in the world — the bliss of Brahman. Such is the intent, not that it is a limb. Thus indeed (the text continues): 'Of this very bliss…'
BS_C01_S01_V19::block-2:
The sūtras, however, are to be explained thus: in 'Brahman is the tail, the foundation,' is Brahman intended as a limb of ānandamaya, or as primary in its own right? On the prima-facie position that, by the word 'tail,' it must be as a limb, it is replied: 'Ānandamaya, on account of repetition (abhyāsa)' — meaning that, in the passage on the ānandamaya Self, in 'Brahman is the tail, the foundation,' Brahman is taught as primary in its own right. This is on account of repetition: in the concluding verse, 'He becomes as if non-existent,' Brahman alone, in itself, is what is being repeated.

'Not on account of the term denoting modification' — if it be objected so, it is not (a fault), 'on account of abundance (prācurya).' The word 'denoting modification' means the word denoting a limb. The objection 'because of the limb-denoting word "tail," Brahman cannot be primary in its own right' must be answered. We answer: this is no fault, because the limb-denoting word can be applied also on account of abundance. Prācurya means prāyāpatti — usage on the basis of the predominance of limbs being spoken of, that is the meaning. For with reference to annamaya etc., having spoken of head and the rest, ending in tail, as their limbs, then having spoken of head and the rest of ānandamaya as further limbs, it is by way of the predominance of limbs (already mentioned) that scripture says 'Brahman is the tail, the foundation,' not with the intention that (Brahman) is a limb. The reason is that, by 'on account of repetition,' Brahman's standing as primary in its own right has already been established.

'And on account of the designation of Him as the cause' — for of the entire host of modifications, including ānandamaya, Brahman is designated as the cause: 'He created all this, whatever there is' (Tai. Up. 2.6.1). And the causal Brahman cannot, in the primary sense, fittingly be a limb of its own modification, the ānandamaya. The other sūtras also are to be understood, as may fit, as establishing only that Brahman which is indicated in the passage about the 'tail.' (12-19)
BS_C01_S01_V20: (That which is) within (the sun and the eye is Brahman), on account of the teaching of His attributes. (20)
BS_C01_S01_V20::block-0:
This is taught: 'Now the puruṣa who is seen within the sun, golden, with golden beard and golden hair, golden up to the very tips of his nails' (Chā. Up. 1.6.6); 'His eyes are like the lotus reddened by the monkey's hindquarters; his name is Ut, for he has risen above all evils; verily he who knows thus rises above all evils' (Chā. Up. 1.6.7) — 'thus, with respect to the deities' (Chā. Up. 1.6.8); 'Now with respect to the body…' (Chā. Up. 1.7.1); 'Now this puruṣa who is seen within the eye…' (Chā. Up. 1.7.5).

Doubt: Is it some transmigrating being, having attained eminence by the merit of vidyā and karma, who is here taught as the object of upāsana within the orb of the sun and within the eye? Or is it the eternally-perfect supreme Lord?

Pūrvapakṣa: It is a transmigrating being. Why? Because of the mention of form: in the case of the sun-puruṣa, form such as 'golden beard' is mentioned; and in the case of the eye-puruṣa, the same form is taught by extension — 'this puruṣa's form is the same as that one's form.'

It is not fitting for the supreme Lord to have form, since śruti says, 'Soundless, touchless, formless, immutable' (Kaṭha Up. 1.3.15); and because of the mention of a locus — 'who is within the sun, who is within the eye.' For the supreme Lord, locus-less, established in His own greatness, all-pervading, no locus can be taught. The śrutis are: 'In what is He, O venerable one, established? In His own greatness' (Chā. Up. 7.24.1); 'Like ākāśa, all-pervading and eternal' (Śat. Br. 10.6.3.2).

Further, because of the mention of the limits of his lordship: 'He has lordship over those worlds beyond him and over the desires of the gods' (Chā. Up. 1.6.8) — such are the limits of the sun-puruṣa's lordship. 'He has lordship over those worlds below him and over the desires of men' (Chā. Up. 1.7.6) — those of the eye-puruṣa. Limited lordship is not fitting for the supreme Lord; the unqualified śruti says, 'He is the Lord of all, the overlord of beings, the protector of beings; He is the embankment, the upholder, of these worlds, that they may not be confused' (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.22). Therefore the supreme Lord is not within the eye and the sun. — Thus the pūrvapakṣa being established, we say:
BS_C01_S01_V20::block-1:
(Sūtra:) 'Within—on account of the teaching of His attributes.' The puruṣa heard of as 'who is within the sun,' 'who is within the eye,' is the supreme Lord alone, not a transmigrating being. Why? On account of the teaching of His attributes (tad-dharma-upadeśa). For attributes of the supreme Lord are here taught.

Thus: having declared 'his name is Ut,' the name of this sun-puruṣa is then etymologically explained as 'he has risen above all evils.' That same etymologized name is by extension applied to the eye-puruṣa: 'whatever is the name (of the one), that is the name (of the other).' Removal from all evils is taught only of the supreme Self in passages such as, 'The Self that is free from evil' (Chā. Up. 8.7.1).

Likewise, of the eye-puruṣa, scripture establishes the nature of being the Ṛk, Sāman and the rest: 'He alone is the Ṛk, that the Sāman, that the Uktha, that the Yajus, that the Brahman.' Such universality is fitting only for the supreme Lord, since being the cause of all entails being the Self of all. Having narrated, with respect to the deities, the Ṛk and Sāman whose nature is earth, fire, etc., and with respect to the body, the Ṛk and Sāman whose nature is speech, prāṇa, etc., it is said, 'His Ṛk and Sāman are these locks of hair' — concerning the deities. Likewise concerning the body: 'Whatever are the locks of that one, those are the locks (of this one).' This is consistent only on the basis of universality.

'Whoever sing on the lute, they sing of him; therefore they earn wealth' (Chā. Up. 1.7.6) — even in worldly songs, His being the one sung is shown. This is consistent only with the acceptance of the supreme Lord, by the Bhagavadgītā passage: 'Whatever being is endowed with majesty, prosperity or vigour, know that to be born of a portion of My splendour' (Bh. Gī. 10.41).

The absolute and unrestricted lordship over worldly desires that is heard of also points to the supreme Lord.

As to what was said—that mention of form such as 'golden beard' is not fitting for the supreme Lord—we say: even of the supreme Lord there may be a māyā-made form by His own will, for the favour of devotees, as is recalled: 'This is the māyā I have created, by which you see Me, O Nārada' (Mahābhārata 12.339.45); 'You should not seek to know Me as endowed with the qualities of all beings' (Mahābhārata 12.339.46).

Further, where the form of the supreme Lord, void of all distinctions, is taught, there scripture says, 'Soundless, touchless, formless, immutable' (Kaṭha Up. 1.3.15) and so on. But on account of His being the cause of all, the supreme Lord, qualified by certain attributes belonging to modifications, is also designated as the object of upāsana, as in 'all-acting, all-desiring, all-fragrance, all-savouring' (Chā. Up. 3.14.2). Likewise, the mention of 'golden beard' and so on is also possible.

As to: 'Because a locus is mentioned, it is not the supreme Lord' — we say: even for one established in His own greatness, the teaching of a particular locus is for the sake of upāsana. Since Brahman is all-pervading like ākāśa, He can be inner to all. The mention of the limits of lordship also is for the purpose of upāsana, with reference to the division between body and deities. Hence the supreme Lord alone is taught as being within the eye and the sun. (20)
BS_C01_S01_V21: And on account of the declaration of difference, (the Lord) is other (than the jīva). (21)
BS_C01_S01_V21::block-0:
And the Lord, the inner controller (antaryāmin), is other than the jīvas who identify with the bodies of the sun and the rest, as is established by the declaration of difference in another śruti: 'He who, dwelling in the sun, is within the sun, whom the sun does not know, whose body the sun is, who controls the sun from within—He is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal' (Bṛ. Up. 3.7.9).

For there, in 'within the sun, whom the sun does not know,' the inner controller, distinct from the sun—that is, distinct from the vijñānātman who is the knower—is clearly designated. He alone here too must be the puruṣa within the sun, on account of the generality of the śruti. Therefore it is established that here the supreme Lord alone is taught. (21)
BS_C01_S01_V22: Ākāśa (is Brahman), on account of His distinguishing mark. (22)
BS_C01_S01_V22::block-0:
This is recited: '"What is the goal of this world?" "Ākāśa," he said. "Verily, all these beings arise from ākāśa alone, and unto ākāśa they return; ākāśa is greater than these, ākāśa is the supreme refuge"' (Chā. Up. 1.9.1).

Doubt: Is the supreme Brahman denoted by the word 'ākāśa,' or is bhūtākāśa (the elemental ether) denoted? Whence the doubt? Because of the observed use (of the word) in both senses. With reference to the particular element, the word 'ākāśa' is well-known both in worldly usage and in the Veda. With reference to Brahman also, it is sometimes seen to be used, where, by the rest of the passage or by the mention of an extraordinary attribute, Brahman is determined—as in 'If this ākāśa were not bliss…' (Tai. Up. 2.7.1), and 'Ākāśa indeed is the bringer-forth of name and form; that within which they are is Brahman' (Chā. Up. 8.14.1). Hence the doubt.

Pūrvapakṣa: What is fitting here? (The reply is:) bhūtākāśa. Why? Because, by its more well-known usage, that meaning rises quickly to the mind. Nor is it possible to understand the word 'ākāśa' as common to both, on pain of the contingency of its having multiple meanings. Therefore, with respect to Brahman, the word 'ākāśa' must be secondary (gauṇa). For Brahman resembles ākāśa in many attributes such as all-pervasiveness. When the primary meaning is possible, the secondary cannot be accepted. And here the primary meaning, the very ākāśa, is possible.

Objection: But if bhūtākāśa is taken, the rest of the passage—'Verily, all these beings arise from ākāśa alone' etc.—is not consistent. Reply: This is no fault, for even bhūtākāśa can be the cause through the gradation of vāyu and the rest. For it is recognized: 'From this very Self, ākāśa arose; from ākāśa, vāyu; from vāyu, fire' (Tai. Up. 2.1.1). Greatness and supreme refuge are also possible for bhūtākāśa with reference to other elements. Therefore, by the word 'ākāśa,' bhūtākāśa is denoted.—Thus being established, we say:
BS_C01_S01_V22::block-1:
'Ākāśa, on account of His distinguishing mark.' Here, by the word 'ākāśa' the apprehension of Brahman is fitting. Why? On account of His distinguishing mark (tal-liṅga). For this is the mark of the supreme Brahman: 'Verily, all these beings arise from ākāśa alone.' For in the Vedānta, the rule is that the origin of beings is from the supreme Brahman alone.

Objection: Even bhūtākāśa has been shown to be the cause through the gradation of vāyu and the rest.

Reply: True, that has been shown. Yet, since the root cause Brahman is not taken in (on that view), the restrictive 'from ākāśa alone' and the qualifier 'all' applied to beings would not be in harmony.

Likewise, 'unto ākāśa they return' is a mark of Brahman; and 'ākāśa is greater than these, ākāśa is the supreme refuge'—greatness and supreme-refuge-ness. Unconditional greatness is recited only of the supreme Self, the One: 'Greater than the earth, greater than the mid-region, greater than heaven, greater than these worlds' (Chā. Up. 3.14.3). Likewise, supreme-refuge-ness, on account of (His) being the ultimate cause, is more fitting only of the supreme Self. The śruti is: 'Brahman is consciousness and bliss; the supreme refuge of the giver of gifts' (Bṛ. Up. 3.9.28).

Further, having censured the position of Śālāvatya for the defect of finitude, Jaivali, intending to declare something infinite, took up ākāśa. Then, having identified ākāśa with udgītha, he concludes: 'This is the highest udgītha, this is the infinite' (Chā. Up. 1.9.2). And that infinity is a mark of Brahman.

As to what was said—that bhūtākāśa is first apprehended on the strength of common usage—we reply: even though first apprehended, on seeing the attributes of Brahman in the rest of the passage, it is not accepted. And the word 'ākāśa' has been shown to apply to Brahman in passages such as 'Ākāśa indeed is the bringer-forth of name and form' (Chā. Up. 8.14.1). Likewise, the use of synonyms for ākāśa with respect to Brahman is also seen: 'In the imperishable, in the supreme vyoman wherein all the gods abide' (Ṛk Saṁhitā 1.164.39); 'This Bhārgavī Vāruṇī Vidyā is established in the supreme vyoman' (Tai. Up. 3.6.1); 'Oṁ kham brahma, kham brahma' (Chā. Up. 4.10.4); 'Kham, the ancient' (Bṛ. Up. 5.1.1). Hence, even when the word 'ākāśa' occurs at the beginning of the passage, on the strength of the rest of the passage, its determination as denoting Brahman is fitting. The word 'agni' in 'Agni recites the anuvāka' (at the beginning of a passage) is even seen to refer to the boy Māṇavaka. Therefore it is established that the word 'ākāśa' (here) denotes Brahman. (22)
BS_C01_S01_V23: For the very same reason, prāṇa (is Brahman). (23)
BS_C01_S01_V23::block-0:
In the udgītha (section), beginning, 'O Prastotṛ, the deity which presides over the prastāva,' it is heard: 'Which is that deity?' (Chā. Up. 1.11.4); 'Prāṇa,' he said. 'Verily, all these beings enter into prāṇa alone, and from prāṇa they rise up; this deity presides over the prastāva' (Chā. Up. 1.11.5).

The doubt and the determination are to be understood as before. In passages such as, 'The mind, dear, is bound to prāṇa' (Chā. Up. 6.8.2), and 'the prāṇa of prāṇa' (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.18), the word 'prāṇa' is seen to refer to Brahman. With reference to the modification of vāyu, however, it is more well-known both in the world and in the Veda. Hence the doubt as to which is to be taken here by the word 'prāṇa.'

What is fitting? (Pūrvapakṣa:) Taking the prāṇa which is the modification of vāyu and has fivefold function. There the word 'prāṇa' is more well-known, as we have said. Objection: Just as before, on account of His distinguishing mark, here too taking Brahman is fitting. For here too, in the rest of the passage, the entry of beings (into it) and their rising forth—a function of the supreme Lord—is recognized. Reply: No, because even in the case of mukhya prāṇa, the entry and rising of beings is observed. Thus indeed it is recited: 'When a man sleeps, then speech goes to prāṇa, sight to prāṇa, hearing to prāṇa, mind to prāṇa; when he awakes, they are again born from prāṇa' (Śat. Br. 10.3.3.6). This is also a matter of direct observation: in sleep, while the function of prāṇa is uninterrupted, the functions of the senses are suspended; on awakening they reappear. Since beings have their essence in the senses, the rest of the passage, speaking of entry and rising of beings, is not in conflict with mukhya prāṇa.

Further, the sun and food, the deities of udgītha and pratihāra, are mentioned next to prāṇa, the deity of prastāva. Neither of them is Brahman. By similarity (sāmānya), prāṇa too is not Brahman. — Thus the pūrvapakṣa being established, the sūtra-author says:
BS_C01_S01_V23::block-1:
'For the very same reason, prāṇa.' 'Tal-liṅgāt' was stated in the previous sūtra. For that very reason—on account of His distinguishing mark—the word 'prāṇa' too can refer to the supreme Brahman. For prāṇa too has connection with the mark of Brahman: 'Verily, all these beings enter into prāṇa alone, and from prāṇa they rise up' (Chā. Up. 1.11.5). The origin and dissolution of all beings, said to be caused by prāṇa, point to the brahman-hood of prāṇa.

Objection: But the entry and rising were said to be unobjectionable even on the acceptance of mukhya prāṇa, by the example of sleep and waking.

Reply: At sleep and waking, the entry and rising taking refuge in prāṇa is observed only of the senses alone, not of all beings. But here, of beings (entire), endowed with senses and bodies, possessed by jīvas — by the śruti 'Verily all these beings.' Even if 'beings' is taken to mean 'great elements,' it is still consistent with the mark of Brahman. Objection: But we also hear of the senses, together with their objects, going to prāṇa and arising from it at sleep and waking — 'When the sleeper sees no dream, then he becomes one in this prāṇa; then speech goes to him along with all names' (Kau. Up. 3.3). Reply: There too, on account of His mark, the word 'prāṇa' (refers to) Brahman alone.

As to what was said about non-brahman-hood of prāṇa from its proximity with sun and food — that is incorrect. When, by the strength of the rest of the passage, the word 'prāṇa' is being apprehended as having Brahman as its referent, mere proximity is of no avail. As to the greater familiarity of the word 'prāṇa' in its fivefold-function sense, the answer is the same as for the word 'ākāśa.' Therefore it is established that prāṇa, the deity of the prastāva, is Brahman.
BS_C01_S01_V23::block-2:
Here some cite, 'the prāṇa of prāṇa' and 'the mind, dear, is bound to prāṇa.' That is incorrect. Because of the difference in word and on account of context, no doubt arises. Just as in the usage 'the father's father,' the father designated by the genitive is other than the (father) designated by the nominative, and is understood as the father's father; in like manner, in 'the prāṇa of prāṇa,' on account of the difference of word, the prāṇa of prāṇa is determined as other than the well-known prāṇa. For the same one cannot fittingly be designated as different from itself.

And in whatever context (prakaraṇa) something is mentioned, even by another name, it is understood as that very thing under discussion in that context. As, in the section on jyotiṣṭoma, in 'In every spring, one should sacrifice with jyotis,' the word 'jyotis' refers to jyotiṣṭoma; even so, in the section on the supreme Brahman, how can the word 'prāṇa,' as heard in 'the mind, dear, is bound to prāṇa,' communicate mere modification of vāyu? Therefore, since this is not a case for doubt, this citation is not apt. But in the prāṇa as deity of the prastāva, the doubt, pūrvapakṣa, and determination have been demonstrated. (23)
BS_C01_S01_V24: Jyotiścaraṇābhidhānāt — (Brahman is meant by 'light'), because of the mention of pāda (foot, quarter). ||24||
BS_C01_S01_V24::block-0:
The following is recited (in the Chāndogya): 'Now, the light that shines beyond this heaven, on the back of all, on the back of everything, in the highest of the highest worlds — verily this is that which is this light here within the puruṣa' (Chā. Up. 3.13.7). Here arises a doubt — is the word jyotis (light) here used to denote the sun and the like, or the supreme Ātman? It has already been stated that even though the word prāṇa has another reference, on the strength of brahma-liṅga (indicators of Brahman) it can refer to Brahman. But here precisely the question is whether such an indicator exists or not.

What then is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa)? — That the sun and the like alone are denoted by the word jyotis. Why? Because of common usage (prasiddhi). The two words tamas (darkness) and jyotis (light) are well known as denoting mutually opposed objects. Darkness is what obstructs the operation of the eye — like the darkness of the night. Light is what favours the same — like the sun and so forth. Likewise the śruti 'shines' (dīpyate) is well known with reference to the sun and the like. Brahman, devoid of form and other qualities, cannot literally be said to shine. Further, because the śruti gives heaven (dyaus) as its limit. Heaven cannot be the limit of Brahman, the seed of all moving and unmoving beings, the Self of all. But for an effected light (kārya-jyotis), which is bounded, heaven could be the limit. The Brāhmaṇa text reads 'the light beyond heaven'.

Objection (āśaṅkā): Since even an effected light is found everywhere, it is incongruous to make heaven its limit. Then let it be the primal radiance (prathamaja tejas) prior to the tripartition (a-trivṛtkṛta). Reply: No, because there is no purpose for an un-tripartitioned tejas. If it be said that being an object of upāsanā (meditation) is itself the purpose — no; for objects like the sun, employed for other purposes, are seen used for upāsanā as well; and the śruti 'I shall make each one of them threefold' (Chā. Up. 6.3.3) speaks without distinction. Nor is heaven's being the limit known of the un-tripartitioned tejas. Then let that very light denoted by jyotis be the tripartitioned tejas.

Objection: But fire and the like, which are jyotis, are perceived also below heaven. Reply: That is no defect; even with respect to a light that is perceived everywhere, the fixing of a particular locus by 'beyond heaven' for purposes of upāsanā is not contradictory. But for Brahman, which has no locus, such fixing of a special place is not appropriate. The mention of multiple supports — 'on the back of all, in the highest of highest worlds' — fits very well with an effected light. And in 'this here is that which is this light within the puruṣa' (Chā. Up. 3.13.7), the supreme light is seen being superimposed (adhyasta) upon the bodily (kaukṣeya) light. Adhyāsa-s arise from similarity, as in 'his head is bhūr — a head and this akṣara are one' (Bṛ. Up. 5.5.3). The kaukṣeya jyotis is well known to be non-Brahman. Because the śruti speaks of its being qualified by warmth and sound — 'this is its sight' (Chā. Up. 3.13.8), 'this is its hearing'. And the śruti 'one should meditate on this as seen and heard'. The text 'he who knows thus becomes endowed with sight, becomes renowned' (Chā. Up. 3.13.8) — because of the mention of a small fruit (alpa-phala) it is non-Brahman. For upāsanā of Brahman is enjoined for a great fruit. Nor is there in the passage itself any other indicator of Brahman like there was for prāṇa and ākāśa. Nor is Brahman mentioned in the preceding passage either, because there the metre (chandas) is referred to in 'all this being is gāyatrī'. Even granting that somehow Brahman were referred to in the previous passage...
BS_C01_S01_V24::block-1:
(Reply / siddhānta): Here jyotis is to be taken as Brahman. Why? caraṇābhidhānāt — that is, because of the mention of pāda (foot, quarter). For in the preceding passage Brahman of four quarters is set forth — 'Such is His greatness; greater than this is the Puruṣa. One quarter of Him is all beings; three quarters of Him are the immortal in heaven' (Chā. Up. 3.12.6). The very tri-pāda immortal of four-pāda Brahman, set forth as connected with heaven (dyu-sambandhin), is recognised here too as referred to by way of its connection with heaven (dyu-sambandhāt). To abandon that and posit a worldly (prākṛta) jyotis would entail the faults of giving up the topic at hand and introducing a foreign one (prakṛta-hāna and aprakṛta-prakriyā). And not only in the jyotis-passage is there this continuation of Brahman; in the next, the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā too, Brahman continues. Therefore here jyotis is to be understood as Brahman.

As to the objection that the words jyotis and dīpyate are familiar in the case of an effected light — this is no defect. When Brahman is ascertained from the context (prakaraṇa), these two words are not exclusive (a-viśeṣaka); since shining is the mark of effected light and Brahman can well be designated by such terms, as in the mantra 'kindled by whose lustre the sun shines' (Tai. Brā. 3.12.9.7). Moreover, the word jyotis is not restricted to that tejas which favours the operation of the eye, for it is seen used elsewhere too — 'he sits with speech itself as light' (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.5), 'let mind, the light, accept' (Tai. Brā. 1.6.3.3). Therefore whatever reveals anything is denoted by jyotis. That being so, since Brahman, of the nature of caitanya (consciousness), is the cause of the manifestation of the entire world, the word jyotis applies to it. So too the śruti — 'Him alone shining all follow; by His lustre this all shines' (Ka. Up. 2.2.15), 'the light of lights, the immortal life — Him the gods worship' (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.16) — and the like.

As to the objection that having heaven as limit does not fit Brahman that is omnipresent — to this we say: even for omnipresent Brahman, the fixing of a particular locus for purposes of upāsanā is not contradictory. Objection: But it was said that fixing a specific locus is not possible for the locus-less Brahman. Reply: This is no defect; even for Brahman, locus-less though it be, the fixing of a particular locus through connection with a particular upādhi (limiting adjunct) is intelligible. Thus upāsanā-s of Brahman in connection with particular loci — the sun, the eye, the heart — are heard. By this the multiplicity of supports indicated in 'on the back of all' is explained.

As to what was urged — that since the supreme light is being superimposed upon the kaukṣeya effected light inferred from warmth and sound, the supreme too must be a mere effected light beyond heaven — that is also untenable. For just as Brahman is meditated upon through symbols (pratīka) such as the name (nāman), so too can it be meditated upon with the kaukṣeya jyotis as its pratīka. The phrase 'one should meditate as seen and heard' will then refer to seeing and hearing through the pratīka. As to its being non-Brahman because a small fruit is mentioned — that too is unsound; for there is no rule that Brahman should be resorted to only for such-and-such a fruit and not for another. Where the supreme Brahman, freed from connection with all distinctions (nirasta-sarva-viśeṣa-sambandha), is taught as one's very Self (Ātman), there mokṣa alone, of one form, is understood as the fruit. But where Brahman is taught as connected with particular guṇa-s or as connected with particular pratīka-s, there fruits high and low, within the sphere of saṃsāra, are seen — 'the eater of food, the giver of wealth, finds...'.
BS_C01_S01_V25: Chandobhidhānān neti cen na, tathā ceto-'rpaṇa-nigadāt; tathā hi darśanam — If it be said that (Brahman is) not (referred to in the prior passage) because the metre is mentioned, no; for the fixing of the mind (on Brahman) by way of the metre is enjoined; thus it is seen elsewhere also. ||25||
BS_C01_S01_V25::block-0:
Now, what was urged — that in the preceding passage too Brahman is not stated, because the metre called gāyatrī is what is mentioned, in 'gāyatrī verily is all this being, whatsoever' (Chā. Up. 3.12.1) — that has to be answered.

How indeed can it be said that Brahman is not stated, when in the very mantra 'Such is His greatness' (tāvān asya mahimā) Brahman of four quarters has been shown? Pūrvapakṣa: That is not so. Beginning with 'gāyatrī verily is all this' the gāyatrī itself is taken up; and after it is explained as differentiated into being, earth, body, heart, speech, prāṇa — 'this same gāyatrī is of four feet, of six kinds; that has been recapitulated by the ṛc (verse): tāvān asya mahimā' (Chā. Up. 3.12.5–6) — how can the mantra cited with regard to that very gāyatrī, already explained, suddenly speak of four-quartered Brahman? And the word brahman occurring in 'that which indeed is brahman' (Chā. Up. 3.12.7) — that too, since the metre is the topic in hand, refers only to the metre. The expression 'who knows this brahma-upaniṣad' (Chā. Up. 3.11.3) is glossed as 'veda-upaniṣad' (the secret of the Veda). Therefore, since the metre is what is spoken of, Brahman is not the topic on hand.

Siddhānta: This is no defect — tathā ceto-'rpaṇa-nigadāt. That is, by way of the metre called gāyatrī, the fixing of the mind (cetaḥ-arpaṇa, citta-samādhāna) on the Brahman that pervades it is enjoined by this Brāhmaṇa text — 'gāyatrī verily is all this'. For the gāyatrī, taken as a mere arrangement of syllables, cannot be the Self of all. Therefore that Brahman, the cause of the world, which pervades the modification (vikāra) called gāyatrī, is here called 'all'. Just as in 'all this verily is Brahman' (Chā. Up. 3.14.1). And we shall demonstrate later, in 'tadananyatvam ārambhaṇa-śabdādibhyaḥ' (Br. Sū. 2.1.14), that the effect (kārya) is non-different from the cause (kāraṇa).

Thus elsewhere too upāsanā of Brahman through a modification is seen — 'the bahvṛcas meditate upon Him in the mahad-uktha, the adhvaryus in fire, the chandogas in the mahāvrata' (Ai. Ār. 3.2.3.12). Therefore even though the metre is mentioned, in the previous passage four-quartered Brahman is set forth. That very Brahman is referred to in the jyotis-passage too for prescribing another upāsanā.

Another (apara) says: by the very word gāyatrī Brahman is denoted directly, owing to commonality of number (saṅkhyā-sāmānya). Just as gāyatrī has four feet of six syllables each, so Brahman has four quarters. And elsewhere too a word denoting a metre is seen used for another object on the strength of commonality of number — as, having begun 'these five and other five being ten — that is what is made', it is said 'this is virāj, the eater of food'. On this view Brahman alone is denoted, and there is no mention of metre at all. In every way, in the previous passage Brahman is the topic on hand. ||25||
BS_C01_S01_V26: Bhūtādi-pāda-vyapadeśopapatteś caivam — And thus, because the designation of beings and the rest as the (one) quarter is intelligible (only on the view that Brahman is the topic). ||26||
BS_C01_S01_V26::block-0:
For this reason also it must be admitted that in the previous passage Brahman is the topic — because the śruti designates beings and the rest as pāda-s. Having mentioned beings, earth, body, heart, the śruti says — 'this same gāyatrī is of four feet, of six kinds' (Chā. Up. 3.12.5). For without resorting to Brahman, the mere metre cannot intelligibly have beings and the rest as its quarters.

Further, without resorting to Brahman this ṛc — 'tāvān asya mahimā' — would not connect. By this ṛc, naturally, Brahman alone is denoted, since 'one quarter of Him is all beings; three quarters of Him are the immortal in heaven' (Chā. Up. 3.12.6) is intelligible only with reference to (Brahman as) the Self of all. In the Puruṣa-sūkta also this same ṛc is recited with reference to Brahman. And the smṛti shows the same form of Brahman — 'pervading this whole, with one part I stand' (Bha. Gī. 10.42).

The expression 'that which is brahman' (Chā. Up. 3.12.7), on this view, is intelligible in its primary (mukhya) sense. And 'these five are brahmapuruṣa-s' (Chā. Up. 3.13.6) — the śruti speaking of brahma-puruṣa-s in the cavities of the heart is possible only when relation to Brahman is intended. Therefore Brahman is the topic on hand in the previous passage. And it is concluded that in the jyotis-passage that very Brahman, recognised through its connection with heaven, is referred to. ||26||
BS_C01_S01_V27: Upadeśa-bhedān neti cen na, ubhayasminn apy avirodhāt — If it be said that (the same Brahman is) not (recognised) because of difference of teaching (regarding heaven), no; for there is no contradiction in either case. ||27||
BS_C01_S01_V27::block-0:
What was further urged — that in the previous passage 'three quarters of Him are the immortal in heaven' (tripādasyāmṛtaṃ divi) heaven is taught as the locus by the seventh case (saptamī, the locative); but here, in 'now the (light) which is beyond this heaven' (atha yad ataḥ paro divaḥ), heaven is taught as the limit (maryādā) by the fifth case (pañcamī, the ablative); therefore, due to difference of teaching, there is no recognition (pratyabhijñāna) of the same — that has to be answered.

To this it is said: This is no defect, since in either case there is no contradiction (avirodha). Whether the upadeśa be in the locative or the ablative ending, recognition is not contradicted. Just as in the world a falcon connected to the tip of a tree is described in two ways — 'the falcon on the tip of the tree' and 'the falcon beyond the tip of the tree' — even so Brahman, while being in heaven, is taught as 'beyond heaven'.

Another (apara) says: Just as in the world a falcon not connected with the tip of a tree is described in two ways — 'the falcon on the tip of the tree' (deemed close to it) and 'the falcon beyond the tip of the tree' — even so, Brahman though beyond heaven is taught as 'in heaven'. Therefore the Brahman set forth previously is recognised here. Hence it is established that the supreme Brahman alone is denoted by the word jyotis. ||27||
BS_C01_S01_V28: Prāṇas tathānugamāt — Prāṇa (in the Pratardana-vidyā is) Brahman, because of (the entire passage) thus following (only on that view). ||28||
BS_C01_S01_V28::block-0:
There is, in the Kauṣītaki-brāhmaṇa-upaniṣad, the narrative of Indra and Pratardana — beginning 'Pratardana, son of Divodāsa, came to the beloved abode of Indra by battle and by valour' (Kau. Up. 3.1). Therein it is heard — 'He said: I am prāṇa, prajñātman; on me as life, as the immortal, meditate' (Kau. Up. 3.2). Likewise further — 'and verily prāṇa, who is prajñātman, having taken hold of this body, raises it up' (Kau. Up. 3.3). And 'one should not seek to know speech, one should know the speaker'. And at the end, 'this same prāṇa, the prajñātman, is bliss, ageless, immortal' (Kau. Up. 3.9), and so on.

Here arises a doubt — is the word prāṇa here used to denote mere wind (vāyu), or the deity (devatātman, i.e. Indra), or the individual self (jīva), or the supreme Brahman? Objection: It has already been declared, in the sūtra 'ata eva prāṇaḥ', that prāṇa refers to Brahman. Here too there are indicators of Brahman — 'bliss, ageless, immortal'. How then can a doubt arise? Reply: We say so because of the perception of multiple indicators (aneka-liṅga-darśana). Not only Brahman-indicators are seen here. There are also other indicators — Indra's words 'know me alone' (Kau. Up. 3.1) is an indicator of devatātman. 'Having taken hold of this body it raises it up' is an indicator of prāṇa. 'One should not seek to know speech, one should know the speaker' and the like are indicators of jīva. Hence the doubt is well founded. There, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) being that on common usage prāṇa is wind, the answer is given —

The word prāṇa is to be understood as Brahman. Why? tathānugamāt — because the passage thus follows (i.e., the import is consistent only on that view). For when the passage is examined as a whole — beginning, middle and end — the syntactic concord (samanvaya) of the words is seen to be aimed at conveying Brahman. At the outset, when Indra said 'choose a boon', Pratardana put forth the supreme puruṣārtha as the boon: 'You yourself choose what you deem most beneficial for man'. The prāṇa taught to him as 'most beneficial' (hitatama) — how can it be other than Paramātman? For except by the knowledge of Paramātman, there is no attainment of the supremely beneficial — by the śruti-s 'knowing Him alone one transcends death; there is no other path for liberation' (Śve. Up. 3.8) and the like.

So too 'whoever knows Me, his world is not lessened by any deed, neither by theft nor by killing of an embryo' (Kau. Up. 3.1) — this fits only when Brahman is taken; for the destruction of all karmas through Brahman-knowledge is well known in śruti-s like 'his deeds perish when That, the higher and lower, is seen'. Being prajñātman (the Self of consciousness) too is intelligible only on the Brahman view — non-conscious wind cannot be prajñātman. So too in the conclusion, 'bliss, ageless, immortal' — these characteristics of bliss and the rest cannot rightly belong to anything other than Brahman. And 'he becomes neither greater by good action nor lesser by bad action; for He alone causes him to do good action whom He wishes to lead up from these worlds; He alone causes him to do bad action whom He wishes to lead down from these worlds', and 'He is the lord of the worlds, the protector of the worlds, the master of the worlds' (Kau. Up. 3.9) — all this can be reconciled (anu-gantum) when supreme Brahman is taken as the referent, not when the principal prāṇa is. Therefore prāṇa is Brahman. ||28||
BS_C01_S01_V29: Na vaktur ātmopadeśād iti cet, adhyātma-sambandha-bhūmā hy asmin — If it be said (prāṇa is) not (Brahman) because the speaker (Indra) teaches his own self, no; for in this passage there is preponderance of inward (adhyātma) reference. ||29||
BS_C01_S01_V29::block-0:
Pūrvapakṣa (objection raised against) — what was stated, namely that prāṇa is Brahman, is now challenged. The supreme Brahman is not denoted by the word prāṇa; why? — because the speaker teaches his own self (vaktur ātmopadeśa). The speaker is one Indra, a particular embodied (vigrahavat) deity, who teaches his own self (svam ātmānam) to Pratardana — beginning 'know me alone' (mām eva vijānīhi) and continuing with the egotic statement (ahaṅkāra-vāda) 'I am prāṇa, prajñātman'. The prāṇa thus taught as the speaker's own self — how can it be Brahman? For Brahman cannot be a speaker, by the śruti-s like 'speechless' (Bṛ. Up. 3.8.8). Likewise he extolled himself by qualities pertaining to an embodied being which cannot belong to Brahman — 'I slew the three-headed son of Tvaṣṭṛ; I gave the Aruṇmukha ascetics over to the wolves' and so on. Indra's being prāṇa (vital power) is intelligible because he is mighty — for it is taught 'prāṇa verily is strength' (prāṇo vai balam), and Indra is well known as the deity of strength. They say 'whatever feat of strength there is, it is Indra's deed'. Being prajñātman is also possible for the deity, since his knowledge is unobstructed (apratihata-jñāna). They say the deities are of unobstructed knowledge. And once it is settled that the teaching is of the deity-Self, the statements about being most beneficial and the rest are to be construed as far as possible as referring to the deity. Therefore, since the speaker Indra teaches his own self, prāṇa is not Brahman. Thus is the objection raised.

Siddhānta: It is answered — adhyātma-sambandha-bhūmā hy asmin. The adhyātma-sambandha is reference to the inner Self (pratyag-ātma-sambandha); its bhūmā is preponderance, abundance — found in this chapter. 'So long as prāṇa dwells in this body, so long is one's life' — this shows the autonomy in the giving and the withdrawing of life of prāṇa, the prajñātman, the inmost (pratyak), and not of some external (parācīna) particular deity. Likewise, 'in their being is the highest good (niḥśreyasa) of the prāṇa-s' — this shows prāṇa as adhyātma, located in the indriyas. So too 'verily prāṇa, the prajñātman, having taken hold of this body raises it up' (Kau. Up. 3.3). And, beginning 'one should not seek to know speech, one should know the speaker' — 'as in the spokes of a chariot the rim is fixed and in the nave the spokes are fixed, even so these elements (bhūta-mātrā) are fixed in the prajñā-mātrā-s, the prajñā-mātrā-s in prāṇa; this same prāṇa is the prajñātman, bliss, ageless, immortal' — by these words the inner Self is brought to a focus, the inner Self into whose knowledge-spokes the activity of the sense-spokes is gathered. And the conclusion 'one should know that as my Self' (sa ma ātmeti vidyāt) is fitting only when the inner Self is taken, not the external. The other śruti also: 'this Ātman is Brahman, the all-experiencer' (Bṛ. Up. 2.5.19). Therefore, owing to preponderance of adhyātma reference, this is a teaching of Brahman (brahmopadeśa), not of the deity-Self. ||29||
BS_C01_S01_V30: Śāstra-dṛṣṭyā tūpadeśo Vāmadevavat — But the teaching (in the form 'know me') is from the standpoint of the śāstra (i.e. the ārṣa-darśana of identity with Brahman), as in the case of Vāmadeva. ||30||
BS_C01_S01_V30::block-0: Then how can it be the teaching of the speaker's own self?
BS_C01_S01_V30::block-1:
(Answer): A deity-Self called Indra, seeing his own Self as Paramātman by the seer's vision (ārṣa-darśana) according to the śāstra — 'I am the supreme Brahman' — teaches: 'know me alone'. As in 'this seeing the ṛṣi Vāmadeva attained: I was Manu and the Sun' (Bṛ. Up. 1.4.10) — and the śruti 'whoever among the gods awoke to It, he became It' (Bṛ. Up. 1.4.10).

What was further urged — that having said 'know me alone', Indra extolled himself by attributes of an embodied being like the killing of the son of Tvaṣṭṛ — that has to be answered. We say: the killing of the son of Tvaṣṭṛ and the rest are not adduced for the praise of Indra as the object of knowledge — 'because I have such deeds, therefore know me'. How then? They are adduced for the praise of knowledge (vijñāna-stuti). For after recounting daring deeds like the killing of the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, he weaves into them the praise of knowledge by the words that follow — 'and even so not a hair of mine is harmed in that state; whoever knows Me, his world is not harmed by any deed' and so on. The meaning is: 'Even though I, who am Brahman, did such cruel deeds, not a hair of mine is hurt; so likewise of any other who knows Me, his world is not hurt by any deed.' But the object of knowledge is Brahman alone, as is going to be stated — 'I am prāṇa, prajñātman'. Therefore this is a Brahman-passage. ||30||
BS_C01_S01_V31: Jīva-mukhya-prāṇa-liṅgān neti cen na, upāsā-traividhyād, āśritatvād iha tad-yogāt — If it be said (this is) not (a Brahman-passage) because of indicators of jīva and of mukhya-prāṇa, no; on account of the threefoldness of the upāsanā, on account of (such designation) being resorted to (elsewhere), and because here (Brahman-indicators are) found in conjunction. ||31||
BS_C01_S01_V31::block-0:
Pūrvapakṣa: Although, on the basis of preponderance of adhyātma reference, the teaching is not of an external deity, still it cannot be a Brahman-passage. Why? — On account of indicators of jīva and of the principal prāṇa (mukhya-prāṇa). An indicator of the jīva is plainly seen here — 'one should not seek to know speech, one should know the speaker' and the rest. For here the jīva, the overseer of body and senses (kārya-karaṇādhyakṣa), engaged through speech and the other instruments, is being declared as the object to be known. Likewise the indicator of the mukhya-prāṇa: 'verily prāṇa, the prajñātman, having taken hold of this body, raises it up'. The bearing of the body is the function of the mukhya-prāṇa; for in the prāṇa-saṃvāda, with reference to speech and other vital functions, it is heard — 'the eldest, prāṇa, said to them: do not be deluded; I alone, dividing myself fivefold and supporting this reed, hold it up' (Pra. Up. 2.3). Those who read 'having taken hold of this body' (instead of 'this jīva') interpret thus — having taken hold of this jīva or this group of senses, it raises up the body. Being prajñātman is intelligible in the jīva, since it is conscious. In the mukhya-prāṇa too, since it is the support of the other prāṇa-s which are instruments of knowledge, it is intelligible. On the view that jīva and mukhya-prāṇa are taken, the indication of non-difference between prāṇa and prajñātman by their co-existence, and indication of difference by their proper natures — both kinds of indication are intelligible: 'that which is prāṇa is prajñā, that which is prajñā is prāṇa', 'these two dwell together in this body and depart together'. But on the Brahman-view, what would be different from what? Hence here either the jīva or the mukhya-prāṇa, or both, are to be understood — not Brahman.

Siddhānta: Not so. On account of upāsā-traividhya (threefoldness of meditation). For on that view, three meditations would have to be admitted — meditation on jīva, meditation on the mukhya-prāṇa, and meditation on Brahman. And it is not proper to admit three different objects in one passage. The unity of a sentence (vākya-aikatva) is determined by upakrama (introduction) and upasaṃhāra (conclusion). Beginning with 'know me alone', having said 'I am prāṇa, prajñātman; meditate on me as life, as the immortal', and ending with 'this same prāṇa, the prajñātman, is bliss, ageless, immortal' — the upakrama and upasaṃhāra are seen to be of one form. There it is fitting to take one meaning. Nor can the Brahman-indicators be turned to refer to something else; for the assigning of the ten bhūta-mātrā-s and the ten prajñā-mātrā-s into anything other than Brahman is unintelligible. And, on the strength of āśritatva — the application of the word prāṇa to Brahman elsewhere on the strength of brahma-liṅga — and of brahma-liṅga-yoga (presence of Brahman-indicators) here too, in the form of mention of hitatama (most beneficial) and the rest, this is understood to be a teaching of Brahman.

As to the indicator of the mukhya-prāṇa shown — 'having taken hold of this body, raises it up' — that is not (decisive); for the activity of prāṇa too depends on Paramātman, and so it can be figuratively (upacāra) referred to Paramātman, by the śruti 'no mortal lives by prāṇa or by apāna; by another do they live, on whom these two depend' (Ka. Up. 2.2.5). As to the jīva-indicator shown — 'one should not seek to know speech, one should know the speaker' — that too does not exclude the Brahman-view. For the jīva is not absolutely different from Brahman, by the śruti-s 'tat tvam asi', 'aham brahmāsmi' and the rest. It is on the strength of the difference set up by the upādhi-s such as the buddhi that Brahman, while really being the jīva, is spoken of as agent and enjoyer. But by giving up the difference made by the upādhi-s, its proper form is just Brahman...
BS_C01_S01_V31::block-1: Or another (apara) interpretation of 'no, on account of upāsā-traividhya, of āśritatva, of tad-yoga here' (sūtra) is this: even in a Brahman-passage, the indicators of jīva and mukhya-prāṇa are not contradictory. How? — On account of upāsā-traividhya. Three kinds of upāsanā of Brahman are intended here — through the property of prāṇa (prāṇa-dharma), through the property of prajñā (prajñā-dharma), and through its own property (svadharma). There 'meditate as life, as the immortal; life is prāṇa', 'having taken hold of this body raises it up', 'therefore one should meditate on this very uktha' — these are by way of prāṇa-dharma. Beginning 'now, how the elements unify with respect to this prajñā, that I shall expound', then 'speech indeed is one limb of it that has been milked; behind it is set the bhūta-mātrā called nāman; mounting on speech by prajñā, one obtains all names through speech' and the rest — these are by way of prajñā-dharma. 'These are the ten bhūta-mātrā-s with regard to prajñā, and the ten prajñā-mātrā-s with regard to bhūta; for if there were no bhūta-mātrā-s there would be no prajñā-mātrā-s, and if there were no prajñā-mātrā-s there would be no bhūta-mātrā-s; for from one alone no form whatever would be accomplished; and these are not different. Just as in the spokes of a chariot the rim is fixed and the spokes in the nave, even so these bhūta-mātrā-s are fixed in the prajñā-mātrā-s and the prajñā-mātrā-s in prāṇa; this same prāṇa is the prajñātman' — this is by way of brahma-dharma. Hence one and the same upāsanā of Brahman is intended as threefold, by the properties of two upādhi-s and by its own property. Elsewhere too, in 'the mind-made, with prāṇa for the body' (Chā. Up. 3.14.2) and the like, upāsanā of Brahman by way of upādhi-properties is resorted to. Here too that fits, since unity of sense of the passage is grasped from upakrama and upasaṃhāra, and indicators of prāṇa, prajñā and Brahman are all found. Therefore this is a Brahman-passage indeed, as established. ||31||
BS_C01_S02_INTRO1::block-0:
In the first pāda, by the sūtra 'janmādyasya yataḥ' (1.1.2) it was declared that Brahman is the cause of the origin and the rest of this entire world beginning with ākāśa. By that very statement, dharmas of such kind belonging to that Brahman who is the cause of the whole jagat — namely all-pervasiveness (vyāpitva), eternality (nityatva), omniscience (sarvajñatva), omnipotence (sarvaśaktitva), and the being-the-Self-of-all (sarvātmatva) — stand stated as a matter of course.

Further, by adducing the reason that certain words ordinarily known (prasiddha) in another sense in fact have Brahman as their referent, certain vākyas which bear clear marks (spaṣṭa-brahma-liṅga) of Brahman, but were under doubt, were determined as having Brahman as their import (brahma-paratayā nirṇītāni).

Now once again other vākyas, which do not bear such clear marks of Brahman (aspaṣṭa-brahma-liṅga), are subject to doubt — do they teach the supreme Brahman, or do they teach some other thing? In order to settle this, the second and third pādas are now commenced —
BS_C01_S02_V01: Sarvatra prasiddhopadeśāt — Because the teaching is of that which is universally famed [as Brahman]. (1.2.1)
BS_C01_S02_V01::block-0:
It is recited thus: 'sarvaṃ khalvidaṃ brahma tajjalāniti śānta upāsīta. atha khalu kratumayaḥ puruṣo yathākratur asmiṃl loke puruṣo bhavati tathetaḥ pretya bhavati sa kratuṃ kurvīta' (Chā. Up. 3.14.1) — 'All this verily is Brahman; as that from which it is born, into which it dissolves, and by which it lives — let one meditate calm-minded. Now, the puruṣa is made of resolve (kratu); as is one's resolve in this world, so does he become on departing — therefore let him form a resolve.' And further, 'manomayaḥ prāṇa-śarīraḥ' (Chā. Up. 3.14.2) — 'mind-formed, with prāṇa as body,' and so on.

Here arises a doubt (saṃśaya): is the embodied self (śārīra ātman) here taught as the object of meditation by the dharmas of being mind-formed and the rest, or is it the supreme Brahman?

pūrvapakṣa: What, then, is the prima facie position? It is that the śārīra is meant. Why? Because for him, the lord of the body and the organs (kārya-karaṇa-adhipati), connection with mind and the rest is well known (prasiddha), but not for the supreme Brahman; for the śruti says 'aprāṇo hyamanāḥ śubhraḥ' (Mu. Up. 2.1.2) — 'breathless, mindless, pure.'

[Objection:] But by the words 'sarvaṃ khalvidaṃ brahma' Brahman has been taken up by its own word; how then can the śārīra be suspected here as the object of meditation?

[Reply:] This is no flaw. This vākya is not concerned with enjoining meditation on Brahman (brahma-upāsanā-vidhi-para). What then? It is concerned with enjoining tranquillity (śama-vidhi-para); for this very reason it says 'sarvaṃ khalvidaṃ brahma tajjalāniti śānta upāsīta' — 'let him meditate calm-minded.' What is meant is this — since all this aggregate of vikāras is verily Brahman, on account of being born from That (taj-jatva), being dissolved into That (tal-latva), and breathing in That (tad-anatva) — and since, all being one Self, attachment and the rest cannot arise — therefore let him be calm-minded. And when [the passage] has tranquillity-injunction as its purport, meditation on Brahman cannot be governed by this vākya. Meditation, however, is enjoined by 'sa kratuṃ kurvīta' — 'let him form a resolve.' kratu means saṅkalpa, dhyāna. And as its content is heard 'manomayaḥ prāṇa-śarīraḥ' — which is a jīva-liṅga.

Therefore we say: this upāsanā has the jīva as its object. The phrase 'sarva-karmā sarva-kāmaḥ' and the rest also can fittingly apply by sequence to the jīva. And 'eṣa ma ātmāntar-hṛdaye 'ṇīyān vrīher vā yavād vā' — 'this Self of mine within the heart, smaller than a grain of rice or barley' — this fact of having the heart as abode, and of being subtler than a grain, fits the jīva who has the measure of an ārā-tip (goad-point), not the unbounded Brahman.

[Counter:] But 'jyāyān pṛthivyāḥ' — 'greater than the earth' — and the rest also do not fit in what is bounded.

[Reply:] To this we say: smallness and greatness, both, cannot be lodged in one and the same thing, because of contradiction (virodha). And on resorting to one of the two, smallness, being heard first (prathama-śruta), is fitting to be resorted to. Greatness will hold by the consideration of the brahma-bhāva (i.e., when the jīva attains identity with Brahman). And, the jīva-viṣayatva being thus settled, even the mention of Brahman at the close — 'etad brahma' (Chā. Up. 3.14.4) — 'this is Brahman' — that too, since it serves to refer back to the topic in hand (prakṛta-parāmarśa), has only the jīva as its referent. Therefore the jīva is to be meditated upon by the dharmas of mind-formedness and the rest — thus being the obtained position, we now reply —
BS_C01_S02_V01::block-1:
siddhānta: It is the supreme Brahman alone that is here to be meditated upon by the dharmas of mind-formedness and the rest. Why? sarvatra prasiddhopadeśāt — because of the teaching of that which is universally famed. That which is, in all the upaniṣads, the well-known referent of the word 'brahman,' the cause of the world (jagat-kāraṇa), and which here too is heard at the very opening of the vākya in 'sarvaṃ khalvidaṃ brahma' — that very thing, qualified by the dharmas of mind-formedness etc., it is fitting should be taught. And this being so, the faults of abandoning the topic in hand (prakṛta-hāna) and introducing what is not in hand (aprakṛta-prakriyā) will not arise.

[Objection:] But it has been said that at the opening of the vākya Brahman was mentioned with the intent of enjoining tranquillity, not with the intent to speak of itself (sva-vivakṣayā).

[Reply:] To this we say — even though Brahman is mentioned with the intent of enjoining tranquillity, still, when mind-formedness and the rest are being taught, it is that very Brahman which is at hand (sannihita); the jīva, on the other hand, is not at hand (na sannihitaḥ), nor has it been taken up by its own word — thus the asymmetry. (1.2.1)
