As for what was said — that from the Śruti of "bridge," and from the bridge fittingly possessing a far-shore, the abode of heaven etc. must be other than Brahman — to this it is replied: by the bridge-Śruti only the function of holding-together (vidhāraṇa-mātra) is intended, not far-shore-hood etc. For when, in the world, no bridge is seen except one made of clay or wood, it does not follow that here too only such a bridge is to be admitted. The very meaning of the word setu is only vidhāraṇa-mātra, and not far-shore-hood etc. — for the etymology of "setu" is from the root ṣiñ in the sense of binding (bandhana-karman). Another says: "Know Him alone as the one Self," which proclaims the knowledge of Self, and "Abandon other words," which proclaims the relinquishment of (other) speech — these, being the means of immortality, are what is referred to by the bridge-Śruti "this is the bridge of immortality"; not the abode of heaven etc. Therefore what was said — that, by reason of the bridge-Śruti, the abode of dyubhū etc. must be other than Brahman — is unfit. (1)
BS_C01_S03_V02: Because of the statement that it is to be approached by the liberated. (2)
BS_C01_S03_V02::block-0:
And from this also it is the supreme Brahman alone that is the abode of heaven, earth, etc.; for it is seen to be designated as approachable-by-the-liberated (mukta-upasṛpya). The samāsa-vigraha: "that which is to be approached (upasṛpya) by the liberated (muktaiḥ)" — mukta-upasṛpya. As to non-Self things such as the body and the rest, the buddhi "I am" — this is avidyā; from that arises rāga in respect of the honouring of the body, dveṣa in respect of insults to it, fear from beholding its destruction, and moha — and so this anartha-vrāta of endless variety is continuous and stands directly perceptible to all of us. By contrast, the abode of heaven and the rest is designated by the text as approachable by those liberated from the doṣas — avidyā, rāga, dveṣa and so on.

How? Having said: "The knot of the heart is loosened, all doubts are cut, and his karmas are exhausted, when That is seen which is both higher and lower" (Mu. Up. 2.2.9), the text declares: "In the same way the wise man, freed from name and form, attains the divine Puruṣa higher than the highest" (Mu. Up. 3.2.8). And the approach-by-the-liberated of Brahman is well known in the śāstra: "When all desires that dwell in his heart are released, then the mortal becomes immortal; here itself he attains Brahman" (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.7) and so on. But of Pradhāna and the rest, no approach-by-the-liberated is anywhere known.

Furthermore, by "Know Him alone as the one Self; abandon other words; this is the bridge of immortality" — the knowability, here, of the abode of heaven and the rest is stated as preceded by relinquishment of (other) speech. And that is seen of Brahman in another Śruti: "That alone the wise Brāhmaṇa, having known, should make pra-jñā his own; let him not muse on many words, for that is verily mere wearying of speech" (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.21). Therefore from this also the abode of heaven, earth, etc. is the supreme Brahman. (2)
BS_C01_S03_V03: It is not what is inferred (the Sāṃkhya Pradhāna), because of there being no word for it. (3)
BS_C01_S03_V03::block-0: Just as a special reason (vaiśeṣika hetu) for establishing Brahman has been stated, in the same way no special reason for establishing anything other (than Brahman) exists — this is what is being said. The anumāna postulated by the Sāṃkhya-smṛti — namely the Pradhāna — is not to be admitted here as the abode of heaven, earth and the rest. Why? Because of "a-tat-śabda" — the absence of its word. The śabda which is the proclaimer of the Pradhāna, that achetana, would be its tat-śabda; the absence of that tat-śabda is a-tat-śabda. For there is no word here that proclaims the achetana Pradhāna, by which the achetana Pradhāna might be apprehended either as kāraṇa or as āyatana. On the contrary, there is here a word proclaiming the very opposite, the chetana: "He who is omniscient, all-knowing" (Mu. Up. 1.1.9) and so forth. For the very same reason, neither is Vāyu accepted here as the abode of heaven, earth, etc. (3)
BS_C01_S03_V04: Nor is it the prāṇabhṛt (the embodied soul). (4)
BS_C01_S03_V04::block-0: Even though for the prāṇa-bhṛt — the vijñāna-ātman — Self-hood and chetana-hood are possible, still, since for one whose knowledge is delimited by upādhis omniscience and the rest are not possible, by this very same a-tat-śabda the prāṇa-bhṛt also is not to be accepted as the abode of heaven, earth, etc. Nor again is the abode-hood of heaven, earth, etc. quite possible for the prāṇa-bhṛt, who is delimited by upādhis and not all-pervading. The separate framing (pṛthag-yoga) of this sūtra is for the sake of what follows. (4)
BS_C01_S03_V05: Because of the statement of difference. (5)
BS_C01_S03_V05::block-0: And from what other reason is the prāṇa-bhṛt not to be accepted as the abode of heaven, earth, etc.? —
BS_C01_S03_V05::block-1: And here a statement of difference (bheda-vyapadeśa) occurs — "Know Him alone as the one Self" — by way of the relation of jñeya (the to-be-known) and jñātṛ (the knower). Among them, the prāṇa-bhṛt is the knower, since he is the seeker of liberation. By the residue (pariśeṣa) it is understood that what is denoted by the word "Self" — namely Brahman — is the jñeya, the abode of heaven, earth, etc., and not the prāṇa-bhṛt. (5)
BS_C01_S03_V06::block-0: And from what further reason is the prāṇa-bhṛt not to be accepted as the abode of heaven, earth, etc.? —
BS_C01_S03_V06::block-1: And this is the prakaraṇa of the supreme Self — for the demand for sarva-vijñāna by means of eka-vijñāna in the words "By the knowledge of what, O Bhagavan, does all this become known?" (Mu. Up. 1.1.3). For when the supreme Self, which is the Self of all (sarva-ātmaka), is known, all this might become known; this cannot be by mere knowledge of the prāṇa-bhṛt alone. (6)
BS_C01_S03_V07::block-0: And from what further reason is the prāṇa-bhṛt not to be accepted as the abode of heaven, earth, etc.? —
BS_C01_S03_V07::block-1:
And in respect of the abode of heaven, earth, etc., in "Two birds, joined as companions" (Mu. Up. 3.1.1), "abiding" (sthiti) and "eating" (adana) are designated. "One of them eats the sweet pippala-fruit" — this is the eating of karma-phala. "The other, not eating, simply looks on" — this is staying-by-way-of-indifference (audāsīnyena avasthāna). And by these two — sthiti and adana — Īśvara and the kṣetra-jña are grasped therein. If Īśvara is intended as the abode of heaven, earth, etc., then the separate mention, of that very Īśvara who is in context, as distinguished from the kṣetra-jña, is fully fitting. Otherwise the mention of one not in context (a-prakṛta-vacana) would be sudden (ākasmika) and unconnected.

Objection: But on your view too, the mention of the kṣetra-jña separately from Īśvara would also be sudden.

Reply: No, because he is not what is principally intended (a-vivakṣitatva). For the kṣetra-jña, as kartṛ and bhoktṛ, conjoined with the upādhis of buddhi etc. in each body, is well known just from worldly experience (loka-prasiddha); he is not what the Śruti, by way of its principal intention (tātparya), is wishing to convey. Īśvara, however, being not well known from worldly experience, is what is wished to be conveyed by the Śruti as its tātparya — hence His mention is not unfitting as sudden.

In "Both having entered the cave (guhā), they are indeed Selves" — there too this same point has been shown: in the ṛk "Two birds," Īśvara and the kṣetra-jña are spoken of. Even if, by the explanation given in the Paiṅgi-upaniṣat, by this same ṛk sattva and kṣetra-jña are spoken of, even so there is no contradiction.

How? Here the prāṇa-bhṛt — apprehended in each body, like the cavities in pots and the like, with the upādhis of sattva and the rest, having identification with them (abhimāna) — is what is denied to be the abode of heaven, earth, etc. But that which is observed in all bodies as without the upādhis (vinā-upādhibhiḥ), He is the supreme alone. Just as the cavities in pots etc., when observed without the upādhis of pots etc., are mahā-ākāśa alone — exactly so, since the prāṇa-bhṛt cannot be other than the supreme, the prohibition would not be possible. Therefore the prohibition of abode-hood of heaven, earth, etc. applies only to the one who has self-identification with the upādhis of sattva and the rest. Therefore the supreme Brahman alone is the abode of heaven, earth, etc.

This very point has already been established by the sūtra: "Because of (the term) of unsee-able-ness and the rest as a quality, on account of the statement of dharmas" (a-dṛśyatv-ādi-guṇako dharma-ukteḥ). For in the very middle of that bhūta-yoni-vākya there is read this: "That in which heaven, earth and the inter-space (are woven)" etc. This (present occasion) is presented merely for elaboration (prapañca-artha). (7)
BS_C01_S03_V08: Bhūman (the Plenum) — for the teaching is given above (the state of) samprasāda. (8)
BS_C01_S03_V08::block-0:
The following is recited in the Chāndogya: "Bhūman (the Plenum) alone is to be sought to be known—Sir, I desire to know Bhūman" (Chā.U. 7.23.1); "Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, knows nothing else, that is Bhūman; but where one sees something else, hears something else, knows something else, that is the limited (alpa)" (Chā.U. 7.24.1) and so forth.

Here arises a doubt — is Bhūman prāṇa, or is it Paramātman (the supreme Self)? Why is there a doubt? Because by the very word bhūman "abundance" is denoted, since the word bhūman is remembered to end in the abstract suffix (bhāva-pratyaya) by the rule "bahor lopo bhū ca bahoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.158). When one further enquires of what nature this abundance is, from the proximity of the statement "Verily prāṇa is greater than hope" (Chā.U. 7.15.1) it appears that prāṇa is Bhūman. Likewise, from the opening of the section — "I have heard from those like your venerable self that he who knows the Self crosses over sorrow; I, Sir, am one who grieves; do you, Sir, ferry me across to the further shore of grief" (Chā.U. 7.1.3) — it also appears that Paramātman is Bhūman. So the doubt arises: which is it proper to accept, and which to reject?

The pūrvapakṣa (prima facie view): Prāṇa is Bhūman. Why? Because no further series of question and answer is seen (beyond prāṇa). For just as the question-answer flow runs "Sir, is there anything greater than name?" — "Speech is verily greater than name"; and again "Sir, is there anything greater than speech?" — "Mind is verily greater than speech" — thus the stream of question and reply proceeds upward from name through to prāṇa; but no such further question "Sir, is there anything greater than prāṇa?" with the answer "Yes, that thing is greater than prāṇa" is seen. Rather, having declared prāṇa itself with elaborate detail to be greater than the items beginning with name and ending with hope by "Verily prāṇa is greater than hope" etc., having approved that the knower of prāṇa is an ativādin (one who declares the higher) by "If one says to him, 'You are an ativādin,' let him say, 'I am an ativādin,' and not deny it," and then carrying on this attribute of being ativādin as the vow of prāṇa with "But he indeed is the (true) ativādin who declares the higher through truth" — without abandoning prāṇa at all, but bringing in Bhūman by the succession beginning with truth (satya) — it is to be understood that prāṇa itself is held to be Bhūman.

If this be objected: when prāṇa is being explained as Bhūman, how then can the description "where one sees nothing else" — which is the defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa) of Bhūman — be made to fit? The answer is: in the state of deep sleep (suṣupti), since the cessation of the activities of seeing and the rest is observed when the senses have been swallowed up into prāṇa, the characteristic "where one sees nothing else" is possible even of prāṇa. And so śruti says — having described, with the words "he does not hear, does not see" etc., the state of deep sleep as the cessation of all sense-activity, it then says "the prāṇa-fires alone keep waking in this city (body)" (Praśna 4.3), thereby showing that in that very state the fivefold prāṇa is awake; this exhibits suṣupti as having prāṇa as its principal. And as for the bliss-nature of Bhūman that is heard in "That which is Bhūman, that is bliss" (Chā.U. 7.23.1) — this too is not contradicted, for in "There this god (the soul) does not see dreams; in this body there is bliss" (Praśna 4.6) bliss is heard precisely in the state of deep sleep. And as for "That which is Bhūman, that is the immortal" (Chā.U. 7.24.1) — that too is not contradicted of prāṇa, since śruti says "prāṇa is verily the immortal" (Bṛ.U. 1.6.3). Then how can one who holds prāṇa to be Bhūman make sense of "the knower of the Self crosses over sorrow"…
BS_C01_S03_V08::block-1:
To this we reply — Paramātman alone deserves to be Bhūman here, not prāṇa. Why? Saṃprasādād adhyupadeśāt — because the teaching is given above (the state of) samprasāda. "Samprasāda" denotes the state of deep sleep, by the etymology samyak prasīdaty asmin — "in which one settles down completely" — and from its being recited along with the dream and waking states in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka. In that samprasāda state prāṇa keeps waking; therefore prāṇa here is intended by the term "samprasāda." The meaning is: because Bhūman is taught above (i.e. higher than) prāṇa. For if prāṇa itself were Bhūman, prāṇa would have been taught as above itself — which would be incoherent. Indeed, name is not taught above name in "greater than name," but a different object distinct from name, namely speech, is taught: "Speech is verily greater than name." Likewise, from speech up to prāṇa, in each case a different object is taught above. In the same way, Bhūman, being taught above prāṇa, must be a thing distinct from prāṇa.

(Pūrvapakṣin objects:) But here there is no question "Sir, is there anything greater than prāṇa?" nor any answer "Yes, there is something greater than prāṇa." How then is it said that Bhūman is taught above prāṇa? And we see that the very ativāditva (the status of being ativādin) which had prāṇa as its object is being carried forward into what follows — "He indeed is the (true) ativādin who declares the higher through truth." Hence there is no teaching above prāṇa.

Reply (siddhānta): It cannot be said that this is the carrying forward of ativāditva connected only with prāṇa, for there is a specifying clause — "who declares through truth." — But may not this very specifying clause too pertain to prāṇa? How? Just as when it is said "This is the agnihotrin who speaks the truth," the status of being an agnihotrin is not (constituted) by speaking the truth — by what then? By the agnihotra alone; truth-speaking is mentioned merely as a particular mark of the agnihotrin. Likewise, when it is said "He indeed is the ativādin who declares through truth," the ativāditva is not (constituted) by truth-speaking — by what then? By the prāṇa-knowledge already under discussion; truth-speaking is intended as a particular mark of the prāṇa-knower.

We reply: No, for that would entail abandonment of the literal meaning of śruti. Here śruti directly conveys ativāditva by truth-speaking — "He who declares through truth, he (alone) is the ativādin." There is no mention here of prāṇa-knowledge. Prāṇa-knowledge would be connected only by the contextual force (prakaraṇa). In that case śruti would be abandoned for the sake of context. Moreover, the word "tu" ("but"), which serves to detach what was previously under discussion, would not fit — "He, however (tu), is the ativādin." And the renewed effort "Truth, however, is to be sought to be known" (Chā.U. 7.16.1) further indicates the intention of speaking of a different object. Hence, just as when the praise of one Veda is in progress and it is said "This indeed is the great Brāhmaṇa, who studies the four Vedas," the four-Veda-knower is praised as a different object from the one-Veda-knowers — so should this be regarded.

Nor is there any rule that the intention to speak of a different object must take only the form of question-and-answer; for the intention to speak of another object is brought about by the impossibility of the contextually given object being connected (with what follows). There Sanatkumāra himself, when Nārada has fallen silent on hearing the instruction up to prāṇa, expounds: that ativāditva which depends on prāṇa-knowledge whose object is mere modification (vikāra) and untruth (anṛta) is in fact non-ativāditva — "He, however, is the (true) ativādin who declares through truth." There by "truth" the supreme Brahman is meant, since it is of the form of the ultimately real (paramārtha-rūpa); and so śruti elsewhere: "Truth, knowledge, infinite, is Brahman"…
BS_C01_S03_V08::block-2: (Bhāṣya continues; here in summary:) Hence Brahman alone, on the strength of the very expression "truth," is what is taught above prāṇa, as the object distinct from prāṇa; the chain of teaching ascends from satya through the further stages and culminates in Bhūman, none of which is possible of prāṇa. Therefore Paramātman alone is Bhūman, and the description "where one sees nothing else" is in its primary sense (mukhya-vṛtti) applicable to that, since in the supreme Self alone is the absence of all duality natural and not borrowed from a state. The prāṇa-interpretation rests only on the secondary (gauṇa) device of suṣupti, in which the absence of seeing etc. is occasional; here, on the contrary, it is intrinsic. Hence siddhānta: bhūmā paramātmaiva.
BS_C01_S03_V09: And because the (described) attributes are coherently established (only of Paramātman). (9)
BS_C01_S03_V09::block-0:
Furthermore, the attributes (dharmas) which are heard concerning Bhūman are coherently established only in Paramātman. "Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, knows nothing else — that is Bhūman" makes us understand the absence of the activities of seeing etc. in Bhūman. And in Paramātman this absence of the activities of seeing etc. is known from another śruti — "But where everything has become the very Self of him, then by what could he see what?" (Bṛ.U. 4.5.15) and similar passages.

As for that absence of the activities of seeing etc. that was spoken of in the suṣupti state — that too was spoken with the intention of indicating the unattachedness (asaṅgatva) of the Self alone, not with the intention of indicating any nature of prāṇa, since the section is about Paramātman. As for the bliss spoken of in that state, that too was said with the intention of indicating the bliss-form of the Self alone, since śruti says "This is His supreme bliss; on a portion of this very bliss other beings live" (Bṛ.U. 4.3.32). And here too, by negating petty (sāmaya) bliss with "That which is Bhūman, that is bliss; in the limited there is no bliss; Bhūman alone is bliss," Brahman alone is shown as the blissful Bhūman.

The immortality (amṛtatva) heard here in "That which is Bhūman, that is the immortal" likewise leads to the supreme cause; for the immortality of effects (vikāras) is only relative, and another śruti says "All else than this is afflicted" (Bṛ.U. 3.4.2). Likewise the dharmas heard here — being satya (true), being established in its own greatness (svamahimapratiṣṭhitatva), all-pervadingness (sarvagatatva), being the Self of all (sarvātmatva) — are coherently established only in Paramātman, nowhere else. Therefore it is established that Bhūman is Paramātman.
BS_C01_S03_V10: (The word) Akṣara (denotes Paramātman) — because of (its) holding up (everything) up to ambara (ākāśa). (10)
BS_C01_S03_V10::block-0:
It is recited: "In what indeed is ākāśa woven, warp and woof?" (Bṛ.U. 3.8.7); "He said — That, O Gārgī, is what the brāhmaṇas call the Imperishable (akṣara), neither gross nor subtle…" (Bṛ.U. 3.8.8) and so on. Here the doubt arises — does the word akṣara denote a phoneme (varṇa), or Parameśvara?

Pūrvapakṣa: Since the word akṣara is well known to mean a phoneme in expressions like akṣara-samāmnāya (the recitation of letters), and since it is improper to overturn well-known usage, and since in another śruti — "Oṁkāra alone is all this" (Chā.U. 2.23.3) — the phoneme too is taken as an object of upāsanā, with all-Self-ness ascertained of it — therefore akṣara here means a phoneme.

Siddhānta: It is said — Paramātman alone is denoted by the word akṣara. Why? Ambarāntadhṛteḥ — because of the holding up of the entire mass of effects from the earth up to ākāśa. For there, having declared the entire mass of effects beginning with earth and divided into the three times to be supported in ākāśa — "in ākāśa indeed is that woven, warp and woof" — by the question "In what indeed is ākāśa woven, warp and woof?" (Bṛ.U. 3.8.7) this akṣara is brought in. So too is it concluded — "In this Imperishable, O Gārgī, ākāśa is woven, warp and woof." And this support of all up to ambara is not possible elsewhere than in Brahman. As for "Oṁkāra alone is all this" — that is to be regarded as a praise (stuti), because of being a means to the realization of Brahman.

Hence, by the etymology na kṣarati "does not perish" and aśnute "pervades" — by virtue of eternity (nityatva) and pervasiveness (vyāpitva) — akṣara is the supreme Brahman alone.
BS_C01_S03_V11: And that (holding up) is on account of (His) ruling. (11)
BS_C01_S03_V11::block-0: Pūrvapakṣa-leading: Suppose this — if the holding up of all that is up to ambara is admitted as the dependence of the effect upon its cause, this is also tenable for the proponent of pradhāna as cause (the Sāṅkhyas); how then is the establishment of the brahmatva of the akṣara from "holding up to ambara"? To this is given the answer in the next sūtra —
BS_C01_S03_V11::block-1: And that holding up to ambara is the action of Parameśvara alone. Why? Praśāsanāt — because of (His) ruling. For ruling is heard here — "Verily, by the ruling of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, sun and moon stand held apart" (Bṛ.U. 3.8.9) and so on. And ruling (praśāsana) is the action of Parameśvara. The ruling of an unconscious (acetana) thing is not possible. For the unconscious causes of pots and the like — clay and so forth — have no ruling power over pots etc.
BS_C01_S03_V12: And from the exclusion of any other (claimant's) being. (12)
BS_C01_S03_V12::block-0:
And from the cause of the exclusion of any other being, Brahman alone is denoted by the word akṣara; the holding up to ambara is its action alone, of no other. What is meant by "exclusion of any other being"? Anyasya bhāvaḥ anyabhāvaḥ; tasmāt vyāvṛttiḥ anyabhāvavyāvṛttiḥ — being-of-another, and exclusion from that. The meaning is: whatever else might be suspected here as the akṣara, distinct from Brahman, śruti excludes from that (suspected being) this akṣara which holds up the (universe) up to ambara — "That, O Gārgī, is the Imperishable: unseen, the seer; unheard, the hearer; unthought, the thinker; uncognized, the cognizer" (Bṛ.U. 3.8.11).

There the designation of being-unseen and so forth is possible even of pradhāna, but the designation of being-the-seer etc. is not possible (of pradhāna), because of its being unconscious. Likewise, by the negation of difference of Self in "There is no other seer than this; no other hearer than this; no other thinker than this; no other cognizer than this," the embodied (śārīra) self with adjuncts (upādhi) is not denoted by the word akṣara either; and by the negation of being-with-adjuncts in "without eye, without ear, without speech, without mind" (Bṛ.U. 3.8.8). And there is no such thing as a śārīra self apart from upādhis. Therefore the conclusion is — the akṣara is the supreme Brahman alone.
BS_C01_S03_V13: He (is the Supreme), because of His being designated as the object of "seeing" (īkṣati). (13)
BS_C01_S03_V13::block-0:
It is recited, beginning with "This, O Satyakāma, is what is both the higher and the lower Brahman, namely Oṁkāra; therefore the wise one attains, through this very abode, one or the other" (Praśna 5.2): "He, however, who meditates on the supreme Person (paraṃ puruṣam) by means of this very imperishable, Oṁ, of three mātrās" (Praśna 5.5).

Doubt: In this passage, is the supreme Brahman taught as the object of meditation, or the lower? Since by this very abode one attains either the higher or the lower, as introduced — there is doubt.

Pūrvapakṣa: It is the lower Brahman. Why? Because the fruit of one who knows it is spoken of as place-limited — "He becomes one with the brilliance, the sun" and "He is led up by the sāmans to the brahmaloka." It is not proper that the knower of the supreme Brahman should attain a fruit limited in place, since the supreme Brahman is all-pervading. Objection: But if the lower Brahman be accepted, the qualification "supreme Person" does not fit. Reply: No defect — for prāṇa can be called "supreme" relatively to the body. Thus the prima facie view.

Siddhānta:
BS_C01_S03_V13::block-1:
The supreme Brahman alone is here taught as the object of meditation. Why? Īkṣatikarma-vyapadeśāt — because of (His) being designated as the object of the action "seeing" (īkṣati). Īkṣati means seeing; the object of "seeing" is what is grasped by sight. In the conclusion of the passage, this Person who is to be meditated on is designated as the object of seeing — "He sees the Person dwelling in the city, higher than this jīvaghana, higher than the highest" (i.e. the Person reposing in the city).

Now, with the verb abhi-dhyāyati (to meditate upon) the object can even be a thing that is not real, since even what is fashioned by mere wishful imagination is an object of "meditating-on." But of īkṣati "seeing" only a real (tathābhūta) thing is found in the world to be an object. Hence it is understood that Paramātman alone, being the object of right knowledge (samyag-darśana), is here designated as the object of īkṣati. And this same Paramātman is recognized here as the one to be meditated upon by the words "para" and "puruṣa."

Objection: In the meditation the supreme Person is spoken of, but in the seeing, one higher than the highest. How is the one recognized as the other? Reply: The words "para" and "puruṣa" are common to both. Nor is the supreme Person, who was contextually introduced as the one to be meditated upon, indicated by the word jīvaghana, such that this Person, higher than that, would be a different (Person) to be seen.

Then what is jīvaghana? "Ghana" means form (mūrti); "jīvaghana" is a ghana (form) characterized by the jīva. Like the lump of salt, that pseudo-individuality (khilya-bhāva) which is in the form of jīva of Paramātman, brought about by upādhi, and which is "para" relative to the senses and sense-objects — that is here called jīvaghana. Another says: the brahmaloka indicated in the immediately preceding sentence "He is led up by the sāmans to the brahmaloka," being "para" relative to other lokas, is here called jīvaghana. For all jīvas, surrounded by their faculties, come together in Hiraṇyagarbha — the very Self of all faculties, dwelling in the brahmaloka — so the brahmaloka is the jīvaghana.

Therefore that Paramātman who is "para" — beyond — that, who is the object of the seeing, is also the object in the meditation, as is understood. The qualification "supreme Person" too holds only when Paramātman is taken; for the supreme Person is Paramātman alone, since there is nothing higher than Him: śruty-antara — "There is nothing higher than the Person; that is the limit, that is the supreme goal." Having divided "the higher and the lower Brahman, namely Oṁkāra," and then immediately saying that one is to meditate upon the supreme Person by means of Oṁkāra, śruti makes us understand that the supreme Person is the supreme Brahman alone. The mention of the fruit of being freed from sin — "As a snake is freed from its slough, so verily is he freed from sin" — also indicates that Paramātman is the one to be meditated on here.

Now as to the objection that for one who meditates on Paramātman a place-limited fruit is improper — to this we say: the fruit of one who meditates on Paramātman by means of the three-mātrā Oṁkāra as ālambana is the attainment of brahmaloka, and thereafter, in succession, the rise of right knowledge (samyag-darśana). Hence this is to be taken as referring to krama-mukti (gradual liberation), and so there is no defect.
BS_C01_S03_V14: The dahara (small space) is (Brahman), because of what follows. (14)
BS_C01_S03_V14::block-0:
The passage is recited: "Now in this city of Brahman (brahma-pura) there is a small (dahara) lotus, an abode; in it, in the inner space (antar-ākāśa), is the small one. What is within that — that should be sought, that verily should be desired to be known" (Chā.U. 8.1.1) and so forth.

Doubt: That small ākāśa heard of as in the small lotus of the heart — is it the elemental ākāśa (bhūta-ākāśa), or the cognizant self (vijñānātman, the jīva), or Paramātman? Why the doubt? Because of the words "ākāśa" and "brahmapura." The word ākāśa is seen used both for the elemental ākāśa and for the supreme. So is the dahara the elemental ākāśa, or is it the supreme? Likewise "brahmapura" — does "brahman" here refer to the jīva, whose city, the body, is the brahmapura, or is it the city of the supreme Brahman? Hence the doubt: of these two, the jīva or the supreme, which is the city's owner whose dahara-ākāśa this is?

Pūrvapakṣa (1): Since the word ākāśa is well established for elemental ākāśa, the word dahara here is the elemental ākāśa. Its smallness is by reference to the smallness of its abode (the heart-lotus). The relation of upamāna and upameya — "As large as is this ākāśa, so large is this ākāśa within the heart" — is brought about by the difference between the outer and the inner. And heaven and earth etc. are placed within it, because as space ākāśa is one.

Pūrvapakṣa (2): Or, the dahara is the jīva — by the word "brahmapura." For this body, being the city of the jīva, is called brahmapura, since it has been earned by his own karma; and the word "brahman" applies to the jīva by metaphor (bhakti). The supreme Brahman has no relation of body-and-owner with the body. The owner of a city is seen to dwell in a corner of the city, like a king. The jīva is conditioned by mind; mind is generally seated in the heart — so the dwelling within the heart is of the jīva. His smallness too is fitting, since he is compared to the tip of a goad. The comparison to ākāśa etc. will then be intended to indicate non-difference from Brahman. Nor is the dahara ākāśa heard here directly as that which is to be sought and known; "that which is within it" is mentioned only as a qualifying phrase of the supreme.
BS_C01_S03_V14::block-1:
Siddhānta: To this we answer — Parameśvara alone deserves to be the dahara-ākāśa here, not the elemental ākāśa nor the jīva. Why? Uttarebhyaḥ — because of the reasons that follow in the rest of the passage. For in answer to the objection raised — "What then is there in it that should be sought, that verily should be desired to be known?" — beginning with "They should say to him" — the reply is given: "He should say: As far as is this ākāśa, so far is this inner ākāśa within the heart. Both heaven and earth are placed in it…" (Chā.U. 8.1.2-3) and so on. There, while the smallness obtained from the smallness of the lotus is being negated by comparison with the well-known (great) ākāśa, śruti also negates the elemental-ākāśa-ness of the dahara-ākāśa. For though the word ākāśa is well established in elemental ākāśa, the comparison of that very ākāśa with itself is incoherent — hence the suspicion of elemental ākāśa is set aside.

Objection: Even of one ākāśa, the upamāna-upameya relation is possible by the imagined difference of outer and inner. Reply: That is not possible. Such a recourse to imagined difference is a way out only when no other course is available. Moreover, even if one imagines such a difference, the relation of comparison cannot make the inner ākāśa equal in measure to the outer ākāśa, since the inner is bounded. Objection: Equality of measure with ākāśa is not possible even of Parameśvara, since another śruti says "greater than ākāśa" (Śat.Br. 10.6.3.2). Reply: No defect — for since the passage aims at negating the smallness obtained from the lotus-enclosure, it does not aim at conveying actual equality. If both were intended, the sentence would be split. Nor in such an imagined-difference treatment can heaven and earth etc. be accommodated in a portion of ākāśa enclosed in a lotus. The qualities "This Self, free from sin (apahata-pāpman), free from old age, free from death, free from sorrow, free from hunger, free from thirst, of true desire, of true resolve" — Self-hood, sinlessness etc. — are not possible in the elemental ākāśa.

Though the word "ātman" is possible in jīva, the suspicion of jīva is also dispelled by the other reasons. The smallness brought about by the lotus-enclosure cannot be negated of the jīva, who is upādhi-bounded and compared to the tip of a goad. If it be said: with the intention of his non-difference from Brahman, all-pervasiveness etc. of jīva are spoken of — then it is reasonable that, in respect of which Self the jīva's all-pervasiveness etc. would be spoken of, of that very Brahman directly the all-pervasiveness etc. should be spoken of.

As to: "brahmapura" — since the city is qualified by jīva, the city's owner is the jīva, who, like a king, dwells in a corner of his own city — to this we say: this body, being the city of the supreme Brahman alone, is called brahmapura, since the word "brahman" applies to Him in its primary sense (mukhya-vṛtti). He too has a relation with this city, as the substratum of cognition (upalabdhy-adhiṣṭhāna), as said in śrutis: "He sees the Person reposing in the city, higher than this jīvaghana, higher than the highest" (Praśna 5.5); "This Person, in all cities, is reposing in the city" (Bṛ.U. 2.5.18). Or, in the city of the jīva, Brahman is figured as present, just as Viṣṇu is figured as present in a śālagrāma. And having said that the fruit of karmas is finite — "Just as here the world won by karma perishes, so there the world won by puṇya perishes" (Chā.U. 8.1.6) — śruti goes on to praise the fruit of the knowledge of the Self as imperishable: "Now those who depart from here, having known the Self…"
BS_C01_S03_V15: (He is the Supreme), because of (the words "going" and "brahmaloka"); for so it is seen (in another śruti); and (there is) a mark too. (15)
BS_C01_S03_V15::block-0:
It has been said that the dahara is Parameśvara on account of the reasons that follow. Those very later reasons are now elaborated.

For this further reason too, Parameśvara alone is the dahara: because in the rest of the dahara passage there are a "going" word (gati-śabda) and a "brahmaloka" word that point to Parameśvara — "All these creatures, going day after day to this brahmaloka, do not find it" (Chā.U. 8.3.2). There the dahara, which is the contextual subject, is referred to by the word brahmaloka, and the going of the creatures (jīvas) — directed towards it — being declared, conveys the brahma-ness of the dahara.

For day after day the going of jīvas in the state of suṣupti to the realm of Brahman is seen in another śruti: "In the existent (sat), my dear, he then becomes merged" (Chā.U. 6.8.1) and the like. In ordinary speech too they say of one fast asleep "He has become Brahman, gone to Brahman-hood." Likewise the word "brahmaloka" applied to the contextual dahara, dispelling the suspicions of jīva and elemental ākāśa, conveys its being Brahman.

Objection: But the word brahmaloka could also point to the loka of the lotus-seated (Brahmā, Hiraṇyagarbha). Reply: It would, if the word were unfolded by the genitive compound "the loka of Brahman" (ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa). But unfolded by sāmānādhikaraṇya (apposition) — "Brahman itself is the loka, hence brahmaloka" — it points to the supreme Brahman alone. And this very day-by-day going to brahmaloka is a mark (liṅga) for taking the word brahmaloka in the apposition reading. For it cannot be imagined that day after day these creatures go to the effected brahmaloka named satyaloka.
BS_C01_S03_V16: And because of (the function of) sustaining (the worlds), and because this greatness is perceived in Him alone. (16)
BS_C01_S03_V16::block-0:
And on account of (the function of) sustaining as the reason, this dahara (the small one within the lotus of the heart) is none other than the Supreme Lord (parameśvara). How? Having introduced the topic with 'A small (dahara) ākāśa (is) within' (Chā. Up. 8.1.1), and having declared the placing of all (worlds) within it after the simile of ākāśa, and having employed in that very (subject) the word ātman, and having taught its connection with such qualities as 'untouched by sin' (apahatapāpmatva) and the rest, the śruti points to that very same (entity), the topic not having lapsed: 'Now this Self (ātman) is the bridge (setu), the upholder (vidhṛti) of these worlds, that they may not be confounded together' (Chā. Up. 8.4.1). There the word vidhṛti, by reason of co-referentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with the word ātman, denotes the upholder (vidhārayitṛ); for the suffix ktic is recorded (in Pāṇinian smṛti) as kartari (in the agent-sense).

Just as in the world a bridge (setu) is the upholder of a stream of water, for the non-confusion of the contents of (different) fields, even so this Ātman is the upholder, the bridge, of these worlds — distinguished as adhyātma and the rest — and of the varṇas, āśramas, and the like, for non-confusion (asaṁbheda), that is, for non-intermixture (asaṅkara). Thus here, in the dahara that is the topic, greatness in the form of upholding (vidhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa) is shown forth.

And this very greatness is, from another śruti, ascertained to be the Supreme Lord's alone — 'Verily, O Gārgī, at the command of this Imperishable, the sun and the moon stand upheld' (Bṛ. Up. 3.8.9), and the like. Likewise, in another passage which is settled to refer to the Supreme Lord, it is heard: 'He is the Lord of all, the overlord of beings, the protector of beings; He is the bridge, the upholder of these worlds, for their non-confusion' (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.22). Thus, on account of upholding (dhṛti) as the reason, this dahara is the Supreme Lord alone. (16)
BS_C01_S03_V17: And on account of (the word ākāśa being) well-known (in the sense of Brahman). (17)
BS_C01_S03_V17::block-0:
On this score also it is the Supreme Lord alone who is meant in 'A small (dahara) ākāśa (is) within' — because the word ākāśa is well-known (prasiddha) as denoting the Supreme Lord. This is seen from such usages as: 'Verily, that which is called ākāśa is the producer (nirvahitṛ) of name and form' (Chā. Up. 8.14.1), and 'All these beings, verily, arise from ākāśa alone' (Chā. Up. 1.9.1).

But in (the sense of) the jīva, the word ākāśa is nowhere seen to be applied. As for the (gross) elemental ākāśa (bhūtākāśa) — although it has the well-known meaning of the word ākāśa, it has been already stated (above) that it is not to be taken here, since the relation of upamāna (object of comparison) and upameya (the thing compared) and the rest cannot subsist (between two cases of the same elemental ākāśa). (17)
BS_C01_S03_V18: If it be said that on account of the reference to the other (the jīva) it (the dahara) is that (jīva) — no, on account of impossibility. (18)
BS_C01_S03_V18::block-0:
(Pūrvapakṣa:) If, by the strength of the supplementary passage (vākya-śeṣa), the dahara is to be taken as the Supreme Lord, then there is, in the supplementary passage, a reference (parāmarśa) to the other (the jīva) as well: 'Now this serene one (saṁprasāda), having risen up from this body and reached the supreme light, manifests in his own form — this is the Self (ātman),' so He said (Chā. Up. 8.3.4 / 8.12.3). For here the word saṁprasāda, since it is seen in another śruti to denote the deep-sleep state, is competent to bring forward the jīva endowed with that state, not anything else. So too, the rising up from the body is possible only of the jīva who has the body as his abode, just as it is possible for wind and the like, which have ākāśa as their abode, to rise from the ākāśa.

And just as the word ākāśa, though not seen in worldly usage with reference to the Supreme Lord, has been admitted in such places as 'Verily that which is called ākāśa is the producer of name and form' (Chā. Up. 8.14.1) to refer to the Supreme Lord, on the strength of the conjoined attributes of the Supreme Lord — even so, here too it may have the jīva for its object. Therefore, on account of the reference to the other (jīva), in 'A small (dahara) ākāśa (is) within' it is the jīva himself who is spoken of — if this be said:

(Siddhānta:) It cannot be so. Why? — Because of impossibility (asaṁbhava). For the jīva, identifying himself with the limitations (upādhi) of the buddhi and the rest, cannot be likened (upamīyate) to the (boundless) ākāśa. Nor are such qualities as 'untouched by sin' (apahatapāpmatva) and the rest possible for one who identifies himself with the attributes of the upādhis. And this has been elaborated under the very first sūtra. To remove the apprehension of redundancy, it has been brought up here once again. And further on too the (sūtrakāra) will say: 'And the reference (parāmarśa) is for another purpose' (Br. Sū. 1.3.20). (18)
BS_C01_S03_V19: If (it be argued) on account of the latter (passage) — (we reply) but (the jīva spoken of there) is one whose true form has been manifested (āvirbhūta-svarūpa). (19)
BS_C01_S03_V19::block-0:
The apprehension of (the dahara being) the jīva, born from the reference to the other, has been refuted on the ground of impossibility. Now, however, as if by the sprinkling of nectar upon the dead, the apprehension of the jīva is once again raised — by the latter Prājāpatya passage. There, having promised that the Self characterized by such qualities as 'untouched by sin' (apahatapāpmā) is to be sought after and to be inquired into, with 'That Self which is untouched by sin,' and saying, 'That Person who is seen in the eye, He is the Self' (Chā. Up. 8.7.4), He points to the seer in the eye, the jīva-ātman.

And by 'But this very (one), I shall further explain to thee' (Chā. Up. 8.9.3), referring to the same again and again, He explains that very jīva as having gone into other states, by 'He who, in dream, moves about being honoured — He is the Self' (Chā. Up. 8.10.1) and 'When, having become asleep, fully composed, serene, he sees no dream — that is the Self' (Chā. Up. 8.11.1). Of that very same (jīva) He shows the qualities of being untouched by sin and the rest: 'This is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman.'

And having noted the defect in the sleep state — 'Lo, indeed, this one does not now know himself thus, that I am he, nor (does he know) these beings' (Chā. Up. 8.11.2) — and beginning, 'But this very (one) I shall further explain to thee, and not (any other) than this,' He, censuring the body-relation, shows by 'This serene one (saṁprasāda), having risen up from this body and reached the supreme light, is manifested in his own form — He is the supreme Person' that the supreme Person is the very jīva risen from the body. Therefore there is the possibility of the attributes of the Supreme Lord (pārameśvara-dharma) in the jīva. Hence, if some one were to say, 'In 'A small (dahara) ākāśa (is) within,' the jīva alone is spoken of,' to him let it be replied — 'But (it is one) whose true form has been made manifest' (āvirbhūta-svarūpas tu).

The word 'tu' (but) is for the purpose of warding off the pūrvapakṣa. The meaning is: not even from this latter passage is there room for the apprehension of the jīva here. Why? — Because there too it is the jīva whose true form has been manifested (āvirbhūta-svarūpa) that is intended to be expounded. He whose svarūpa (true form) has become manifest — this is the etymology of āvirbhūta-svarūpa; the (continued) designation as jīva is by way of 'what was previously so' (bhūta-pūrva-gati).

This is the import: by 'He who is in the eye,' having pointed out the seer characterized by (residence in) the eye, having dislodged him from identification with the body by means of the Udaśarāva-brāhmaṇa, having drawn him back again and again as the very thing to be expounded by 'But this very (one) I shall (further explain) to thee,' and proceeding through the exposition of dream and deep sleep, by 'reaching the supreme light, is manifested in his own form,' He explains that very jīva by way of that which is his pāramārthika (ultimately real) svarūpa, the supreme Brahman — not by his (apparent) jaiva form. The 'supreme light' that is to be reached, as heard, is the supreme Brahman; and that has the qualities of being untouched by sin and the rest. And that alone is the pāramārthika (truly real) form of the jīva — by such scriptures as 'That thou art' (tat tvam asi) — not the other one, fashioned by upādhis.

For so long as one does not, by causing to cease that avidyā which has the form of duality — like the (false) cognition of a man in a (mere) post — apprehend the Self that is of the form of the unchanging eternal seer (kūṭastha-nitya-dṛk-svarūpa) as 'I am Brahman' (ahaṁ brahmāsmi), so long is there the jīva-hood of the jīva. But when, raised up by the śruti from the aggregate of body, sense-organs, manas and buddhi, he is roused with: 'Thou art not the aggregate of body, sense-organs, manas, buddhi; thou art not a transmigrator (saṁsārin); but rather — that which is real, that is the Self, of the nature of pure consciousness alone — 'tat tvam asi' — then, awakening to the Self of the form of the unchanging eternal seer, rising up from the identification with this body and the rest, he becomes that very unchanging eternal (Brahman). (19)
BS_C01_S03_V20: And the reference (to the jīva) is for another purpose. (20)
BS_C01_S03_V20::block-0:
Now, the reference to the jīva that has been shown in the supplementary passage of the dahara — 'Now this serene one (saṁprasāda)' (Chā. Up. 8.3.4) and the rest — when the dahara is being expounded as the Supreme Lord, would not be a teaching of the worship of the jīva, nor would it be a teaching of any peculiarity of the topic at hand, and so it would attain the status of being purposeless. To meet this, (the sūtrakāra) says: this reference to the jīva is for another purpose (anyārtha) — it does not terminate in the jīva's own form (jīva-svarūpa-paryavasāyī), but rather terminates in the form of the Supreme Lord (parameśvara-svarūpa-paryavasāyī).

How? The jīva, designated by the word saṁprasāda — having become, in the waking transactions, the overseer of the cage of body and sense-organs, having experienced through the channels (nāḍī-cara) the dreams fashioned out of the impressions left by that (waking life), wearied, and seeking refuge — rising up from his identification with both forms of the body, in the deep-sleep state, reaches the supreme light, designated as ākāśa, the supreme Brahman, and giving up specialized cognition (viśeṣa-vijñānavattva), is manifested in his own form. That supreme light which is to be reached, that by reason of which he is manifested in his own form, that very Self, possessed of qualities such as being untouched by sin and the rest, is to be worshipped — for such a purpose this reference to the jīva is fitting even for the upholder of the Supreme Lord doctrine. (20)
BS_C01_S03_V21: If it be said (the dahara is the jīva) on account of the smallness heard of (in the śruti) — (we reply) that has (already) been answered. (21)
BS_C01_S03_V21::block-0:
What was also said (in the pūrvapakṣa) — that the smallness of the ākāśa heard of in 'A small (dahara) ākāśa (is) within' is not appropriate to the Supreme Lord, but the smallness, compared to the tip of an awl (ārāgra), is fitting in the case of the jīva — for that the refutation must be stated. The refutation has been (already) given, viz. that even of the Supreme Lord a relative smallness (āpekṣika alpatva) is fitting, in the sūtra 'On account of (the description of) smallness of dwelling and the (consequent) designation, (it is the jīva and) not (Brahman) — if so, no, on account of the (declared) being-the-object-of-meditation thus, and like the sky' (Br. Sū. 1.2.7). The same refutation is to be borne in mind here too — this the sūtra hints at.

And by the śruti itself this (apparent) smallness has been countered, by the comparison made through the well-known ākāśa: 'As large as is this (great) ākāśa, so large is this ākāśa within the heart' (Chā. Up. 8.1.3). (21)
BS_C01_S03_V22: (He is the supreme Self) on account of (His being followed in) shining-after, and on account of His (light by which all this shines). (22)
BS_C01_S03_V22::block-0:
(Pūrvapakṣa:) They recite: 'There the sun shines not, nor moon and stars; these lightnings shine not — whence then this fire? Him alone shining, all shines after; by His shining all this shines forth' (Mu. Up. 2.2.10 / Kaṭha 5.15). There, He whom shining all shines after, by whose shining all this shines forth — is He some luminous element (tejo-dhātu), or the Prājña-Ātman? — In this doubt, it is first attained that He is some luminous element. Why? — Because what is denied (here) is the shining of luminous things alone, viz. the sun and the rest. For it is well-known that the moon, stars and the like, themselves of luminous nature, do not shine when the sun, of luminous nature, is shining in the day. Likewise, that in which all this — moon, stars and the rest, together with the sun — does not shine must itself be of some luminous nature, it is understood. Shining-after, also, is fitting only in the case of one of luminous nature, since 'following' (anukāra) is seen in the case of those of similar nature; as in 'he goes after one going.' Hence let it be some luminous element — when this is attained, we say:

(Siddhānta:) This is fit to be the Prājña-Ātman alone. Why? — Because of (the said) anukṛti (after-imitation, after-shining); 'anukaraṇa' (imitation) is anukṛti. This 'shining-after' — viz. 'Him alone shining, all shines after' — fits if the Prājña is taken; for they recite the Prājña-Ātman as 'of the form of light, of true resolves' (bhārūpaḥ satyasaṅkalpaḥ — Chā. Up. 3.14.2). It is, however, not well-known that the sun and the rest shine after some (other) luminous element. And, since the luminous things, the sun and the rest, are equal in their luminosity, there is no need (for them) of another luminous element which they should follow as it shines. Lamp does not shine after lamp.

As for the contention that 'following' (anukāra) is seen in those of similar nature alone — this is not an absolute rule. For the following (anukāra) is seen also in those of differing nature — as a fully-heated iron-ball, imitating fire, scorches after the scorching fire, and the dust of the earth blows after the wind that blows.

'Anukṛteḥ' (the sūtra-word) suggested 'shining-after' (anubhāna). 'Tasya ca' suggests the fourth quarter of the (Mu. Up.) verse. 'By His shining all this shines forth' — the (statement that the) shining of the sun and the rest is caused by Him brings to mind the Prājña-Ātman. They recite the Prājña-Ātman as 'Him the gods worship as the Light of lights, as life, as immortal' (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.16). It is not well-known, and indeed contradictory, that the luminosity of the sun and the rest shines forth by another luminous thing — for one luminous thing is obstructed by another.

Or else, this caused-by-Him-shining is not (only) of the sun and the rest enumerated in the verse. What then? — On account of the unrestricted śruti 'sarvam idam' (all this), the manifestation of every aggregate of name, form, action, doer, and fruit has, as its (sustaining) cause, the existence (sattā) of the brahma-jyotis — just as the manifestation of every aggregate of forms has, for its cause, the existence of the light of the sun and the rest.

And in 'There (tatra) the sun shines not,' bringing in the word 'there,' it indicates the prakṛta (the topic at hand). And the prakṛta is Brahman, by 'In whom the heaven, the earth, and the mid-region are woven' (Mu. Up. 2.2.5) and the rest, and immediately after by 'In the supreme golden sheath is Brahman, stainless, partless. That, the pure, the Light of lights, that which the knowers of Self know.' How is it the Light of lights? — to (answer) this, this (passage) has arisen — 'There the sun shines not.'

As for what was said — that the negation of the shining of the sun and the rest is fitting only with reference to another luminous element, like (it is fitting) for the rest with the sun — there it has been shown that no other such (different) luminous element is possible. And in (the case of) Brahman too, this negation of the shining of these is fitting. Because: whatever is apprehended is apprehended only by Brahman as light. But Brahman is not apprehended by another light, being itself self-luminous in nature (svayañ-jyotiḥ-svarūpatva); by which (the lights) the sun and the rest shine in It. For Brahman makes other things manifest, but Brahman is not made manifest by another — by the śruti texts: 'He sits with this very Self as light' (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.6), 'He is ungraspable, for He is not grasped' (Bṛ. Up. 4.2.4 / 3.9.26), and the rest. (22)
BS_C01_S03_V23: And further, (it is) remembered (in the smṛti, viz. the Bhagavad-gītā). (23)
BS_C01_S03_V23::block-0:
And further, this same form (of being the Light of lights) is, of the Prājña-Ātman alone, remembered (smaryate) in the Bhagavad-gītā: 'Neither the sun lights it, nor the moon, nor fire; whither having gone they return not — that is My supreme abode' (Bh. Gī. 15.6).

And: 'That light which, residing in the sun, illumines the entire world, and that which is in the moon and in the fire — know that light to be Mine' (Bh. Gī. 15.12). (23)
BS_C01_S03_V24: From the word itself (it is) ascertained. (1.3.24)
BS_C01_S03_V24::block-0:
It is heard, ‘The puruṣa of the measure of a thumb stands in the middle, in the Self’; and likewise, ‘The puruṣa of the measure of a thumb, like a smokeless flame, is the lord of what was and what shall be; He alone is today, He alone tomorrow. This verily is That’ (Kaṭha Up. 2.1.13). There, regarding this puruṣa of thumb-measure that is heard of, the doubt arises — is it the vijñānātman (the individual cognising self), or is it the Paramātman (Supreme Self)?

There, the pūrvapakṣa first obtains: because a measure is taught, it must be the vijñānātman. For, of the Paramātman, who has neither end nor extent, the measure of a thumb cannot be reasonably accommodated. But of the vijñānātman, since it is endowed with limiting adjuncts (upādhi-mat), the state of being thumb-sized is possible by some figurative imagination. And from smṛti too — ‘Then from the body of Satyavat, bound and brought under his sway by the noose, Yama by force drew out the puruṣa of thumb-size’ (Mbh 3.297.17). For the Supreme Lord cannot possibly be drawn out by force by Yama. Hence what is denoted there is the transmigrating self of thumb-measure. The very same is here too — when this is the prima facie position, we reply:
BS_C01_S03_V24::block-1: It is the Paramātman alone that should be taken to be this puruṣa of thumb-measure. On what ground? From the word — ‘the lord of what was and what shall be’. For none other than the Supreme Lord is the unrestrained ruler of past and future. And ‘This verily is That’ — by this it relates back to the topic that was previously asked. ‘This verily is That’ — that which was asked of as Brahman, is the meaning. And here Brahman alone was asked of — ‘That which thou seest as other than dharma, other than adharma, other than this done and undone, other than past and other than future, that tell me’ (Kaṭha Up. 1.2.14). ‘From the word itself’ — that is, from the very word of designation: from the word ‘Īśāna’ (lord), the Supreme Lord is here understood. This is the meaning. (1.3.24)
BS_C01_S03_V25: But with reference to the heart, because (the śāstra) has men for its qualified subject. (1.3.25)
BS_C01_S03_V25::block-0: But how can a measure be taught of the all-pervading Paramātman? On this we say:
BS_C01_S03_V25::block-1:
Even of the all-pervading Paramātman, this thumb-measure is spoken of with reference to His abiding in the heart — just as for ākāśa, residing in a bamboo-joint, the measure of a forearm (is spoken of with reference to that joint). For directly, of the Paramātman who exceeds all measure, thumb-size is impossible. And none other than the Paramātman is fit to be apprehended here, by reason of words such as ‘Īśāna’ — this has been stated.

‘But, since the hearts of beings differ from being to being and are not of fixed dimension, even with reference to that, the thumb-measure is not made out’ — to this the answer is given: ‘because (the śāstra) has men as its qualified subjects’. ‘The śāstra, though it proceeds without distinction (towards all), yet authorises men alone for adhikāra; for they alone are capable, are seekers, are not excluded, and on account of the upanayana-śāstra etc. — this has been described in the chapter on adhikāra-lakṣaṇa’ (Jaim. Sūtra 6.1). And men have a body of fixed dimension; suitably, their heart too is of fixed dimension, namely the size of the thumb. Hence, since the śāstra has men for its qualified subjects, the thumb-measure of the Paramātman with reference to His residing in the human heart is reasonable.

As to what was said — that, owing to the teaching of measure and from smṛti, this thumb-measured one is to be understood as the saṃsārin alone — to that the answer is: just as in ‘That Self thou art’ (sa ātmā tat tvam asi) and the like, so here also, of the saṃsārin who is of thumb-measure, Brahman-hood is being taught. For the activity (pravṛtti) of vedānta-vākyas is twofold — at some places it is directed at setting forth the very nature of the Paramātman; at others it is directed at the teaching of the oneness of the vijñānātman with the Paramātman. Here too the oneness of the vijñānātman with the Paramātman is taught; thumb-measuredness is not taught of any. This very meaning is made explicit further on — ‘The puruṣa of thumb-size, the inner Self, is ever seated in the heart of men. Him let one draw forth from one’s body steadily, as a stalk from muñja-grass. Him let one know as the pure, the immortal’ (Kaṭha Up. 2.3.17). (1.3.25)
BS_C01_S03_V26: And above them too (gods etc. are qualified), says Bādarāyaṇa, because it is possible. (1.3.26)
BS_C01_S03_V26::block-0:
It has been said that the śruti about thumb-size is with reference to the human heart, because the śāstra has men as its qualified subjects. In that connection this is now stated. Granted, the śāstra qualifies men. But there is no rule here, in regard to the knowledge of Brahman, that it is men only. Above those men there are gods and others — them too the śāstra qualifies; this is the view of Bādarāyaṇa the ācārya. Why? Because it is possible (sambhavāt). For of them too the conditions of qualification — desire (arthitva) and so on — are possible. There, desire for liberation (mokṣa-viṣaya arthitva) is possible even for the gods, occasioned by the contemplation of the impermanence of even the highest sovereignty over modifications. Likewise their capacity (sāmarthya) too is possible, since their possessing bodies and so on is known from mantras, arthavādas, itihāsa, purāṇa, and worldly tradition. Nor is there any prohibition for them. Nor is their qualification negated by the upanayana-śāstra, since the upanayana exists for the sake of vedic study, while for them the Veda shines forth of itself (svayam-pratibhāta-veda).

Moreover, scripture shows brahmacarya etc. for the sake of their grasping of vidyā — ‘Verily for one hundred and one years did Maghavan dwell as a brahmacārin under Prajāpati’ (Chānd. Up. 8.11.3); ‘Bhṛgu, the son of Varuṇa, approached his father Varuṇa and said, “Sir, teach me Brahman”’ (Tait. Up. 3.1.1) — and so on. As for the reasons given for non-qualification in karma — ‘Not the gods, because there is no other deity (for them to worship)’, ‘Not the ṛṣis, because there is no other ārṣeya (lineage for them)’ (Jaim. Sū. 6.1.6, 7) — those do not apply to the vidyās. For when Indra and the rest are qualified for vidyās, there is no rite to be performed by them addressed to Indra and the rest as the deity. Nor for Bhṛgu and others, with reference to being of the Bhṛgu-gotra and so on. Therefore, by what is the gods’ etc. qualification in the vidyās precluded? Even when the gods are qualified, the śruti about thumb-measure is, with reference to their own thumbs, not contradicted. (1.3.26)
BS_C01_S03_V27: If it be objected that there is contradiction with respect to (sacrificial) action, (we reply) no, for the assumption of many forms is seen. (1.3.27)
BS_C01_S03_V27::block-0:
It might be said: pūrvapakṣa — if, by accepting the corporeality etc. of the gods, qualification in the vidyās is to be set forth, then, since they have bodies, just like ṛtviks etc., Indra and the rest would also have to be admitted as ancillaries to the rite by their personal presence; and then there would be a contradiction with regard to karma. For Indra and the others are not seen to function as ancillaries to a sacrifice by personal presence. Nor is it possible — since at many sacrifices going on simultaneously the personal presence of one Indra cannot be made out.

Siddhānta — this contradiction does not exist. Why? Because there is the apprehension of many forms (aneka-pratipatteḥ). Even of one deity-self, the simultaneous adoption of many forms is possible. How is this known? From observation (darśanāt). Thus, beginning with ‘How many gods are there?’ (Bṛh. Up. 3.9.1), the śruti having explicated, ‘Three and three hundred, and three and three thousand’ (3.9.1), then on the question, ‘Which are these?’ (3.9.1), declaring, ‘These are but the powers of those; the gods (proper) are thirty-three only’ (3.9.2), the śruti shows that one and the same deity-self has many simultaneous forms. So too, after enfolding the thirty-three by stages — six and so forth — into one, ‘Which is the one god? Prāṇa,’ — showing the singleness in the form of Prāṇa of the gods, it shows the simultaneous many-formedness of that very one Prāṇa.

Likewise smṛti — ‘O bull of the Bharatas, of the (yogi) Self there are many bodies; the yogi having attained power may make them, and with all of them go upon the earth. With some he may enjoy objects, with some practise stern tapas; and again he gathers them in, like the sun his rays’ — and so on, shows even of yogins who have attained aṇimā and other supremacies the simultaneous yoking of many bodies; what is to be said of the gods who are siddha by birth (ājāna-siddha)? Thus, since apprehension in many forms is possible, each single deity, dividing herself into many forms, simultaneously becomes ancillary in many sacrifices, and is not seen by others, by reason of yoga-power of vanishing and the like — this stands established.

Another explanation of ‘from the seeing of many apprehensions’ — even with respect to corporeal beings as enjoined in their ancillary role in karma, plurality of apprehension is observed; in some places one corporeal being does not become ancillary at many places at once — as one brāhmaṇa is not simultaneously fed by many feeders; in some places one corporeal being does become ancillary at many places at once — as one brāhmaṇa is simultaneously saluted by many salutants. Likewise here, since a sacrifice consists in the dedication of an offering to a particular addressee (uddeśa-parityāgātmaka), even of one corporeal deity, addressing her, many will at once give up their own respective dravya. Thus, even with the corporeality of the gods admitted, there is no contradiction with respect to karma. (1.3.27)
BS_C01_S03_V28: If it be said (there is contradiction) regarding the word, (we reply) no, since from this very (word) is the origination, by perception (śruti) and inference (smṛti). (1.3.28)
BS_C01_S03_V28::block-0: Pūrvapakṣa — Be it so that, on accepting the corporeality of the gods, no contradiction is incurred in karma. But contradiction would be incurred with regard to the word. How? The pramāṇya of the Veda has been established, by relying on the natural (autpattika) connection of word with meaning, on the ground that ‘it is independent (anapekṣatva)’ (Mīm. Sū. 1.1.5). But now, if a corporeal deity is admitted, then though, by virtue of sovereignty, she may eat the offerings related to many simultaneous rites, yet, by reason of having a body, she would be subject to birth and death like ourselves. So, when the eternal connection of the eternal word with the eternal meaning has been understood, the pramāṇya of the vedic word that has been settled would be contradicted. — Reply: this contradiction too does not exist. Why? Because from this (very vedic word) is the origination (ataḥ prabhavāt). For from the vedic word itself the world of gods etc. originates.
BS_C01_S03_V28::block-1:
Doubt — at ‘That from which is the origin of this etc.’ (Brahmasūtra 1.1.2) the world’s origination from Brahman has been ascertained; how is its origination from word said here? Moreover, even granting that its origin is from the vedic word, how, by so much, is the contradiction in regard to the word removed? For the entities ‘Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, Viśvedevas, Maruts’ are non-eternal, having an origin. And, on their non-eternality, what shall preclude the non-eternality of the vedic words ‘Vasu’ etc., which name them? It is well known in the world that when a son is born to Devadatta, the name ‘Yajñadatta’ is fashioned for him.

Reply — no, because the connection of word with meaning in cases like ‘cow’ is seen to be eternal. For though the individual cow has origination, the ākṛti (universal form) does not have origination too. Of substance, quality, and action, only the individuals (vyakti) come to be, not the ākṛtis. And the connection of words is with the ākṛti, not with the individuals — for, since the individuals are infinite, the apprehension of connection (with each) is impossible. While individuals are originating, since the ākṛtis are eternal, no contradiction is seen in words like ‘cow’. Similarly, even on accepting the origination of individual deities etc., since the ākṛti is eternal, there is no contradiction in regard to words like ‘Vasu’. The specific ākṛti of the gods is to be understood from mantra, arthavāda, and the like, where their being possessed of a body etc. is gathered. And words like ‘Indra’ have a connection grounded in a particular station, like ‘senāpati’ etc. (a generalship-name): therefore whoever ascends to that station is denoted by ‘Indra’ etc. — so there is no defect.

Nor is this ‘śabda-prabhavatva’ (origination from word) to be taken in the upādāna sense as ‘Brahma-prabhavatva’ is. Then how? It is said: in the eternal word abiding as designator (vācakātmanā nitya), connected eternally with its meaning, there occurs the production (niṣpatti) of meaning-individuals fit for word-usage. This is what is meant by ‘ataḥ prabhavaḥ’.

How is it known that the world originates from the word? By prratyakṣa and anumāna; pratyakṣa is śruti, on account of independence in regard to authority; anumāna is smṛti, on account of dependence (on something else) in regard to authority. They both show that creation is preceded by the word: ‘Saying ete iti, Prajāpati created the gods; saying asṛgram iti, men; indavaḥ iti, the manes; tiraḥ-pavitraṃ iti, the grahas; āśavaḥ iti, the stotra; viśvāni iti, the śastra; abhi-saubhagā iti, other beings’ — thus says the śruti. So elsewhere — ‘He united with vāc as a couple by the mind’ (Bṛh. Up. 1.2.4) etc. — there too creation preceded by word is heard. Smṛti also — ‘Beginningless and endless, eternal, vāc was emitted by the Self-existent’ (Mbh 12.232.24); ‘At the beginning, divine, made of the Veda, from which all pravṛttis (proceed)’ (Kūrma Pu. 2.27); — and this ‘emission’ of vāc is to be understood as the inauguration of tradition (sampradāya-pravartana), since for what is beginningless and endless any other kind of emission is impossible. So too — ‘the names and forms of beings, and the regulation of their actions, that great Lord at the beginning fashioned from the Veda-words alone’ (Mbh 12.232.26; Viṣṇu Pu. 1.5.63); ‘He fashioned distinctly the names and acts of all, and their distinct stations, from the Veda-words alone, at the beginning’ (Manu 1.21). Furthermore, when one is to perform an intended thing, one first remembers the word denoting it, and then performs the thing — this is everyone’s pratyakṣa.
BS_C01_S03_V28::block-2: What is the nature of word that is intended in saying that the world originates from word? Sphoṭa, he says. For on the varṇa-pakṣa, since the varṇas (phonemes) come and perish, the origination of god-individuals etc. from eternal words would not be made out. And the varṇas come and perish, since at every utterance they are apprehended differently. Thus, even when not seen, a particular person is determined merely by hearing the sound of his recitation — ‘this is Devadatta who recites; this is Yajñadatta who recites’. Nor is this differential apprehension regarding varṇas mistaken cognition (mithyā-jñāna), since there is no contradicting cognition. Nor is the apprehension of meaning from the varṇas reasonable. For no single varṇa can convey a meaning, because of vyabhicāra (deviation). Nor is there a cognition of the aggregate (samudāya) of varṇas, since the varṇas are sequential. If it be said that the last varṇa, accompanied by the saṃskāras produced by the experiences of the previous varṇas, will convey the meaning, that is not so. For a word, requiring the grasping of the connection (with meaning), is itself apprehended and then conveys the meaning, like smoke etc. But of the last varṇa, accompanied by saṃskāras produced by experiences of the previous varṇas, there is no apprehension, since saṃskāras are not perceptible. If it be said that the last varṇa, accompanied by saṃskāras inferred from their effect, will convey the meaning, no — for the effect of the saṃskāra, namely smaraṇa, is itself sequential. Therefore the word is sphoṭa alone. And it, when on the seed sown by the apprehensions of each individual varṇa the apprehension of the last varṇa brings ripening in the cognising one (pratyayin), as the object of one cognition, suddenly flashes into view. And this single cognition is not a remembrance of the varṇas, since the varṇas being many, their being the object of one cognition is impossible. And, since at every utterance it is recognised, it is eternal — the cognition of difference being only of the varṇas. Hence, from the eternal word in the form of sphoṭa, as designator, the world of action, agent, and fruit, as that to be designated, originates.
BS_C01_S03_V28::block-3:
‘But the word is the varṇas alone’ — so says Bhagavān Upavarṣa. — But it has been said that the varṇas come and perish? — Not so, on account of recognition (pratyabhijñāna) — ‘these are the same.’ — If it be said that the recognition is by similarity (sādṛśya), as in hairs etc., not so — for the recognition cannot be sublated by another pramāṇa. — If it be said that the recognition is grounded in ākṛti, no — for it is the recognition of the individuals (vyakti) themselves. For if at every utterance other and other individual varṇas were apprehended, as with cow-individuals, then the recognition would be grounded in ākṛti. But this is not the case. The varṇa-individuals themselves are recognised at every utterance. The cognition is — ‘the word “go” has been uttered twice’; not — ‘two “go”-words.’ — But it has been said that varṇas too appear differentiated by difference of utterance, since by hearing the recitation-sound the difference between Devadatta and Yajñadatta is known. — On this we say: when, regarding varṇas, recognition is established, since varṇas are manifested by saṃyoga and vibhāga (conjunction and disjunction), this varied cognition regarding varṇas is grounded in the variety of the manifesters (abhivyañjaka), not in the inherent nature (svarūpa) of the varṇas.

Moreover, even one who maintains the distinction of varṇa-individuals must, for the sake of recognition, postulate varṇa-ākṛtis; and in those, an extraneous (paropādhika) cognition of difference must be admitted. Better, then, that on varṇa-individuals themselves the cognition of difference be paropādhika and the recognition svarūpa-grounded — this is lighter in postulation. And this very recognition is the contradicting cognition (bādhaka-pratyaya) of the cognition of difference regarding varṇas. For how, in one and the same time, when many utter, can a single ‘ga’-kāra be at once of many forms — udātta, anudātta, svarita, sānunāsika, niranunāsika? — Or rather, this differential cognition is produced by dhvani (sound), not by the varṇa — so there is no defect. — What then is this dhvani? — It is that which enters the ear-path of one listening from afar, who does not yet make out the distinction of varṇas; and on coming nearer, sets attributes such as paṭu, mṛdu, etc. upon the varṇas. The differences such as udātta etc. are grounded in that, not in the very nature of the varṇas, since the varnas themselves are recognised at every utterance. And on this view, the cognitions of udātta etc. will have a real basis (sālambana). Otherwise (on the alternative view), since the varṇas, being recognised, are without distinction, distinctions like udātta etc. would have to be imagined as produced by saṃyoga and vibhāga; and as saṃyoga and vibhāga are not perceptible, distinctions grounded in them cannot be ascertained on the varṇas — hence these cognitions of udātta etc. would be without object (nirālambana).

Moreover one should not insist thus: that the recognised varṇas should differ owing to differences of udātta etc. For one thing’s difference cannot bring about the difference of another thing that remains unbroken. One does not regard the genus (jāti) as differentiated by the difference of individuals (vyakti). And, since meaning-cognition is possible from the varṇas themselves, the postulation of sphoṭa is purposeless. — If it be said: I do not postulate sphoṭa; I apprehend it directly (pratyakṣam), since on the cognition into which the saṃskāras of grasping each varṇa have been laid, it suddenly flashes — no. For this very cognition too has the varṇas as its content. For this single cognition that comes after the grasping of each varṇa, ‘gauḥ’, has all the varṇas together as its content, not any other content. How is this known? Because in this cognition too the varṇas ‘ga’ etc. recur, not ‘da’ etc. If this cognition were of something other than ‘ga’ etc. …
BS_C01_S03_V28::block-4: Even granting that at every utterance other and other varṇas obtain, still, since varṇa-sāmānyas (universals of varṇas) must be admitted as objects of recognition, the procedure of conveying meaning that has been worked out in the varṇas must be transferred to the sāmānyas. And so, the origination of god-individuals etc. from eternal words is not contradicted. (1.3.28)
BS_C01_S03_V29: And from this very (origination from word follows) eternity. (1.3.29)
BS_C01_S03_V29::block-0: When, by the absence of remembrance of an independent author and the like, the eternity of the Veda is established, the doubt of contradiction with it on the supposition of the origination of god-individuals etc. having been raised, and resolved by ‘from this is the origin (ataḥ prabhavāt)’, that very eternity of the Veda thus established is now strengthened — ‘And from this very (cause), the eternity’. From this very (fact), namely that the world consisting of gods etc. of fixed ākṛti has its origination from the word of the Veda, the eternity of the word of the Veda also is to be understood. So too the mantra-text — ‘By sacrifice they followed the path of speech; they found her, that had entered into the ṛṣis’ (Ṛk Saṃ. 10.71.3) — shows speech as already abiding, only being recovered. And Vedavyāsa too remembers thus — ‘At the end of an age (yuga) the Vedas, hidden, with their itihāsas, the great ṛṣis, granted permission by the Self-existent, attained again of old by tapas’. (1.3.29)
BS_C01_S03_V30: And from sameness of name and form, even in (cosmic) recurrence there is no contradiction, on account of seeing (in śruti) and from smṛti. (1.3.30)
BS_C01_S03_V30::block-0:
It might still be said: pūrvapakṣa — if individuals such as gods, like animal-individuals, were to arise and perish in continuous succession, then, from the unbroken continuity of the conventions of designator, designated, and designators (abhidhāna, abhidheya, abhidhātṛ), the contradiction in regard to the word would be removed by the eternity of the relation. But when the entire trailokya, having put off names and forms, dissolves utterly, and another arises afresh — as the śruti and smṛti texts declare — then how is there no contradiction? — To this we say: ‘from the sameness of name and form (samāna-nāmarūpatva)’. There too the beginninglessness (anāditva) of saṃsāra must be admitted. The ācārya will establish the beginninglessness of saṃsāra at ‘It is reasonable, and is also seen (in śruti)’ (Brahmasūtra 2.1.36). And in beginningless saṃsāra, just as, even where the dissolution and emergence of sleep and waking are heard of, on account of the continuance of activity in the post-waking state matching the pre-sleep, no contradiction arises, so too in the dissolution and emergence of one kalpa and another — this is to be seen.

The dissolution and emergence in sleep and waking are heard — ‘When one asleep does not see any dream, then he becomes one in this Prāṇa alone; then speech, with all names, withdraws into him; the eye, with all forms, withdraws into him; the ear, with all sounds, withdraws into him; the manas, with all dhyānas, withdraws into him. When he awakes, just as from a blazing fire sparks fly forth in all directions, even so from this Self all the prāṇas issue forth to their respective stations; from the prāṇas the gods (sense-organs); from the gods the lokas (their objects)’ (Kauṣ. Up. 3.3).

It may be objected — in sleep, since the dealings of other persons continue without break, and since the one asleep on awakening can connect his pre-sleep dealings, there is no contradiction. But in the great dissolution (mahāpralaya), since all dealings are cut off, and since dealings of an inter-kalpa kind, like dealings of another birth, cannot be re-connected, the case is dissimilar. — Reply: this is no fault. Even at the great dissolution, where all dealings are cut off, by the grace of the Supreme Lord (parameśvarānugrahāt), the lords (īśvaras) such as Hiraṇyagarbha and others have the connecting up of inter-kalpa dealings. Although ordinary creatures (prākṛtāḥ prāṇinaḥ) are not seen to connect dealings of another birth, the lords (īśvaras) need not be like the ordinary. Just as, even where the status as a living being is not different, in the spectrum from man down to a tuft of grass, the obstruction to knowledge and sovereignty is seen to be greater and greater downwards, so among living beings — from man up to Hiraṇyagarbha — the manifestation of knowledge and sovereignty etc. likewise is greater and greater upwards. This is heard repeatedly in śruti and smṛti texts; it cannot be denied as ‘not so’.
