Hence, of the lords such as Hiraṇyagarbha, who in the past kalpa had performed eminent jñāna and karma and who at the beginning of the present kalpa appear, having received the grace of the Supreme Lord, the connecting up of inter-kalpa dealings is reasonable, like that of one awakened from sleep. So says the śruti — ‘He who creates Brahmā in the beginning, and who indeed sends forth the Vedas to him — to that God who illumines my own intellect, do I, desirous of liberation, take refuge’ (Śvet. Up. 6.18). And Śaunaka and others remember — ‘By Madhucchandas etc. as ṛṣis the daśatayī (Ṛksaṃhitā) was seen’ (Śaun. Ṛk-anuk. 4). And for each Veda, similarly, the kāṇḍa-ṛṣis and the like are remembered. The śruti too shows that ritual undertaking with a mantra is preceded by the knowledge of the ṛṣi — ‘He who, with a mantra of which the ṛṣi, metre, deity, and brāhmaṇa are not known, makes another sacrifice, or teaches…’
BS_C01_S03_V31: Jaimini (holds) non-qualification, on account of (qualification) being impossible in (vidyās) such as the madhu-vidyā etc. (1.3.31)
BS_C01_S03_V31::block-0:
Here that which was earlier set forth — that gods etc. too have qualification in brahma-vidyā — is reversed. Jaimini the ācārya holds that gods and the rest are not qualified. Why? On account of impossibility in (vidyās) such as madhu-vidyā etc. For if qualification in brahma-vidyā is admitted, then, since vidyā is not different in kind, qualification would have to be admitted in vidyās such as madhu-vidyā etc. as well; and that is not possible.

How? At ‘Yonder sun is the divine madhu’ (Chānd. Up. 3.1.1), men are to upāsanā the sun by superimposition (adhyāsa) of madhu. But if gods themselves are admitted as upāsakas, what other sun is the sun to upāsanā? Again, after enumerating the five amṛtas — red and the rest — that depend on the sun, and teaching that the five groups of gods, Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, Maruts, and Sādhyas, in turn live upon them, the śruti says: ‘He who knows thus this nectar, becomes one of the Vasus alone, and through Agni as mouth, sees this very nectar, and is satisfied’ (Chānd. Up. 3.6.3) — and so on, showing those who know the nectars on which the Vasus etc. live attaining to the glory of the Vasus and so on. But what other Vasus etc., living on amṛta, will the Vasus and so on themselves know? Or what other glory of the Vasus etc. shall they aspire to obtain?

Likewise — ‘Agni is one foot, Vāyu one foot, the Sun one foot, the directions one foot’; ‘Vāyu indeed is the saṃvarga’ (Chānd. Up. 4.3.1); ‘Āditya is Brahman — this is the teaching’ (Chānd. Up. 3.19.1) — in such upāsanās of deities as the Self, qualification of those very deity-Selves themselves is not possible. So too in ‘These two indeed are Gotama and Bharadvāja; this verily is Gotama, this verily is Bharadvāja’ (Bṛh. Up. 2.2.4) — in such upāsanās connected with ṛṣis, the qualification of those very ṛṣis themselves is not possible. (1.3.31)
BS_C01_S03_V32: And because of (mere) being in the (case of) luminary. ॥ 32 ॥
BS_C01_S03_V32::block-0: [Leading bhāṣya] And on what further ground is there non-eligibility (anadhikāra) for the gods and the rest? —
BS_C01_S03_V32::block-1:
This luminous orb (jyotir-maṇḍala), stationed in the heavenly region (dyu-sthāna), revolving (bambhramat) by means of day and night (ahorātrābhyām), illumines the world; with regard to it the words "Āditya" and the rest, which are designations of deities (devatā-vacanāḥ śabdāḥ), are employed; and this on the strength of common usage in the world (loka-prasiddhi) and on the strength of the established sense in the supplementary portion of the Vedic sentence (vākya-śeṣa-prasiddhi). And it is not possible to comprehend that the luminous orb has any connection with a body (vigraha) endowed with heart and the rest, with sentiency (cetanatā), or with desire and so on (arthitvādi), since it is apprehended as non-sentient (acetana) like clay and the like (mṛd-ādi-vat). By this same (reasoning) Agni and the rest stand explained.

[pūrvapakṣa] Should it be objected: "Since, from the mantras, arthavādas, itihāsa, purāṇa and the world's usage, the possession of bodies (vigrahavattva) and the rest by the gods is apprehended, this defect (of non-eligibility) does not arise"—we reply, no. To begin with, the (mere) world (loka) is not by itself any independent means of valid cognition (svatantra-pramāṇa). It is only an object established by the means of cognition such as perception (pratyakṣa) and the rest, taken without distinguishing examination (avicārita-viśeṣa), that is spoken of as "established by the world" (loka-prasiddha). And here none of the means of cognition such as perception is operative. Itihāsa and purāṇa too, being of human origin (pauruṣeya), require some other means of valid cognition as their root. The arthavādas also, being of one syntactic unity (eka-vākyatva) with the injunction (vidhi) and serving the purpose of eulogy (stutyartha), do not as a separate matter (pārthag-arthya) become a cause for the establishment of bodies and the rest of the gods. Mantras too, applied (viniyukta) by śruti and the like, being concomitant with ritual usage (prayoga-samavāyin) and aimed at expression (abhidhānārtha), are not, as it is declared, a means of valid cognition for any (independent) object. Therefore there is absence of eligibility (adhikārābhāva) for the gods and the rest. ॥ 32 ॥
BS_C01_S03_V33: But (the) being (of eligibility) Bādarāyaṇa (holds), for it is (so). ॥ 33 ॥
BS_C01_S03_V33::block-0:
[siddhānta] The word "tu" ("but") turns aside the prior view (pūrvapakṣa). The ācārya Bādarāyaṇa, however, holds that there is eligibility (adhikārasya bhāva) even for the gods and the rest. Although in the Madhu-vidyā and similar meditations (vidyās) which are intermixed with the deities themselves there is the impossibility of (the deities') being eligible (since they would then have to meditate on their own selves), nevertheless in the pure brahma-vidyā there is the possibility (sambhava). For eligibility depends on desire (arthitva), capacity (sāmarthya), the absence of prohibition (apratiṣedha) and the like. And it is not the case that, simply because somewhere there is impossibility, the eligibility should be denied even where there is possibility. Even among men, eligibility for all the rājasūya and other rites does not arise for all the brāhmaṇas and the rest; the rule (nyāya) that holds there will hold here also. Moreover, with regard to brahma-vidyā, there is found a śrauta indication suggesting the eligibility of gods and the rest — "Whoever among the gods awoke to It, he indeed became That; so among the ṛṣis, so among men" (Bṛ.U. 1.4.10), and "They said: Come, let us seek out that Self, having sought out which Self one obtains all worlds and all desires; Indra (alone) of the gods set forth, and Virocana of the asuras" (Ch.U. 8.7.2), and so forth. There is also the smṛti (evidence such as) the dialogue of Gandharva and Yājñavalkya.

As to what was said, "And because of being in (the case of) luminary" (sūtra 32) — to that we say: even those words such as "Āditya", whose objects are luminaries and the like and which designate deities, convey those several deity-Selves (devatātman) endowed with sentiency (cetanāvat) and lordship (aiśvarya) and the rest, since in mantras, arthavādas and the like, usage proceeds in that manner. There exists indeed in the deities, by reason of (their) lordship, the capacity to abide as the selves of luminaries and the rest, and to assume at will any body whatever. Thus is it heard in the arthavāda of subrahmaṇyā — "Of Medhātithi, the ram" — "Indra, becoming a ram, carried off Medhātithi the Kāṇvāyana" (Ṣaḍviṃśa-Br. 1.1); and it is recorded — "Āditya, becoming a person, approached Kuntī." Even in clay and the rest sentient presiding deities (cetana adhiṣṭhātāraḥ) are admitted, on the strength of "the clay said", "the waters said", and the like. Of luminary and the rest, however, in the elemental aspect (bhūta-dhātu) — that is, the Āditya etc. (qua physical body) — non-sentience is admitted; but the sentient presiding deity-Selves (are admitted), through usage in mantras, arthavādas and the like, as has been stated.

As to what was further said — that mantra and arthavāda, having other purposes (anyārthatva), have no capacity to disclose the body and the rest of the deities — to that we say: cognition or non-cognition (pratyaya-apratyaya) is the cause of the existence or non-existence (sad-bhāva-asad-bhāva) of an object; not its having other purpose or not having other purpose. For one going forth on a different errand, on perceiving on the path a fallen blade of grass or leaf, surely apprehends "this exists." Here it is said: the comparison is unequal. There, perception with respect to the blade of grass and the like has set forth, by which its existence is apprehended. Here, however, in the arthavāda which is for the purpose of eulogy through unitary syntactic relation with the injunctive enunciation (vidhy-uddeśa-eka-vākya-bhāva), there cannot be ascertained any separate engagement (pravṛtti) with the matter as an independent object. For when a great sentence (mahāvākya) conveys the meaning, the subordinate sub-sentence does not have a separate conveying-power. Thus, in the negative sentence "One should not drink surā", from the relation of the three words, only the single sense — the prohibition of drinking surā — is grasped; and not also, from the relation of the two words "surām pibet", an injunction of drinking surā. To this we reply: the comparison is unequal. It is fitting that in "One should not drink surā", because of the unitariness of the syntactical connection, the subordinate sentence-meaning is not grasped. But in (the case of) the injunctive enunciation and the arthavāda, the words occurring in the arthavāda first apprehend a separate connection pertaining to the matter (vṛttānta-viṣaya), and only thereafter, as required by the question "to what end?" (kaimarthya), do they take up — willingly — the eulogising of the injunction. Thus, in "One desirous of prosperity should offer a white (animal) to Vāyu" — there the words "vāyavya" etc., occurring in the injunctive enunciation, are connected with the injunction; not so the words "Vāyu indeed is the swiftest deity; one approaches Vāyu by his own offering portion; he indeed leads him to prosperity" — the words occurring in the arthavāda. For we do not have "One should offer to Vāyu" or "one should offer to the swiftest deity", and so on. Rather, having apprehended a subordinate (avāntara) connection by way of the recital of the natural character of Vāyu, they thus eulogise the injunction (saying) "this rite has such-and-such deity". Therefore, where that subordinate sentence-meaning is the sphere of another means of cognition (pramāṇāntara), there the arthavāda proceeds by way of restatement (anuvāda) of it. Where it is contradictory to another means of cognition, there it proceeds by way of figurative description (guṇavāda). Where, however, both these are absent — there the question is whether, on account of the absence of any other means of cognition, it should be a guṇavāda; or whether, on account of the non-contradiction with any other means of cognition, it should be a statement of (an actually) existing thing (vidyamāna-vāda). Those who take cognition (pratīti) as their refuge should resort to the vidyamāna-vāda, not the guṇavāda. By this very (reasoning) the mantra (case) too is explained. Moreover, by the very injunctions enjoining oblations consecrated to Indra and other deities, the proper form (sva-rūpa) of Indra and the rest is required. For Indra and the rest, devoid of (any) proper form, cannot be raised in the mind (cetasi āropayitum); and to a deity not raised in the mind oblation cannot be offered. And (the śruti) declares — "Of whichever deity the oblation has been taken, on her one should meditate while about to utter Vaṣaṭ" (Ait. Br. 3.8.1); and a mere word cannot be the proper form of a thing, since word and thing are different. Therefore, that proper form of Indra and the rest which is apprehended in mantra and arthavāda — that, of such a kind, it is not proper to dismiss by means of (mere) verbal authority. Itihāsa and purāṇa too, by the path explained, having mantra and arthavāda as their possible source, are competent to establish the body and the rest of the deities. They are also possible as having perception and the rest as their source. For what is non-perceptible to us is perceptible to those of olden times. Thus it is recorded that Vyāsa and the rest have direct dealings with gods and the like. As for one who would say — that just as for those of the present day, so for the men of old too, there is no capacity to deal with gods and the rest...
BS_C01_S03_V34: Grief is his (i.e. arises in him), from the hearing of the disregard of him, and from running towards that, it is hinted at; for it is so. ॥ 34 ॥
BS_C01_S03_V34::block-0:
[Introduction] Just as the rule restricting eligibility (adhikāra-niyama) to men was set aside and eligibility for the gods and the rest in vidyās was declared, so likewise, by way of an exception (apavāda) to the rule restricting eligibility to the twice-born (dvijāti), there might be eligibility for the śūdra also — to ward off this very doubt, this section (adhikaraṇa) is begun. There, to begin with, the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) is reached: there is eligibility for the śūdra also; because of the possibility of (his having) desire (arthitva) and capacity (sāmarthya); because, unlike "Therefore the śūdra is unfit for sacrifice" (Tai. Saṃ. 7.1.1.6), no prohibition like "the śūdra is unfit for vidyā" is heard. And as for the absence of fire (anagnitva) which is a cause of non-eligibility for the śūdra in (Vedic) rites, that is no indicatory mark (liṅga) cancelling eligibility for vidyās. For it is not the case that without the āhavanīya and other (fires) the vidyā cannot be known. There is also a śrauta liṅga reinforcing the śūdra's eligibility. For in the Saṃvarga-vidyā, the śruti refers to Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa, who was eager to listen, by the word "śūdra" — "Aha hāre tvā śūdra, may that (wealth) along with the cows remain with you alone" (Ch.U. 4.2.3). Vidura and others, although born of śūdra wombs, are remembered as endowed with distinguished knowledge. Therefore the śūdra is eligible for the vidyās — when this prima facie view is reached, we say:

[siddhānta] The śūdra has no eligibility, because of the absence of Vedic study (vedādhyayana). For only one who has studied the Veda, knowing the Veda's meaning, is eligible for the matters of Vedic meaning. And there is no Vedic study for the śūdra, because Vedic study is preceded by upanayana, and upanayana pertains to (only) the three varṇas. As for the desire (arthitva), it is not a cause of eligibility in the absence of capacity. Nor is mere worldly capacity by itself a cause of eligibility, since in a śāstric matter śāstric capacity is required. And the śāstric capacity stands set aside by the setting aside of (Vedic) study. And as for "the śūdra is unfit for sacrifice" — that, since it has the rule (nyāya) as its basis, indicates non-fitness in vidyā too, the rule being common (sādhāraṇa). As for the hearing of the word "śūdra" in the Saṃvarga-vidyā, which you took as a liṅga — that is no liṅga, since there is no rule (nyāya). For only when there is a stated rule does the seeing of an indicatory mark (liṅga-darśana) become indicative. And here there is no rule. And, granted, this word "śūdra" might make the śūdra eligible only in this single Saṃvarga-vidyā, since that is its scope; not in all the vidyās. But, since it occurs in an arthavāda, it is not capable of making the śūdra eligible anywhere at all. And this word "śūdra" can be construed as having the eligible (kṣatriya) for its object. How? It is gathered thus — to Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa, who had heard, from the speech of the swans (haṃsa-vākya), "How indeed do you, sir, speak of him, such (a great person) as he is, like Raikva of the cart?" (Ch.U. 4.1.3) — this disregard of himself, there arose grief (śuk). The ṛṣi Raikva indicated him by this word "śūdra" in order to declare his own knowledge of the remote (parokṣa-jñatā). Because the one who is a śūdra by birth (jāti-śūdra) has no eligibility. How then is the grief that has arisen indicated by the word "śūdra"? It is replied — by his running towards (it) — "he ran towards grief", or "he was overrun by grief", or "he ran towards Raikva by means of grief" — hence śūdra; because the etymological sense (avayava-artha) is possible (śucā ādravaṇāt), and because the conventional sense (rūḍhi-artha) is impossible. And this sense is seen (to be borne out) in this very narrative (ākhyāyikā). ॥ 34 ॥
BS_C01_S03_V35: And from the recognition of (his) being a kṣatriya, in the latter (passage), through (his association with) the Caitraratha, from the indicatory mark. ॥ 35 ॥
BS_C01_S03_V35::block-0: And on this further ground Jānaśruti is not a born śūdra (jāti-śūdra): the reason being that, by examination of the context (prakaraṇa-nirūpaṇa), his being a kṣatriya is gathered from the indicatory mark of his being mentioned together (samabhivyāhāra) in the latter (portion) with Abhipratārin Caitrarathi, who is a kṣatriya. For in the latter passage, in the supplementary portion of the Saṃvarga-vidyā, Caitrarathi Abhipratārin is mentioned as a kṣatriya — "Then a brahmacārin begged of Śaunaka Kāpeya and Abhipratārin Kākṣaseni, who were being served (a meal)" (Ch.U. 4.3.5). And Abhipratārin's being a Caitrarathi is to be apprehended from his connection with the Kāpeyas; for the connection of Citraratha with the Kāpeyas is established — "By this (rite) the Kāpeyas caused Citraratha to perform sacrifice" (Tāṇḍya Br. 20.12.5). And those who sacrifice for those of one lineage (samāna-anvaya) are themselves generally of one lineage. And from "Therefore there was born a single kṣatra-pati named Caitrarathi" — from the apprehension of his being a kṣatra-pati, his being a kṣatriya is to be gathered. The mention of Jānaśruti together with that kṣatriya Abhipratārin in a single (common) vidyā suggests Jānaśruti's being a kṣatriya as well. For mention together generally pertains to those of equal (status). The apprehension of Jānaśruti's being a kṣatriya is also gained from his connection with the lordship (aiśvarya) of dispatching kṣattṛs and the like. Hence the śūdra has no eligibility. ॥ 35 ॥
BS_C01_S03_V36: Because of the reference to saṃskāras (purificatory rites) and because of the declaration of their absence (in the case of the śūdra). ॥ 36 ॥
BS_C01_S03_V36::block-0: And on this further ground there is no eligibility for the śūdra: that in the contexts of vidyās the saṃskāras such as upanayana and the rest are referred to — "Him he initiated" (Śat. Br. 11.5.3.13), "Reverend sir, teach me — saying so he approached" (Ch.U. 7.1.1), "Devoted to Brahman, established in Brahman, seeking the supreme Brahman, (saying) 'this revered one will declare all that' — they, with fuel in hand, approached the revered Pippalāda" (Pra.U. 1.1) — and so on. Even from "Without initiating them at all" (Ch.U. 5.11.7), it is clearly indicated that initiation (upanayana) is the (normal) rule. And the absence of saṃskāra for the śūdra is declared, because of the smṛti "The śūdra is the fourth varṇa, of one birth (eka-jāti)" (Manu Smṛ. 10.4); and because of "There is no sin in the śūdra, nor is he fit for saṃskāra" (Manu Smṛ. 10.126), and the like. ॥ 36 ॥
BS_C01_S03_V37: And because, when the absence of that (śūdra-status) was ascertained, (the teacher) proceeded (to initiate). ॥ 37 ॥
BS_C01_S03_V37::block-0: And on this further ground there is no eligibility for the śūdra: that, when by truthful speech the absence of śūdra-hood (śūdratva-abhāva) was ascertained, Gautama proceeded to initiate and instruct Jābāla — "This (truthfulness) one who is not a brāhmaṇa cannot speak; bring fuel, dear; I shall initiate you, since you have not departed from truth" (Ch.U. 4.4.5) — from the indicatory mark in the śruti. ॥ 37 ॥
BS_C01_S03_V38: And because of the prohibition, in smṛti, of (his) hearing, study and (engagement in) the meaning of (the Veda). ॥ 38 ॥
BS_C01_S03_V38::block-0: And on this further ground there is no eligibility for the śūdra: that for him there is, in the smṛti, the prohibition of hearing, study, and the meaning (i.e. application). The prohibition of hearing the Veda, the prohibition of studying the Veda, and the prohibition of knowing and acting on its meaning is recorded for the śūdra. As for the prohibition of hearing — "Then for him who overhears the Veda, the (penalty is) filling up the ears with tin and lac"; and "This śūdra is a moving cremation-ground; therefore one should not study near a śūdra." Hence also the prohibition of study. For one near whom one should not study, how shall he, the unheard-of one, study? And there is also "For uttering the Veda, the cutting of the tongue; for retaining (it), the cutting of the body" (Gautama Dh. Sū. 2.3.4). Hence also, by implication, there is the prohibition of knowing and acting on the meaning — "One should not give counsel (concerning dharma) to a śūdra" (Manu Smṛ. 4.80), and "Of the twice-born are study, sacrifice, and giving (of gifts)" (Gautama Dh. Sū. 2.1.1). For those, however, in whom — like Vidura, Dharmavyādha and the rest — knowledge arises by virtue of saṃskāras done in former (births), the obtaining of the fruit cannot be prohibited; for knowledge is unfailingly fruitful (ekāntika-phala). And from "One should make (it) heard by the four varṇas" (Mahābh. 12.327.49), there is the smṛti of the eligibility of the four varṇas in the knowing of itihāsa and purāṇa. But for the śūdras there is no eligibility based on (the study of) the Veda — this stands established. ॥ 38 ॥
BS_C01_S03_V39::block-0:
[Introduction] The incidental discussion of eligibility (prāsaṅgika adhikāra-vicāra) is concluded. We shall now bring forward the very investigation of the meaning of the (originally) intended sentences. "All this whatsoever, the world, having issued forth, trembles in the prāṇa. (It is) a great fear, an upraised thunderbolt; those who know This become immortal" (Kaṭha U. 2.3.2) — this sentence has been pointed out by following up the meaning of the root "ej", which means "trembling" ("ejṛ kampane"). In this sentence it is heard that all this world, depending on prāṇa, throbs (spandate); that something great, the cause of fear, called "vajra" (thunderbolt), stands raised; and that from the knowledge of It comes the attainment of immortality. There, since there is non-comprehension as to who that prāṇa is and what that fearful thunderbolt is, when an investigation is undertaken, the prima facie position is reached: by common usage (prasiddhi), the five-functioned vāyu (pañca-vṛtti vāyu) is prāṇa. And by usage itself, the lightning-bolt (aśani) would be the vajra. And here the greatness of vāyu is being recited. How? All this world, established in the five-functioned vāyu called "prāṇa", trembles. And it is by reason of the vāyu that the great fearful thunderbolt is raised. For when vāyu transforms (vivartamāna) as the rain-cloud, lightning, thunder, rain and lightning-bolt are seen to evolve, as is declared. And from the knowledge of vāyu alone is this immortality. So another śruti — "Vāyu indeed is the (separate) distribution (vyaṣṭi); vāyu is the aggregate (samaṣṭi); he conquers re-death who knows thus." Therefore vāyu is to be apprehended here — when this prima facie position is reached, we say:

[siddhānta] It is Brahman alone that is to be apprehended here. How? From considering the prior and subsequent (passages). For in the prior and subsequent textual portions we find Brahman alone being indicated. How here, suddenly, in the middle, could we understand vāyu as being indicated? In the prior (passage), to begin with, Brahman is indicated by "That alone is the bright (śukra), that is Brahman, that alone is called the immortal; on it all worlds are based, and none transcends it" (Kaṭha U. 2.3.1). That same (Brahman) is indicated here too, from proximity (sannidhāna), and from the recognition of (the same characteristic of) being the support of the worlds (loka-āśrayatva-pratyabhijñāna), in "All this world trembles in prāṇa". The word "prāṇa" too is employed in the supreme Self alone, as is seen in "the prāṇa of the prāṇa" (Bṛ.U. 4.4.18). The character of being the cause of trembling (ejayitṛtva) too is fitting only for the supreme Self, not for mere vāyu. Thus it is said — "Not by prāṇa, nor by apāna does any mortal live; but by another do they live, on which these two depend" (Kaṭha U. 2.2.5). In the subsequent (passage) too, "Through fear of It fire blazes; through fear (of It) the sun blazes; through fear (of It) Indra and Vāyu (act); and Death, the fifth, runs" (Kaṭha U. 2.3.3) — Brahman alone is indicated, not vāyu, since the world together with vāyu is declared to fear It. That same is indicated here too, from proximity, and from the recognition of (the same characteristic of) being the cause of fear (bhaya-hetutva) in "a great fear, an upraised thunderbolt". The word "vajra" too is employed by the commonness of being a cause of fear. For just as one acts under the rule of a king and the rest by the fear "the upraised thunderbolt should fall on my head if I do not carry out his command", so too this world consisting of fire, vāyu, sun and the rest, fearing this very Brahman, acts in its own functions under rule — hence Brahman is fearful, likened to the thunderbolt. So another śruti regarding Brahman — "Through fear of It Vāyu blows; through fear (of It) the sun rises; through fear of It fire and Indra; and Death, the fifth, runs" (Tai.U. 2.8.1). And from the hearing of immortality as the fruit, it is also gathered that this is Brahman alone. For from the knowledge of Brahman comes the attainment of immortality, as in the mantra-text "Knowing Him alone one passes beyond death; there is no other path for going (to liberation, mokṣa)" (Śve. U. 6.15). As for the immortality which is somewhere said to come from the knowledge of vāyu, that is relative (āpekṣika). For there itself, in another passage, after declaring the supreme Self, the perishability (ārta-tva) of vāyu and the rest is stated in "Other than this is suffering" (Bṛ.U. 3.4.2). From the context (prakaraṇa) too, here, the determination is of the supreme Self. For the question is asked concerning the supreme Self — "That which you see (as) other than dharma, other than adharma, other than what is done and not done, other than the past and the future — tell That" (Kaṭha U. 1.2.14). ॥ 39 ॥
BS_C01_S03_V40: (It is Brahman that is meant by) jyotis (light), because (Brahman) is seen (to be the topic). ॥ 40 ॥
BS_C01_S03_V40::block-0: It is heard (in the śruti): "This serene one (samprasāda), having risen up from this body and having attained the supreme jyotis (light), manifests in his own form" (Chā. Up. 8.12.3). Here a doubt is raised — does the word jyotis denote the well-known luminous (tejas) which dispels darkness, the object of the eye, or does it denote the supreme Brahman? What, then, is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa)? The well-known luminous (tejas) is what is denoted by the word jyotis. On what ground? Because the word jyotis is conventionally fixed (rūḍha) in that meaning. In the case of "jyotiścaraṇābhidhānāt" (Br. Sū. 1.1.24), the word jyotis abandons its own primary meaning and stands for Brahman owing to the prakaraṇa (contextual indication); but here no such reason for abandoning its own meaning is seen. Likewise in the section on the nāḍīs — "And when he departs from this body, then he ascends upwards by these very rays" (Chā. Up. 8.6.5) — the attainment of the sun by the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu) is declared. Therefore the word jyotis means only the well-known luminous (tejas). When this is the position arrived at, we reply —
BS_C01_S03_V40::block-1: The word jyotis denotes the supreme Brahman alone. Why? Because of darśana — because Brahman is seen (to be the contextual subject). For in this prakaraṇa the continued reference (anuvṛtti) of Brahman as the topic to be expounded is observed; for at the beginning of the section "That Self, free from sin" (Chā. Up. 8.7.1) — the Ātman characterized by the qualities such as freedom from sin and the rest is announced (pratijñā) as that which is to be sought after (anveṣṭavya) and to be inquired into (vijijñāsitavya); and the connecting words "This very same I shall expound to you again" (Chā. Up. 8.9.3) confirm the continuity. And because the attaining of the jyotis is here explained as the attaining of the bodiless state — "Verily, while one is bodiless, pleasure and pain do not touch him" (Chā. Up. 8.12.1); and because the bodiless state cannot be established anywhere except in the state of being Brahman. The qualifications "the supreme jyotis" and "He is the supreme Person" (Chā. Up. 8.12.3) also confirm this. As for the objection that the attainment of the sun was declared for the seeker of liberation — that is not the absolute (ātyantika) mokṣa, since it is connected with going (gati) and departure (utkrānti). For in the absolute mokṣa there is neither going nor departing — this we shall establish later. ॥ 40 ॥
BS_C01_S03_V41: ākāśa (in the text) is (Brahman) because of the designation as something other (than name and form) and the like. ॥ 41 ॥
BS_C01_S03_V41::block-0: It is heard (in the śruti): "That which is called ākāśa is the bearer (nirvahitṛ) of name and form (nāmarūpa); that within which they are is Brahman, that is the immortal, that is the Ātman" (Chā. Up. 8.14.1). Here, in the inquiry whether the word ākāśa denotes the supreme Brahman or the well-known elemental ākāśa, (the pūrvapakṣa is) — the acceptance of the (elemental) bhūta is appropriate, because the word ākāśa is conventionally fixed (rūḍha) in that meaning; and because the bearing (nirvahaṇa) of name and form can be ascribed to it through its providing space (avakāśadāna); and because no clear mark (liṅga) of Brahman such as creatorship is heard here. When this is the position arrived at, we declare —
BS_C01_S03_V41::block-1: It is the supreme Brahman alone that the word ākāśa here is fit to denote. Why? Because of the designation as something other (than name and form) and the like (arthāntaratva-ādi-vyapadeśāt). For "that within which they are — that is Brahman" — thus the text designates ākāśa as something other than name and form. And nothing other than Brahman can be other than name and form, because the entire mass of effects (vikāra) has been differentiated (vyākṛta) by name and form themselves. Nor can the unrestricted (niraṅkuśa) bearing of name and form be in anything other than Brahman, since it is heard to be the act of Brahman — "Having entered (the elements) by means of this jīva-Ātman, let me differentiate name and form" (Chā. Up. 6.3.2). One may object: even for the jīva there is directly perceptible bearing of names and forms. Granted, there is. But here non-difference (abheda — between jīva and Brahman) is what is intended to be conveyed. By the very statement of the bearing of name and form, the marks (liṅgas) of Brahman such as creatorship are stated. "That is Brahman, that is the immortal, that is the Ātman" (Chā. Up. 8.14.1) — these are the marks of the Brahman-doctrine (brahmavāda). This is merely the elaboration (prapañca) of the (earlier) sūtra "ākāśas tal-liṅgāt" (Br. Sū. 1.1.22). ॥ 41 ॥
BS_C01_S03_V42: (The supreme Lord is meant) because of the designation as different (from the embodied self) in deep sleep (suṣupti) and at departure (utkrānti). ॥ 42 ॥
BS_C01_S03_V42::block-0: "Vyapadeśāt" continues (from the previous sūtra). In the sixth prapāṭhaka of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka, beginning with "Which is the Ātman? — That puruṣa here who, made of vijñāna, is amid the prāṇas, the inner light within the heart" (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.7), an extensive elaboration on the topic of the Ātman is made. There the doubt arises — is the passage simply intended to expound the nature of the transmigrating self (saṁsārin), or is it intended to set forth the nature of that which transcends transmigration (asaṁsārin)? What, then, is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa)? It is solely concerned with the nature of the saṁsārin. On what ground? From the opening (upakrama) and the conclusion (upasaṁhāra). At the upakrama, "That puruṣa here, made of vijñāna, amid the prāṇas" — by the mark of the embodied (śārīra). And at the upasaṁhāra, "Verily this great unborn Ātman is this very one made of vijñāna amid the prāṇas" (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.22) — that very same is not abandoned. In the middle too, by the introduction of the states such as the waking state (buddhānta), only that same (saṁsārin) is elaborated. When this is the position arrived at, we reply —
BS_C01_S03_V42::block-1: This passage is solely intended to teach the supreme Lord (parameśvara), not merely to expound the embodied self. Why? Because in deep sleep (suṣupti) and at departure (utkrānti), the supreme Lord is designated as different from the embodied self. In suṣupti — "This puruṣa, embraced by the prājña-Ātman, knows nothing without nor within" (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.21) — the supreme Lord is designated as different from the embodied self. There the puruṣa would be the embodied self (śārīra), since the cognizership belongs to him; and since on the contingency of cognizing the outer and the inner, the negation of that becomes possible. The prājña is the supreme Lord, since (he is) eternally unseparated from the prajñā which is of the nature of omniscience. So too at departure — "This embodied Ātman, mounted upon by the prājña-Ātman, departs sending forth (groans)" (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.35) — the supreme Lord is designated as different from the jīva. There too the embodied (śārīra) would be the jīva, since he is the owner of the body. The prājña indeed is the supreme Lord himself. Therefore, since in suṣupti and utkrānti the designation is by way of difference, it is understood that the supreme Lord alone is intended here. As to what was said — that owing to the marks of the embodied at the beginning, end, and middle, the passage purports the saṁsārin — to this we reply: at the upakrama, by "That puruṣa here, made of vijñāna, amid the prāṇas," the nature of the saṁsārin is not what is meant to be conveyed — what then? — having referred to the nature of the saṁsārin, his identity (ekatā) with the supreme Brahman is meant to be conveyed. For from "He meditates as it were, he moves as it were" onwards, the subsequent text is seen to be devoted to the negation of the attributes of the saṁsārin. Likewise at the upasaṁhāra, the text concludes precisely as it began — "Verily this great unborn Ātman is this very one made of vijñāna amid the prāṇas." The meaning is: this very one made of vijñāna amid the prāṇas, who is apparently the saṁsārin, has been by us expounded as the great unborn Ātman, the supreme Lord himself. As for the one who, on account of the introduction of the states such as the waking state (buddhānta) in the middle, supposes that the nature of the saṁsārin is intended — he, when started toward the east, would also be made to settle in the west! For by the introduction of the states such as the waking state, neither the having-of-states nor the saṁsāritva is what is meant — what then? — the absence of states (avasthārahitatva) and the absence of saṁsāritva. How is this understood? From the fact that step by step (the disciple) asks — "From beyond this, teach me only liberation" (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.14); and step by step (the teacher) replies — "He is not followed by that, for this puruṣa is unattached (asaṅga)" (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.15); and "He is not followed by merit, not followed by demerit; verily then he has crossed all the sorrows of the heart" (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.22). Therefore it is to be understood that this passage is solely devoted to setting forth the nature of that which transcends transmigration (asaṁsārin). ॥ 42 ॥
BS_C01_S03_V43: (The supreme Lord is meant) on account of the words "pati" (lord) and the like. ॥ 43 ॥
BS_C01_S03_V43::block-0: From this also it is to be understood that this passage is solely devoted to the exposition of the nature of that which transcends transmigration (asaṁsārin); since in this passage the words "pati" and the rest are devoted to expounding the nature of the asaṁsārin and to the negation of the nature of the saṁsārin. "He is the controller of all, the ruler of all, the overlord of all" — words of this kind are devoted to the exposition of the nature of the asaṁsārin. "He does not become greater by good karma, nor lesser by evil karma" — words of this kind are negations of the nature of the saṁsārin. Therefore it is understood that the asaṁsārin, the supreme Lord (parameśvara), is the one taught here. ॥ 43 ॥
BS_C01_S04_INTRO1::block-0: Having promised the inquiry into Brahman (brahmajijñāsā), the lakṣaṇa of Brahman has been stated — "That from which the origination etc. of this (world proceeds)" (Br. Sū. 1.1.2). The doubt that this lakṣaṇa might be common to pradhāna also was negated on the ground that pradhāna is not based on any śabda (scriptural word) — "īkṣater nāśabdam" (Br. Sū. 1.1.5). And it has been elaborated by the preceding text (granthena) that the uniformity of import (gati-sāmānya) of all the Vedānta-vākyas is toward the doctrine that Brahman is the cause (kāraṇa) and not toward the doctrine that pradhāna is the cause. But this much remains now to be raised — that the statement that pradhāna is not based on śabda is not established (asiddha), since in some recensions (śākhās) words are heard which appear to point to the pradhāna. Hence the causality of pradhāna is well established by the Veda itself, and has been accepted by the great supreme ṛṣis (paramarṣis) such as Kapila and others — this is the unwelcome consequence (prasaṅga). So long as the import of those words as referring to something else (anyaparatva) is not established, the position already settled — that the omniscient Brahman is the cause of the world — would itself be confused. Hence in order to show that those words have a different import, the next section of the text proceeds. ॥
BS_C01_S04_V01: If it be said that the inferred (entity, i.e. pradhāna) is also (referred to) in some (recensions) — no; for the grasp (of the word avyakta) is in connection with what is placed in the metaphor of the body (śarīra-rūpaka), and (the text) shows (this). ॥ 1 ॥
BS_C01_S04_V01::block-0: (Objection): The inferred (ānumānika) — that is, what is established by inference — namely the pradhāna, is found word-wise (śabdavat) in some recensions of śākhās. For in the Kāṭhaka it is read — "Beyond the mahat is the avyakta; beyond the avyakta is the puruṣa" (Ka. Up. 1.3.11). There the very same mahat, avyakta, and puruṣa, of the very same names and in the very same order as are well known in smṛti (the Sāṁkhya tradition), are recognized (pratyabhijñāyante) here. Among them, by "avyakta" — owing to the fame of the term in smṛti, and because the etymological derivation "that which is not vyakta (manifest) — being devoid of sound and the like — is avyakta" is possible — what is intended is the pradhāna well known in smṛti. Hence, since pradhāna has śabda-support, its non-being-in-śabda (aśabdatva) is untenable. And it itself is the cause of the world — by the establishment of śruti, smṛti, and reasoning (nyāya) — if so, no, this is not so. For this Kāṭhaka passage is not concerned with affirming the existence of mahat and avyakta as understood in smṛti. For here that which is recognized is not a pradhāna of the kind well known in smṛti — namely independent (svatantra), the cause, possessed of three guṇas. Only the bare word "avyakta" is recognized here. And that word, being yaugika (etymological) — "that which is not vyakta is avyakta" — is applied to anything else also that is subtle and very difficult to discern. Nor is it conventionally fixed (rūḍha) on anything in particular. As for the conventional fixity (rūḍhi) which the pradhāna-vādins assume, it is merely their technical usage (pāribhāṣikī), and does not have causal status in determining the meaning of the Veda. Nor does the mere similarity of order (krama) bring about the apprehension of identical meaning, in the absence of recognition of that same form. For one who, on seeing a cow in a horse-stable, is not deluded does not conclude "this is a horse." When the prakaraṇa is examined here, no pradhāna as imagined by others is apprehended, owing to the grasp (gṛhīti) of what is placed in the metaphor of the body (śarīra-rūpaka). For here the body, which has been laid down in the metaphor of the chariot (ratha-rūpaka), is grasped by the word "avyakta." On what ground? On the ground of prakaraṇa and pariśeṣa (residual elimination). For the immediately preceding text shows the imagery (kḷpti) of the chariot-rider (rathin), the chariot, etc., for the Ātman, body, and so forth — "Know the Ātman as the chariot-rider, the body verily as the chariot; know the buddhi as the charioteer, and the manas as the reins" (Ka. Up. 1.3.3); "They call the indriyas the horses, the viṣayas (objects) their pasture-grounds; the wise call the Ātman, joined with indriyas and manas, the enjoyer" (Ka. Up. 1.3.4). And having shown that by these — when the indriyas etc. are unrestrained — one attains saṁsāra, but when restrained one attains the further shore of the path, the supreme abode of Viṣṇu (tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṁ padam), then in answer to the expectancy as to what that further shore of the path, the supreme abode of Viṣṇu, is, he shows the Paramātman, beyond those very same indriyas etc., as the further shore of the path, the supreme abode of Viṣṇu — "Beyond the indriyas verily are the objects (arthas); beyond the objects is the manas; beyond the manas is the buddhi; beyond the buddhi is the great Ātman (mahān). Beyond the mahat is the avyakta; beyond the avyakta is the puruṣa; beyond the puruṣa there is nothing — that is the culmination, that is the supreme goal" (Ka. Up. 1.3.10–11). There, the very same indriyas etc., which were originally introduced in the previous chariot-metaphor as horses and the rest, are themselves grasped here, in order to avoid abandoning what is contextually current (prakṛta) and introducing what is not contextual (aprakṛta-prakriyā). There, indriya, manas, and buddhi are the same words in the previous (verse) and here. As for the arthas — those śabdas etc., the viṣayas, which were referred to as the pasture of the indriya-horses — their being beyond the indriyas (is established because) the indriyas are graha (the seizers) and the viṣayas atigraha (super-seizers), as known from śruti. The manas is beyond the viṣayas, since the activity of viṣayas and indriyas is rooted in the manas. Beyond the manas is the buddhi — for the buddhi…
BS_C01_S04_V02: But (it is) the subtle (sūkṣma — i.e. the body in its subtle, causal state that is meant by avyakta), because of fitness for that (designation). ॥ 2 ॥
BS_C01_S04_V02::block-0: It has been said that, by prakaraṇa and pariśeṣa, the body is what is meant by the word avyakta, not the pradhāna. Now this doubt is raised — how is the body fit for the term avyakta, when, on the contrary, this body is gross (sthūla) and so is more than evident, fit for the term "vyakta," while the term "avyakta" denotes what is unmanifest? Hence the reply is given — sūkṣmaṁ tu — here it is the body in its causal nature (kāraṇātmanā) that is intended to be expressed; for the subtle is fit for the term avyakta. Although this gross body is not by itself fit for the term avyakta, nevertheless its initiating cause — the subtle bhūta (bhūta-sūkṣma) — is fit for the term avyakta. The word denoting the prakṛti (cause) is seen to be applied to the vikāra (effect) — as in "Refresh the vexed one with the cows" (Ṛk Saṁ. 9.46.4 — where "cows" denotes products of cows). And śruti — "Verily this was then unevolved (avyākṛta)" (Bṛ. Up. 1.4.7) — shows that this very world, which is later differentiated into name and form (vyākṛta-nāmarūpa-vibhinna), in its prior state, having abandoned the differentiated name and form and remaining in the state of bīja-śakti (the power of the seed), is fit for the term avyakta. ॥ 2 ॥
BS_C01_S04_V03: (That prior state of the world is) meaningful (i.e. real and admissible), since it is dependent on Him (the supreme Lord). ॥ 3 ॥
BS_C01_S04_V03::block-0: Here the objector says: If this world, with name and form unmanifested, in the seed-state (bīja-ātmaka) of its prior condition, is admitted as fit for the term avyakta, and if the body too — taken under that aspect — is declared to be fit for the term avyakta, then thereby the very pradhāna-kāraṇa-vāda would result; for this very prior state of the world has been accepted (by us) as the pradhāna. To this we reply: If we accepted some self-existent (svatantra) prior state as the cause of the world, then we should be involving ourselves in the pradhāna-kāraṇa-vāda. But by us this prior state of the world is admitted as dependent on the supreme Lord (parameśvara-adhīnā), not as svatantra. And it must necessarily be admitted; for it is meaningful (arthavatī). For without it the supreme Lord's creatorship would not be established, since for one devoid of śakti (power), pravṛtti (initiating activity) is impossible. And the non-rebirth of the liberated (would not be established). On what ground? Because by vidyā (true knowledge) the dāha (burning up) of that bīja-śakti (takes place). For this avidyātmika bīja-śakti (the seed-power constituted of avidyā), denoted by the word avyakta, supported on the supreme Lord (parameśvara-āśrayā), māyāmayī (constituted of māyā), is the great deep sleep (mahāsuṣupti) — wherein the saṁsārin jīvas, devoid of awareness of their own essential nature, lie sleeping. This very same avyakta is in some places denoted by the word ākāśa — "In this very imperishable, O Gārgī, the ākāśa is woven, warp and woof" (Bṛ. Up. 3.8.11), as śruti says; in some places it is uttered by the word akṣara — "Beyond the akṣara is what is higher" (Mu. Up. 2.1.2), as śruti says; in some places it is hinted by the term māyā — "Know māyā as prakṛti, and the wielder of māyā as the great Lord" (Śv. Up. 4.10), in the very mantra. For māyā is avyakta — since its tattvānyatva (whether it is identical or different from Brahman) is unable to be determined. Such is what is said in "Beyond the mahat is the avyakta" — when the buddhi pertaining to Hiraṇyagarbha is mahat, that mahat originates from the avyakta. When the jīva is mahat, even then, since the state of being a jīva is dependent on the avyakta, it is said that the avyakta is beyond the mahat. For avidyā is avyakta. It is by virtue of being possessed of avidyā (avidyāvattvena) that all the dealings of the jīva continue uninterruptedly. And that beyond-ness which pertains to the avyakta is, by way of figurative non-difference (abheda-upacāra), imposed on its effect, the body. Even though the indriyas etc. are likewise effects (vikāras) just as the body, the grasping by the word avyakta is of the body alone, by way of the abheda-upacāra, since the indriyas etc. are taken by their own respective words, and the body alone is left over (pariśiṣṭa).
BS_C01_S04_V03::block-1: Others, however, explain thus — the body is of two kinds, gross (sthūla) and subtle (sūkṣma); gross — that which is here perceived; subtle — that which will be spoken of later, in "In attaining a different (body), it goes embraced (by the subtle elements), as is shown by the question and the answer" (Br. Sū. 3.1.1). Both these bodies, without distinction, were referred to in the previous text as the chariot. Here, however, the subtle is grasped by the word avyakta, since the subtle is fit for the term avyakta; and since on it depends the dealings of bondage and liberation, it is beyond the jīva. Just as, owing to the dependence of the activity of indriyas on objects, the objects are beyond the indriyas. To them, this is to be said — since both bodies were referred to as the chariot in the previous text without distinction, and since both are equally prakṛta (contextually current) and pariśiṣṭa (residual), how is only the subtle body grasped here, and not also the gross? If it be said: we are competent to apprehend the meaning of what is recited, but not to question what is recited; and the recited word avyakta is competent to expound only the subtle, not the other, since it is vyakta — to that we reply: no. Because the apprehension of meaning is dependent on construing the passages as one (eka-vākyatā). For these previous and subsequent passages, recited together, do not, without falling into the unity of statement, expound any meaning; otherwise the contingency of abandoning what is contextually current and introducing what is not contextual would arise. And without expectancy (ākāṅkṣā) there is no apprehension of unity-of-statement (ekavākyatā). There, when the expectancy is the same regarding the grasp-ability (grāhyatva) of both bodies, if the connection is not admitted as the expectancy demands, the very ekavākyatā is undermined — whence the apprehension of the meaning of what is recited? Nor is this to be supposed — that since the subtle body is hard to purify, only it is here grasped, while the gross — being seen to be revolting and easy to purify — is not grasped. For here no purification of anything is intended to be conveyed. There is no statement here enjoining purification. By being immediately referred to, what is intended to be conveyed here is — what is that supreme abode of Viṣṇu? For having said "this is beyond that, this is beyond that," the text declares "beyond the puruṣa there is nothing." Even in any case, since the negation of the inferred (ānumānika — pradhāna) is established, let it be so as you wish; nothing of ours is broken thereby. ॥ 3 ॥
BS_C01_S04_V04: And because it is not stated to be an object of knowledge.
BS_C01_S04_V04::block-0: The Sāṅkhyas, on their part, do remember the pradhāna as an object of knowledge, since they declare that liberation (kaivalya) arises from the discriminative knowledge of the difference between the guṇas and the puruṣa. For without first knowing the proper nature of the guṇas, the otherness of the puruṣa from the guṇas cannot be cognised. In some places they also remember the pradhāna as an object of knowledge for the attainment of certain special powers (vibhūti). But here, in the passage under examination, the avyakta is not at all spoken of as an object of knowledge. The word avyakta occurs as a mere term in the chariot-figure; there is no sentence here saying "the avyakta is to be known" or "is to be meditated upon." And one cannot reasonably maintain that knowledge of an object that has not been enjoined as something to be known is a human end (puruṣārtha). Therefore, on this ground also, the word avyakta does not denote the pradhāna. According to our siddhānta, on the contrary, this presentation, following out the chariot-figure with its imagined body and the rest, has only this purpose: to point out the supreme abode (paramaṁ padam) of Viṣṇu. Hence the construction is wholly unobjectionable.
BS_C01_S04_V05: If it be said that the text does declare it (as an object of knowledge), we reply, no — for what is so referred to is the prājña (the all-knowing Self), as is established by the context.
BS_C01_S04_V05::block-0: Here the Sāṅkhya, voicing the pūrvapakṣa, says: "Your assertion that 'it is not stated to be an object of knowledge' is unestablished. How? Because in a subsequent passage one indeed hears the pradhāna, denoted by the word avyakta in the chariot-figure, being declared to be an object of knowledge — namely, 'That which is soundless, touchless, formless, undecaying, likewise tasteless, eternal, odourless, beginningless, endless, beyond the mahat, fixed — by discerning that, one is released from the mouth of death' (Kaṭha Up. 1.3.15). For here, just such a pradhāna, devoid of sound and the rest, beyond the mahat, as is set forth in the smṛti, is pointed out as that which is to be discerned (nicāyya). Therefore this very thing is the pradhāna, and the same is what was indicated by the word avyakta." To this we reply: the pradhāna is not here pointed out as the object to be discerned; rather, it is the prājña, the supreme Ātman, that is so pointed out. How is this known? From the context (prakaraṇa). For the context dealing with the prājña runs through, as shown by such utterances as "There is nothing higher than the puruṣa: he is the consummation, he is the supreme goal"; and by the statement of his hard-knowability, "This Ātman, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth," which itself raises the longing to know that very Ātman; and by the prescription, made for the sake of His knowledge alone, "The wise should restrain speech in the mind" — which enjoins the restraint of speech and the rest. Further, the fruit there spoken of is release from the mouth of death; and the Sāṅkhyas themselves do not admit that by merely discerning the pradhāna one is released from the mouth of death. Their own admission is that release from the mouth of death follows only from the knowledge of the conscious Self. In all the Vedānta-texts, it is of the prājña Ātman alone that the absence of sound and the rest is asserted. Hence neither does the pradhāna here have the character of an object of knowledge, nor is it what is denoted by the word avyakta.
BS_C01_S04_V06: And it is only of three (objects) that there is in this manner the introduction and the question.
BS_C01_S04_V06::block-0: And on this further ground, too, the pradhāna is neither the denotandum of the word avyakta nor an object of knowledge here: namely, that in this work, the Kaṭha-vallī, by virtue of the boon-granting (varapradāna) only three padārthas — the (Naciketas) Fire, the jīva, and the supreme Ātman — are seen to be brought forward as topics to be expounded; and the questions, too, concern only these. There is no question and no introduction of any other thing besides these. There, first, the question concerning the Fire: "That Fire which leads to heaven, O Death, do thou tell to me, the faithful one" (Kaṭha Up. 1.1.13). Then the question concerning the jīva: "This doubt that there is regarding a man departed — some say, 'he is,' others, 'he is not' — let me, taught by thee, know this; this is the third of my boons" (Kaṭha Up. 1.1.20). Then the question concerning the supreme Ātman: "That which thou seest as other than dharma and other than adharma, other than this done and not-done, other than the past and the future, that tell me" (Kaṭha Up. 1.2.14). The replies, too: "He told him that Fire which is the beginning of the worlds — the bricks, how many, of what kind" (Kaṭha Up. 1.1.15) concerns the Fire. "Lo, I shall declare to thee this hidden, eternal Brahman, and how, having reached death, the Ātman becomes, O Gautama" (Kaṭha Up. 2.2.6); "Some embodied beings enter into a womb to obtain a body; others go to the unmoving — according to their work, according to their hearing" (Kaṭha Up. 2.2.7) — these, though intervening, concern the jīva. And "He, the Wise, is not born, nor does He die" (Kaṭha Up. 1.2.18) and the rest — a great expansion — concerns the supreme Ātman. There is no question whatever concerning the pradhāna; and not having been asked about, it is not fit to be introduced.
BS_C01_S04_V06::block-1: Here it is objected: this question regarding the Self — "This doubt that there is regarding a man departed" — is it the very same that is brought up again in "Other than dharma, other than adharma," or is it some other, fresh question that is raised? What follows from this distinction? If it be said that the same question is brought up again, then the two questions concerning the Self merge into one, and there are only two questions in all — that on the Fire and that on the Self; hence one ought not to say there is the introduction of three questions. If, on the other hand, it be said that this is a different, fresh question that is being raised, then, just as a question can be conceived of even apart from the boon-granting without fault, so also, apart from any question, the introduction of the pradhāna would be conceivable without fault.
BS_C01_S04_V06::block-2: To this we reply: we do not, beyond the boon-granting, imagine any further question whatsoever, owing to the force of the opening of the discourse. The connected sentence-flow, beginning from the boon-granting, in the form of a dialogue between Death (Mṛtyu) and Naciketas, is found to run through the Kaṭha-vallī to its very close. Death, indeed, granted three boons to Naciketas who had been sent by his father. With the first boon Naciketas chose his father's good-mindedness; with the second, the knowledge of the Fire (agnividyā); with the third, the knowledge of the Self (ātmavidyā) — as is indicated by the linking signs "This doubt regarding a man departed" and "this is the third of my boons." If now, in "Other than dharma," some other, fresh question were raised, then, by imagining a question apart from the boon-granting, the sentence-context would be violated. (The pūrvapakṣin urges:) But by reason of the difference of the thing to be enquired into, this may justly be a fresh question. The earlier question concerned the jīva, since it spoke of the doubt as to whether the man departed exists or not. The jīva, being within the range of dharma and the rest, does not warrant the question "Other than dharma"; but the prājña, being beyond dharma and the rest, does warrant the question "Other than dharma." The colour of the two questions is also not the same: the former concerns the existence or non-existence (of the soul after death); the latter concerns a reality beyond dharma and the rest. Hence, since there is no recognition (pratyabhijñā) of the same thing, there is a difference of question, and the earlier question is not being merely drawn forward to the later place. (Siddhānta:) No — for the jīva and the prājña are accepted as one. Difference of question due to difference of thing to be asked about would hold good only if the jīva were other than the prājña. But there is no such otherness, by reason of such other Vedāntic ścriptures as "That thou art" (Tat tvam asi). And here also the answer to the question "Other than dharma" — "He, the Wise, is not born, nor does He die" — by the denial of birth and death establishes the non-difference between the embodied (śārīra) and the supreme Lord. For a denial only takes effect when there is an actual occasion for the thing denied. The occasion of birth and death belongs, through contact with the body, to the embodied one, not to the supreme Lord. Likewise: "By which (Self) one perceives both the dream-state and the waking-state — having known that great, all-pervading Self, the wise man does not grieve" (Kaṭha Up. 2.1.4). Here too, by indicating the cessation of grief through reflection (manana) on the very jīva — the perceiver of dream and waking — qualified now as great and all-pervading, the text shows that the jīva is none other than the prājña. For it is the established siddhānta of the Vedānta that release from grief comes from the knowledge of the prājña. So again, further on: "What is here, that is there; what is there, that is here. From death to death he goes who sees here as if there were any difference" (Kaṭha Up. 2.4.10) — this rejects the view that sees difference between jīva and prājña. Likewise: after the question concerning the existence and non-existence of the jīva, beginning with "Choose another boon, O Naciketas," Death tempts Naciketas with various objects of desire; and when Naciketas was not moved, Death, exhibiting the distinction between abhyudaya (worldly prosperity) and niḥśreyasa (the supreme good), and again the distinction between vidyā and avidyā, praises him with "Naciketas I deem to be one who longs for true knowledge; the manifold objects of desire have not enticed thee" (Kaṭha Up. 1.2.4). And, while praising even Naciketas's question, he speaks: "That hard-to-be-seen, lodged in the depth, set in the cave, abiding in the cavern, ancient God — having known Him by the application of yoga in the inner Self, the wise man leaves joy and sorrow behind" (Kaṭha Up. 1.2.12). By this also it is understood that here the non-difference between jīva and prājña is what is meant to be conveyed.
BS_C01_S04_V07: And as in the case of (the word) mahat (the term avyakta need not denote what the Sāṅkhyas hold).
BS_C01_S04_V07::block-0: Just as the word mahat, though employed by the Sāṅkhyas in the sense of the first-born (intellect) which has only the bare quality of being, does not, in Vedic usage, signify that very thing — for in such passages as "The Mahān Ātman is higher than the buddhi" (Kaṭha Up. 1.3.10), "the great, all-pervading Self" (Kaṭha Up. 1.2.22), "I have known this great Puruṣa" (Śvet. Up. 3.8), and so forth, the conjunction with the word ātman and other reasons preclude such a meaning — so likewise the word avyakta, in Vedic usage, does not warrant the meaning pradhāna. Hence what is established only by inference (ānumānika) has not the support of scripture (śabdavattva).
BS_C01_S04_V08: (The mantra about the unborn one cannot establish the pradhāna,) just as in the case of the camasa (cup), there being no specifying mark.
BS_C01_S04_V08::block-0: The advocate of the pradhāna again rises and says: the soundlessness (aśabdatva) of the pradhāna, that is, that it has no scriptural basis, is not established. From what? From the mantra: "There is one unborn (female), red, white, and black, who brings forth many progeny resembling herself; one unborn (male), enjoying her, lies by her; another unborn one leaves her, having had her enjoyments" (Śvet. Up. 4.5). For here, in this mantra, by the words red, white, and black are denoted rajas, sattva, and tamas. Red is rajas, since rajas is of the nature of colouring (rañjana); white is sattva, being of the nature of light; black is tamas, being of the nature of covering. Their state of equipoise is referred to by the dharma of their constituents — "red-white-black." "She is unborn (ajā)" because she is not produced — for it is admitted that "the root-prakṛti is no modification." The objection: But the word ajā is rūḍha (conventionally) for she-goat. Granted; but that conventional sense cannot be resorted to here, owing to the context of vidyā. And she brings forth many progeny endowed with the three guṇas. One unborn puruṣa, enjoying (juṣamāṇa) her — that is, taking pleasure in or making use of her — lies by (anuśete) her: he, taking her by avidyā as the Self and thinking "I am happy, I am sorrowful, I am deluded" through non-discrimination, transmigrates. Another unborn puruṣa, in whom discriminating knowledge has arisen, having become detached, leaves her — leaves the prakṛti whose enjoyments have been had, that is, whose role of being the place of bhoga and apavarga is finished — that is, he is liberated. Therefore, the conception of the pradhāna and the rest by the Kāpilas does have a scriptural basis. Such is the pūrvapakṣa.
BS_C01_S04_V08::block-1: We reply: by this mantra the Sāṅkhya doctrine cannot be claimed to have the support of scripture. For this mantra by itself is not capable of establishing any particular doctrine. Since by some imagination or other the property of being "unborn" and the rest can be constructed in any object, there is no specific ground (viśeṣāvadhāraṇakāraṇa) for assuming that the Sāṅkhya doctrine alone is here intended. As in the case of the camasa: just as in the mantra "There is a cup with its mouth downward and its bottom upward" (Bṛhad. Up. 2.2.3), it is not possible to determine, on the strength of the mantra alone, that this or that particular cup is meant — since the property of having the mouth downward and so forth can somehow be conceived in anything — so here too, in regard to "that one ajā," there is no specifying mark. It cannot be determined that in this mantra it is the pradhāna alone that is meant by the term ajā.
BS_C01_S04_V09: But (the ajā is one) beginning with light (i.e., fire), since some thus recite it.
BS_C01_S04_V09::block-0: There, in the camasa-mantra, from the rest of the sentence — "This is that head; for this is a cup with its mouth downward and bottom upward" — the apprehension of a particular cup arises. Here again, what is this ajā that is to be cognised? On this we say: —
BS_C01_S04_V09::block-1: This ajā is to be apprehended as the cause of the four-fold class of beings — that is, the prakṛti in the form of light (tejas), water (ap), and food (anna), arisen from the supreme Lord (parameśvara), and beginning with light. The word tu ("but") is used by way of restriction: this ajā is to be known as having the form of the three elements alone, not as having the form of the three guṇas. Why? Because some Vedic schools, after handing down the origin of light, water, and food from the supreme Lord, hand down the very ruddy and other forms of these themselves: "That which is the ruddy form of fire is the form of light; that which is white belongs to the waters; that which is black belongs to food." These very tejas, ap, and anna are recognised here on the strength of the common occurrence of the words ruddy and the rest, and because the words ruddy and the rest are primary in respect of forms of colour and only secondary in respect of guṇas. And it is held to be reasonable to settle a doubtful matter by means of an undoubted one. So here too, the discourse opens with "The expounders of Brahman speak. What is the cause? Brahman?" (Śvet. Up. 1.1) and proceeds — "They, following the path of meditation, perceived the power of the divine Self, hidden by His own guṇas" (Śvet. Up. 1.3) — wherein at the very opening the all-fashioning power belonging to the supreme Lord is intimated. In the rest of the sentence too — "Know māyā as prakṛti, and the great Lord as the māyin"; "He, the One, who presides over each womb" (Śvet. Up. 4.11) — that very (power) is intimated. Hence it cannot be said that any independent prakṛti called pradhāna is set forth by the ajā-mantra. Rather, on the strength of the context, that very divine power, with name and form not yet manifested (avyākṛtanāmarūpā), the antecedent state of name and form, is intimated by this mantra also. And her three-formedness is spoken of by the three-formedness pertaining to her own modifications.
BS_C01_S04_V10: And because there is the teaching of (its being a mere) figure — as in the case of "honey" and the rest — there is no contradiction.
BS_C01_S04_V10::block-0: How can the ajā, three-formed, be apprehended through the three-formedness of tejas, ap, and anna, considering that no shape of an actual she-goat exists in tejas, ap, and anna; nor, since no jāti of "goat" is heard of in regard to tejas, ap, and anna, is the word ajā possible as based on the genus of goats? To this objection the next sūtra gives the reply: —
BS_C01_S04_V10::block-1: This word ajā has no reference to the shape of a she-goat; nor is it etymological (yaugika). Then what? It is a teaching of figurative imagination (kalpanopadeśa): the figurative construction of an ajā is here employed, and is taught in regard to the womb of the moving and the unmoving, characterised by tejas, ap, and anna. Just as in the world some chance she-goat may be of red, white, and black hue, with many kids resembling herself, and one he-goat, finding pleasure in her, lies by her, while another leaves her after enjoying her — so this elemental prakṛti, characterised by tejas, ap, and anna, three-coloured, brings forth in great variety the manifold offspring of moving and unmoving things which resemble her; she is enjoyed by the kṣetrajña who is ignorant, and is left behind by the kṣetrajña who is wise. Nor should this be feared: "Because one kṣetrajña enjoys, and another forsakes, therefore a real (pāramārthika) difference of kṣetrajñas, such as our opponents desire, becomes established." For this passage has no intention to teach a difference of kṣetrajñas. Rather, its intention is to teach the systematic distinction between bondage and liberation. The well-known difference is only restated, in order to teach the distinction between bondage and liberation. The difference itself is due to upādhi, fashioned by mithyā-jñāna; it is not real (pāramārthika); as is shown by such ścriptures as "One God, hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner Self of all beings" (Śvet. Up. 6.11). As in the case of "honey" and the like — just as the honey-ness of the sun, which is not honey, the cow-ness of speech, which is not a cow, the fire-ness of the heavenly worlds and the rest, which are not fires, are figuratively conceived (kalpyate) — so here, the goat-hood of what is not a she-goat is figuratively conceived; this is the meaning. Hence there is no contradiction in employing the word ajā in regard to tejas, ap, and anna.
BS_C01_S04_V11: Nor (does the pradhāna become scriptural) by reason of the inclusion of the (twenty-five) numbers — because of their diverse nature, and because there is something over and above them.
BS_C01_S04_V11::block-0: Even when the ajā-mantra has been thus disposed of, the Sāṅkhya again takes his stand, this time on another mantra: "In whom the five five-folk and ākāśa rest, that very one I deem to be the Self; knowing that, I, immortal, become the immortal Brahman" (Bṛhad. Up. 4.4.17). In this mantra, by "five five-folk," another five-fold number which has the (preceding) five for its scope is heard of — since the word "five" appears twice. These five fives become twenty-five. And by this number twenty-five, just as many tattvas as are required to fill out the count are precisely those that are enumerated by the Sāṅkhyas: "The root-prakṛti is no modification; the great (mahat) and the rest, seven, are both prakṛti and modifications; the group of sixteen is modification; the puruṣa is neither prakṛti nor modification." Hence, by the inclusion of those twenty-five tattvas, established (only) in smṛti, in the number twenty-five established in śruti, the pradhāna and the rest do, after all, possess scriptural support — so the pūrvapakṣa.
BS_C01_S04_V11::block-1: We reply: even from this inclusion of number, no scriptural support for the pradhāna and the rest may be hoped for. Why? Because of nānābhāva — these twenty-five tattvas are diverse. There is no common dharma running through them five-by-five whereby, within the twenty-five, further numbers of "five and five" might be lodged. For unless there is some single basis, the numbers two and the rest do not get lodged in things which are diverse. (Pūrvapakṣa:) But the very number twenty-five is here indicated through its parts, just as people, when they say "Indra rained not for five and seven years," indicate a twelve-year drought; so here too. (Reply:) That too does not fit. The defect in this view is precisely that one would have to fall back on lakṣaṇā (figurative meaning). Moreover, here the latter word "five" is compounded with the word "folk" (jana) — "pañcajanāḥ" — as is determined by the bhāṣika accent (the unitary accentuation showing it is a single word). And in another usage too — "of thee, of the five five-folk" (Tait. Saṁ. 1.6.2.2) — by the unitariness of word, accent, and case-inflexion (aikapadya, aikasvarya, ekavibhaktikatva), it is recognised. Because of being compounded, no vīpsā (repetitive doubling) is meant in "pañca pañca." Hence "pañca pañca" does not denote two fives. Nor again is one "five" qualified by another following "five" — for an upasarjana (subordinate member) is not joined with a qualifier. (Pūrvapakṣa:) But once "jana" has acquired the number five, this very five-numbered thing is again qualified by "five" and so apprehended as twenty-five — as in "five bundles of fives" twenty-five sheaves are understood; so here too. (Reply:) No. There it is fitting, because the word "pañcapūlī" intends a collective whole, so that on the question "how many?" arising — that is, when there is desire (ākāṅkṣā) for a numerical distinction — "five pañcapūlīs" works as a qualification. But here, when from the very start the differentiation has been brought in by "pañca janāḥ," the question "how many?" does not arise; hence there is no desire for distinction such that "pañca pañcajanāḥ" should serve as a qualifier. Even if such a qualification did stand, it would still be a qualification of the number five only — and there the previously stated defect comes back. Therefore "pañca pañcajanāḥ" does not intend the twenty-five tattvas. Furthermore, because of atireka (excess), "pañca pañcajanāḥ" cannot intend the twenty-five tattvas. For there is an excess, beyond the twenty-five, of Ātman and ākāśa. Ātman, indeed, is here pointed out as the support (ādhāra) for the act of resting, by "yasmin" — the locative — drawn forward by "the very one I deem to be the Self." Ātman is the conscious puruṣa; and he is included within the twenty-five, so it is not fitting that he should be both the support and the supported. To take him in some other sense would lead to an excess of tattvas beyond the count, which contradicts the (Sāṅkhya) siddhānta. Likewise, "ākāśa, too, rests therein" — ākāśa, being included within the twenty-five, ought not to be mentioned separately; and to take it in another sense incurs the same fault stated above. Moreover, when only the (twenty-five) number is heard, how could there be inclusion of unmentioned twenty-five tattvas? The word jana is not rūḍha for "tattva"; even with the inclusion of some other meaning, the number would still hold good. Then how is "pañca pañcajanāḥ"? We say: by the exception in the rule "with dik (direction) and saṅkhyā (number) in the case of a name (saṁjñā)" (Pāṇini 2.1.50), the word pañca is compounded with the word jana only when the compound denotes a name (saṁjñā). Hence, in the sense of a (proper) name (rūḍhi), some particular "five-folk" (pañcajanāḥ) is intended — not the Sāṅkhya tattvas. To the question "how many are they?", the answer comes again as "five." The meaning is: those whoever are named pañcajanāḥ — they are five only — just as one says "the seven sages are seven."
BS_C01_S04_V12::block-0: Now, who indeed are these "five peoples" (pañca pañcajanāḥ)? This is now stated —
BS_C01_S04_V12::block-1: In the mantra following "yasmin pañca pañcajanāḥ" ("in whom the five fivefold-peoples [abide]"), for the purpose of setting forth the very nature of Brahman, five entities beginning with prāṇa are indicated — "They who know the prāṇa of prāṇa, the eye of the eye, the ear of the ear, the food of food, the mind of mind" (Bṛ. Up.). These, occurring in the supplementary portion of the passage (vākya-śeṣa), are by reason of their proximity intended as the "five peoples." But how can the word "jana" (people) be applied to prāṇa and the rest? Or, [if some other view be taken,] how can the word "jana" be applied to the [twenty-five] tattvas [of the Sāṅkhyas]? Since the transgression of accepted usage is equal in both cases, by the force of the supplementary passage prāṇa and the rest alone are to be taken. Moreover, by reason of their connexion with persons (jana), prāṇa and the rest become entitled to the designation "jana." Indeed, the word "puruṣa," which denotes a "jana," is employed with respect to the prāṇas — "These verily are the five Brahma-puruṣas" (Chā. Up. 3.13.6). And the Brāhmaṇa-text says, "prāṇa is the father, prāṇa is the mother" (Chā. Up. 7.15.1), and so forth. Furthermore, by the force of the compound (samāsa), the conventional fixity (rūḍhi) of the aggregate [as denoting prāṇa-group] is not contradicted. But how can a conventional meaning (rūḍhi) be resorted to when there is no prior usage? It can be resorted to, just as in the case of [terms like] udbhid and the like — so [the bhāṣyakāra] says: when a word of unestablished meaning is employed in proximity to a context of established meaning, it gets restricted to that meaning by collocation; thus in "Let one sacrifice with the udbhid," "He cuts the post," "He makes the altar." In the same way this word "pañcajana" too, since by the explanation of the compound it is understood as a designation seeking its denotatum, will pertain to prāṇa and the rest collocated in the supplementary passage. Some, however, have explained the "five peoples" as gods, fathers, gandharvas, asuras, and rākṣasas. Others have taken them as the four varṇas with the Niṣāda as the fifth. And in some place an application of the word "pañcajana" referring to subjects (prajā) is found — "yat pāñcajanyayā viśā" (Ṛg. Saṁ. 8.63.7). Even on accepting that, there is no contradiction here. The ācārya [Bādarāyaṇa], however, holding that the cognition of the twenty-five tattvas is not present here, said "prāṇādayo vākya-śeṣāt" with that very intent. ॥ 12 ॥
BS_C01_S04_V13::block-0: Now, prāṇa and the rest may indeed be the "five peoples" for the Mādhyandinas, who recite "food" among the prāṇas. But for the Kāṇvas, who do not recite "food" among the prāṇas, how can prāṇa and the rest be the five peoples? — to this is given the following answer:
BS_C01_S04_V13::block-1: Even when there is no "food" for the Kāṇvas, by the "light" (jyotis) the count of five for them is fulfilled. For they too, in the mantra preceding "yasmin pañca pañcajanāḥ," recite the "light" precisely for setting forth the nature of Brahman: "That is the gods' light of lights" (tad devā jyotiṣāṁ jyotiḥ). But how is it that this "light" — read alike by both [recensions] within mantras of the same Veda — is taken by some as included in the count of five within that mantra, and by others not? "From a difference of requirement (apekṣā)," he says — for the Mādhyandinas, since the five "peoples" of prāṇa etc. have already been obtained from the same mantra, there is no requirement for the "light" recited in another mantra. But for the Kāṇvas, since that is not obtained, the requirement does arise. From this difference of requirement, even though the mantra is the same, the "light" is taken in one case and not in the other. Just as in the same atirātra sacrifice, by reason of differing scriptural injunctions, the ṣoḍaśin cup is taken in one case and not taken in another — so it is here. Thus there is, in any case, no Vedic establishment for [Sāṅkhya's] pradhāna being the subject. The establishment by smṛti and reasoning will be set aside [in what follows]. ॥ 13 ॥
BS_C01_S04_V14::block-0: The defining mark (lakṣaṇa) of Brahman has been propounded. The unanimity of all the Vedānta-passages with respect to Brahman has been propounded. And the non-Vedicness of [Sāṅkhya's] pradhāna has been propounded. Now this further objection is raised — Neither can the causality with respect to origination etc. be established for Brahman, nor can the unanimity of Vedānta-passages with respect to Brahman be established. Why? Because of the appearance of disagreement (vigāna). For in each Vedānta a different creation is found, by reason of variation in order and the like. Thus — in some place a creation beginning with ākāśa is recited: "From the Self ākāśa arose" (Tai. Up. 2.1.1). In some place one beginning with tejas: "It [Sat] sent forth tejas" (Chā. Up. 6.2.3). In some place one beginning with prāṇa: "He sent forth prāṇa, from prāṇa śraddhā" (Pra. Up. 6.4). In some place the production of the worlds is recited without sequence: "He created these worlds — ambhas, marīcis, mara, the waters" (Ai. Up. 1.1.2).
