Likewise, in some place a creation preceded by non-being is read: "Verily, non-being was this in the beginning. From it being arose" (Tai. Up. 2.7.1), and "Non-being verily was this in the beginning; that became being; that grew" (Chā. Up. 3.19.1). In some place, by way of refuting the doctrine of non-being, the procedure preceded by being is enjoined: beginning with "Some say non-being verily was this in the beginning" (Chā. Up. 6.2.1), [it continues] "How indeed, dear, could it thus be? he said. How could being be born from non-being? Truly, dear, this in the beginning was being alone" (Chā. Up. 6.2.2). In some place the differentiation (vyākriyā) of the world is described as self-doing: "This indeed was then undifferentiated; it became differentiated by name and form alone" (Bṛ. Up. 1.4.7). Thus, since there is disagreement of many kinds, and since alternative options are inadmissible in the matter of an existent thing, it is not just that Vedānta-texts should be ascertained as having the world-cause for their import. Rather, by smṛti and reasoning, the acceptance of some other cause is more proper — to this prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) we say —
BS_C01_S04_V14::block-1: Although there is a discrepancy regarding the order etc. in the products beginning with ākāśa in different Vedāntas, there is no discrepancy at all regarding the Creator (sraṣṭā). How? Because of the statement [of the Creator] as described — for as the all-knowing, all-mighty, the Self of all, one without a second, has been declared as Cause in one Vedānta, even as such alone is He declared in the other Vedāntas too. Thus — "Brahman is truth, knowledge, infinite" (Tai. Up. 2.1.1). Here, by the word "knowledge" and by the further reference to His desiring ("may I be many"), Brahman is described as conscious. By His not being moved by another, Brahman is taught as the īśvara, the Cause. By the further word "ātman" referring to Him, and by the entry through the succession of sheaths beginning with the body, He is determined as the inner Self of all. By the desire concerning the Self — "May I be many, may I be born forth" (Tai. Up. 2.6.1) — by the eulogy of becoming many, the non-difference of the products created from their Creator is announced. Likewise by "He sent forth all this, whatsoever this is" (Tai. Up. 2.6.1), through the indication of the entire world-creation, He declares the Creator without a second prior to creation. So that of which here Brahman is known as Cause with such a defining mark — that very Brahman with that same defining mark is known elsewhere too: "Being alone, dear, was this in the beginning, one only without a second" (Chā. Up. 6.2.1). "It thought: may I be many, may I be born forth. It sent forth tejas" (Chā. Up. 6.2.3). Likewise, "In the beginning verily, this was the Self alone, one only — nothing else whatsoever moved. He thought, let me create the worlds" (Ai. Up. 1.1.1). Such a class of passages, devoted to ascertaining the nature of the Cause, is unanimous in import (avigītārtha) throughout every Vedānta. Disagreement is, however, observed with respect to effects (kārya): in one place a creation beginning with ākāśa, in another with tejas, and so forth. But it cannot be said that, because of disagreement regarding effects, even Brahman as the Cause — known as unanimous throughout all the Vedāntas — should not be intended; for that would lead to absurd consequence. The Ācārya himself will resolve the disagreement regarding effects beginning with "Not ākāśa, on account of the absence of scriptural mention to the contrary" (Br. Sū. 2.3.1). And it may well be so, that there is disagreement regarding effects — for they are not what is to be propounded. For this expanse of creation etc. is not what is meant to be taught (pratipipādayiṣita). For no human end (puruṣārtha) is seen or heard as bound up with it. Nor can it be supposed [as the chief import], since by introduction and conclusion (upakrama-upasaṁhāra), unity of statement with the passages dealing with Brahman is grasped at every place. He also shows the purposive direction of the creation-expanse etc. towards the cognition of Brahman — "Through food, dear, as the sprout, seek out the waters as root; through waters, dear, as the sprout, seek tejas as root; through tejas, dear, as the sprout, seek Sat as root" (Chā. Up. 6.8.4). And by the analogies of clay etc., it is understood that the expanse of creation is taught only to convey the non-difference of effect from cause. Thus also the knowers of tradition say — "The creation that is taught, otherwise [than as it actually is], by [analogies of] clay, iron, sparks and the like, is a means for [our] descent [into the truth]; there is no difference whatsoever" (Mā. Kā. 3.15). And the fruit bound up with the cognition of Brahman is heard — "The knower of Brahman attains the highest" (Tai. Up. 2.1.1), "The knower of the Self crosses sorrow" (Chā. Up. 7.1.3), "Knowing Him alone one passes beyond death" (Śve. Up. 3.8). And this fruit is one cognized by direct experience (pratyakṣāvagama) — when the cognition arises through "That thou art" (tat tvam asi) of the Self as not bound by saṁsāra... [text truncated]
BS_C01_S04_V15::block-0: Now, that disagreement concerning the Cause that was shown — "Verily, non-being was this in the beginning" (Tai. Up. 2.7.1) and the like — that has to be removed; on this it is now said —
BS_C01_S04_V15::block-1: "Verily, non-being was this in the beginning" (Tai. Up. 2.7.1) — here "non-being" devoid of self is not made out as cause. For, having refuted the doctrine of non-being by "He becomes verily non-existent who knows Brahman as non-being. He who knows that Brahman exists — they know him as existent" (Tai. Up. 2.6.1), and having determined Brahman, characterized by existence, as the inner Self, through the succession of sheaths beginning with the food-sheath, and having drawn back this very topic by "He desired," and made the creation, with its expanse, to be heard from That, and concluded with "That they call the True" — and saying "On this also there is this verse," he cites this verse precisely with the same topic in view — "Verily, non-being was this in the beginning" (Tai. Up. 2.7.1). If, on the other hand, by this verse one were to mean non-being devoid of self, then, since one thing has been drawn back as topic and another is cited as illustration, the passage would become incoherent. Therefore, since the word "sat" is well-established as referring chiefly to a thing differentiated by name and form, with reference to the absence of such differentiation prior to origination, Brahman, [though] in fact existent (sat), is figuratively spoken of as if non-existent (asat). The same construction also applies in "Non-being verily was this in the beginning" (Chā. Up. 3.19.1), since "that became being" is brought in by the resumptive draw-back; for if utter non-existence were accepted, what would be drawn back by "that became being"? In "Some say non-being verily was this in the beginning" (Chā. Up. 6.2.1) too, this presentation of one [school's] view is not made with the intent of [agreement with] another scriptural text — since alternative options regarding a real thing, as in regard to action, are impossible. Therefore it should be seen that this presentation of the non-being view, fashioned by the dull-witted, is set forth precisely for the firmness of the being-view (sat-pakṣa) embraced by the śruti, and is then refuted. In "Then this was undifferentiated" (Bṛ. Up. 1.4.7) too, no differentiation of the world without an overseer is being stated, since by "He, this very [Self], having entered here up to the very tips of the nails," the entry of the overseer into the differentiated effect is implicitly drawn in. For if differentiation without an overseer were accepted, by what could the connected pronoun "saḥ" (he) — depending on the previous topic — be drawn in as entering into the effect? And it is the entry of this conscious Self into the body that is heard, since the consciousness of the entered one is heard — "seeing as eye, hearing as ear, thinking as mind." Moreover, just as today this world being differentiated by name and form is differentiated with an overseer, so is it understood at the very first creation as well, since the supposition contrary to what is observed is unwarranted. Another śruti also — "Having entered with this living self, let me differentiate name and form" (Chā. Up. 6.3.2) — shows the world's differentiation as having an overseer alone. The form "vyākriyata," too, taking the karmakartṛ usage of the suffix, must be understood as referring to ease relative to the supreme Lord (parameśvara), who is the actual differentiator — just as "the field gets reaped of itself," while there is in fact a full reaper. Or else this suffix is in the karman sense alone, and is to be understood as implying an agent supplied by context — just as in "the village gets gone to." ॥ 15 ॥
BS_C01_S04_V16::block-0: In the Kauṣītaki-brāhmaṇa, in the dialogue between Bālāki and Ajātaśatru, it is heard — "O Bālāki, he indeed who is the maker of these persons (puruṣas), and whose deed (karma) this is — he indeed is to be known" (Kau. Brā. 4.18). Now there is a doubt: is the jīva taught as the one to be known, or the chief prāṇa, or the supreme Self (paramātman)? What now obtains [as pūrvapakṣa]? — that it is the prāṇa. Why? From the hearing of "and whose this deed (karma)." Because the activity characterized by motion has prāṇa for its substrate. And in the supplementary passage (vākyaśeṣa) is found the word "prāṇa": "Then in this very prāṇa they become unified." And the word "prāṇa" is well-established as denoting the chief prāṇa. Of those persons whom Bālāki had earlier indicated — "the puruṣa in the sun, the puruṣa in the moon," etc. — the prāṇa would be the maker, since the deities of the sun and the rest are particular states of prāṇa, as established by another śruti — "Which is the one God? prāṇa, He is Brahman, they call Him That" (Bṛ. Up. 3.9.9). Or it may be the jīva that is here taught as the one to be known. Of him, too, the deed characterized by dharma and adharma can be made out by "and whose this deed." He, too, since he is the experiencer (bhoktṛ), is suitable as the maker of these puruṣas which are the instruments of his enjoyment. And in the supplementary passage a mark (liṅga) of the jīva is recognized — for, intending to wake up Bālāki, who had come for the cognition of the maker of the puruṣas posited as the one to be known, Ajātaśatru calls a sleeping man and, by the man's not hearing the call, makes known the non-experiencership of prāṇa and the rest, and then by raising him with a stroke of the staff he awakens [Bālāki to] the jīva, the experiencer, distinct from prāṇa and the rest. Likewise later too the mark of the jīva is gathered — "As the master enjoys with his retainers, or as the retainers enjoy [with] their master, so does this prajñā-Self enjoy by means of these selves [organs], and so do these selves enjoy this Self" (Kau. Brā. 4.20). And since the jīva sustains the prāṇas (prāṇa-bhṛt), the application of the word "prāṇa" to him is reasonable. Therefore one of the two — jīva or chief prāṇa — should be taken here, not the supreme Lord (parameśvara), since His mark is not perceived. To this prima facie position we say —
BS_C01_S04_V16::block-1: It must indeed be the supreme Lord (parameśvara) who is the maker of these puruṣas. Why? From the force of the introduction (upakrama). For here Bālāki began the discussion with Ajātaśatru saying, "Let me declare Brahman to thee." And he, having spoken of certain seats — the sun and the rest — entitled to a non-primary contemplation as Brahman (amukhya-brahma-dṛṣṭi), fell silent. Ajātaśatru, dismissing him as one teaching a non-primary Brahman with "You have spoken to me falsely; let me declare Brahman to thee," puts forth as the one to be known another, the maker of these. If even He were entitled merely to a non-primary contemplation as Brahman, the introduction would be set aside. Hence it must indeed be the supreme Lord. And the makership of these puruṣas, in independence (svātantrya), is fitting of none other than the supreme Lord. "And whose this deed (karma)" — this is no reference to motion-characterized activity nor to dharma-adharma activity; for neither of those is the topic, nor are they verbally indicated. Nor is this a reference to the puruṣas, since they have already been indicated by "the maker of these puruṣas," and on grounds of disagreement in gender and number. Nor is it a reference to the action sense of the verb-root "kṛ" with the puruṣas as object, or to the fruit of the action — for both of those are already conveyed by the word "kartā" (maker). By the method of remainder (pāriśeṣya), it is by "this" (etat) — a pronoun pointing to what is directly proximate — that the world is referred to. And "that which is done" — that very world is the deed (karma). But surely the world too is unmentioned and verbally unindicated [as a topic]. True, this is so. Yet, in the absence of any specifying acquisition, by general meaning, the reference is by mere proximity to a present thing — and not to any particularized one — since there is no particular proximity. And in the foregoing, since particular puruṣas which are parts of the world were specifically taken up, here it is understood that the world itself is taken up unspecified. The meaning is this: he who is the maker of these puruṣas which are parts of the world — why this restriction? — he whose deed is the entire world unrestrictedly — the word "vā" serves to exclude makership confined to a part. The specific mention is for declaring the non-Brahmanhood of the puruṣas which Bālāki regarded as Brahman. Thus, after the manner of the brāhmaṇa-and-mendicant illustration (one being a particular case of the other being the general), by the general and particular, the maker of the world is taught as the one to be known. And the supreme Lord has been ascertained throughout all the Vedāntas as the maker of the entire world. ॥ 16 ॥
BS_C01_S04_V17::block-0: Now, that which was said — that since there is a mark of the jīva and a mark of the chief prāṇa in the supplementary passage, the proper grasping is of one of those two and not of the supreme Lord — that has to be removed. Here it is said: this has been removed under "Not [the jīva], on account of the threefold contemplation, on account of [the term ātman] being relied upon [for Brahman], and on account of the connexion here" (Br. Sū. 1.1.31). For if it were so, a triple contemplation (upāsana) would result here — contemplation of the jīva, of the chief prāṇa, and of Brahman. And that is not proper. For from the introduction and conclusion (upakrama-upasaṁhāra) the Brahman-character of this passage is grasped. There the introduction has indeed been shown as having Brahman for its subject. Of the conclusion too, by the hearing of an unsurpassed fruit, the Brahman-character is seen — "Striking off all sins, he attains supremacy, sovereignty, lordship over all beings, who knows thus." But surely, if so, by the very ascertainment in the Pratardana-passage this passage too should be ascertained. It is not so ascertained, since there "and whose this deed" was not determined as having Brahman for its subject. Therefore the doubt as to jīva and chief prāṇa, springing up again here, is removed. The word "prāṇa" too is seen as having Brahman for its subject — "For mind, dear, has prāṇa as its tether" (Chā. Up. 6.8.2). The mark of the jīva too, since the introduction and conclusion have Brahman for their subject, must be construed with the intent of non-difference (abheda). ॥ 17 ॥
BS_C01_S04_V18::block-0: Moreover, here it is not even to be disputed whether this passage is jīva-principal or Brahman-principal. For Jaimini, the ācārya, holds that in this passage the reference to the jīva is for another purpose (anyārtha) — namely for the cognition of Brahman. Why? From the question and the explanation (praśna-vyākhyāna). For the question — namely after the awakening of the sleeping man, whereby the jīva distinct from prāṇa and the rest is awakened — is found to have for its content something distinct from the jīva: "Where, O Bālāki, did this puruṣa lie? Where indeed was he? Whence did he come back?" (Kau. Brā. 4.19). The reply too — "When he is asleep and sees no dream, then he becomes one within prāṇa" (Kau. Brā. 4.20) and so on, and "From this Self the prāṇas issue forth, each to its own seat; from the prāṇas the gods, from the gods the worlds." In deep sleep the jīva attains oneness with the supreme Brahman; and from the supreme Brahman the world beginning with prāṇa arises — this is the Vedānta limit. Therefore, that wherein this jīva has its sleep characterized by absence of consciousness and sheer transparency — namely the very nature [of the Self] free from particular knowledge born of upādhis, from which a coming-forth (āgamana) takes place as a deviation — that is here taught as the supreme Self, as the one to be known. Moreover, thus do certain śākhins, the Vājasaneyins, in this very Bālāki-Ajātaśatru dialogue, having clearly designated the jīva by the word "vijñānamaya," teach the supreme Self as distinct from him: "This vijñānamaya puruṣa — where was he then? Whence did he come back?" (Bṛ. Up. 2.1.16) — in the question. In the reply also: "This [Self] which is in the inner ākāśa of the heart, in that he sleeps" (Bṛ. Up. 2.1.17). The word "ākāśa" too is employed for the supreme Self in "In it [the heart] there is a small inner ākāśa" (Chā. Up. 8.1.2). And by "All these selves issue forth" — by teaching the issuing-forth of selves bound to upādhis from somewhere else, they teach the supreme Self alone as the cause. The refutation of prāṇa, by means of the awakening of the sleeping man, is also a corroborative addition (abhyuccaya) to the teaching of [the Self as] distinct from prāṇa and the rest. ॥ 18 ॥
BS_C01_S04_V19::block-0: In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka, in the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa, it is recited: beginning with "Not, indeed, for love of the husband" — "Not, indeed, for love of all is all dear; rather, for love of the Self is all dear. The Self, dear, is to be seen, to be heard, to be reflected upon, to be meditated upon, O Maitreyī. By seeing, hearing, reflecting and cognizing the Self, dear, all this is known" (Bṛ. Up. 4.5.6). Here this is the doubt: is it the cognitive self (vijñānātman) that is taught here under the form of "to be seen, to be heard," etc., or is it the supreme Self? Whence indeed this doubt? From the introduction by the experiencer (bhoktṛ) — the Self indicated by "dearness" (priya) — it appears to be the teaching of the cognitive self. Likewise, from the teaching of the cognition of all by the cognition of the Self, it [appears to be] the teaching of the supreme Self. What now obtains [as pūrvapakṣa]? — the teaching of the cognitive self. Why? From the force of the introduction. The whole world of objects of enjoyment — husband, wife, sons, wealth and the rest — is dear by way of subserving the Self; and after introducing the experiencer Self indicated by such dearness, of what other Self could the immediately following teaching of seeing etc. of the Self be? In the middle too — "This great being, infinite, boundless, is a sheer mass of consciousness; rising up out of these elements, it gets destroyed along with them; after departing there is no consciousness" (Bṛ. Up. 2.4.12) — by speaking, in the form of the cognitive self, of the rising-up out of the elements of the very great being already taken up as to-be-seen, he shows that this seeability belongs precisely to the cognitive self. Likewise, by concluding with the agent-word "Whereby would one know the Knower (vijñātṛ), my dear?" (Bṛ. Up. 2.4.14), he shows that what is here taught is precisely the cognitive self. Hence the saying that "by the cognition of the Self there is the cognition of all" is figurative, since the totality of objects of experience exists for the sake of the experiencer — to this prima facie position we say —
BS_C01_S04_V19::block-1: This is indeed the teaching of the supreme Self. Why? From the syntactic concord of the passage (vākyānvaya). For this passage, examined in its prior-and-posterior connexion, is observed to have its members fitting together with reference to the supreme Self. How? This is now made out — having heard from Yājñavalkya, "Of immortality, however, there is no hope through wealth," she said: "Whereby I should not become immortal, what shall I do with that? What my lord knows, that very thing tell me." Yājñavalkya is here teaching this knowledge of the Self to Maitreyī, who desires immortality. And Vedic and smṛti texts proclaim that there is no immortality apart from the cognition of the supreme Self. Likewise, the statement that by the cognition of the Self there is the cognition of all is, in its primary sense, fitting nowhere except in the cognition of the supreme Cause. Nor can this be taken as figurative, since after the proposition that by the cognition of the Self there is the cognition of all, the immediately following text supports just that very [primary sense] — by "Brahman casts him aside who knows Brahman as other than the Self," and so on. For he who sees the world consisting of brahmins, kṣatriyas, etc., as having attained existence independently apart from the Self, that very world of brahmins, kṣatriyas, etc., wrongly seen by him, casts off that wrong-seer — thus refuting the perception of difference, and by "All this, namely this Self," he establishes the non-difference of every thing-class from the Self. By the analogies of drum and the like (Bṛ. Up. 4.5.8), he firms up that very non-difference. By "This — the Ṛg-veda — is the breathing-out of this great being" (Bṛ. Up. 4.5.11) etc., expounding the causality of the Self under topic with respect to the expanse of name, form, and action, he leads us to the supreme Self. Likewise, in the passage on the One Resort (ekāyana) too, expounding the One Resort of the expanse of objects, organs, and inner organ as the unbroken, unbounded, all consciousness-mass — he leads us to the supreme Self. Therefore it is understood that this teaching of seeing etc. is of the supreme Self alone. ॥ 19 ॥
BS_C01_S04_V20::block-0: Leading Bhāṣya: As to what was urged (in the pūrvapakṣa) — that since the introduction speaks of being signified by what is dear, this teaching of seeing and the rest concerns the vijñānātman (the individual cognising self) alone — to this we now reply.
BS_C01_S04_V20::block-1: Bhāṣya: There exists here a pratijñā (declaration), namely, ‘When the Ātman is known, all this becomes known,’ and ‘All this is what this Ātman is.’ Of that pratijñā, this — the proclaiming of the seeability and so forth of the Ātman that is signified by what is dear — serves as the liṅga (indicatory mark) suggesting its establishment. For if the vijñānātman were other than the Paramātman, then even when the Paramātman were known, the vijñānātman would remain unknown; and thus the pratijñā that ‘by the knowing of one, all is known’ would collapse. Therefore, for the establishment of the pratijñā, the introduction proceeds in the aspect of non-difference between the vijñānātman and the Paramātman — such is the view of the ācārya Āśmarathya.
BS_C01_S04_V21::block-0: Bhāṣya: It is the vijñānātman itself which, having become turbid through contact with the upādhi (limiting adjunct) consisting of the body, sense-organs, mind and intellect aggregate, and then thoroughly purified by the practice of the means such as jñāna and dhyāna, departs upward (utkramaṇa) from the body-aggregate; since for such a one the attainment of identity with the Paramātman is intelligible, the introduction proceeds in the form of non-difference — such is the view of the ācārya Auḍulomi. And the śruti is to this effect: ‘This serene one, rising up from this body, attaining the Supreme Light, becomes manifest in his own form’ (Chā. U. 8.12.3). And in some places it is intimated, by the illustration of rivers, that nāmarūpa (name-and-form) too has the jīva as its locus: ‘As rivers flowing onward come to their setting in the ocean, abandoning name-and-form, so the knower, freed from name-and-form, attains the divine Puruṣa, higher than the high’ (Mu. U. 3.2.8). Just as in the world rivers, abandoning the very name-and-form that has them for its locus, enter the sea, even so the jīva too, abandoning the very name-and-form lodged in him, attains the supreme Puruṣa — such is the meaning understood there, in keeping with the parity of dṛṣṭānta and dārṣṭāntika (illustration and that-to-be-illustrated).
BS_C01_S04_V22::block-0: Bhāṣya: Because this very Paramātman abides also in the form of the vijñānātman, this introduction by way of non-difference is intelligible — such is the view of the ācārya Kāśakṛtsna. And so the brāhmaṇa-passage: ‘Having entered (these) by this jīvātman, let me unfold name-and-form’ (Chā. U. 6.3.2) — such utterances show the abiding of the supreme Ātman itself in the form of the jīva. And the mantra-text too: ‘The Wise One, having fashioned all forms and having made names, sits uttering them’ (Tai. Ā. 3.12.7) — and the like. Nor is any separate creation of the jīva heard of in the creation of fire and the rest, by which the jīva would be a transformation of, and other than, the supreme Ātman. According to the ācārya Kāśakṛtsna’s view, the jīva is the unmodified (avikṛta) Parameśvara himself, not another. As for Āśmarathya, although he too intends the non-otherness of the jīva from the Supreme, yet from the use of ‘for the establishment of the pratijñā,’ which states a relativeness, some kind of cause-effect relation (kāryakāraṇabhāva) is also seen to be intended. In the position of Auḍulomi, on the other hand, difference and non-difference clearly relative to different states (avasthāntara) are understood. Among these, the view of Kāśakṛtsna is in conformity with śruti — for it is in keeping with the purport sought to be established in śrutis like ‘That thou art’ (tat tvam asi). And only thus is immortality from the knowledge of That intelligible. For if the jīva be admitted to be transformatory (vikārātmaka), then the prakṛti-relation of a transformation entails its dissolution at pralaya, so immortality through that knowledge would not be intelligible. Hence, since name-and-form having the Self for its locus is impossible, name-and-form located in the upādhi is figuratively imputed (upacaryate) to the jīva. For this very reason the ‘origination’ of the jīva, where heard of with the example of fire and sparks, is to be understood as resting only on the upādhi.
BS_C01_S04_V22::block-1: Bhāṣya: As to what was further said — that, the great Being under discussion, who is to be seen, is shown rising up from the bhūtas in the form of the vijñānātman, and so it is the seeability of the vijñānātman alone that is being shown — there too this same group of three sūtras must be applied. ‘Pratijñāsiddher liṅgam āśmarathyaḥ’ — here is the pratijñā: ‘When the Ātman is known, all this becomes known,’ and ‘All this is what this Ātman is’ (Bṛ. U. 2.4.6); and it has been substantiated that the entire prapañca (manifold) of name, form and action arises from one and is dissolved into one, and that the non-difference of cause and effect has been propounded by such illustrations as the dundubhi (drum). The establishment of that very pratijñā is what this liṅga suggests — namely, the saying that the great Being, who is to be seen, rises up from the bhūtas in the form of the vijñānātman — so the ācārya Āśmarathya holds; for the pratijñā that all is known by knowing one is intelligible only when there is non-difference. ‘Utkramiṣyata evaṃbhāvād ity auḍulomiḥ’ — for the vijñānātman about to depart, made serene by the power of jñāna and dhyāna, identity with the supreme Ātman is possible, and hence this assertion of non-difference — so the ācārya Auḍulomi holds. ‘Avasthiter iti kāśakṛtsnaḥ’ — because the very Paramātman abides also in the form of the vijñānātman, this assertion of non-difference is intelligible — so the ācārya Kāśakṛtsna holds. But surely (śaṅkā) — ‘Having risen up from these bhūtas, it perishes after them; there is no consciousness after departing’ (Bṛ. U. 2.4.12) — this looks like a declaration of annihilation; how is it an assertion of non-difference? Not so — there is no fault. This statement of perishing has in view the perishing of viśeṣavijñāna (particularised cognition), not the annihilation of the Ātman. For when questioned, ‘Here itself the Bhagavān has bewildered me — there is no consciousness after departing,’ the śruti herself shows the other meaning: ‘I do not, my dear, speak bewilderment; this Self is indeed indestructible, of an inexhaustible nature; there is, however, dissociation from the mātrās (constituents).’ The purport is this: this Ātman, dense with vijñāna, is kūṭastha-nitya (immutably eternal); there is no occasion for its destruction. But its dissociation from the mātrās — namely the bhūtas and indriyas, which are products of avidyā — comes about by vidyā (true knowledge). And in the absence of that association, since the viśeṣavijñāna produced by it is also absent, ‘there is no consciousness after departing’ has been said. As to what was further said — that by the closing kartṛ-vacana word ‘How indeed could one know the knower?’ (vijñātāram are kena vijānīyāt), the seeability of the vijñānātman alone is meant — that too is to be removed by the very view of Kāśakṛtsna. Moreover, beginning with ‘Where there is, as it were, duality, there one sees another’ (Bṛ. U. 2.4.15), the text elaborates the viśeṣavijñāna in the form of seeing and the rest in the domain of avidyā, and then by ‘But where for him all has become the very Ātman, there what should one see and by what?’ etc., it asserts the absence of viśeṣavijñāna in the form of seeing and the rest in the domain of vidyā. Then again, anticipating that even in the absence of objects one might know the Ātman, it says, ‘How indeed could one know the knower?’ Therefore, since the sentence aims at substantiating the absence of viśeṣavijñāna, the verb-root vijñā alone, taken in its prior state (bhūtapūrva-gati), is referred to by the kṛt-suffix tṛc with kartṛ-sense — so it is understood. The conformity to śruti of Kāśakṛtsna’s position has already been shown. Therefore, the difference between the vijñānātman and the Paramātman is occasioned by the upādhi consisting of body and the rest, fashioned out of name-and-form set up by avidyā; it is not pāramārthika (ultimately real) — this is…
BS_C01_S04_V23::block-0: Sūtra 23: ‘And (Brahman is) also the prakṛti (material cause), because of non-contradiction of the pratijñā and the dṛṣṭānta.’
BS_C01_S04_V23::block-1: Bhāṣya (pūrvapakṣa): It has been said that, just as dharma (religious duty) is to be enquired into because it is the cause of abhyudaya (worldly prosperity), so Brahman is to be enquired into because it is the cause of niḥśreyasa (the highest good). And Brahman has been characterised by ‘That from which the origination etc. of this (universe proceed)’ (BS 1.1.2). Now, that lakṣaṇa is equally compatible with prakṛti-hood — like clay or gold for the pot, ornament and so on — and with nimitta-hood — like the potter, the goldsmith and the like; hence this consideration arises: of what nature, then, is Brahman’s causality? Therein, at first sight, it seems that it should be only the nimitta-kāraṇa (efficient cause). Why? Because agency preceded by īkṣaṇa (deliberation) is heard of — Brahman’s agency is known to be preceded by īkṣaṇa, from such śrutis as ‘He deliberated’ (Pra. U. 6.3) and ‘He created prāṇa’ (Pra. U. 6.4); and agency preceded by īkṣaṇa is seen in the world only among efficient causes such as the potter. Further, the accomplishment of the fruit of an action is seen in the world to be preceded by many kārakas (factors); and that nyāya may rightly be transferred even to the primal Maker. From the well-known sense of īśvara too — for of īśvaras like kings, Vaivasvata and the rest, only the nimitta-cause-hood is known; correspondingly, of the Parameśvara also only the nimitta-cause-hood is fitting to admit. Moreover, this effect, the world, is seen to be composite (sāvayava), insentient (acetana) and impure (aśuddha). Its cause too must be of the same kind, since likeness between cause and effect is seen. But Brahman is not understood as having such characteristics — from śrutis like ‘partless, actionless, tranquil, faultless, stainless’ (Śve. U. 6.19). By exclusion, then, some other upādāna-kāraṇa, possessed of impurity etc., known from smṛti, must be admitted; the śruti of Brahman’s causality terminates merely in efficient-causality. Thus the pūrvapakṣa being established, we now reply (siddhānta).
BS_C01_S04_V23::block-2: Bhāṣya (siddhānta): Brahman must be admitted both as prakṛti (material/upādāna cause) and as nimitta-kāraṇa, not merely as nimitta. Why? Because of the non-contradiction of the pratijñā and the dṛṣṭānta. For only thus are the śrauta pratijñā and dṛṣṭānta not contradicted. The pratijñā is: ‘Did you ask for that ādeśa by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought thought, the unknown known?’ (Chā. U. 6.1.3) — therein it is intimated that by knowing one, all else, even though unknown, becomes known. And that is possible upon knowing the upādāna-cause, since the kārya is non-different from the upādāna-cause. The kārya is not non-different from the nimitta-cause — for in the world the carpenter is seen to be different from the palace. The dṛṣṭānta too — ‘Just as, dear one, by one lump of clay, all that is made of clay would be known; the modification is mere talk, a name; clay alone is real’ (Chā. U. 6.1.4) — is taught only with reference to the upādāna-cause. So too: ‘By one lump of metal, all that is made of metal would be known’ (Chā. U. 6.1.5); ‘By one nail-cutter, all that is made of black iron would be known’ (Chā. U. 6.1.6). And elsewhere also — ‘In whom, sir, when known, does all this become known?’ (Mu. U. 1.1.3) is the pratijñā; ‘As herbs spring up upon the earth’ (Mu. U. 1.1.7) is the dṛṣṭānta. Likewise, ‘When the Self is seen, heard, thought of and known, all this is known’ (Bṛ. U. 4.5.6) is the pratijñā; ‘As when a drum is being beaten one cannot grasp the outer sounds, but by grasping the drum or the drummer the sound is grasped’ (Bṛ. U. 4.5.8) is the dṛṣṭānta. Thus, for each Vedānta, pratijñā and dṛṣṭānta establishing prakṛti-hood are to be acknowledged as occasion warrants. The fifth-case ending in ‘from which (yataḥ)’ in ‘That from which these beings are born’ (Tai. U. 3.1.1), by the special smṛti ‘the prakṛti is the apādāna of the genitor (janikartuḥ prakṛtiḥ)’ (Pā. Sū. 1.4.30), is to be taken as the apādāna in the sense of prakṛti. Nimitta-hood, however, is to be inferred from the absence of any other adhiṣṭhātṛ (presiding agent). For just as in the world clay, gold and the like, the upādāna-causes, function in dependence on the potter, goldsmith and the like as adhiṣṭhātṛs, no such other adhiṣṭhātṛ different from the upādāna-cause Brahman is to be sought — from the determination ‘one only, without a second’ before creation. The absence of any other adhiṣṭhātṛ, too, is to be understood as having been stated by the very non-contradiction of the pratijñā and the dṛṣṭānta — for if any adhiṣṭhātṛ other than the upādāna were admitted, the impossibility of all-knowledge by one-knowledge would again contradict the pratijñā and the dṛṣṭānta. Therefore, from the absence of any other adhiṣṭhātṛ, the Self’s agency follows; and from the absence of any other upādāna, its prakṛti-hood follows.
BS_C01_S04_V24::block-0: Sūtra 24: ‘And because of the teaching of abhidhyāna (deliberate willing).’
BS_C01_S04_V24::block-1: Leading Bhāṣya: Whence further the agency and prakṛti-hood of the Ātman?
BS_C01_S04_V24::block-2: Bhāṣya: The teaching of abhidhyāna (deliberate willing) intimates the agency and prakṛti-hood of the Ātman — ‘He desired: May I be many, may I be born forth’ (Tai. U. 2.6.1), and ‘He deliberated: May I be many, may I be born forth’ (Chā. U. 6.2.3). There, since the activity (pravṛtti) springs from autonomy preceded by abhidhyāna, the Ātman is understood as kartṛ. Since the abhidhyāna of becoming many has the inner Self for its very content (‘May I be many’), the Ātman is also understood as the prakṛti.
BS_C01_S04_V25::block-0: Sūtra 25: ‘And directly, because of the recital of both (origination and dissolution from Brahman).’
BS_C01_S04_V25::block-1: Bhāṣya: This is an additional confirmation of prakṛti-hood. Hence too Brahman is the prakṛti, because both origination and dissolution are recited taking Brahman directly as the cause: ‘All these beings indeed arise from ākāśa alone, and into ākāśa they go to their setting’ (Chā. U. 1.9.1). For that from which a thing arises, and in which it dissolves, is well-known to be its upādāna — as the earth is for paddy, barley and the rest. The word ‘directly’ (sākṣāt) shows the non-acceptance of any other upādāna — by ‘from ākāśa alone.’ And the dissolution of an effect is not seen anywhere except in its upādāna.
BS_C01_S04_V26::block-1: Bhāṣya: Hence too Brahman is the prakṛti, because in the brahma-prakriyā (account of Brahman) it is shown that the Self is both the karma (object) and the kartṛ (agent) — ‘He made Himself, by Himself’ (tad ātmānaṃ svayam akuruta, Tai. U. 2.7.1); ‘ātmānam’ shows the karma-hood, ‘svayam akuruta’ shows the kartṛ-hood. But how can the being-made-character be made out for one already established as standing in agency? We say: through transformation (pariṇāma) — for the Ātman, though already established, transformed Himself into the special transformatory form (vikārātmanā). And transformation into a vikāra-form is observed in such prakṛtis as clay. Also, from the qualifier ‘svayam (by Himself),’ independence from any other instrumental cause is understood. Or ‘pariṇāmāt’ may form a separate sūtra. Its meaning is: hence too Brahman is the prakṛti, because the transformation of Brahman itself into the form of the vikāra is recited by way of co-referentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), as in ‘It became the manifest (sat) and the unmanifest (tyat); the defined and the undefined…’ (Tai. U. 2.6.1) and so on.
BS_C01_S04_V27::block-0: Sūtra 27: ‘And because (Brahman) is also sung as the yoni (source).’
BS_C01_S04_V27::block-1: Bhāṣya: Hence too Brahman is the prakṛti, because Brahman is also called yoni in the Vedāntas — ‘the Maker, the Lord, the Puruṣa, the Brahma-yoni’ (Mu. U. 3.1.3), and ‘by knowing whom, the wise behold the yoni of the bhūtas’ (Mu. U. 1.1.6). The word ‘yoni’ is well-attested in the world in the sense of prakṛti — ‘the earth is the yoni of herbs and forest-trees.’ Even the female yoni, through its own constituents, has upādāna-causality with respect to the embryo. Sometimes the word yoni is also seen in the sense of place — ‘O Indra, a yoni has been made for thy seating’ (Ṛk Saṃ. 1.104.1). But here, by the supplement of the passage, the sense of prakṛti is grasped — from such an utterance as ‘As the spider sends forth and draws back…’ (Mu. U. 1.1.7). Thus the prakṛti-hood of Brahman stands established. As to what was further said — that agency preceded by īkṣaṇa is seen in the world only among efficient causes such as the potter, not among upādāna-causes, etc. — to that we reply: here it should not be as in the world. For this is not a matter to be reached by anumāna (inference); it being a matter to be known from śabda (śruti), it must be here as the śabda has it. And the śabda, we have said, propounds the prakṛti-hood of Īśvara who is the īkṣitṛ. We shall again expound all this at length.
BS_C01_S04_V28::block-0: Sūtra 1.4.28: "By this all (other doctrines) are explained, are explained." Beginning from "Ikṣaternāśabdam" (BS 1.1.5), the doctrine of pradhāna as cause was repeatedly anticipated and refuted by the sūtras themselves — for certain seeming-marks supportive of that view appear superficially in the Vedānta texts to slow-witted persons. And it is, by the admission of non-difference between effect and cause, close to the Vedāntic doctrine, and was adopted in their own works by certain dharmasūtra-authors such as Devala and others. Hence great effort has been made in refuting it, but not so much in refuting the doctrines that hold the atom etc. as cause. Yet those too must be refuted, since they are counter-positions to the doctrine of Brahman as cause. For some Vedic seeming-mark supportive of them too might superficially appear to slow-witted persons. Therefore, by the maxim of "crushing the principal wrestler," the sūtra extends (the refutation): "By this" — by this group of arguments refuting the pradhāna-cause doctrine — "all" doctrines holding the atom etc. as cause too are to be known as "explained," that is, refuted. For these too, like the pradhāna, are non-Vedic (aśabda) and contradictory to scripture. The repetition of the words "vyākhyātāḥ vyākhyātāḥ" indicates the conclusion of the adhyāya.
BS_C02_S01_INTRO1::block-0: Introduction to Adhyāya 2, Pāda 1: In the first adhyāya it has been established by the demonstration of the harmonious purport of the Vedānta sentences that — the Omniscient, the Lord-of-all is the cause of the origination of the world, just as clay and gold are of pots and ornaments respectively; that He is the cause of the maintenance of the originated world by His ruling-power, like a magician of his magic; that He is the cause of the re-absorption of the expanded world back into His own Self, like the earth of the four-fold class of beings; and that He alone is the inner Self of all. The doctrines of pradhāna and the like as cause have been refuted as being non-Vedic (aśabda). Now, in order to set forth this further matter — namely, the rebuttal of objections from smṛti and reasoning against our own position; the showing that the doctrines of pradhāna etc. are propped up by mere semblance of reasoning; and the non-contradictoriness of the procedure of creation etc. as taught in each Vedānta — the second adhyāya is begun. Therein, first the contradiction-with-smṛti is brought forward and answered:
BS_C02_S01_V01::block-0: Sūtra 2.1.1: "If it be objected that (the doctrine of Brahman as cause) entails the fault of leaving the smṛti without scope — (we reply) no, because (then) the fault of leaving other smṛtis without scope would equally arise."
BS_C02_S01_V01::block-1: Pūrvapakṣa: That which has been said — that Brahman alone, omniscient, is the cause of the world — is improper. Why? Because it entails the fault of leaving smṛti without scope. The smṛti called "the Tantra," composed by the supreme ṛṣi (Kapila) and accepted by the cultured, and the other smṛtis that follow it, would all on this view be left without scope. For in them the unconscious pradhāna, independent, is laid down as the cause of the world. The smṛtis of Manu and others have scope by furnishing what is required for the dharmas indicated by Vedic injunction such as the agnihotra and the like — "of this varṇa, at this time, by this rule, the upanayana; such-and-such conduct; thus the study of the Veda; thus the samāvartana; thus the union with a cohabiting wife." They likewise prescribe the manifold human ends and the duties of varṇas and āśramas. Not so the smṛtis of Kapila and others — they have no scope in any matter to be performed. For they are composed precisely with reference to right knowledge as the means of mokṣa. If they too are left without scope (there), the very purposelessness of those smṛtis would result. Therefore the Vedānta texts must be expounded so as not to contradict them. But how is it that the meaning of the śruti, which has been ascertained by the grounds beginning with "ikṣati" etc. as: Brahman alone, omniscient, is the cause of the world — how is it brought back into question by the alleged fault of leaving smṛti without scope? Such an objection would not arise for those of independent insight; but most people, of dependent insight, being unable independently to ascertain the meaning of śruti, lean on smṛtis composed by famous authors and through their force seek to grasp the meaning of śruti, and would not have confidence in our exposition because of the great regard they have for the authors of the smṛtis. Of Kapila and others, the ārṣa knowledge is recorded as unobstructed; and there is the śruti, "He who, when first born, beheld the ṛṣi Kapila, brought forth, supported by knowledges" (Śve. U. 5.2). Therefore their view cannot be supposed to be unreal. They establish the matter on the strength of reasoning. Hence too, by the strength of smṛti, the Vedānta texts must be expounded — thus the renewed objection.
BS_C02_S01_V01::block-2: Siddhānta: Its resolution — "No, because the fault of leaving other smṛtis without scope would equally arise." If by the alleged fault of leaving smṛti without scope the doctrine of the Lord as cause be challenged, then on the same showing other smṛtis that hold the Lord as cause would be left without scope. We shall cite them. Beginning with "That which is subtle, unknowable" — referring to the supreme Brahman — and saying "He alone is called the inner Self of beings and the kṣetrajña," it states: "Therefrom is born the Unmanifest, threefold-guṇa-ed, O best of the twice-born" (Mahābhārata 12.334.29-31). And elsewhere likewise: "The Unmanifest, O brāhmaṇa, dissolves into the guṇa-less Puruṣa" (MBh. 12.339.31). "Therefore hear this brief account: Nārāyaṇa, the Ancient, is all this. He at the time of creation makes all and at the time of dissolution again devours that" (Brahma-purāṇa 1.1.174). And in the Bhagavad-gītā: "I am the origin and likewise the dissolution of the entire world" (BhG 7.6). Āpastamba too, taking up the supreme Self, says: "From Him spring all the bodies; He is the root, eternal, He is permanent" (Āp. Dh. Sū. 1.8.23.2). Thus in many places in the smṛtis the Lord is set forth as cause and as material-cause. Since the opponent stands on the strength of smṛti, the answer too is offered on the strength of smṛti — hence the bringing forward of "the fault of leaving other smṛtis without scope." The purport of the śruti towards the doctrine of the Lord as cause has already been demonstrated. And in case of mutual contradiction among smṛtis, when one must be inevitably accepted and the other rejected, the smṛtis that follow śruti are authoritative; the others are not to be regarded. As stated in the section on means of knowledge: "In conflict, however, (the smṛti) is to be disregarded; for, when (śruti) is present, there is the inference (of its non-Vedic root)" (Jaimini-sūtra 1.3.3). And it is not possible to suppose that anyone can apprehend supersensuous matters without śruti, there being no occasioning ground. If it be said that this is possible for siddhas like Kapila etc. because their knowledge is unobstructed — no. For even siddhi is itself dependent (on something else). For siddhi depends on the performance of dharma, and that dharma is characterized by Vedic injunction. And so the meaning of the prior-established injunction cannot be put in doubt by reliance on the words of a later-established person. Even if one were to take refuge in (some) siddha, since the siddhas are many, given the conflict among smṛtis as shown, there is no other ground of decision than reliance on śruti. For one of dependent insight too, mere arbitrary partiality towards a particular smṛti is not proper, since if anyone, anywhere, takes a partial position, by the diversity of human opinion the established truth would not stand. Therefore, even for him, by setting forth the conflict among smṛtis and by discriminating which follow śruti and which do not, insight should be gathered onto the right path. As for the śruti shown to indicate the supreme knowledge of Kapila — by it one cannot believe a Kāpila view that is contrary to śruti, for "Kapila" is only a generic term in the śruti, and another Kapila is remembered, named Vāsudeva, who scorched the sons of Sagara, and the citing of a passage which has another sense and which is not connected with the topic is not probative. There is also another śruti proclaiming the greatness of Manu: "Whatever Manu has said is medicine" (Tai. Saṁ. 2.2.10.2). And Manu has said: "Seeing the Self in all beings and all beings in the Self, sacrificing to the Self, one attains svārājya" (Manu-smṛti)...
BS_C02_S01_V02::block-0: Sūtra 2.1.2: "And on account of the non-perception of the others."
BS_C02_S01_V02::block-1: Leading bhāṣya: How further is the alleged "absence of scope for smṛti" not a fault?
BS_C02_S01_V02::block-2: Bhāṣya: Those things — mahat etc. — which, other than pradhāna, are imagined in smṛti as the transformations of pradhāna are not perceived in the Veda or in the world. The bhūtas and indriyas are well known in the world and in the Veda, and so can be remembered. But mahat and the rest, being established neither in the world nor in the Veda — like a sixth sense-object — cannot have any scope of remembrance. Even if at some place a śruti seemingly bearing on this appears, it has been already explained as not really pertaining to it under "Ānumānikam api ekeṣām" (BS 1.4.1). Since the smṛti about the effect (mahat etc.) is non-authoritative, the smṛti about the cause (pradhāna) too may justly be held non-authoritative — this is the import. Therefore on this score too, the alleged absence of scope for smṛti is no fault. The reliance on reasoning will be uprooted starting from "Na vilakṣaṇatvāt" (BS 2.1.4).
BS_C02_S01_V03::block-1: Bhāṣya: "By this" — by this rejection of the Sāṅkhya smṛti — the Yoga smṛti too is to be regarded as rejected — thus an extension is made. Even there, against śruti, pradhāna alone is held to be the independent cause, and the mahat etc., not established in the world or in the Veda, are imagined as effects. But on this footing, the same reasoning being common, this is already covered by what went before; why then is it again extended? Because here a further apprehension lies — Yoga is taught in the Veda as a means of complete realization — "It should be heard, reflected upon, contemplated" (Bṛ. U. 2.4.5); and in Śvetāśvataropaniṣad an elaborate prescription of Yoga is seen, with the imagining of postures etc., beginning "Holding the body upright with the three (parts) elevated" (Śve. U. 2.8). And Vedic indications concerning Yoga are met with by the thousand: "They consider that Yoga, the steady holding of the senses" (Ka. U. 2.3.11), "this knowledge and the entire method of Yoga" (Ka. U. 2.3.18), and so on. In the Yoga-śāstra also: "Now, Yoga is the means of the seeing of reality" — Yoga is recognized as the means of complete realization. Hence, on the principle that, when one part of the matter is conceded, like the Aṣṭakā etc. smṛtis, the Yoga smṛti too cannot be set aside — this further apprehension is removed by the extension, since even when one part of an idea is conceded, conflict on another part has been seen, as already shown. Among many smṛtis bearing on the inner Self, effort is made only to refute the Sāṅkhya and Yoga smṛtis; for the Sāṅkhya and Yoga are renowned in the world as means of the supreme human end, accepted by the cultured and supported by Vedic mark — "Knowing that cause attainable through Sāṅkhya and Yoga, the divine, one is freed from all bonds" (Śve. U. 6.13). The refutation, however, is this: by Sāṅkhya knowledge or Yoga path independent of the Veda, supreme good is not attainable. For śruti precludes any other means of supreme good besides the Vedic knowledge of the oneness of the Self: "Knowing Him alone one passes beyond death; there is no other path to go by" (Śve. U. 3.8). The Sāṅkhyas and Yogins are dualists; they do not see the oneness of the Self. As for the passage "That cause attainable through Sāṅkhya and Yoga," it is precisely Vedic knowledge and meditation that are denoted by the words "Sāṅkhya" and "Yoga" by proximity (of meaning) — so it is to be understood. Insofar as they do not contradict (śruti), the Sāṅkhya and Yoga smṛtis indeed have their proper scope; for example, the purity of the puruṣa, established in śruti such as "This puruṣa is unattached" (Bṛ. U. 4.3.16), is admitted by the Sāṅkhyas in their account of the guṇa-less puruṣa. And by the Yogins too, the abiding in withdrawal (nivṛtti), established in śruti such as "Now the wandering monk, of soiled garments, shaven, possessionless" (Jāb. U. 5), is followed in their teaching of pravrajyā etc. By this all the smṛtis based on reasoning are to be refuted. If it be said, "They too aid the knowledge of reality by reasoning and demonstration" — let them aid. But the knowledge of reality arises from the Vedānta sentences alone — "None other than a knower of the Veda thinks of that great one" (Tai. Br. 3.12.9.7), "That upaniṣadic Puruṣa I ask of you" (Bṛ. U. 3.9.26), and other such śrutis.
BS_C02_S01_V04::block-0: Sūtra 2.1.4: "Not (so), because of the dissimilarity of this (world from Brahman); and (Brahman's) being so (i.e., dissimilar) is from scripture."
BS_C02_S01_V04::block-1: Pūrvapakṣa-introduction: The objection that "Brahman is the efficient and material cause of the world" — this objection occasioned by smṛti has been disposed of. The objection occasioned by reasoning is now to be disposed of. But what scope is there for an objection occasioned by reasoning, when the meaning of the āgama has thus been ascertained? Surely, like dharma, with regard to Brahman too, the āgama may be independent of all corroboration. — Such reliance would hold if this object (Brahman) were inaccessible to other means of knowledge and known only by the āgama, like dharma which is of the form of something to be performed. But Brahman is apprehended as already-existent in form. And in the case of an existent thing, other means of knowledge have scope, as in the case of earth etc. And just as, when there is mutual conflict among the śrutis, by the force of one the others are interpreted, so when there is conflict between śruti and another means of knowledge, by the force of that the śruti would have to be interpreted. And reasoning, sustaining an unseen object by an analogy with the seen, draws near to direct experience; but śruti is far removed, telling its meaning merely as tradition (aitihya). And the knowledge of Brahman, terminating in direct experience, the dispeller of avidyā and the means of mokṣa, is desired as an object having a seen result. The śruti also, by enjoining "reflection" beyond "hearing" — "It should be heard, reflected upon" — shows that reasoning too is to be honored here. Hence the objection occasioned by reasoning is again raised: "Not, because of dissimilarity."
BS_C02_S01_V04::block-2: Pūrvapakṣa-bhāṣya: That which has been said, that conscious Brahman is the cause and material-cause of the world — this is not tenable. Why? Because of the dissimilarity of this (effect, the world) from (its supposed) prakṛti. For this world, intended as the effect of Brahman, is seen as dissimilar to Brahman, unconscious and impure. And Brahman is heard of as dissimilar to the world, conscious and pure. And in case of dissimilarity, the relation of prakṛti and effect is not seen. Pots-and-the-like, modifications, do not have clay as their prakṛti; nor do dishes etc. have gold as their prakṛti. Modifications follow upon clay and are produced as endowed with clay; and so endowed with gold. Likewise this world too, unconscious and endowed with pleasure, pain, and delusion, can only be the effect of an unconscious cause whose nature is itself pleasure, pain, and delusion — not of dissimilar Brahman. The dissimilarity of this world from Brahman is to be understood from its observed impurity and unconsciousness. For this world is impure, since it is the cause of joy, suffering, despair, etc. by being constituted of pleasure, pain, and delusion, and since it is the high-and-low expanse of heaven, hell, etc. And this world is unconscious, since towards conscious (selves) the body and the senses go in the role of instruments-of-action and means-of-experience. There is no relation of helper-and-helped where there is parity. Two lamps do not aid each other. — But may not the body and senses, even if conscious, aid the experiencer in the manner of master and servant? — No; for in the master-servant relation also it is precisely the unconscious portion that aids the conscious. The accessory of one conscious being — the unconscious portion such as the buddhi etc. — is what aids another conscious being; not that the conscious itself aids or harms another conscious. Conscious selves are non-active and unsurpassed (in their state) — so the Sāṅkhyas hold. Hence body and senses are unconscious. There is no evidence for the consciousness of wood, clods, and the like. The division between conscious and unconscious is well established in the world. Therefore, owing to the dissimilarity from Brahman, this world cannot have Brahman as its prakṛti. As to one who might object: "Having heard from śruti the world's having a conscious prakṛti, on its strength alone I shall apprehend the entire world as conscious, since the form of the prakṛti is seen continued in the effect; the non-perception of consciousness will be due to a particular transformation. As consciousness is not perceived even of selves, whose consciousness is well manifest, in states of sleep, swoon, etc., similarly the consciousness of wood and clods etc. will not be perceived. Precisely from the difference made by perceived/non-perceived, by the presence and absence of form etc., though body-senses and selves are alike conscious, the relation of subordinate and principal will not be obstructed. Just as, although flesh, soup, rice, etc. are alike earthen, by their individual particularities they aid each other, so here too. Even the established division will not on this account be obstructed." — Even by him, somehow the dissimilarity of conscious-and-unconscious might be removed; but the dissimilarity of pure-and-impure cannot be removed at all. Nor can the other dissimilarity be removed — so it is said: "and that-being-so is from scripture." For this universal consciousness of all things is not actually apprehended in the world; it is merely conjectured by mere word, taking refuge in scripture, on hearing of the conscious prakṛti. And that very thing is contradicted by scripture itself, since from scripture also this dissimilarity is apprehended. "Tathātvam" expresses dissimilarity from the prakṛti. For scripture itself, by saying "Both knowledge and ignorance" (Tai. U. 2.6.1), declares the unconsciousness of some division and (thus) shows it as dissimilar from conscious Brahman...
BS_C02_S01_V05::block-0: Sūtra 2.1.5: "But the designation as 'identifier' (i.e., presiding deity) — by reason of distinction and continuance."
BS_C02_S01_V05::block-1: Leading bhāṣya: But surely consciousness is heard of in the very bhūtas and indriyas which are reputed unconscious — for example, "the clay said," "the waters said" (Śat. Br. 6.1.3.2.4); "that fire saw" (Ch. U. 6.2.3), "those waters saw" (Ch. U. 6.2.4), and other such śrutis on consciousness in the bhūtas. So too on the indriyas: "These prāṇas, disputing among themselves about who was best, went to Brahman" (Bṛ. U. 6.1.7), "They said to Speech, 'Sing for us'" (Bṛ. U. 1.3.2), and so on. Hence the answer is given:
BS_C02_S01_V05::block-2: Bhāṣya: The word "tu" ("but") removes the apprehension. By such-like śrutis as "the clay said," the consciousness of bhūtas and indriyas need not be feared, since this is the designation of an identifier (abhimānin). The conscious deities who identify themselves with clay etc. and with speech etc. are designated when activities proper to the conscious — like speaking, conversing — are spoken of, not the bhūtas and indriyas alone. Why? "Because of distinction and continuance." The distinction characterized by the division of conscious and unconscious between experiencer-selves and bhūtas-with-indriyas has already been stated. On a universal consciousness this would not hold. Moreover, in the dialogue of the prāṇas in the Kauṣītaki text, in order to remove the suspicion that mere instruments are meant and to identify the presiding conscious-being, they characterize them by the word "deity" — "These deities, disputing among themselves about who was best," and "All these deities, knowing supreme good in prāṇa" (Kau. U. 2.12). And the conscious deities who are identifiers are everywhere known from mantra, arthavāda, itihāsa, purāṇa, etc. The śruti "Agni having become Speech entered the mouth" (Ai. Ā. 2.4.2.4), and so on, shows that the deity favoring activities follows the indriyas. And in the conclusion of the prāṇa-dialogue, "Those prāṇas approached the father Prajāpati and said" (Ch. U. 5.1.7) — for ascertaining who is best they go to Prajāpati; by his word, by departing one by one, by anvaya-vyatireka, the establishment of the supremacy of the prāṇa is reached; the bringing of bali to him — such procedure being seen as among ourselves, the designation as identifier is confirmed. "That fire saw" too is to be regarded as designation of this seeing as belonging to the supreme presiding deity which has continued into its own modifications. Therefore this world is precisely dissimilar to Brahman; and being dissimilar, it cannot have Brahman as prakṛti.
BS_C02_S01_V06::block-1: Leading bhāṣya: When (the dissimilarity-objection) has thus been raised, (the siddhāntin) responds:
BS_C02_S01_V06::block-2: Bhāṣya: The word "tu" ("but") sets aside the (pūrvapakṣa) view. What was said — that, owing to dissimilarity, this world cannot have Brahman as prakṛti — is not exclusively so. For it is seen in the world that from puruṣa etc., who are well known as conscious, hair, nails, and the like, dissimilar (to them), arise; and from cow-dung etc., well known as unconscious, scorpions etc. (arise). — But surely the bodies of puruṣa etc. are themselves unconscious, the causes of unconscious hair etc.; and the scorpion-bodies too are unconscious, effects of unconscious cow-dung etc. — Reply: even so, some unconscious thing comes to be the abode of consciousness, some not — there is dissimilarity all the same. And there is a great difference of nature, due to transformation, between puruṣa-etc. and hair-nail-etc. by difference of essential nature, and likewise between cow-dung etc. and scorpion etc. In total identity-of-form, the very relation of prakṛti and effect would lapse. — But it might be said: "There is some commonness — earthen-ness etc. — in puruṣa-etc. that continues into hair-nails-etc., and in cow-dung-etc. into scorpions-etc." — Then the nature of Brahman characterized as existence (sattā) is also seen continuing into ākāśa etc. And he who would refute the world's having Brahman as prakṛti by the ground of dissimilarity must say: is the meaning that no portion of Brahman's nature continues, or some portion or other, or specifically consciousness? On the first option, the relation of prakṛti and effect itself collapses — there is no "prakṛti and effect" without some excess (in the cause). On the second, that is unestablished, since the existence-nature of Brahman has been said to continue in ākāśa etc. On the third, no example exists. For where would what is seen "not pervaded by consciousness" be cited as "not having Brahman as prakṛti" against the upholder of Brahman as cause, since the entire mass of things is admitted to have Brahman as prakṛti? The contradiction with āgama is clear, since the purport of āgama as: "conscious Brahman is the cause and prakṛti of the world" has been demonstrated. As to what was said — that since Brahman is parinispanna, other means of knowledge can have scope — that is mere wishful thinking. Owing to absence of form etc., this object is not the field of pratyakṣa; and owing to absence of liṅga etc., not of inference and the like. This object, like dharma, is to be apprehended only by āgama. And so the śruti — "This thought is not to be reached by reasoning; declared by another it is for true comprehension, dearest" (Ka. U. 1.2.9). And: "Who knows truly? Who in this can declare? — Whence this creation has come about" (Ṛk. Saṁ. 10.129.7), these two ṛks indicating the difficulty of comprehension of the world's cause even for the established lords. There is also the smṛti: "Indeed, things that are inconceivable should not be joined with reasoning," and "This is said to be unmanifest, this is inconceivable, this is unchangeable" (Bh. Gītā 2.25), and "The hosts of devas know not my origin, nor the great ṛṣis. For I am the source of devas and of the great ṛṣis in every way" (Bh. Gītā 10.2), and so forth. As to what was said — that scripture, by enjoining reflection beyond hearing, shows that reasoning too is to be honored — under this pretext mere dry reasoning has no foothold here. Only the reasoning that is favored by śruti, as a limb of experience, is here taken: from the mutual deviation of the dream-and-waking states, the non-relation of the Self with both; and in the state of deep sleep, by the abandoning of all phenomena, attaining oneness with sat-self, one apprehends the phenomena-less Self...
BS_C02_S01_V07::block-0: Sūtra 7: "If it be objected that [the effect would then be] non-existent [prior to production], we reply: no, since [this objection] is mere negation [without an actual object to be negated]."
BS_C02_S01_V07::block-1: Pūrvapakṣa: If Brahman, which is conscious, pure, and devoid of sound and the like, is held to be the cause of an effect that is its opposite — non-conscious, impure, and possessed of sound and the like — then it would follow that the effect was non-existent (asat) prior to its production. And this is unacceptable to you, the upholder of the satkārya-vāda (the doctrine that the effect pre-exists in the cause).
BS_C02_S01_V07::block-2: Siddhānta: This is no defect, because [the objection] is mere negation (pratiṣedha-mātratvāt). For this is only a bare negation; this negation has no real object that can be negated. This negation cannot establish the non-existence of the effect prior to production. How so? Just as even now this effect exists in the form of its cause (kāraṇātmanā sat), so too it is to be understood as existing in that very form prior to production. For even now this effect does not stand independently apart from the essential nature of the cause, as is heard in the śruti: "Whoever knows everything as other than the Self, all that abandons him" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.6). Hence, in the form of the cause, the effect's existence prior to production is not different [from its existence now].
BS_C02_S01_V07::block-3: Objection: But Brahman is devoid of sound and the like, [whereas the world possesses sound]. — Granted; but it is not the case that the effect, possessed of sound and the like, is ever — either prior to production or now — devoid of the essential nature of the cause. Therefore it cannot be said that prior to production the effect is non-existent. We shall expound this at length under the doctrine of the non-difference of effect and cause (kārya-kāraṇa-ananyatva-vāda).
BS_C02_S01_V08::block-0: Sūtra 8: "At dissolution (apītau), since [the cause would become] like that [the effect], it is incongruous (asamañjasam)."
BS_C02_S01_V08::block-1: Pūrvapakṣa: Here it is objected — If an effect characterized by grossness, having parts, non-consciousness, limitation, impurity, and so on, be admitted to have Brahman as its cause, then at dissolution (apītau, pralaya), the effect being reabsorbed and attaining non-distinction (avibhāga) from the cause, would taint the cause with its own attributes. Thus at dissolution, the cause Brahman too would acquire the form of impurity and the like, just like the effect. Hence the Aupaniṣada view that the omniscient Brahman is the cause of the world is incongruous.
BS_C02_S01_V08::block-2: Further, since the entire manifold differentiation would attain non-distinction, in the subsequent re-emergence there would be no determining cause for the differentiation into experiencer (bhoktṛ), object of experience (bhogya), and the rest. Hence such differentiated emergence would not occur — this too is incongruous.
BS_C02_S01_V08::block-3: Further, when those experiencers who have attained non-distinction from the supreme Brahman in the dissolution caused by karma and the like are admitted to re-emerge, then the re-emergence of even the liberated (mukta) would follow — also incongruous.
BS_C02_S01_V08::block-4: Now, if it be supposed that even at dissolution this world remains distinct from the supreme Brahman, then there would be no real apīti (dissolution) at all, and an effect non-distinct from the cause would not be established — so this too is incongruous.
BS_C02_S01_V09::block-0: Sūtra 9: "But not [so], owing to the existence of [contrary] examples (dṛṣṭānta-bhāvāt)."
BS_C02_S01_V09::block-1: Leading bhāṣya: Here it is replied —
BS_C02_S01_V09::block-2: Siddhānta: There is no incongruity at all in our view. As to what was said — that the effect, on returning into the cause, would taint the cause with its own attributes — this charge is itself the defect. Why? Because of the existence of examples (dṛṣṭānta-bhāvāt). There are indeed examples in which the effect, on returning into the cause, does not taint the cause with its own attributes.
BS_C02_S01_V09::block-3: Thus: dishes and other modifications having clay as their material cause (mṛt-prakṛtikā), being various — high, low, and middling — in the state of differentiation, when they return into their material cause, do not pollute it with their own attributes. So too the modifications of gold, like the necklace, at dissolution do not pollute the gold with their attributes. The fourfold class of beings, which is a modification of earth, does not at dissolution pollute the earth with its own attributes. But for your view there is no example at all. Indeed, there could be no apīti at all, if the effect were to subsist in the cause with its own distinct attributes.
BS_C02_S01_V09::block-4: Even though effect and cause are non-different, the effect has the nature of the cause (kāryasya kāraṇātmatvam), but not the cause the nature of the effect — as we shall expound under "On account of the words 'origination' etc." (Brahma-sūtra 2.1.14). And the present objection is too feeble: that the effect at dissolution would taint the cause with its own attributes. The same predicament applies even in the state of subsistence (sthiti), since the non-difference of effect and cause is admitted there too. For the śruti repeatedly declares the non-difference of effect from cause in all three times: "All this is what this Self is" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.6), "All this is verily the Self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2), "This immortal Brahman alone is in front" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.12), "All this verily is Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1).
BS_C02_S01_V09::block-5: There the resolution — that the effect and its attributes are superimposed by avidyā (avidyā-adhyāropita) and so do not pollute the cause — applies equally at dissolution. There is also this further example: just as a magician (māyāvī) is not in any of the three times touched by the māyā that he himself spreads forth — because of its non-substantiality (avastutva) — so the supreme Self too is not touched by the māyā of saṃsāra. And just as the one dreamer is not touched by the māyā of dream-vision, since [the dream] is not carried over into waking and deep sleep (susupti), so the unchanging witness of the three states is not touched by the three states which are themselves changing.
BS_C02_S01_V09::block-6: For the appearance of the supreme Self (paramātman) as having the form of the three states is mere māyā, like the appearance of a serpent and the like in a rope. Here the teachers who know the tradition of the Vedānta meaning have said: "When the jīva, asleep due to beginningless māyā (anādi-māyā), is awakened, then he knows the unborn, sleepless, dreamless, non-dual" (Māṇḍūkya Kārikā 1.16). Hence what was said — that at dissolution the cause too would suffer the defects of grossness etc., like the effect — is unsound.
BS_C02_S01_V09::block-7: Then, regarding what was said — that with the entire differentiation having attained non-distinction, no determining cause can be found for the re-differentiated emergence — this too is no defect, again because of an example. Just as even when there is the natural attainment of non-distinction in deep sleep (suṣupti), samādhi, and the like, since false knowledge (mithyā-jñāna) has not been removed, on awakening the differentiation arises just as before — so it will be here too. The śruti also bears this: "All these creatures, having merged in the Existent, do not know 'we have merged in the Existent'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.9.2); "Whatever they are here — tiger, lion, wolf, boar, worm, moth, gnat, mosquito — they become that" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.9.3). For just as in non-distinction with the supreme [Self...] [text continues]
BS_C02_S01_V10::block-0: Sūtra 10: "And because of [the same] defect in [the opponent's] own view (svapakṣa-doṣāt)."
BS_C02_S01_V10::block-1: These same defects would arise in the opponent's own view as common faults. How? Take what was said — that this world is not derived from Brahman as its material cause because of dissimilarity (vailakṣaṇya). The same applies even when pradhāna is taken as the material cause, since you too admit the origination of a world possessed of sound and the like from a pradhāna devoid of sound and the like.
BS_C02_S01_V10::block-2: And precisely because the origination of an effect dissimilar [to its cause] is admitted, the same predicament — namely the asat-kārya-vāda prior to production — equally applies. Likewise, because non-distinction of the effect from the cause at dissolution is admitted, the predicament of "becoming like that" (tadvat-prasaṅga) is also equally common.
BS_C02_S01_V10::block-3: Likewise, when at dissolution all distinctions among the modifications are erased and they have attained non-distinction, the determinate distinctions found prior to dissolution for each individual — "this is the material substrate of this puruṣa, this of that" — cannot be re-determined as such in the new origination, since the determining cause is gone. And if regulation be admitted without a cause, then by parity of cause-lessness even the liberated would face the predicament of fresh bondage.
BS_C02_S01_V10::block-4: If you say that some distinctions attain non-distinction at dissolution while others do not — then those that do not attain non-distinction would not qualify as effects of the pradhāna. Thus these defects, being common to both, cannot be urged against either side alone. Their non-defect-status is thereby strengthened, since [non-distinction at dissolution] must necessarily be admitted (avaśya-āśrayitavyatvāt).
BS_C02_S01_V11::block-0: Sūtra 11: "If it be said: 'Owing to the non-establishment of reasoning (tarka-apratiṣṭhāna), it may be inferred otherwise' — even so, there would be the predicament of non-liberation (avimokṣa-prasaṅga)."
BS_C02_S01_V11::block-1: For this reason too, in a matter accessible only through scripture (āgama), one should not stand on bare reasoning alone (kevala tarka). Reasonings unanchored in scripture, resting only on the speculation of [some] person, are unestablished, since speculation is unbridled. Thus reasonings constructed with great effort by some experts are seen to be refuted by others more expert; and those too, having been speculated, are refuted by yet others — so the establishment of reasonings cannot be relied on, owing to the diversity of human intellects.
BS_C02_S01_V11::block-2: If you take refuge in the position that the reasoning of some person of well-known greatness — say Kapila or some other — is established, even so it remains unestablished. For among teachers held to be of well-known greatness — Kapila, Kaṇabhuk and the rest — mutual contradiction is seen.
BS_C02_S01_V11::block-3: Pūrvapakṣa: We shall infer otherwise, in such a way that the defect of non-establishment will not arise. Surely it cannot be said that no reasoning at all is established — for this very non-establishment of reasonings is itself established by reasoning, namely, by inferring from the non-establishment seen in some reasonings to the non-establishment of others of the same class. And if all reasoning be unestablished, worldly transaction would collapse, since by parity of past, present, [and future], one is seen to act for the future too — for attaining pleasure and avoiding pain. And in cases of conflict over the meaning of śruti, accurate ascertainment of meaning by exclusion of mere semblances of meaning is achieved through reasoning itself, in the form of investigating the construction of sentences.
BS_C02_S01_V11::block-4: Manu also thinks thus: "Perception, inference, and śāstra of varied tradition — these three should be well known to one desirous of purifying dharma"; and "He alone knows dharma, none other, who follows up the rishi-given instruction in dharma with reasoning not contrary to the Veda and śāstra" (Manu-smṛti 12.105–106). And this is the very ornament of reasoning — namely, its (apparent) non-establishment. For only thus, by abandoning faulty reasoning, is sound reasoning to be embraced. There is no proof that because one's predecessor was confused, one must oneself remain confused. Hence non-establishment of reasoning is not a defect.
BS_C02_S01_V11::block-5: Siddhānta: Even so, there is the predicament of non-liberation. Even if in some domain reasoning is found to be established, in the domain at hand the defect of non-establishment of reasoning leading to non-liberation is unavoidable. For this exceedingly profound true nature of being (bhāva-yāthātmya), the cause of liberation, cannot even be speculated about apart from āgama. Since it is devoid of form and the like, this matter is not the field of perception (pratyakṣa); and since it lacks linga (mark) etc., it is not the field of inference and the rest, as we have said.
BS_C02_S01_V11::block-6: Further, all who hold mokṣa hold that liberation comes from right knowledge (samyag-jñāna). And right knowledge is of one form, since it is dependent on the object (vastu-tantra). For that which abides in one form is the supreme reality (paramārtha); knowledge concerning it is called right knowledge in the world — like "fire is hot." Such being the case, divergence among persons regarding right knowledge is unintelligible. But in respect of reasoning-based knowledges, mutual divergence is well-known, owing to their mutual contradiction. What one tārkika has established as 'this alone is right knowledge' is overturned by another; what he has established is overturned by another — this is well-known in the world. How can right knowledge, springing from reasoning, whose object is not established as one form [be liberation-giving]? [text continues]
BS_C02_S01_V12::block-0: Sūtra 12: "By this [refutation], the [doctrines] not accepted by the cultured (śiṣṭa-aparigrahāḥ) are also explained."
BS_C02_S01_V12::block-1: Bhāṣya: Since the Vaidika doctrine is closer at hand, endowed with greater strength of reasoning, and accepted in some respect by certain cultured ones (śiṣṭas) who follow the Veda, the objection raised on the basis of reasoning against the Vedānta-vākyas was first taken up — by attacking the pradhāna-cause-doctrine — and refuted.
