Now, lest a similar reasoning-based objection be raised again against the Vedānta-vākyas by some dull-witted persons taking refuge in atomistic and other doctrines, [Bādarāyaṇa] extends the refutation by the maxim of "slaying the principal wrestler" (pradhāna-malla-nibarhaṇa-nyāya).
BS_C02_S01_V12::block-2: Etymology: "Parigrahāḥ" — those that are accepted (parigṛhyante); "aparigrahāḥ" — those that are not accepted; "śiṣṭa-aparigrahāḥ" — those not accepted by the cultured. "By this" — by the present cause for the refutation of the pradhāna-cause-doctrine — those atomistic and other cause-doctrines that are not accepted in any respect by śiṣṭas like Manu, Vyāsa, and others, must also be regarded as explained — that is, refuted — by way of being negated. Since the cause of refutation is the same, there is here nothing further to be apprehended.
BS_C02_S01_V12::block-3: Equally applicable here too: the unfathomability of the supreme cause of the world by reasoning, the non-establishment of reasoning, the predicament of non-liberation in alternative inference, and contradiction with āgama — such are the causes of refutation.
BS_C02_S01_V13::block-0: Sūtra 13: "If [it be objected that] non-distinction [would result] from [the cause's] becoming the experiencer (bhoktṛ-āpatteḥ), [we reply:] it may be (syāt) — like in the world (lokavat)."
BS_C02_S01_V13::block-1: Bhāṣya: From another side, the doctrine of Brahman as cause is again challenged by the strength of reasoning. Although śruti is a means of knowledge in its own domain, when its object is preempted by some other means of knowledge, it must be taken as having a different intent — like mantras and arthavādas. Reasoning too, in a domain other than its own, may be unestablished — as in the case of dharma and adharma. — "What follows from this?" — From this it is improper to overturn what is established by other means of knowledge by means of śruti.
BS_C02_S01_V13::block-2: Pūrvapakṣa: How then is the meaning established by other means of knowledge overturned by śruti? Here it is said: well-known in the world is this distinction between experiencer (bhoktṛ) and the object of experience (bhogya) — the experiencer is the conscious embodied being (śārīra), the objects of experience are sound and the like, — as Devadatta is the experiencer and rice the food. The non-being of this distinction would follow if the experiencer became the object of experience, or the object of experience became the experiencer. And their mutual transformation would follow from non-difference from the supreme cause Brahman. It is not proper to overturn this well-established distinction. As the distinction of experiencer and object is now seen, so it must be inferred for past and future. Hence the assertion of Brahman-causality is improper, owing to the predicament of non-being of this well-known distinction.
BS_C02_S01_V13::block-3: Siddhānta: To one who raises this objection, one would reply: "It may be — like in the world" (syāl lokavat). This distinction is consistent even on our view, since it is so seen in the world. Thus: even though foam, ripples, waves, bubbles and the like are non-different from the seawater that is their essence, mutual distinction among them, and transactions of mutual contact and so on, are observed. And though non-different from the seawater that is their essence, foam, waves and the like do not undergo mutual transformation. Nor, on account of their non-mutual-transformation, do they become different from the essence of the sea.
BS_C02_S01_V13::block-4: Likewise here — the experiencer and object of experience do not undergo mutual transformation, nor will they become different from the supreme Brahman. Although the experiencer is not [strictly] a vikāra of Brahman — as is heard in "Having created that, He entered into that very [creation]" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6.1), where experiencer-hood is heard of the unmodified Creator who has entered into the effect — yet for one who has entered into the effect there is a distinction conditioned by the upādhi (limiting adjunct), as in the case of space conditioned by jar and other upādhis. Thus, even though there is non-difference from the supreme cause Brahman, the distinction characterized as experiencer-and-object is consistent on the analogy of sea and waves — as has been said.
BS_C02_S01_V14::block-0: Sūtra 14: "Their non-difference (tad-ananyatvam) [is established] from the words 'origination' (ārambhaṇa-śabda) and the like."
BS_C02_S01_V14::block-1: Bhāṣya: While granting this empirical (vyāvahārika) distinction of experiencer-and-object, the resolution "like in the world" was given. But this distinction does not exist in the highest sense (paramārthatas), since the non-difference of effect and cause is to be known. The effect is the manifold world beginning with space; the cause is the supreme Brahman. From that cause the effect's non-difference in the highest sense — its non-being apart [from the cause] — is to be known. Whence? From the words "origination" and the like (ārambhaṇa-śabda-ādibhyaḥ).
BS_C02_S01_V14::block-2: The word "origination" first occurs after the proposition "by knowing one, all is known," when an example is sought: "As, dear one, by [knowing] a single lump of clay, all that is made of clay would be known — modification (vikāra) being a name based on speech alone (vāc-ārambhaṇa); 'clay' alone is real (mṛttiketyeva satyam)" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.4). The meaning is: by truly knowing a single lump of clay in its essence as clay, all that is made of clay — pot, dish, jar and so on — would be known, since they are non-different from clay in essence. Because — "vāc-ārambhaṇaṁ vikāro nāmadheyam" — "modification" is initiated only by speech: "It is a vikāra — pot, dish, jar." In actual fact (vastu-vṛttena) there is no modification at all. It is only a name (nāmadheya), and unreal (anṛta). "Clay alone is real" — this is the example offered for Brahman.
BS_C02_S01_V14::block-3: There, from the heard word "vāc-ārambhaṇa," it is known that even in the dārṣṭāntika (the thing illustrated), the multitude of effects has no being apart from Brahman. Again, having declared the Brahman-effect-hood of fire, water, and food, [the śruti] declares the non-being of their effects apart from fire, water, and food: "The fire-ness of fire has departed; modification is a name based on speech alone; the three forms alone are real" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.4.1) and so on.
BS_C02_S01_V14::block-4: By the "and the like" in "ārambhaṇa-śabda-ādibhyaḥ," passages such as: "All this has That as its essence; That is real; That is the Self; That thou art" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7); "All this is what this Self is" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.6); "Brahman alone is all this"; "All this is verily the Self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2); "There is no plurality whatever here" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.19) — and other passages teaching the oneness of the Self — are to be cited. Otherwise, the knowing of all by knowing one would not be established. Hence, just as the spaces enclosed in pots, jars, and the like are non-different from the great space (mahākāśa), and as the water of mirage is non-different from the saline waste — being seen and then vanishing, and uncharacterizable in their own form — so too, this entire world of objects, experiencer, and the rest is non-existent apart from Brahman. Thus it is to be seen.
BS_C02_S01_V14::block-5: Pūrvapakṣa (alternate Bhedābheda-leaning view): But Brahman is manifold in nature. Just as a tree has many branches, so Brahman is endowed with manifold powers and activities. Hence both oneness and manyness are real — as 'tree' is oneness, 'branches' is manyness; as in the form of the sea oneness, in the form of foam-and-wave manyness; as in the form of clay oneness, in the form of pot-and-dish manyness. There the empirical activity of liberation through knowledge will be established by the aspect of oneness (ekatvāṁśena), while worldly and Vaidika transactions resting on the karma-kāṇḍa will be established by the aspect of manyness (nānātvāṁśena). And thus the examples of clay and the like will become apt.
BS_C02_S01_V14::block-6: Siddhānta: It is not so. For in the example, only the material cause (prakṛti-mātra) is determined as real — "mṛttikā ity eva satyam"; and by the word "vāc-ārambhaṇa," the multitude of modifications is declared unreal. In the dārṣṭāntika too, only the supreme cause as one (paramakāraṇasya ekasya) is determined as real — "All this has That as its essence; That is real"; and the embodied [self] is taught to be Brahman: "That is the Self, That thou art, O Śvetaketu."
BS_C02_S01_V14::block-7: Indeed, this Brahman-Self-hood of the embodied (śārīra) is self-established (svayaṁ-prasiddha), and is being taught — not something to be accomplished by another effort. Hence this scriptural (śāstrīya) Brahman-Self-hood, when known, becomes the sublator (bādhaka) of the natural [false] embodied-self-hood (svābhāvika śārīrātmatva), as the rope-cognition is to the serpent-cognition. And when embodied-self-hood is sublated, all the natural transactions resting on it are sublated; and for the sake of establishing those, no further "aspect of manyness" of Brahman need be assumed.
BS_C02_S01_V14::block-8: And it is shown: "But where for him all has become the very Self, then by what should he see what?" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15) and so on — declaring, for the seer of Brahman-Self-hood, the absence of all transactions characterized as kriyā, kāraka, and phala. Nor is it proper to say that this absence of transactions is grounded in some particular state, since "That thou art" — Brahman-Self-hood — is not grounded in any particular state. By the example of the thief (taskara-dṛṣṭānta), [the śruti] shows the bondage of one bound to the unreal and the liberation (mokṣa) of one bound to the real, thereby showing that oneness alone is the one paramārthika, and that manyness is the play of mithyā-jñāna (false knowledge).
BS_C02_S01_V14::block-9: If both were real, how could even the creature engaged in transactions be called 'bound to the unreal'? "He goes from death to death who sees as if there were plurality here" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.19) — by censuring the bheda-vision, [the śruti] shows precisely this. Nor in this view is "liberation through knowledge" inconsistent: rather, no kind of mithyā-jñāna sublatable by samyag-jñāna is admitted as the cause of saṁsāra [on the bhedābheda view] — and on dual-reality, how can the knowledge of plurality be sublated by the knowledge of oneness?
BS_C02_S01_V14::block-10: Objection: But on the absolute affirmation of oneness, due to the absence of plurality, the worldly means of knowledge — perception and the rest — would be voided of their object, like the cognitions of "man" and the like in a post (sthāṇu). Likewise the śāstra of injunction and prohibition, depending on bheda, would be voided in its absence. So too the mokṣa-śāstra, depending on bheda among teacher, taught, and so forth, would be voided. And how could the oneness of the Self taught by an unreal mokṣa-śāstra be real?
BS_C02_S01_V14::block-11: Siddhānta: There is no defect. For all transactions, prior to the realization of Brahman-Self-hood, are valid (satya), as the dream-transactions are valid prior to waking. As long as there is no realization of the true oneness of the Self (sat-ya-ātmā-aikatva-pratipatti), in the modifications characterized as means of knowledge, objects, and fruits, the cognition of unreality does not [arise]... [text continues]
BS_C02_S01_V15::block-0: Sūtra 15: bhāve copalabdheḥ — "And on account of perception only when [the cause] exists." The non-difference of the effect from the cause is established by the fact that the effect is perceived only when the cause is present, never in its absence.
BS_C02_S01_V15::block-1: From this further reason too the effect is non-different from the cause: namely, because the effect is perceived only when the cause exists (bhāve eva kāraṇasya), never in its absence (na abhāve). Thus, when clay is present a pot is perceived; when threads are present a cloth is perceived. Nor is it observed as an invariable rule that, on the existence of one thing, another thing is perceived. A horse, being other than a cow, is not perceived merely on the existence of a cow. Nor is a pot perceived solely on the existence of the potter, although there is between them the relation of efficient cause and effect (nimitta-naimittika-bhāva), because of [their] otherness.
BS_C02_S01_V15::block-2: Objection: Surely the perception of one thing on the existence of another is seen to be invariable, as smoke on the existence of fire. We reply: not so; for even when the fire has been extinguished, smoke held within the cowherd's vessel and the like is still perceived. Should one then specify smoke by some particular state — "smoke of such-and-such a kind does not exist without fire" — even so there is no fault [against our position]. For we declare that what proves the non-difference of effect and cause is the cognition (buddhi) tinged by the very being of [the cause]; and this does not exist in the case of fire and smoke.
BS_C02_S01_V15::block-3: Or [the sūtra may be read] bhāvāc copalabdheḥ — "and from the existence of perception". The meaning is: not only from scriptural word (śabda) is the non-difference of effect and cause established, but also from the existence of direct perception (pratyakṣa-upalabdhi) of their non-difference. For there is direct perception of effect and cause as non-different. Thus, in a cloth that has the configuration of threads, no effect named "cloth" is at all perceived apart from the threads (tantu-vyatirekeṇa); only the threads themselves, with their warp and woof (ātāna-vitāna), are perceived directly. Likewise the filaments in the threads, and in the filaments their constituent parts.
BS_C02_S01_V15::block-4: By this same direct perception [we proceed]: from these are inferred the three colours red, white, black; from those, mere air and mere ākāśa; and beyond that, the one Brahman alone, without a second (ekam eva advitīyam). Therein lies the final resting-place of all means of valid knowledge (sarva-pramāṇānām niṣṭhā), as we have already declared.
BS_C02_S01_V16::block-0: Sūtra 16: sattvāc cāvarasya — "And because the later [effect] [pre-]exists [in the cause]." The non-difference of the effect from the cause is also established because the later effect is heard in scripture as already existing in the cause, in the form of the cause itself, prior to its production.
BS_C02_S01_V16::block-1: From this further reason too the non-difference of the effect from the cause [is to be admitted]: namely, because the existence of the later (avara-kālīna) effect in the cause, in the very form of the cause, prior to production, is taught in scripture — "Being alone, dear one, this was in the beginning" (Chā. Up. 6.2.1), "This was indeed the Self alone in the beginning" (Ai. Ār. 1.1.1) — by reason of the co-ordinate predication (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of the effect, denoted by the word "this" (idam), with the cause.
BS_C02_S01_V16::block-2: And that which does not exist in some thing in some essential form — that does not arise from that thing, as oil does not arise from sands. Therefore, since [the effect] is non-different prior to production, it is understood that the produced effect too is non-different from the cause.
BS_C02_S01_V16::block-3: And just as the cause, Brahman, does not deviate from existence (sattva) through the three times (past, present, future), so the effect, the world, also does not deviate from existence through the three times. And existence is one. From this also follows the non-difference of the effect from the cause.
BS_C02_S01_V17::block-0: Sūtra 17: asad-vyapadeśān neti cen na dharmāntareṇa vākya-śeṣāt — "If it be objected that, owing to the designation [of the world] as 'non-existent' [prior to creation, the effect is not pre-existent], we reply: not so, for the [non-existence is spoken of] in respect of a different attribute, as appears from the remainder of the passage."
BS_C02_S01_V17::block-1: Pūrvapakṣa: But surely, scripture in some places speaks of the non-existence of the effect prior to production — "Non-existent indeed was this in the beginning" (Chā. Up. 3.19.1), and "Non-existent indeed was this in the beginning" (Tai. Up. 2.7.1). Therefore, on account of the designation "non-existent" (asad-vyapadeśa), the effect was not existent prior to production.
BS_C02_S01_V17::block-2: Siddhānta: We say, no. This designation of non-existence regarding the effect prior to production is not made with the intention of absolute non-existence (atyanta-asattva). Then with what intention? It is by reason of a different attribute (dharmāntara) — namely, that the attribute of unmanifest name-and-form (avyākṛta-nāmarūpatva) is a different attribute from manifest name-and-form (vyākṛta-nāmarūpatva). It is by this different attribute that this designation of non-existence is applied to the effect, which prior to production was indeed existent, being non-different from the cause in the form of the cause.
BS_C02_S01_V17::block-3: How is this understood? From the remainder of the passage (vākya-śeṣa). When the meaning of a sentence is doubtful at its beginning, it is determined from its conclusion. Here too, that which was indicated at the beginning by the word "non-existent" — "Non-existent indeed was this in the beginning" — is again referred to by the word "that" and qualified as "existent": "That was existent". And the absolutely non-existent has no connection with prior or later time, and the word "āsīt" ("was") would be inapplicable [to the absolutely non-existent].
BS_C02_S01_V17::block-4: Likewise, in "Non-existent indeed was this in the beginning" (Tai. Up. 2.7.1), in the remainder "It made itself by itself" (Tai. Up. 2.7.1), the qualification rules out absolute non-existence. Therefore this designation of non-existence regarding the effect prior to production is solely by reference to a different attribute. For in worldly usage that thing is well-known as deserving the word "existent" (sat) which has its name-and-form manifested. Hence, prior to the manifestation of name-and-form, [the effect] is figuratively spoken of as if (iva) it were non-existent.
BS_C02_S01_V18::block-0: Sūtra 18: yukteḥ śabdāntarāc ca — "And from reasoning, and from another scriptural text [the pre-existence of the effect is established]."
BS_C02_S01_V18::block-1: From reasoning (yukti) too, the pre-existence and non-difference of the effect from the cause prior to production is understood, and from another scriptural word (śabdāntara).
BS_C02_S01_V18::block-2: Reasoning is first set forth: in the world, those who desire curd, a pot, an ornament, etc., are seen to take up specifically determined causes — milk, clay, gold, and so on. Those who desire curd do not take up clay; those who desire a pot do not take up milk. This would not be intelligible on the doctrine of non-existent effect (asat-kārya-vāda). For if, prior to production, all things were undistinguishedly non-existent everywhere, why should curd arise only from milk and not from clay, and a pot only from clay and not from milk?
BS_C02_S01_V18::block-3: If it be replied: even though there is undistinguished prior non-existence, yet there is some excellence (atiśaya) in milk for curd, but not in clay; and some excellence in clay for the pot, but not in milk — then, since the prior state has excellence, the doctrine of non-existent effect collapses and the doctrine of pre-existent effect (sat-kārya-vāda) is established.
BS_C02_S01_V18::block-4: And the potency (śakti) of the cause, postulated in order to fix it to a particular effect, can be neither different [from the cause] nor non-existent and yet determine the effect — since both would be equally non-existent, and the otherness would be equally undifferentiated. Therefore the potency is of the very nature of the cause, and the effect is of the very nature of the potency.
BS_C02_S01_V18::block-5: Moreover, since there is no cognition of difference between effect and cause, between substance and qualities, etc., as there is between a horse and a buffalo, identity (tādātmya) must be admitted. Even on the postulation of inherence (samavāya), if a relation between samavāya and the inherent terms is admitted, another relation must be postulated for that relation, and so on — leading to infinite regress. If not admitted, separation results.
BS_C02_S01_V18::block-6: If it be said that samavāya, being itself of the nature of relation, relates without depending on a further relation, then conjunction (saṃyoga) too, being itself of the nature of relation, would relate without depending on samavāya. And since the cognition of identity in respect of substance, qualities, etc., is given, the postulation of samavāya is purposeless.
BS_C02_S01_V18::block-7: Further: how would the effect, the whole-substance (avayavi-dravya), reside in the causes, the part-substances (avayava-dravya)? Would it reside in all the parts together, or in each part severally? If in all together, the whole would not be perceived, since contact with all the parts simultaneously is impossible — for plurality residing in all its loci together is not grasped by grasping its loci separately.
BS_C02_S01_V18::block-8: If it resides in all the parts part by part (avayava-śaḥ), then over and above the originating parts, further parts of the whole must be postulated by which it could reside part-wise in the originating parts — for a sword pervades the scabbard by parts other than the scabbard's parts. And this would lead to infinite regress, since further parts would have to be postulated to make those reside in those parts.
BS_C02_S01_V18::block-9: If it resides in each part severally, then while operating in one place, there would be inactivity in another. Devadatta, while present at Srughna, is not on that very day present also at Pāṭaliputra. From simultaneous presence in many places, plurality would result — like Devadatta and Yajñadatta dwelling in Srughna and Pāṭaliputra.
BS_C02_S01_V18::block-10: If it be said: as in the case of cow-ness etc., where the universal is wholly present in each individual, there is no fault — no, because such cognition is absent. Were the whole-substance present like cow-ness wholly in each individual, then just as cow-ness is grasped directly in each individual, so the whole-substance would be grasped directly in each part. But it is not so grasped invariably.
BS_C02_S01_V18::block-11: And if the whole were severally complete in each part, then since the whole is one and is qualified by its function, the cow could perform the udder's function with its horn, and the back's function with its breast. But this is not seen.
BS_C02_S01_V18::block-12: And if the effect were non-existent prior to production, production would be agentless and selfless. Production is an action, and an action must have an agent. [The text is truncated here.]
BS_C02_S01_V18::block-13: And from another scriptural word (śabdāntara) too this is known. Since in the previous sūtra a word designating non-existence was cited, another word designating existence is "another scriptural word" — "Being alone, dear one, this was in the beginning, one only without a second" (Chā. Up. 6.2.1) and the like. Having mentioned the view of asat — "Some say: non-existent indeed was this in the beginning" — and refuted it with "How could the existent arise from the non-existent?", scripture concludes "Being alone, dear one, this was in the beginning".
BS_C02_S01_V18::block-14: Since therein the co-ordinate predication of the effect, denoted by "this", with the cause, denoted by "sat", prior to production, is heard, the existence and non-difference [of the effect] are established. If, on the contrary, the effect were non-existent prior to production, and being later produced were inhered in the cause, it would be other than the cause; and then the proposition "that by which what is unheard becomes heard" (Chā. Up. 6.1.3) would be violated. By the establishment of pre-existence and non-difference, this proposition is sustained.
BS_C02_S01_V19::block-0: Sūtra 19: paṭavac ca — "And as in the case of a cloth." Just as a folded cloth, when spread out, manifests itself, so the effect, latent in its causal state, becomes manifest through the operation of agencies.
BS_C02_S01_V19::block-1: And just as a folded-up cloth is not clearly grasped — "is this a cloth, or is it some other substance?" — but when spread out, the very same substance which was folded is grasped, manifested by spreading, as just "a cloth".
BS_C02_S01_V19::block-2: And just as, although it is grasped at the time of folding as "a cloth", its specific length and breadth are not grasped, but at the time of spreading the same is grasped with specific length and breadth — not as "this cloth is something different from the folded form" — even so the cloth-like effect, which abides in the state of its cause as threads etc., being unclear, when manifested by the operation of the agents — shuttle, weaving-comb, weaver and so on — is grasped clearly.
BS_C02_S01_V19::block-3: Hence, by the very analogy of the folded and spread-out cloth, the effect is non-different from the cause. This is the meaning.
BS_C02_S01_V20::block-0: Sūtra 20: yathā ca prāṇādi — "And as in the case of the prāṇa and the rest." The non-difference of the effect from the cause is illustrated by the example of the various vital airs, which, when restrained by prāṇāyāma, abide in the form of the cause alone, and when re-active produce additional effects.
BS_C02_S01_V20::block-1: And as in the world, when the various breaths — prāṇa, apāna and the rest — are restrained by prāṇāyāma and abide in the form of the cause alone, only the bare effect of being-alive (jīvana-mātra) is accomplished, and not other effects such as bending and stretching. When those very vital divisions are once again active (pravṛtta), additional effects beyond mere life — bending, stretching, etc. — are also accomplished.
BS_C02_S01_V20::block-2: And the various vital divisions of one possessing them are not other than prāṇa itself, since they do not differ in their essential nature as motion (samīraṇa-svabhāva). Even so the effect is non-different from the cause.
BS_C02_S01_V20::block-3: And from this — that the entire world is the effect of Brahman and is non-different from It — the scriptural proposition is established: "That by which what is unheard becomes heard, what is unthought becomes thought, what is uncognised becomes cognised" (Chā. Up. 6.1.3).
BS_C02_S01_V21::block-0: Sūtra 21: itara-vyapadeśād dhitākaraṇādi-doṣa-prasaktiḥ — "On account of the designation of the other [the individual self as Brahman], there would arise the defect of [Brahman's] not doing what is beneficial, etc."
BS_C02_S01_V21::block-1: Pūrvapakṣa: Now the doctrine of a conscious cause is differently challenged: if a conscious being is taken as the cause in the cosmic process, the defects of "not doing what is beneficial" etc. (hitākaraṇa-ādi-doṣa) follow. How? On account of the designation of the other (itara-vyapadeśa). Scripture designates the embodied self (śārīra) as having Brahman for its self — "That is the Self, That thou art, O Śvetaketu" (Chā. Up. 6.8.7) — by way of awakening.
BS_C02_S01_V21::block-2: Or alternatively, scripture designates Brahman as having the embodied self for its self: "Having created that, He entered into it" (Tai. Up. 2.6.1), since Brahman, the unmodified creator, is shown to have embodied selfhood by entry into the effect; and "By this living self (jīva) entering as the Self, let me differentiate names and forms" (Chā. Up. 6.3.2), where the Supreme Deity, designating the jīva by the word "self" (ātman), shows that the embodied self is not different from Brahman.
BS_C02_S01_V21::block-3: Therefore that creatorship which belongs to Brahman belongs to the embodied self alone. Hence, being an independent agent, the embodied self would do only what is beneficial — what produces good cheer for itself — and not what is unbeneficial: the manifold web of evils such as birth, death, old age, disease and the rest. For no one not under another's power makes a prison-house and enters it himself.
BS_C02_S01_V21::block-4: Nor would one who is himself perfectly stainless take on a perfectly stained body as his self. Even what has been somehow done, if it brought misery, he would abandon by his will; and he would take up what brought happiness. He would also remember: "This variegated cosmic image was made by me". For everyone, having clearly accomplished an effect, remembers "This was done by me".
BS_C02_S01_V21::block-5: And just as a magician at will withdraws, without effort, the magical display he himself has spread out, so the embodied self would withdraw this creation. But the embodied self cannot withdraw even his own body without effort. Thus, since beneficial action and the like are not seen, the cosmic process from a conscious [individual] being is unjustified — so it is concluded [by the pūrvapakṣa].
BS_C02_S01_V22::block-0: Sūtra 22: adhikaṃ tu bheda-nirdeśāt — "But [Brahman is] something more [than the embodied self], on account of the indication of difference."
BS_C02_S01_V22::block-1: The word "tu" ("but") rebuts [the previous] view. That Brahman which is omniscient (sarvajña), all-powerful (sarva-śakti), of the nature of eternally pure, conscious, and free (nitya-śuddha-buddha-mukta-svabhāva), other than and over and above the embodied self — that we declare to be the creator of the world. To Him the defects of "not doing what is beneficial" etc. do not apply. For there is nothing beneficial that He has yet to do, nor anything unbeneficial to be avoided, since His nature is eternally liberated (nitya-mukta-svabhāva).
BS_C02_S01_V22::block-2: Nor is there anywhere any obstruction to His knowledge or to His power, since He is omniscient and omnipotent. The embodied self is not of this kind. Hence in him the defects of not doing the beneficial etc. arise; but it is not him that we declare to be the creator of the world.
BS_C02_S01_V22::block-3: How is this known? From the indication of difference (bheda-nirdeśa) — "The Self, my dear, is to be seen, to be heard, to be reflected upon, to be deeply meditated upon" (Bṛ. Up. 2.4.5), "He is to be sought, He is to be enquired into" (Chā. Up. 8.7.1), "Then, my dear, he is united with sat" (Chā. Up. 6.8.1), "The embodied self has been mounted upon by the Wise Self" (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.35) — such indications of the difference of agent, object, and so on, show Brahman as something more than the jīva.
BS_C02_S01_V22::block-4: Objection: But indication of non-difference is also shown — "That thou art" and the like. How can difference and non-difference, being mutually contradictory, both be possible? This is no fault, since the possibility of both has been established in various places by the analogy of ākāśa and the ākāśa within a pot (ākāśa-ghaṭākāśa-nyāya).
BS_C02_S01_V22::block-5: Moreover, when through indication of non-difference, like "That thou art", non-difference is awakened, then the jīva's transmigratoriness (saṃsāritva) and Brahman's creatorship are both removed; for the entire empirical activity (vyavahāra) of difference, which is the play of false knowledge (mithyā-jñāna-vijṛmbhita), is sublated by right knowledge (samyag-jñāna). In that condition, where indeed is creation, and where the defects of not doing the beneficial and the rest?
BS_C02_S01_V22::block-6: We have declared again and again: the delusion (bhrānti), characterised by saṃsāra of the form of doing-the-beneficial etc., arises from non-discrimination (aviveka) of the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) — namely, the body-and-organ-aggregate (kārya-karaṇa-saṅghāta) constructed by name-and-form set up by avidyā — and is not real in the highest sense, like the conceit of birth, death, cutting, dividing and so on.
BS_C02_S01_V22::block-7: But when the empirical activity of difference is unsublated, then by indications of difference such as "He is to be sought, He is to be enquired into", the something-more-ness of Brahman is grasped, which precludes the possibility of the defects of not doing the beneficial etc.
BS_C02_S01_V23::block-0: Sūtra: And as in the case of stones and the like, the alleged objection (tad-anupapattiḥ) does not stand. Just as among stones, though all share the common nature of being earthen, manifold variety is observed, so too one Brahman can produce a variegated world.
BS_C02_S01_V23::block-1: Bhāṣya: For in the world, even among stones which all share the common attribute of being of the earth (pṛthivītva-sāmānya-anvita), some are highly precious gems such as diamond and lapis-vaiḍūrya; others are of middling power such as the sun-stone (sūryakānta) and the like; and yet others are inferior pebbles fit only to be flung at dogs and crows—thus a manifold variety (aneka-vidha-vaicitryam) is seen. And just as among seeds resting upon the very same earth (eka-pṛthivī-vyapāśraya), a manifold variety of leaves, flowers, fruits, scents and tastes is observed in sandalwood, kiṁpāka and the like. And just as from the single sap of food (eka-anna-rasa), variegated effects arise as blood and the rest, and again as hairs of the head, body-hairs and the rest. In the very same way, even from the single Brahman, the diversity of the jīva and the prājña, and the variegation of effects, is fully consonant. Therefore tad-anupapattiḥ—meaning that the defect imagined by the opponent (para-parikalpita-doṣa) does not stand. And by the further authority (prāmāṇya) of śruti, and because every modification (vikāra) is a mere matter of speech (vāca-ārambhaṇa-mātra) as taught at Chā. Up. 6.1.4, and like the variety of dream-objects (svapna-dṛśya-bhāva-vaicitryavat) seen in one dreamer—this is the cumulative reinforcement (abhyuccaya) of the siddhānta.
BS_C02_S01_V24::block-0: Sūtra: If it be objected that Brahman cannot be cause because we observe causes operating only by gathering together (upasaṁhāra) of subsidiary instruments — not so; for it is like milk, which transforms itself without any external aid.
BS_C02_S01_V24::block-1: Bhāṣya: Pūrvapakṣa: It has been said that conscious Brahman, one and without a second (eka-advitīya), is the cause of the world; this does not stand. Why? Because of the observation of upasaṁhāra (collection of accessories). For in the world, potters and the like, who are makers of pots, cloths and so on, are seen producing their respective effects only when furnished with means by gathering together many causal factors (kāraka)—the clay, staff, wheel, string, water and the rest. But Brahman, on your view, is unaccompanied (asahāya). When other instruments are not gathered for it, how can creatorship (sraṣṭṛtva) be coherent? Therefore Brahman is not the cause of the world. Siddhānta: This defect does not arise. For it stands by the special nature of substances, like milk (kṣīravat). Just as in the world milk or water transforms itself by its own nature into curd, snow, hail and the like without depending on any external instrument, so it will be here. Pūrvapakṣa-objection: But milk too, while transforming into curd and the rest, does require an external instrument like heat. How then is it said kṣīravad-hi? Reply: This is no defect. For milk by itself does undergo whatever degree and measure of modification (pariṇāma-mātrā) it does undergo; it is merely accelerated by heat and the rest toward the state of curd. If milk did not by itself have the disposition (śīlatā) to become curd, then even by force of heat it would not be brought to curdhood; for wind or ākāśa is never compelled into curdhood by heat. The fullness (pūrṇatā) of finite causes is brought about by an aggregate of accessories. But Brahman is of plenary power (paripūrṇa-śaktika); its fullness need not be supplied by any other. And there is the śruti — “There is no work for it, nor any organ; there is none its equal nor any superior; its highest power (parā śaktiḥ) is heard of as manifold, the natural action of knowledge and strength” (Śve. Up. 6.8). Therefore even from one Brahman, by reason of its conjunction with manifold powers (vicitra-śakti-yoga), variegated transformation like that of milk is fully coherent.
BS_C02_S01_V25::block-0: Sūtra: Also (the case is) like that of gods and the like in the world; conscious agents too can act unaided.
BS_C02_S01_V25::block-1: Bhāṣya: Pūrvapakṣa: Be it so — that for non-conscious things like milk, the state of becoming curd or the like is coherent without any external means, for that is observed. But conscious agents such as potters are seen to engage in their respective effects only by depending on an aggregate of instruments. How then could Brahman, while being conscious (cetana) and unaccompanied (asahāya), engage? Reply: We say — devādivat. Just as in the world the gods, ancestors, ṛṣis, and so on—although themselves conscious and possessed of mighty power—are observed, by reason of a special yoga of sovereign lordship (aiśvarya-viśeṣa-yoga), to bring forth, without depending on any external instrument and by mere willing-meditation (abhidhyāna-mātra), many bodies, mansions, chariots and the like of varied configurations, on the authority (prāmāṇya) of mantra, arthavāda, itihāsa and purāṇa. Likewise the spider (tantunābha) emits its threads by itself; the female crane (balākā) conceives without contact with seed (śukra); the lotus-plant (padminī), without recourse to any conveyance, moves from one lake to another. Thus conscious Brahman too, without depending on external means, will of itself project the world. Should the opponent reply: These illustrations of gods and the rest taken with respect to Brahman are not on a par (na samāna) with the dārṣṭāntika, Brahman; for it is the body itself, which is non-conscious (acetana), that is the material in the production of further bodies and powers in the case of the gods—not the conscious Self. The spider's saliva, hardening from the eating of very minute creatures, becomes thread; the female crane conceives by hearing the rumble of thunder (stanayitnu); and the lotus-plant, prompted by a conscious agent (cetana-prayuktā), travels from lake to lake by means of a non-conscious body, like a creeper upon a tree—not by itself as non-conscious in the act of moving from lake to lake. Hence these are not parallels for Brahman — to him we reply: this is no defect. For only the contradistinction (vailakṣaṇya) from the potter-illustration is intended (vivakṣita); just as, both potters and gods being equally conscious, potters depend on external means for initiating an effect while the gods do not, so too Brahman, though conscious, will not depend on external means — only this much do we mean to convey by the example of the gods. Thus, what is seen as the capacity (sāmarthya) of one need not, in absolute uniformity (ekānta), be required of all; this is the import.
BS_C02_S01_V26::block-0: Sūtra: There would result the prasakti (prima-facie consequence) that the whole (kṛtsna) of Brahman becomes effect; or else the violation (kopa) of the words declaring it partless (niravayavatva).
BS_C02_S01_V26::block-1: Bhāṣya: It is settled that conscious Brahman, one and without a second, transforms by itself, like milk and like the gods, without depending on external means, and is the cause of the world. But for the further purification of the meaning of the śāstra, an objection is raised. Pūrvapakṣa: Kṛtsna-prasakti — there would arise the prasakti that the whole of Brahman is transformed into the form of effect, because of niravayavatva (partlessness); for if Brahman were endowed with parts (sāvayava) like earth and the rest, then one part of it might transform and another part remain. But Brahman is known from śruti to be partless — “without parts, without action, tranquil, blameless, stainless” (Śve. Up. 6.19); “for the divine Puruṣa is formless, both within and without, unborn” (Mu. Up. 2.1.2); “this is the great Being, infinite, boundless, a mass of consciousness” (Bṛ. Up. 2.4.12); “this Self is described as ‘not thus, not thus’” (Bṛ. Up. 3.9.26); “neither gross nor subtle” (Bṛ. Up. 3.8.8) — and so on, all of which negate every distinction (sarva-viśeṣa-pratiṣedhinī). Then, since transformation of one part is impossible, there results the prasakti of total transformation, and consequently uprooting of the very basis (mūlocchedaḥ) — the upadeśa “he is to be seen” (draṣṭavyatā) would be rendered fruitless, because the effect would be seen with no effort, and there would be no Brahman over and above the effect. There would also be violation (kopa) of words declaring unbornness (ajatva) and the rest. Or, if to remove this defect Brahman were admitted to be sāvayava, then the words declaring partlessness which have been cited would be violated; and being possessed of parts entails non-eternity (anityatva). Thus by neither alternative can this thesis be made to fit — so does the opponent object.
BS_C02_S01_V27::block-0: Sūtra: But (tu) — because of śruti, and because (Brahman) is rooted in the Word (śabda-mūlatva), there is no defect.
BS_C02_S01_V27::block-1: Bhāṣya: By the word tu the objection is refuted. Siddhānta: Indeed, on our side there is no defect at all. There is no kṛtsna-prasakti. Why? Because of śruti — for just as the origination of the world from Brahman is heard, so too is heard Brahman's continuance apart from the modification (vikāra-vyatireka), by way of differentiated reference to prakṛti and vikāra: “That very deity reflected: ‘Let me, having entered into these three deities by means of this jīva-self, differentiate name and form (nāma-rūpa)’ ” (Chā. Up. 6.3.2); “Such is its greatness, and yet greater than this is the Puruṣa; one foot of his is all beings, and three feet are the immortal in heaven” (Chā. Up. 3.12.6) — and the like. Likewise from the statement that the heart is its abode (hṛdayāyatana) and from the statement of attainment to Sat (sat-sampatti) — for were the entire Brahman engaged in the form of effect, the qualification “he becomes united with Sat, my dear” (Chā. Up. 6.8.1) regarding deep sleep would not be coherent, since one would already be eternally united with the modified Brahman, and there would be no unmodified Brahman to attain. Likewise from the prohibition of Brahman’s being a sense-object, while modification can be a sense-object. Hence the unmodified Brahman exists. Nor is there violation of the words of partlessness (niravayavatva-śabda-kopa), since partlessness too is admitted exactly as it is heard (śrūyamāṇatva). Brahman is rooted in the Word (śabda-mūla); its pramāṇa is śabda, not the senses or the rest. Therefore it must be admitted as the Word declares. And the Word teaches both about Brahman: non-totality of becoming-effect (akṛtsna-prasakti) and partlessness. Even the powers of mundane gems, mantras and herbs, varying with place, time and occasion, are seen to issue in mutually contrary effects; even those cannot be ascertained by mere reasoning apart from instruction (upadeśa) — that ‘this thing has these many powers, with these aids, on these objects, for these purposes’. How much more is the form (rūpa) of Brahman of inconceivable nature (acintya-svabhāva) not to be ascertained without the Word. Thus also the puranic seers say: “Those entities (bhāvāḥ) which are inconceivable, one must not yoke to reasoning (tarka); that which is beyond prakṛti is the very mark (lakṣaṇa) of the inconceivable.” Therefore knowledge of the true nature (yāthātmya) of supra-sensible objects is rooted only in the Word (śabda-mūla). Objection: But not even by the Word can a contradictory matter be communicated — that Brahman is partless and yet transforms, and not wholly. If Brahman is partless, it cannot transform at all, or must transform wholly. If it transforms in some respect (rūpa) and stays in another, then by positing distinction of forms (rūpa-bheda-kalpanā) it would inevitably be sāvayava. In ritual matters, in such phrases as “he takes the ṣoḍaśin at the atirātra” and “he does not take the ṣoḍaśin at the atirātra,” although contradiction is perceived, recourse to option (vikalpa) removes the contradiction, since performance is human-dependent (puruṣa-tantra). But here, since the matter is non-human-dependent (apuruṣa-tantra), even by recourse to option there is no removal of contradiction. Hence this is impossible. Reply: This is no defect, because the distinction of forms is admitted as fashioned by avidyā (avidyā-kalpita). For the substance does not become sāvayava by a distinction of forms imagined through avidyā. Just as the moon, seen as if many by an eye dimmed by timira, does not actually become many. By a distinction of forms, characterized as nāma-rūpa, fashioned by avidyā, of the form of vyākṛta-avyākṛta, indescribable as either identical with or different from Brahman (tattva-anyatva-abhyām anirvacanīyena), Brahman attains the status of being the locus of all transactions including transformation. But by its supreme real form (pāramārthika), it remains beyond all transactions, untransformed; its modification is mere vāca-ārambhaṇa (matter of speech). [text truncated]
BS_C02_S01_V28::block-0: Sūtra: And it is so even in (the dreamer's) Self; for in him too manifold (creations) are seen.
BS_C02_S01_V28::block-1: Bhāṣya: Moreover, here there is nothing to dispute — how could a manifold creation arise in one Brahman without disturbing its own form (svarūpa-anupamarda). For even in one Self that is the dreamer (svapna-dṛś), a manifold creation without disturbing its own form is taught — “There are no chariots there, no yokings of chariots, no roads; but he creates chariots, yokings of chariots and roads” (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.10) and the like. Even in the world, in the case of gods and of magicians (māyāvin), variegated creations of elephants, horses and the rest are seen without disturbing their own form. So in the case of one Brahman, a manifold creation without disturbing its own form will be.
BS_C02_S01_V29::block-0: Sūtra: And because the (alleged) defect afflicts the opponent's own thesis (sva-pakṣa) equally.
BS_C02_S01_V29::block-1: Bhāṣya: For others too the same defect is shared in their own thesis. The pradhāna-vādin (Sāṅkhya) holds that pradhāna, partless, unbounded, devoid of sound and the rest, is cause of the effect, which is endowed with parts (sāvayava), bounded, possessed of sound and the rest. There too, kṛtsna-prasakti results from the partlessness of pradhāna, or else the violation of the admission of partlessness. Objection: They do not admit pradhāna to be partless — for sattva, rajas, tamas are three guṇas; their state of equilibrium (sāmyāvasthā) is pradhāna; by these very guṇas as parts (avayava), it is sāvayava. Reply: By such sāvayavatva the present defect cannot be averted, since each one of sattva, rajas, tamas is itself partless (niravayavatva) — and one alone, aided by the other two, is the upādāna of a homogeneous (sajātīya) world — so the proximate defect of the sva-pakṣa is the same. If, fearing tarka's instability (tarka-apratiṣṭhāna), they say sāvayavatva itself, then non-eternity (anityatva) and other defects ensue. If their intention is that ‘powers’ (śakti), inferred from the variety of effects, are the avayavas — those powers are equally available to the Brahmavādin, undistinguished. Likewise for the aṇu-vādin (Vaiśeṣika): an aṇu in conjunction with another aṇu, being partless, if it conjoined with the whole, then because no extension (prathiman) would arise, the prasaṅga of remaining aṇu-sized would follow; if with a part, then the partlessness-admission is violated — the same defect attends sva-pakṣa. Since the defect is shared, it should not be raised against one side only. The Brahmavādin has parried the defect on his own side.
BS_C02_S01_V30::block-0: Sūtra: And (Brahman) is endowed with all (powers), because of the seeing thereof (in śruti).
BS_C02_S01_V30::block-1: Bhāṣya: It has been said that even from one Brahman, by reason of conjunction with manifold powers (vicitra-śakti-yoga), the variegated stream of modification is coherent. But how is it known that the supreme Brahman is endowed with manifold powers? It is told — sarva-upetā ca tad-darśanāt — and the supreme Deity (parā devatā) must be admitted as endowed with all powers (sarva-śakti-yukta). Why? Because of the seeing thereof (tad-darśanāt). Thus śruti shows the conjunction of the supreme Deity with all powers — “Of all action, of all desire, of all scent, of all taste, encompassing this whole, speechless, indifferent” (Chā. Up. 3.14.4); “of true desire, of true resolve” (Chā. Up. 8.7.1); “He who is all-knowing, all-wise” (Mu. Up. 1.1.9); “Verily, Gārgī, by the command of this Imperishable, the sun and moon are held apart” (Bṛ. Up. 3.8.9) — and the like.
BS_C02_S01_V31: If it be objected that, since (Brahman) is devoid of organs (vikaraṇa), it cannot be the cause — that has already been answered.
BS_C02_S01_V31::block-0: Pūrvapakṣa: Let this be said — the scripture teaches that the Supreme Deity is vikaraṇa, devoid of organs, in passages such as ‘acakṣuṣkam aśrotram avāg amanāḥ’ — ‘without eye, without ear, without speech, without mind’ (Bṛ.U. 3.8.8). How then could that Deity, even granted to be possessed of all powers (sarva-śakti-yukta), be capable of producing an effect? For the gods and so on, who are sentient and although endowed with all powers, are observed to be capable of one or another effect only when furnished with the inner organs and outer instruments (ādhyātmika-kārya-karaṇa-sampanna). And how, again, can the conjunction with all powers (sarva-śakti-yoga) be possible for that Deity, from whom every distinguishing feature has been negated by ‘neti neti’ — ‘not thus, not thus’ (Bṛ.U. 3.9.26)? Siddhānta: Whatever has to be said here has indeed been stated already in the earlier portion. This Brahman, profoundly deep, is to be plumbed only by the Śruti and not to be plumbed by reasoning (tarka). Nor is there any rule that whatever capacity is observed in one thing must necessarily belong to another in the same way. That, even for Brahman from whom every distinguishing feature has been negated, the conjunction with all powers is possible — this too has already been declared by setting forth the difference of forms imagined through avidyā (avidyā-kalpita-rūpa-bheda). And accordingly the scripture says, ‘apāṇi-pādo javano grahītā paśyaty acakṣuḥ sa śṛṇoty akarṇaḥ’ — ‘without hands and feet He grasps swiftly; without eye He sees, without ear He hears’ (Śve.U. 3.19), thus showing that, even though Brahman is without organs (akaraṇa), there is yet conjunction of all capacity in Him. ॥ 31 ॥
BS_C02_S01_V32: (Brahman is) not (the cause of the world), because (creative) activity must have a purpose (prayojana). ॥ 32 ॥
BS_C02_S01_V32::block-0: Pūrvapakṣa: Once again it is objected that the world cannot have a sentient agent for its maker — surely the sentient Supreme Self (cetana paramātmā) cannot fashion this great mirror-image which is the world. Why? Because all activities (pravṛtti) presuppose a purpose (prayojanavattva). For in the world a sentient being who acts deliberately (buddhi-pūrva-kārī) is never seen undertaking even a slight activity that does not serve some purpose of his own (ātma-prayojana), let alone an undertaking of greater magnitude. And the Śruti, echoing common observation, declares: ‘na vā are sarvasya kāmāya sarvaṃ priyaṃ bhavati, ātmanas tu kāmāya sarvaṃ priyaṃ bhavati’ — ‘not for the sake of all is everything dear; rather it is for the sake of the Self that everything is dear’ (Bṛ.U. 2.4.5). And this activity is one of vast magnitude — namely, fashioning the variegated mirror-image of high and low that is the world. If even this activity of the sentient Supreme Self were imagined to subserve some purpose of His own, then the perfect contentment (paritṛptatva) of the Supreme Self that is heard of in the Śruti would be contradicted. If, on the other hand, there were no purpose, then there would be no activity either. Now, if it be said that just as one who is sentient yet deranged is observed acting from defect of intellect (buddhy-aparādha) without any self-serving purpose, so the Supreme Self too will act — then in such a case the omniscience (sarvajñatva) of the Supreme Self that is heard of in the Śruti would be contradicted. Therefore creation does not consist with a sentient (cause). ॥ 32 ॥
BS_C02_S01_V33: But (the activity of the Lord is) mere līlā (sport), as in the world. ॥ 33 ॥
BS_C02_S01_V33::block-0: Siddhānta: By the word ‘tu’ (‘but’) the objection is set aside. Just as in the world, in the case of some king or chief minister whose desires are all fulfilled (āpta-eṣaṇa), there occur activities of the form of sport alone (līlā-rūpa) in play and recreation, without aiming at any further purpose; and just as breathing in and breathing out and the like proceed naturally, without aiming at any external purpose; so too, of the Īśvara, there will be an activity that is mere sport (līlā-rūpa) by very nature, without depending on any other purpose. For of the Īśvara no other purpose can be made out, whether by reasoning or from Śruti. Nor can svabhāva (intrinsic nature) be questioned. Although to us this fashioning of the world-mirror appears like a vast undertaking, yet to the Supreme Lord it is mere sport, since His power is unlimited (aparimita-śaktitva). And even granting that in the world some subtle purpose may be conjectured even in sports, here no purpose whatever can be conjectured, on account of the Śruti ‘āpta-kāmaḥ’ — ‘He whose desires are fulfilled.’ Nor again is there absence of activity or deranged activity, on account of the Śruti of creation and the Śruti of omniscience. And this Śruti of creation does not concern the supreme reality (paramārtha); for it lies within the sphere of dealings with names and forms imagined through avidyā (avidyā-kalpita-nāma-rūpa-vyavahāra-gocara), and its purport is the conveying of the Brahman-Self identity (brahma-ātma-bhāva-pratipādana) — this too is by no means to be forgotten. ॥ 33 ॥
BS_C02_S01_V34: Inequality (vaiṣamya) and cruelty (nairghṛṇya) (cannot be charged against the Lord), because of (His) dependence (on karma); and so the Śruti shows. ॥ 34 ॥
BS_C02_S01_V34::block-0: Pūrvapakṣa: Once more the Lord’s being the cause of the origin etc. of the world is challenged, in order to fortify the position already proposed, after the manner of the post-driving illustration (sthūṇā-nikhanana-nyāya). The Lord is not tenable as the cause of the world. Why? Because there would arise the contingency of inequality (vaiṣamya) and cruelty (nairghṛṇya) — fashioning some such as the gods to be sharers in extreme bliss, others such as beasts to be sharers in extreme suffering, and others such as men to be sharers in middling enjoyments. From such a Lord who fashions an unequal creation, attachment and aversion (rāga-dveṣa) just like that of an ordinary person would follow, and there would result the loss of the Lord’s nature of pure transparency (svacchatva) which is firmly established by Śruti and Smṛti. Likewise, there would result cruelty (nairghṛṇya) and extreme harshness, despicable even among ignoble men, by His allotting suffering and by His withdrawing all creatures (in pralaya). Therefore, owing to the contingency of inequality and cruelty, the Lord is not the cause — when this stance is reached, we say: Siddhānta: Inequality and cruelty do not adhere to the Lord. Why? Because of His dependence (sāpekṣatva). For if the Lord, independent and alone (nirapekṣa), fashioned an unequal creation, those two faults would arise — inequality and cruelty. But the Lord is not a fashioner without dependence. He fashions an unequal creation depending (on something). On what does He depend? — we answer, He depends on dharma and adharma. Hence the unequal creation is dependent on the dharma and adharma of the creatures being created, and there is no fault in the Lord. The Lord is to be regarded like the rain-cloud (parjanya) — just as the rain-cloud is the common cause in the sprouting of paddy, barley and the like, but in the diversity among paddy, barley and so forth, the unique potencies (asādhāraṇa-sāmarthya) belonging to the respective seeds are the cause; even so, the Lord is the common cause in the creation of gods, men and the like, but in the diversities among gods, men and the like, the unique karmas belonging to those several jīvas are the cause. Thus the Lord, being dependent (sāpekṣa), is not vitiated by inequality and cruelty. But how is it known that the Lord, depending (on karma), fashions a saṃsāra of low, middling and high? Because the Śruti shows it thus: ‘eṣa hy eva sādhu karma kārayati taṃ yam ebhyo lokebhya unninīṣate, eṣa u evāsādhu karma kārayati taṃ yam adho ninīṣate’ — ‘He alone causes him whom He would lead up from these worlds to do good action; He alone causes him whom He would lead downward to do evil action’ (Kau.U. 3.8); and ‘puṇyo vai puṇyena karmaṇā bhavati pāpaḥ pāpena’ — ‘holy verily by holy action one becomes, sinful by sinful’ (Bṛ.U. 3.2.13). The Smṛti too shows that the Lord’s graciousness and chastisement depend solely on the specific karma of the creatures: ‘ye yathā māṃ prapadyante tāṃs tathaiva bhajāmy aham’ — ‘in whatever way they take refuge in Me, in that very way I requite them’ (Bh.G. 4.11), and the like. ॥ 34 ॥
BS_C02_S01_V35: If it be objected that (karma cannot be the regulating factor), because of non-distinction (avibhāga) (prior to creation) — no, because (saṃsāra is) beginningless (anāditva). ॥ 35 ॥
BS_C02_S01_V35::block-0: Pūrvapakṣa: From the determination ‘sad eva somyedam agra āsīd ekam evādvitīyam’ — ‘in the beginning, dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second’ (Chā.U. 6.2.1), avibhāga (non-distinction) is established prior to creation; hence there exists no karma in dependence on which the creation could be unequal. For karma depends upon the differentiation of bodies and the like, which is post-creation; and the differentiation of bodies and the like depends upon karma — so mutual dependence (itaretarāśrayatva) would arise. Therefore, after differentiation, let the Lord act depending on karma; but prior to differentiation, since the karma which is the cause of variety is absent, the first creation must come out uniform — if this be objected: Siddhānta: This is no defect, on account of the beginninglessness (anāditva) of saṃsāra. This defect would arise if saṃsāra had a beginning. But in a beginningless saṃsāra, like seed and sprout (bīja-aṅkura) by the relation of cause and effect (hetu-hetumad-bhāva), the operation of karma and of the diversity of creation does not contradict (each other). ॥ 35 ॥
BS_C02_S01_V36: And (the beginninglessness of saṃsāra) is reasonable, and is also observed (in Śruti and Smṛti). ॥ 36 ॥
BS_C02_S01_V36::block-0: Leading bhāṣya: But how is it known that this saṃsāra is beginningless? In answer, He recites:
BS_C02_S01_V36::block-1: Siddhānta: The beginninglessness of saṃsāra is reasonable (upapadyate). For if saṃsāra had a beginning, since it would have arisen suddenly out of nothing, even the liberated would face the contingency of saṃsāra’s arising again, and there would result the contingency of acquiring what was not earned (akṛta-abhyāgama), since the inequality of pleasure, pain and the like would be without cause. And it has already been said that the Lord is not the cause of inequality. Nor is avidyā alone the cause of inequality, since it is uniform in nature (eka-rūpatva). But avidyā, dependent upon karma propelled by the latent impressions of the kleśas like rāga and the rest (rāgādi-kleśa-vāsanā-ākṣipta-karma-apekṣā), would generate inequality. And karma cannot exist without a body, and a body cannot exist without karma — so mutual dependence (itaretarāśrayatva) would arise. But on (saṃsāra’s) beginninglessness, by the maxim of seed and sprout (bīja-aṅkura-nyāya), it is reasonable, and no fault arises. The beginninglessness of saṃsāra is also observed (upalabhyate) from Śruti and Smṛti. In Śruti, ‘anena jīvenātmanā’ — ‘by means of this jīva-self’ (Chā.U. 6.3.2): at the very forefront of creation, addressing the embodied Self with the term jīva, on account of its sustaining the prāṇas (prāṇa-dhāraṇa-nimitta), it shows that saṃsāra is beginningless. If saṃsāra had a beginning, how could one — not having previously sustained prāṇas — be addressed at the very forefront of creation by the term jīva, whose etymological ground is the sustaining of prāṇas? Nor could He be so addressed because He will (in future) sustain — for of a future relation, a past relation is stronger, since it is already accomplished (abhiniṣpanna). The mantra ‘sūryācandramasau dhātā yathāpūrvam akalpayat’ — ‘the Disposer fashioned the sun and the moon as before’ (Ṛg-Saṃhitā 10.190.3) likewise shows the existence of a previous kalpa. In Smṛti, too, the beginninglessness of saṃsāra is observed: ‘na rūpam asyeha tathopalabhyate, nānto na cādir na ca sampratiṣṭhā’ — ‘its form is not perceived here as such, nor end, nor beginning, nor base’ (Bh.G. 15.3). And in the Purāṇa it is established that of the past and future kalpas there is no measure. ॥ 36 ॥
BS_C02_S01_V37: And because all the (causal) attributes (sarva-dharma) are tenable (only in Brahman). ॥ 37 ॥
BS_C02_S01_V37::block-0: Siddhānta: The Vedic sense being firmly settled — that the cetana (sentient) Brahman is the cause and the material (prakṛti) of the world — the Ācārya has refuted such defects as ‘dissimilarity (vailakṣaṇya)’ and the like raised by the opponents. Now, about to commence a chapter principally devoted to refuting the opposing positions, He concludes the chapter principally devoted to the establishment of His own position. Because, in this Brahman being accepted as the cause, all the dharmas of a cause come out tenable in the manner shown — namely, that ‘Brahman is omniscient (sarvajñam), all-powerful (sarva-śakti) and possessed of great māyā (mahāmāyam)’ — therefore this Aupaniṣada darśana is not to be doubted at all. ॥ 37 ॥
BS_C02_S02_INTRO1::block-0: Introductory bhāṣya: Although this śāstra has commenced for the purpose of determining the import (aidaṃparya) of the Vedānta-vākyas, and has not commenced — like a tarka-śāstra — for the purpose of establishing or refuting some siddhānta merely by reasonings (yukti) alone, still, by those who would expound the Vedānta-vākyas, the Sāṅkhya and other darśanas, which are opposed to the right vision (samyag-darśana), must be refuted; and to that end the next pāda commences. Since the determination of the meaning of Vedānta is for the sake of right vision, the establishment of one’s own position by such determination has been effected first — that being more honoured than the refutation of the opposing positions. Objection: For seekers of liberation (mumukṣus), it is fitting to do only the establishment of one’s own position by way of investigating samyag-darśana, which is the means to mokṣa. What is the use of refuting the opponent’s position, which produces dislike of the opponents? Reply: Quite so. Yet, on observing that the great schools of the Sāṅkhyas and others, accepted by great men, have proceeded under the appearance of being samyag-darśana, there might arise the expectation in some dull-minded people: ‘these too are to be adopted for samyag-darśana,’ since reasoning may seem cogent in them, and since they may be supposed to have been spoken by an omniscient one, and they have a measure of faith in them — therefore an effort is made to establish the unsoundness (asāratā) of those (schools). Objection: Even before, in ‘īkṣater nāśabdam’ (Br.Sū. 1.1.5), ‘kāmāc ca nānumāna-apekṣā’ (Br.Sū. 1.1.18) and ‘etena sarve vyākhyātā vyākhyātāḥ’ (Br.Sū. 1.4.28), the positions of Sāṅkhya and others have been refuted. Why again do what has been done? Reply: To this it is said — the Sāṅkhyas and others, in order to establish their own positions, even cite Vedānta-vākyas and explain them by joining them only to suit their own positions; whatever exposition of theirs there is, that is a semblance of exposition (vyākhyāna-ābhāsa), not a right exposition — only this much was done before; here, however, the refutation of their reasonings is undertaken independently, without depending on (Vedānta) statements — this is the distinguishing feature.
BS_C02_S02_V01::block-0: Sūtra 2.2.1: "And because of the impossibility of [intelligent] construction, [pradhāna] is not the inferential ground." The insentient pradhāna of the Sāṅkhyas cannot be inferred as the world's cause, since orderly fashioning of effects is never seen apart from a conscious agent.
BS_C02_S02_V01::block-1: Bhāṣya: Here the Sāṅkhyas hold that — just as differences such as pots, saucers and the like, being pervaded by the nature of clay, are seen in the world to have for their antecedent the common substratum that is clay, in the same way all differences whatsoever, external (bāhya) and inward (ādhyātmika), being pervaded by the nature of pleasure, pain and delusion (sukha-duḥkha-moha), must necessarily have for their antecedent a common substratum whose nature is pleasure, pain and delusion. That common reality whose nature is pleasure, pain and delusion is the three-stranded pradhāna (triguṇa-pradhāna); and being insentient like clay, it engages by its own nature alone, through its variegated transformative form, in order to accomplish the purpose (artha) of the conscious puruṣa. By marks such as limited magnitude (parimāṇa) and the rest also they infer that very pradhāna.
BS_C02_S02_V01::block-2: Bhāṣya — siddhānta reply: To this we say — if this were determined merely by the strength of the example (dṛṣṭānta-bala), nowhere in the world is anything insentient seen, unguided by a conscious being and acting independently, fashioning specific transformations capable of accomplishing the determinate purposes of a person. For houses, palaces, beds, seats, places of recreation and so forth are seen in the world to be constructed by skilled craftsmen possessed of intelligence, in such a way as to be fit, at the proper time, for the gaining of pleasure and the avoidance of pain. In just the same way this entire world — earth and the rest externally, and the body and the rest inwardly, fitted for the experience of the fruits of manifold karmans, joined to manifold species, possessed of an exactly determinate arrangement of parts, the substratum for the experience of the fruits of many actions — though seen, is such that even craftsmen of the very highest conceivable intelligence could not so much as picture it in thought; how then could insentient pradhāna fashion it? Such a thing has never been seen in clods, stones and the like. Even in clay and the like, when presided over by a potter and so on, fashioning of a determinate shape is seen — by parity, pradhāna too would have to be presided over by some other conscious entity. Nor is there any restrictive ground for saying that the root cause must be ascertained only by that property which inheres in the material self-nature of clay and the like, and not by that which depends upon an external potter and the rest. And on this view nothing is contradicted; on the contrary, śruti is supported, since a conscious cause is delivered. Therefore, on the ground that orderly construction is not possible (racanānupapatti), the world's cause is not to be inferred as insentient. "And because of the failure of co-presence (anvaya) and the rest" — by the word "and" (ca) the unestablishedness of the proposed reason is also gathered up. For the co-presence of external and inward differences with the natures of pleasure, pain and delusion is not warranted, because pleasure and the rest are cognized as inward, while sound and the rest are cognized as not of that form, and as the occasioning conditions of those (pleasures); and even when sound and the rest are uniform, the differences in pleasure and the rest are obtained only through differences in mental disposition (bhāvanā-viśeṣa). So too, having seen that limited differences such as roots, sprouts and the rest are antecedently composite (saṃsarga-pūrvaka), and inferring on that ground that external and inward differences too, being limited, are antecedently composite — there would be the consequence that sattva, rajas and tamas themselves are antecedently composite, since the limitedness is uniform. As for the cause-effect relation (kārya-kāraṇa-bhāva), it is seen in beds, seats and the like, which are made through forethought; therefore from the cause-effect relation it cannot be supposed that external and inward differences have an insentient antecedent. ||1||
BS_C02_S02_V02::block-0: Sūtra 2.2.2: "And because of [the impossibility of independent] activity (pravṛtti)." The very initial activity by which the equipoise of the guṇas is broken cannot belong to an insentient pradhāna acting on its own.
BS_C02_S02_V02::block-1: Bhāṣya: Let the matter of construction (racanā) be set aside for the moment. Even that activity (pravṛtti) by means of which it is to be accomplished — namely, the falling away from the state of equipoise (sāmyāvasthāna), the entering of sattva, rajas and tamas into the relation of subordinate and principal (aṅgāṅgi-bhāva), and the becoming directed towards a determinate effect — even that is not warranted in the case of insentient pradhāna acting independently, since it is nowhere seen in clay, chariots and the like. For neither clay and the rest, nor chariots and the rest, being themselves insentient, are seen, when not presided over by conscious agents — by potters and the rest, by horses and the rest — to engage in activity directed towards a determinate effect. And from the seen the unseen is established (dṛṣṭāc cādṛṣṭa-siddhiḥ). Therefore, on the ground of the impossibility of activity (pravṛtty-anupapatti) too, the world's cause is not to be inferred as insentient.
BS_C02_S02_V02::block-2: Bhāṣya — pūrvapakṣa: Now [you will say], activity is not seen in the conscious one either, when isolated. True; yet activity is seen in an insentient thing such as a chariot, when conjoined with the conscious; whereas activity is not seen in the conscious one when conjoined with the insentient. Which then is here proper — that activity belongs to that in which it is seen, or that it belongs to that on conjunction with which it is seen? Surely the proper view is that activity belongs to that in which it is seen, since both [the locus and the activity] are perceptible; but the conscious one in isolation is not perceptible like a chariot as the locus of activity. The existence of the conscious one is established only as conjoined with body and the rest, which are the locus of activity — for the living body is observed to differ from the merely insentient chariot and the like. For just this reason the Lokāyatikas have concluded that consciousness too belongs to the body itself, since it is perceived where the body is and not perceived where it is not. Hence activity belongs to the insentient itself.
BS_C02_S02_V02::block-3: Bhāṣya — siddhānta: To this it is replied: We do not say that activity does not belong to that insentient thing in which it is seen. Let it indeed belong to that. But we say that it arises from the conscious — being where the conscious is and not being where the conscious is not. Just as the modification (vikriyā) characterized as burning, illumination and the like, though resorting to wood and the rest [as locus] and not perceived in fire taken alone, nevertheless arises from fire alone, being seen in conjunction with it and not seen in its absence — just so. Even for the Lokāyatikas, the conscious body alone is seen as the prompter of insentient chariots and the rest; thus the prompter-status of the conscious is not contradicted. — Objection: But on your view too, since for the Self conjoined with body and the like, apart from being mere consciousness in nature (vijñāna-svarūpa-mātra), no activity is warranted, prompter-status is unwarranted. — Reply: No. For prompter-status is warranted even for what lacks activity, as in the case of the loadstone (ayaskānta) and of colour and the rest. As the loadstone, itself devoid of activity, becomes the prompter of iron, or as colour and the other objects, themselves devoid of activity, become prompters of the eye and the rest, so the Lord (Īśvara), though devoid of activity, being all-pervading, the Self of all, omniscient and all-powerful, may prompt all — this is warranted. — Objection: Owing to oneness (ekatva), since there is nothing to be prompted, prompter-status is not warranted. — Reply: No. For this has been refuted again and again by recourse to the māyā-immersion of names and forms presented through avidyā (avidyā-pratyupasthāpita-nāmarūpa-māyāveśa). Therefore activity is possible on omniscience as the cause, but not on insentience as the cause. ||2||
BS_C02_S02_V03::block-0: Sūtra 2.2.3: "If [it be said,] like milk and water [pradhāna acts spontaneously], even there [a conscious presider is required]." The example of milk flowing for the calf or water flowing for the world does not establish independent insentient activity, since even there a conscious presider is implied.
BS_C02_S02_V03::block-1: Bhāṣya — pūrvapakṣa: Let it be thus — just as milk, though insentient, flows by its very own nature for the growth of the calf, and just as water, though insentient, flows by its very own nature for the welfare of the world, so pradhāna, though insentient, will engage in activity by its very own nature for the accomplishment of the puruṣa's purpose.
BS_C02_S02_V03::block-2: Bhāṣya — siddhānta: This is not well said, for there too we infer that the activity of milk and water belongs to them only as presided over by a conscious entity, since in a chariot and the like — accepted as insentient by both disputants — activity is never seen in isolation. And the śāstra — "He who, abiding in the waters … who within the waters governs them" (Bṛhad-Āraṇyaka Up. 3.7.4), "By the rule of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, some rivers flow eastward" (Bṛhad-Āraṇyaka Up. 3.8.9), and texts of this class — proclaim that the entire world-process is presided over by Īśvara. Therefore the comparison "like milk and water" is no real ground, since the example itself is lodged within the very thesis to be proved (sādhya-pakṣa-nikṣiptatva). For the cow, being conscious, is the prompter of the milk through her affection [for the calf], and the milk is also drawn out by the calf's sucking. Nor is water altogether independent, since flow depends on lower terrain and the like; and dependence on the conscious has been pointed out everywhere. As for the [earlier] sūtra "Not, since there is observation of recombination — no, for it is like milk" (Brahma-sūtra 2.1.24), there it was illustrated, by way of common worldly observation, that an effect may proceed even from its own substratum without dependence on an external instrumental cause. From the standpoint of śāstra, however, dependence on Īśvara everywhere is implied and is not set aside. ||3||
BS_C02_S02_V04::block-0: Sūtra 2.2.4: "And because [pradhāna stands] devoid of relation [to anything other than itself], owing to non-dependence (anapekṣatva)." Since pradhāna depends on nothing extrinsic to itself, it could not, on its own account, alternately transform and not transform.
BS_C02_S02_V04::block-1: Bhāṣya: For the Sāṅkhyas, the three guṇas standing in equipoise are pradhāna; and there is nothing extrinsic to it — to be looked to as a prompter or restrainer of pradhāna — that abides as something external. Puruṣa is indifferent (udāsīna), neither prompter nor restrainer; therefore pradhāna is non-dependent (anapekṣa). And being non-dependent, that pradhāna should at one time transform into the form of mahat and the rest, and at another time not transform — this is unwarranted. In the case of Īśvara, however, since He is omniscient, all-powerful and the great wielder of māyā (mahā-māyatva), [the alternation of] activity and non-activity stands in no contradiction. ||4||
BS_C02_S02_V05::block-0: Sūtra 2.2.5: "And not, like grass and the rest, owing to absence elsewhere (anyatra-abhāva)." The example of grass turning into milk does not support pradhāna's spontaneous transformation, since even there an instrumental cause is observed.
BS_C02_S02_V05::block-1: Bhāṣya — pūrvapakṣa: Let it be thus — as grass, leaves, water and the like, without dependence on any other instrumental cause, are spontaneously transformed into milk and the like, so pradhāna too will be spontaneously transformed into the form of mahat and the rest. — How is it concluded that grass and the rest are independent of any other instrumental cause? — From the non-apprehension of any other instrumental cause; for if any instrumental cause were apprehended, we should at will, by means of it, take grass and the rest and produce milk; but we do not so produce. Therefore the transformation of grass and the rest is spontaneous (svābhāvika). So too in the case of pradhāna.
BS_C02_S02_V05::block-2: Bhāṣya — siddhānta: To this it is replied — pradhāna's transformation might indeed be spontaneous, like that of grass and the rest, if even the transformation of grass and the rest were granted to be spontaneous; but this is not granted, since another instrumental cause is apprehended. — How is another instrumental cause apprehended? — On account of absence elsewhere (anyatra-abhāva). For only when consumed by a milch cow does grass and the rest become milk, not when discarded, nor when consumed by a draught-bull and the like. If this were without instrumental cause, then grass and the rest would become milk even apart from connection with the cow's body. Nor does the mere fact that human beings cannot at will produce it make it without cause. For some effects are producible by men and others by destiny. Even men can, by an appropriate means, take grass and the rest and produce milk: those desiring abundant milk feed the cow abundant fodder and pasture her, and thence obtain abundant milk. Therefore the transformation of pradhāna is not spontaneous after the manner of grass and the rest. ||5||
BS_C02_S02_V06::block-0: Sūtra 2.2.6: "Even if [spontaneous activity be] granted, owing to the absence of [any] purpose (artha-abhāva)." Even granting pradhāna's spontaneous activity, no coherent purpose for it can be assigned.
BS_C02_S02_V06::block-1: Bhāṣya: It has been established that pradhāna's activity is not spontaneous. But even if, accommodating your conviction, we should grant pradhāna's activity to be spontaneous, defect would still attach. Whence? From the absence of any purpose (artha-abhāva). If, in the first place, it be said that pradhāna's activity is spontaneous and looks to nothing else here, then, just as it looks to no auxiliary, so it will look to no purpose either; in which case the very thesis — "pradhāna engages in activity in order to accomplish the puruṣa's purpose" — would lapse. — Should the opponent say: it looks to no auxiliary alone, but does look to a purpose — then too the purpose of pradhāna's activity must be discriminated: would it be enjoyment (bhoga), or release (apavarga), or both? If enjoyment — what kind of enjoyment can there be for the puruṣa to whom no excellence can be added (anādheyātiśaya)? And the consequence would be that there is no liberation (anirmokṣa-prasaṅga).
