If release — since release is established even prior to activity, the activity becomes purposeless; and the consequence would be the non-apprehension of sound and the rest. Even granting both purposes, since the things to be enjoyed — the modifications of pradhāna — are infinite, the consequence of non-liberation still stands. Nor is activity for the cessation of restlessness (autsukya-nivṛtti); for restlessness is not possible in insentient pradhāna, nor in the puruṣa, who is unstained and partless. If activity is for fear of the futility of the powers of seeing and of creating (dṛk-śakti and sarga-śakti) — then, since the power of seeing is uninterrupted and the power of creation is likewise uninterrupted, the saṃsāra would be uninterrupted, and the consequence of non-liberation again. Therefore that pradhāna's activity is for the puruṣa's purpose is not warranted. ||6||
BS_C02_S02_V07::block-0: Sūtra 2.2.7: "If [it be objected,] like the [lame and blind] person and the loadstone — even so [the same defect remains]." The analogies of a lame man riding a blind man, or a loadstone moving iron, do not save the Sāṅkhya position; the defect of non-liberation persists.
BS_C02_S02_V07::block-1: Bhāṣya — pūrvapakṣa: Let it be thus — as a man endowed with the power of sight but devoid of the power of motion, a lame man, mounting upon another man endowed with the power of motion but devoid of the power of sight, a blind man, prompts him; or as the loadstone (ayaskānta), itself non-moving, prompts iron — so will puruṣa prompt pradhāna; — thus, by trust in [these] examples, the opponent stands his ground again.
BS_C02_S02_V07::block-2: Bhāṣya — siddhānta: To this it is replied — even so, no escape from the defect is possible. For first, the abandonment of one's own admission attaches as defect, since pradhāna's activity has been admitted to be independent (svatantra), and puruṣa's prompter-status has not been admitted. Further, how should puruṣa, being indifferent, prompt pradhāna? For even the lame prompts the blind by speech and the like. There is, however, no operation of prompting whatsoever in puruṣa, since he is actionless (niṣkriya) and free from attributes (nirguṇa). Nor could he prompt by mere proximity (sannidhi-mātra) as the loadstone does, since on that view, proximity being permanent, activity too would be the consequence as permanent. As for the loadstone — its proximity is impermanent, so it has its own operation of approach, and it requires polishing and the like — therefore the comparison "like the loadstone (puruṣāśmavat)" is no real ground. So too, since pradhāna is insentient and puruṣa indifferent, and since there is no third entity to bring the two into relation, the relation itself is unwarranted. And on a relation grounded in fitness (yogyatā-nimitta), since fitness is not destroyed, the consequence of non-liberation again. As before, here too the absence of purpose is to be considered. — But for the supreme Self, indifference (audāsīnya) is intrinsic, dependent on his own nature (svarūpa-vyapāśraya), and prompter-status is dependent on māyā (māyā-vyapāśraya); thus the [Vedāntin's] preeminence stands. ||7||
BS_C02_S02_V08::block-0: Sūtra 2.2.8: "And because of the impossibility of the relation of subordinate and principal (aṅgi-tva-anupapatti)." In the state of equipoise, the guṇas cannot enter into the relation of subordinate and principal, hence the production of mahat and the rest is impossible.
BS_C02_S02_V08::block-1: Bhāṣya: For this further reason too, pradhāna's activity is not warranted — for the state of pradhāna is the abiding of sattva, rajas and tamas in equipoise, by their mere self-form, having abandoned the relation among themselves of guṇa and principal (anyonya-guṇa-pradhāna-bhāva). In that state, since their self-forms are non-dependent (anapekṣa-svarūpa) and there is fear of the destruction of their self-forms, the mutual entry into the relation of subordinate and principal (paraspara-aṅgāṅgi-bhāva) is not warranted; and since there is no external agitator (kṣobhayitṛ), the production of mahat and the rest, occasioned by the disequilibrium of the guṇas (guṇa-vaiṣamya-nimitta), would not occur. ||8||
BS_C02_S02_V09: And even on a different inference, because of the absence of the power of cognition (jña-śakti) [in pradhāna, the difficulties remain] (sūtra 9).
BS_C02_S02_V09::block-0: Now suppose [the Sāṅkhya] should plead thus: We infer [the guṇas] in another way, such that the immediately preceding fault would not arise. For we do not admit the guṇas to be of an absolutely independent nature and immutable (kūṭastha), since there is no pramāṇa for that. Rather, the nature of the guṇas is admitted only as conformable to their effects (kārya-vaśena). In whatever way the production of the effect is intelligible, in that way alone is their nature admitted; and there is also the admission that ‘the functioning of the guṇas is unsteady (calaṁ guṇa-vṛttam).’ Therefore, even in the state of equilibrium (sāmya-avasthā), the guṇas remain such as to be capable of inequality (vaiṣamya-upagama-yogyāḥ). — Even so, since pradhāna is devoid of the power of cognition (jña-śakti-viyogāt), the previously stated faults — the impossibility of arrangement (racanā-anupapatti) and the rest — stand exactly as before. Moreover, one who would infer also a power of cognition [in pradhāna] would, by that very fact, cease to be a counter-disputant (prativādī), since he would slide into the Brahma-vāda — namely, that the one conscious [principle] is the material cause (upādāna) of this manifold expanse of the world. Further, even guṇas fit to assume inequality, in the state of equilibrium, would either never enter into inequality, due to the absence of any occasioning cause (nimitta), or, if they did, they would, since the absence of any occasioning cause is uniform [at all times], be in inequality always. Thus this immediately following fault as well becomes inevitable (sūtra 9).
BS_C02_S02_V10: And [the Sāṅkhya doctrine is] inconsistent on account of mutual contradiction (vipratiṣedha) (sūtra 10).
BS_C02_S02_V10::block-0: This admission of the Sāṅkhyas is also mutually self-contradictory. Somewhere they enumerate seven sense-organs (indriyāṇi), elsewhere eleven; somewhere they teach the creation of the tan-mātras from mahat, elsewhere from ahaṁ-kāra; somewhere they describe three internal organs (antaḥkaraṇāni), elsewhere only one. Moreover, well-known is their conflict with Śruti, which proclaims Īśvara as the cause, and with Smṛti that follows it. Therefore on this ground also the doctrine of the Sāṅkhyas is inconsistent (asamañjasa).
BS_C02_S02_V10::block-1: Here [the pūrvapakṣin] objects: But the doctrine of the Aupaniṣadas (Vedāntins) is itself inconsistent, because they do not admit a difference of category (jāty-antara-bhāva) between the experiencer of pain (tapya) and the inflicter of pain (tāpaka). For those who admit one Brahman, of the nature of all (sarvātmaka), as the cause of the entire expanse, must admit that the tapya and tāpaka are merely two aspects (viśeṣau) of one and the same Self, not of distinct categories. And if these tapya and tāpaka be aspects of one Self, that [Self] could never be released from these two — so the śāstra teaching right knowledge (samyag-darśana) for the cessation of suffering would be rendered futile. For the lamp, whose dharmas are heat and light, while remaining as such, cannot be released from these two. As for the illustration of water with its waves, ripples, foam and so on — even there the waves and the rest are eternal as aspects of the water-self under the modes of manifestation and non-manifestation (āvirbhāva-tirobhāva); hence the water-self has equally no release from waves and the rest. Moreover, the difference of category between tapya and tāpaka is well-established in the world. Thus: the seeker (arthin) and the object sought (artha) are observed to be mutually distinct. If the artha were not other than the arthin in itself, then [say] the artha which is the object of his desire would already be eternally accomplished; and so he would have no desire for it — just as for a lamp, whose self is light, the so-called artha ‘light’ is already eternally accomplished, and he has no longing toward it; for desire pertains only to an unattained object. Likewise, the artha would no longer be artha. If it were so, it would be its own artha. But this is not the case. ‘Arthin’ and ‘artha’ are correlative terms (sambandhi-śabdau). And relation is between two correlatives, not of a single thing with itself. Therefore artha and arthin are distinct. So too anartha and the one to whom anartha pertains. The favourable to the arthin is artha; the unfavourable is anartha. With these two, one [puruṣa] is connected by turn. There, since artha is meagre and anartha abundant, both artha and anartha together are anartha alone; that is called tāpaka. The puruṣa is the tapya, who alone is connected with both alternately. Hence, on the supposition that tapya and tāpaka are one Self, mokṣa would be impossible. But if there be a difference of category, then by removing the cause of their conjunction, mokṣa might at some time be intelligible.
BS_C02_S02_V10::block-2: Here we reply: No. From oneness itself, the relation of tapya and tāpaka is impossible. — This fault would arise if, on the unity-of-Self view, tapya and tāpaka assumed a relation of viṣaya–viṣayī (object–subject) toward each other. But this is not the case, precisely because of unity. For fire, being one, does not burn its own self, nor illumine itself, even though there is a distinction of dharmas such as heat, light, etc., and even though it is subject to modification. How much less, then, in the immutable (kūṭastha) Brahman, which is one, can the tapya–tāpaka relation arise? — Where, then, is this tapya–tāpaka relation? — We say: Why do you not see — the living body, being the karma-product, is the tapya; the sun and the like is the tāpaka. — But surely, ‘scorching’ (tapti) means pain, and pain belongs to the conscious one (cetayitṛ), not to the insentient body. For if the pain belonged to the body alone, it would perish of itself with the perishing of the body, and one would not need to seek means for its destruction. — We answer: In the absence of the body, no pain has been observed for the conscious one taken alone. Nor do you yourself accept that pain, qua transformation (vikriyā), pertains to the conscious one taken alone. Nor again is there union (saṁhata-tva) of body and consciousness, for the fault of admixture of impurity etc. would follow. Nor do you admit pain of pain itself. How then can you yourself uphold the tapya–tāpaka relation? — If [the Sāṅkhya says] sattva is tapya and rajas is tāpaka, [we reply] no, for it is impossible to admit the union of consciousness with these two. — If [it be said] that since the conscious one conforms to sattva, it is, as it were, scorched (tapyate iva) — then by the use of the word ‘iva,’ in truth it is not scorched at all. And if it is not scorched, the word ‘iva’ does no harm. For a non-poisonous water-snake (ḍuṇḍubha) does not become poisonous merely by being likened to a serpent (sarpa iva), nor does a serpent become non-poisonous by being likened to a water-snake. Hence this tapya–tāpaka relation is brought about by avidyā (avidyā-kṛta) and is not absolutely real (pāramārthika) — this must be admitted. And if so, nothing in our position is impaired. But if you admit the experience of being scorched of the conscious one as absolutely real, then on your own view non-liberation (anirmokṣa) follows all the more, since you also admit the eternality of the tāpaka. — If [you reply] that although the powers of tapya and tāpaka are eternal, since pain (tapti) depends on a conjunction occasioned by a [particular] cause, when the occasioning of the conjunction is no longer perceived (adarśana-nivṛtti), there is absolute cessation of conjunction and consequently absolute mokṣa is intelligible — [we say] no. For you admit the eternality of darkness (tamas), the non-perceiving (adarśana). And since the rising and suppression (udbhava-abhibhava) of the guṇas are not regulated, the cessation of the occasioning of conjunction is also not regulated; thus separation (viyoga) too is unregulated, and non-liberation (anirmokṣa) becomes unavoidable for the Sāṅkhya himself. As for the Aupaniṣada, since the unity of the Ātman (ātma-ekatva) is admitted, since the viṣaya–viṣayī relation in one [Self] is impossible, and since the difference of modification is heard [in Śruti] to be merely a matter of speech (vāc-ārambhaṇa-mātra), the apprehension of non-liberation does not arise even in dream. As for vyavahāra — there, where the tapya–tāpaka relation is observed in such-and-such manner, there in just that manner it stands; it is neither to be challenged nor to be defended (sūtra 10).
BS_C02_S02_V11: Or [the production of an effect of dissimilar quality is] like the great-and-long [arising] from the short-and-spherical (sūtra 11).
BS_C02_S02_V11::block-0: [Leading bhāṣya:] The doctrine that pradhāna is the cause has been refuted; now the doctrine that the atoms (paramāṇu) are the cause must be refuted. First, the fault that the atom-vādin imagines against the Brahma-vādin is to be answered. Here is the admission of the Vaiśeṣikas: the guṇas inhering in the cause-substance (kāraṇa-dravya-samavāyinaḥ) initiate, in the effect-substance (kārya-dravya), another guṇa of the same class — for from white threads is observed the production of a white cloth, and the contrary is not observed. Therefore, when conscious Brahman is admitted as the cause of the world, consciousness should also inhere in the world as effect; but it is not observed; hence conscious Brahman cannot be the cause of the world. — He refutes this very admission by their own procedure:
BS_C02_S02_V11::block-1: This is their procedure: the paramāṇus, for some time not having begun any effect, remain endowed with form etc. according to their nature, and have the dimension called pārimāṇḍalya (sphericality of the smallest order). Then, preceded by adṛṣṭa and aided by saṁyoga (conjunction), they begin the entire host of effects in the order of dyad (dvy-aṇuka) and so on; and the cause-guṇas initiate other guṇas in the effect. When two paramāṇus initiate a dyad, the special guṇas inhering in the paramāṇus — whiteness etc., qualities of form etc. — initiate other whitenesses etc. in the dyad. But the special paramāṇu-guṇa pārimāṇḍalya does not initiate another pārimāṇḍalya in the dyad, since the dyad is admitted to be associated with a different dimension. For they describe two dimensions inhering in the dyad — minuteness (aṇutva) and shortness (hrasvatva). When two dyads initiate a quaternary (catur-aṇuka), the dyad-inhering whitenesses etc. likewise initiate; but the dyad-inhering aṇutva and hrasvatva do not initiate, since the quaternary is admitted to be associated with the dimensions of greatness (mahattva) and length (dīrghatva). And when many paramāṇus, or many dyads, or a paramāṇu together with a dyad, produce an effect, the same scheme applies. Thus: just as from the spherical (parimaṇḍala) paramāṇu arises a dyad which is minute (aṇu) and short (hrasva), and from that the great and long triad (try-aṇuka) etc., not the spherical; or just as from the dyad which is minute and short arises the great and long triad, not the minute, not the short — so also from conscious Brahman an unconscious world will be born; on this admission, what has been mutilated for you?
BS_C02_S02_V11::block-2: Now, if you think: the effect-substance — dyad etc. — is invaded by an opposed dimension (virodhinā parimāṇāntareṇa ākrāntam), and so the cause-resident pārimāṇḍalya etc. are not initiators — that I admit; but the world is not invaded by any guṇa opposed to consciousness, by reason of which the cause-resident consciousness should fail to initiate another consciousness in the effect; for there is no guṇa called ‘unconsciousness (acetanā)’ opposed to consciousness, it being merely the negation of consciousness. Therefore, by the very disparity from pārimāṇḍalya etc., consciousness must be an initiator. — Do not think so: just as pārimāṇḍalya etc., though present in the cause, are non-initiators, so also is consciousness — for in this respect the cases are alike. And the invasion by another dimension is not the cause of the non-initiating character of pārimāṇḍalya etc., because pārimāṇḍalya etc. could very well be initiators prior to the initiation of the other dimension; for it is admitted that the initiated effect-substance, prior to the initiation of [its] guṇas, remains for one moment without guṇas. Nor [is it the case that] pārimāṇḍalya etc., being engaged in the initiation of another dimension, do not initiate a dimension of their own class — for the [other] dimension is admitted to have a different cause: the Kāṇabhuja sūtras run, ‘Greatness comes from plurality of cause, magnitude of cause, and a special accumulation’ (Vai.Sū. 7.1.9), ‘The contrary is the minute’ (7.1.10), ‘By this, length and shortness are explained’ (7.1.17). Nor can it be said that, owing to a special proximity from some [factor], they initiate only ‘plurality of cause’ etc. and not pārimāṇḍalya etc., for when another substance or guṇa is being initiated, all the cause-guṇas have equal inherence in their own substrate. Therefore by their very nature pārimāṇḍalya etc. are non-initiators; thus also is consciousness to be regarded.
BS_C02_S02_V11::block-3: Moreover, since substances and so on of dissimilar nature are observed to arise from conjunction, the rule of arising-of-the-same-class is broken (samāna-jātīya-utpatti-vyabhicāra). — If [you say] that when substance is the topic, citing a guṇa as illustration is improper — no; for the illustration is meant only to show the initiation of something dissimilar. There is no rule that for substance only a substance should be cited as illustration, or for a guṇa only a guṇa; the sūtra-author of yours himself has cited a guṇa for substance: ‘Of perceptible-imperceptible objects, owing to the imperceptibility of conjunction, the five-elemental [body] does not exist’ (Vai.Sū. 4.2.2) — meaning, just as conjunction inhering in the perceptible-imperceptible earth and ether is itself imperceptible, so a body inhering in the five elements (some perceptible, some imperceptible) would be imperceptible; but the body is perceptible; therefore it is not made of the five — that is, conjunction is a guṇa, body is a substance. The arising of the dissimilar has also been elaborated here in ‘But it is observed’ (Brahma-Sūtra 2.1.6). — But if so, that very [argument] has covered this case. — No, we say; that was directed against the Sāṅkhya, this against the Vaiśeṣika. — But the extension was made on the ground of equal logic in ‘By this, the unaccepted-by-the-instructed are also explained’ (Brahma-Sūtra 2.1.12). — True; but at the very inception of the examination of the Vaiśeṣika, this elaboration is being made by an illustration drawn from their own procedure (sūtra 11).
BS_C02_S02_V12: On either alternative, no activity (karma) [in the atoms is possible]; therefore the absence of that [creation/dissolution] (sūtra 12).
BS_C02_S02_V12::block-0: Now [Śaṅkara] refutes the doctrine that the paramāṇus are the cause. The doctrine arises thus: in the world, things-with-parts (sāvayava) such as cloths and so on are observed to be initiated by substances of their own connatural sort like threads, accompanied by conjunction. By the universality, whatever is sāvayava is initiated by such-and-such connatural substances accompanied by saṁyoga. The point at which the avayava–avayavin division ceases is the limit of decrement, the paramāṇu. All this — mountains, oceans, etc. — is sāvayava; and being sāvayava, it has a beginning and end. There cannot be an effect without a cause; therefore the paramāṇus are the cause of the world — this is Kaṇabhuk’s view. Observing the four bhūtas — earth, water, fire, air — as having parts, four kinds of paramāṇus are conceived. Since these are at the limit of decrement, division beyond them being impossible, when earth etc. are perishing, division goes only down to the paramāṇus; that is the time of dissolution (pralaya). Then at the time of creation, in the air-paramāṇus, depending on adṛṣṭa, action (karma) arises. That action conjoins the paramāṇu in which it resides with another paramāṇu. From that, by the order of dyad etc., air arises; so fire; so water; so earth; and so the body together with the senses (sendriya). Thus this whole world arises from atoms. And from form etc. inhering in the atoms arise the forms etc. inhering in the dyad etc., on the analogy of thread and cloth — so think the Kāṇādas.
BS_C02_S02_V12::block-1: Here we say: First, the conjunction of the atoms in their state of separation (vibhāga-avasthāna) must be admitted as dependent on action (karma-apekṣa); for conjunction is observed in things possessing action, like threads. And since karma is itself an effect, some occasioning cause (nimitta) must be admitted for it. If not admitted, in the absence of nimitta, no first action could occur in the atoms. Even if admitted, if effort (prayatna) or impact (abhighāta) etc. — observed [causes] — were assumed as the nimitta for action, [their] impossibility would prevent any first action in the atoms. For in that state effort, an attribute of the Self, is impossible, since there is no body. For only when there is conjunction of the Self with the mind which is body-resident does prayatna, an attribute of the Self, arise. By this very [argument], impact and other observed nimittas are also rejected. For all those occur only after creation — none of them can be a nimitta for the first action. — Now if it be said that adṛṣṭa is the nimitta of the first action — that adṛṣṭa would either inhere in the Self (ātma-samavāyī) or in the atom (aṇu-samavāyī). On either alternative, action in the atoms could not be occasioned by adṛṣṭa, because adṛṣṭa is unconscious. The unconscious, unguided by the conscious, does not function or cause to function on its own — this has been laid down in the Sāṅkhya-prakriyā [examination]. And the Self, in that state, having unmanifest consciousness, is itself unconscious. Even on the supposition of inherence in the Self (ātma-samavāyitva), adṛṣṭa cannot be the nimitta for action in the atoms, owing to non-relation. — If [it be said] that the puruṣa possessing adṛṣṭa is connected with the atoms, [we reply] that owing to the constancy of relation, constancy of activity (pravṛtti-sātatya) would follow, since there is no other regulator. Thus, in the absence of any regulated nimitta of action, no first action in the atoms is possible. In the absence of action, the conjunction depending on it would not be; and in the absence of conjunction, the dyad etc. depending on it would not arise. — Further, the conjunction of an atom with another atom — would it be by the whole [atom] or by a part (eka-deśa)? If by the whole, since accumulation would be unintelligible (upacaya-anupapatti), the result would be the persistence of mere atom-magnitude, contrary to what is observed; for conjunction of an extended substance is seen only with another extended substance through their parts. If by a part, it follows that the atom has parts (sāvayava-tva). — If [it be said] that the parts (pradeśas) of the paramāṇus are imagined (kalpita), [we reply] that what is imagined is unreal, and so the conjunction would be unreal; consequently, for the real effect there would be no non-inherent cause (asamavāyi-kāraṇa); and in the absence of the non-inherent cause, the effect-substance dyad etc. would not arise. Just as, at the first creation, action of the atoms for the production of conjunction is not possible owing to absence of nimitta, so also, at the great dissolution (mahā-pralaya), action of the atoms for the production of separation (vibhāga) is not possible. For there too no regulated nimitta is observed. And adṛṣṭa, being for the establishment of enjoyment (bhoga-prasiddhi), not for that of dissolution — for this reason, in the absence of nimitta, action of the atoms for production of conjunction or production of separation cannot exist. Hence, in the absence of conjunction and separation, the absence of creation and dissolution depending on them follows. Therefore the doctrine of paramāṇu-causality is unintelligible (sūtra 12).
BS_C02_S02_V13: And from admitting samavāya (inherence), owing to parity, [there results] non-finality (regress) (sūtra 13).
BS_C02_S02_V13::block-0: ‘And from admitting samavāya — therefore the absence of that’ — this is connected with the present refutation of the atom-doctrine. You admit that a dyad arising from two atoms, while absolutely distinct from those two atoms, inheres in those two by samavāya. But one who admits this cannot establish atom-causality. Why? Owing to parity, non-finality (sāmyāt anavasthiteḥ). For just as the dyad, being absolutely distinct from the two atoms, is connected with them by the relation called samavāya, so also samavāya itself, being absolutely distinct from its samavāyins (its relata), would be connected with them by yet another such samavāya-relation, owing to parity in absolute distinctness. From that, yet another and another relation must be conceived for that one — and thus regress (anavasthā) becomes inevitable. — But samavāya is the object of the cognition ‘here’ (iha-pratyaya-grāhya); it is grasped as eternally connected (nitya-sambaddha) with its samavāyins, not as unconnected and depending on a further relation. Hence no further relation need be conceived for it; thus there is no regress. — No, we reply: in that case, conjunction (saṁyoga) too, [analogously,] is eternally connected with its conjuncts (saṁyogins), and so, like samavāya, would not require another relation. — If [you say] that conjunction, being a different category-thing (artha-antara), requires another relation, then samavāya too, being a different category-thing, must require another relation. Nor can it be properly said that conjunction requires another relation because it is a guṇa, while samavāya, being a non-guṇa, does not — since the ground of requirement is equal in both, and the convention of [calling something a] ‘guṇa’ is not authoritative here. Therefore, for one admitting samavāya as a distinct entity (artha-antara), regress is unavoidable. And when regress is unavoidable, since the failure to establish one [link] entails the failure of all (eka-asiddhau sarva-asiddheḥ), the dyad cannot arise from the two atoms. Therefore on this ground also the doctrine of atom-causality is unintelligible (sūtra 13).
BS_C02_S02_V14: And [there would be] perpetual existence [of pravṛtti or nivṛtti] (sūtra 14).
BS_C02_S02_V14::block-0: Further, the atoms are admitted either as pravṛtti-svabhāva (of the nature of activity), or as nivṛtti-svabhāva (of the nature of cessation), or as both (ubhaya), or as neither (anubhaya) — there being no other alternative. None of the four is intelligible. — On the supposition of pravṛtti-svabhāva, since pravṛtti would be perpetual, it would follow that there is no pralaya (cosmic dissolution). On the supposition of nivṛtti-svabhāva, since nivṛtti would be perpetual, it would follow that there is no sarga (creation). The supposition of both at once is inconsistent (asamañjasa) by reason of contradiction (virodha). On the supposition of neither, when pravṛtti and nivṛtti are admitted as occurring through the influence of nimitta, since the nimitta — adṛṣṭa etc. — is always present (nitya-sannidhāna), perpetual pravṛtti would follow; and if adṛṣṭa etc. is held to be inoperative (atantra), then perpetual non-pravṛtti would follow. Therefore on this ground also the doctrine of atom-causality is unintelligible (sūtra 14).
BS_C02_S02_V15: And because of possessing form etc. (rūpādimat-tva), the contrary [of atomicity and eternality] follows, by observation (sūtra 15).
BS_C02_S02_V15::block-0: What the Vaiśeṣikas admit — that the four kinds of paramāṇus, possessing form etc. (rūpādimantaḥ), at the limit of decrement when sāvayava substances are divided part by part, are the initiators of the four kinds of bhautika (elemental and elemental-derivative) products possessing form etc., and are eternal — this admission is groundless. For, owing to the rūpādimat-tva (possession of form etc.) of the paramāṇus, the contrary of atomicity and eternality follows. That is: as compared to the supreme cause, they would be gross (sthūla) and non-eternal (anitya), the very contrary of what is intended. Why? Because so it is observed in the world. For whatever in the world is rūpādimat is observed to be gross and non-eternal in relation to its own cause; for instance, cloth is gross and non-eternal in relation to threads, and threads in relation to fibres — and these atoms too are admitted by them as rūpādimat. Therefore they too, being possessed of cause, will turn out to be gross and non-eternal in relation to that cause. — The reason they have given for eternality, ‘What is real (sat) and uncaused is eternal’ (Vai.Sū. 4.1.1), does not, on this view, apply to atoms, since on the said showing the atoms also turn out to be possessed of a cause. — The second reason given for eternality, ‘There is no specific denial that they are anitya’ (Vai.Sū. 4.1.4), does not necessarily establish the eternality of the paramāṇus. For unless there be some [other] eternal thing, the compounding of the negation with the word ‘nitya’ would not be possible. But it is not necessarily the eternality of paramāṇus that is meant; the eternal supreme cause Brahman exists. And mere usage of word and meaning does not establish the existence of any object, for the usage of word and meaning operates on objects established by other pramāṇas. — The third reason given, ‘And avidyā,’ if it be expounded thus: ‘the non-perception by perception of the existing causes of effects observed (sat-kāraṇānāṁ pratyakṣeṇa-agrahaṇam) is avidyā’ — then the eternality of the dyad would also follow. If qualified as ‘[not being] a substance’ (a-dravya-tve sati), then merely uncausedness becomes the ground of eternality, and since that has already been stated, ‘And avidyā’ (Vai.Sū. 4.1.5) would be a tautology. — Or if it be expounded as ‘the impossibility of any third destruction-cause besides the disjunction of the cause (kāraṇa-vibhāga) and the destruction of the cause (kāraṇa-vināśa) is avidyā, and that proclaims the eternality of paramāṇus’ — there is no rule that a perishable thing must perish only by these two causes. This would hold if a substance were admitted to be initiated only by another substance accompanied by saṁyoga and consisting of more than one [unit]. But when the cause is admitted to be a generic state (sāmānya-ātmaka), with its specifics removed, undergoing transformation into a state with specifics as initiator, then destruction is intelligible by mere dissolution of the [former] form — as in the melting of the hardness of ghee. Therefore, owing to rūpādimat-tva, the contrary of what is intended would befall the paramāṇus. Therefore on this ground also the doctrine of paramāṇu-causality is unintelligible (sūtra 15).
BS_C02_S02_V16: And on either alternative, owing to fault [the doctrine fails] (sūtra 16).
BS_C02_S02_V16::block-0: Earth has the four guṇas of smell, taste, form, and touch and is gross; water has form, taste and touch and is subtle; fire has form and touch and is subtler; air has touch and is subtlest — thus these four bhūtas, with successively diminishing or increasing guṇas, with the gradation of gross, subtle, subtler, subtlest, are observed in the world. Now, are paramāṇus likewise to be conceived as having such increase and decrease of guṇas, or not? On either alternative, the inevitable application of fault is unavoidable. — Suppose increase and decrease of guṇas be admitted; then, since the increase of guṇas implies an increase of bulk (mūrti-upacaya), the paramāṇus would lose their atomicity (a-paramāṇu-tva). Nor can it be said that there can be increase of guṇa without increase of bulk, since in the bhūta-effects an increase of bulk is observed wherever there is an increase of guṇa. — Suppose increase and decrease of guṇas be not admitted, in order to preserve the parity of paramāṇu-status. Then if all are conceived as having one guṇa each only, there would be no perception of touch in fire, of form-and-touch in water, of taste-form-and-touch in earth — for the qualities of the effect follow the qualities of the cause. — But if all be conceived as having all four guṇas, then there would be perception of smell also in water, of smell-and-taste in fire, of smell-form-and-taste in air. And this is not observed. Therefore on this ground also the doctrine of paramāṇu-causality is unintelligible (sūtra 16).
BS_C02_S02_V17: And on account of its non-acceptance (by the wise), there is absolute disregard (of the atomic doctrine).
BS_C02_S02_V17::block-0: The doctrine of pradhāna as the cause has been set forth in part by some who know the Veda, such as Manu and others, with the intention of utilizing certain aspects like the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (sat-kāryatva). But this doctrine of atoms as the cause has not been accepted, even in any single aspect, by any of the wise. Therefore it deserves absolute disregard from those who follow the Veda. Moreover, the Vaiśeṣikas accept six categories (padārtha) which are the subject-matter of their system — substance (dravya), quality (guṇa), action (karma), generality (sāmānya), particularity (viśeṣa), and inherence (samavāya) — as absolutely distinct, having distinct definitions, just as a man, a horse, and a hare are distinct. Having admitted this, they yet hold that the rest depend upon substance, which contradicts that very admission; this is not tenable. How so? Just as in the world a hare, a kuśa-grass, and a palāśa-leaf, being absolutely distinct from one another, do not depend on one another, so too, since substances and the rest are absolutely distinct, qualities and the rest cannot at all depend on substance. If, on the other hand, qualities and the rest do depend on substance, then since they exist when the substance exists and do not exist when the substance is absent, the substance alone, owing to differences of configuration and so on, would come to be the object of various words and concepts — just as Devadatta, though one, becomes the object of various words and concepts owing to different conditions. In that case the position of the Sāṅkhya siddhānta would be entailed, and there would be a contradiction with their own siddhānta. "But surely, smoke, though distinct from fire, is seen to depend on fire?" True, it is so seen. Yet there, on account of the cognition of difference, the otherness of fire and smoke is established. Here, however — "the blanket is white," "the cow is red," "the lotus is blue" — since the substance itself is cognized as qualified by this or that attribute, there is no cognition of difference between substance and quality such as exists between fire and smoke. Therefore quality is of the nature of substance. By this the substance-nature of action, generality, particularity, and inherence is also explained.
BS_C02_S02_V17::block-1: When it is said that qualities depend on substance because of the non-separateness (ayuta-siddhatva) of substance and quality, this non-separateness must mean either non-separateness of locus, or non-separateness of time, or non-separateness of essential nature. In none of these ways is it tenable. If first non-separateness of locus is asserted, their own admission would be contradicted. How so? The cloth produced by threads is admitted to occupy the locus of the threads, not its own locus as cloth. But the qualities of the cloth — whiteness and the like — are admitted to occupy the locus of the cloth, not the locus of the threads. Thus they say: "Substances commence another substance, and qualities another quality" (Vai. Sū. 1.1.10). For threads, being causal substances, commence the effect-substance, the cloth; and the qualities of the threads, whiteness and the rest, commence in the effect-substance, the cloth, other qualities such as whiteness — this is what they admit. That admission would be nullified if non-separateness of locus between substance and quality were granted. If, again, non-separateness of time were called non-separateness, then non-separateness of the left and right horns of a cow would also follow. And in the case of non-separateness of essential nature being non-separateness, no distinction of selfhood between substance and quality is possible, since it is cognized as identity itself.
BS_C02_S02_V17::block-2: "The relation of two things separately established is conjunction (saṃyoga); of two not separately established it is inherence (samavāya)" — this admission of theirs is empty, since the cause, which is established prior to the effect, cannot be non-separately established from the effect. If this admission were made with regard to one alone — that the relation of the not-separately-established effect with the cause is inherence — even so, the relation of an effect that is not yet established and has not yet attained existence with its cause is not tenable, for relation depends upon two relata. If it be said that having become established it then becomes related, then if the establishment of the effect is admitted prior to its relation with the cause, since there is no non-separate-establishment, the statement "there is no conjunction or disjunction between cause and effect" would be ill-spoken. Just as the relation of a just-produced inactive effect-substance with the all-pervading substances such as ākāśa is admitted to be conjunction alone and not inherence, so too the relation with the causal substance also would be conjunction alone and not inherence. Nor is there any pramāṇa for the existence of the relation, whether conjunction or inherence, apart from the relata. If it be said that on account of seeing words and concepts of conjunction and inherence apart from the words and concepts of the relata, their existence is established — no, because even when there is unity, owing to dependence on the intrinsic and extrinsic forms, manifold words and concepts are seen. Just as Devadatta, though one in the world, becomes the object of manifold words and concepts when his own form and his relational form are considered — "man," "brāhmaṇa," "vedic scholar," "liberal," "boy," "youth," "elder," "father," "son," "grandson," "brother," "son-in-law"; and just as a single line, by being placed in different positions, undergoes the difference of words and concepts as one, ten, hundred, thousand, and so on — so too the very relata, apart from the words and concepts of the relata, are fit to be the objects of the words and concepts of conjunction and inherence, and not on account of any separate entity existing — thus, by the non-perception of what should have been perceived if it existed (upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta-anupalabdhi), there is the absence of any further entity. Nor is there the contingency of an unbroken sequence of words and concepts of relation when their object is the relata, since the answer has already been given that it is by reference to intrinsic and extrinsic forms. Likewise, since atoms, the Self, and the mind are without spatial parts (apradeśa), conjunction is not possible, for it is seen that a substance with parts has conjunction with another substance with parts. If it be said that imagined parts will exist for atoms, the Self, and the mind — no, because if non-existing things are imagined, the establishment of every desired thing would follow. Only this much that does not exist, whether opposed or unopposed, is to be imagined, no more — there is no rule-establishing reason; and since imagination is at one's own disposal and may be in profusion, there is no reason that prevents the Vaiśeṣikas from imagining a hundred or a thousand more categories beyond the six they imagined. Therefore whatever is pleasing to anyone would be established. Some compassionate person might imagine: "Let there not be saṃsāra, full of misery for living beings"; another addicted person might imagine the rebirth even of the liberated; who would prevent these two? And another point — there cannot be any cohesion of the dyad (dvy-aṇuka), which has parts, with two atoms which have no parts, just as there cannot be such cohesion with ākāśa. For there is no cohesion of ākāśa and earth and the rest as there is between lac and wood. If it be said that the relation of substratum and superstratum (āśrita-āśraya-bhāva) between the effect-substance and the cause-substance is not otherwise tenable, and so inherence must necessarily be imagined — no, because of mutual dependence (itaretarāśraya). For the establishment of the relation of substratum and superstratum between cause and effect depends on the establishment of their distinction, and the establishment of their distinction depends on the establishment of the relation of substratum and superstratum — and so on.
BS_C02_S02_V17::block-3: And another point — since atoms are limited (paricchinna), they would have as many parts as there are directions — six, eight, or ten — and being possessed of parts, they would also be non-eternal; thus the admission of their eternality and partlessness would be nullified. If it be said: "The very parts you imagine as differentiated by the difference of directions are themselves my atoms" — no, for owing to the gradation of grossness and subtlety, destruction up to the supreme cause is tenable. Just as earth, though grosser than the dyad and the rest and being a real entity, perishes; and after that, what is subtle and subtler within the same class as earth perishes; and after that, the dyad perishes — so too the atoms also, being of one class with earth, must perish. If it be said: "Even when they perish, they perish only by separation of parts" — there is no fault here, for we have already stated that destruction is tenable also like the melting of the hardness of ghee. For just as the hardness of ghee, gold, and the like, even though their parts are not divided, is destroyed by attainment of fluidity through conjunction with fire, so too in the case of atoms, the destruction of form and so on will occur through their reaching the state of the supreme cause. Likewise the production of an effect does not occur solely by the conjunction of parts, since the production of effects such as curd, hail, and the like from milk, water, and the like is seen even without any further conjunction of parts. Thus, since this doctrine is woven together by the most worthless reasoning, since it contradicts the śruti which speaks of Īśvara as the cause, and since it has not been accepted by the wise inclined to śruti such as Manu and others, those who desire the highest good must show absolute disregard towards this doctrine of atoms as the cause — this is the supplied completion of the sentence.
BS_C02_S02_V18: Even granting an aggregate of two kinds of cause, that aggregate cannot be brought about.
BS_C02_S02_V18::block-0: It has been said that the doctrine of the Vaiśeṣikas should not be regarded, on account of its faulty reasoning, contradiction with the Veda, and non-acceptance by the wise. That doctrine is half-destructionist (ardha-vaināśika); since the doctrine of the total destructionists (sarva-vaināśika) shares this destructionist character, all the more should it not be regarded — this we now establish. That doctrine is of many kinds, owing to differences of conception or differences among disciples. Among them there are three sets of disputants — some hold that all things exist (sarvāstitvavādin); some hold that only consciousness exists (vijñānāstitvamātravādin); others again hold that all is void (sarvaśūnyatvavādin). Among these, those who hold that everything exists, accepting both external and internal entities — element (bhūta) and elemental (bhautika), mind (citta) and mental (caitta) — to them we first reply. Among these, the elements are the earth-element and the rest; the elemental are the colours and the rest, and the eyes and the rest. The atoms of earth and the rest, of the four kinds, have the natures of hardness, viscidity, heat, and motion respectively, and they are aggregated as earth and the rest — so they hold. Likewise, the five aggregates (skandha) called colour (rūpa), consciousness (vijñāna), feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), and dispositions (saṃskāra) — these too, internally, are aggregated as the basis of all dealings (vyavahāra) — so they hold.
BS_C02_S02_V18::block-1: Now this is said — this aggregate (samudāya) of two kinds, of two sorts, that is intended by the opponents — the one having atoms as cause, in the form of the aggregation of element and elemental, and the other having skandhas as cause, in the form of the five skandhas — even when this aggregate of two kinds is held in mind, there would be its non-attainment (tad-aprāpti); that is, the non-attainment of the aggregate, the non-tenability of the very being of the aggregate. How so? Because the constituents of the aggregate are non-conscious. And because the kindling of the citta itself depends on the establishment of the aggregate. And because no other conscious enjoyer (bhoktṛ) or ruler (praśāsitṛ) — a stable aggregator — is admitted. And because, if independent activity (nirapekṣa-pravṛtti) were admitted, the cessation of activity (pravṛtti-anuparama) would not occur. And because the receptacle (āśaya) cannot be defined as either different or non-different. And because, owing to the admission of momentariness (kṣaṇikatva) and consequent inactivity, activity is not tenable. Therefore the aggregate is not tenable; and if the aggregate is not tenable, then the worldly course (loka-yātrā) which depends on it would be cut off.
BS_C02_S02_V19: If it be said that owing to mutual causation (the aggregate is established), it is not so, on account of (mutual causation) being merely the cause of origination.
BS_C02_S02_V19::block-0: Even though no conscious enjoyer (bhoktṛ) or ruler (praśāsitṛ) — a stable aggregator — is admitted, yet the worldly course is tenable owing to the mutual causation (itaretara-kāraṇatva) of avidyā and the rest. And when that is tenable, nothing further need be looked for. These — avidyā, saṃskāra, vijñāna, name, form, the six fields of sense (ṣaḍāyatana), contact, feeling, craving (tṛṣṇā), grasping (upādāna), becoming (bhava), birth (jāti), old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection — and the like, mutually causing one another, are sometimes briefly indicated and sometimes elaborately set forth in the system of the Bauddhas. This series of avidyā and the rest cannot be set aside by any of them. So when this series of avidyā and the rest revolves ceaselessly like a series of pots on a water-wheel by mutual relation of cause and effect, the aggregate (saṅghāta) is implicitly required by the very meaning — this is the pūrvapakṣa view; we say, no. Why? Because of the mere causality of origination (utpatti-mātra-nimittatva) — the aggregate would be tenable if any cause for the aggregate were ascertained, but it is not ascertained; for though there is mutual causation among avidyā and the rest, the previous one becoming the mere cause of origination of each succeeding one is what occurs, but no cause is possible for the origination of the aggregate. "But the aggregate is implicitly required by the very meaning of avidyā and the rest," so it has been said. Here it is replied — if this is the intent: avidyā and the rest, not gaining their own being apart from the aggregate, require the aggregate, then some cause must be stated for that aggregate. And that is not possible even when the eternal atoms admitted (by Vaiśeṣikas) and the enjoyers as substratum and superstratum exist, as has been stated in the examination of the Vaiśeṣikas; how much less when the atoms are momentary, when there is no enjoyer, and when there is no substratum-superstratum relation, as admitted (by Bauddhas)? But if this is the intent — that avidyā and the rest are themselves the cause of the aggregate — how can they, depending on the very aggregate for their own being, be its cause? If you think — "In beginningless saṃsāra, aggregates alone follow in succession, and avidyā and the rest depend on them" — even so, an aggregate produced from another aggregate must either by rule be produced as similar alone, or without rule be produced either similar or dissimilar. If rule is admitted, the human personality would never reach the conditions of god, animal, or hell-being. If no rule is admitted, then the human personality at some moment might become an elephant, and then a god, or again a human — this would result. Both alternatives contradict the admission. Moreover, if the aggregate were for the sake of enjoyment, you do not admit a stable jīva as the enjoyer. From that it follows that enjoyment is for the sake of enjoyment alone, not to be sought by another. Similarly, liberation (mokṣa) is for the sake of liberation alone, and there should be no other seeker of liberation (mumukṣu). If sought by another, then both — enjoyment and liberation — would require a being that abides through the times of enjoyment and of liberation. If there is abiding, then there is contradiction with the admission of momentariness (kṣaṇikatva). Therefore, even if avidyā and the rest are mere causes of origination of one another, let it be so; yet the aggregate is not established, owing to the absence of an enjoyer — this is the import.
BS_C02_S02_V20: And on account of the cessation of the prior at the arising of the subsequent (cause-effect relation is impossible).
BS_C02_S02_V20::block-0: It has been said that, owing to mere causality of origination of avidyā and the rest, the aggregate is not established. But further it is now shown that even that mere causality of origination is not tenable. The admission of the proponents of momentary destruction (kṣaṇa-bhaṅga-vādin) is this — at the arising of the subsequent moment, the prior moment is destroyed. By one who admits thus, the cause-effect relation between prior and subsequent moments cannot at all be brought about, since the prior moment, being either being destroyed or already destroyed, is in the grip of non-existence and so cannot be the cause of the subsequent moment. If, again, the intent be that the prior moment, while in its consummated state of being, is the cause of the subsequent moment, even so it is not tenable, for if a further activity is imagined for what is in the state of being, the relation with another moment would follow. If the intent be that being itself is its activity, even so it is not tenable, for an effect not coloured by the nature of the cause cannot arise. And if the colouring by the cause's nature is admitted, then since the cause's nature would abide through the time of the effect, the admission of momentary destruction would have to be given up. If one admits the cause-effect relation without any colouring by the cause's nature, then over-extension would occur, since it would obtain everywhere. Moreover, origination and destruction must be either the very nature of the entity, or another state of the entity, or quite another entity — in none of these ways are they tenable. If, first, origination and destruction were the very nature of the entity, then the words "entity," "origination," and "destruction" would become synonymous. If it be thought there is some difference — that by the words "origination" and "destruction" the initial and final states of the intermediate entity are denoted — even so, since the entity would be related to three moments, the initial, final, and middle, the admission of momentariness would be lost. If origination and destruction were absolutely distinct from the entity — like a horse and a buffalo — then the entity, being unconnected with origination and destruction, would result in the eternality of the entity. If origination and destruction were the seeing and not-seeing of the entity, even so, since these are properties of the seer (draṣṭṛ) and not properties of the entity (vastu), the eternality of the entity would still follow. Therefore the doctrine of the Bauddhas is incoherent in this respect also.
BS_C02_S02_V21: If (the effect arises) when (the cause) is non-existent, the proposition is contradicted; if otherwise, simultaneity (of cause and effect would result).
BS_C02_S02_V21::block-0: It has been said in the doctrine of momentary destruction that the prior moment, being in the grip of destruction, cannot be the cause of the subsequent moment. If now one were to say that the effect arises even when the cause is non-existent, then the proposition would be contradicted — the proposition "having depended on the four kinds of causes, the citta and caittas arise" would be abandoned. And if origination be without cause, since there is no restriction, anything would arise anywhere. If, again, one were to say that the prior moment abides only as long as the subsequent moment is being produced, then there would be simultaneity (yaugapadya) of cause and effect; even so, there would still be the contradiction of the proposition — the proposition "all saṃskāras are momentary" (kṣaṇikāḥ sarve saṃskārāḥ) would be obstructed.
BS_C02_S02_V22: Conscious and unconscious destruction (pratisaṃkhyā- and apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) are not attainable, on account of non-interruption.
BS_C02_S02_V22::block-0: Moreover, the destructionists imagine that there are three things — apart from the ones cognized by buddhi — that are saṃskṛta and momentary. Of these three again — the conscious destruction (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), the unconscious destruction (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), and ākāśa — they speak. They hold all three to be non-entities (avastu), mere absences (abhāvamātra), without any positive description (nirupākhya). The deliberate destruction of entities is called pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha. Its opposite is apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha. Mere absence of obstruction is ākāśa. Their (view of) ākāśa will be refuted later. Now the two destructions are refuted — "the non-attainment" of pratisaṃkhyā- and apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha means their impossibility. Why? On account of non-interruption (avicchedāt) — these two, pratisaṃkhyā- and apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha, must concern either the series (santāna) or the entity (bhāva). They cannot concern the series, since in all series the interruption of the series is impossible due to the unbroken cause-effect relation among the constituents of the series. Nor can they concern the entity — for an absolute, indescribable destruction without continuity (niranvaya, nirupākhya vināśa) is not possible for entities, since in all states the unbroken continuity (anvayin avicchedaḥ) is seen by the strength of recognition (pratyabhijñā), and even in states where recognition is unclear, by inference from the unbroken continuity seen elsewhere. Therefore the two destructions imagined by the opponents are not tenable.
BS_C02_S02_V23: And on account of fault either way.
BS_C02_S02_V23::block-0: This destruction of avidyā and the rest, falling within pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha as imagined by the opponents — does it come about through right knowledge (samyag-jñāna) together with its accompaniments, or by itself? On the former alternative, the admission of causeless destruction (nirhetuka-vināśa) would be lost. On the latter alternative, the teaching of the path (mārgopadeśa) would become useless. Thus, since fault arises either way, this view is incoherent.
BS_C02_S02_V24: And in the case of ākāśa also, on account of non-difference (the same fault).
BS_C02_S02_V24::block-0: What they hold further — that the two destructions and ākāśa are without positive description (nirupākhya) — has already had the indescribability of the two destructions refuted earlier. Now that of ākāśa is refuted. The admission of the indescribability of ākāśa is unjustified, since the apprehension of its substantiality (vastutva) is no different from that of pratisaṃkhyā- and apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha. By the authority of scripture (āgama-prāmāṇyāt) first — from such śrutis as "From the Self ākāśa was born" (Tai. Up. 2.1.1) — the substantiality (vastutva) of ākāśa is well-known. Against the disputants, however, its inference through its quality of sound must be stated — for qualities such as smell and the like are seen to depend on substantial entities such as earth and the rest. Moreover, for those who would have ākāśa be the mere absence of obstruction, when one bird is flying, since the obstruction exists (in that part), there would be no room for another bird wishing to take off. If it be said: "Wherever there is absence of obstruction, there it will fly," then that whereby the absence of obstruction is qualified must itself be ākāśa as a real substantial entity, not the mere absence of obstruction. Moreover, for the Bauddha who holds ākāśa to be mere absence of obstruction, contradiction with his own admission would arise. For in the Bauddha system, in the flow of question and answer beginning with "In what does the earth, O Lord, abide?", at the end of (questions concerning) earth and the rest, to the question "In what does air abide?" the answer is "Air abides in ākāśa." That would be incoherent if ākāśa were a non-entity. Therefore the non-substantiality of ākāśa is also unjustified. Moreover, that all three — the two destructions and ākāśa — are non-entities, indescribable, and yet eternal, is contradictory. For of a non-entity neither eternality nor non-eternality is possible, since the dealing of property and property-bearer (dharma-dharmi-vyavahāra) presupposes substantiality. If there is the relation of property and property-bearer, then like a pot and the rest, there must be substantiality, not indescribability.
BS_C02_S02_V25::block-0: Sūtra 25 — "And from recollection (anusmṛti)." The momentariness doctrine is further refuted because the very fact of recognitive recollection, which presupposes one continuous cogniser persisting through the moments of perception and remembrance, cannot be accounted for if every cogniser is destroyed in a single moment.
BS_C02_S02_V25::block-1: Bhāṣya: Moreover, the destructionist (vaināśika), accepting the momentariness of every entity, must also accept the momentariness of the cogniser (upalabdhṛ). But that is not possible, on account of recollection (anusmṛti). Anusmṛti is precisely the remembrance that arises consequent upon a prior experience or perception (anubhava, upalabdhi). And such recollection is intelligible only when there is one and the same agent for both the perception and the remembrance, since we never observe one person remembering what some other person has perceived. For how could there arise the cognition "I saw that — I now see this," if there were not one and the same seer in the prior and later moments?
BS_C02_S02_V25::block-2: Furthermore, the recognitive cognition (pratyabhijñā-pratyaya), which has one and the same agent for seeing and remembering, is directly evident and well-established for the entire world — "I saw that — I see this." If the agent of seeing and the agent of remembering were different, then the cognition would have the form "I remember — but it was another who saw"; yet no one has such a cognition. Wherever such a split cognition does occur, the whole world recognises a different agent for seeing and remembering, as in "I remember — but it was someone else who saw that." Here, however, in "I saw that," even the destructionist himself recognises one and the same Self (ātman) as the agent both of seeing and of remembering. He does not deny the established fact of his own seeing by saying "I am not (the seer)," any more than one can deny that fire is hot and luminous.
BS_C02_S02_V25::block-3: This being so, with one cogniser linked to two moments — the moment of seeing and the moment of remembering — the destructionist's tenet of momentariness is unavoidably overthrown. Likewise, the destructionist himself recognises a single agent in his own successive cognitions up to his very last breath, and reaches back, gathering all past cognitions from birth as having the Self alone as their one agent — how then is the proponent of momentary destruction (kṣaṇa-bhaṅga-vāda) not ashamed?
BS_C02_S02_V25::block-4: If he should say, "This will be accounted for by mere similarity (sādṛśya)," we reply: similarity, being of the form "this is similar to that," depends on a pair, and for the proponent of momentariness there is no single grasper of the two similar entities; therefore the explanation "recognition is due to similarity" is mere false babble (mithyā-pralāpa). And if there were one grasper of the similarity between the prior and later moments, then, since one entity would persist over two moments, the thesis of momentariness would itself be wounded.
BS_C02_S02_V25::block-5: Suppose he says: "The cognition 'this is similar to that' is just another, fresh cognition; it does not require the apprehending of the two prior and later moments together." No — for the very expression "this similar to that" employs two distinct referents ("this" and "that"). If the cognition of similarity were merely a separate isolated cognition, then the linguistic usage "this is similar to that" would be meaningless; only the bare term "similarity" would arise. When a fact established for the world is not accepted by examiners, then whatever is uttered, whether to establish one's own thesis or to find fault with the opponent's, fails to take root in the minds of either the examiners or oneself as truly significant. One ought to state only what is settled in the form "the matter is just so." Anything else uttered merely advertises one's own garrulity.
BS_C02_S02_V25::block-6: Nor is this verbal practice based on similarity, for what is grasped is the very identity (tat-bhāva) of the thing, not its mere being-similar to something else (tat-sadṛśa-bhāva). With external objects there may sometimes arise the doubt, due to the possibility of deception, "Is this the very same, or only similar to it?" But with respect to the cogniser there is never even a doubt of the form "Am I the very same, or only similar to him?" — because of the apprehension, "the very I who saw yesterday am the very I who remember today," wherein identity itself (tad-bhāva) is grasped with certainty. For this reason too the destructionist's doctrine is untenable.
BS_C02_S02_V25::block-7: Siddhānta: The persisting Self that connects perception and recollection is established; the Buddhist thesis of momentariness collapses against the universal datum of recognitive memory.
BS_C02_S02_V26::block-0: Sūtra 26 — "Not from the non-existent, since that is never observed." The arising of an existent effect from a sheer non-existent cause is rejected, for nowhere in experience is such origination ever witnessed.
BS_C02_S02_V26::block-1: Bhāṣya: For this further reason the destructionist's tenet is untenable: those who do not accept any abiding, continuous cause incur the consequence that an entity (bhāva) arises from sheer non-entity (abhāva). They themselves expressly teach origination from non-being: "Without the destruction (of the cause) there is no manifestation (of the effect)." For, they say, the sprout arises from a destroyed seed; curd from destroyed milk; the pot from a (broken) clay-lump. If, on the contrary, the effect arose from an unmodified, immutable (kūṭastha) cause, then since there would be no distinction (among causes), anything could arise from anything. Therefore, since sprouts and the like arise from seeds and the like that have already lapsed into non-being, an effect arises from non-being — so they think.
BS_C02_S02_V26::block-2: Pūrvapakṣa: An entity arises from non-entity, since seeds and the like, when destroyed, produce sprouts and the like.
BS_C02_S02_V26::block-3: Siddhānta: To this it is replied — "Not from the non-existent, because of non-observance." An entity does not arise from a non-entity. Were a positive effect to arise from a sheer non-entity, then, since there is no distinction (aviśeṣa) within bare non-existence, the positing of a particular cause would become meaningless. For between the non-existence of destroyed seeds and the non-existence of a hare's horn there is no distinction qua non-existence — both being equally bereft of self-nature (niḥsvabhāva); so there is nothing in virtue of which one could meaningfully say "the sprout arises from a seed only, curd from milk only."
BS_C02_S02_V26::block-4: If a featureless non-entity were granted causal power, then a sprout might equally arise from a hare's horn — and that is never seen. If, on the other hand, distinctions within non-entities were admitted (like blueness and the rest in lotuses), then non-entity, by virtue of having distinctions, would itself become an entity, like the lotus. Nor again can a non-entity be the cause of anything, precisely because it is non-existent, like a hare's horn.
BS_C02_S02_V26::block-5: Further, if existents were to arise from non-existents, every effect would be permeated by non-existence (abhāva-anvita). But we never see this; rather every entity is apprehended as existent in its own form (sva-rūpeṇa bhāva-ātmanā). No one accepts that pots and saucers, which are modifications of clay, are pervaded by thread or its modifications. The world apprehends the modifications of clay as pervaded by clay alone.
BS_C02_S02_V26::block-6: It was urged: "Without the dissolution of its own form, no immutable (kūṭastha) thing can be a cause; therefore origination from non-being is necessary." That is ill-said. For we observe that gold and the like, recognised through change (pratyabhijñāyamāna) as having stable nature, stand in cause–effect relation with bracelets and the like (which are their products). Even in seeds and similar things where dissolution of form is observed, it is not the dissolved prior state that is taken as the cause of the later state; rather the persisting, undestroyed component-parts of the seed are admitted as the cause of the sprout.
BS_C02_S02_V26::block-7: Therefore, since origination of the existent from non-existents like a hare's horn is never observed, and origination of the existent from existents like gold is observed, the assumption "existent arises from non-existent" is unsustainable.
BS_C02_S02_V26::block-8: Moreover, the destructionists themselves admit that mind and mental factors (citta-caitta) arise from four (causal conditions, pratyaya), and that the aggregate constituting elements and elementals (bhūta-bhautika) arises from atoms (paramāṇu); having admitted this, they then turn around to imagine origination of being from non-being, denying their own admission, and thereby throw all worldly intelligibility into confusion.
BS_C02_S02_V27::block-0: Sūtra 27 — "And on this view there would be the attainment (of desired ends) even by those who are inactive." If being arose from sheer non-being, then even those who undertake no effort would obtain the fruits of effort, since non-being is universally available.
BS_C02_S02_V27::block-1: Bhāṣya: If origination of being from non-being were admitted, then on that view even people who are wholly indifferent (udāsīna) and not striving (anīhamāna) would attain their desired ends, because non-existence is everywhere readily at hand. The farmer who does not exert himself in field-work would still obtain a harvest of grain. The potter not striving in clay-preparation would still obtain pots. The weaver, even without weaving the threads, would obtain cloth just like one who weaves. And no one would need to exert himself in any way for heaven (svarga) or final liberation (apavarga / mokṣa).
BS_C02_S02_V27::block-2: But this is neither rationally tenable nor accepted by anyone. Therefore on this further ground also the assumption that being arises from non-being is untenable.
BS_C02_S02_V28::block-0: Sūtra 28 — "Non-existence (of external objects) is not (tenable), because of (their) being apprehended." The vijñāna-vādin's denial of external reality is refuted on the simple ground that external things are universally apprehended through the means of cognition.
BS_C02_S02_V28::block-1: Pūrvapakṣa (vijñāna-vāda — the Yogācāra Buddhist): Having raised objections such as the impossibility of an aggregate against the realist (bāhya-artha-vāda) Buddhist, the vijñāna-vādin Buddhist now stands forth: it is said that, perceiving that some disciples were attached to external objects, the doctrine of external reality was framed for their sake alone. That was not the real intention of the Sugata (the Buddha). His own true position is the doctrine of vijñāna alone as the sole skandha. On that doctrine of vijñāna-vāda, the entire transactional usage of pramāṇa, prameya and phala stands within consciousness in a form impressed upon the buddhi; for even granting external objects, no transaction of the means of knowledge can take place save through their appearing to consciousness.
BS_C02_S02_V28::block-2: How then is it determined that all this transaction is internal alone, that there is no external object distinct from consciousness? Because such an external object is impossible, he says. For the supposed external object would have to be either atoms (paramāṇu) or aggregates of atoms such as pillars and the rest. Now atoms cannot be objects of cognitions like the cognition of a pillar, since no cognition has the form of atoms. Nor can their aggregates — pillars and the like — be such objects, since these aggregates can be defined neither as identical with nor as different from the atoms. Likewise classes (jāti) and the rest are to be rejected.
BS_C02_S02_V28::block-3: Furthermore, the cognition of a particular object — "this is the cognition of a pillar, this of a wall, this of a pot, this of cloth" — given that bare cognition itself is a single common nature, cannot be accounted for without admitting some intrinsic differentiation in the cognition itself. Hence one must necessarily admit that cognition has the form of its object (viṣaya-sārūpya). Once that is admitted, the object's form is already comprehended within cognition itself, so the supposition of an external object becomes pointless. Furthermore, by the rule of co-apprehension (saha-upalambha-niyama), object and cognition turn out to be non-different — for never is one apprehended without the other; and this is unaccountable if their natures were truly distinct, since there is no such constraint between truly separate things. Hence too no external object exists.
BS_C02_S02_V28::block-4: Like dream and the rest, so should waking experience be regarded — for just as the cognitions in dream, in māyā, in mirage-water, in the gandharva-city and so on arise without any external object, presenting themselves in the forms of grasper and grasped, even so the cognitions of pillars and the like in the waking sphere can well arise without external objects, since they are equally just cognitions.
BS_C02_S02_V28::block-5: How then, without an external object, is the variety of cognitions accounted for? By the variety of latent dispositions (vāsanā-vaicitrya), he says — for in the beginningless saṃsāra, vijñānas and vāsanās stand to one another as seed and sprout, mutually conditioning each other, so the variety is unobjectionable. Furthermore, by positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) it is established that the variety of cognitions is grounded in vāsanās alone, not in objects: in dreams and so on, cognition-variety arises without external objects (and is conceded by both of us), while cognition-variety without vāsanās is not admitted by me. Hence too the non-being of the external object. Such is the pūrvapakṣa.
BS_C02_S02_V28::block-6: Siddhānta: To this we reply — "Non-existence is not (tenable), because of apprehension." The non-existence of the external object cannot be conclusively determined. Why? Because of apprehension — at every cognitive event the external object is apprehended: "a pillar, a wall, a pot, a cloth." And what is being apprehended cannot be non-existent. Just as one who is eating, while the satisfaction (tṛpti) born of eating is being directly experienced, were to declare "I am not eating, nor am I being satisfied," so too one who is himself apprehending the external object through sense-contact, were to say "I do not apprehend, and there is no such thing," — how could his speech be authoritative?
BS_C02_S02_V28::block-7: Objection: I do not say "I apprehend nothing whatever"; I say only "I apprehend nothing distinct from apprehension itself." — Indeed you say so, since your tongue is unrestrained, but you do not say it with reason. For from the very nature of apprehension (upalabdhi) one is forced to admit the object as something other than apprehension itself. No one apprehends apprehension itself as the pillar or the wall; rather, all worldly people apprehend pillars, walls and the like as the objects of apprehension. And this is just how all worldly people apprehend — even those who deny external reality say "that which has the form of an inner cognisable shines forth as if outside (bahir-vat avabhāsate)." Even they, gaining the universally established awareness of "outer" appearance, while wishing to repudiate the external object, are forced to insert the suffix vat ("as if"). Why else would they say "as if outside"? No one says "Viṣṇumitra appears like the son of a barren woman."
BS_C02_S02_V28::block-8: Therefore those who follow experience faithfully should admit that things truly appear outside (bahir eva avabhāsate), not merely "as if outside." — Objection: "Because external reality is impossible, we conclude that it merely appears as if outside." — That is no sound conclusion. For possibility and impossibility are determined by the operation or non-operation of pramāṇas, not the other way round. What is apprehended by even one of the pramāṇas — perception, etc. — is possible; what is apprehended by no pramāṇa is impossible. Here, since the external object is apprehended by all the pramāṇas in their proper modes, how can it be declared impossible by alternatives like "distinct from / not distinct from cognition"? Apprehension itself answers.
BS_C02_S02_V28::block-9: Nor does the cognition's having the form of its object (viṣaya-sārūpya) entail destruction of the object, since (a) without any object, sārūpya itself is unintelligible, and (b) the object is apprehended outside (bahir upalabdheḥ). For this very reason the rule of co-apprehension (saha-upalambha-niyama) too is to be admitted as grounded in the means-and-end relation (upāya-upeya-bhāva) between cognition and object, not as grounded in their non-difference.
BS_C02_S02_V28::block-10: Furthermore, in "pot-cognition" and "cloth-cognition" the difference belongs to the qualifiers (viśeṣaṇa) — pot and cloth — not to the qualified (viśeṣya), namely cognition. Just as in "white cow" and "black cow" the distinction lies in whiteness and blackness, not in cowness. Difference of one is established by reference to two, and difference of two by reference to one; hence object and cognition are different. Likewise with "pot-seeing" and "pot-remembering" — here the difference lies in the qualifieds, seeing and remembering, not in the qualifier, the pot — just as in "milk-smell" and "milk-taste" the difference is in smell and taste, not in milk.
BS_C02_S02_V28::block-11: Moreover, two cognitions, prior and posterior, each terminating in their own self-cognition (sva-saṃvedana), cannot stand to each other in the relation of grasper and grasped. From this it follows that vijñāna-bheda (difference among consciousnesses) too cannot itself be established on Yogācāra premises — and hence the doctrine collapses.
BS_C02_S02_V29::block-0: Sūtra 29 — "And not (waking is) like dream and the rest, on account of the difference of properties." Waking experience cannot be assimilated to dream-cognitions, since the two differ essentially in being subject or not subject to subsequent cancellation.
BS_C02_S02_V29::block-1: Bhāṣya: It was urged by the denier of external objects that, just as dream-cognitions arise without external objects, so too pillar-cognitions and the like in the waking sphere can arise without external objects, since both are equally cognitions (pratyayatva-aviśeṣāt). To this we reply: the cognitions of waking are not like those of dream. Why? On account of difference of properties (vaidharmya). For there is a difference of properties between dream and waking. What is that difference? — being-cancelled and not-being-cancelled (bādha–abādha), we say.
BS_C02_S02_V29::block-2: What was apprehended in dream is cancelled (bādhyate) by the awakened person — "Falsely (mithyā) did I apprehend a great gathering of folk; I have no such gathering; rather my mind was overcome by sleep, and that delusion arose accordingly." In just this way, in the case of māyā and the rest, there is appropriate cancellation. But what is apprehended in waking — pillars and the like — is not cancelled in any state.
BS_C02_S02_V29::block-3: Furthermore, dream-seeing is recollection (smṛti), whereas waking-seeing is direct apprehension (upalabdhi). The difference between recollection and direct apprehension is itself directly experienced by every person, taking the forms of disjunction from and conjunction with the object — "I remember my beloved son, I do not (now) apprehend him, I wish to apprehend him."
BS_C02_S02_V29::block-4: This being so, it cannot be said that "waking apprehension is false because it is an apprehension, like dream-apprehension" — for both the speaker and the hearer themselves directly experience the difference, and renunciation of one's own immediate experience is not befitting one who claims wisdom. Furthermore, being unable to maintain that waking cognitions are intrinsically without external support (svatas-nirālambana), the opponent must invoke a (mere) similarity (sādharmya) with dream-cognitions. But what is not the intrinsic property of one thing cannot accrue to it merely on account of similarity with another. Fire, experienced as hot, will not become cold by similarity with water. The difference of dharmas between dream and waking has been shown.
BS_C02_S02_V30::block-0: Sūtra 30 — "There is no being (of vāsanās), because (of you) there is non-apprehension (of external objects)." The Yogācārin's appeal to vāsanās to explain cognitive variety fails, since vāsanās themselves require external objects as their occasioning causes.
BS_C02_S02_V30::block-1: Bhāṣya: It was further said that even without external objects, variety of cognitions is intelligible from variety of vāsanās alone — to this we reply. We say: there is no being (sambhava) of vāsanās on your view, since on your view there is non-apprehension of external things. For the manifold vāsanās, varying with each object, are caused by the apprehension of objects. If, however, no objects are apprehended, what could be the occasioning cause of variegated vāsanās?
BS_C02_S02_V30::block-2: Even granting beginninglessness, the situation is analogous to a chain of blind men leading blind men — there is no foundation (apratiṣṭha) and there is destructive infinite regress (anavasthā), which would obliterate all transactional usage; one's intended doctrine would not be established.
