BS_C02_S02_V30::block-3: And even the positive and negative concomitances (anvaya-vyatireka) put forward by the denier of external objects — "this whole class of cognitions is caused by vāsanās, not by objects" — should themselves be regarded as refuted in this connection, since vāsanās are unintelligible without prior apprehension of objects. Indeed, since (a) we admit apprehension of objects even without vāsanās, and (b) we do not admit the arising of vāsanās without prior apprehension of objects — these very anvaya-vyatirekas in fact establish the existence of objects.
BS_C02_S02_V30::block-4: Furthermore, vāsanās are a kind of saṃskāra. And saṃskāras are not intelligible without a substrate (āśraya); so it is observed in the world. But on your view there is no substrate of vāsanās, since none is apprehended by any pramāṇa.
BS_C02_S02_V31::block-0: Sūtra 31 — "And on account of momentariness." The Yogācārin's posited ālaya-vijñāna, being itself momentary, cannot be the abiding substrate that vāsanās require.
BS_C02_S02_V31::block-1: Bhāṣya: The so-called ālaya-vijñāna, postulated as the substrate of vāsanās, since it too is admitted to be momentary, has an unstable nature (anavasthita-svarūpa), like the ordinary functioning consciousness (pravṛtti-vijñāna), and cannot serve as the locus of vāsanās. For the entire transaction of laying-down vāsanās, recollecting them, gathering them together (pratisaṃdhāna), depending on place, time and occasion (deśa-kāla-nimitta), is impossible without either one continuous self spanning the three times, or an immutable (kūṭastha) all-seeing (sarvārtha-darśin) Self. If, on the other hand, ālaya-vijñāna is accorded a stable nature, the very Buddhist tenet (siddhānta) is given up.
BS_C02_S02_V31::block-2: Furthermore, since the postulate of momentariness is shared by the vijñāna-vāda also, all the objections grounded on momentariness that were raised against the realist Buddhist (bāhya-artha-vāda) — beginning with "Upon the arising of the later, since the earlier has already perished" (uttara-utpāde ca pūrva-nirodhāt) — are to be carried over here as well.
BS_C02_S02_V31::block-3: Thus both the destructionist positions, the realist (bāhya-artha-vādin) and the cognition-only (vijñāna-vādin), have been refuted. The śūnya-vāda (doctrine of the void) is contradicted by every pramāṇa, and so no pains are taken to refute it; for one cannot deny the world of transaction established by all pramāṇas without first establishing some other tattva, since the general rule (utsarga) holds in the absence of an exception (apavāda).
BS_C02_S02_V32::block-0: Sūtra 32 — "And on account of total non-tenability." Examined from every angle, the Buddhist doctrine collapses; nothing in it stands as rationally tenable.
BS_C02_S02_V32::block-1: Bhāṣya: What more need be said? In every way (sarva-prakāreṇa), the more the destructionist's tenet is examined for tenability, the more it crumbles like a well dug in sand. We see no tenability anywhere in it. Therefore the entire transactional usage of the destructionist system is untenable.
BS_C02_S02_V32::block-2: Moreover, by teaching the three mutually contradictory positions — bāhya-artha-vāda, vijñāna-vāda, and śūnya-vāda — the Sugata has himself made plain his own incoherent garrulity (asambaddha-pralāpitva). Or else (we may surmise) hostility (pradveṣa) towards the creatures: "By apprehending mutually contradictory teachings, may these creatures be confounded." In every way, then, the Sugata's doctrine is to be disregarded by those desirous of the highest good (śreyas-kāmin) — such is the import.
BS_C02_S02_V33::block-0: Sūtra 33: "Not (so) in one, on account of impossibility." Contradictory attributes such as being and non-being cannot coexist in one and the same substrate, and hence the Jaina syād-vāda doctrine collapses.
BS_C02_S02_V33::block-1: Bhāṣya: The doctrine of the Sugata (Buddha) has been refuted. Now the doctrine of the Vivasanas (the unclothed, i.e., the Jainas, Digambaras) is being refuted. Seven categories (padārthas) are accepted by them, namely: jīva (the living), ajīva (the non-living), āsrava (inflow of karma), saṃvara (restraint), nirjarā (wearing off of karma), bandha (bondage) and mokṣa (liberation). In brief, however, there are only two categories, called jīva and ajīva, since the others are, as appropriate, included within these two — so they hold. They expound a further elaboration of these two, called the five astikāyas (extended substances), namely: jīvāstikāya (the soul-extension), pudgalāstikāya (matter-extension), dharmāstikāya (the medium of motion), adharmāstikāya (the medium of rest) and ākāśāstikāya (space-extension). They also describe many subdivisions of all of these as fancied in their own scriptures. And everywhere they introduce a procedure (nyāya) called the seven-fold mode of predication (sapta-bhaṅgī-naya): "in some respect it is" (syād asti), "in some respect it is not" (syān nāsti), "in some respect it is and is not" (syād asti ca nāsti ca), "in some respect it is inexpressible" (syād avaktavyaḥ), "in some respect it is and is inexpressible" (syād asti cāvaktavyaś ca), "in some respect it is not and is inexpressible" (syān nāsti cāvaktavyaś ca), "in some respect it is and is not and is inexpressible" (syād asti ca nāsti cāvaktavyaś ca). In just this way they apply this seven-fold mode of predication even to oneness, eternality and the like.
BS_C02_S02_V33::block-2: To this we reply: this assumption is not reasonable. Why? Because of the impossibility (of contradictory attributes) in one (substrate). For it is not possible that contradictory attributes such as existence and non-existence should simultaneously coexist in one and the same property-bearer (dharmin), as is the case with cold and heat. Those seven categories which have been determined to be just so many and of such-and-such a form must either be just thus, or not at all thus. Otherwise, if cognition were of an undetermined form — "may be thus, may be not thus" — it would, like doubtful cognition, be no valid means of knowledge (apramāṇa) at all. (Pūrvapakṣa:) But surely a cognition that arises with a determined form, namely "a thing is of manifold nature," does not deserve to be invalid like doubtful cognition. (Siddhānta:) We say no — for one who professes manifoldness (anekānta) without restriction in all things, since the act of determination (nirdhāraṇa) is itself a thing not different (from other things), the very modes "in some respect it is, in some respect it is not" must intrude into it as well, and hence it would itself be of an indeterminate nature. Thus the determiner and the fruit of the determination would in one alternative possess being and in another alternative possess non-being. This being so, how could a Tīrthaṅkara, even though held to be a means of valid knowledge, be able to teach when the means of knowledge (pramāṇa), the object known (prameya), the knower (pramātṛ) and the act of knowing (pramiti) are all undetermined? Or how would those who follow his intention engage with regard to the matter taught by him when it is of an indeterminate form? For only when the fruit is determined to be one-pointed (aikāntika) does the whole world unhesitatingly engage in the performance of its means; not otherwise. And hence one who composes a śāstra of indeterminate purport would be like a drunkard or a madman, his speech unworthy of acceptance. Likewise the number five of the five astikāyas, when subjected to the alternative "either it is or it is not," would in one alternative be present and in another not — and so it would come to be either less or more in number. Nor is it possible that these categories should be inexpressible (avaktavya). If they are inexpressible, they ought not to be expressed; but they are expressed and are also called inexpressible — this is self-contradictory. And further, when they are expressed, either they are determined to be just so or they are not so determined. Likewise the fruit of that determination — right vision (samyag-darśana) — either is or is not; and similarly its opposite, wrong vision (asamyag-darśana), either is or is not. He who babbles thus belongs only to the camp of the drunken and the mad, not to the camp of those worthy of trust. And in the case of heaven (svarga) and final release (apavarga) too, in one alternative there is existence and in another non-existence; likewise eternality in one alternative and non-eternality in another — and on such non-determination there is no possibility of pravṛtti (purposive activity). Moreover, beings such as the beginningless jīva, whose nature is determined in their own śāstra, would have their nature undetermined contrary to that determination. Thus, in jīva and the other categories, since contradictory properties such as being and non-being cannot coexist in one property-bearer, and since when one property of being is present another property of non-being cannot subsist, and likewise when non-being is present being cannot subsist, the Ārhata (Jaina) doctrine is incoherent. By this very (refutation), the doctrines of manifoldness (anekānta) — that of being one and many, eternal and non-eternal, separate and non-separate, and the like — should be regarded as refuted. As for their fancy that aggregates arise from atoms named pudgala, that stands refuted by the prior refutation of the atomic doctrine itself, and hence no separate effort is made for refuting it. (Sūtra 33)
BS_C02_S02_V34::block-0: Sūtra 34: "And thus (would follow) the non-completeness of the Self." On the Jaina view that the jīva is the size of the body, the Self would be partial and impermanent, and thus untenable.
BS_C02_S02_V34::block-1: Bhāṣya: Just as the impossibility of contradictory properties in one property-bearer is a defect that befalls the syād-vāda, so too another defect — the non-completeness (akārtsnya, partiality) of the Ātman, namely the jīva — would befall it. How? The Ārhatas hold that the jīva is of the size of the body. If it is of the size of the body, then the Self becomes incomplete (akṛtsna), non-omnipresent (asarvagata), and limited (paricchinna); hence, like a pot and similar things, the Self would have to be impermanent. And since bodies are of variable size, when a human jīva, which has been of human-body size, attains the birth of an elephant by some maturation of karma, it would not pervade the entire elephant body. And when it attains the birth of an ant (puttikā), it would not be fully contained in the ant's body. The same defect applies even within a single birth, in the states of childhood, youth and old age. (Pūrvapakṣa:) It might be said: the jīva has infinite parts (avayavas); those very parts contract in a small body and expand in a large one. (Siddhānta:) Of those infinite parts of the jīva it must then be stated whether they are mutually obstructed in occupying the same locus or not. If there is mutual obstruction, then infinite parts cannot be contained within a limited region. If there is no obstruction, then since all parts could occupy the locus of one part, none of the parts having any extent (prathiman), the jīva would be reduced to atomic size (aṇu-mātratva). Furthermore, the infinitude of jīva-parts limited only by the size of the body cannot even be conceived. (Sūtra 34)
BS_C02_S02_V35::block-0: Sūtra 35: "Nor (is there) absence of contradiction even by succession (alternation), on account of (defects of) modification and the like." Even the alternative of parts coming and going by turns does not save the Jaina view, because of defects of modification, impermanence and the rest.
BS_C02_S02_V35::block-1: Leading bhāṣya: It might be said that some parts of the jīva are added when it attains a large body, and some are removed when it attains a slender body. To that also it is said —
BS_C02_S02_V35::block-2: Bhāṣya: Even by succession (paryāya), through addition and removal of parts (avayavopagama-apagama), the body-sized character of the jīva cannot be established without contradiction. Why? Because of the consequence of defects such as modification (vikāra) and the rest. For the jīva, being constantly filled up and reduced through the addition and removal of parts, would inevitably possess the property of modification (vikriyāvattva). And if it possesses modification, then like skin (carma) and similar things impermanence (anityatva) would befall it. Thereupon the very acceptance of bondage and liberation would be obstructed — the doctrine, namely, that the jīva, surrounded by the eightfold karma and submerged like a gourd (alābū) in the ocean of saṃsāra, after the cessation of bondage moves upward (ūrdhva-gāmin). Furthermore: since the parts that come and go possess the property of arising and ceasing, they are non-self (anātmā), like the body and the rest. And so it would have to be that some abiding part is the Ātman; but no such part can be pointed out as "this is it." Furthermore: regarding the jīva-parts that come, it must be said whence they arise; and regarding those that go, where they dissolve. They cannot arise from the elements (bhūtas) or dissolve in them, because the jīva is non-elemental (abhautika). Nor can any other locus, common or special, of the jīva-parts be pointed out, for there is no pramāṇa for it. Furthermore: in this case the Self would be of indeterminate nature, since the parts that come and go are of indeterminate measure. Thus, on account of these and other defects, even by succession the addition and removal of parts cannot be ascribed to the Self. Or else: by the previous sūtra, regarding the Self that is body-sized, when the consequence of incompleteness (akārtsnya) was pressed in respect of taking up larger and smaller bodies, and impermanence was urged, one might raise the further objection: even if there is non-establishment of measure by alternation, by the principle of the permanence of the continuity of a stream (srotaḥ-santāna-nityatā-nyāya), the Ātman would be eternal — just as the impermanence of cognitions (vijñāna) of the Red-Robes (rakta-paṭa, i.e., the Buddhists) is compatible with the permanence of their continuum, so it is for the impermanence (visici) (of jīva-parts) too. Apprehending such an objection, the answer is given by this sūtra: if the continuum is unreal (avastu), the doctrine of no-self (nairātmya-vāda) would result; and if it is real (vastu), then on account of the defects of modification etc. in the Self, this view does not hold. (Sūtra 35)
BS_C02_S02_V36::block-0: Sūtra 36: "And on account of the abiding (permanence) of the final (state), and the eternality of both (sizes), there would be non-difference." Since the Jainas accept that the final size of the jīva in liberation is permanent, the prior sizes too would have to be permanent, and so all the body-sized stages would collapse into non-difference.
BS_C02_S02_V36::block-1: Bhāṣya: Moreover, the final size of the jīva that obtains in the state of liberation (mokṣāvasthā) is held by the Jainas to be eternal. Like that, the consequence would be that the two prior sizes too — the initial (ādya) and the middle (madhyama) — would have to be eternal; and hence the consequence of non-difference (aviśeṣa). It would then be the case that there is only one body-sized state, and not the attainment of larger and smaller other bodies. Or else: because the final size of the jīva is abiding, in the two prior states also the jīva would be of an abiding size. Hence, without distinction, the jīva must always be acknowledged as either atomic (aṇu) or large (mahān), and not body-sized. Therefore the Ārhata doctrine, like that of the Saugata, is incoherent and to be set aside. (Sūtra 36)
BS_C02_S02_V37::block-0: Sūtra 37: "(The doctrine) of the Lord (as mere efficient cause) (is to be rejected) on account of incoherence." The view that Īśvara is only the directing efficient cause and not the material cause cannot be sustained, on account of multiple incoherences.
BS_C02_S02_V37::block-1: Bhāṣya: Now the doctrine of Īśvara as a mere directing cause (kevala-adhiṣṭhātṛ-īśvara-kāraṇa-vāda) is being refuted. How is this known (to be the topic)? Because in the (sūtras) "And the prakṛti (material cause), on account of non-contradiction of the proposition and the illustration" (Br. Sū. 1.4.23) and "And on account of the teaching of resolve (abhidhyā)" (Br. Sū. 1.4.24), the Ācārya (Bādarāyaṇa) himself has established that Īśvara is of dual nature — both as material cause (prakṛti) and as directing cause (adhiṣṭhātṛ). If, however, here the doctrine of Īśvara as cause were to be refuted indiscriminately, it would follow that the sūtra-author contradicts himself, his utterances mutually conflicting between earlier and later. Therefore the view that Īśvara is only the efficient cause (nimitta-kāraṇa), being a directing cause without being the material cause — this view, since it opposes the oneness of Brahman ordained by the Vedānta (vedānta-vihita-brahmaikatva-pratipakṣa), is here refuted with effort. Now this fancying of an Īśvara outside the Veda (vedabāhya-īśvara-kalpanā) is of many kinds. Some, leaning on Sāṅkhya and Yoga, fancy that Īśvara is a mere directing efficient cause, the directing principle over Pradhāna and Puruṣa; that Pradhāna, Puruṣa and Īśvara are mutually distinct. The Māheśvaras hold: the five categories — kārya (effect), kāraṇa (cause), yoga (union), vidhi (procedure) and duḥkhānta (cessation of suffering) — are taught by the Lord Paśupati (Īśvara) for the release of paśus (souls) from their paśas (bonds); Paśupati is Īśvara, the efficient cause. Likewise the Vaiśeṣikas and others, in some manner, in accordance with their own systems, describe Īśvara as the efficient cause.
BS_C02_S02_V37::block-2: Hence the answer is given: "on account of incoherence in the case of the Lord" (patyur asāmañjasyāt). The lordship (jagat-kāraṇatva) of the Lord (pati = Īśvara) by way of being the directing cause over Pradhāna and Puruṣa is not tenable. Why? On account of incoherence (asāmañjasya). What is this incoherence? Since Īśvara apportions distinctions of beings as low (hīna), middling (madhyama) and high (uttama), the consequence would be the application of defects such as attachment (rāga) and aversion (dveṣa) to Īśvara, and hence non-lordship (anīśvaratva), like ourselves. (Pūrvapakṣa:) There is no defect, since (Īśvara) depends on the karma of beings. (Reply:) No; for in that case karma and Īśvara would have to be respectively the prompted (pravartya) and the prompter (pravartayitṛ), and the defect of mutual dependence (itaretarāśraya) would arise. (Pūrvapakṣa:) Not so, because of beginninglessness (anāditva). (Reply:) No; for as in the present, so even in past times the defect of mutual dependence is the same, and the consequence would be the principle of an endless succession of the blind (andha-paramparā-nyāya). Furthermore, "defects have prompting (to action) as their characteristic" (pravartanā-lakṣaṇā doṣāḥ) — this is the view of the knowers of nyāya (Nyāya-Sūtra 1.1.18). For no one is seen acting in his own interest or another's interest unless prompted by some defect. And every person, prompted by self-interest, acts even in the interest of another — and so this also is incoherent, since being possessed of self-interest, Īśvara would incur the consequence of non-lordship. And further, since Īśvara is held to be a kind of puruṣa (puruṣa-viśeṣa), and puruṣa is held to be indifferent (audāsīnya), there is incoherence. (Sūtra 37)
BS_C02_S02_V38::block-0: Sūtra 38: "And on account of the impossibility of relation." The mere efficient-cause Īśvara cannot stand in any tenable relation to Pradhāna and Puruṣa.
BS_C02_S02_V38::block-1: Bhāṣya: Once again there is just incoherence — for an Īśvara distinct from Pradhāna and Puruṣa cannot be the ruler of Pradhāna and Puruṣa without some relation. Now a relation of the form of conjunction (saṃyoga-lakṣaṇa-sambandha) is not possible, since Pradhāna, Puruṣa and Īśvara are all-pervading (sarvagata) and partless (niravayava). Nor is a relation of the form of inherence (samavāya-lakṣaṇa-sambandha), since the relation of substrate and resident-in-substrate (āśraya-āśrayi-bhāva) cannot be specified. Nor can any other relation knowable through effects be supposed, since the cause-effect relation itself is up to now unestablished. (Pūrvapakṣa:) How then for the Brahman-vādin? (Reply:) No; for him the relation of the form of identity (tādātmya-lakṣaṇa-sambandha) holds. And further, the Brahman-vādin determines the form of cause and so on by the strength of scripture (āgama-bala), and so it is not necessarily incumbent upon him to accept everything just as observed (yathādṛṣṭa) — there is no such restriction. But for the opponent, who determines the form of cause and so on by the strength of an illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta-bala), it is incumbent that everything be accepted just as observed — this is the additional point (atiśaya). (Pūrvapakṣa:) The opponent too has scripture composed by an omniscient being, so the strength of āgama is the same. (Reply:) No; for the consequence of mutual dependence (itaretarāśraya) arises — the establishment of omniscience from confidence in āgama, and the establishment of āgama from the confidence (gained by) omniscience. Therefore the fancying of an Īśvara by the Sāṅkhya-Yoga-vādins is unsustainable. In the same way, in other extra-Vedic fancyings of Īśvara also, incoherence is to be applied as appropriate. (Sūtra 38)
BS_C02_S02_V39::block-0: Sūtra 39: "And on account of the impossibility of (presiding over) a substrate." The Tārkika-imagined Īśvara cannot have anything to preside over.
BS_C02_S02_V39::block-1: Bhāṣya: From this further point too, the Tārkika-imagined Īśvara is impossible. For He, being imagined like a potter (kumbhakāra) presiding over clay and the like, would have to set Pradhāna and the rest in motion by presiding over them; but this does not hold. For Pradhāna, being imperceptible (apratyakṣa) and devoid of form (rūpa) and the rest, cannot be a substrate to be presided over by Īśvara, since it is unlike clay and so on. (Sūtra 39)
BS_C02_S02_V40::block-0: Sūtra 40: "If (it be said that Īśvara presides over Pradhāna) as (the puruṣa over) the sense-organs, no, on account of (the consequence of) experience and the rest." The analogy of the puruṣa presiding over imperceptible sense-organs fails, because it would saddle Īśvara with worldly experience.
BS_C02_S02_V40::block-1: Bhāṣya: It might be said: just as the puruṣa presides over the array of sense-organs (karaṇa-grāma) — the eye and the rest — which are also imperceptible and devoid of form etc., so too Īśvara will preside over Pradhāna. Even so it does not hold. For the fact that the array of sense-organs is presided over is known from the observation of experience (bhoga) and the like; but here (in the case of Īśvara presiding over Pradhāna) experience and the rest are not seen. And if parity with the array of sense-organs is accepted, then, like transmigrating beings (saṃsārins), even Īśvara would incur experience and the rest.
BS_C02_S02_V40::block-2: Or else the two sūtras are explained otherwise. "Adhiṣṭhāna-anupapatteś ca" — from this point too the Tārkika-imagined Īśvara is impossible. For in the world a king is seen to be the lord of a country only as one who has a substrate (sādhiṣṭhāna), namely as embodied (sa-śarīra), not as without a substrate (niradhiṣṭhāna). And hence for one who wishes to imagine the unseen Īśvara on the basis of that (worldly) example, even Īśvara must be described as having some body (śarīra) as the seat of His instruments (karaṇāyatana). But that cannot be described, because the body comes into being only after creation, and prior to creation it is not possible. And without a substrate, the prompting power (pravartakatva) of Īśvara is not possible — for thus is it observed in the world. "Karaṇavac cen na bhogādibhyaḥ" — now if, following observation in the world, one were to imagine for Īśvara too some body that is the seat of His instruments — even this does not hold. For if He is embodied, then like a transmigrating being, the consequence of experience and the rest would befall, and Īśvara too would incur the consequence of non-lordship (anīśvaratva). (Sūtra 40)
BS_C02_S02_V41::block-0: Sūtra 41: "Or [there would result] finitude or non-omniscience [for the Lord postulated by the logicians]."
BS_C02_S02_V41::block-1: There is a further inconsistency in the Īśvara fabricated by the logicians (tārkika-parikalpita Īśvara — the Naiyāyika-Vaiśeṣika theistic position). For He is admitted by them to be omniscient (sarvajña) and infinite (ananta); pradhāna (primordial nature) too is admitted to be infinite, and the puruṣas (selves) are admitted to be infinite in number and mutually distinct (mitho bhinnāḥ). Now, the question arises: does the omniscient Īśvara know the precise extent (iyattā) of pradhāna, of the puruṣas, and of His own Self, or does He not know it? In either alternative, fault is unavoidable.
BS_C02_S02_V41::block-2: How so? In the first alternative, since pradhāna, the puruṣas, and Īśvara would all be measured out by a definite extent, finitude (antavattva) becomes inevitable for them, because such is invariably observed in the world. For whatever object in the world is delimited by a definite extent — such as a pot and the like — is seen to be finite (antavat). In the same way, the triad of pradhāna, puruṣas, and Īśvara, being delimited by definite extent, would be finite. Their numerical measure (saṅkhyā-parimāṇa) is fixed by the very form of the triad — pradhāna, puruṣas, and Īśvara. Their qualitative measure of nature (svarūpa-parimāṇa) too, inhering in them, would be ascertained by Īśvara. There is also the great number (mahāsaṅkhyā) inhering in the puruṣas.
BS_C02_S02_V41::block-3: Consequently, among those whose extent is thus delimited, those puruṣas who are released from saṃsāra (transmigration) — for them saṃsāra has an end, and their condition of being a transmigrator (saṃsāritva) has an end. Likewise, as the others too become liberated in succession, both saṃsāra and the saṃsārins (transmigrators) would come to an end. And pradhāna, together with its modifications (savikāra), is held to be the substratum to be presided over by Īśvara for the puruṣa's purpose, in the form of saṃsāritva. When that is exhausted, over what would Īśvara preside? With respect to what would His omniscience and lordship (sarvajñatā and īśvaratā) subsist?
BS_C02_S02_V41::block-4: Moreover, if pradhāna, puruṣas, and Īśvara were finite in this manner, the unwanted consequence (prasaṅga) of their having a beginning (ādimattva) would follow; and from being possessed of beginning and end (ādyantavattva), the consequence of the doctrine of voidness (śūnyavāda — the Mādhyamika position) would follow.
BS_C02_S02_V41::block-5: Now, suppose to avoid this fault the second alternative were adopted — that the extent of pradhāna, of the puruṣas, and of His own Self is not ascertained by Īśvara. Then another fault arises: the abandonment of the very tenet that Īśvara is omniscient (sarvajñatva-abhyupagama-hāni). Therefore on this ground also the doctrine of Īśvara as cause, as accepted by the logicians, is incoherent (asaṅgata). (41)
BS_C02_S02_V42::block-0: Sūtra 42: "On account of the impossibility of origination [the Bhāgavata-Pāñcarātra view is also untenable]."
BS_C02_S02_V42::block-1: Those who hold that Īśvara is merely the efficient cause (kevala-nimitta-kāraṇa) — being the presider (adhiṣṭhātā) but not the material (aprakṛti) — their view has been refuted. Now, the view of those who hold that Īśvara is both the material (prakṛti) and the presider (adhiṣṭhātā), being thus a cause of both natures (ubhayātmaka-kāraṇa), is being refuted.
BS_C02_S02_V42::block-2: Pūrvapakṣa (objection): But by recourse to śruti also, Īśvara has been previously determined to be precisely of this form — both prakṛti and adhiṣṭhātā. And smṛti, when conformable to śruti (śruty-anusāriṇī), is established as a valid means (pramāṇa). On what ground, then, is this view sought to be refuted?
BS_C02_S02_V42::block-3: Siddhānta (reply): It is said — although in this respect of being [both material and efficient cause] there is similarity and hence no occasion for disagreement, yet there is another aspect which is a locus of disagreement. Therefore the refutation is undertaken with respect to that.
BS_C02_S02_V42::block-4: Therein, the Bhāgavata holds: Bhagavān alone, the one Vāsudeva, of the nature of unstained knowledge (nirañjana-jñāna-svarūpa), is the supreme reality (paramārtha-tattva). He, dividing Himself into four, is established — in the form of the Vāsudeva-vyūha, the Saṅkarṣaṇa-vyūha, the Pradyumna-vyūha, and the Aniruddha-vyūha. Vāsudeva is called Paramātman; Saṅkarṣaṇa is called the jīva (individual self); Pradyumna is called manas (mind); Aniruddha is called ahaṅkāra (ego-sense). Among these, Vāsudeva is the supreme prakṛti, and the others — Saṅkarṣaṇa and the rest — are effects (kārya). One who, having worshipped this Bhagavān, the supreme Lord so constituted, for a hundred years through abhigamana (approach to the temple), upādāna (procuring materials of worship), ijyā (offering), svādhyāya (recitation), and yoga (meditative concentration), and whose afflictions (kleśa) are exhausted, attains Bhagavān Himself.
BS_C02_S02_V42::block-5: Now, what is said here — that Nārāyaṇa, well known as the supreme Self (Paramātman) beyond the unmanifest (avyakta), the Self of all (sarvātman), having distributed Himself into many forms by His own Self, abides — that is not refuted, since the manifoldness (anekadhā-bhāva) of the Paramātman is established by śrutis such as "He becomes one, He becomes threefold" (Chāndogya 7.26.2) and the like. Likewise, what is intended as constant, single-pointed (ananya-citta) worship of that Bhagavān in the form of abhigamana etc. — that too is not prohibited, since in śruti and smṛti the meditative dedication to Īśvara (īśvara-praṇidhāna) is well established.
BS_C02_S02_V42::block-6: But what is further said — that from Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa is born; from Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna; and from Pradyumna, Aniruddha — concerning this we say: it is not possible for the jīva called Saṅkarṣaṇa to originate from the Paramātman called Vāsudeva, because the unwanted consequences (prasaṅga) of impermanence (anityatva) and the like would follow. For if the jīva were originated, the faults of impermanence and so forth would attach to it. And consequently, there would be no liberation (mokṣa) for it as attainment of Bhagavān, since on attaining the cause, the effect would be liable to dissolution (pravilaya). The Ācārya himself will refute the origination of the jīva in: "The Self [is] not [originated], on account of non-mention in śruti, and on account of [its] eternality, [as established] from these [śrutis]" (Brahmasūtra 2.3.17). Therefore this fancy is incoherent. (42)
BS_C02_S02_V43::block-0: Sūtra 43: "And [it cannot be admitted that] from the agent the instrument [arises]."
BS_C02_S02_V43::block-1: On this further ground also this fancy is incoherent — namely, because nowhere in the world is it observed that from an agent (kartṛ) such as Devadatta, an instrument (karaṇa) such as an axe and the like is born. The Bhāgavatas, however, declare that from the agent jīva called Saṅkarṣaṇa, the instrument manas called Pradyumna is born; and from that manas, which is born from an agent, the ahaṅkāra called Aniruddha is born. We cannot determine such a thing without an analogous instance (dṛṣṭānta). Nor do we find any śruti to this effect. (43)
BS_C02_S02_V44::block-0: Sūtra 44: "Or, if [Saṅkarṣaṇa etc.] are of the nature of [supreme] knowledge etc. [i.e., are themselves Īśvaras], even then there is no warding off of that [defect of impossibility of origination]."
BS_C02_S02_V44::block-1: Pūrvapakṣa: It might be said — Saṅkarṣaṇa and the rest are not regarded as being of the nature of jīva and so forth; rather, all of these are admitted to be Īśvaras themselves, endowed with the lordly qualities (aiśvara-dharma) of jñāna (knowledge), aiśvarya (lordship), śakti (power), bala (strength), vīrya (vigour), and tejas (splendour) — all of them being Vāsudevas, free of fault (nirdoṣa), without [external] presider (niradhiṣṭhāna), and free from blemish (niravadya). Therefore the fault of the impossibility of origination as described does not arise.
BS_C02_S02_V44::block-2: Siddhānta: Here it is replied — "Even so, there is no warding off of that" (tad-apratiṣedhaḥ) — that is, there is no warding off of the impossibility of origination; this fault of impossibility of origination obtains in another manner. The intent is this. How? If the intention is this — that these four, Vāsudeva and the rest, are mutually distinct Īśvaras of equal qualities (tulya-dharmāṇaḥ), and there is no oneness of essence (ekātmakatva) among them — then the postulation of multiple Īśvaras becomes purposeless (anarthakya), since the work of an Īśvara can be accomplished by a single Īśvara alone. There is also abandonment of [their own] siddhānta (sva-siddhānta-hāni), since their own admission is that Bhagavān, the one Vāsudeva alone, is the supreme reality.
BS_C02_S02_V44::block-3: If, on the other hand, the intention is — that these four vyūhas are of one and the same Bhagavān, all having equal qualities — even then the impossibility of origination remains as it was. For from Vāsudeva the origination of Saṅkarṣaṇa cannot occur, nor from Saṅkarṣaṇa that of Pradyumna, nor from Pradyumna that of Aniruddha, owing to the absence of any superiority (atiśaya). Between cause and effect there must necessarily be some excess on one side, as between clay and the pot. For without superiority, it is not intelligible to call one a cause and the other an effect (kārya-kāraṇa).
BS_C02_S02_V44::block-4: Nor is any difference among Vāsudeva and the rest — whether in any one of them or in all — admitted by the Pāñcarātra siddhāntins as arising from a graded scale (tāratamya) of knowledge, lordship, etc. For all the vyūhas are upheld as Vāsudevas alone, without distinction (nirviśeṣa). Nor would these vyūhas of the Bhagavān remain confined to the number four, since the entire world from Brahmā down to a clump of grass is understood to be a vyūha of Bhagavān. (44)
BS_C02_S02_V45::block-0: Sūtra 45: "And on account of [internal] contradictions [in the Pāñcarātra teaching, this fancy is untenable]."
BS_C02_S02_V45::block-1: Internal contradiction (vipratiṣedha) of many kinds is found in this śāstra — characterised by the postulation of [a difference and yet non-difference between] guṇa (quality) and guṇin (qualified). On the one hand jñāna, aiśvarya, śakti, bala, vīrya, and tejas are spoken of as guṇas (qualities); on the other, they are said to be the very Selves — "these blessed Vāsudevas are the Selves themselves" — and so on. Such mutually conflicting statements are seen.
BS_C02_S02_V45::block-2: There is also contradiction with the Veda (veda-vipratiṣedha): for it is found that, having failed to obtain the supreme good (paraṃ śreyas) from the four Vedas, Śāṇḍilya took to this śāstra (the Pāñcarātra) — and such censure of the Veda (veda-nindā) is seen. Therefore it is established that this fancy (kalpanā) is incoherent (asaṅgata). (45)
BS_C02_S03_INTRO1::block-0: Introduction to Pāda 3: In the various Vedānta texts, śrutis pertaining to origination (utpatti-śruti) of differing tenor (bhinna-prasthāna) are met with. Some declare the origination of ākāśa (space/ether), some do not. Likewise, some declare the origination of vāyu (air), some do not. The same holds for the jīva (individual self) and the prāṇas (vital breaths). And in like manner, contradiction (vipratiṣedha) by way of order of creation (krama) and the rest is also observed in different śruti passages.
BS_C02_S03_INTRO1::block-1: By [pointing to] internal contradiction, the unworthiness of the opposing schools' tenets has been established. In the same way, with respect to one's own position too (svapakṣa) one might suspect non-authoritativeness on the very ground of mutual contradiction. Therefore, in order to clarify the meaning of the creation-śrutis (sṛṣṭi-śruti) found across all the Vedāntas, this further extended discussion (prapañca) is undertaken. The fruit of this clarification is just the dispelling of the suspicion as stated. Among these topics, first ākāśa is taken up for inquiry —
BS_C02_S03_V01::block-0: Sūtra 1: "Not [does] vyat (space/ether arise), because of non-mention in śruti."
BS_C02_S03_V01::block-1: Pūrvapakṣa-Siddhānta inquiry: Does ākāśa (space) have origination, or does it not? Therein it is first propounded — "Not vyat, because of non-mention": ākāśa surely does not originate. Why? Because of non-mention in śruti (aśruteḥ) — for there is no scriptural utterance regarding its origination in the section dealing with origination (utpatti-prakaraṇa).
BS_C02_S03_V01::block-2: For in the Chāndogya, having taken up Brahman, denoted by the word sat, in "Existence (sat) alone, dear one, this was in the beginning, one only without a second" (Chāndogya 6.2.1), the origination of just three [elements] — tejas (fire), ap (water), and anna (food/earth) — is taught, beginning with tejas as the first among the five mahābhūtas (gross elements): "It (Sat) reflected" and "It created tejas" (Chāndogya 6.2.3).
BS_C02_S03_V01::block-3: And śruti is for us the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for the rise of knowledge regarding supersensuous matters (atīndriya-artha-vijñāna). And here there is no śruti propounding the origination of ākāśa. Therefore there is no origination of ākāśa. (1)
BS_C02_S03_V02::block-0: Sūtra 2: "But it does exist [i.e., there is a śruti for ākāśa's origination]."
BS_C02_S03_V02::block-1: The word tu ("but") indicates the adoption of an alternative position (pakṣāntara-parigraha). Granted, in the Chāndogya there is no origination of ākāśa. But in another śruti there is. For the Taittirīyakas declare — having taken up "Brahman is truth, knowledge, infinite" ("satyaṃ jñānam anantaṃ brahma", Taittirīya Up. 2.1.1) — "From that very Self, this ākāśa came forth" ("tasmād vā etasmād ātmana ākāśaḥ saṃbhūtaḥ", Taittirīya Up. 2.1.1).
BS_C02_S03_V02::block-2: Hence there is a contradiction between the two śrutis: in one place creation begins with tejas, in another with ākāśa. Pūrvapakṣa: But surely the harmonising as one statement (eka-vākyatā) of these two śrutis is proper. Reply: Granted, that would be proper, but it cannot be ascertained.
BS_C02_S03_V02::block-3: Why? Because the once-mentioned creator in "It created tejas" cannot be syntactically connected with two objects of creation — "It created tejas", "It created ākāśa". Pūrvapakṣa: But it is observed that even a once-mentioned agent is connected with two objects of action — for example, "having cooked the soup, he cooks the rice" — likewise I shall construe "having created ākāśa, He created tejas".
BS_C02_S03_V02::block-4: Reply: That is not proper. For in the Chāndogya the priority of birth (prathamajatva) belongs to tejas; in the Taittirīyaka, to ākāśa. Both cannot be the first-born. By this very reasoning the conflict with the very wording of the other śruti is also explained — in "From that very Self, this ākāśa came forth" (Taittirīya Up. 2.1.1) too: "From that, ākāśa came forth", "From that, tejas came forth" — the once-mentioned point of origin (apādāna) and act of coming-forth (sambhavana) cannot simultaneously be connected with both vyat (space) and tejas. And from "From vāyu, agni" (Taittirīya Up. 2.1.1) it is mentioned separately. (2)
BS_C02_S03_V03::block-0: In this apparent contradiction, someone (the pūrvapakṣin) speaks thus —
BS_C02_S03_V03::block-1: There is no origination of ākāśa (space/ether), simply because no scripture teaches it. As for that other śruti which has been cited as declaring the origination of ākāśa, it deserves to be taken in a secondary (gauṇa) sense. Why? Because origination is impossible (asambhava). For the origination of ākāśa cannot be admitted as possible, so long as those who follow the view of the venerable Kaṇabhuk (Kaṇāda, founder of Vaiśeṣika) are alive. They indeed prevent the origination of ākāśa on the ground that the requisite assemblage of causes (kāraṇa-sāmagrī) is not possible. For according to them, everything that comes into being is produced from the inherent cause (samavāyi-kāraṇa), the non-inherent cause (asamavāyi-kāraṇa) and the efficient cause (nimitta-kāraṇa). And the inherent cause of a substance is many substances of the same class (samāna-jātīyaka). But there exists no plurality of substances of the same class which could be the originating material for ākāśa, such that, when this inherent cause is present, and when there is conjunction (saṃyoga) of these as the non-inherent cause, ākāśa might come into being. And in the absence of these, the efficient cause that operates in conjunction with them is far removed in the case of ākāśa. Further, in the case of fire and the rest, which are originated, a difference between the prior and posterior states is conceivable — before origination the effects such as illumination did not exist, and afterwards they exist. But in the case of ākāśa no difference between prior and posterior states can be conceived. For who can ascertain that prior to origination it was without space, without porousness, without aperture? Moreover, from its dissimilarity (vaidharmya) with earth and the rest, namely from its characteristic of all-pervasiveness (vibhutva) and so on, the unbornness (ajatva) of ākāśa is established. Therefore, just as in worldly speech such expressions as “make ākāśa,” “ākāśa has come into being” are secondary (gauṇa) usages, and just as in such phrases as “the ākāśa of a pot,” “the ākāśa of a water-jug,” “the ākāśa of a house” the designation of distinction within the one undivided ākāśa is secondary — even in the Veda, “Let them sacrifice in forest-spaces” — in the same way, the śruti speaking of origination is also to be regarded as secondary.
BS_C02_S03_V04::block-0: Indeed śabda (scriptural word) proclaims the unbornness (ajatva) of ākāśa, since it says — “Vāyu and the inter-space, this is amṛta (immortal)” (Bṛ. U. 2.3.3); for of that which is amṛta no origination is possible. And in the passage “Like ākāśa, all-pervading and eternal” (Śat. Brā. 10.6.3.2), Brahman is being likened to ākāśa through the two attributes of all-pervasiveness and eternality, and thereby suggests that those two attributes belong also to ākāśa itself. And of that which is so (eternal and all-pervasive) origination is not possible. Likewise the citation, “As this ākāśa is endless, even so the Self is to be known as endless,” and “Brahman whose body is ākāśa” (Tai. U. 1.6.2), and “Ākāśa is the Ātman” (Tai. U. 1.7.1). For if ākāśa were possessed of origination, the qualification of Brahman by it would not be possible — as is the qualification of the lotus by blueness (which presupposes the lotus already exists). Therefore it is understood that Brahman, eternal in nature, is uniformly common with ākāśa (in eternality).
BS_C02_S03_V05::block-0: This sūtra is supplementary to the previous one (padottara). The objector (pūrvapakṣin) says: But how is it possible that one and the same word ‘sambhūta’ (came into being), occurring in the passage “From this very Self ākāśa came into being” (Tai. U. 2.1.1), should be primary (mukhya) in respect of the subsequent items, fire and the rest, and yet secondary (gauṇa) in respect of ākāśa? To this the reply is given — Yes, it is possible that one and the same word ‘sambhūta’ should, owing to the difference of its objects, be used both secondarily and primarily, like the word ‘brahman’; just as the one word ‘brahman’ in the passage “Seek to know Brahman through tapas; Brahman is tapas” (Tai. U. 3.2.1) is used secondarily with reference to food and the rest, and primarily with reference to Bliss (ānanda); and just as the word ‘brahman’ is applied figuratively (bhaktyā) to tapas which is the means to the knowledge of Brahman, but is applied primarily to the Brahman that is to be directly known — even so here.
BS_C02_S03_V05::block-1: But, if ākāśa is not originated, how is the declaration “One only, without a second” (Chā. U. 6.2.1) sustained? For surely with ākāśa as a second, Brahman would be possessed of a second. And how would Brahman’s being known render everything known? To this it is said — “One only” is, first, intelligible with reference to its own effects (svakārya). Just as in the world someone, having seen on the previous day clay, staff, wheel and the rest in a potter’s house, and on the next day having seen various pots laid out, might say “Yesterday clay alone was, without companion” — by such a determination he means that on the previous day the assemblage of clay’s products was not, not that staff, wheel and the rest were not — even so the śruti “without a second” (advitīya) excludes any other ruler (adhiṣṭhāṛ). For just as a potter is seen as the ruler over clay which is the material for pots, so there is no other ruler over Brahman which is the material of the world. Nor does ākāśa as a second occasion Brahman’s having a second. For diversity (nānātva) is occasioned by difference of defining marks (lakṣaṇa). And before origination there is no difference of defining marks between Brahman and ākāśa, just as there is none between milk and water mixed together, on account of their sharing the common attributes of all-pervasiveness, formlessness and the rest. But at the time of creation Brahman alone exerts itself to bring forth the world; the other (ākāśa) remains motionless — through this their difference is recognised. Likewise, from such śrutis as “Brahman whose body is ākāśa” (Tai. U. 1.6.2) the figurative non-difference (abheda-upacāra) between Brahman and ākāśa is established. And just on this account is established the cognition of all by the cognition of Brahman. Moreover, every effect when it comes into being arises in a place and time non-different from that of ākāśa, and ākāśa exists in a place and time non-different from that of Brahman; therefore, when Brahman together with its effects is known, ākāśa is known along with them — just as when into a pot full of milk a few drops of water are thrown, they get apprehended by the very apprehension of the milk; for there does not remain a separate apprehension of the water-drops over and above the apprehension of the milk; even so, owing to non-difference of place and time with Brahman and its effects, ākāśa stands apprehended by the very apprehension of Brahman. Therefore the śruti of ākāśa’s origination is figurative (bhākta).
BS_C02_S03_V06::block-0: When this is the position established (by the pūrvapakṣa), this (siddhānta) is now stated —
BS_C02_S03_V06::block-1: “By which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought thought, the unknown known” (Chā. U. 6.1.3); “Verily when the Self is seen, heard, thought, and known, all this is known” (Bṛ. U. 4.5.6); “What is that, O Bhagavan, by knowing which all this becomes known?” (Mu. U. 1.1.3); “There exists no knowledge other than from me” — such a pratijñā (declaration) is recognised throughout each Vedānta. There would be no abandonment of, no contradiction to, that declaration only if there is non-difference (avyatireka) of the entire mass of things from Brahman the object to be known. For if there were difference, the declaration that by knowing one thing all is known would be set aside. And such non-difference is intelligible only if the entire mass of things has originated from the one Brahman. The establishment of the declaration is also understood from the words of śruti, on the very principle of non-difference between cause and effect (prakṛti-vikāra-avyatireka-nyāya). Thus indeed, having declared “by which the unheard becomes heard,” the declaration is supported by such illustrations as that of clay (mṛd), which aim at establishing the non-difference of effect and cause. And to establish that very point the subsequent words are: “Being alone, my dear, was this in the beginning, one only without a second” (Chā. U. 6.2.1), “It thought,” “It created tejas” (Chā. U. 6.2.3) — having shown thus the assemblage of effects from Brahman, they show its non-difference: from “All this has That as its Self” (Chā. U. 6.8.7) up to the end of the chapter (prapāṭhaka). If, then, ākāśa were not the effect of Brahman, ākāśa would not be known when Brahman is known. And from this would follow the abandonment of the declaration. But it is not proper to make the Veda inauthoritative by abandoning its declaration. Likewise, throughout each Vedānta, those various words by means of those various illustrations make known that very same declaration — “All this is what this Self is” (Chā. U. 2.4.6), “Brahman alone, immortal, is in front” (Mu. U. 2.2.12), and so on. Therefore ākāśa too originates, just like fire and the rest.
BS_C02_S03_V06::block-2: Now, what was said — that ākāśa is not originated because there is no scriptural mention thereof — that is unsound; for another śruti dealing with the origination of ākāśa has been pointed out, “From this very Self ākāśa came into being” (Tai. U. 2.1.1). True, it has been pointed out, but it is in conflict with the other śruti “It created tejas.” Not so, because of the unity of import (eka-vākyatva) of all the śrutis. Let there be unity of import where there is no contradiction. But here a contradiction has been stated: from the impossibility of one creator (heard of only once) being related to two objects of creation, from the impossibility of both being first-born, and from the impossibility of either an alternative (vikalpa) or a combination (samuccaya). This objection does not stand. For in the Taittirīyaka the creation of tejas is read as third in order: “From this very Self ākāśa came into being; from ākāśa, vāyu; from vāyu, agni” (Tai. U. 2.1.1). This śruti cannot be interpreted otherwise. But the Chāndogya śruti can be reinterpreted: having created ākāśa and vāyu, it is said “It created tejas.” For this śruti, having as its principal subject the origination of tejas, cannot exclude the origination of ākāśa established by the other śruti, since one sentence cannot perform two functions. The single creator can in succession create many objects of creation — when this construction is possible, the śruti should not be abandoned as expressing a contradictory meaning. And we do not maintain that the creator (heard of only once) is connected with two objects of creation, since the additional object of creation is included by virtue of the other śruti. Just as in the passage “All this is verily Brahman; from That it springs, into That it dissolves, in That it breathes” (Chā. U. 3.14.1), where the directly heard origination of all things from Brahman does not exclude the order of origination beginning with tejas declared elsewhere — even so the heard origination of tejas from Brahman cannot exclude the order of origination beginning with ākāśa declared in another śruti. Now (the pūrvapakṣin says) this passage is for the purpose of enjoining tranquillity (śama), as is heard from the śruti “One should meditate on it as ‘from That it springs’ etc., being tranquil.” It is not a creation-passage. Therefore it cannot oppose the order established elsewhere. But “It created tejas” is a creation-passage. Hence here the order should be taken as it is heard. We say: not so. For on the strength of the priority of tejas, we cannot abandon the entity ākāśa established by another śruti, since order is a property of the entities (padārtha-dharma). Moreover, in “It created tejas” there is no word at all expressly denoting order. Order is understood only by implication. And that order is set aside by the order established by the other śruti, “From vāyu, agni” (Tai. U. 2.1.1). And alternative (vikalpa) and combination (samuccaya) regarding the first-bornness of either ākāśa or tejas are excluded by the impossibility (of vikalpa) and by their non-acceptance (of samuccaya). Therefore there is no contradiction between the two śrutis. Furthermore, in the Chāndogya, in order to support the declaration “by which the unheard becomes heard,” heard at the very commencement of the passage, even though ākāśa is not mentioned, it must be supplemented in the origination; how much more, then, can the ākāśa expressly mentioned in the Taittirīyaka not be included? And as for what was said — that since ākāśa is non-different in place and time from everything, it stands known along with Brahman and its effects, hence the declaration is not abandoned, and there is no violation of the śruti “One only without a second,” by reason of the non-difference of Brahman and ākāśa being intelligible like that of milk and water — to this we reply: this knowledge of all by knowledge of one cannot be carried through on the analogy of milk and water. (text truncated)
BS_C02_S03_V07::block-0: Now to that which has been said — that the śruti of ākāśa’s origination is secondary on account of the impossibility (of its being primary) — here we say —
BS_C02_S03_V07::block-1: The word ‘tu’ (“but”) serves to dispel the apprehension of impossibility. Indeed, no apprehension of impossibility regarding the origination of ākāśa is to be entertained. For whatever modification (vikāra) is observed — be it pots, jars, vessels and the like; or bracelets, armlets, earrings and the like; or needles, arrows, swords and the like — only that much division (vibhāga) is observed in the world. But not any unmodified thing is found divided from anything. And the division of ākāśa from earth and the rest is recognised. Therefore that too must be a modification (vikāra). By this is also explained the effect-nature of direction (dik), time (kāla), mind (manas), atoms (paramāṇu), and the rest. But (it might be objected) the Self too is divided from ākāśa and the rest, so its being an effect like a pot would also follow. No, because of the śruti “From the Self ākāśa came into being” (Tai. U. 2.1.1). For if the Self too were a modification, then since beyond it nothing is heard of, ākāśa and all that follows, being effects of the Self, would be devoid of self (nirātmaka). And thus the doctrine of voidness (śūnyavāda) would result. And from the very fact of being the Self, the apprehension of denying the Self does not stand. For the Self is not adventitious to anyone, being self-established (svayaṃ-siddha). The Self is not established by depending upon a means of knowledge regarding itself. For instruments of knowledge such as perception are taken up for establishing the unestablished objects of knowledge. Ākāśa and the like, the various entities, are not accepted by anyone as self-established without dependence upon a means of knowledge. But the Self, being the very ground of the operation of pramāṇa and the rest, is established prior to the operation of pramāṇa. And of such a thing denial is not possible. For an adventitious thing is denied, not one’s own nature. He who denies — that very fact is his own nature. The heat of fire is not denied by fire. So too: ‘I alone now know the present thing, I alone knew the past and the more remote past, I alone shall know the future and the more distant future’ — even though the object known undergoes change as past, future and present, no change of the knower exists, since he is always of the nature of the present. Likewise, even when the body is reduced to ashes, no annihilation of the Self can be conceived, nor can a nature different from his ever-present nature be conceived. Thus from the very fact that his nature cannot be denied, the Self is non-effect (akārya), and ākāśa is effect (kārya).
BS_C02_S03_V07::block-2: Now what was said — that there is no plurality of cause-substances of the same class (samānajātīya) for ākāśa — to that we reply: there is no rule that only the same-class produces, not the different-class. For there is no sameness of class between threads and their conjunctions, since they are accepted (by Vaiśeṣikas) as substance and quality respectively. Nor is there a rule of sameness of class even regarding efficient causes such as shuttle, loom, and the rest. Now (the opponent says): the acceptance of sameness of class refers only to the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa), not to other causes. But that too is inconclusive (anaikāntika). For a single rope is seen being made out of threads and cow-tails of unlike classes. Likewise variegated blankets are spread out from threads and wools and the like. Or, if sameness of class is to be conceived with reference to existence (sattva), substance-ness (dravyatva), and so on, the rule becomes purposeless, since everything is of the same class as everything (in those respects). Nor is there a rule that only many produce, not one. For the first action of an atom (aṇu) and of mind (manas) is accepted (by Vaiśeṣikas). For each individual atom and mind, it is accepted, initiates the first action, not by combining with other substances. If it be said: the rule of producer being many (anekārambhakatva) holds only in the case of substance-origination — no. For pariṇāma (transformation) is accepted. This rule would obtain if it were accepted that a substance, with the auxiliary of conjunction, originates another substance. But it is accepted that the very same substance, undergoing a special new state, is what is called effect (kārya). And that, in some cases, transforms as many — clay, seed and the rest, into the form of pot, sprout, and so on; in some cases as one — milk and the rest, into curd and the like. There is no Lord’s decree that only multiple causes produce an effect. Therefore by the authority of śruti it is determined: from the one Brahman, the world has come into being through the order of origination of the great elements (mahābhūta) beginning with ākāśa. As also has been said: “If it be said that (Brahman cannot be the cause), since the contrary is observed, no — for it is so as in the case of milk” (Br. Sū. 2.1.24).
BS_C02_S03_V07::block-3: And as for what was said — that no difference of prior and posterior states is conceivable in the origination of ākāśa — that is unsound. By that very specific characteristic by which ākāśa is now ascertained, as having its own form distinguished from earth and the rest, by that very specific characteristic it is understood that prior to origination ākāśa did not exist. And just as Brahman is not possessed of the natures of the gross and the rest, the natures of earth and the rest — from the śrutis “Not gross, not subtle” (Bṛ. U. 3.8.8) and so on — even so it is understood from śruti that Brahman is not possessed of the nature of ākāśa, that it is not ākāśa (anākāśa). Therefore it stands established that prior to origination there was no ākāśa. And as for what was said — that from dissimilarity (vaidharmya) with earth and the rest the unbornness of ākāśa is established — that too is wrong. For when there is contradiction with śruti, the inference of impossibility of origination is fallacious; and the inference for origination has been shown. (Inferences also exist:) ākāśa is non-eternal, since it is the support of non-eternal qualities, like a pot — such a syllogism is also possible. If it be said this is inconclusive in the case of the Self — no. For the Self of the Upaniṣads is not established as the support of non-eternal qualities. And all-pervasiveness and the rest of ākāśa are not established for one who maintains its origination. As for what was said — “and from śabda” — there the śruti of immortality with respect to ākāśa is to be understood like “the immortal dwellers of heaven” (relatively immortal), since origination and dissolution have been demonstrated. The expression “like ākāśa, all-pervading and eternal” (Śat. Brā. 10.6.3.2) is using ākāśa, well-known for its greatness, as an upamāna (standard of comparison) for unsurpassed greatness, not for equality with ākāśa — just as “the sun runs like an arrow” is used for swiftness of movement, not for equality of speed with the arrow. By this the śruti of comparison with respect to endlessness is also explained. And from such śrutis as “Greater than ākāśa,” the smaller measure (ūnaparimāṇatva) of ākāśa as compared with Brahman is established. “There is no likeness of Him” (Śve. U. 4.19) shows the incomparability of Brahman. “Other than This is afflicted” (Bṛ. U. 3.4.2) shows the afflicted character of all other than Brahman, including ākāśa. The secondariness (gauṇatva) of the śruti of ākāśa’s origination — like the use of the word ‘brahman’ in the case of tapas — has been refuted by the śruti of ākāśa’s origination and by inference. Therefore it stands established that ākāśa is the effect of Brahman.
BS_C02_S03_V08::block-0: This is an extension (atideśa). By this exposition concerning ākāśa (vyat), mātariśvan (vāyu) too, which has ākāśa as its support, is explained. There also the various positions are to be arranged accordingly. The first view: vāyu does not originate, since in the Chāndogya origination-passage there is no mention of it. The other view: there is mention in the Taittirīyaka origination-passage, “From ākāśa, vāyu” (Tai. U. 2.1.1). And consequently when there is conflict between the two śrutis, the śruti of vāyu’s origination is secondary, since origination is impossible — this is another opinion. And the impossibility (according to the pūrvapakṣin) follows from “This is the deity that never sets, namely vāyu” (Bṛ. U. 1.5.22), which negates its setting, and from the śruti of immortality and the rest. The siddhānta is: vāyu originates, by reason of non-violation of the declaration (pratijñā) and acceptance of division (vibhāga) being co-extensive with modification (yāvad-vikāra). The negation of setting is relative, in the sphere of lower knowledge (apara-vidyā), since vāyu does not have a setting like fire and the rest. And the śruti of immortality has been answered (in the previous adhikaraṇa). Now (someone may ask): for vāyu and ākāśa, both equivalent in being mentioned (in the Taittirīyaka) and not mentioned (in the Chāndogya) in the origination-passage, let there be only one adhikaraṇa with both as the subject — what is the use of the extension when there is no difference? — to this we reply: True, this is so. Yet for the dispelling of the apprehension occasioned in dull-witted persons by the mere word, this extension (atideśa) is performed — for from hearing in the saṃvarga-vidyā and the like the high status of vāyu as an object of meditation, and from the negation of its setting and the like, there might arise in someone the apprehension of its eternality.
BS_C02_S03_V09::block-0: Hearing of the origination of ākāśa and vāyu, whose origination was thought impossible, someone might form the opinion that even Brahman might have origination from somewhere. Likewise, hearing that subsequent modifications originate from prior modifications such as ākāśa and the rest, someone might think that even ākāśa originates only from a modification, namely Brahman. To dispel this apprehension is the present sūtra —
BS_C02_S03_V09::block-1: “But there is no origination (of Brahman).” For of Brahman, whose nature is sat (Existence), origination from anywhere else is not to be apprehended. Why? Because of the impossibility (anupapatti). For Brahman is mere Existence (sanmātra). Of it, origination from mere Existence itself is not possible, since when there is no excellence (atiśaya), the relation of cause-effect (prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva) is not possible. Nor (origination) from a particular existent (sad-viśeṣa), since this would contradict observation — for the particulars are seen to originate from the general; pots and the like from clay; not the general from particulars. Nor from non-existence (asat), since it is devoid of self (nirātmaka). And also from hearing the rejection “How can the existent be born from the non-existent?” (Chā. U. 6.2.2). And the śruti “He is the cause, the lord of the lord of the senses; of Him there is no progenitor, no overlord” (Śve. U. 6.9) excludes any progenitor of Brahman. The origination of ākāśa and vāyu has been demonstrated, but it is not so with Brahman — herein lies the asymmetry. Nor, from the observation of one modification originating from another modification, can Brahman also be a modification, since not accepting a root-prakṛti (mūla-prakṛti) would entail an infinite regress (anavasthā). And whatever root-prakṛti is accepted is for us nothing but Brahman — so there is no contradiction.
BS_C02_S03_V10::block-0: In the Chāndogya, tejas is taught as having sat as its source (sanmūla); but in the Taittirīyaka, as having vāyu as its source (vāyumūla). Now, regarding the source of tejas, when there is conflict in śruti, the prima facie view (prāpta) is that tejas has Brahman as its source. Why? Because, having commenced with “Existence alone” (sat eva), the teaching is “It created tejas.” Also because the declaration of all-cognition by Brahman’s cognition is intelligible only when everything has Brahman as its source; and from “In That it springs, in That it dissolves, in That it breathes” (Chā. U. 3.14.1), where there is no specification (aviśeṣa-śruti). And also because, having begun with “From this is born prāṇa” (Mu. U. 2.1.3), in another śruti everything is taught as Brahman-born without specification (aviśeṣa); and in the Taittirīyaka, from “He, having performed tapas, created all this — whatever there is” (Tai. U. 2.6.1), there is non-specific śravaṇa. Therefore — “From vāyu, agni” (Tai. U. 2.1.1) is to be taken as a teaching of order: agni came into being immediately after vāyu.
BS_C02_S03_V10::block-1: When this prima facie view is established, it is replied: tejas is born “from this” (atas), namely from mātariśvan. Why? Because the śruti so declares — “From vāyu, agni.” For if tejas were born immediately from Brahman without intermediate, and not from vāyu, then this śruti “From vāyu, agni” would be wrenched out of meaning. Now, it might be said that this śruti has order as its purport — to that we say: no. For in the prior passage “From this very Self ākāśa came into being” (Tai. U. 2.1.1), the Self, which is the source (apādāna) of origination, is shown by the fifth-case ending (pañcamī), and that very ‘sambhū’ (originate) is in operation here, and likewise in the subsequent context “From earth, the herbs” (Tai. U. 2.1.1) the fifth-case ending of source is observed; therefore in “From vāyu, agni” the fifth-case ending is also that of source. Furthermore, the connection of word and meaning required in “Above vāyu agni came into being” is conjectural (kalpya), but the connection of grammatical case-meaning (kāraka-artha) “From vāyu, agni came into being” is established (kḷpta). Therefore this śruti makes known that tejas has vāyu as its source. But (it might be objected) the other śruti makes known that tejas has Brahman as its source — “It created tejas.” No, because even if it (tejas) is born through a chain (pāramparya), there is no contradiction. For even when it is conceived that, having created ākāśa and vāyu, Brahman, having attained the form of vāyu, created tejas, even then tejas being Brahman-born is not contradicted, just like in “its (the cow’s) milk boiled, its curd, its butter,” and so on. And the śruti shows Brahman’s assuming the form of modification — “He himself made his Self” (Tai. U. 2.7.1). Likewise the smṛti of the Lord — having enumerated “buddhi, jñāna, lack of delusion” and the rest (Bha. Gī. 10.4), it says “The various states of beings come from Me alone” (Bha. Gī. 10.5). For though buddhi and the rest are seen to come about directly from their causes, even then everything in the realm of beings, either directly or through a chain, is descended from the Lord. By this, those śrutis which speak of simultaneous creation (akrama-sṛṣṭi) are also explained — they are intelligible in every way, while those which speak of orderly creation (krama-vat-sṛṣṭi) are not otherwise intelligible. The declaration too requires only descent from sat, not direct birth without intermediate — so there is no contradiction.
BS_C02_S03_V11::block-0: The phrase ‘ataḥ — tathā hyāha’ (‘from this; for thus says the śruti’) continues from the previous sūtra. Water (āpaḥ) arises from this — i.e., from fire (tejas). On what authority? ‘Tathā hyāha’ — for the scripture so declares: ‘tad-apo'sṛjat’ (‘That [fire] created water’) (citation), and ‘agner āpaḥ’ (‘from fire, water’) (citation). When the scriptural statement is explicit, there is no doubt. Having explained the production of fire, and intending now to explain the production of earth, the sūtrakāra interposes water in the middle by composing the sūtra ‘āpaḥ.’ ‖ 11 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V12: Earth (is meant by the word ‘anna’) — because of the topic, because of the colour-form (rūpa) and because of other (corroborating) words. ‖ 12 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V12::block-0: Pūrvapakṣa: It is heard in the śruti, ‘tā āpa aikṣanta bahvyaḥ syāma prajāyemahīti tā annam asṛjanta’ — ‘Those waters reflected: “May we be many, may we propagate”; they emitted anna’ (Chā. Up. 6.2.4) (citation). Here arises a doubt — does this word ‘anna’ denote rice, barley and the like that are eaten, or cooked rice and similar prepared foods, or rather earth (pṛthivī)? On this the prima facie view is that rice, barley, cooked rice and the like must be taken. For in common usage the word ‘anna’ is well known in this sense. The remainder of the passage also strengthens this meaning — ‘tasmād yatra kva ca varṣati tad eva bhūyiṣṭham annaṁ bhavati’ (‘therefore wherever it rains, there food becomes most abundant’) (citation). For when there is rainfall it is rice, barley and so on that grow abundantly, not earth.
BS_C02_S03_V12::block-1: Siddhānta: To this prima facie view we reply — it is earth itself which, as arising from the waters, is meant to be conveyed by the word ‘anna.’ Why? Because of the topic (adhikāra), because of the colour-form (rūpa), and because of another corroborating word (śabdāntara). First, the topic: the context of ‘tat tejo'sṛjata’ (‘that created fire’) and ‘tad apo'sṛjat’ (‘that created water’) deals with the great elements (mahābhūtas). It is improper, leaping over earth — the great element that comes next in due sequence — to suddenly grasp at rice and the like. Likewise the rūpa appearing in the rest of the passage agrees with earth — ‘yat kṛṣṇaṁ tad annasya’ (‘that which is black is of anna’) (citation). For there is no fixed blackness in cooked rice and other foods, nor in rice, barley and so on. Objection: even earth has no fixed blackness, since fields milk-white in colour and red as embers are also seen. Reply: this is no defect, for the rule rests on predominance. The black colour is most prevalent in earth; whiteness and redness are not so. The Paurāṇikas too teach that night is the shadow of the earth, and that shadow appears black — hence blackness as the rūpa is fittingly applied to earth. Another śruti having the same import is also found — ‘adbhyaḥ pṛthivī’ (‘from the waters, the earth’) (citation), and ‘tad yad apāṁ śara āsīt tat samahanyata sā pṛthivy abhavat’ (‘that which was the froth of the waters became compacted, and that became the earth’) (Bṛ. Up. 1.2.2) (citation). And from earth the production of rice and the like is shown — ‘pṛthivyā oṣadhayaḥ oṣadhībhyo'nnam’ (‘from the earth, the herbs; from the herbs, food’) (citation). Thus, when the topic and other indicators establish earth, how can rice and the like be the import? The well-known popular sense is also overridden by these (topic, etc.). The remainder of the passage too should be seen as suggesting, by the earthiness of food, that earth itself springs from the waters through that very route. Therefore, in this passage the word ‘anna’ denotes earth. ‖ 12 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V13: But (the elements arise) only from His meditation upon them, that being a mark thereof — He (the Lord is the agent). ‖ 13 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V13::block-0: Pūrvapakṣa: Do these elements — ether and the rest — themselves emit their own modifications, or is it the Supreme Lord alone who, abiding within each as their (inner) self and meditating, brings forth each modification? On this doubt arising, the prima facie view is that they themselves emit them. Why? Because of the scriptural mention of independence: ‘ākāśād vāyuḥ vāyor agniḥ’ (‘from ether, air; from air, fire’) (Tai. Up. 2.1.1) (citation). Objection: but for non-conscious things acting independently, activity (pravṛtti) has been denied! Reply: this is no defect, since scriptural mention of consciousness in the elements themselves is found — ‘tat teja aikṣata’ (‘that fire reflected’) (Chā. Up. 6.2.3), ‘tā āpa aikṣanta’ (‘those waters reflected’) (Chā. Up. 6.2.4) (citation).
BS_C02_S03_V13::block-1: Siddhānta: To this we reply — it is that very Supreme Lord who, abiding within each as their (inner) self and meditating, emits each modification. Why? Because of the mark thereof (tal-liṅgāt). Thus the śāstra: ‘yaḥ pṛthivyāṁ tiṣṭhan pṛthivyā antaro yaṁ pṛthivī na veda yasya pṛthivī śarīraṁ yaḥ pṛthivīm antaro yamayati’ (‘He who, dwelling in the earth, is within the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body the earth is, who controls the earth from within’) (Bṛ. Up. 3.7.3) (citation), and similar passages, show that the elements function only when overseen (by the inner ruler). Likewise, beginning with ‘so'kāmayata bahu syāṁ prajāyeyeti’ (‘He desired: “May I become many, may I be born”’) (Tai. Up. 2.6.1), and continuing ‘sac ca tyac cābhavat’ (‘He became the manifest and the unmanifest’) (Tai. Up. 2.6.1), and ‘tad ātmānaṁ svayam akuruta’ (‘He of Himself made Himself’) (Tai. Up. 2.7.1) (citation), the texts show that He alone is the Self of all. As for the īkṣaṇa (reflection) heard of regarding water and fire, it must be understood as solely owing to the indwelling of the Supreme Lord — for there is the negation of any other reflector: ‘nānyo'to'sti draṣṭā’ (‘there is no other seer than this’) (Bṛ. Up. 3.7.23) (citation), and because the īkṣitṛ (reflector) under discussion is none other than Sat (Pure Being) referred to in ‘tad aikṣata bahu syāṁ prajāyeyeti’ (‘That reflected: “May I become many, may I be born”’) (Tai. Up. 2.6.1) (citation). ‖ 13 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V14: But the order (of dissolution) is in the reverse, and that stands to reason. ‖ 14 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V14::block-0: Pūrvapakṣa: The order of origination of the elements has been considered. Now the order of their dissolution (apyaya) is to be considered: is the dissolution in some indeterminate order, or in the same order as origination, or in the reverse? All three — origination, sustenance, and dissolution of the elements — are heard in scripture as dependent on Brahman: ‘yato vā imāni bhūtāni jāyante. yena jātāni jīvanti. yat prayanty abhisaṁviśanti’ (‘That from which all these beings are born, by which when born they live, into which on departing they enter’) (Tai. Up. 3.1.1) (citation). Hence on this matter, since there is no special indication, the prima facie view is indeterminacy. Or else, since the order of origination is heard, the dissolution also — which awaits some order — should follow that very same order.
BS_C02_S03_V14::block-1: Siddhānta: To this prima facie view we reply — but the order of dissolution is in the reverse, that is, from the order of origination, must it be. For so it is seen in the world: by whatever sequence one ascends a staircase, by the reverse one descends. Further, it is observed that the pot, dish and so on born from clay, at the time of dissolution, return to the state of clay, and the snow, hail and so on born from water, return to the state of water. And on this ground also it stands to reason: that the earth, having been born from water, when its time of subsistence is past, dissolves into water; the waters, having been born from fire, dissolve into fire. Thus, by stages, every effect — entering its immediately prior, more subtle cause — is finally to be known as merging into the supreme cause and supremely subtle Brahman. For the dissolution of an effect into the cause-of-the-cause, leaping over its own immediate cause, is improper. In smṛti also the order of dissolution is shown, here and there, only as the reverse of the order of origination — ‘jagat-pratiṣṭhā devarṣe pṛthivy apsu pralīyate. jyotiṣy āpaḥ pralīyante jyotir vāyau pralīyate’ (‘O divine seer, the support of the world: earth dissolves in water, water dissolves in fire, fire dissolves in air’) (citation), and so on. The order of origination, however, being heard only in the context of origination, cannot apply to dissolution; nor is it sought there, as it is unsuitable. For while the effect remains, the dissolution of its cause is unreasonable, since on the cause’s dissolution the effect cannot subsist. But on the dissolution of the effect, the subsistence of the cause is reasonable — as is observed in clay and the like. ‖ 14 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V15: If it be said that, in between, the (origination and dissolution of the) intellect (vijñāna) and the mind (manas) must be inserted in due order — because of the mark thereof — (we reply,) no; on account of non-distinction. ‖ 15 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V15::block-0: Pūrvapakṣa: It has been said that the origination and dissolution of the elements proceed by the forward and reverse orders respectively; and it has also been said that origination begins with the (individual) self and dissolution ends in the self. Now the existence of the mind (manas) along with the senses, and of the intellect (buddhi), is well known both in śruti and smṛti, by such marks as ‘buddhiṁ tu sārathiṁ viddhi manaḥ pragraham eva ca’ (‘know the intellect to be the charioteer, and the mind, indeed, the rein’) (Ka. Up. 1.3.3), ‘indriyāṇi hayān āhuḥ’ (‘they call the senses the horses’) (Ka. Up. 1.3.4) (citation), and the like. Their origination and dissolution too must be accommodated, in due order, somewhere in the interval — since every existing thing is acknowledged as born of Brahman. Moreover, in the Ātharvaṇa-(Muṇḍaka), in the section on origination, the instruments are enumerated in the interval between the elements and the self — ‘etasmāj jāyate prāṇo manaḥ sarvendriyāṇi ca. khaṁ vāyur jyotir āpaḥ pṛthivī viśvasya dhāriṇī’ (‘from this arise prāṇa, mind and all the senses; ether, air, fire, water and earth, the supporter of all’) (Mu. Up. 2.1.3) (citation). Hence the order of origination and dissolution of the elements stated earlier is in danger of being broken. Siddhānta: If so, (we reply:) no, on account of non-distinction (aviśeṣāt). First, if the instruments are bhautika (composed of the elements), then through the very origination and dissolution of the elements there occurs their origination and dissolution; no separate order need be sought for these two. And there is a mark for the bhautika nature of the instruments — ‘annamayaṁ hi somya mana āpomayaḥ prāṇas tejomayī vāk’ (‘mind, dear one, is made of food; prāṇa is made of water; speech is made of fire’) (Chā. Up. 6.5.4) (citation), and the like. The (occasional) interchange of names between the elements and the instruments should be understood on the principle of the ‘brāhmaṇa-parivrājaka’ (where ‘parivrājaka’ stands also for the brāhmaṇa). On the other hand, if the instruments are non-elemental (abhautika), even then the order of origination of the elements is not qualified by the instruments — whether the instruments arise first and the elements last, or the elements first and the instruments last.
