In the Ātharvaṇa it is only the order of mention (samāmnāya-krama) of the instruments and elements; no order of origination is taught there. And elsewhere also the order of the instruments is mentioned separately from the order of the elements — ‘prajāpatir vā idam agra āsīt sa ātmānam aikṣata sa mano'sṛjata tan mana evāsīt tad ātmānam aikṣata tad vācam asṛjata’ (‘Prajāpati alone was this in the beginning; he viewed himself; he created the mind; that was just mind; that viewed itself; it created speech’) (citation), and so on. Therefore there is no breach of the order of origination of the elements. ‖ 15 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V16: But (origination and dissolution) are in dependence on the moving and the unmoving (bodies); the use of those (terms ‘birth’ and ‘death’) with reference to the soul is figurative, since (its use depends) on the existence of those (bodily states). ‖ 16 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V16::block-0: Pūrvapakṣa-doubt: Someone may suppose that the soul (jīva) too has origination and dissolution, on the strength of common usage like ‘Devadatta is born,’ ‘Devadatta is dead,’ and on the strength of the prescriptions of saṁskāras such as the jātakarman (birth-rite) and the like. We dispel that. The soul does not undergo origination and dissolution, since otherwise the connection of scripture with its fruit would not stand. For if the soul perished along with the body, the prescriptions and prohibitions, aimed at obtaining what is desired and avoiding what is undesired in the next body, would be purposeless. The śruti also says — ‘jīvāpetaṁ vāva kiledaṁ mriyate na jīvo mriyate’ (‘this (body) verily dies when forsaken by the soul; the soul itself does not die’) (Chā. Up. 6.11.3) (citation). Objection: but the worldly designation of birth and death has been shown of the soul itself. True, it has been shown — but this designation of ‘birth’ and ‘death’ of the soul is figurative (bhākta). Where then is the principal (mukhya) usage, with reference to which this is figurative? It is answered: in dependence on the moving and the unmoving (carācara-vyapāśraya). The words ‘birth’ and ‘death’ refer primarily to the bodies of the moving (animate) and the unmoving (inanimate). For it is moving and unmoving beings that are born and die. Hence these words ‘birth’ and ‘death,’ being primary with reference to those, are then transferred to the indwelling soul, on account of the soul’s being conditioned by the existence of those (bodily states) (tad-bhāva-bhāvitvāt) — for the words ‘birth’ and ‘death’ obtain only when there is the manifestation and disappearance of the body, not where there is none. The soul is never noticed by anyone as being born or dying apart from connection with a body. The śruti also: ‘sa vā ayaṁ puruṣo jāyamānaḥ śarīram abhisampadyamānaḥ sa utkrāman mriyamāṇaḥ’ (‘that very person, while being born, attains a body; while departing, dies’) (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.8) (citation), shows that the words ‘birth’ and ‘death’ have as their occasion only the conjunction with and disjunction from the body. The injunction of jātakarman and the rest, too, must be understood as concerned only with the manifestation of the body, since there is no manifestation of the soul itself. Whether the soul has, like ether and the rest, an origination from the supreme Self or not, will be stated in the next sūtra. By this sūtra it has been stated that the soul’s gross body-dependent origination and dissolution do not exist. ‖ 16 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V17: The (individual) self is not (originated), because of the absence of scriptural mention (of its origination), and because of the eternality (heard) from those (śruti texts). ‖ 17 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V17::block-0: Pūrvapakṣa: There exists a self, called the jīva, which is the overlord of the cage of body and senses, and is connected with the fruits of action. Does this jīva, like ether and the rest, originate from Brahman, or like Brahman itself does it not originate? On this there is doubt because of conflict in scriptural statements. In some śrutis, the origination of the individual self from the supreme Brahman is stated through illustrations such as fire and sparks; in others, the very same supreme Brahman, unmodified, is known as having entered into the effects (and thereby) acquired jīva-hood — and no origination is mentioned. On this the prima facie view is that the jīva is originated. Why? On the strength of the consistency of the (scriptural) declaration alone — the declaration ‘ekasmin vidite sarvam idaṁ viditam’ (‘by the knowing of the One all this becomes known’) (citation) would not be consistent unless every existing thing arose from Brahman; if the jīva were a separate principle, this declaration would be infringed. Nor can the unmodified supreme Self itself be regarded as the jīva, because of the difference in characteristics (lakṣaṇa-bheda): the supreme Self is endowed with such qualities as ‘sinlessness’ and the rest, while the jīva is the very opposite. Its modificatory nature is also established by partition (vibhāga): whatever, beginning with ākāśa, is partitioned, is all a modification (vikāra). And the origination of ākāśa and the rest has been ascertained. The jīva-self too, as endowed with merit and demerit, joined with pleasure and pain, is partitioned in each body; hence it too, on the occasion of the world’s manifestation, must be (regarded as) originated. Further, ‘yathāgneḥ kṣudrā visphuliṅgā vyuccaranty evam evāsmād ātmanaḥ sarve prāṇāḥ’ (‘as from a fire tiny sparks fly forth, so from this Self all prāṇas fly forth’) (Bṛ. Up. 2.1.20) (citation) — having taught the creation of prāṇa and the like (the entire object of enjoyment), it then teaches in ‘sarva ete ātmāno vyuccaranti’ (‘all these selves fly forth’) (citation) the separate creation of the experiencing selves. And ‘yathā sudīptāt pāvakād visphuliṅgāḥ sahasraśaḥ prabhavante sarūpāḥ. tathākṣarād vividhāḥ somya bhāvāḥ prajāyante tatra caivāpiyanti’ (‘as from a brightly blazing fire sparks of like form spring forth in thousands, so, dear one, manifold beings come forth from the imperishable, and there alone they merge back’) (Mu. Up. 2.1.1) (citation) — here the origination and dissolution of the individual selves are taught, since the word ‘sarūpa’ (of like form) is used: for the individual selves are of like form with the supreme Self by reason of consciousness. Nor is mere absence of mention in one place able to debar what is heard elsewhere; for whatever is heard in another śruti, if not contradicted, is to be incorporated everywhere. The śruti of ‘entering’ (praveśa), accordingly, is also to be explained as the assumption of the modificatory state — as in ‘tad ātmānaṁ svayam akuruta’ (‘He of Himself made Himself’) (Tai. Up. 2.7.1) (citation) and the like. Therefore the jīva is originated.
BS_C02_S03_V17::block-1: Siddhānta: To this prima facie view we reply — the self, the jīva, is not originated. Why? Because of the absence of scriptural mention (aśruteḥ): for there is no mention of its origination in the topical sections on origination, in many places. Objection: but it has been said that absence of mention in one place does not debar what is heard elsewhere. Granted — but we say that origination itself is impossible for it. Why? ‘And on account of eternality (heard) from those’ — by the word ‘ca’ (‘and’) being included also unbornness and immutability — for its eternality is known from the śrutis, and so also its unbornness and immutability, since the unmodified Brahman alone abides as the jīva-self and as the Brahman-self. And origination of one of such nature is not feasible. Which śrutis are those? ‘na jīvo mriyate’ (‘the soul does not die’) (Chā. Up. 6.11.3); ‘sa vā eṣa mahān aja ātmā'jaro'maro'mṛto'bhayo brahma’ (‘that great unborn Self is undecaying, undying, immortal, fearless, Brahman’) (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.25); ‘na jāyate mriyate vā vipaścit’ (‘the wise One is neither born nor dies’) (Ka. Up. 1.2.18); ‘ajo nityaḥ śāśvato'yaṁ purāṇaḥ’ (‘unborn, eternal, perpetual, ancient is this’) (Ka. Up. 1.2.18); ‘tat sṛṣṭvā tad evānuprāviśat’ (‘having created that, He entered into that very thing’) (Tai. Up. 2.6.1); ‘anena jīvenātmanānupraviśya nāmarūpe vyākaravāṇi’ (‘entering by this living self, let me unfold name and form’) (Chā. Up. 6.3.2); ‘sa eṣa iha praviṣṭa ā nakhāgrebhyaḥ’ (‘He has entered here, even up to the tips of the nails’) (Bṛ. Up. 1.4.7); ‘tat tvam asi’ (‘That thou art’) (Chā. Up. 6.8.7); ‘ahaṁ brahmāsmi’ (‘I am Brahman’) (Bṛ. Up. 1.4.10); ‘ayam ātmā brahma sarvānubhūḥ’ (‘this Self is Brahman, the experiencer of all’) (Bṛ. Up. 2.5.19) — these and similar passages, declaring eternality, debar the origination of the jīva. Objection: but it has been said that, since (it is) partitioned, it is a modification, and being a modification, it is originated. To this we reply: it has no partition of its own — for the śruti says, ‘eko devaḥ sarvabhūteṣu gūḍhaḥ sarvavyāpī sarvabhūtāntarātmā’ (‘the one God, hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner Self of all beings’) (Śve. Up. 6.11) (citation). The appearance of partition is occasioned by the upādhis (limiting adjuncts) such as buddhi and the rest — like the partition of ākāśa appearing through connection with pots and the like. The śāstra also: ‘sa vā ayam ātmā brahma vijñānamayo manomayaḥ prāṇamayaś cakṣurmayaḥ śrotramayaḥ’ (‘this very Self is Brahman, made of vijñāna, made of mind, of prāṇa, of eye, of ear’) (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.5) (citation), and the like, shows that this single, unmodified Brahman is multiform as buddhi and the rest. And its (jīva’s) being ‘made-of-that’ should be understood as bearing the character of being coloured by that, on account of its own intrinsic nature distinct from that not being manifested — in the manner of common expressions like ‘the wretch is woman-made’ (i.e., enthralled by women). And whatever mention is made elsewhere of its origination and dissolution, that too should be construed in this very way through connection with the upādhis: by the origination of the upādhi its origination, by its dissolution its dissolution. So it is shown — ‘prajñānaghana evaitebhyo bhūtebhyaḥ samutthāya tāny evānu vinaśyati na pretya saṁjñāsti’ (‘a mere mass of cognition, having arisen from these elements, perishes along with them; there is no consciousness after death’) (Bṛ. Up. 4.5.13) (citation); and that here it is the dissolution of the upādhi only, not the dissolution of the Self, is taught with the question and answer: ‘atraiva mā bhagavān mohāntam āpīpadan na vā aham imaṁ vijānāmi na pretya saṁjñāsti’ — (‘here itself the Lord has confounded me; I do not understand this — that there is no consciousness after death’); and the answer — ‘na vā are'haṁ mohaṁ bravīmy avināśī vā are'yam ātmā'nucchitti-dharmā mātrā'saṁsargas tv asya bhavati’ (‘I am not, dear one, telling thee anything bewildering; this Self, dear one, is verily indestructible, of an indestructible nature; it has only a non-conjunction with the elements’) (Bṛ. Up. 4.5.14) (citation). Even the consistency of the declaration (‘by knowing one all is known’) is preserved by acknowledging that the very Brahman, unmodified, has assumed jīva-hood; the difference of characteristics between the two is also occasioned by the upādhis alone; and ‘ata ūrdhvaṁ vimokṣāyaiva brūhi’ (‘teach me thereafter for the sake of liberation’) (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.15) (citation) shows that, by setting aside all the dharmas of saṁsāra from this very vijñānamaya self under discussion, its identity with the supreme Self is established. Therefore the Self is neither originated nor dissolved. ‖ 17 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V18: (The self is) a knower, for that very reason. ‖ 18 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V18::block-0: Pūrvapakṣa: Is the (Self) — like the view of the Kāṇabhujas (Vaiśeṣikas) — possessed of adventitious consciousness, intrinsically non-conscious, or — like the view of the Sāṅkhyas — of the very nature of eternal consciousness? On this dispute among the schools, doubt arises. What then is the prima facie view? It is held that the consciousness of the Self is adventitious (āgantuka), produced by the contact of the self and the manas, just as the quality of redness and the like is produced by the contact of fire and the pot (in baking). For if it were eternally conscious, then those who are asleep, swooning or possessed would also possess consciousness; but they, when questioned, say, ‘we were not conscious of anything’; while when in normal state they are seen to be conscious. Hence, since consciousness is occasional, the Self has adventitious consciousness — so says the Vaiśeṣika.
BS_C02_S03_V18::block-1: Siddhānta: To this we reply: ‘jñaḥ’ — this Self is of the nature of eternal consciousness — ‘ata eva’ — for that very reason that it is not originated; the supreme Brahman itself, unmodified, abides in the form of the jīva through the contact of upādhis. For the supreme Brahman’s nature as consciousness has been declared in such śrutis as: ‘vijñānam ānandaṁ brahma’ (‘Brahman is consciousness and bliss’) (Bṛ. Up. 3.9.28); ‘satyaṁ jñānam anantaṁ brahma’ (‘Brahman is truth, knowledge, infinite’) (Tai. Up. 2.1.1); ‘anantaro'bāhyaḥ kṛtsnaḥ prajñānaghana eva’ (‘without inside or outside, entire, a very mass of consciousness’) (Bṛ. Up. 4.5.13) (citation), and the like. If that very supreme Brahman is the jīva, it follows that the jīva also is of the nature of eternal consciousness — like the heat and light of fire. In the section on the vijñānamaya there are also śrutis such as: ‘asuptaḥ suptān abhicākaśīti’ (‘the unsleeping one views those who sleep’) (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.11); ‘atrāyaṁ puruṣaḥ svayaṁjyotir bhavati’ (‘here this person becomes self-luminous’) (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.9); ‘na hi vijñātur vijñāter viparilopo vidyate’ (‘for there is no break in the knowership of the knower’) (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.30) (citation), and so on. Also, ‘atha yo vededaṁ jighrāṇīti sa ātmā’ (‘he who is aware “let me smell this,” he is the Self’) (Chā. Up. 8.12.4) (citation) — by the connecting cognition through all the doors of the senses, ‘this I know, this I know,’ its (the Self’s) being of that (cognitive) nature is established. Objection: if consciousness is its eternal nature, then smelling and the rest become purposeless. Reply: not so, since they serve to differentiate the particular objects, smell and the like. Thus it is shown — ‘gandhāya ghrāṇam’ (‘the nose is for smell’) (citation), and so on. As to the contention that the sleeping and the rest are not conscious, the reply has been given by the śruti itself, with reference to deep sleep: ‘yad vai tan na paśyati paśyan vai tan na paśyati; na hi draṣṭur dṛṣṭer viparilopo vidyate'vināśitvāt; na tu tad dvitīyam asti tato'nyad vibhaktaṁ yat paśyet’ (‘when he does not see, he is verily seeing though he does not see; for there is no break in the seer’s seeing, since he is imperishable; but there is then no second other than him, separate, which he might see’) (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.23) (citation), and so on. The meaning is this: this absence of consciousness is owing to the absence of objects, not from absence of consciousness — just as the non-manifestation of the sky-located light is from absence of objects to be illumined, not from absence of its own form. Such is the case here. The reasonings of the Vaiśeṣika and the rest, when they conflict with śruti, are merely fallacious appearances. Therefore we conclude that the Self is verily of the nature of eternal consciousness. ‖ 18 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V19: On account of (the scriptural mention of the jīva’s) going-out, going, and returning. (II.iii.19)
BS_C02_S03_V19::block-0: Now is taken up the inquiry: of what magnitude (parimāṇa) is the jīva — is he atomic (aṇu-parimāṇa), or of medium magnitude (madhyama-parimāṇa, i.e. body-sized), or of vast magnitude (mahā-parimāṇa, all-pervading)? An objection (pūrvapakṣa-style demur): It has already been established that the Self is not produced and is of the nature of eternal Consciousness. From this it follows that the supreme Self alone is the jīva. And of the supreme Self infinitude (anantatva) has been declared in scripture. Where then is the room for an inquiry into the magnitude of the jīva? Reply (siddhāntin): True, this is so; yet the scriptural statements about (his) going-out, going, and returning impel us toward a (notion of his) being limited (paricchinna), and his own designating words (sva-śabda) in some places affirm his atomicity (aṇu-parimāṇatva). To remove the seeming confusion in all this, this section is begun. The position first reached (prāptam — pūrvapakṣa) is this: because we hear of his going-out, going, and returning, the jīva is limited and atomic in size. Going-out — ‘When he departs from this body, he departs along with all these (organs)’ (Kau. U. III.4); going — ‘All those who depart from this world go to the moon alone’ (Kau. U. I.2); returning — ‘From that world he comes back again to this world for (further) action’ (Bṛ. U. IV.4.6). From hearing of these — going-out, going and returning — it follows that the jīva is limited; for of an all-pervading entity (vibhu) movement is impossible. Once limitedness is admitted, since the alternative of his being body-sized has been refuted in the examination of the Ārhata (Jaina) view, it follows that the Self is atomic. (II.iii.19)
BS_C02_S03_V20: And on account of (these movements pertaining to) his very own self, in the case of the latter two. (II.iii.20)
BS_C02_S03_V20::block-0: Going-out (utkrānti) might, even of one who does not himself move, be conceivable through the cessation of ownership-of-the-body upon the exhaustion of karma — just as one ceases to be the headman of a village without himself moving away. But the latter two — going (gati) and returning (āgati) — are not possible for one who does not himself move. For these two are connected with him by his very own self (svātmanā), since the action denoted by the root ‘gam’ (to go) resides in the agent (kartṛ-stha-kriyā). And going and returning are possible only for one who is non-medium-sized — that is, only on the supposition of atomicity. Moreover, when going and returning are real, even going-out is understood as nothing but actual departure from the body; for of one who has not departed from the body, going and returning could not occur. The parts of the body are also stated as the points of departure (apādāna) in connection with going-out: ‘From the eye, or from the head, or from other regions of the body’ (Bṛ. U. IV.4.2). And from ‘He, gathering up these particles of light, descends into the heart itself’ (Bṛ. U. IV.4.1) and ‘Taking the (subtle) seed, he again returns to (his former) place’ (Bṛ. U. IV.3.11), it is seen that going and returning of the embodied one occur even within the body itself. From this also the atomicity of the jīva is established. (II.iii.20)
BS_C02_S03_V21: If it be said: he is not atomic, since scripture speaks otherwise (i.e. of his vastness) — (we reply) no, because that pertains to the Other (the supreme Self). (II.iii.21)
BS_C02_S03_V21::block-0: Now there might be this objection (pūrvapakṣa): The Self is not atomic. Why? Because of statements that say otherwise (a-tat-śruti) — i.e. because magnitudes opposed to atomicity are heard of: ‘Verily, this great unborn Self, who is this one made of consciousness amid the vital airs’ (Bṛ. U. IV.4.22), ‘(He is) all-pervading like ākāśa, and eternal’ (Śat. Br. X.6.3.2), ‘Truth, knowledge, the infinite — Brahman’ (Tai. U. II.1.1) — texts of this class would clearly contradict the atomicity of the Self. (Reply, siddhāntin:) This is no fault. Why? Because the context concerns the Other (itara-adhikārāt) — for these utterances of a different magnitude occur within an exposition of the supreme Self; the supreme Self is the principal subject taught in the Vedānta as that which is to be known, and from ‘Pure, beyond ākāśa’ and similar passages it is clear that everywhere the special context (viśeṣa-adhikāra) belongs to the supreme Self alone. Objection: But ‘this one made of consciousness amid the vital airs’ (Bṛ. U. IV.4.22) seems to designate the embodied jīva (śārīra) himself as connected with greatness. (Reply:) From the standpoint of scripture, this designation should be understood after the manner of the Vāmadeva passage (‘I was Manu, I was the sun’ — where the seer realised his identity with the supreme). Hence, since the scriptural mention of another magnitude pertains to the supreme (Prājña), the atomicity of the jīva is not contradicted. (II.iii.21)
BS_C02_S03_V22: And on account of (his) own designating word and (the scriptural) measurement. (II.iii.22)
BS_C02_S03_V22::block-0: From this also the Self is atomic, since a word directly denoting his atomicity is heard: ‘This atomic Self is to be known by the mind (cetas), into whom the prāṇa entered fivefold’ (Mu. U. III.1.9). And from his connection with prāṇa it is understood that it is the jīva himself who is here described as atomic. So too the (scriptural) measurement (unmāna) makes us understand the minuteness (aṇimā) of the jīva: ‘The hundredth part of the tip of a hair, divided again into a hundred — that part is to be known as the jīva’ (Śve. U. V.9). And another measurement: ‘Of the size of the point of a goad (ārā-agra) is the lower (one) seen’ (Śve. U. V.8). (II.iii.22)
BS_C02_S03_V23: And there is no contradiction, as in the case of sandal-paste. (II.iii.23)
BS_C02_S03_V23::block-0: Objection (leading bhāṣya): If the jīva be atomic, then his perceiving (sensations) throughout the whole body, while himself residing in a single spot, is contradicted. Yet it is observed that those plunged in the pool of the Gaṅgā feel coldness in all their limbs, and in the hot season the heat is felt over the whole body. To this the reply is given (in the sūtra) —
BS_C02_S03_V23::block-1: Just as a drop of yellow sandal-paste (haricandana-bindu), though connected only with one part of the body, produces a delight pervading the whole body, so the Self also, residing in one part of the body, will produce perception pervading the whole body. And through his connection with the skin (tvac), his sensation throughout the whole body is not contradicted. For the relation between skin and Self subsists in the entire skin, and the skin pervades the whole body. (II.iii.23)
BS_C02_S03_V24: If it be said (that the example fails) on account of the specific location (in the case of sandal-paste being directly seen) — no, because (such location of the Self) is admitted, for (he is) in the heart. (II.iii.24)
BS_C02_S03_V24::block-0: Here an objection (pūrvapakṣa) is raised: What was said — ‘there is no contradiction, as in the case of sandal-paste’ — is improper, because the example (dṛṣṭānta) and the thing exemplified (dārṣṭāntika) are not parallel. The sandal-paste illustration would apply only if the Self’s being located in one part of the body were already established. In the case of sandal, its specific location (avasthiti-vaiśeṣya) — its being in one part — and the delight pervading the whole body, are both directly perceived (pratyakṣa). But of the Self, only the perception pervading the whole body is directly perceived; not his being located in one part. If it be said that this is to be inferred (anumeya) — even so, inference cannot succeed here; for there remains the unresolved doubt: is the Self’s sensation throughout the body due to his being himself all-pervading in the body like the organ of skin, or like the all-pervading ākāśa, or like an atomic drop of sandal located in one spot? (Reply, siddhāntin:) This is no fault. Why? Because (such location) is admitted (abhyupagama). For the Self too, like sandal-paste, is admitted to dwell in one part of the body, and to have specific location (avasthiti-vaiśeṣya). How? It is replied: For in the Vedānta this Self is taught to be in the heart (hṛdi) — ‘For this Self is in the heart’ (Pra. U. III.6), ‘Verily, this Self is in the heart’ (Chā. U. VIII.3.3), ‘Which is the Self? — This person made of consciousness, amid the vital airs, the inner light within the heart’ (Bṛ. U. IV.3.7), and similar teachings. Therefore, since example and exemplified are not unequal, this is fitting indeed: ‘There is no contradiction, as in the case of sandal-paste.’ (II.iii.24)
BS_C02_S03_V25: Or rather (the perception throughout the body is) on account of (his) attribute (of consciousness pervading the body), as in the world. (II.iii.25)
BS_C02_S03_V25::block-0: Or rather, by the pervasion of his attribute of consciousness (caitanya-guṇa-vyāpti), the function (kārya) of the jīva, though atomic, pervading the whole body is not contradicted — just as in the world the radiance (prabhā) of a gem, lamp, and the like, though they reside in one part of a chamber, while pervading the (whole) chamber performs its function throughout it. So here. Apprehending the doubt: ‘It might possibly be that, since sandal has parts, by the spreading-out of its subtle particles (sūkṣma-avayava-visarpaṇa) it produces delight throughout the whole body; but the atomic jīva has no parts by which he might spread out through the whole body’ — (the sūtrakāra) has therefore said ‘Or rather, by the attribute, as in the world.’ (II.iii.25)
BS_C02_S03_V26: (The attribute may extend) beyond (the substance), as in the case of fragrance. (II.iii.26)
BS_C02_S03_V26::block-0: Objection (leading bhāṣya): But how can an attribute (guṇa) reside elsewhere, apart from its substrate (guṇin)? It is not seen that the white attribute of a cloth resides anywhere apart from the cloth. If it be said: ‘Like the radiance of a lamp’ — no, for that too is admitted to be a substance (dravya). For the lamp is a fiery substance with closely-packed particles, and its radiance is the same fiery substance with sparser particles. To this objection the reply is given —
BS_C02_S03_V26::block-1: Just as fragrance (gandha), though it is an attribute, has functioning apart from the fragrance-bearing substance — for the fragrance of flowers and the like is perceived even when the fragrance-bearing flowers are not (directly) reached — so too, of the jīva, though atomic, his attribute of consciousness will function beyond (himself). And so this argument is shown to be inconclusive (anaikāntika): namely, that ‘because (consciousness) is an attribute, it cannot, like form etc., function apart from its substrate.’ For we see in fragrance, which is itself an attribute, functioning apart from its substrate. Objection (Vaiśeṣika-style): ‘Even fragrance separates only along with its substrate (i.e. along with subtle particles).’ Reply: No; for then the original substance from which (those particles) separate would be liable to diminish (kṣaya-prasaṅga). (Yet) it is also seen as not diminishing from its prior state. Otherwise it would lose its original weight and the like. Objection: ‘It might be that the separated parts of the fragrance-bearing substance are so small that, even if the difference is real, it is not noticed; for the subtle fragrance-paramāṇus, spreading on every side, produce the cognition of fragrance without (themselves) entering the cavity of the nose.’ Reply: No; for paramāṇus are beyond the senses (atīndriya), and yet there is clear apprehension of fragrance in nāgakeśara (mesua) flowers and the like. Nor is the popular cognition ‘the fragrance-bearing substance has been smelt’; rather, ordinary people apprehend ‘the fragrance itself has been smelt.’ Objection: ‘Since in the case of form (rūpa) and the rest no functioning apart from the substrate is observed, in the case of fragrance too such functioning is improper.’ Reply: No; because (it is) directly perceived (pratyakṣa), inference (to the contrary) cannot operate. Therefore, those who reason rightly should infer of a thing exactly as it is observed in the world, not otherwise. For from the fact that the attribute taste (rasa) is apprehended only by the tongue, it cannot be ruled that the attributes of form etc. too should be apprehended only by the tongue. (II.iii.26)
BS_C02_S03_V27::block-0: Having stated that the self has the heart as its seat (hṛdayāyatanatvam) and is of atomic dimension (aṇu-parimāṇatvam), (scripture) likewise shows of that very (self) its pervasion of the entire body through the quality of consciousness (caitanya-guṇa), by the text ‘from the (tips of the) hairs to the (tips of the) nails’ (Chā. Up. 8.8.1) (citation). (27)
BS_C02_S03_V28::block-0: Also from ‘having ascended the body by intelligence’ (Kau. Up. 3.6) (citation) — because of the separate teaching of the self and its intelligence as agent (kartṛ) and instrument (karaṇa) — it is understood that this (self) pervades the body only through the quality of consciousness. And the teaching ‘taking the cognition of these prāṇas through the cognition (of the self)’ (Bṛ. Up. 2.1.17) (citation) — wherein the cognition of the agent is taught as separate from the bodily (organs) — reinforces just this same purport. Therefore the self is atomic. (28)
BS_C02_S03_V29: But (the designation of atomicity etc.) is the designation of that (self) on account of (its) being predominantly characterised by the qualities of that (intellect), as in the case of the prājña (Supreme Self). (29)
BS_C02_S03_V29::block-0: Thus when (the pūrvapakṣa) is established, we say (siddhānta):
BS_C02_S03_V29::block-1: The word ‘tu’ (but) negates the (preceding) view. This is not so — that the self is atomic. Because no (text on its) origination is heard, and because the entry (into the body) is heard only of the supreme (Brahman), and because of the teaching of identity (tādātmya), it has (already) been said that the jīva is just the supreme Brahman itself. And if the jīva is just the supreme Brahman, then the jīva ought to be precisely co-extensive with the supreme Brahman. The all-pervasiveness (vibhutva) of the supreme Brahman is recorded (in scripture). Therefore the jīva is all-pervading (vibhu). And in this way the doctrines of all-pervasiveness pertaining to the jīva, both śrauta and smārta, of the kind ‘Verily, this great unborn Self, who is among the prāṇas, made of cognition’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.22) (citation), become substantiated. Nor is sensation pervading the entire body intelligible if the jīva be atomic. If it be said: it is by reason of (its) connection with the skin — no; for then even at a thorn-prick the sensation would arise as pervading the entire body — for the contact of skin and thorn obtains over all the skin, and the skin pervades the whole body; yet only on the sole of the foot, when pricked by the thorn, do they experience sensation. Nor is the pervasion of (the body) by the quality (of consciousness) of an atomic (self) intelligible, since a quality (resides) in the locus of its possessor; for to be a quality at all is forfeited by a quality if it does not depend on its possessor. And the lamp's flame (prabhā) being a separate substance has (already) been explained. As for fragrance, since it is admitted to be a quality, it must travel only along with its substratum, otherwise it would forfeit its qualityhood; thus it has been said by Dvaipāyana: ‘If the unskilled, on perceiving fragrance in waters, were to declare it (resident) there, one should know it (to belong) only to the earth, taking refuge in waters and air’ (citation). And if consciousness were to pervade the entire body of the jīva, the jīva would not be atomic; for consciousness itself is its very essential nature, as heat and light are of fire — there is no division of quality and quality-possessor here, as has been said. Body-sized dimension has also been refuted. By the residue (pariśeṣa), the jīva is all-pervading.
BS_C02_S03_V29::block-2: How then the designation of atomicity etc.? To this he says: ‘But on account of (its) being predominantly characterised by the qualities of that (intellect), is the designation of that (self).’ ‘Tad-guṇāḥ’ — the qualities of that intellect, viz. desire, aversion, pleasure, pain etc.; that self of which, in (its) saṃsāric state, the qualities of that (intellect) are the essence (sāra), the principal — that is ‘tad-guṇa-sāra’; the abstract of that is ‘tad-guṇa-sāratva’. For there is no saṃsāric state for the self alone, apart from the qualities of the intellect. The state of saṃsāra characterised by agency, enjoyership etc., (belongs) to the self — which is in truth a non-agent, a non-enjoyer, non-saṃsāric, ever-free — only because of the superimposition of the attributes of the limiting adjunct, the intellect. Therefore on account of being thus predominantly characterised by the qualities of that (intellect), the designation of (its) measure is by the measure of the intellect, and the designation of (its) ‘departing’ etc. is by the departing etc. of that (intellect), not by itself (intrinsically). Thus too: ‘Of the hundredth part of the tip of a hair, divided into a hundred — that part is to be known as the jīva; and that (very same) is fit for infinity’ (Śve. Up. 5.9) (citation) — having stated atomicity of the jīva, scripture again declares the very same (jīva) to be infinite. And this could be coherent only thus — if the atomicity of the jīva be figurative (aupacārika), and the infinity be real (pāramārthika). For both cannot be primary. Nor can infinity be understood as figurative, since in all the Upaniṣads the identity of self and Brahman is what is intended to be conveyed. Likewise in that other measurement: ‘Through the quality of intellect and the quality of self, one is seen as small as the tip of a goad’ (Śve. Up. 5.8) (citation) — by connection with the quality of intellect alone is the goad-tip-measure taught, not by the self in its own nature. ‘This atomic Self is to be known by the mind’ (Mu. Up. 3.1.9) (citation) — here too, atomic measure of the jīva is not being taught, since the supreme Self alone — being ungraspable by eye etc. and attainable by the grace of knowledge — is the topic in context, and since primary atomic measure is also not possible for the jīva. Therefore this statement of atomicity is to be regarded as having the import of (the self's) being hard to know, or as having the import of the limiting adjunct (upādhi). So too in difference-teachings of the kind ‘having ascended the body by intelligence’ (Kau. Up. 3.6) (citation), the construction is to be made thus: the jīva, having ascended the body by intellect alone (which serves) as the upādhi; or it is mere (figurative) designation, like ‘the body of the stone-son’ etc. For here, as has been said, there is not even any division of quality and quality-possessor. The statement of (the heart as) seat too (applies), because (the heart) is the seat only of the intellect. Likewise, in the case of departure etc., (scripture) shows their dependence on the upādhi: ‘In whose departure shall I depart, in whose remaining shall I remain?’ (Pra. Up. 6.3) (citation). ‘He created prāṇa’ (Pra. Up. 6.4) (citation); for if there were no departure, the absence of going and coming too would be known. For going and coming would not be possible for one who has not departed from the body. Thus, on account of (its) being predominantly characterised by the qualities of the upādhi, the designation of atomicity etc. of the jīva, is like that of the prājña (Supreme Self). Just as in the saguṇa upāsanās of the prājña, the supreme Self, the designation of being smaller-than-small etc., is on account of (its) being predominantly characterised by the qualities of the upādhi — ‘Smaller than a grain of rice or a grain of barley’ (Chā. Up. 3.14.3), ‘made of mind, having prāṇa as body … of all fragrance, of all taste’, ‘of true desire, of true resolve’ (Chā. Up. 8.7.1) (citation) — exactly so (here too). (29)
BS_C02_S03_V30: And there is no defect, on account of (the connection with the intellect) lasting as long as the self (continues in saṃsāra), since this is seen (in scripture). (30)
BS_C02_S03_V30::block-0: It might be (objected) thus: if the saṃsāra-state of the self be conceived on account of (its) being predominantly characterised by the qualities of the intellect, then since the conjunction of two distinct (entities), intellect and self, must necessarily come to an end, when there is severance from the intellect, the self being separated would be unperceivable, hence non-existent or non-saṃsāric — would result. To this he replies in answer:
BS_C02_S03_V30::block-1: This apprehension of the defect just stated is not to be entertained. Why? Because the conjunction with the intellect lasts as long as the self (continues in saṃsāra) — as long as this self is in saṃsāra, as long as its saṃsāra-state does not cease through right vision (samyag-darśana), so long does its conjunction with the intellect not cease. And just so long as there is this connection with the upādhi (limiting adjunct) of the intellect, just so long is its jīva-hood and saṃsāra-state. In ultimate truth (paramārthatas), however, there is no jīva apart from the form fashioned by the upādhi of the intellect. For no second sentient principle, distinct from the ever-free omniscient Lord, is found in the inquiry into the meaning of Vedānta — from hundreds of śrutis like ‘There is no other seer than this, no other hearer, no other thinker, no other cogniser’ (Bṛ. Up. 3.7.23) (citation), ‘There is no other seer, hearer, thinker, cogniser than this’ (Chā. Up. 3.8.11) (citation), ‘That thou art’ (Chā. Up. 6.8.7) (citation), ‘I am Brahman’ (Bṛ. Up. 1.4.10) (citation). But how is it understood that the conjunction with the intellect lasts as long as the self? He says: ‘because that is seen.’ For thus scripture shows: ‘This puruṣa, who is among the prāṇas, made of cognition, who is the inner light within the heart — he, remaining the same, wanders through both worlds; he as it were thinks, he as it were moves’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.7) (citation), and so forth. There ‘vijñānamaya’ means ‘buddhi-maya’ (made of intellect); for in another passage ‘made of cognition, made of mind, made of prāṇa, made of eye, made of ear’ — vijñānamaya is read along with mind etc. And by buddhi-mayatva precisely tad-guṇa-sāratva is meant — just as in worldly usage Devadatta is called ‘woman-made’ (strī-maya) because he has passion for women etc. as predominant — exactly so. ‘He, remaining the same, wanders through both worlds’ — by this scripture shows non-separation from the intellect even when going to other worlds. ‘The same as’ what? It is understood, from the proximity (of the context), as ‘the same as that very intellect.’ And this it shows: ‘he as it were thinks, he as it were moves’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.7) (citation). What is meant is this — he himself does not think, nor does he move; when the intellect thinks, he as it were thinks; when the intellect moves, he as it were moves. Moreover, this connection of the self with the upādhi of the intellect is preceded by mithyā-jñāna (false cognition). And there is no cessation of mithyā-jñāna other than by samyag-jñāna (right knowledge); hence as long as there is no awakening to the identity of self and Brahman, just so long this connection with the intellect-upādhi does not cease. And (scripture) shows this: ‘I know this great Puruṣa, of sun-like splendour, beyond darkness; knowing Him alone one transcends death; there is no other path for going (to liberation)’ (Śve. Up. 3.8) (citation). (30)
BS_C02_S03_V31: Like manhood etc. — because of the possibility of (the conjunction's) being manifested as (something) existing (in seed-form). (31)
BS_C02_S03_V31::block-0: But surely in deep sleep (suṣupti) and in cosmic dissolution (pralaya) the conjunction of the intellect with the self cannot be admitted, because of the text ‘he becomes united with Being, my dear, then; he goes back into his own’ (Chā. Up. 6.8.1) (citation), and because the dissolution of all modifications is admitted. How then can the conjunction with the intellect last as long as the self? To this it is said:
BS_C02_S03_V31::block-1: Just as in the world manhood (puṃstva) etc., though existing only in seed-form (bīja-ātmanā) and not perceived in childhood etc. — being intended as if non-existent — yet manifest in youth etc. They do not arise as non-existent (then becoming existent), for then there would be the unwarranted consequence of their arising even in eunuchs etc. — exactly so this conjunction with the intellect, existing in seed-form (śaktyātmanā), manifests again in waking and re-creation, in deep sleep and in dissolution. For only thus is this intelligible. There is no causeless arising of anything, on pain of over-extension. And (scripture) shows that the rising from deep sleep is brought about by the existence of the seed in the form of avidyā (nescience): ‘Becoming united with Being, they do not know “We have become united with Being”’ (Chā. Up. 6.9.2) (citation), ‘Whatever they were here — tiger or lion …’ (Chā. Up. 6.9.3) (citation) and so forth. Therefore this is established — the connection with the upādhis (such as) the intellect lasts as long as the self (continues in saṃsāra). (31)
BS_C02_S03_V32: Otherwise, the consequence of perpetual perception or non-perception (would result), or the restriction to one of the two. (32)
BS_C02_S03_V32::block-0: And that (which is) the upādhi of the self is variously named in various places as antaḥkaraṇa (inner organ), manas (mind), buddhi (intellect), vijñāna (cognition), and citta. In some places by the division of (its) functions — as having functions like doubt etc. it is called manas, as having functions like ascertainment etc. it is called buddhi. And such an antaḥkaraṇa must necessarily be admitted to exist; for otherwise — if it is not admitted — there would be the consequence of perpetual perception or non-perception. When the means of perception, viz. the self, the sense-organs, and the objects, are present, perception would always result. Or, if even with the concurrence of the cause there were absence of the effect, there would be perpetual non-perception. Neither is seen to be so. Or else, the obstruction of the capacity of one of the two — the self or the sense-organ — would have to be admitted. The obstruction of capacity is not possible for the self, since it is changeless. Nor is it (possible) for the sense-organ. For its capacity, being unobstructed in the prior and posterior moments, would not suddenly get obstructed. Therefore, that on whose attentiveness or inattentiveness perception or non-perception depends — that is mind. And so the śruti: ‘I was elsewhere-minded, I did not see; I was elsewhere-minded, I did not hear’ (Bṛ. Up. 1.5.3) (citation), and ‘with the mind alone one sees, with the mind one hears’ (Bṛ. Up. 1.5.3) (citation). And it shows desire etc. as its (the mind's) modifications: ‘Desire, resolve, doubt, faith, faithlessness, firmness, non-firmness, modesty, intelligence, fear — all this is mind alone’ (Bṛ. Up. 1.5.3) (citation). Therefore this is right — that the designation of the (self) is on account of (its) being predominantly characterised by the qualities of that (intellect). (32)
BS_C02_S03_V33: (The jīva is) an agent, on account of scripture having (thereby) a purpose. (33)
BS_C02_S03_V33::block-0: Under the same topic of being predominantly characterised by the qualities of that (intellect), another property of the jīva is being elaborated. And this jīva must be an agent. Why? Because (only thereby) does scripture have a purpose. Thus (only) injunction-scripture of the form ‘one should sacrifice (yajeta),’ ‘one should offer oblations (juhuyāt),’ ‘one should give (dadyāt)’ becomes purposeful. Otherwise it would be purposeless. For it teaches an action to be performed by one who is (already) an agent. And this would not be possible in the absence of agency. Likewise this scripture too becomes purposeful: ‘For this is the seer, hearer, thinker, comprehender, doer, the cogniser-self, the puruṣa’ (Pra. Up. 4.9) (citation). (33)
BS_C02_S03_V34: Because of the teaching of (its) sport (vihāra). (34)
BS_C02_S03_V34::block-0: Hence too is the agency of the jīva, since in the topic of the jīva, in the intermediate state (sandhya, i.e. dream), (scripture) teaches (its) sport — ‘He moves there immortal, wherever he desires’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.12) (citation), and ‘he moves about in his own body as he pleases’ (Bṛ. Up. 2.1.18) (citation). (34)
BS_C02_S03_V35::block-0: For this further reason too the jīva is the agent (kartṛ): inasmuch as, in the very procedure dealing with the jīva, scripture proclaims his ‘taking up’ (upādāna) of the instruments (karaṇa) — ‘Then taking the cognition (vijñāna) of these prāṇas by his cognition’ (Bṛ. U. 2.1.17) (citation), and ‘having grasped the prāṇas’ (Bṛ. U. 2.1.18) (citation). The act of seizing/taking-up (upādāna) is properly the act of an agent, not of a mere instrument; hence the jīva, being shown to take up the instruments, is established as the agent. ‖ 35 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V36: And from the (grammatical) designation in respect of action; and if it were not so there would be a reversal of the case-ending (nirdeśa-viparyaya). ‖ 36 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V36::block-0: For this further reason too the jīva is the agent: scripture designates him as agent in laukika (worldly) as well as vaidika (Vedic) actions — ‘Vijñāna spreads out the sacrifice; it spreads out the works as well’ (Tai. U. 2.5.1) (citation). [Pūrvapakṣa:] But the word ‘vijñāna’ is well established as denoting the buddhi; how then is the jīva’s agency indicated by it? [Siddhānta:] Not so, we reply — this designation is of the jīva alone, not of the buddhi. For if it were not of the jīva, there would be a reversal of the case-ending (nirdeśa-viparyaya): scripture would have said ‘by vijñāna’ (instrumental, vijñānena) instead. So indeed, where the buddhi is meant elsewhere, the word ‘vijñāna’ is seen used in the instrumental case, denoting it as karaṇa — ‘Then taking the cognition of these prāṇas by his cognition’ (Bṛ. U. 2.1.17) (citation). But here, in ‘Vijñāna spreads out the sacrifice’ (Tai. U. 2.5.1) (citation), since vijñāna is placed in grammatical co-reference (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with the agent, what is signified is precisely the agency of the ātman, distinct from the buddhi. Hence there is no fault. ‖ 36 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V37: Like cognition (upalabdhi), there is no rule (aniyama) [restricting agency to good results only]. ‖ 37 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V37::block-0: [Pūrvapakṣa:] Here it is objected — if the jīva, distinct from the buddhi, were the agent, then being independent (svatantra) he would, as a rule, bring about for himself only what is dear and beneficial, never the contrary. But he is observed to bring about the contrary as well. And such conduct, devoid of regulation (aniyama), cannot fit an independent ātman. To this the answer is given —
BS_C02_S03_V37::block-1: [Siddhānta:] Just as this ātman, though independent in respect of cognition (upalabdhi), still cognises both the desired and the undesired indiscriminately (aniyamena), so too will he produce, indiscriminately, both the desired and the undesired. — [Pūrvapakṣa:] But even in cognition there is no full independence, since cognition is found to depend on the procurement (upādāna) of its causes (sense-organs, object, light, etc.). — Not so. The causes of cognition serve only to set forth the object (viṣaya-prakalpanā-mātra-prayojana); but in cognition itself the ātman depends on nothing else, since cognition belongs to it intrinsically through its own consciousness (caitanya-yoga). Furthermore, even in producing effects (artha-kriyā) the ātman is not absolutely independent: it must depend on particularities of place, time, and instrumental occasion. And the agency of an agent does not lapse merely because he requires assistants — even one cooking, who depends on fuel, water, and the like, remains the cook. So, owing to the variety of co-operating factors (sahakāri-vaicitrya), unregulated activity (pravṛtti aniyamena) toward desired and undesired effects is not contradictory in the ātman. ‖ 37 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V38: Because [otherwise] there would be a reversal of capacities (śakti-viparyaya). ‖ 38 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V38::block-0: For this reason also the jīva, distinct from vijñāna [= buddhi], must be the agent. For if instead the buddhi denoted by the word ‘vijñāna’ were itself the agent, there would arise a reversal of capacities (śakti-viparyaya): the buddhi would lose its instrumental capacity (karaṇa-śakti) and acquire the agentive capacity (kartṛ-śakti). And once the buddhi is granted agentive capacity, it must also be admitted as the object of the I-notion (aham-pratyaya-viṣayatva), since everywhere activity is observed to be preceded by the I-sense (ahaṃkāra) — ‘I go, I come, I eat, I drink.’ Then, for this buddhi endowed with agentive capacity, some other organ that performs all functions would have to be postulated; for an agent, even though capable, is seen to engage in actions only by taking up an instrument. And in that case the dispute would be merely about a name (saṃjñā-mātre vivādaḥ), not about any difference of substance — since [in either case] agency, distinct from the instrument, has been admitted. ‖ 38 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V39: And because of the impossibility of samādhi (samādhi-abhāva) [if agency be denied]. ‖ 39 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V39::block-0: That samādhi too which is taught in the Upaniṣads with the aim of attaining the Aupaniṣada Self — characterised in such words as ‘Verily, the Self, my dear, is to be seen, to be heard about, to be reflected upon, to be steadfastly meditated on’ (Bṛ. U. 2.4.5) (citation), ‘He is to be sought after, He is to be enquired into’ (citation), ‘Meditate on the Self with the syllable Oṃ’ (Mu. U. 2.2.6) (citation) — that too would not be possible were the ātman not the agent. Hence too his agency is established. ‖ 39 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V40: And it is as in the case of the carpenter (takṣan): in both ways. ‖ 40 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V40::block-0: Thus, by reasons such as the meaningfulness of scripture (śāstra-arthavattva) and the rest, the agency of the embodied (śārīra) has been demonstrated. Now arises the consideration: is this agency natural (svābhāvika) or is it conditioned by an upādhi (adjunct)? — On the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) the very same reasons (meaningfulness of scripture, etc.) would establish that agency is natural, since no contrary ground (apavāda-hetu) is found. — To this prima facie position we reply (siddhānta): natural agency is not possible for the ātman, for that would entail the impossibility of liberation (anirmokṣa-prasaṅga). For if agency were the very nature of the ātman, no release from agency would be possible — just as fire cannot be released from heat. And one not freed from agency cannot attain the supreme human goal (puruṣārtha), since agency is by nature painful (duḥkha-rūpatva). [Pūrvapakṣa:] Even with the capacity for agency remaining, puruṣārtha will be achieved by avoiding the effects of agency; and these effects are avoided by removing their occasioning causes (nimitta) — just as fire, though endowed with the burning capacity, has no burning effect when separated from fuel. — Not so; for the occasioning causes too, being bound by the relation called ‘capacity’ (śakti), cannot be absolutely got rid of. [Pūrvapakṣa:] By the prescription of the means of liberation, liberation will be accomplished. — Not so; what depends on means is non-eternal (anitya). Moreover, mokṣa is held to be established by the very teaching of the eternally pure, ever-free Self (nityaśuddhamuktātma); and such a teaching of the Self would be inadmissible if agency were natural. Therefore, agency belongs to the ātman only through the superimposition of the properties of an upādhi (upādhi-dharma-adhyāsa), not by nature. So too śruti — ‘He as it were thinks, he as it were trembles’ (Bṛ. U. 4.3.7) (citation), and ‘The wise call the Self joined with body, sense, and mind the enjoyer’ (Ka. U. 1.3.4) (citation) — shows that the particularising attainment of enjoyer-hood and the like belongs to the Self only when conjoined with upādhis. For to discriminating sages there exists no jīva named ‘agent’ or ‘enjoyer’ different from the Supreme — as in ‘There is no other seer than This’ (Bṛ. U. 4.3.23) (citation). [Objection:] Then the Supreme itself would be the transmigrator, agent, and enjoyer! — [Or alternatively:] If a conscious jīva different from the Supreme is the agent, it must be other than the aggregate of buddhi etc. — Not so; agency and enjoyership are presented through avidyā (avidyā-pratyupasthāpita). And so scripture: ‘Where there is duality as it were, there one sees another’ (Bṛ. U. 2.4.14) (citation) — having shown agency and enjoyership in the state of avidyā, removes those very (agency and enjoyership) in the state of vidyā: ‘But where for him all has become the very Self, then by what should one see what?’ (Bṛ. U. 2.4.14) (citation). Likewise, having recounted to the ātman, in the dream and waking states, the toil arising from contact with upādhis — like a hawk flying to and fro in the sky — scripture announces the absence of that toil in deep sleep, when the ātman is enfolded by the prājña Self: beginning ‘That, indeed, is his form, in which all his desires are attained, in which the Self is the only desire, which is desireless and beyond sorrow’ (Bṛ. U. 4.3.21) (citation) and concluding ‘This is his supreme goal, this his supreme attainment, this his supreme world, this his supreme bliss’ (Bṛ. U. 4.3.32) (citation).
BS_C02_S03_V40::block-1: This very point the Ācārya states: ‘And as in the case of the takṣan, in both ways.’ The ‘ca’ here is read in the sense of ‘tu’ (‘but’). It must not be thought that agency is natural to the ātman, like heat to fire. Rather, just as in the world a carpenter (takṣan), with adze and other tools in hand, is an agent and undergoes toil, but the very same one, on reaching home, having laid aside the adze and the rest, becomes self-poised, content, free of activity, happy — even so the ātman, conjoined with the duality presented by avidyā, becomes the agent, full of pain, in the dream and waking states; and to remove that fatigue, entering its own Self, the supreme Brahman, freed from the aggregate of body and sense-organs, it becomes a non-agent and happy in the state of deep sleep (samprasāda); likewise, in the state of liberation also, having dispelled the darkness of avidyā by the lamp of vidyā (vidyā-pradīpa), the Self alone, solitary, content, blissful, remains. The takṣan-illustration is to be taken to this extent: the takṣan is an agent, in the various activities of carpentry, only with reference to the specific instruments — adze and the like — but in respect of his own body alone he is not an agent. Even so, this ātman is an agent in all activities only in dependence on the instruments such as the manas; in respect of his own self he is not an agent. Yet, unlike the takṣan, the ātman has no limbs by which, as the takṣan with hands and the like takes up or sets down adze etc., the ātman could take up or lay down the instruments such as manas.
BS_C02_S03_V40::block-2: What was urged — that by reasons such as the meaningfulness of scripture, the ātman’s agency is natural — that is wrong. The injunction-scripture (vidhi-śāstra) takes up agency as already given (yathāprāptam), and merely teaches some particular duty; it does not establish agency for the ātman. We have already said that natural agency belongs not to the ātman, since brahmātmatva is taught. Hence the injunction-scripture proceeds taking up only the agency that is brought about by avidyā. Likewise, scripture of the form ‘the agent is the vijñānātmā, the puruṣa’ — being of the nature of an anuvāda (re-statement), merely re-states the agency that is already given through avidyā. With this the [appeal to] vihāra (sporting in dream) and upādāna (taking up the prāṇas) is also disposed of, since those passages too are of the nature of anuvāda. [Objection:] But in the saṃdhya (intermediate) state, while the sense-organs are asleep, ‘he moves about in his own body as he pleases’ — this teaching of vihāra implies the agency of the ātman alone. Likewise in the upādāna passage ‘then taking the cognition of these prāṇas by his cognition’ (Bṛ. U. 2.1.17) (citation), where instrumental and accusative case-endings are heard upon the karaṇas, it conveys the agency of the ātman alone. — To this we reply: in the saṃdhya state there is no absolute cessation of the karaṇas for the ātman, for śruti also there mentions connection with the dhī (intellect): ‘together with intellect, having become a dreamer, he transcends this world’ (Bṛ. U. 4.3.7) (citation). And the smṛti: ‘When, on the cessation of the senses, the manas remains unceased and resorts only to its objects — that one should know to be the dream-vision.’ Desires and the like are functions of the manas, says śruti; and these are seen in dream. Therefore he sports in dream only as one with manas (samanāḥ). And the sporting there is itself of the nature of impressions (vāsanāmaya), not real (pāramārthika). Thus too the śruti describes dream-activity tied with the particle ‘iva’ (‘as it were’): ‘as if rejoicing with women, as if laughing, as if also seeing fearful things’ (Bṛ. U. 4.3.13) (citation). And in worldly speech too people thus relate dream: ‘I as it were ascended a mountain peak, I as it were saw a row of trees.’ Likewise in the upādāna passage, although the case-endings of action and instrument are used in respect of the karaṇas, agency is to be seen as belonging only to the ātman in conjunction with them, since agency in the ātman alone has been shown impossible. And in the world there are many ways of speaking — ‘the soldiers fight,’ ‘the king fights with his soldiers.’ Moreover, in this upādāna only the cessation of the activity of the karaṇas is what is meant — not anyone’s independence; for cessation of karaṇa-activity in sleep is observed even apart from any deliberate (buddhi-pūrvaka) act. As for the designation cited, ‘vijñāna spreads out the sacrifice’ — this leads only to the agency of the buddhi: for the word ‘vijñāna’ is well established in that sense; for it is recited immediately after manas; and from ‘śraddhā is its head’ (Tai. U. 2.4.1) (citation) — by which śraddhā etc. are mentioned as limbs of the vijñānamaya-ātman, and śraddhā etc. are well known as properties of the buddhi; and from the closing sentence ‘all the gods worship vijñāna as the eldest Brahman’ (Tai. U. 2.5.1) (citation) — eldership and the property of being first-born are well established in the buddhi; and from another śruti ‘this is the further-and-further sequence in the form of speech and mind, namely the sacrifice,’ where the sacrifice is determined to be accomplished by speech and intellect. Nor does the admission of the karaṇas’ agency entail a reversal of the buddhi’s capacity (śakti-viparyaya), since for all the kārakas (case-factors) agency is necessarily present in their own respective operations. But in relation to upalabdhi these karaṇas remain karaṇas… [text continues]
BS_C02_S03_V41: But [it is] from the Supreme, because of the śruti to that effect. ‖ 41 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V41::block-0: Now is undertaken the consideration: this agency of the jīva, occasioned by upādhi in the state of avidyā, does it occur independently of Īśvara, or does it depend on Īśvara? On the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) it would seem that the jīva does not depend on Īśvara for agency. Why? Because there is no purpose served by such dependence. For this jīva, himself impelled by faults such as rāga and dveṣa, equipped with the rest of the kāraka-aggregate, is able to undergo agency. What will Īśvara do for him? Nor is there in worldly experience the recognition that, as in actions like ploughing the ox is necessary, so Īśvara is to be relied upon. Moreover, were Īśvara to associate creatures with toilsome agency, the fault of cruelty (nairghṛṇya) would attach to him, and the inequality of fruits dispensed in their agency would entail partiality (vaiṣamya). [Objection:] Has it not already been said: ‘There is no partiality or cruelty, because [Īśvara] is dependent (sāpekṣatva)’ (Br. Sū. 2.1.34) (citation)? — True, that has been said, but only on the supposition that Īśvara’s dependence is possible; and Īśvara’s dependence is possible only when there exist the dharma and adharma of creatures, and they exist only when the jīva has agency. If that very agency requires Īśvara, then, with reference to what is Īśvara said to be dependent? And so the akṛtābhyāgama-fault (encountering what one has not done) would attach to the jīva. Hence the jīva’s agency is from himself alone. — This prima facie view is set aside by the word ‘tu’ (‘but’), and the established conclusion (siddhānta) is announced: ‘from the Supreme’ (parāt). In the state of avidyā, when the jīva, blinded by the darkness of avidyā and seeing no distinction between himself and the body-organ-aggregate, undergoes the saṃsāra of agency and enjoyership, this comes about from the Supreme Self — the Overseer of works, the Indweller of all beings, the Witness, the Conscious One, Īśvara — by his permission (anujñā). And mokṣa, accomplished by vijñāna, can come about only as caused by His grace (anugraha). Why? Because of the śruti to that effect (tac-chruteḥ). Even though the jīva is impelled by faults and equipped with the means, and even though in worldly actions like ploughing Īśvara’s causality is not popularly recognised, still, in all actions Īśvara is the principal cause (hetu-kartā), as is determined from śruti. So śruti — ‘He, indeed, makes him whom he wishes to lead up out of these worlds perform good action; and he, indeed, makes him whom he wishes to lead downward perform evil action’ (Kau. U. 3.7) (citation), and ‘He who, dwelling in the Self, controls the Self from within’ (citation), and the like. ‖ 41 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V42: But [Īśvara] takes account of the effort already made [by the jīva], because of the non-futility of injunctions and prohibitions and other [reasons]. ‖ 42 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V42::block-0: [Pūrvapakṣa:] But if Īśvara is thus the maker-cause, the faults of partiality (vaiṣamya) and cruelty (nairghṛṇya) will arise, and the jīva will encounter the akṛtābhyāgama (the meeting with what one has not done). — Not so, we reply —
BS_C02_S03_V42::block-1: The word ‘tu’ serves to ward off the urged faults. Whatever effort (prayatna) is made by the jīva, of the form of dharma and adharma, taking that very effort into account Īśvara causes him to act. Hence the urged faults do not arise — Īśvara, depending on the inequality of dharma and adharma made by the jīvas, allots the various fruits unequally; like Pārjanya (the rain-cloud), only as the bare instrumental cause (nimitta-mātra). Just as in the world Pārjanya is the common cause (sādhāraṇa-nimitta) of the various clusters, shrubs, paddy, barley, etc. produced from their own respective uncommon seeds (asādhāraṇa-bīja) — for without Pārjanya the differences of taste, flower, fruit, leaf, etc., do not arise, nor without their own respective seeds — so Īśvara, depending on the effort of the jīva, dispenses good and evil to them. This is fitting. [Objection:] But the dependence on effort made by the jīva does not fit if his agency is dependent on Another (parāyatta). — No fault; even when agency is dependent on Another, the jīva does act; Īśvara causes that very acting one to act. Moreover, He causes him to act now, depending on his prior effort, and earlier He caused him to act, depending on a still earlier effort — for saṃsāra is beginningless (anāditva). Hence no defect. — How is it known that Īśvara takes account of the made effort? — From the non-futility of the enjoined and the prohibited, and so on (vihita-pratiṣiddha-avaiyarthya etc.). For thus, ‘One who desires heaven should sacrifice,’ ‘A brāhmaṇa is not to be killed,’ and the like, retain their non-futility. Otherwise they would be purposeless. Īśvara himself would be the one enjoined upon by injunction and prohibition, since the jīva is utterly dependent on Another. So too He would link the doer of the enjoined with calamity and the doer of the prohibited with reward. Then the authority of the Veda would lapse. And if Īśvara were absolutely independent (atyanta-anapekṣatva), worldly human exertion (puruṣakāra) would also be in vain, as would place, time, and instrumental occasion. The earlier-stated faults too would attach. The like host of faults is indicated by the word ‘ādi’ (‘etc.’). ‖ 42 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V43: (The jīva is) a part (aṁśa), because of the declaration of difference (nānā-vyapadeśa); and because also otherwise (i.e., in another way too non-difference is taught), some (śākhins) read (the jīva) as being of the nature of fishermen, gamblers, and the like (dāśa-kitavādi). ‖ 43 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V43::block-0: The relation of being benefited and benefactor (upakārya-upakāraka-bhāva) between the jīva and Īśvara has been stated. Such a relation in the world is seen only between things that stand in some (specific) connection — as between master and servant (svāmi-bhṛtya), or as between fire and its sparks (agni-visphuliṅga). Hence, since the relation of upakārya-upakāraka is admitted between the jīva and Īśvara as well, a doubt (vicikitsā) arises: is the relation like that of master and servant, or like that of fire and sparks? In this doubt either non-restriction (aniyama) follows, or — since lordship and being-ruled (īśitṛ-īśitavya-bhāva) is well established (prasiddha) only in the case of master-and-servant types — it would follow that the relation must be of that very kind. (pūrvapakṣa)
BS_C02_S03_V43::block-1: Therefore (the Sūtra-kāra) declares: ‘aṁśaḥ’ — (the jīva) is a part. The jīva deserves to be a part of Īśvara, just as a spark is of fire. ‘Aṁśa’ here means ‘aṁśa-iva aṁśaḥ’ (a part as it were); for of that which is partless (niravayava) a primary (mukhya) part is not possible. (Objection:) But on account of partlessness, why should not (the jīva) be just (Brahman) itself? (Reply:) Because of the declaration of difference (nānā-vyapadeśa). Such expressions of difference as ‘He is to be sought, He is to be inquired into’ (saḥ anveṣṭavyaḥ saḥ vijijñāsitavyaḥ) (citation), ‘Knowing this very (Self) one becomes a sage’ (etam eva viditvā munir bhavati) (citation), and ‘He who, dwelling in the Self, controls the Self from within’ (yaḥ ātmani tiṣṭhan ātmānam antaro yamayati) (citation) are not consistent if there is no difference at all. (Objection:) But this declaration of difference would fit far better in the master-and-servant model. To this (the bhāṣya-kāra) says: ‘anyathā cāpi’ — and otherwise also. The conclusion of part-hood is not derived from the declaration of difference alone. Then how? Otherwise also there is a declaration teaching non-difference (anānātva). Thus some śākhins, the Atharvaṇikas, in the Brahma-sūkta declare Brahman to be of the very nature of fishermen, slaves, gamblers, and so on (dāśa-kitavādi-bhāva): ‘Brahman are the fishermen (dāśāḥ), Brahman are the slaves, Brahman alone are these gamblers (kitavāḥ)’ (brahma dāśā brahma dāsā brahmaiva ime kitavāḥ) (citation). The well-known fishermen (kaivartas), and these slaves who waste themselves away in the service of masters, and these other gamblers (kitavas, dice-players) — all of these are Brahman alone; thus by citing low-born creatures (hīna-jantu-udāharaṇena) (the Śruti) declares the Brahman-nature of all jīvas who have entered the aggregate of effect (kārya, body) and instrument (karaṇa, sense-organs) fashioned by name and form (nāma-rūpa-kṛta). The same purport is also expounded elsewhere in the very treatment of Brahman: ‘Thou art woman, Thou art man, Thou art the youth or also the maiden; Thou, aged, walkest with a staff; born, Thou art with face turned every-way’ (tvaṁ strī tvaṁ pumān asi tvaṁ kumāra uta vā kumārī, tvaṁ jīrṇo daṇḍena vañcasi tvaṁ jāto bhavasi viśvatomukhaḥ) (Śve. U. 4.3) (citation), and ‘Having devised all forms, the wise One, having made names, sits uttering them’ (sarvāṇi rūpāṇi vicitya dhīro nāmāni kṛtvā abhivadan yad āste) (citation). And from such Śrutis as ‘There is no other seer than this’ (nānyo’to’sti draṣṭā) (Bṛ. U. 3.7.23) (citation) the same meaning is established. And consciousness (caitanya) is undifferentiated (aviśiṣṭa) in jīva and Īśvara, just as heat is in fire and spark. Therefore, from the apprehension of both difference and non-difference (bheda-abheda-avagamābhyām), part-hood (aṁśatva) is apprehended. (siddhānta) ‖ 43 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V44: And from a Mantra-passage (mantra-varṇa) also (the part-hood of the jīva is established). ‖ 44 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V44::block-1: A Mantra-passage also (mantra-varṇa) makes this very meaning known: ‘So great is His glory, and yet greater than this is the Puruṣa. One foot of His is all beings, His three feet are immortal in heaven’ (tāvān asya mahimā tato jyāyāṁś ca pūruṣaḥ; pādo’sya sarvā bhūtāni tripād asyāmṛtaṁ divi) (Chā. U. 3.12.6) (citation). Here by the word ‘bhūtāni’ (beings) the stationary and moving things, of which jīvas are the chief, are meant — as in the usage ‘not injuring any beings (sarva-bhūtāni) except at sacred fords (tīrthas)’ (citation); and ‘aṁśa,’ ‘pāda’ (foot), ‘bhāga’ (portion) are not different in meaning. Hence too part-hood is apprehended. ‖ 44 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V45: And it is also remembered (in the Smṛti). ‖ 45 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V45::block-1: In the Īśvara-gītā (Bhagavad-gītā) too, the part-hood of the jīva (relative to) Īśvara is remembered: ‘A part (aṁśa) of Mine alone, becoming the eternal jīva (jīva-bhūtaḥ sanātanaḥ), in the world of jīvas …’ (mamaivāṁśo jīvaloke jīvabhūtaḥ sanātanaḥ) (Bh. Gī. 15.7) (citation). Hence too part-hood is apprehended. As to what was said — that in the world the relation of ruler and ruled (īśitṛ-īśitavya-bhāva) is well established only in the case of master, servant, and the like — although this prasiddhi exists in the world, yet in this matter it is from Śāstra alone that the part-and-whole relation (aṁśa-aṁśitva) and the ruler-ruled relation are determined. And Īśvara, endowed with adjuncts that are unsurpassable (niratiśaya-upādhi-sampanna), governing the jīvas endowed with very inferior adjuncts (nihīna-upādhi-sampanna) — there is nothing contradictory in this. ‖ 45 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V45::block-2: Here it is objected (pūrvapakṣa): But if part-hood of the jīva relative to Īśvara is admitted, then by reason of the experience of saṁsāric suffering belonging to the jīva, there would be sufferer-hood for Īśvara, the whole (aṁśin), as well — just as in the world, by suffering located in any one limb such as hand or foot, the embodied being (aṅgin) Devadatta is a sufferer. And then those who attain Him (i.e., liberation in Him) would attain still greater suffering. Therefore better that saṁsāra remain just in its previous state — there would thus follow the futility (anarthakya) of correct insight (samyag-darśana). To this it is replied (siddhānta) —
BS_C02_S03_V46: Like light and so on (prakāśādi-vat); the Supreme (paraḥ) is not so. ‖ 46 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V46::block-0: We declare that the Supreme (para) Īśvara does not experience (saṁsāric suffering) as the jīva does. The jīva, by virtue of being possessed by avidyā, having as it were entered into identification with body and the rest (dehādy-ātma-bhāva), conceives the suffering wrought by avidyā — ‘I am the sufferer’ — through that identification. Not so the Supreme Lord; for Him there is neither identification with the body etc. nor the conceit of suffering. Even the jīva’s conceit of suffering arises only from non-discrimination (aviveka-bhrama) due to the adjuncts (upādhi) — body, sense-organs, etc. — fashioned out of the names and forms produced by avidyā; it is not real (pāramārthika). Just as he experiences, through the delusion of identification, the suffering occasioned by burning, cutting, etc. in his own body, in the same way he experiences also the suffering pertaining to son, friend, and so on, through the delusion of identification — clinging to son, friend, etc. through affection, thinking ‘I am the son, I am the friend.’ Hence it is conclusively understood: the experience of suffering is occasioned solely by the delusion of false identification (mithyā-abhimāna-bhrama-nimitta). And from the seeing of (corresponding) absence (vyatireka-darśana) it is so understood. Thus, when many are seated together — those who have the conceit of relationship (with sons, friends, etc.) and the others — and the proclamation is made ‘the son has died, the friend has died,’ suffering on that account arises only in those who have the conceit of being possessors of son, friend, etc., not in those free from this conceit such as Parivrājakas (renunciates). Hence it is observed that even for the worldly person, samyag-darśana has its purpose; what then to say of one who, beholding no thing other than the object-less Self, is of the nature of pure eternal consciousness alone (nitya-caitanya-mātra-svarūpa)? Hence there is no contingency of futility of samyag-darśana. The phrase ‘prakāśādi-vat’ is by way of citing illustrations. As the light of the sun or moon, pervading the sky and standing thus, by reason of contact with adjuncts (upādhi) such as a finger and so on, when these become straight or crooked, appears to assume that very (straight or crooked) state, but does not in reality assume that state; and as space (ākāśa), even though it appears to be moving when pots and the like move, does not in reality move; and as the sun, even when its reflection (pratibimba) in a pot of water trembles due to the trembling of the vessel, does not himself tremble — even so, when the part called jīva, conjured up by avidyā and limited by the intellect and the rest (buddhy-ādy-upahita), suffers, the possessor (of that part), Īśvara, does not suffer. And the jīva’s undergoing of suffering too is itself caused only by avidyā, as has been said. And accordingly, by setting aside (vyudāsa) the avidyā-caused jīva-state, the Vedānta-texts establish for the jīva nothing but Brahman-state (brahma-bhāva-eva), in such passages as ‘That thou art’ (tat tvam asi) (citation). Therefore there is no contingency of the Supreme Self being a sufferer through the jīva’s suffering. (siddhānta) ‖ 46 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V47::block-0: And Vyāsa and the rest remember (in Smṛti) — that the Supreme Self does not suffer through the jīva’s suffering: ‘There, that which is the Supreme Self, He is remembered as eternal and attributeless (nityo nirguṇaḥ);’ (citation) ‘He is not tainted by results, even as a lotus-leaf is not by water. But that other one, the agent-self (karmātmā) — he is bound by liberation and bondage (mokṣa-bandhaiḥ);’ (citation) ‘He is again joined with the seventeen-fold aggregate (saptadaśakena rāśinā)’ (citation). By the word ‘ca’ (and), the supplement of the sentence is: ‘they also declare’ — ‘Of the two (birds), one eats the sweet pippala-fruit; the other, not eating, looks on’ (tayor anyaḥ pippalaṁ svādvatti anaśnann anyo abhicākaśīti) (Śve. U. 4.6) (citation), and ‘The One, in like manner, the inner-Self of all beings, is not tainted by the world’s suffering, being outside’ (ekas tathā sarva-bhūta-antarātmā na lipyate loka-duḥkhena bāhyaḥ) (Ka. U. 2.2.11) (citation). ‖ 47 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V47::block-1: Here it is objected (pūrvapakṣa): If, then, there be only one inner-Self (antarātman) of all beings, how can the worldly and Vedic injunctions and prohibitions (anujñā-parihārau) be (sustained)? (Reply:) But it has been said that the jīva is a part (aṁśa) of Īśvara; from the difference resulting from this, the injunctions and prohibitions, resting upon that, become unmingled (avyatikīrṇa) and well-established. What then is being objected here? (Counter:) It is replied — not so. For Śrutis teaching non-difference also establish the partlessness (anaṁśatva) of the jīva: ‘Having created that, He entered into that very thing’ (tat sṛṣṭvā tad eva anuprāviśat) (Tai. U. 2.6.1) (citation), ‘There is no other seer than this’ (nānyo’to’sti draṣṭā) (Bṛ. U. 3.7.23) (citation), ‘He goes from death to death who sees as if there were many here’ (mṛtyoḥ sa mṛtyum āpnoti ya iha nāneva paśyati) (Bṛ. U. 4.4.19) (citation), ‘That thou art’ (tat tvam asi) (Chā. U. 6.8.7) (citation), ‘I am Brahman’ (ahaṁ brahmāsmi) (Bṛ. U. 1.4.10) (citation) — such and the like. (Counter-reply:) But it has been stated that part-hood is established by the apprehension of both difference and non-difference (bheda-abheda). (Reply:) That would be so, were both difference and non-difference intended to be expounded. But here non-difference alone (abheda eva) is intended to be expounded, since the puruṣārtha (the goal of human life) is accomplished in the realization of one’s identity with Brahman (brahma-ātmatva-pratipatti). Difference, however, attained as a matter of natural state (svabhāva-prāpta), is merely re-stated (anūdyate). And it has been stated that of partless (niravayava) Brahman a primary part — the jīva — is not possible. Therefore the Supreme alone, being one, is the inner-Self of all beings, abiding (apparently) in the jīva-form; so the consistency of injunctions and prohibitions has to be stated. We state it —
BS_C02_S03_V48: Injunctions and prohibitions (apply) because of connection with bodies (deha-sambandha), like fire and the rest (jyotirādi-vat). ‖ 48 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V48::block-0: ‘One should approach one’s wife in (her) season’ (ṛtau bhāryām upeyāt) (citation) is an injunction (anujñā); ‘one should not approach the guru’s wife’ (gurv-aṅganāṁ na upagacchet) (citation) is a prohibition (parihāra). Likewise: ‘he should immolate the animal sacred to Agni and Soma’ (agnīṣomīyaṁ paśuṁ saṁjñapayet) (citation) is an injunction, and ‘one should not injure any beings’ (na hiṁsyāt sarvā bhūtāni) (citation) is a prohibition. So too in the world: ‘a friend should be served’ — injunction; ‘an enemy should be avoided’ — prohibition. Such injunctions and prohibitions, even when the Self is one (ekatve’pi), would be possible from connection with bodies (deha-sambandha). The connection with bodies — what is it? It is the arising of the contrary cognition in the Self: ‘this aggregate of body and the rest is verily I.’ And this very (cognition) is observed in all beings — ‘I go,’ ‘I come,’ ‘I am blind,’ ‘I am not blind,’ ‘I am deluded,’ ‘I am undeluded,’ — of this nature. There is nothing other than samyag-darśana that can ward this off. Prior to samyag-darśana this delusion is uninterrupted (pratata) in all beings. Thus, on account of the difference produced by connection with body and other adjuncts caused by avidyā, even in the admission of one-Self-ness (aikātmya-abhyupagama) injunctions and prohibitions are warranted. (Objection:) Then for the samyag-darśin, the injunctions and prohibitions would become purposeless. (Reply:) Not so, because for him, on account of his being one whose end is accomplished (kṛtārtha), the qualification of being-enjoined (niyojyatva) is not possible — for one to whom there is something to be embraced (upādeya) or to be rejected (heya), he would be one to be enjoined. But (one) who, beyond the Self, sees no other thing as fit to be embraced or rejected — how could he be enjoined? Nor can the Self be enjoined to (act towards) the Self alone. (Objection:) Niyojyatva belongs only to one who sees difference from the body (śarīra-vyatireka-darśin). (Reply:) No; for the conceit of niyojyatva belongs to him precisely because, on account of his identification (with the body, etc.) (saṁhatatva-abhimāna), he does not see the Self as unconnected with the body etc., like space (vyomādi-vat). For no injunction is observed for one who sees the Self as unconnected with the body etc. — what then to say of one who sees the one-Self (aikātmya-darśin)?
