Nor, because of the absence of injunction, does there follow for the samyag-darśin behaving as he wills (yatheṣṭa-ceṣṭā), since in all cases it is identification (abhimāna) alone that is the impeller (pravartaka), and for the samyag-darśin there is absence of identification (abhimāna-abhāva). Therefore from connection with the body alone do injunctions and prohibitions arise — like in the case of fire etc. (jyotir-ādi-vat). Just as, even though fire is one, the kravyāt fire (cremation-pyre fire) is shunned, but not the other; just as the light of the one sun, when in contact with an impure place, is shunned, but not the same light when standing on pure ground; just as earthen substances such as diamond and lapis-lazuli (vajra-vaiḍūrya-ādi) are received, even though earthen, while bodies of corpses in cemeteries (naraka-lebara-ādi), also earthen, are avoided; just as cow-urine and dung are accepted as purifying, but the same in another species are rejected — even so. ‖ 48 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V49: And because of non-extension (asantateḥ), there is no admixture (avyatikara). ‖ 49 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V49::block-0: (Objection:) Let injunctions and prohibitions indeed obtain even for one Self by reason of conjunction with particular bodies. But this connection of action and result (karma-phala-sambandha) — would not this become mingled (vyatikīryeta) on the admission of one-Self-ness, since the master (svāmin) is one? (Reply:) Not so; on account of non-extension (asantateḥ). For the Self, as agent and enjoyer, has no extended (santata) connection with all bodies. The jīva is dependent on the upādhi (upādhi-tantra), as has been said. And, since the upādhis are not extended (asantāna) (across all bodies), there is no extension of jīvas — and hence there will be no admixture of action (karma-vyatikara) or admixture of result (phala-vyatikara). ‖ 49 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V50: And (the jīva is) only a semblance (ābhāsa). ‖ 50 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V50::block-0: And this jīva is to be apprehended as merely a semblance (ābhāsa) of the Supreme Self, like the reflection of the sun in water (jala-sūrya-ka), and not as that itself (directly), nor yet as another thing. And accordingly, just as when one reflection of the sun in water trembles, another reflection of the sun in water does not tremble, even so, when one jīva is connected with karma-phala, there is no such connection for another jīva. Even so, there is non-admixture (avyatikara) only of action and result. And, the semblance being avidyā-fashioned (avidyā-kṛta), the consequent saṁsāra resting upon it has its avidyā-causedness well-warranted; and, by setting that (saṁsāra) aside, the teaching of the truly real Brahman-Self-state (pāramārthika brahma-ātma-bhāva) is warranted. But for those who hold many selves, all of them all-pervading (sarva-gata) — for them alone this admixture obtains. How? (Sāṅkhya pūrvapakṣa:) The selves are many, all-pervading (vibhu), of the form of pure consciousness alone (caitanya-mātra-svarūpa), attributeless (nirguṇa), and without any pre-eminence over one another (niratiśaya). For their (purposes) is the common Pradhāna; and from this comes about the accomplishment of (their) experience and liberation (bhoga-apavarga-siddhi) — so the Sāṅkhyas. (Vaiśeṣika pūrvapakṣa:) Even granted plurality and all-pervadingness, the selves, similar to pots, walls, and the like, of the nature of mere substance (dravya-mātra-svarūpa) and unconscious by themselves (svato’cetana), and their adjuncts the manases, atomic and unconscious — there, by the conjunction of self-substances and mind-substances, the nine special qualities of the self (vaiśeṣikā ātma-guṇāḥ) such as desire (icchā) etc. arise; and these inhere in the (respective) selves separately without admixture (avyatikareṇa) — that is saṁsāra. The absolute non-arising of those nine self-qualities is mokṣa — so the Kāṇādas (Vaiśeṣikas). Now, for the Sāṅkhyas first: since all the selves are of the nature of consciousness, and there is no difference among them in respect of proximity etc., the connection of suffering and pleasure with one would entail the connection of all selves with that suffering and pleasure. (Sāṅkhya rejoinder:) That may be — but since the activity of Pradhāna is for the kaivalya (isolation/liberation) of the puruṣa, restriction (vyavasthā) will obtain. Otherwise the activity of Pradhāna would be for displaying its own glory (sva-vibhūti-khyāpana-artha), and absence of liberation would result. (Refutation:) This has no substance — for restriction whose grounding is (merely) the desired result cannot be cognized (as such); only by means of some logical proof (upapatti) can restriction be stated. In the absence of such proof, let the desired puruṣa-kaivalya, you may have, fail to obtain. But due to absence of any cause of restriction, admixture (vyatikara) follows. (For the Kāṇādas) too: when one self is conjoined with mind, since there is no difference in proximity etc., conjunction with the other selves also would be unavoidable. And then, since the cause is the same, the result must also be the same; thus when one self is connected with pleasure and pain, all the selves alike would have to be sufferers and enjoyers. (pūrvapakṣa refuted: Sāṅkhya, Vaiśeṣika) ‖ 50 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V50::block-1: (Sāṅkhya/Vaiśeṣika rejoinder:) Let it be objected: there will be a restriction occasioned by adṛṣṭa (the unseen, i.e., karma). (The Sūtra-kāra) says ‘No’ —
BS_C02_S03_V51: Because of the non-restriction of the unseen (adṛṣṭa). ‖ 51 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V51::block-0: When the selves are many, all-pervasive like ākāśa, and equally present within and without each body, the unseen (adṛṣṭa) characterised as dharma and adharma is generated through mind, speech and body. Now, on the view of the Sāṅkhyas, that adṛṣṭa inheres not in the self but resides in pradhāna; and since pradhāna is common (sādhāraṇa) to all selves, no determinant arises whereby the experience of pleasure and pain should be apportioned to each particular self. As for the Kāṇādas (Vaiśeṣikas), even though they hold the adṛṣṭa to be brought about by the conjunction of self and mind, since — as already shown — that conjunction too is common (to all selves alike), there is no ground (hetu) for the restriction ‘this adṛṣṭa belongs to this very self and not to another’; thus the very same defect attaches to them. ‖ 51 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V51::block-1: It might be urged (pūrvapakṣa): ‘But intentions and the like — “let me obtain this fruit, let me avoid this, let me strive thus, let me act thus” — being themselves operative in each individual self, will themselves regulate the relation of owner and owned (sva-svāmi-bhāva) between the adṛṣṭa and the selves.’ To this he replies, ‘No,’ as follows —
BS_C02_S03_V52: And in the case of intentions and the rest also, it is similarly so. ‖ 52 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V52::block-0: Even intentions and the like, since they too are produced through the very same common conjunction of self and mind in the proximity of all selves alike, cannot serve as the ground of restriction; hence the aforesaid defect attaches inevitably here too. ‖ 52 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V53: If it be said ‘by reason of locus (pradeśa)’ — no, because of inclusion (antarbhāva). ‖ 53 ‖
BS_C02_S03_V53::block-0: It might be urged (pūrvapakṣa): ‘Although the self is all-pervasive, its conjunction with the mind, which abides within the body, will occur only in that locus (pradeśa) of the self which is delimited by the body; hence, by reason of difference of locus, there will be a settled apportionment of intentions and the rest, of the unseen (adṛṣṭa), and of pleasure and pain.’ This too does not stand. Why? Because of inclusion (antarbhāvāt). For, by parity of all-pervasiveness, all selves alike are included within all bodies. Therein the Vaiśeṣikas cannot fancy a body-delimited locus of the self. And even were such a locus imagined, since the self has no parts, that locus, being merely imagined, can never regulate any real effect (pāramārthikaṁ kāryam). Nor can the body itself, arising in the proximity of all selves alike, be restricted as ‘of this very self and not of others.’ Even granting a particular locus, since two selves having a common share of pleasure and pain might at some time obtain enjoyment through one and the same body — for it is possible that two selves should have adṛṣṭa belonging to the same locus. To explain: in whatever locus Devadatta experienced pleasure and pain, when his body has departed from that locus and Yajñadatta's body has come to occupy that very locus, an experience of pleasure and pain identical with the former's is observed in him also. This would not be so unless Devadatta and Yajñadatta had adṛṣṭa pertaining to a common locus. The pradeśa-vādin would also incur the consequence that there is no enjoyment of heaven and the like, since the adṛṣṭa is generated in body-loci such as those of brāhmaṇas, while heavenly enjoyment lies in another locus altogether. Moreover, the all-pervasiveness of many selves cannot be established, there being no example (dṛṣṭānta). Pray tell — what are these things that are many and yet share a common locus? If you say ‘colour and the rest (rūpādayaḥ),’ no; for they too do not differ in their nature as ‘substantial qualities’ (dharmy-aṁśena), and they differ from one another in characteristic (lakṣaṇa-bhedāt) — but among the many selves there is no difference of characteristic. If you say ‘distinction is established by ultimate-particulars (antya-viśeṣa)’, no; for the supposition of distinction and the supposition of ultimate-particulars would mutually depend on each other (itaretarāśraya). And as to ākāśa and the rest, their all-pervasiveness is not established for the Brahma-vādin, since he holds them to be effects (kārya). Therefore, only on the doctrine of the unity of the Self (ātma-aikatva-pakṣa) is there freedom from all defects. Thus stands established. ‖ 53 ‖
BS_C02_S04_INTRO1::block-0: The śruti-conflict regarding ākāśa and the rest (the elements) was resolved by the third pāda. Now, by the fourth, the conflict regarding the prāṇas (vital functions and sense-organs) is being resolved. There, in the first place, in such passages of the creation-section as ‘That generated tejas’ (Chā. U. 6.2.3) and ‘Verily from this Self ākāśa came forth’ (Tai. U. 2.1.1) and so on, the origination of the prāṇas is not recorded. And in some places their very non-origination is recorded — ‘Verily this was non-being in the beginning’ (Tai. U. 2.7.1). ‘They ask: What was that non-being? — “Sages indeed they were, who in the beginning were that non-being.” They ask: Who were these sages? — “The prāṇas verily are the sages”’ — for here, prior to creation, the existence (sad-bhāva) of the prāṇas is heard. Elsewhere, however, the origination of the prāṇas too is read — ‘As from a fire tiny sparks fly forth, even so from this Self all prāṇas’; ‘From This is born prāṇa, mind, and all sense-organs’ (Mu. U. 2.1.3); ‘Seven prāṇas come forth from It’ (Mu. U. 2.1.8); ‘He created prāṇa; from prāṇa, śraddhā, ākāśa, vāyu, jyotis, āpas, pṛthivī, indriya, manas, and anna’ (Pra. U. 6.4) and the like. Therein, since there is conflict among the śrutis and no determinant of preference is in evidence, doubt arises (apratipatti). Or else: since the existence of the prāṇas prior to origination is heard, the śruti as to the origination of prāṇas must be taken figuratively (gauṇī) — this view obtains. Hence the following reply is read —
BS_C02_S04_V01::block-0: ‘Likewise the prāṇas’ — But how is this ‘likewise’ (tathā) consistent with the order of letters, when no upamāna (object of comparison) has been introduced? — for what was discussed at the close of the immediately preceding pāda was the refutation of the doctrine of plurality of all-pervading selves. To begin with, that cannot serve as upamāna, since there is no similitude. For comparison would obtain only where there is similitude — as in ‘Balavarman is like a lion.’ Should it be said: ‘this is to bring out parity with the unseen (adṛṣṭa) — that just as the adṛṣṭa, arising in proximity to all selves alike, is non-restricted, so the prāṇas too are not restricted to particular selves’ — even that would amount to mere repetition (punarukta), since the same was already stated in the case of bodies and their non-restriction. Nor can the prāṇas be likened to the jīva, for that would conflict with the siddhānta — for the non-origination of the jīva has been declared, while the origination of the prāṇas is the very thing now to be stated. Therefore the word ‘likewise’ would seem disconnected. — Not so. The connection is fitting through an upamāna conveyed by the citation. For here the upamāna is the body of texts that affirm the origination of the prāṇas — such as ‘From this Self all prāṇas, all worlds, all gods, all beings come forth’ (Bṛ. U. 2.1.20) and the like. There, the meaning is: just as worlds and the rest are originated from the supreme Brahman, so too the prāṇas. Likewise in passages such as ‘From This is born prāṇa, mind, all sense-organs, ākāśa, vāyu, jyotis, āpas, pṛthivī, the supporter of all’ (Mu. U. 2.1.3) — the origination of the prāṇas is to be regarded as on a par with that of ākāśa and the rest. Or else, since in such sūtras as ‘And likewise in the case of pāna-vyāpat’ (Jai. Sū. 3.4.15) recourse is taken to a connection with an upamāna stated at a remove (vyavahita) — the meaning will be: just as ākāśa and the rest, declared in the earlier portion of the immediately preceding pāda, are ascertained to be modifications of the supreme Brahman, so too the prāṇas are modifications of the supreme Brahman; thus the construction is to be made. — But what is the ground for the prāṇas being modifications? — Their being so heard (śrutatvam eva). — But it has been objected that in some places the origination of the prāṇas is not heard. — That is no defect, since it is heard in other places. For, the non-mention in some places cannot annul what is mentioned in another. Hence, by uniformity of śruti-mention (śrutatva-aviśeṣa), like ākāśa and the rest the prāṇas too are originated. Thus the sūtra is well-stated. ‖ 1 ‖
BS_C02_S04_V02: Because the figurative is not possible. ‖ 2 ‖
BS_C02_S04_V02::block-0: What was urged — that, since the existence of the prāṇas prior to origination is heard, the śruti as to the origination of the prāṇas must be figurative (gauṇī) — that is answered by ‘Because the figurative is not possible.’ ‘Gauṇy-asambhavaḥ’ means: the impossibility of the figurative. For the śruti as to the origination of prāṇas cannot be figurative, since that would entail abandonment of the pratijñā (initial declaration). Indeed, having declared at the start ‘That by the knowing of which all this becomes known’ (Mu. U. 1.1.3) — i.e., the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one — for the establishment of that very point is read ‘From This is born prāṇa’ (Mu. U. 2.1.3) and the like. And that pratijñā is established only when the entire universe beginning with prāṇa is a modification of Brahman, since apart from the prakṛti there is no vikāra. But if the śruti as to the origination of prāṇas were figurative, this very pratijñā would be abandoned. And accordingly he sums up the matter declared, as: ‘Puruṣa indeed is all this — karma, tapas, Brahman, the supreme Immortal’ (Mu. U. 2.1.10) and ‘Brahman alone is all this; this is the highest’ (Mu. U. 2.2.12). Likewise in such śrutis as ‘Verily, dear, by the seeing, hearing, reflecting, and knowing of the Self all this is known’ — this very same pratijñā is to be applied. — But how is the existence of the prāṇas prior to origination heard? — That is not in respect of the mūla-prakṛti (root-prakṛti, viz. Brahman), since the affirmation that the mūla-prakṛti is devoid of all particularities such as prāṇa is established by ‘Without prāṇa, without manas, pure, higher than the high Imperishable’ (Mu. U. 2.1.2). It is to be understood as relating to the intermediate prakṛti (avāntara-prakṛti) — the establishment of the existence of the prāṇas prior to origination, with reference to their own modifications, since śruti and smṛti are familiar with prakṛti-vikāra-relation among many vyākṛta states (manifested conditions). Now, in the Viyad-adhikaraṇa, since ‘gauṇy-asambhavāt’ was a pūrvapakṣa-sūtra, it was explained as: ‘the śruti about birth is figurative, because [the literal] is not possible.’ And there the siddhānta was set forth by the abandonment of the pratijñā. But here, since it is a siddhānta-sūtra, it is explained as: ‘because the figurative interpretation of the śruti about birth is not possible.’ Whereas those who, conforming to that earlier reading, here too explain ‘the śruti about birth is figurative, because not possible,’ would have neglected the abandonment of the pratijñā. ‖ 2 ‖
BS_C02_S04_V03: And because of its [the verb ‘is born’] being heard earlier with reference to that [prāṇa]. ‖ 3 ‖
BS_C02_S04_V03::block-0: On this further ground also, the śruti about birth in the case of the prāṇas, like that in the case of ākāśa and the rest, is principal (mukhyā): the single word denoting birth, ‘jāyate’ (‘is born’), heard earlier in connection with prāṇa, is carried over to the subsequent items, ākāśa and the rest. In ‘From This is born prāṇa’ (Mu. U. 2.1.3) the principal sense of birth has been already established for ākāśa and the rest. By parity with that, in the case of the prāṇas too, birth must be in the principal sense. For one cannot decide that, in a single section and a single sentence, a single word uttered once and connected with several items, should be principal in some places and figurative in others — this would entail incongruity (vairūpya). Likewise, in ‘He created prāṇa, from prāṇa śraddhā’ (Pra. U. 6.4) too, the verb ‘sṛjati’ (‘creates’), heard with reference to the prāṇas, is carried over to the subsequent originated items, śraddhā and the rest. And where the verb of origination is heard later and is connected with the earlier items, this same maxim applies — as in ‘all beings come forth (vyuccaranti),’ where ‘vyuccaranti,’ read at the end, is connected even with the earlier items, prāṇa and the rest. ‖ 3 ‖
BS_C02_S04_V04: Because speech is preceded by that [tejas, ap, anna]. ‖ 4 ‖
BS_C02_S04_V04::block-0: Although in the section ‘That generated tejas’ (Chā. U. 6.2.3), the origination of the prāṇas is not read — only the origination of the three elements tejas, ap, and anna being heard there — yet, since vāk, prāṇa, and manas are declared to be preceded by tejas, ap, and anna which have Brahman as their prakṛti (ground), and by parity with that, the prāṇas in their entirety are established as having Brahman as their source. To explain — in this very section the priority of tejas, ap, and anna to vāk, prāṇa, and manas is recorded thus: ‘Mind, dear one, is constituted of anna; prāṇa is constituted of āpas; speech (vāk) is constituted of tejas’ (Chā. U. 6.5.4). There, if the constitution of these as anna and the rest is taken in the principal sense, then their having Brahman as their source obtains directly. If, on the other hand, it is figurative, even then — since the differentiation of name and form (nāma-rūpa-vyākriyā) is heard as effected by Brahman, and from the upakrama (commencement) ‘by which the unheard becomes heard’ (Chā. U. 6.1.3), and from the upasaṁhāra (conclusion) ‘All this has That as its Self’ (Chā. U. 6.8.7), and from the established declaration in other śrutis — it is to be inferred that the assertion of mind and the rest as constituted of anna and so on is meant precisely to elaborate the fact that they are effects of Brahman. Hence too the prāṇas are established as modifications of Brahman. ‖ 4 ‖
BS_C02_S04_V05: ‘Seven, on account of the going and on account of the specification.’ (5)
BS_C02_S04_V05::block-0:
The śruti-conflict regarding the origination of the prāṇas has been removed (in the previous adhikaraṇa). The conflict regarding their number is now being settled. Among the prāṇas, the chief (mukhya) prāṇa will be discussed later; at present the question being deliberated is — how many are the other prāṇas? Here too there is doubt because of conflicting śruti-statements: in some places seven prāṇas are enumerated — ‘From Him are produced the seven prāṇas’ (Muṇḍ. Up. 2.1.8); in some places eight prāṇas are enumerated as grahas with their corresponding qualities — ‘There are eight grahas and eight atigrahas’ (Bṛh. Up. 3.2.1); in some places nine — ‘Verily seven prāṇas are seated in the head and two are downward-going’ (Tait. Saṃ. 5.1.7.1); in some places ten — ‘There are nine prāṇas in the puruṣa and the navel as the tenth’; in some places eleven — ‘These are the ten prāṇas in the puruṣa and the ātman as the eleventh’ (Bṛh. Up. 3.9.4); in some places twelve — ‘Of all touches, skin is the sole resort’ (Bṛh. Up. 2.4.11); in some places thirteen — ‘the eye and what is to be seen’ (Praśna Up. 4.8). Thus the śrutis are at variance regarding the number of the prāṇas. What then (is the prima facie position) obtained? — That the prāṇas are seven only. Why? — Because of ‘going’ (gati), that is, because so many are made known in the śrutis such as ‘From Him are produced the seven prāṇas’ (Muṇḍ. Up. 2.1.8); and they are specified as such in ‘Verily seven prāṇas are seated in the head’ (pūrvapakṣa). 

Objection: But the repetition (vīpsā) ‘the seven, seven prāṇas hidden in the cave’ is heard; and that suggests prāṇas in excess of the seven. 

Reply: This is no fault. The repetition is intended with reference to difference of persons — that there are seven, seven prāṇas in each person; it is not intended with reference to difference of substance — that there are seven and seven other and other prāṇas. 

Objection: But the numbers eight and so forth have been enumerated of the prāṇas; how then can they be seven only? 

Reply: True, they have been enumerated; but on account of the conflict, some one number must be settled upon. Therein, since the rule is to lean toward the lesser assumption, the determination is on the number seven. The mention of other numbers is to be regarded as referring to differences of function (vṛtti-bheda). Such is the (pūrvapakṣa) view. (5)
BS_C02_S04_V06: ‘But the hands and the rest, since (the difference) is established, hence not so.’ (6)
BS_C02_S04_V06::block-1:
(Siddhānta:) But the hands and the rest, other prāṇas in excess of the seven, are heard of in śrutis such as — ‘The hands verily are a graha; that is grasped by the atigraha karma; for with the hands one performs action’ (Bṛh. Up. 3.2.8). When the surplus over seven is established, sevenness can be regarded as included within it. For when there is conflict between a smaller and a larger number, the larger number must be accepted; the smaller is included in it, but not the larger in the smaller. Hence it should not be thought — ‘On the strength of the principle of leaning toward the lesser, the prāṇas are seven only.’ Rather, on the strength of the higher number, the prāṇas are eleven only. So too the śruti has been cited — ‘These are the ten prāṇas in the puruṣa and the ātman as the eleventh’ (Bṛh. Up. 3.9.4); and the word ‘ātman’ here denotes the antaḥkaraṇa, since the topic is the karaṇas (instruments). 

Objection: But over and above eleven, twelve and thirteen have been enumerated. 

Reply: True, they have been enumerated; but there is no class of effects beyond the eleven for the sake of which an additional instrument should be postulated. The objects śabda, sparśa, rūpa, rasa, gandha give five differences of cognition (buddhi-bheda); for them are the five buddhīndriyas. Speech, grasping, locomotion, evacuation, generation are the five differences of action (karma-bheda); for them are the five karmendriyas. The mind which extends to all objects and operates over the three times is one only, with many functions. The same, by reason of difference of function, is sometimes designated as if differentiated — ‘mind, intellect, ego, citta.’ And so the śruti, after enumerating various functions such as desire and so forth, says — ‘all this is just mind’ (Bṛh. Up. 1.5.3). 

Moreover, for one who holds that there are only seven śīrṣaṇya prāṇas, only four prāṇas would in fact be intended; for, being four, on account of difference of place they are counted as seven — ‘two ears, two eyes, two nostrils, one speech.’ And it is not possible to say that the other prāṇas are mere differences of function of these, for the functions of the hands and the rest are utterly heterogeneous (atyanta-vijātīya). 

Likewise in ‘Nine prāṇas in the puruṣa, the navel as the tenth,’ ten prāṇas are spoken of with reference to the differences of bodily orifices, not with reference to differences of prāṇa-substance, as is shown by the statement ‘the navel as the tenth.’ For there is no prāṇa known by the name ‘navel.’ But the chief prāṇa has the navel also as one specific seat — therefore it is said ‘the navel as the tenth.’ Sometimes prāṇas are enumerated for the sake of upāsana, sometimes for indication. Thus, since the enumeration of the prāṇas is variegated, it has to be discriminated where the enumeration has what purport. On the strength of the variety of effects, the enumeration of eleven is the standard regarding the prāṇas — this is the conclusion (sthitam).
BS_C02_S04_V06::block-2:
Here is another way of construing this pair of sūtras (alternate yojanā): The prāṇas are seven only, since the going (utkrānti) of seven only is heard of — ‘When that one departs, prāṇa departs after him; when prāṇa departs, all the prāṇas depart after him’ (Bṛh. Up. 4.4.2). 

Objection: But the word ‘all’ (sarva) is read here; how then is the going of seven only being asserted? 

Reply (pūrvapakṣa-continuation): On account of specification (viśeṣitatvāt) — for it is precisely seven prāṇas, the eye and the rest down to the skin, that are specified as the topic here, by the enumeration ‘When the puruṣa of the eye turns away, then he becomes ignorant of forms,’ ‘He becomes one, they say he does not see’ (Bṛh. Up. 4.4.1–2), and so on. The word ‘all’ refers to what is contextually under discussion (prakṛtagāmin); just as in ‘all the brāhmaṇas should be fed,’ those brāhmaṇas who are invited and under reference are alone meant by ‘all,’ not others — even so here, the seven prāṇas under reference are alone denoted by ‘all,’ not others. 

Objection: But here vijñāna as the eighth has not been enumerated; how then is there enumeration of seven only? 

Reply: This is no fault. Since manas and vijñāna are non-different in essence, even though differing in function, sevenness is sustained. Hence the prāṇas are seven only. Such is the prima facie view. 

This being so, we say (siddhānta) — But the hands and the rest, other prāṇas in excess of the seven, are made known in śrutis like ‘The hands verily are a graha’ (Bṛh. Up. 3.2.8). And graha-hood is the state of being a bond — that by which the kṣetrajña is grasped, that is, bound, by this bondage called ‘graha.’ And that kṣetrajña is bound not in one body alone, since the bondage is alike in other bodies. Therefore this bondage called ‘graha’ migrates from one body to another — this is the implied meaning. So too smṛti — ‘He is connected with the puryaṣṭaka liṅga beginning with prāṇa; bondage is of one bound by it, and liberation is of one freed from it’ — shows that till liberation there is no separation from the bondage called graha. And in the Atharvaṇa (Praśna), in the enumeration of viṣayas and indriyas, ‘the eye and what is to be seen’ (Praśna Up. 4.8), the hands and the rest of the indriyas, along with their objects, are equally enumerated — ‘the hands and what is to be grasped, the generative organ and what is to be enjoyed, the anus and what is to be evacuated, the feet and what is to be traversed’ (Praśna Up. 4.8). Likewise — ‘These are the ten prāṇas in the puruṣa and the ātman as the eleventh; when they go forth from this mortal body, then they make to weep’ (Bṛh. Up. 3.9.4) — shows the going forth of eleven prāṇas. 

The word ‘all’ also, when joined with the word ‘prāṇa,’ denoting the prāṇas without remainder, cannot be confined to seven on the strength of context, since the word is stronger than context (prakaraṇāt śabdasya balīyastvāt). Even in ‘all brāhmaṇas should be fed,’ the inclusion of all brāhmaṇas of the earth would be the just construction by virtue of the strength of the word ‘all’; only because feeding all is impossible is the word ‘all’ there construed as referring just to those invited. But here there is no reason to restrict the meaning of the word ‘all.’ Therefore by ‘all’ here all the prāṇas without remainder are taken in. The enumeration of seven is for indicative purposes (pradarśanārtha) — and so it is unobjectionable. Therefore the prāṇas are eleven only — both by śruti and by their effects. Thus is it established. (6)
BS_C02_S04_V07::block-0:
Now another nature of the prāṇas themselves is being adduced (abhyuccinoti). The prāṇas under reference are also to be understood as ‘atomic’ (aṇu). And their atomicity is subtlety and limitedness in extent (sūkṣmya and paricchedau), not equality with the paramāṇu, since on that view there would be the contingency of the impossibility of an effect pervading the entire body. — These prāṇas are subtle; if they were gross, then at the time of death, going forth from the body like a snake from a hole, they would be perceived by the bystanders of the dying. They are limited in extent; if they were all-pervading, the śrutis about going forth, going to other regions and returning would be set at naught (vyākopa), and the ‘being-the-essence-of-the-jīva’s-qualities’ (taj-jīva-guṇa-sāratva) of the jīva would not be established. 

Objection: Even if all-pervading, they may have their function (vṛtti-lābha) only in the locus of the body. 

Reply: No; for it stands to reason that the function alone is the karaṇa-hood. For whatever is the means of cognition — be it the function or anything else — that alone, with us, is the instrument; the dispute would be merely about the name. Hence positing pervasiveness for the karaṇas is purposeless. Therefore we determine that the prāṇas are subtle and limited. (7)
BS_C02_S04_V08::block-0:
By way of extension (atideśa), it is taught that the chief prāṇa also, like the other prāṇas, is a modification of Brahman (brahma-vikāra). Now the brahma-vikāra-hood of all prāṇas in general has been declared — ‘From Him are produced prāṇa, mind and all the indriyas’ (Muṇḍ. Up. 2.1.3) where the origination of prāṇa is heard of distinct from the indriyas and the mind, and from passages such as ‘He created prāṇa’ (Praśna Up. 6.4). 

Then what is the purpose of the extension (atideśa)? — To remove a particular doubt. For in the Nāsadāsīya hymn dealing primarily with Brahman, there is the mantra-passage — ‘Death was not, nor immortality then; there was no sign of night or day. That One breathed without air by its own power; other than That there was nothing whatever beyond’ (Ṛg. Saṃ. 8.7.17 / RV 10.129.1ff). By the use of the verbal root meaning ‘breathed’ (ānīt), it is suggested as if prāṇa existed prior to creation. Hence someone might form the opinion ‘prāṇa is unborn (aja)’; that opinion is removed by the extension (atideśa). The word ‘ānīt’ also does not indicate the existence of prāṇa prior to creation, because of the qualifier ‘avātam’ (without breath/air), and because the root prakṛti is shown to be free of all the particularizations like prāṇa and so forth — ‘Without prāṇa, without mind, pure’ (Muṇḍ. Up. 2.1.2). Hence this word ‘ānīt’ is intended only to indicate the existence of the cause. 

The word ‘śreṣṭha’ here denotes the chief (mukhya) prāṇa, by reason of the śruti-statement ‘Prāṇa indeed is the eldest and the best’ (Chānd. Up. 5.1.1). Prāṇa is the eldest (jyeṣṭha) because his function (vṛtti-lābha) commences from the moment of the impregnation of the semen. If at that moment he did not obtain his function, the semen deposited in the womb would putrefy, or would not develop. But the śrotra and the rest obtain their function only after the formation of their respective seats like the ear-cavity and so forth — hence they are not jyeṣṭha. And he is śreṣṭha (the best), by reason of his pre-eminence in qualities — by the śruti ‘We shall not indeed be able to live without you’ (Bṛh. Up. 6.1.13). (8)
BS_C02_S04_V09: ‘Not air or function, on account of the separate teaching.’ (9)
BS_C02_S04_V09::block-0: Now what is the essential nature of that chief prāṇa? That is being inquired into. Therein the prima facie position obtained is — by śruti, prāṇa is air (vāyu). For so it is heard — ‘That which is prāṇa, that is vāyu; that very vāyu is fivefold — prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, samāna.’ Or, on the view of another tantra (the Sāṅkhya), the prima facie view obtained is that prāṇa is the common function of all the karaṇas; for thus speak the followers of another tantra — ‘The common function of the karaṇas is the five airs beginning with prāṇa.’
BS_C02_S04_V09::block-1:
(Siddhānta:) To this it is replied — Prāṇa is neither vāyu, nor a function of the karaṇas (karaṇa-vyāpāra). Why? Because of separate teaching (pṛthag-upadeśa). For of vāyu first, prāṇa is taught separately — ‘Prāṇa is the fourth foot of Brahman; it shines and warms with vāyu as its light’ (Chānd. Up. 3.18.4). Were prāṇa nothing but vāyu itself, it could not be taught as separate from vāyu. So too, of the karaṇa-function, separate teaching obtains, since after enumerating the karaṇas like speech and so forth, prāṇa is mentioned separately in those very contexts; and there is non-difference between function and the function-possessor. Were prāṇa nothing but the function of the karaṇas, it could not be taught separately from the karaṇas. So also passages such as ‘From Him are produced prāṇa, mind and all the indriyas; ether, vāyu’ (Muṇḍ. Up. 2.1.3) — the separate teaching of prāṇa from vāyu and from the karaṇas — should be followed up. 

Further, of all the karaṇas there cannot be one common function, since each one has its own respective function, and an aggregate cannot be an agent (samudāyasya akārakatvāt). 

Objection: Will it not be by the analogy of moving the cage (pañjara-cālana-nyāya) — just as eleven birds dwelling in one cage, each having its specific activity, jointly move the one cage, so the eleven prāṇas dwelling in one body, each having its respective function, will jointly attain a single function called prāṇa? 

Reply: That is not so. There it is fitting that the birds, each with its individual activity but each activity being of a kind that contributes to moving the cage, should jointly move the one cage — for so it is observed. But here it is not fitting that the prāṇas, severally engaged in such heterogeneous functions as hearing, etc., should jointly engage in prāṇana (vital activity), since there is no pramāṇa for it, and prāṇana is utterly heterogeneous in kind from hearing and the like. Likewise the proclamation of the prāṇa’s pre-eminence (śreṣṭhatva), and the assumption of subordination of speech and the rest to him, would not fit if prāṇa were a mere karaṇa-function. 

Therefore prāṇa is other than air and the function. Then how is this śruti — ‘That which is prāṇa is vāyu’? It is replied — That very vāyu, having entered into the adhyātma (the inner organism) and arranged in fivefold formation (pañca-vyūha), abiding as a particular self-modification, is called prāṇa; he is not a separate substance (tattvāntara), nor mere vāyu either. Hence both śrutis — those of difference and those of non-difference — do not conflict. (9)
BS_C02_S04_V10: ‘But like the eye and the rest, on account of being taught together with them, etc.’ (10)
BS_C02_S04_V10::block-0: It might be thought (pūrvapakṣa) — Prāṇa too, then, like the jīva, must obtain independence in this body, since he is the chief, and since speech and the other indriyas accept subordination toward him. For thus, manifold glory of prāṇa is heard of in the śruti — when speech and the rest are asleep, prāṇa alone keeps awake; prāṇa alone is unattained by death; prāṇa, the saṃvarga, swallows up speech and the rest; prāṇa protects the other prāṇas like a mother protects her sons. Hence the contingency of independence (svātantrya-prasaṅga) of prāṇa also, just like the jīva. He removes (parihṛti) this —
BS_C02_S04_V10::block-1: (Siddhānta:) The word ‘tu’ (but) excludes the independence of prāṇa, like that of the jīva. Just as the eye and the rest, like the king’s subjects, are instruments (upakaraṇa) of the jīva towards his agentship and enjoyment, and not independent — so too the chief prāṇa, like the king’s minister, is the instrument of the jīva for accomplishing all his purposes, and is not independent. Why? — From his being taught together (with them) and so forth (tat-saha-śiṣṭyādibhyaḥ); for prāṇa is taught together with those eye and the rest in the prāṇa-saṃvāda passages and so forth; and joint teaching is fitting for those of similar dharma, like bṛhad-rathaṃtara, etc. By the word ‘ādi’ are indicated such reasons negating prāṇa’s independence as composite-ness (saṃhata-tva), insentience (acetana-tva) and so forth. (10)
BS_C02_S04_V11: ‘And on account of his not being a karaṇa there is no defect; thus indeed (the śruti) shows.’ (11)
BS_C02_S04_V11::block-0: It might be objected (pūrvapakṣa) — If, like the eye and the rest, prāṇa’s being a karaṇa to the jīva is admitted, then it would have to have a separate object like rūpa and so forth; for it is by their respective functions of perceiving rūpa and so on that the eye and the rest become karaṇas to the jīva. Moreover, only eleven classes of effects beginning with the perception of form have been enumerated, for the sake of which eleven prāṇas have been comprehended; but no twelfth class of effect is known, for the sake of which this twelfth prāṇa is being postulated. To this objection he gives the reply (sūtra) —
BS_C02_S04_V11::block-1: (Siddhānta:) The contingency of a separate object is no defect, since prāṇa is not a karaṇa (akaraṇatva). For prāṇa’s being a karaṇa by way of delimiting an object, like the eye and the rest, is not what is admitted. Nor is there absence of effect (kāryābhāva) in him merely because of that. Why? — For thus indeed the śruti shows (tathā hi darśayati) the special effect (vaiśeṣikam kāryam) of the chief prāṇa, which is impossible in the other prāṇas, in the prāṇa-saṃvāda passages and elsewhere — beginning with ‘Then the prāṇas disputed about who was the best’ (Chānd. Up. 5.1.6) and stating ‘He on whose departure the body would appear most wretched, he is your best’ (Chānd. Up. 5.1.7), and showing through the departure of speech and so forth one by one that life continues as before, deficient only in the function of that one — and showing further that on the chief prāṇa’s being about to depart, speech and the rest become loose and the body is on the verge of falling. Thus the śruti shows the dependence of the body and indriyas on prāṇa. And the śruti says this same purport: ‘Then the chief prāṇa said to them, Do not fall into delusion; I myself, dividing my self fivefold, holding up and supporting this reed (the body)’ (cf. Praśna Up. 2.3). And ‘Guarding the lower nest by prāṇa’ (Bṛh. Up. 4.3.12) — when the eye and the rest are asleep, the śruti shows the protection of the body by prāṇa. ‘From whichever limb prāṇa departs, that very (limb) dries up’ (Bṛh. Up. 1.3.19) and ‘With what he eats and drinks, by that he sustains the other prāṇas’ — show the body’s and the indriyas’ nourishment caused by prāṇa. ‘In what departing shall I depart? In what abiding shall I abide? — He created prāṇa’ — show that the jīva’s departure (utkrānti) and abiding (pratiṣṭhā) are caused by prāṇa. (11)
BS_C02_S04_V12: ‘He is taught as having five functions, like the manas.’ (12)
BS_C02_S04_V13::block-0: This principal vital-breath (mukhya-prāṇa) too is to be understood as atomic (aṇu), like the other prāṇas. Here also ‘atomicity’ (aṇutva) means subtlety (saukṣmya) and limitedness (paricchedaḥ) — not equality with a paramāṇu (ultimate atom), since by its five functions (prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, samāna) it pervades the entire body. The prāṇa is subtle (sūkṣma), because at the time of departure (utkrānti) it is not perceived by one standing close by; and it is limited (paricchinna), on account of the scriptural statements (śruti) of departure, going forth, and returning (utkrānti-gati-āgati). Objection (nanu): But all-pervasiveness (vibhutva) too is recorded (samāmnāyate) of the prāṇa — in passages such as ‘Equal to a small fly, equal to a mosquito, equal to an elephant, equal to these three worlds, equal to all this’ (samaḥ pluṣiṇā samo maśakena samo nāgena sama ebhistribhirlokaiḥ samo'nena sarveṇa) (Bṛ. U. 1.3.22) and the like. To this it is replied: That all-pervasiveness is recorded only of the ādhidaivika (cosmic) prāṇa-self in its collective (samaṣṭi) and distributive (vyaṣṭi) aspects, namely Hiraṇyagarbha — not of the ādhyātmika (individual) prāṇa. Moreover, by the very statement of equality, ‘equal to a small fly’ etc., what is shown is precisely the limitedness (paricchedaḥ) of the prāṇa as residing in each living being. Hence there is no defect. ‖ 13 ‖
BS_C02_S04_V14: But (the prāṇas) have light (Agni) etc. as their presiding deities, because that is so taught. ‖ 14 ‖
BS_C02_S04_V14::block-0: Now, regarding those prāṇas already discussed: do they engage in their respective functions by their own might (svamahimnā), or do they engage as presided over by deities (devatādhiṣṭhitāḥ)? — this is now investigated. Here first the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) is reached: since each is endowed with the power for its own work, the prāṇas should function by their own might. Moreover, if the engagement of the prāṇas is admitted to be presided over by deities, then since the very deities that preside would become the experiencers (bhoktṛ), the experiencership of the embodied self (śārīra) would be lost. Hence, their engagement must be by their own might. — When this position has been arrived at, the established conclusion (siddhānta) is stated: ‘But (they have) light (jyotis = Agni) etc. as their presiding principle’. The word ‘tu’ (‘but’) sets aside the pūrvapakṣa. The complex of organs beginning with speech (vāgādi-karaṇa-jāta), presided over by the deities such as Agni and the rest who identify themselves with fire and so on, engages in its own work — this is asserted. The ground is now expounded: ‘because that is so taught’ (tadāmananāt). Thus they declare: ‘Agni, becoming speech, entered the mouth’ (agnirvāgbhūtvā mukhaṃ prāviśat) (Ai. U. 1.2.4) and so on. This becoming speech and entering the mouth on the part of Agni is spoken of by accepting his presidership as the deity-self; for setting aside the deity-relation, no special relation of Agni with speech or the mouth is observed. Likewise, ‘Vāyu, becoming prāṇa, entered the nostrils’ (vāyuḥ prāṇo bhūtvā nāsike prāviśat) (Ai. U. 1.2.4) and so on must be construed similarly. So too elsewhere, ‘Speech indeed is the fourth foot of Brahman; it shines and burns by Agni as light’ (vāgeva brahmaṇaścaturthaḥ pādaḥ so'gninā jyotiṣā bhāti ca tapati ca) (Chā. U. 3.18.3) — by such statements that speech etc. are illumined as Agni etc. as light, this same point is reinforced. And ‘He first transcended speech; when she was freed from death, she became Agni’ (sa vai vācameva prathamāmatyavahatsā yadā mṛtyumatyamucyata so'gnirabhavat) (Bṛ. U. 1.3.12) — by such statements declaring the attainment of the state of Agni etc. by speech etc., the same is illustrated. Everywhere too, the enumeration of speech etc. and Agni etc. follows in the order of adhyātma and adhidaivata, by precisely this proximity. In smṛti also: ‘The knowers of truth, the brāhmaṇas, declare speech to be the adhyātma; that which is to be spoken is the adhibhūta; and Agni there is the adhidaivata’ — by such statements the presidership of deities such as Agni over speech etc. is shown elaborately. As to what was said — that owing to the connection of each with the power for its own work, the prāṇas should function by their own might — that is not correct, since even capable instruments such as carts (śakaṭa) etc. are seen to function only when presided over by oxen etc. And both views being possible (ubhayathopapattau), it is decisively established by scripture (āgama) that the speech etc. are presided over by deities. ‖ 14 ‖
BS_C02_S04_V15: (The connection of the prāṇas is) with the one possessing prāṇa (i.e., the embodied soul), because of scripture. ‖ 15 ‖
BS_C02_S04_V15::block-0: (Leading bhāṣya:) Now, that which was urged — that the experiencership would devolve upon the deities who are the presiders, not upon the embodied self — that is now removed:
BS_C02_S04_V15::block-1: Even when there are deities presiding over the prāṇas, the connection of these prāṇas is, from scripture, understood to be only with the embodied self (śārīra), the master of the aggregate of effect-and-organs (kārya-karaṇa-saṅghāta-svāmin), the ‘possessor of prāṇa’ (prāṇavān). Thus the śruti: ‘Now, where this space is enveloped by the eye, there the puruṣa is of the eye; the eye is for the sake of seeing. Now, he who knows ‘let me smell this’ — he is the ātman; the nose is for the sake of smell.’ (atha yatraitadākāśamanuviṣaṇṇaṃ cakṣuḥ sa cākṣuṣaḥ puruṣo darśanāya cakṣuratha yo vededaṃ jighrāṇīti sa ātmā gandhāya ghrāṇam) (Chā. U. 8.12.4) — and statements of this kind make known the connection of the prāṇas with the embodied self alone. Moreover, since the presiding deities are many — one for each organ — the experiencership in this body cannot rest with them. For one alone — this embodied experiencer — is in this body the experiencer, as is understood from the possibility of pratisandhāna (recollective synthesis) and the like. ‖ 15 ‖
BS_C02_S04_V16: And on account of his (the embodied soul’s) permanence (with respect to the body’s experience). ‖ 16 ‖
BS_C02_S04_V16::block-0: And of that embodied self there is permanence (nityatva) as the experiencer in this body — because the touch of merit and demerit (puṇya-pāpa-upalepa) is possible for him, and the enjoyment of pleasure and pain (sukha-duḥkha-upabhoga) is possible for him — not for the deities. For they, abiding in the lordly supreme station (paramaiśvara pada), are not fit to attain experiencership in this lowly body. And the śruti is: ‘Only puṇya goes to him (the deity); pāpa indeed does not go to the gods’ (puṇyamevāmuṃ gacchati na ha vai devānpāpaṃ gacchati) (Bṛ. U. 1.5.20). And the connection of the prāṇas is permanent with the embodied self alone, since their following him is observed at the time of departure (utkrānti) etc. — from such śrutis as: ‘When he departs, the prāṇa departs after him; when the prāṇa departs, all the prāṇas depart after it’ (tamutkrāmantaṃ prāṇo'nūtkrāmati prāṇamanūtkrāmantaṃ sarve prāṇā anūtkrāmanti) (Bṛ. U. 4.4.2) and the like. Hence, even when there are deities controlling the organs (karaṇa-niyantṛ), the experiencership of the embodied self is not lost. For the deity belongs to the side of the organ (karaṇa-pakṣa), not to the side of the experiencer (bhoktṛ-pakṣa). ‖ 16 ‖
BS_C02_S04_V17: They (the eleven prāṇas) are sense-organs (indriyāṇi), because of being so designated, except for the chief one (śreṣṭha = mukhya-prāṇa). ‖ 17 ‖
BS_C02_S04_V17::block-0: The principal one (mukhya), and the other eleven prāṇas, have been enumerated. Now this further doubt arises: are the other prāṇas mere modal-functions (vṛtti-bhedāḥ) of the principal prāṇa itself, or are they distinct realities (tattvāntarāṇi)? What then is the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa)? — That the others are mere modes of the principal (mukhyasyaiva itare vṛtti-bhedāḥ). Why? From the śruti. For the śruti, after placing the principal and the other prāṇas in proximity, declares the others to be of the nature of the principal: ‘Come, indeed, all became its form’ (hantāsyaiva sarve rūpamasāmeti ta etasyaiva sarve rūpamabhavan) (Bṛ. U. 1.5.21). And from the use of the single word ‘prāṇa’ for them, oneness is concluded. Otherwise, the word ‘prāṇa’ would have multiple meanings, which is unjustifiable, or else it would be primary in one place and secondary (lākṣaṇika) in another. Hence, just as of the one prāṇa there are five modes — prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, samāna — so too the eleven beginning with speech are merely modes. — When this position has been arrived at, we say: speech etc., are realities distinct from prāṇa (tattvāntarāṇi vāgādīni prāṇāt). Why? On account of the difference of designation (vyapadeśa-bheda). What is this difference of designation? Of those prāṇas under discussion, leaving aside the chief (śreṣṭha), the remaining eleven are designated as ‘sense-organs’ (indriyāṇi); for in śruti such designation is found — ‘From this are born the prāṇa, the mind, and all the senses’ (etasmājjāyate prāṇo manaḥ sarvendriyāṇi ca) (Mu. U. 2.1.3) — in passages of this kind, prāṇa is designated separately and the indriyas are designated separately. Objection (nanu): Then the mind too, like prāṇa, would be excluded from being an indriya — since separate designation is seen in ‘the mind and all the senses’. True; yet in smṛti the mind is included as an indriya — under ‘the eleven indriyas’ — along with hearing etc. But for prāṇa, indriya-hood is not established either in śruti or in smṛti. And this difference of designation is intelligible only on the view that they are distinct realities (tattva-bheda-pakṣa). On the view of identity of essence (tattva-aikatva), it would be self-contradictory that the same one being prāṇa should both obtain and not obtain the designation of indriya. Hence, the others are distinct realities from the principal one. ‖ 17 ‖
BS_C02_S04_V18: Because of the scriptural mention of difference. ‖ 18 ‖
BS_C02_S04_V18::block-0: (Leading bhāṣya:) And why are they distinct realities? —
BS_C02_S04_V18::block-1: Prāṇa is heard of everywhere as differentiated from speech etc. — beginning with ‘To them they said to speech’ (te ha vācamūcuḥ) (Bṛ. U. 1.3.2), then introducing how speech etc. were vitiated by the demon-evil (asura-pāpma-vidhvasta), and after concluding the topic of speech etc., commencing afresh: ‘Now they said to this prāṇa located in the mouth’ (atha hememāsanyaṃ prāṇamūcuḥ) — there is a separate commencement for the principal prāṇa as the destroyer of demons (asura-vidhvaṃsin). Likewise: ‘He made the mind, speech, and prāṇa his own’ (mano vācaṃ prāṇaṃ tānyātmane'kuruta) — such ‘difference-śrutis’ (bheda-śruti) too should be cited. Hence too, the others are distinct realities from the principal. ‖ 18 ‖
BS_C02_S04_V19: And on account of dissimilarity (of properties). ‖ 19 ‖
BS_C02_S04_V19::block-0: (Leading bhāṣya:) And why are they distinct realities? —
BS_C02_S04_V19::block-1: There is dissimilarity (vailakṣaṇya) between the principal one and the others: while speech etc. are asleep, the principal alone keeps awake (jāgarti); and it alone is unattained by death (mṛtyunā anāptaḥ), while the others are attained by it; and by its abiding and departure alone the body is sustained or falls — not by the indriyas; and the cognising of objects (viṣayālocana) is by the indriyas, not by prāṇa. Such manifold differences of characteristic (lakṣaṇa-bheda) exist between prāṇa and the indriyas. Hence too is the establishment of their being distinct realities. As for what was said — that from the śruti ‘all became its form’ (te etasyaiva sarve rūpamabhavan) (Bṛ. U. 1.5.21) prāṇa itself is the indriyas — that is not correct, for there too, by considering what comes before and after (paurvāparyālocana), distinction is understood. Thus: ‘ ‘‘I shall speak indeed’’ — speech resolved’ (vadiṣyāmyevāhamiti vāgdadhre) (Bṛ. U. 1.5.21) — having so enumerated the indriyas beginning with speech, and ‘Death, becoming weariness, took possession of them ... therefore speech becomes weary’ (tāni mṛtyuḥ śramo bhūtvopayeme ... tasmācchrāmyatyeva vāk) — having declared the seizure of speech etc. by death in the form of weariness, then ‘But this one — the middle prāṇa — death did not reach’ (athememeva nāpnodyo'yaṃ madhyamaḥ prāṇaḥ) (Bṛ. U. 1.5.21) — separately enumerating the prāṇa as unconquered by death; and ‘He indeed is our chief’ (ayaṃ vai naḥ śreṣṭhaḥ) (Bṛ. U. 1.5.21) — affirming his eminence. Hence, without contradicting that, what is to be understood is that the obtaining of motion (parispanda) by speech etc. is dependent on prāṇa — and that is what is meant by speech etc. ‘becoming its form’ — but not identity (tādātmya). And from this very fact follows the establishment of the secondary (lākṣaṇika) usage of the word ‘prāṇa’ for the indriyas. So the śruti — ‘They all became its form; therefore these are designated by this name, ‘prāṇas’ ’ (te etasyaiva sarve rūpamabhavaṃstasmādeta etenākhyāyante prāṇāḥ) (Bṛ. U. 1.5.21) — shows the secondary application (lākṣaṇikī vṛtti) of the term ‘prāṇa’ (which has the principal prāṇa as its primary scope) to the indriyas. Hence the indriyas — speech etc. — are realities distinct from prāṇa. ‖ 19 ‖
BS_C02_S04_V20: But the construction of name and form (saṃjñā-mūrti-kḷpti) belongs to Him who makes (the elements) tripartite (tri-vṛt-kurvat), because of the (scriptural) teaching. ‖ 20 ‖
BS_C02_S04_V20::block-0: In the procedure of (creation as expounded in the chapter beginning) ‘Existent’ (sat-prakriyā), after expounding the creation of fire, water, and food (tejas-ap-anna), it is taught: ‘That deity reflected: ‘‘Come, let me, having entered into these three deities by means of this jīva-self (jīvenātmanā), unfold name and form (nāmarūpe vyākaravāṇi)’’ ’ (seyaṃ devataikṣata hantāhamimāstisro devatā anena jīvenātmanānupraviśya nāmarūpe vyākaravāṇīti) (Chā. U. 6.3.2). ‘ ‘‘Of these, let me make each one tripartite, tripartite’’ ’ (tāsāṃ trivṛtaṃ trivṛtamekaikāṃ karavāṇīti) (Chā. U. 6.3.3). Here arises a doubt: is this unfolding of name and form done by the jīva, or is it done by the Supreme Lord (parameśvara)? On this it is at first reached: this unfolding of name and form is done by the jīva alone (jīva-kartṛkam). Why? Because of the qualifying ‘by means of this jīva-self’ — just as in the world, in usages such as ‘Having entered the enemy’s army by means of a spy, let me defeat them’, although the defeat of the army is done by the spy, the king, by virtue of being the cause-agent (hetu-kartṛtva), superimposes the agency upon himself by using the first person — ‘let me defeat’; similarly, although the unfolding of name and form is done by the jīva, the deity, by virtue of being the cause-agent, superimposes the agency upon herself by using the first person — ‘let me unfold’. Moreover, in names like Dittha, Davittha etc. and in forms like pots, dishes etc., the unfolding-agency (vyākartṛtva) is observed only on the part of the jīva. Hence this unfolding of name and form is done by the jīva alone. — When this is reached, it is replied: ‘But the construction of name and form (saṃjñā-mūrti-kḷpti)…’. By the word ‘tu’ (‘but’) the (pūrvapakṣa) view is set aside. ‘Saṃjñā-mūrti-kḷpti’ means the unfolding of name and form (nāmarūpa-vyākriyā). ‘Of him who makes (them) tripartite’ (tri-vṛt-kurvataḥ) indicates the Supreme Lord, since in the act of tri-vṛt-karaṇa (rendering tripartite) His agency is mentioned without exception (nirapavāda-kartṛtva-nirdeśa). This construction of name (saṃjñā-kḷpti) and form (mūrti-kḷpti) — namely, ‘Agni, Āditya, Candramas, Vidyut’, and again in such things as kuśa, kāśa, palāśa etc., and in cattle, deer, men etc., differentiated according to species (pratyākṛti) and individual (prativyakti), in many ways — all this can be the doing only of the Supreme Lord, the maker of fire, water, and food. Why? On account of the (scriptural) teaching: thus, beginning with ‘That deity reflected’, by the use of the first person ‘let me unfold’ (vyākaravāṇi), the unfolding-agency is here taught of the supreme Brahman alone. Objection (nanu): From the qualifying ‘by means of the jīva’, the agency of the jīva in the unfolding has been concluded. — Not so. The phrase ‘by means of the jīva’ is connected with ‘having entered’ (anupraviśya), because of immediate proximity (ānantaryāt); not with ‘let me unfold’ (vyākaravāṇi) — for if so connected, this first person ‘let me unfold’ as referring to the deity would have to be construed metaphorically (aupacārika). Furthermore, in the manifold names and forms of mountains, rivers, oceans etc., the jīva who is not the Lord (anīśvara) has no capacity for unfolding. And even where he has capacity, even that is dependent on the Supreme Lord. And the jīva is not utterly different from the Supreme Lord — like a spy from the king — because of the qualifying word ‘ātmanā’ (as one’s own self), and because the jīva-state rests merely on adjuncts (upādhi-mātra-nibandhana). Hence even what is done by him is in truth done by the Supreme Lord. And it is the established conclusion (siddhānta) of all the upaniṣads that the Supreme Lord alone is the unfolder of name and form, on the strength of śrutis such as ‘ākāśa indeed, by name, is the unfolder of name and form’ (ākāśo vai nāma nāmarūpayornirvahitā) (Chā. U. 8.14.1). Hence, the unfolding of name and form is the act of the Supreme Lord, who renders (the elements) tripartite. The unfolding of name and form spoken of here is intended to be preceded by the tri-vṛt-karaṇa (rendering tripartite), since the unfolding of name and form for each (element) individually has already been stated by the very statements of the origination of fire, water, and food. And that tri-vṛt-karaṇa, the śruti shows, applies to fire, sun, moon, and lightning: ‘Whatever red form fire has, that is the form of fire (tejas); the white is of water; the black is of food’ (yadagne rohitaṃ rūpaṃ tejasastadrūpaṃ yacchuklaṃ tadapāṃ yatkṛṣṇaṃ tadannasya) (Chā. U. 6.4)… [bhāṣya truncated in source]
BS_C02_S04_V21: Flesh and the rest are of earthly origin, in accordance with the scriptural statement; and likewise of the other two (water and fire). (21)
BS_C02_S04_V21::block-0: Of those three deities (fire, water, earth), after they have been made tripartite externally, a further internal (adhyātma) tripartition has been declared — ‘These three deities, on reaching the puruṣa, each becomes tripartite, tripartite’ (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.4.7). That very (process) the ācārya now exhibits in conformity with the scriptural text, intending to remove a certain apprehended objection —
BS_C02_S04_V21::block-1: Of earth that has been made tripartite (trivṛt-kṛtā), when consumed by the puruṣa, the effect — flesh and so forth — is produced in accordance with the scriptural text. For thus says the śruti: ‘The food that is eaten is divided into three; its grossest constituent (sthaviṣṭho dhātuḥ) becomes faeces, the middle one becomes flesh, and the subtlest becomes mind’ (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.5.1). The intent is that it is precisely this trivṛt-kṛta earth that is consumed in the form of food such as rice, barley and the like. Of it, the grossest form goes outward as faeces; the middle, internally (adhyātmam), nourishes the flesh; and the subtlest becomes the mind. In the same way, of the other two — water and fire — the effects are to be understood in accordance with the scriptural text: urine, blood, and prāṇa are the effects of the waters; bone, marrow, and speech are of fire. (21)
BS_C02_S04_V22: But on account of preponderance, that designation; that designation. (22)
BS_C02_S04_V22::block-0: Here it is objected (pūrvapakṣa): If everything — every gross element and every elemental product — has been made tripartite, by reason of the undifferentiated scriptural statement, ‘He made each one of these tripartite, tripartite,’ then by what is occasioned this distinct designation — ‘this is fire, these are the waters, this is food (earth)’ — and likewise with respect to the body: ‘this — flesh and so on — is the effect of food eaten; this — blood and the rest — is the effect of waters drunk; this — bone and so on — is the effect of fire ingested’? To this it is replied (siddhānta) —
BS_C02_S04_V22::block-1: By the word ‘tu’ (but) he removes the objection raised. The state of being viśeṣa (predominant) is vaiśeṣya — that is, ‘being more abundant.’ Even though there is the trivṛt-karaṇa (tripartition), in some places a preponderance of one elemental constituent over another is observed — fire has a preponderance of fire (tejas), water of water (ap), earth of food (anna). And this trivṛt-karaṇa is for the sake of establishing common usage (vyavahāra). Common usage, when one-ness has come about — as in the case of a tripartite-twisted rope (trivṛt-kṛta-rajju) — could not, with respect to ordinary people, be established as having for its scope the three elements separately. Therefore, even with the trivṛt-karaṇa, the designation of fire (tejas), water (ap), and food (anna) as distinct, with reference to the gross elements and their products, is justified precisely by virtue of preponderance (vaiśeṣya). The repetition of the phrase ‘tadvādaḥ tadvādaḥ’ (‘that designation, that designation’) indicates the conclusion of the adhyāya. (22)
BS_C03_S01_INTRO1::block-0: In the second adhyāya, the conflict with smṛti and reasoning regarding the brahma-darśana taught in the Vedānta has been removed; the irrelevance of the rival schools has been demonstrated; and the seeming mutual contradiction of śruti texts has been resolved. There it has been stated that the principles other than the jīva — being instruments of the jīva — are born from Brahman. Now, in the third (adhyāya), the following themes will be examined: the manner of the saṃsāric movement of the jīva endowed with such instruments; the differing states it undergoes; the true nature of Brahman; the difference and non-difference among the (various) vidyās; the gathering and non-gathering of the (meditative) qualities; the attainment of the puruṣārtha through samyag-darśana; the diversity of injunctions concerning the means to samyag-darśana; the absence of restriction with regard to the fruit of liberation — and likewise any other matter that comes up incidentally. There, in the first pāda, taking up the pañcāgnividyā (doctrine of the five fires), the various courses of saṃsāra are exhibited for the sake of (engendering) dispassion (vairāgya) — for at the conclusion (of that vidyā) one hears, ‘Therefore one should feel disgust (with saṃsāra)’ (‘tasmāj-jugupseta’). It has been ascertained that the jīva, accompanied by the chief prāṇa (mukhya-prāṇa), endowed with the senses, possessed of mind, taking on the prajñā formed by previous avidyā and karma, leaves the previous body and assumes another body — this from the saṃsāra-prakaraṇa text beginning with ‘Then these prāṇas approach him’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.1) and ending with ‘He fashions another newer, fairer form’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.4); and from the very possibility of the experience of the fruits of dharma and adharma. The point under consideration (cintā) is: does he go un-enveloped by the subtle elements that are the seeds of the (next) body, or enveloped by them?
BS_C03_S01_INTRO1::block-1: Now, what (view) presents itself first (as pūrvapakṣa)? — That he goes un-enveloped. Why? Because there is no scriptural mention of the appropriation of the (gross) elements as there is of the appropriation of the senses. For (the text) ‘He, taking up these portions of light (tejomātrāḥ)’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.1) — here by the word ‘tejomātrāḥ’ celebrates the appropriation of the senses (karaṇas), since in the rest of the passage the eye and the others are mentioned. There is no such mention of the appropriation of portions of (gross) elements (bhūta-mātrāḥ). Moreover, portions of the (gross) elements are easy to obtain everywhere; wherever a body is to be initiated, there itself they are present. And therefore conveying them along would be without purpose. Hence (the jīva) goes un-enveloped (by them) — when this (pūrvapakṣa) is reached, the ācārya states (the siddhānta) —
BS_C03_S01_V01: On the attainment of another (body), (the soul) goes enveloped (by subtle elements), as is known from the question and the answer. (1)
BS_C03_S01_V01::block-0: ‘On the attainment of another (body), it goes enveloped.’ ‘Tad-antara-pratipattau’ — at the time of attaining another body, ‘sam-pariṣvaktaḥ’ — enveloped by the subtle elements that are the seeds of the body, ‘raṃhati’ — goes; thus is to be understood. Whence? From the question and from the answer (praśna-nirūpaṇābhyām). For thus the question: ‘Do you know how, at the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called ‘puruṣa’?’ (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.3.3). And the determination is the answer (prati-vacana), wherein, having shown five oblations — having the forms of śraddhā, soma, rain, food, and semen — in the five fires, viz., heaven, the rain-cloud, earth, man, and woman, (it concludes,) ‘Thus indeed at the fifth oblation the waters come to be called ‘puruṣa’ (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.9.1). Therefore it is understood that the jīva, surrounded by waters, ‘raṃhati’ — goes. But surely another śruti shows that, like a leech, (the jīva) does not give up the previous body until it has set foot upon another body — ‘Just as a leech (tṛṇa-jalāyukā)’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.3). Even there, what is being compared by the leech-simile is only the prolonged duration of the bhāvanā (ideation) directed toward the body-to-be-attained — that body which is presented by karma — for the jīva who is (already) enveloped by the waters; thus there is no contradiction. The manner of attaining another body being thus stated by śruti, those imaginings which arise from human cognition — namely: (i) that the senses (karaṇas) and the ātman are all-pervading, and merely a renewal of their function (vṛtti-lābha) takes place there at the attainment of another body, by force of karma; (ii) that of the ātman alone the renewal of function takes place there; (iii) that the senses, like the body, are produced afresh in each successive seat of experience; (iv) that the mind alone, by itself, takes hold of the seat of experience; (v) that the jīva alone, springing forth, attains another body from a body, like a parrot from tree to tree — all such (notions) are not to be entertained, since they conflict with śruti. (1)
BS_C03_S01_V02: But (it goes enveloped by all elements) on account of (the body's) being constituted of three elements, on account of preponderance. (2)
BS_C03_S01_V02::block-0: But (an objection): from the cited question and answer, what is obtained is that he goes enveloped only by waters alone, by force of the scriptural mention of the word ‘āpaḥ’ (waters). How then is it concluded in general that he goes enveloped by all the subtle elements? In reply to this he states the following —
BS_C03_S01_V02::block-1: By the word ‘tu’ (but) he removes the apprehension that has been raised. The waters are tri-constitutive (try-ātmikā) — by the śruti of trivṛt-karaṇa. When these are accepted as initiating (the body), the other two elements also must necessarily be accepted. The body too is tri-constitutive (try-ātmaka), since the effects of all three — fire, water, and earth — are observed in it. Again it is tri-constitutive in being three-humoured (tri-dhātu) — having the three (humours), wind, bile, and phlegm. It cannot be initiated by waters alone, rejecting the other elements. Therefore in the question and answer ‘the waters come to be called puruṣa,’ the word ‘āpaḥ’ has reference to preponderance (bhūyastva), not to exclusiveness (kaivalya). For in all bodies a preponderance of fluid substances such as the chyle, blood, and the like is observed. — But surely the earthen constituent is observed to be most abundant in bodies. — This is no fault: in comparison with the others, the waters will be more abundant. Even in the body-seed, namely semen and blood, abundance of fluid is observed. And karma is the efficient cause (nimitta-kāraṇa) in the initiation of another body; and the karmas, agnihotra and the like, depend upon fluid substances such as soma, ghee, milk, and so on. And the waters intimately connected with karma, designated by the word ‘śraddhā’, will be said to be offered along with the karmas in the fire called dyu-loka. Hence too the well-known abundance of waters. By reason of (this) abundance, the appropriation of all the subtle elements that are the seeds of the body, by the word ‘āpaḥ,’ is unobjectionable. (2)
BS_C03_S01_V03: And on account of the going of the prāṇas. (3)
BS_C03_S01_V03::block-0: Of the prāṇas also, going forth at the attainment of another body is heard about — by such śrutis as ‘When he departs, prāṇa departs after him; when prāṇa departs, all the prāṇas depart after it’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2). And the going of the prāṇas is not possible without a substratum (āśraya); hence, occasioned by the going of the prāṇas, the going also of the waters which are their substratum, attended by the other elements, is to be inferred. For the prāṇas without a substratum do not go anywhere, nor do they remain (anywhere) — as is observed in the case of the living. (3)
BS_C03_S01_V04: If it be said (that they do not go) on account of the scriptural statement of the going of (vāk and the rest) into agni and the rest, (we say) no, on account of (its being) figurative. (4)
BS_C03_S01_V04::block-0: Be it so (says the pūrvapakṣin) — the prāṇas do not at all go along with the jīva at the attainment of another body, on account of the scripture of (their) going to fire and the rest. For thus the śruti shows that the prāṇas vāk and the rest, at the time of death, go to the deities agni and the rest — ‘When this person dies, his speech enters into fire, his prāṇa into wind’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.2.13) etc. — If this be said, (the answer is) no, on account of (its being) figurative (bhāktatva). The śruti about vāk and the rest going to agni and the rest is secondary (gauṇī) — because (the going) is not observed in the case of the body-hairs (loma) and the head-hairs (keśa). For there it is recited, ‘the herbs are the body-hairs, the trees the head-hairs’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.2.13); but it is not possible that body-hairs and head-hairs spring forth and go to herbs and trees. Nor can the going of the jīva be accounted for if the prāṇa-upādhi is rejected. Nor again is enjoyment in another body intelligible without the prāṇas. The going of the prāṇas along with the jīva has been clearly stated elsewhere by śruti. Therefore, with reference to the cessation, at the time of death, of the helping (function) of the deities — agni and the rest — who preside over and assist vāk and the rest, it is figuratively (upacaryate) said that vāk and the rest go to agni and the rest. (4)
BS_C03_S01_V05: If it be said that (the waters are not mentioned) in the first (fire), (we reply) no, for those very (waters) are referred to (by ‘śraddhā’), on account of intelligibility. (5)
BS_C03_S01_V05::block-0: Be it so (the pūrvapakṣin objects) — how then can it be ascertained that ‘at the fifth oblation the waters come to be called puruṣa’ (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.3.3), seeing that in the first fire there is no scriptural mention at all of waters? For here five fires beginning with dyu-loka are taught as the receptacles of the five oblations. And at the head of these, having posited ‘That world (heaven) verily is the fire, O Gautama’ (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.4.1), it is declared, ‘In this fire the gods offer śraddhā’ (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.4.2) — śraddhā is taught as the substance to be offered (homya-dravya). The waters are not there mentioned as the homya-dravya. Even granting that in the latter four fires beginning with parjanya, the homya-dravya-status of waters might be supposed — let it be supposed, since the soma and the rest, taken as oblations there, may be of large water-content — yet it is rash to abandon the śraddhā that is heard of in the first fire and imagine waters that are not heard of. ‘Śraddhā’ moreover is the name of a particular cognition (pratyaya-viśeṣa), by force of established usage. Therefore, the puruṣa-hood of the waters at the fifth oblation is not justified — if this be said, no, this is no defect. For there too, in the first fire, those very waters are intended by the word ‘śraddhā.’ Whence? On account of intelligibility (upapatti). For thus, by harmonization of beginning, middle, and end, this single sentence stands without confusion. Otherwise, on the question being asked about the manner of the waters becoming puruṣa at the fifth oblation, if at the time of the answer, in the place of the first oblation, one were to introduce, in place of the homya-dravya which is not waters, a thing called ‘śraddhā,’ then the question would be of one kind and the answer of another, and there would be no unity of statement. And concluding with ‘Thus indeed at the fifth oblation the waters come to be called puruṣa,’ (the text) shows precisely this. The effect of śraddhā — soma, rain, and so forth — is observed to be a thickening (mass) abundant in waters; and that is the ground (yukti) for śraddhā being water. For the effect is in conformity with the cause. Nor can the cognition called śraddhā, which is a property of the mind or the jīva, be extracted from the substrate (dharmin) and taken as the offering — as the heart and the rest can be (extracted) from animals and so forth. Hence the very waters must be (here) the meanings of the word ‘śraddhā.’ The word ‘śraddhā’ does fit the waters, by the observation of Vedic usage — ‘śraddhā are verily the waters.’ Because the waters going forth as body-seeds attain subtlety, a likeness to śraddhā, they are designated by the word śraddhā — just as a man of lion-like prowess is designated by the word ‘siṃha’ (lion). And on account of (their) inhering in (or accompanying) actions preceded by śraddhā, the word śraddhā is fit for waters — like the word ‘mañca’ (platform) for the people (sitting on it). And on account of (their) being the cause of (the rise of) śraddhā, the word ‘śraddhā’ is justified, by the śruti ‘The waters bend his śraddhā toward holy karma.’ (5)
BS_C03_S01_V06: ‘If [the objection be raised] that [the souls' going] is not heard of (aśrutatva), [we reply] no, because of the cognition (pratīti) of those who perform iṣṭa-pūrta and the like.’ (6)
BS_C03_S01_V06::block-0: [Pūrvapakṣa]: It might still be urged — by the question and answer (praśna-prativacana), it is the waters that, through the sequence beginning with śraddhā, attain a human form in the fifth oblation; but the jīvas enveloped (samparisvakta) by them do not travel (raṃheyuḥ), because that is not heard of (aśrutatva); for here there is no scriptural utterance (śabda) which makes the jīvas heard of, as there is in the case of the waters. Therefore the statement ‘he travels enveloped (raṃhati samparisvaktaḥ)’ is unfounded — if such be the objection, [Siddhāntin replies:] this is no fault. Why? ‘Because of the cognition of those who perform iṣṭa-pūrta and the like.’ Beginning with ‘Now those who in the village practise sacrifices, public works, and gifts, as a means of worship — they go to the smoke’ (Chā. Up. 5.10.3) (citation), [the śruti] narrates the attainment of the moon by the performers of iṣṭa-pūrta etc. via the path of the fathers (pitṛyāṇa) marked by smoke and the rest, [saying] ‘from ākāśa [they go] to the moon — that is Soma the king’ (Chā. Up. 5.10.4) (citation). Those very same [persons] are cognised here too, by the parity of śruti seen in ‘In that fire the gods offer śraddhā; out of that oblation Soma the king arises’ (Chā. Up. 5.4.2) (citation). And of these [performers] the curd, milk and the rest — being the means (sādhana) of agnihotra, darśa-pūrṇamāsa and other rites — are, by reason of being predominantly liquid, perceptibly waters. These, when offered into the āhavanīya, become subtle, oblation-formed (āhuti-rūpa), and assume the apūrva-rūpa (the unseen efficacy-form); they take refuge in those iṣṭa-doers. And of these [performers] the body, in the final fire, is offered by the ṛtviks according to the rite ordained for death (naidhana-vidhāna) — ‘Hail (svāhā) to that for the heavenly world.’ Thereupon those waters, conjoined with the rite preceded by śraddhā, oblation-formed and bearing the apūrva-rūpa, envelop those iṣṭa-doing jīvas and lead them to that [other] world for the bestowal of fruit. This is what is here designated by the verb juhoti — ‘they offer śraddhā’ (Bṛ. Up. 6.2.9) (citation). And likewise in the agnihotra, by the supplementary passage in the form of the explanation of the six questions (ṣaṭ-praśnī-nirvacana) — ‘these two oblations, when offered, ascend’ (citation) and so forth — the attainment of another world for the inception of the fruit of the agnihotra-oblations is shown. Therefore it stands fitting (śliṣyate): the jīvas, enveloped by oblation-formed waters, travel for the experience of the fruit of their own karma. (6)
BS_C03_S01_V07: ‘But [the term ‘food’] is figurative (bhākta), because of [their] not being knowers of the Self; for [śruti] shows it thus.’ (7)
BS_C03_S01_V07::block-0: [Pūrvapakṣa, leading bhāṣya]: But how is this travelling of the iṣṭa-doers asserted to be ‘for the experience of the fruit of one's own karma’, when, having ascended to the moon by the path marked by smoke, [śruti] shows their being food (anna-bhāva) — ‘That is Soma the king; that is the food of the gods; the gods eat him’ (Chā. Up. 5.10.4) (citation)? And another śruti having the same import: ‘On reaching the moon they become food; there the gods eat them, as one says to Soma the king, “Wax, wane!”’ (Bṛ. Up. 6.2.16) (citation). And just as those eaten by tigers and the like cannot have any enjoyment, [so it cannot be here]. To this objection [the Sūtrakāra] reads the answer —
BS_C03_S01_V07::block-1: [Siddhānta]: The word ‘vā’ (‘but/or’) serves to ward off the objection just raised. Their being ‘food’ is figurative (bhākta), not primary (mukhya). For if their being food were taken in the primary sense, the adhikāra-śruti of the kind ‘he who desires heaven should sacrifice (svarga-kāmo yajeta)’ would be obstructed. And if in the moon-orb (candra-maṇḍala) there were no enjoyment for the iṣṭa-doers, why should the qualified (adhikārin) perform the iṣṭa rites that involve great toil? Moreover, the word ‘food’ (anna), by its general property of being a cause of enjoyment (upabhoga-hetu), is seen used figuratively even of what is not literally food — as in ‘the people are food of kings, cattle are food of the people.’ Therefore, just as the joyful sport which the gods derive from beloved wives, sons, friends, servants and the like — [all these] standing in a subordinate position (guṇa-bhāva) — is itself their ‘eating’, so too [is it here]: it is not chewing or swallowing as in the case of sweetmeats. ‘The gods, indeed, neither eat nor drink; merely beholding this nectar (amṛta) they are satisfied’ (Chā. Up. 3.6.1) (citation) — this also wards off any chewing-and-similar activity on the part of the gods. And although the iṣṭa-doers stand in a subordinate position to the gods, an enjoyment is for them quite tenable — like the dependents (parijana) of those who live off the king. And ‘because of [their] not being knowers of the Self’, the iṣṭa-doers' condition of being objects of enjoyment to the gods is established. For thus śruti indicates the enjoyability by gods of those who do not know the Self: ‘Now whoever worships another deity [thinking] “he is one and I am another” does not know; he is like a [domestic] beast (paśu) for the gods’ (Bṛ. Up. 1.4.10) (citation).
