Such a one, here in this world too, by gladdening the gods through iṣṭa-pūrta and other rites, is helpful to them like a beast; and in that other world too, living off them and enjoying the fruit assigned by them, he is helpful to them just like a beast — so it is gathered.
BS_C03_S01_V07::block-2: [Alternative explanation by the same Bhāṣyakāra]: Another exposition of ‘because of [their] not being knowers of the Self; for it shows thus’ — these iṣṭa-doers are non-knowers of the Self; they are mere ritualists (kevala-karmin), not practitioners of the conjunction of jñāna and karma (jñāna-karma-samuccaya-anuṣṭhāyin). The pañcāgni-vidyā is here, by the context, designated as ‘ātma-vidyā’. And it is on account of these iṣṭa-doers' lack of pañcāgni-vidyā that their condition of being food is set forth in a figurative sense (guṇa-vāda) for the praise of pañcāgni-vijñāna. For pañcāgni-vidyā is what is here intended to be enjoined, as is gathered from the import (tātparya) of the passage. And another śruti also shows the existence of enjoyment in the moon-orb: ‘Having experienced eminence (vibhūti) in the world of Soma, he returns again’ (Pra. Up. 5.4) (citation). And yet another śruti: ‘Now there are a hundred joys of the conquered-world fathers… one of these is the joy of the karma-devas, who through karma attain godhood’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.33) (citation) — this shows the attainment of enjoyment by iṣṭa-doers dwelling together with the gods. Thus, since the statement of their being food is figurative (bhākta), it is grasped that here it is the iṣṭa-doer jīvas that travel. Therefore ‘he travels enveloped (raṃhati samparisvaktaḥ)’ stands fittingly stated. (7)
BS_C03_S01_V08: ‘At the exhaustion (kṛta-atyaya) [of the karma], [he descends] possessed of a residue (anuśayavān), [as is known] from perception (dṛṣṭa) and from smṛti, by the same path as he came (yathetam) and not by the same (anevam ca).’ (8)
BS_C03_S01_V08::block-0: [Pūrvapakṣa established as prima facie view]: For the iṣṭa-doers who have ascended to the moon-orb by the path marked by smoke, having experienced their enjoyment, the descent (pratyavaroha) from there is recited — beginning with ‘Having dwelt there as long as their saṃpāta lasts, they return again by that very path, as they came’ (Chā. Up. 5.10.5) (citation), [and continuing] up to: ‘those of pleasant conduct (ramaṇīya-caraṇa) attain the womb of a brāhmaṇa or the like; those of foul conduct (kapūya-caraṇa) attain the womb of a dog and the like.’ The matter to be examined here is: do they descend devoid of any residue (niranuśaya), having exhausted all their karma; or with a residue (sānuśaya)? What, then, is the prima facie view? That they descend devoid of residue. Why? On account of the qualifier ‘yāvat-saṃpātam’ — by the word ‘saṃpāta’ here is meant the karmāśaya (the stock of karma), since by it they fly together (saṃpatanti) from this world to that for the experience of fruit. ‘Yāvat-saṃpātam uṣitvā’ (‘having dwelt as long as the saṃpāta lasts’) shows that all of that [karma] which had been performed has been enjoyed there itself. The same import is shown by another śruti: ‘When for them that [karma] is fully exhausted (paryavaiti)’ (Bṛ. Up. 6.2.16) (citation). It might be supposed: ‘I shall posit that one consumes only as much karma as is to be experienced in that world.’ It is impossible to posit thus, for elsewhere there is the [unrestricted] reference ‘yat kiṃca’ (whatever): ‘Having reached the end of his karma — whatever he does here, from that world he comes again to this world for [further] karma’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.6) (citation) — this further śruti, by the unqualified reference ‘yat kiṃca’, shows the exhaustion there of all the karma performed here. Moreover, departure (prāyaṇa) is the manifester (abhivyañjaka) of all karma whose fruit has not yet begun (anārabdha-phala); for, prior to departure, there cannot be the manifestation of [karma] obstructed by another karma whose fruit has begun (ārabdha-phala). And that [departure], by lack of distinction, is the manifester of whatever has not yet started its fruit. For, when the cause is common, the effect cannot be uncommon: it is unintelligible that, when the lamp is equally near, the pot should be manifested but not the cloth. Therefore [it is concluded that] they descend without residue. Such being the prima facie position, we say —
BS_C03_S01_V08::block-1: [Siddhānta]: ‘At the exhaustion [of karma], [he is] possessed of a residue.’ With the bundle of karmas (karma-bṛnda) by which they ascended to the moon for the experience of fruit, when that is exhausted by enjoyment — that watery body (ammaya śarīra) of theirs, which had been formed in the moon for the sake of enjoyment, dissolves (pravilīyate) by contact with the fire of grief at seeing the exhaustion of enjoyment, just as snow-stones (himakaraka) [melt] by contact with the sun's rays, and the solidity of ghee by contact with the flame of fire. Then, ‘at kṛta-atyaya’ — i.e., when by the experience of fruit there is the exhaustion of the karma performed (the iṣṭa and the rest) — they descend to this [world] only as ‘sānuśaya’ (with a residue). By what reason? He says: ‘from dṛṣṭa and smṛti.’ For thus the directly perceived śruti shows the descent of those with residue: ‘And there those of pleasant conduct here — they have a likely prospect of attaining a pleasant womb, the womb of a brāhmaṇa, kṣatriya, or vaiśya; whereas those of foul conduct — they have a likely prospect of attaining a foul womb, the womb of a dog, a hog, or a caṇḍāla’ (Chā. Up. 5.10.7) (citation). That by the word ‘caraṇa’ here the anuśaya is indicated will be expounded [later]. And what is perceived (dṛṣṭa) — the high-and-low forms of enjoyment apportioned to each living being from birth itself, since their being haphazard is impossible — points to the existence of anuśaya, since the śāstra has established in general that abhyudaya and pratyavāya have sukṛta and duṣkṛta as their causes. Smṛti also shows the descent of only those with residue: ‘The varṇas and āśramas, established in their own duties, having departed and experienced the fruit of their karma, then by the residue (śeṣa) attain birth distinguished by region, jāti, family, form, lifespan, learning, conduct, wealth, happiness, and intelligence’ (Gau. Dh. Sū. 2.2.29) (citation).
BS_C03_S01_V08::block-2: [On the nature of anuśaya — Pūrvapakṣa view of ‘some’ thinkers]: But what, again, is this anuśaya? Some, indeed, say: a remnant (avaśeṣa) of the karma whose fruit (heaven) has been enjoyed — that is anuśaya, like the oil clinging to the vessel (bhāṇḍa-anusāri-sneha). Just as a vessel of oil being emptied is not emptied entirely — some residue of oil clinging to the vessel still remains — so too is anuśaya. [Objection]: But for an adṛṣṭa (unseen result of karma) whose fruit has been enjoyed, a remnant's persistence is not reasonable, being contrary to its having borne effect (kārya-virodhitva). [Reply]: This is no fault. For we do not assert that the karma has borne fruit completely (sarvātmanā). [Objection]: But they ascended to the moon-orb for the consumption of the entire fruit of the karma, [did they not]? [Reply]: Granted; but even so, with a mere small residue of karma it is impossible to remain there. Just as some servant who has approached the king's court with all the paraphernalia of service, after long sojourn, when his ample means are spent and he is left with only an umbrella, sandals and so on, can no longer dwell in the king's court — even so, one taking up residence with only the residue cannot remain in the moon-orb.
BS_C03_S01_V08::block-3: [Refutation of this view, and statement of correct view]: But this is not seemly. For the persistence of a remnant of the karma whose fruit (heaven) has been enjoyed is not tenable, on account of contradiction with its having borne effect (kārya-virodhitva) — as already stated. [Objection]: But it has been said too — the entire karma whose fruit is heaven will not have its fruit fully enjoyed. [Reply]: That is unsubtle. The notion that the karma which is for heaven's sake produces the entire heaven-fruit only for one in heaven, and even after he falls from heaven produces some little fragment of fruit — for those whose pramāṇa is the word [of śruti], such a hypothesis is not admissible. In the case of the oil-vessel, the persistence of an oil-remnant is intelligible because directly observed; and the persistence of a fragment of paraphernalia for the servant is also seen. But here no such persistence of a fragment of the heaven-fruit-yielding karma is seen, nor can it be hypothesised, for it would contradict the śāstra fixing it as having heaven for its fruit. Indeed it must be known thus: the anuśaya is not the fragment of the iṣṭa-and-the-rest karma (which has heaven for its fruit) persisting like the oil clinging to the vessel. For if the very sukṛta-karma — iṣṭa etc. — by which they enjoyed heaven were posited as having some fragment which is the anuśaya, then the anuśaya would be wholly pleasant (ramaṇīya), never adverse. The śruti dividing anuśaya — ‘there those of pleasant conduct here… now those of foul conduct here…’ (Chā. Up. 5.10.7) (citation) — would thereby be obstructed. Therefore the anuśaya is the karma of another sort, the bearer of a this-worldly fruit (aihika-phala), which remains over after the experience of the karma-aggregate that bore the other-worldly fruit (āmuṣmika-phala). Possessed of that, they descend.
BS_C03_S01_V08::block-4: [Refutation of pūrvapakṣa's remaining arguments]: As for what was said — that on account of the unrestricted reference ‘yat kiṃca’, they descend without residue, having reached the end of all the karma performed here by enjoyment of the fruit — this is not so. Since the existence of anuśaya is established, what is to be understood is: ‘whatever karma performed here yielding other-worldly fruit had begun its enjoyment, all that they consume by enjoyment of the fruit.’ As for what was further said — that departure (prāyaṇa), by lack of distinction, manifests every karma whose fruit has not yet begun, and that therefore the division ‘by some karma fruit is begun in that world, by some in this’ is impossible — that too is rebutted by the very establishment of anuśaya. Moreover, by what reason is departure declared to be the manifester of karma whose fruit has not yet begun? It must be stated. If it be said that, since the rising-up of activity (vṛtti-udbhava) of one karma is impossible while it is obstructed by another karma whose fruit has begun, the rising-up of activity comes about at the time of departure due to the cessation of that obstructer — then it must be stated thus: just as, prior to departure, the rising-up of activity of one karma is impossible while it is obstructed by another whose fruit has begun, even so, at the time of departure too — since manifold karmas with mutually contrary fruits cannot simultaneously start their fruits — the rising-up of activity of the weaker, obstructed by the stronger, is impossible. For one cannot say that, by the mere generic feature of having unbegun fruit, manifold karmas — even those whose fruits are to be enjoyed in another jāti — being simultaneously manifested in a single departure, give rise to one [single] jāti, since this contradicts their having a determinate fruit (pratiniyata-phalatva). Nor can one say that, of some karma there is manifestation at departure and of some there is uccheda (annihilation), since this contradicts their having an inevitable fruit (aikāntika-phalatva). For without causes such as prāyaścitta and the like, the annihilation (uccheda) of karmas is not conceivable. Smṛti also shows that another karma, when obstructed by a karma of contrary fruit, remains for long: ‘Sometimes a sukṛta karma stays here as if fixed (kūṭa-stham), while [the soul] is sinking in saṃsāra, until he is freed from sorrow’ (Mahābhārata 12.290.18) (citation), and the like. And if all karma of unbegun fruit, manifested in a single departure, were to start a single jāti, then — there being no adhikāra in the wombs of heaven, hell, and the animal kingdom, and no arising of dharma or adharma there — there would be no occasion for a subsequent jāti, since the cause [of further karma] would be absent; and the smṛti-teaching that a single karma like brahma-hatyā is the cause of many births would be obstructed. Nor can any cause beyond śāstra be conceived for the cognition of the nature, fruit, and means of dharma and adharma. Nor can departure be the manifester of a karma whose fruit is seen [in this very life], such as kārīrī etc. — therefore this hypothesis of departure being the manifester is also non-pervasive (avyāpaka). The illustration of the lamp too is set aside merely by indicating the strong-and-weak [relation] of karmas. And it is to be regarded as analogous to the manifestation and non-manifestation of gross and subtle forms: just as a lamp, even with equal proximity, manifests gross form but not subtle, even so departure, even when there is equality regarding the having-attained-occasion of the karma-aggregate of unbegun fruit, brings forth the activity of the strong karma and not of the weak. Therefore, by contradiction with śruti, smṛti and reasoning (nyāya), this assumption of the manifestation of all karma is incoherent. As for ‘if there be a residue of karma there will be the contingency of non-liberation’ — this too is needless agitation, since śruti declares the destruction of all karma upon samyag-darśana. Therefore this stands established: they descend possessed of residue (anuśayavantaḥ). And these descending ones descend ‘by the same path as they came’ (yathetam) and ‘not by the same’ (anevam). ‘Yathetam’ means ‘by the path by which they had gone’. ‘Anevam’ means ‘not in that very [same] manner’ [— here the bhāṣya text is truncated].
BS_C03_S01_V09: ‘[Pūrvapakṣin]: “If [the rebirth be said to be] from caraṇa (conduct), [we say] no, [for the term caraṇa is] meant for upalakṣaṇa (indication of anuśaya)” — so [holds] Kārṣṇājini.’ (9)
BS_C03_S01_V09::block-0: [Pūrvapakṣa]: It might still be urged — that śruti which was cited for the establishment of anuśaya, ‘And there those of pleasant conduct here’ (Chā. Up. 5.10.7) (citation), in fact shows the attainment of a womb from caraṇa (conduct), not from anuśaya. ‘Caraṇa’ and ‘anuśaya’ are different things — caraṇa is cāritra, ācāra, śīla (conduct, character, disposition), these being non-different terms; while anuśaya is intended to mean a karma over and above the karma whose fruit is enjoyed. And śruti speaks distinguishingly of karma and caraṇa: ‘As one acts, as one conducts, so one becomes’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.5) (citation), and ‘Such karmas as are not blamable, those should be performed; not the others. Such of our actions as are well-conducted (sucarita), those are to be revered by you’ (Tai. Up. 1.11.2) (citation). Therefore, since the śruti speaks of the attainment of a womb from caraṇa, the establishment of anuśaya is not [thereby] proved. — If such be the objection, [Siddhāntin replies]: this is no fault. For this caraṇa-śruti is meant only as an upalakṣaṇa (indication) of anuśaya — so does the ācārya Kārṣṇājini hold. (9)
BS_C03_S01_V10: ‘[Pūrvapakṣin]: “[That would entail] purposelessness (ānarthakya) [of caraṇa].” [We say] no, on account of [karma] depending upon that [caraṇa].’ (10)
BS_C03_S01_V10::block-0: [Pūrvapakṣa]: It might still be — why, then, should the śruti-given śīla be set aside and the figurative (lākṣaṇika) anuśaya be conveyed by the word caraṇa? Indeed, the very śruti-given śīla, being enjoined or prohibited and of good or bad character, will produce as its fruit the attainment of an auspicious or inauspicious womb. And some fruit of śīla too must necessarily be admitted; otherwise mere purposelessness (ānarthakya) of śīla would be entailed. — If such be the objection, [Siddhāntin replies]: this is no fault. Why? On account of [karma's] depending on that [caraṇa]. For the iṣṭa-and-the-rest karma-aggregate depends on caraṇa. No one bereft of good conduct (sad-ācāra) is qualified [for sacrifice] — by smṛtis like ‘the Vedas do not purify one bereft of conduct (ācāra-hīnaṃ na punanti vedāḥ)’ (citation). Even when conduct is itself a puruṣārtha, it is not purposeless. For when the iṣṭa-and-the-rest karma-aggregate is producing fruit, conduct, depending on it, will produce there itself some excellence (atiśaya). And ‘karma achieves all ends’ — so is the established teaching of śruti and smṛti. Therefore karma alone, indicated by śīla and constituting the anuśaya, is the cause in the attainment of a womb — such is the view of Kārṣṇājini. For when karma is available, the womb-attainment from śīla is not reasonable. One who is able to flee on his feet does not need to travel on his knees — so [the saying]. (10)
BS_C03_S01_V11: ‘But [the words ‘rāmaṇīya-caraṇa’ etc. mean] sukṛta and duṣkṛta themselves — so [holds] Bādari.’ (11)
BS_C03_S01_V11::block-0: [Bādari's view]: But the ācārya Bādari holds that by the word caraṇa, sukṛta and duṣkṛta themselves are conveyed. ‘Caraṇa’, ‘anuṣṭhāna’, and ‘karma’ are non-different terms (anarthāntara). For the verb ‘carati’ is seen used without distinction with regard to karma in general — one who performs the meritorious karma characterised as iṣṭa and the rest, of him laymen say ‘this great soul practises (carati) dharma.’ Even ācāra is just dharma-viśeṣa (a particular form of dharma). The differential reference to karma and caraṇa is intelligible by the analogy of brāhmaṇa-parivrājaka (where ‘parivrājaka’, though already a brāhmaṇa, is distinguished). Therefore the conclusion is: ramaṇīya-caraṇāḥ are those of praiseworthy karmas (praśasta-karman); kapūya-caraṇāḥ are those of blamable karmas (nindita-karman). (11)
BS_C03_S01_V12: ‘And [the going to the moon] is heard [in śruti] also of those who do not perform iṣṭa and the like.’ (12)
BS_C03_S01_V12::block-0: [Pūrvapakṣa here]: It has been said that the iṣṭa-doers go to the moon. As to the others — those who do not perform iṣṭa and the like — it is now examined whether they too go to the moon or do not go. There they say: that ‘only iṣṭa-doers go to the moon’ — that is not so. Why? Because the going to the moon-orb is heard [in śruti] of those also who do not perform iṣṭa and the like. For the Kauṣītakins recite without distinction: ‘Whosoever indeed depart from this world, all of them go to the moon’ (Kau. Up. 1.2) (citation). And the inception of a body for those being reborn is impossible without the attainment of the moon, by the rule of the count of oblations stated in ‘in the fifth oblation’. Therefore all should reach the moon. — If it be objected that it is not proper to give the iṣṭa-doers and the others the same path — [we reply] no, since for the others there is no enjoyment in the moon-orb. (12)
BS_C03_S01_V13: ‘But in the saṃyamana (Yama's realm) [the others] experience [their fruit]; the ascent and descent of the others [is otherwise], because of the recital of their going [there in śruti].’ (13)
BS_C03_S01_V13::block-0: [Siddhānta]: The word ‘tu’ (‘but’) wards off the [pūrvapakṣa] alternative. This is not so — that all go to the moon. Why? Because the ascent to the moon is for the sake of enjoyment (bhoga), not purposeless (niṣprayojana); nor is it merely for the sake of descent — just as one who climbs a tree does so for the gathering of flowers and fruits, not purposelessly nor merely to fall. And it has been said that for the non-iṣṭa-doers there is no enjoyment in the moon. Therefore the iṣṭa-doers alone ascend to the moon, not the others. The others, descending into the saṃyamana — Yama's realm (yamālaya) — and experiencing the Yāmī sufferings (yātanā) corresponding to their own duṣkṛta, again descend to this world. Such are their ascent and descent. Why? ‘Tad-gati-darśanāt’ — because the going thither is shown. For thus a śruti, in the very form of a Yama-utterance (yama-vacana-sa-rūpā), shows the bondage to Yama (yama-vaśyatā) for the deceased non-iṣṭa-doers: ‘To the immature (bāla), revelling, deluded by the infatuation of wealth, no other-world (sāmparāya) appears. “This world is, no other” — so deeming, again and again he comes under my sway’ (Ka. Up. 1.2.6) (citation). And there is much such evidence indicating attainment of subjugation to Yama, like ‘the son of Vivasvat (vaivasvatam) — the gathering-place of men.’ (13)
BS_C03_S01_V14::block-0: Moreover, the venerable ones — Manu, Vyāsa and the rest — record in narrations such as the story of Naciketas that, in the city of Saṃyamana, the ripening of evil deeds (kapūya-karma-vipāka) is under the sway of Yama (yama-āyatta). ‖ 14 ‖
BS_C03_S01_V15: And, moreover, the seven (hells are recorded). ‖ 15 ‖
BS_C03_S01_V15::block-0: Moreover, the seven hells, headed by Raurava, are recorded by the authors of the Purāṇas (paurāṇikas) as the realms wherein the fruits of evil deeds (duṣkṛta-phala-upabhoga-bhūmi) are experienced. Those who do unwished-for deeds and the like (aniṣṭādi-kāriṇaḥ) reach those (hells). Whence, then, could they reach the moon? — this is the purport. ‖ 15 ‖
BS_C03_S01_V16: There also (in those hells), there is no contradiction, because of his (Yama's) functioning (vyāpāra). ‖ 16 ‖
BS_C03_S01_V16::block-0: [Leading bhāṣya — pūrvapakṣa-doubt:] But surely this is contradictory — that the doers of evil deeds, being subject to Yama (yama-āyatta), undergo torments — inasmuch as in those very (hells) Raurava and the rest, others such as Citragupta are recorded as various overseers (nānā-adhiṣṭhātāraḥ). [The siddhānta replies:] No (it is not so) — and says:
BS_C03_S01_V16::block-1: [Siddhānta:] Even in those seven hells, since the office of overseership (adhiṣṭhātṛtva-vyāpāra) of that very Yama himself is admitted, there is no contradiction. For those overseers, Citragupta and the rest, are themselves recorded as functioning only when set in motion by Yama (yama-prayuktāḥ). ‖ 16 ‖
BS_C03_S01_V17: But (the words ‘of these two paths’ refer) to (the path) of knowledge and (the path) of works, because that is the topic under discussion (prakṛta). ‖ 17 ‖
BS_C03_S01_V17::block-0: In the Pañcāgni-vidyā, on the occasion of answering the question ‘How is it that yonder world (asau lokaḥ) does not become full?’ (Chā. Up. 5.3.3), it is heard: ‘Now, by neither of these two paths (etayoḥ pathoḥ) (do they go); they become these tiny creatures, returning again and again — “be born, die” — this is the third state; therefore yonder world does not become full’ (Chā. Up. 5.10.8). There, ‘of these two paths’ means ‘of the (path of) knowledge and (the path of) works’ (vidyā-karmaṇoḥ). Why so? Because they are what is under discussion (prakṛtatvāt). For knowledge and works are the topic with reference to the obtaining of the path of the gods (devayāna) and the path of the fathers (pitṛyāṇa) — by ‘they who know thus’ (tad ya itthaṃ viduḥ) (Chā. Up. 5.10.1), knowledge (is mentioned), by which the path-of-the-gods (devayāna) is to be reached, and which is proclaimed (as such); by ‘sacrifices, public works (iṣṭāpūrta), and gifts (dattam)’ (Chā. Up. 5.10.3), work (is mentioned), by which the path-of-the-fathers (pitṛyāṇa) is to be reached, and which is proclaimed (as such). In that very procedure, the text ‘by neither of these two paths’ is heard. This is what is said: those who are not, by means of knowledge as instrument, qualified for the devayāna, nor by means of works for the pitṛyāṇa — for them, this third path, characterised by tiny creatures, returning again and again (asakṛd-āvartin), is reserved. Therefore, the moon is not reached even by those who do unwished-for deeds and the like (aniṣṭādi-kārins). [Pūrvapakṣa-objection:] Suppose this — that they too will mount the orb of the moon, and from there, descending, attain the state of tiny creatures. [Siddhānta:] That too is not, because the ascent would be purposeless (āroha-anarthakyāt). And, moreover, if all the departed (prayants) were to reach the lunar world, that world would become full of those passing on (prayadbhiḥ sampūryeta) — and thus the answer would become contradictory to the question (praśna-viruddhaṃ prativacanam); for the answer must be given in such a way that yonder world is not filled up. [Pūrvapakṣa:] If we admit a (consequent) descent (avaroha), the non-filling-up is established. [Siddhānta:] No, because such (descent) is not heard of (in the text — aśrutatvāt). True, even by descent, the non-filling-up is intelligible. But the Śruti shows the non-filling-up by mentioning the third state — ‘this is the third state; therefore yonder world does not become full’ (Chā. Up. 5.10.8). Hence, it is fitting (to hold) that the non-filling-up is due solely to non-ascent (anārohād eva). For, if descent were uniformly (avaroha-aviśiṣṭatva) admitted even in the case of those who perform iṣṭa and the like, the mention of the third state would become purposeless (tṛtīyasthāna-ukti-ānarthakya-prasaṅga). The word ‘tu’ (‘but’) cuts off the apprehension of the going of all without exception (aśeṣa-gamana-āśaṅkā), which arises from the statement of another recension (śākhāntarīya-vākya). This being so, the word ‘all’ (sarva) in the other-recension passage stands as having reference (only) to those qualified (adhikṛta-apekṣa) — viz. ‘whichsoever qualified ones depart from this world, they all (sarve) go to the moon alone’. ‖ 17 ‖
BS_C03_S01_V18: Not in the third (state is the rule of five oblations to be regarded), since (the obtaining of that state is) thus apprehended (without that rule). ‖ 18 ‖
BS_C03_S01_V18::block-0: [Leading reference to pūrvapakṣa:] What was again said — that all are entitled to go to the moon for the obtaining of a body, on the strength of the rule of the number of oblations stated by ‘at the fifth oblation’ (pañcamyām āhutau) — to that this is the answer:
BS_C03_S01_V18::block-1: [Siddhānta:] In the third state, the rule of the number five of oblations is not to be insisted upon for the obtaining of a body. Why? Because it is so apprehended (tathā-upalabdheḥ). For thus the obtaining of the third state is apprehended in the manner already described, even without the rule of number of oblations — ‘“Be born, die” — this is the third state’ (Chā. Up. 5.10.8). And further, the number of oblations is mentioned in ‘at the fifth oblation, the waters take on the designation “person” (puruṣa-vacasaḥ)’ (Chā. Up. 5.3.3) as the cause of a human body, not as the cause of bodies of insects, moths, and the like, since the word ‘puruṣa’ refers to the human species (manuṣya-jāti). Moreover, what is being taught is that, at the fifth oblation, the waters bear the designation ‘person’; it is not being prohibited that, in the absence of the fifth oblation, they should not bear that designation — for that would entail the fault of the sentence having two purports (vākyasya dvyartha-tā-doṣāt). There, for those whose ascent and descent are possible, the body will arise at the fifth oblation. But for others, even without the rule of the number of oblations, the body will be commenced through waters that are aided (upasṛṣṭa) by other elements. ‖ 18 ‖
BS_C03_S01_V19: And it is also recorded in the world (in Smṛti). ‖ 19 ‖
BS_C03_S01_V19::block-0: Moreover, it is recorded in the world (smaryate loke) — the womb-less origination (ayoni-jatva) of Droṇa, Dhṛṣṭadyumna and the rest, and of Sītā, Draupadī and the rest. There, in the case of Droṇa and the others, the one oblation pertaining to the female (yoṣid-viṣayā) is absent. In the case of Dhṛṣṭadyumna and the others, both the oblations — pertaining to female and male (yoṣit-puruṣa-viṣaya) — are absent. And just as in those (cases) the rule of the number of oblations is disregarded (ādara-anādaraḥ), so it shall be elsewhere too. The female crane (balākā) too, by popular convention (loka-rūḍhi), is said to conceive without the seminal flow (retaḥ-seka). ‖ 19 ‖
BS_C03_S01_V20::block-0: Moreover, in the four-fold class of beings (bhūta-grāma) characterized as womb-born (jarāyu-ja), egg-born (aṇḍa-ja), sweat-born (sveda-ja), and sprout-born (udbhij-ja) — in the case of the sweat-born and the sprout-born, the origination is observed without the rural rite (grāmya-dharma, i.e. sexual congress). Hence the disregard of the number of oblations (āhuti-saṃkhyā-anādaraḥ) is established. So shall it be elsewhere too. ‖ 20 ‖
BS_C03_S01_V21: The third term comprehends what is sweat-born (saṃśoka-ja). ‖ 21 ‖
BS_C03_S01_V21::block-0: [Leading bhāṣya — pūrvapakṣa-objection:] But surely, ‘there are only three seeds (bījas) of these beings — egg-born, viviparous (jīva-ja), and sprout-born’ (Chā. Up. 6.3.1) — there only a three-fold class of beings (tri-vidha bhūta-grāma) is heard of. How then has the four-fold-ness of the class of beings been propounded (in the previous sūtra)? To this it is replied:
BS_C03_S01_V21::block-1: [Siddhānta:] In ‘egg-born, viviparous, sprout-born’ (Chā. Up. 6.3.1), the inclusion of the sweat-born (sveda-ja-upasaṃgrahaḥ) is to be understood as accomplished by that very third word ‘udbhij-ja’ (sprout-born) — because in the case of both, the sweat-born and the sprout-born, the property of arising by emergence from earth and water (bhūmi-udaka-udbheda-prabhavatva) is alike. But the emergence of the moving (jaṅgama-udbheda) is distinct (vilakṣaṇa) from the emergence of the stationary (sthāvara-udbheda) — hence elsewhere there is the doctrine of the difference (bheda-vāda) of the sweat-born and the sprout-born. Thus there is no contradiction. ‖ 21 ‖
BS_C03_S01_V22: Attainment of similarity (to ākāśa etc.), because (only thus) is it intelligible. ‖ 22 ‖
BS_C03_S01_V22::block-0: It has been said that those who perform iṣṭi (sacrifices) and other rites, having ascended to the moon and having dwelt there for as long as the residue of their karma lasts, descend with a remainder (sānuśayāḥ). Now the manner of the descent is being examined. There is, in this connection, this descent-śruti: ‘Then they return again by the very path they came — to ākāśa, from ākāśa to vāyu; having become vāyu, one becomes smoke; having become smoke,’ (Chā. Up. 5.10.5) ‘one becomes mist; having become mist, one becomes a cloud; having become a cloud, one rains down’ (Chā. Up. 5.10.6). Here arises the doubt: do those descending attain the very nature (svarūpa) of ākāśa and the rest, or only similarity (sāmya) to ākāśa and the rest? On this, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is obtained first — they attain the very nature of ākāśa and the rest. Why? Because the śruti speaks thus. Otherwise it would be lakṣaṇā (secondary signification). And when there is a conflict between śruti (literal) and lakṣaṇā (figurative), śruti is the proper recourse, not lakṣaṇā. Likewise, the syllables ‘having become vāyu, one becomes smoke,’ and the like, work out straightforwardly when the very nature of those (vāyu, smoke etc.) is obtained. Hence, attainment of the very nature of ākāśa and the rest. — When such a position is reached, we say (siddhānta): they attain similarity to ākāśa and the rest. The watery body originated in the moon-orb for the purpose of enjoyment, when enjoyment is exhausted, dissolves and becomes subtle, similar to ākāśa. Then it comes under the sway of vāyu. Then it becomes mingled with smoke and so on. This is what is stated by ‘to ākāśa as it came, from ākāśa to vāyu’ (Chā. Up. 5.10.5) and so forth. How is this established? ‘Because (thus alone) is it intelligible (upapatteḥ)’ — for thus alone does it become intelligible. For one thing’s becoming another in the primary sense is not intelligible. And were attainment of the very nature of ākāśa accepted, the descent in the order of vāyu and so on would not be intelligible. Further, since ākāśa is all-pervading and hence eternally connected (with the soul), no relation with it is possible other than attainment of similarity to it. And when śruti (in its literal sense) is impossible, recourse to lakṣaṇā is altogether proper. Therefore, attainment of equality with ākāśa and the rest is here metaphorically spoken of as becoming ākāśa and the rest. ‖ 22 ‖
BS_C03_S01_V23: Not for very long, because of the (śruti’s) specific statement. ‖ 23 ‖
BS_C03_S01_V23::block-0: There, with regard to the attainment of ākāśa and the rest, prior to the attainment of paddy and the rest, there arises a doubt — do they remain for a long, long time in each preceding similarity and (then) pass on to the succeeding similarity, or only for a short, short time? On this, since there is no scriptural rule (śāstra) that fixes a determinate measure, there results indeterminacy (anirayama) — when this position is reached, this is said: ‘Not for very long.’ Remaining for a short, short time in the state of ākāśa and the rest, they fall down to this earth along with the streams of rain. How is this established? Because of the specific statement (viśeṣa-darśanāt). For thus, just after attainment of the state of paddy and the rest, (the śruti) qualifies — ‘from this it is indeed very difficult to escape’ (Chā. Up. 5.10.6). One ‘ta’ should be understood to be elided in the Chāndasa formation. Durniṣprapatataram means ‘harder to come out of’ — the meaning is that escape from this state of paddy and the rest is more painful than that. By thus showing in this case the painful nature of departure, (the śruti) shows in the previous (states) the easy nature of departure. And this difference of pleasure and pain in departure is conditioned by the shortness or length of time, because in that interval there is no enjoyment, since no body is produced for enjoyment. Hence, prior to the attainment of the state of paddy and the rest, the descent must be in but a short time. ‖ 23 ‖
BS_C03_S01_V24: Into (plants) presided over by others, as before, because of the (mode of) statement. ‖ 24 ‖
BS_C03_S01_V24::block-0: In that very descent, just after the rainfall, it is read — ‘Here they are born as paddy and barley, herbs and trees, sesamum and beans’ (Chā. Up. 5.10.6). Here arises the doubt — at this stage, do those with residual karma (anuśayinaḥ), having attained the species of immobile beings (sthāvara), enjoy the pleasures and pains of immobile beings, or do they only undergo a mere conjunction with bodies of immobile beings that are presided over by other kṣetrajñas (selves)? What, then, is the pūrvapakṣa? — Having attained the species of immobile beings, they enjoy the pleasures and pains thereof. Why? Because the verb ‘to be born’ (jan) properly applies in its primary sense; because of the established usage of śruti and smṛti as to the state of immobile beings being a place of enjoyment; and because, since iṣṭi and other karma involve the slaying of animals etc., it is intelligible that they should yield undesirable fruits. Hence, this birth of those with residue as paddy and the rest is in the primary sense, like the birth as a dog and so on — just as ‘either a dog’s womb, or a hog’s womb, or a Caṇḍāla’s womb,’ where the birth of those with residue as a dog and the rest is primary and accompanied by the pleasures and pains thereof, so also the birth as paddy and the rest. — When such (pūrvapakṣa) is reached, we say (siddhānta) —
BS_C03_S01_V24::block-1: Those with residue undergo only a mere conjunction with paddy and other (plants) presided over by other jīvas, and do not enjoy their pleasures and pains; ‘as before’ (pūrvavat) — just as the becoming vāyu, smoke and the rest of those with residue is mere conjunction with them, so also the becoming paddy and the rest is mere conjunction with the immobile beings of (those) species. How is this established? From the mode of statement (abhilāpa) being just like that. What is the ‘being like that’ of the statement? The mention without reference to the activity of karma — just as in (the descent through) ākāśa and the rest, ending with rainfall, the (śruti) does not refer to any activity of karma, so also in the birth as paddy and the rest. Hence here there is no enjoyment of pleasure and pain by those with residue. But where (the śruti) intends enjoyment of pleasure and pain, it does refer to the activity of karma — ‘those of pleasing conduct’, ‘those of foul conduct’. Moreover, were the birth of those with residue as paddy and the rest in the primary sense, then when paddy and the rest are reaped, threshed, cooked, and eaten, those with residue who identify themselves with them would have to depart. For it is well-known that whatever body a jīva identifies with, he departs from it when it is afflicted. In that case, the becoming-the-shedder-of-semen of those with residue (after) the state of paddy and the rest could not be expressed. Hence, those with residue have only a mere conjunction with paddy and the rest presided over by others. By this, the (claim of) the verb ‘to be born’ being in its primary sense and the (claim of) immobile state being a place of enjoyment have been answered. Nor do we deny that the immobile state is a place of enjoyment. Let it be so for other beings who have come to the immobile state through the power of demerit — for them this is a place of enjoyment. But of those with residue descending from the moon, we declare that they do not enjoy the immobile state. ‖ 24 ‖
BS_C03_S01_V25: If it be said (the sacrificial karma is) impure, (we say) no, because of (scriptural) word. ‖ 25 ‖
BS_C03_S01_V25::block-0: Now what was said — that, on account of being conjoined with the slaying of animals and the like, the sacrificial (ādhvarika) karma is impure (aśuddha), and hence yielding even an undesirable fruit is intelligible, and so let the birth of those with residue as paddy and the rest be primary, and the figurative (gauṇī) construal be needless — that is now refuted. No (na), because the means of cognition of dharma and adharma is śāstra (scripture). It is śāstra alone that is the cause of the cognition ‘this is dharma, this is adharma,’ because both are beyond the senses (atīndriya). Also because (dharma and adharma) are not bound to fixed place, time, and occasion — for that very dharma which is performed in a certain place, time, and occasion becomes adharma in other places, times, and occasions. Hence, apart from śāstra, no one has any cognition concerning dharma and adharma. And by śāstra, the jyotiṣṭoma, which is of the nature of (sacrificial) slaying-and-favouring (himsānugrahādyātmaka), has been ascertained as dharma; how can it be called impure? — But surely the very śāstra ‘Let one not slay any beings’ teaches us that himsā concerning beings is adharma. Quite so — but that is the general rule (utsarga). The exception (apavāda) is ‘Let one immolate the animal devoted to Agnīṣoma.’ And the general rule and the exception have their own determinate spheres (vyavasthita-viṣayatva). Therefore Vedic karma is pure (viśuddha); because it is performed by the cultured (śiṣṭa) and is not censured by them. Hence its corresponding fruit is not the state of immobile beings. Nor is the birth as paddy and the rest comparable to the birth as a dog and the rest. For that (latter) is spoken of with reference to those of foul conduct (kapūya-caraṇa). There is here no such distinct adhikāra (governing context). Therefore, of those with residue who have fallen from the moon-orb, mere conjunction with paddy and the rest is metaphorically called ‘becoming’ them. ‖ 25 ‖
BS_C03_S01_V26: Then connection with one who sheds (the seed). ‖ 26 ‖
BS_C03_S01_V26::block-0: For this further reason too is the becoming paddy and the rest mere conjunction with paddy and the rest — namely, that, just after the state of paddy and the rest, the state of becoming the shedder-of-semen (retaḥsig-bhāva) is mentioned of those with residue: ‘Whoever eats food, whoever sheds semen, becomes that very thing’ (Chā. Up. 5.10.6). And here the primary becoming-the-shedder-of-semen is not possible. For (a being) becomes a shedder of semen only when, born long ago, he has attained youth. How could one with residue, who has accompanied the food being eaten, attain a non-figurative (anupacarita) ‘becoming-the-shedder-of-semen’? There, then, only connection (yoga) with the shedder-of-semen must necessarily be admitted as the ‘becoming-shedder-of-semen.’ Like that, the becoming paddy and the rest is also mere connection (yoga) with paddy and the rest. Thus there is no contradiction. ‖ 26 ‖
BS_C03_S01_V27::block-0: Now, after the state of becoming the shedder-of-semen, when the semen is deposited in the womb, the body of those with residue is born from the womb (yoneḥ adhi) for the enjoyment of the fruit of the residue, says the śāstra — ‘Now those who here are of pleasing conduct’ (Chā. Up. 5.10.7) and so on. Hence too it is understood that during the descent, at the stage of becoming paddy and the rest, that very (paddy etc.) body is not the (body) accompanied by pleasure and pain (of the soul with residue). Hence it is established that the birth of those with residue (in paddy etc.) is mere conjunction with paddy and the rest. ‖ 27 ‖
BS_C03_S02_INTRO1::block-0: In the previous pāda, by adducing the Pañcāgni-vidyā, the various transmigratory courses of the jīva have been elaborated. Now, the various states (avasthā-bheda) of that very (jīva) are being elaborated. This is what (the śruti) declares — beginning with ‘When he sleeps’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.9) and continuing with ‘There are no chariots there, no chariot-yokings, no roads; then he creates chariots, chariot-yokings, roads,’ and so on. Here the doubt arises — is the creation in dream, like that in the waking state, ultimately real (pāramārthikī), or is it only māyā-like (māyāmayī)? Here first this is propounded —
BS_C03_S02_V01: In the intermediate (state, dream-state), creation; for (the śruti) says so. ‖ 1 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V01::block-0: In the sandhya (intermediate state) the creation is real (tathya-rūpā). The word ‘sandhya’ designates the dream-state, since this usage is observed in the Veda — ‘the sandhya, the third, is the dream-state.’ Or (it is so called) because it occurs at the junction (sandhi) of the two world-states (waking and deep sleep) or of the states of waking-perception and deep tranquillity (saṃprasāda); hence ‘sāndhya.’ In that intermediate state (sandhya-sthāna), the creation must necessarily be real in form. Why? Because the śruti, which is an authoritative pramāṇa, says so — ‘then he creates chariots, chariot-yokings, roads’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.10) and so on. And from the concluding statement ‘for he is the agent (kartā)’ this very (conclusion) is understood. ‖ 1 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V02: And some [recension] [declare the Self to be] the fashioner [of desires], and [the desires are] sons and the like. (II)
BS_C03_S02_V02::block-0: (Pūrvapakṣa continued — establishing that the dream-creation is real:) Moreover, [the followers of] one recension recount that, in this very intermediate (sandhya) state, the Self is the fashioner (nirmātṛ) of desires — ‘That Person who, while [the senses] are asleep, remains awake, fashioning desire after desire’ (Kaṭha Up. 2.2.8). And by ‘desires’ (kāmāḥ) here are meant sons and the like — they are called ‘kāmāḥ’ because they are objects of longing (kāmyante iti kāmāḥ — nirvacana). It might be objected: ‘But by the word kāma only specific cognitions of desire (icchā-viśeṣāḥ) are spoken of.’ Not so; for, in the same context, having begun with ‘Choose sons and grandsons of a hundred years of age’ (Kaṭha Up. 1.1.23), [Death] concludes with ‘I make thee an enjoyer of [these] kāmas’ (Kaṭha Up. 1.1.24) — the word ‘kāma’ is there applied to the previously mentioned sons and the rest. And this fashioner we ascertain to be the Prājña (the all-knowing Lord) on the strength of the section (prakaraṇa) and the supplementary sentence (vākya-śeṣa). For the section is precisely concerning the Prājña — ‘Other than dharma, other than adharma...’ (Kaṭha Up. 1.2.14) etc.; and the supplementary text too belongs to that very topic — ‘That alone is the Bright, that is Brahman, that alone is called the immortal. On That all the worlds rest; none transcends That’ (Kaṭha Up. 2.2.8). Now, a creation having the Prājña as its agent has been ascertained, in the waking-sphere, to be of factual nature (tathya-rūpā); thus the dream-resting creation too deserves to be [factual]. The Śruti likewise attests this — ‘And further they say: this [dream-region] of his is the very same as the waking-region; for whatever he sees while awake, that he sees while asleep’ (Bṛh. Up. 4.3.14) — proclaiming the parity of method between dream and waking. Hence the dream-creation is of factual nature. (II)
BS_C03_S02_V03: But [it is] mere illusion (māyā-mātra), because of the non-manifestation of [its] nature in entirety. (III)
BS_C03_S02_V03::block-0: (Leading-bhāṣya:) The pūrvapakṣa having thus been obtained, [the siddhāntin] replies —
BS_C03_S02_V03::block-1: (Siddhānta:) The word ‘tu’ (but) excludes the [pūrvapakṣa] view. What was said — that the dream-creation is paramārthika (absolutely real) — is not so. The dream-creation is mere illusion (māyā); not even a whiff of absolute reality is in it. Whence? ‘From its nature not being manifest in entirety’ (kārtsnyena anabhivyakta-svarūpatvāt). For the dream is not, in entirety, manifest with the attributes of a real entity (paramārtha-vastu-dharmeṇa). What, then, is meant here by ‘entirety’? The conjunction of [appropriate] place, time, and cause, together with non-sublatability (abādha). For the appropriate place, time, and cause that pertain to absolutely real things, and non-sublatability, are not possible in dream. First, no fitting place for chariots and the like is possible in a dream — for chariots cannot find room within the confined region of the body. (Pūrvapakṣa-objection within siddhānta:) ‘Let it be granted that he sees the dream outside the body, since he apprehends objects situated in distant regions. The Śruti also teaches that dream is outside the body — ‘Roving immortal beyond the nest [of the body], he, the immortal, goes wherever he likes’ (Bṛh. Up. 4.3.12). And the variation in cognitions of staying and moving cannot be reconciled if the creature has not gone out.’ (Reply:) Not so, we say — for it is not credible that a sleeping creature, in a mere instant, should have the capacity to traverse a region a hundred yojanas away and return again. And in some cases [the Śruti] proclaims a dream that lacks any return — ‘Today as I lay sleeping, overpowered by sleep, I went in dream to the Pañcālas, and [yet] awakened here’; if [the dreamer] had departed from the body, he should have woken up among the Pañcālas, where he had gone. But in fact he wakes up among the Kurus only. And the body, by means of which he fancies himself to attain another region, is seen by other persons standing nearby in the very place of his couch. Moreover, the regions which he sees in dream are not, in fact, such as he sees them; if he were truly running about, he would apprehend an actually existent object as in waking. The Śruti too declares that the dream is within the body itself — having begun with ‘When he wanders about with this dream-stuff’, [it concludes] ‘he moves about in his own body as he likes’ (Bṛh. Up. 2.1.18). Hence, since the [‘outside’ reading] conflicts with both Śruti and reasoning, the text ‘outside the nest’ must be construed figuratively (gauṇī-vyākhyātavyā) — ‘the immortal [Self], roving as it were outside the nest’; for one who, though dwelling in the body, makes no use of it, is as if outside the body. The variation in cognitions of staying and moving, on this view, must simply be admitted to be a delusion (vipralambha eva).
BS_C03_S02_V03::block-2: Moreover, there is incongruity of time in dream — sleeping in the night, one fancies it to be daytime in Bhārata-varṣa; in a dream lasting only a muhūrta one sometimes lives through many groups of years. Nor are there in dream causes appropriate either to cognition or to action. Owing to the withdrawal of the sense-organs, he has no eyes and so on for grasping chariots and the like. Even for the constructing of chariots, whence has he the capacity, or the timber, in a moment? And these chariots etc. seen in dream are sublated upon waking. Indeed, even within the dream itself they are easily sublated, since contradiction is seen between the beginning and the end — what is determined in dream as ‘this is a chariot’ becomes a man in a moment, what is determined as ‘this is a man’ becomes a tree in a moment. The Śāstra clearly teaches the absence of chariots and the like in dream — ‘There [in the dream-state] there are no chariots, no chariot-yokes, no roads’ (Bṛh. Up. 4.3.10), and so on. Therefore the dream-experience is mere māyā. (III)
BS_C03_S02_V04: And [dream is] indicative (sūcaka), because of Śruti, and the knowers of dreams say so. (IV)
BS_C03_S02_V04::block-0: (Objection:) ‘If, then, [dream] is mere māyā, no whiff of paramārtha is present in dream at all?’ — Not so, we reply: dream is indicative (sūcaka) of good and evil yet to come. Thus the Śruti declares — ‘When in [the performance of] kāmya rites one sees a woman in dreams, in that vision in dream let him recognize success’ (Chānd. Up. 5.2.8). And by such dreams as ‘he sees a black man with black teeth — he kills him’ (the Śruti) makes known that one is to be short-lived. The knowers of the dream-treatise (svapnādhyāya-vidaḥ) likewise say — ‘mounting an elephant and so on in dream are auspicious; riding on an ass and the like are inauspicious’. Some hold that certain dreams, conditioned by particular mantras, deities or substances, carry a whiff of true import. Even there, let it be granted that the thing indicated (sūcyamāna-vastu) is true; but the indicative dream-content itself — the seeing of the woman and the like — is false (vaitathya), being sublatable. Such is the intent. Hence dream’s being mere māyā is established.
BS_C03_S02_V04::block-1: What was said — ‘He says...’ [‘sa hi kartā’] — must, in this view, be explained figuratively (bhāktam vyākhyātavyam). Just as ‘the plough draws the bullocks etc.’ is said only in virtue of being an instrumental cause (nimitta-mātratvāt), and not that the plough literally draws the bullocks, so by being merely the occasion, the sleeper is said to ‘create chariots’, and ‘he is the agent’ — but the sleeper does not literally create chariots. His being the cause is to be stated in the sense that, owing to the cognition of chariots etc., delight, terror, and the like arise in him, and he is therefore the agent of their cause, namely sukṛta and duṣkṛta (good and evil deeds). Moreover, in waking, owing to the contact of objects with the sense-organs and the intermixing of sun-light and other lights, the self-luminosity (svayaṃ-jyotiṣṭva) of the Self is hard to discriminate; hence the dream-state has been adduced for that discrimination [in the Bṛhad-Āraṇyaka]. There, if the talk of the creation of chariots etc. were taken in its primary sense (śrutyā), then self-luminosity would not stand established. Hence the statement of absence of chariots etc. is to be taken in the literal śruti-sense, while the statement of dream-creation of chariots etc. is to be construed figuratively (bhakti). By this, the Śruti about ‘fashioning’ (nirmāṇa-śravaṇa) is also explained. As to what was said — ‘they declare him to be the Prājña-fashioner’ — that too is unsound, because in another Śruti — ‘Having himself struck down [the body], having himself fashioned [dream-objects], by his own splendour, by his own light, he sleeps’ (Bṛh. Up. 4.3.9) — the activity of the jīva is heard. So here too, in ‘That Person who, while [the senses] are asleep, remains awake’ (Kaṭha Up. 2.2.8), this very jīva, by an anuvāda of what is well-known, is celebrated as fashioner of desires. But by the supplementary text — ‘That alone is the Bright, that is Brahman’ — his jīva-status is set aside and his Brahman-status is taught, just as in ‘That thou art’ (Chānd. Up. 6.9.4) etc.; thus the Brahma-prakaraṇa is not violated. Nor is the activity of the Prājña denied even in dream by us, since he, being Lord of all, may serve as the substratum-controller (adhiṣṭhātṛ) in all states. But that this sandhya-creation is not absolutely real (pāramārthika), like the creation of ether and so on (vyad-ādi-sarga) — only this much is being established. Nor is the creation of ether and so on absolutely real either. For we have already established, under ‘Their non-difference [from Brahman, follows] from words like ārambhaṇa etc.’ (B.S. 2.1.14), that the entire phenomenal world is mere māyā. Yet, prior to the realization of Brahman as the Self, the cosmic phenomenon of ether and so on retains a settled form (vyavasthita-rūpa). The sandhya-resting phenomenon, on the other hand, is sublated every day. Hence this special distinctive (vaiśeṣika) māyā-only-character of the sandhya-state has been declared. (IV)
BS_C03_S02_V05: But [the jīva’s knowledge and lordship are] concealed [from the Supreme]; through meditation upon Him [arise their disclosure], for from Him alone are this [jīva’s] bondage and its reverse. (V)
BS_C03_S02_V05::block-0: (Pūrvapakṣa:) Yet again it might be urged: ‘The jīva is a part (aṃśa) of the Supreme Self — like a spark of fire. Now, just as fire and the spark have the powers of burning and illumining in common, so the jīva and the Lord have the powers of knowledge and lordship in common. Hence, in virtue of the jīva’s knowledge and lordship, the dream-creation of chariots and the like will be sāṅkalpikī (constructed by his volition).’ (Siddhānta replies:) Even granting the jīva-Lord part-whole relation, that the jīva has attributes contrary to the Lord’s is a matter of direct experience (pratyakṣam eva). Then is there no commonality with the Lord at all in the jīva? It is not absent: it exists, but is concealed (tirohitam) by the obstruction of avidyā and the like. That [commonality], though concealed, becomes manifest only in some accomplished one (saṃsiddhasya kasyacid eva) — through the grace of the Lord, by meditating on the Supreme Lord, with diligent effort, having dispelled the darkness — like the power of vision concealed by cataract becomes manifest by the potency of medicine. It does not arise spontaneously in all creatures. How? ‘Tato hi’ — for from Him, from the Lord as cause, this jīva’s bondage and liberation arise — bondage from non-knowledge of the Lord’s essential nature, and liberation from knowledge of His essential nature. So says the Śruti — ‘By knowing God, [there comes] the dropping off of all fetters; with afflictions exhausted, [there comes] the cessation of birth and death; by meditating on Him, [there is] the third [stage], on the breaking of the body — universal lordship; and, [in the fourth,] solitary, having attained all desires’ (Śvet. Up. 1.11), and so on. (V)
BS_C03_S02_V06: Or rather, that [concealment of the jīva’s knowledge-lordship arises] from connection with the body. (VI)
BS_C03_S02_V06::block-0: (Objection:) Why, then, is the jīva — being a part of the Supreme Self — afflicted with concealment of knowledge and lordship? Rather, the non-concealment of knowledge and lordship would be fitting, as in the case of the spark with respect to burning and illuminating. (Reply:) True, that is so. Yet that very concealment of the jīva’s knowledge and lordship arises from connection with the body (deha-yogāt) — that is, from connection with body, sense-organs, mind, intellect, objects, sensations, and the like. There is also an analogy here: just as fire, though endowed with the powers of burning and illuminating, has those powers concealed when shut up in the kindling-wood (araṇi-gata), or as when covered by ashes — so, by connection with the upādhis of body and the rest, brought about by the avidyā-projected name-and-form, and through the delusion of non-discrimination from them, the jīva’s knowledge and lordship are concealed. The word ‘vā’ (‘or’) is meant to ward off the doubt that the jīva is something other than the Lord. (Pūrvapakṣa:) ‘Let the jīva, then, be other than the Lord — since his knowledge and lordship are concealed. What use is the postulation of body-connection?’ (Reply:) Not so, we say — for it is impossible that the jīva be other than the Lord, since, having begun ‘That deity reflected’ (Chānd. Up. 6.3.2), [the Śruti] makes a back-reference to the jīva by the word ‘Ātman’ in ‘Having entered with this jīva-Self’ (Chānd. Up. 6.3.2); and [the Śruti] teaches the jīva his identity with the Lord — ‘That is the Real, that is the Self, That thou art, O Śvetaketu’ (Chānd. Up. 6.8.7). Hence the jīva, being non-different from the Lord, has his knowledge and lordship concealed by connection with the body. Therefore, no sāṅkalpikī dream-creation of chariots etc. by the jīva is tenable. If a sāṅkalpikī dream-creation by the jīva were possible, no one would ever see an undesirable dream — for no one wills (saṅkalpayati) the undesirable. As to what was said — that the Śruti about ‘the same as the waking-region’ proclaims the truth of dream — that statement of similarity is not meant to convey [absolute] truth, since it would conflict with self-luminosity, and since the very Śruti has also shown the absence of chariots etc. in dream. Rather, it intends only that, since dream is fashioned out of the latent impressions (vāsanā) sprung from waking, it has a semblance similar to that. Therefore the dream’s being mere māyā stands established. (VI)
BS_C03_S02_V07: The absence of that [dream-experience occurs] in the nāḍīs and in the [Supreme] Self, on the strength of Śruti to that effect. (VII)
BS_C03_S02_V07::block-0: (Introduction:) The dream-state has been examined. Now the deep-sleep state (suṣupti) is examined. There are these Śruti-passages on the topic of suṣupti. In one place we hear — ‘When at the time he is asleep, fully composed, and sees no dream, he has crept into these nāḍīs’ (Chānd. Up. 8.6.3). Elsewhere, after enumerating the nāḍīs, [the Śruti] says — ‘By them having returned, he lies in the purītat (the pericardium)’ (Bṛh. Up. 2.1.19). And again, after enumerating the nāḍīs — ‘He is in them at the time when, asleep, he sees no dream; then he becomes one with this Prāṇa’ (Kauṣ. Up. 4.19). And elsewhere — ‘He sleeps in this ākāśa within the heart’ (Bṛh. Up. 2.1.17). And in another place — ‘At that time, dear, he becomes united with the Sat (Existent), he becomes merged in his own’ (Chānd. Up. 6.8.1). And also — ‘Embraced by the Prājña-Self, he knows nothing external nor internal’ (Bṛh. Up. 4.3.21).
BS_C03_S02_V07::block-1: (Pūrvapakṣa-saṃśaya:) Now, there is a doubt: are these — the nāḍīs and the rest — independent of one another, distinct loci of suṣupti? Or are they, taken in mutual reference, a single locus of suṣupti? What, then, is the prima-facie view? They are distinct. Why? Because they have a single function (eka-arthatvāt). For things having a single function are nowhere seen to need each other — like rice, barley, etc. The nāḍīs and the rest do have a single function in suṣupti, since the locative case-form (saptamī-nirdeśa) — ‘he has crept into the nāḍīs’ (Chānd. Up. 8.6.3), ‘he lies in the purītat’ (Bṛh. Up. 2.1.19) — is uniformly used in each instance. (Counter:) ‘But no such locative is seen in ‘He becomes united with the Sat, dear’ (Chānd. Up. 6.8.1)’. (Reply:) That is no defect; even there the locative-meaning is implicit — for the supplementary text speaks of the jīva, in search of a resting-place, taking refuge as Sat — ‘Failing to find a resting place elsewhere, he resorts to Prāṇa alone’ (Chānd. Up. 6.8.2); for there, by the word ‘Prāṇa’, the previously-introduced Sat is taken up. ‘Resting-place’ is the locative-meaning, and the locative-form too is seen in the supplementary text — ‘Becoming merged in Sat, they do not know, [thinking] ‘we are merged in Sat’’ (Chānd. Up. 6.9.2). And everywhere suṣupti is uniformly characterized as cessation of particular cognition (viśeṣa-vijñāna-uparama-lakṣaṇa). Therefore, the nāḍīs etc., being of a single function, are reached for sleep optionally (vikalpena), one place sometimes — such is [the pūrvapakṣa].
BS_C03_S02_V07::block-2: (Siddhānta:) The pūrvapakṣa having thus been obtained, [the sūtra] says: ‘their absence [is] in the nāḍīs and in the Self’. ‘Their absence’ — the absence of the previously-mentioned dream-experience is suṣupti; that is the meaning. ‘In the nāḍīs and in the Self’ — by way of conjunction (samuccaya) the [sleeper] resorts to these — the nāḍīs and the rest — for sleep, not by alternation (vikalpena); that is the sense. Whence? ‘Tac-chruteḥ’ — for so the Śruti declares; for of all of them — nāḍīs etc. — the locus-of-suṣupti-status is heard, in this place and that. And that is gathered together as conjunction. If they were taken alternately, in one alternative there would be sublation. ‘But because of single function, the nāḍīs etc. ought to be alternative, like rice and barley’ — has been urged. Not so, we say. Mere unity of case-ending does not entail unity of function and alternation, since unity of case-ending is also seen in the case of multiple meaning and conjunction — as in ‘he sleeps in the palace, he sleeps on the couch’; so here too ‘he sleeps in the nāḍīs, in the purītat, and in Brahman’ is tenable as conjunction. So too the Śruti — ‘He is in them at the time when, asleep, he sees no dream; then he becomes one with this Prāṇa’ (Kauṣ. Up. 4.19) — declares the conjunction of nāḍīs and Prāṇa in suṣupti, since both are taken in a single sentence. And the Brahman-status of Prāṇa has been already established under ‘And Prāṇa, owing to subsequent reference’ (B.S. 1.1.28). Even where the nāḍīs are mentioned as if independent — ‘he has crept into these nāḍīs’ (Chānd. Up. 8.6.3) — even there, since Brahman, established elsewhere, is not negated, it is understood that, by way of the nāḍīs, [the jīva] rests in Brahman alone. Nor is the locative ‘in the nāḍīs’ thus contradicted; for one who reaches Brahman by way of the nāḍīs is indeed crept into the nāḍīs — just as one who reaches the ocean by way of the Gaṅgā is verily on the Gaṅgā. And here, since the path to Brahmaloka, consisting of the rays and nāḍīs, is intended, the mention of ‘creeping in’ is meant in praise of the nāḍīs — having said ‘he has crept into the nāḍīs’ (Chānd. Up. 8.6.3), [the Śruti] praises the nāḍīs by adding ‘no sin touches him’ (Chānd. Up. 8.6.3). And it states the cause of non-touch by sin — ‘for he then becomes united with the tejas’ (Chānd. Up. 8.6.3) — meaning, ‘pervaded in his organs by the tejas in the nāḍīs called bile, he no longer beholds external objects’. Or else, ‘by tejas’ here is a reference to Brahman itself, since in another Śruti — ‘Brahman alone is light alone’ (Bṛh. Up. 4.4.7) — the word ‘tejas’ is applied to Brahman. ‘He becomes united with Brahman through the nāḍīs; therefore no sin touches him’ — that is the meaning. And that union with Brahman is the cause of non-touch by sin — established by ‘Therefore all sins return; for this Brahmaloka is sinless’ (Chānd. Up. 8.4.1) and similar Śrutis. And thus, the conjunction of nāḍīs, accompanied by Brahman established elsewhere as the suṣupti-locus, is established. So too, since the purītat is also mentioned in the Brahma-procedure, its suṣupti-locus-status is understood in conformity with that — having begun ‘He sleeps in this ākāśa within the heart’ (Bṛh. Up. 2.1.17) (the suṣupti-locus, the heart-ākāśa, is taken up), it is then said ‘he lies in the purītat’ (Bṛh. Up. 2.1.19). The purītat is the wrapping of the heart. The [text continues], ‘residing in that wrapping...’
BS_C03_S02_V08::block-0: And since the Self alone is the locus of sleep, it is for that very reason that the awakening is taught (śiṣyate) — invariably (nityavat) — from this Self in the sleep-section. Thus, in the answer to the question ‘Whence has it come?’ (Bṛh. Up. 2.1.16), with passages such as ‘As tiny sparks issue from a fire, so from this Self issue forth all the prāṇas’ (Bṛh. Up. 2.1.20) and the like, and ‘Coming from Sat they do not know that ‘we have come from Sat’’ (Chānd. Up. 6.10.2). If, however, the suṣupti-loci were taken alternatively, [the Śruti] would have taught: ‘sometimes he awakes from the nāḍīs, sometimes from the purītat, sometimes from the Self’. Therefore, also from this consideration, the Self alone is the sleep-locus. (VIII)
BS_C03_S02_V09: But the same [jīva returns from sleep], on the strength of [continuance of] action, recollection, scripture, and injunction. (IX)
BS_C03_S02_V09::block-0: (Pūrvapakṣa-saṃśaya:) On awakening from that union with Sat, is it the very same one who had become merged in Sat that awakens, or some other? Such is the inquiry. The prima-facie position is: there is no fixed rule (aniyamaḥ). Why? When a drop of water is cast into a body of water, it then becomes the body of water itself; and to extract that very same drop of water again would be impossibly difficult. Likewise, the sleeper, having attained unity with the Supreme, becomes composed; he is not bound to rise as the very same. Therefore, either the same one — the Lord himself, that is, or some other jīva — awakens.
BS_C03_S02_V09::block-1: (Siddhānta:) The pūrvapakṣa being thus established, [the sūtra] says: but it is the very same jīva that, having gone to sleep and attained well-being, rises again, and not another. How? ‘Karma-anusmṛti-śabda-vidhibhyaḥ’ (from action, recollection, scriptural statement, and injunction). I shall show the reason in detail. First, from the observed performance of the remainder of action: he alone is fit to rise, and not another. Thus, on the next day one is seen continuing what was begun on the day before — and another cannot rightly engage in completing an action half-done by another, since that would entail an undue extension. Hence the same person is grasped as agent of the same action on the previous day and on the day after. From this also it is the same who arises: for the recollection later, ‘On the previous day I saw that’, of one previously experienced, is not possible upon the rising of another. For one cannot remember what was seen by another. Nor is the self-recollection ‘I am that one’ possible if another self has arisen. From scriptural words too his very rising is gathered. Thus — ‘He returns again, in the same way, by the same path, to the waking-state’ (Bṛh. Up. 4.3.16); ‘All these creatures, going day by day to this Brahmaloka, do not find it’ (Chānd. Up. 8.3.2); ‘Whatsoever they become here — tiger, lion, wolf, boar, worm, moth, gnat, mosquito — that they become there’ (Chānd. Up. 6.9.3) — these and similar passages, recited under the head of sleeping and waking, would not fit if another self arose. From karma- and vidyā-injunctions also it is gathered just so. Otherwise, the karma- and vidyā-injunctions would be without purpose. For on the view that another rises, the consequence would be that one is liberated by mere going to sleep. If that were so, tell me — what would be accomplished by an action whose fruit comes after a long time, or by knowledge? Furthermore, on the other-rising view: if a jīva that is engaged in some other body should rise [in this body], the activities native to that other body would be lost. If, on the other hand, a sleeper [in another body] should rise [in this body], the supposition would be without purpose. For of what gain is the supposition: ‘he who slept in one body rises not in that, but he who slept in another body rises in another’? If a liberated one were to rise, mokṣa would have an end; and the rising again of one in whom avidyā has ceased is impossible. By this, the rising of the Lord [as the awakener] is also rejected, since in Him avidyā is eternally in cessation. And on the other-rising view, both akṛta-abhyāgama (the visiting of unperformed action) and kṛta-vipraṇāśa (the loss of performed action) would be unavoidable. Hence the same one rises, not another. As to what was urged — that, like a drop of water cast into a body of water that cannot be raised, the jīva merged in Sat cannot rise again — that is repelled: in the case of the water-drop, non-extraction is fitting because there is no cause of distinction (viveka-kāraṇa-abhāva); but here, the cause of distinction is present — karma and avidyā — hence the disparity. We see also that, in our own kind, even hard-to-discriminate things, like milk and water mingled, are discriminated by the swan. Furthermore, there is no jīva at all distinct from the Supreme, who could be sifted from the existent Sat as a drop from a body of water. The Sat alone, by association with upādhi, is figuratively spoken of as ‘jīva’ — as has been expounded again and again. This being so, so long as bondage continues with reference to one and the same upādhi, there is the usage of one jīva; on the continuation of bondage with reference to another upādhi, there is the usage of another jīva. The very same upādhi, in sleep and awakening, persists by the maxim of seed and sprout (bīja-aṅkura-nyāya) — therefore...
BS_C03_S02_V10: In the swooned state, there is half-attainment (of the state of deep sleep), since this is what remains after exclusion (of the other possibilities). ‖ 10 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V10::block-0: There is something called ‘mugdha’ (the swooned), whom worldly people call ‘mūrcchita’ (the one who has fainted). On enquiry as to what state he is in, it is said: three states of the embodied jīva are well known — waking (jāgarita), dream (svapna) and deep sleep (suṣupta). The fourth is the departure from the body (i.e. death). But no fifth state of the jīva is established either in śruti or in smṛti. Hence (the pūrvapakṣin says) the swoon must be one among these four states alone.
BS_C03_S02_V10::block-1: When this is the position attained, we reply: the swooned man cannot indeed be in the waking state, for he does not perceive objects through the senses. It might be urged — by the analogy of the arrow-maker (iṣukāra-nyāya) he will be (regarded as) swooned: just as the arrow-maker, even while waking, on account of his mind being attached to the arrow, does not perceive other objects, so the swooned man, even while waking, on account of his mind being engrossed in the experience of the pain produced by the falling of a club and the like, does not perceive other objects. (We reply:) No — because of his being unconscious. The arrow-maker, indeed, with his mind engaged, says: ‘During this much time I was perceiving the arrow alone’; whereas the swooned man, on regaining consciousness, says: ‘During this much time I had been cast into blind darkness; nothing was sensed by me.’ Further, even of the waking man whose mind is attached to a single object, the body is held upright; but the body of the swooned man falls to the ground. Therefore he is not in the waking state. Nor does he see dreams, since he is devoid of consciousness. Nor is he dead, on account of the presence of breath and warmth — for, in regard to a swooned creature, when people are in doubt, ‘Is this one dead or not dead?’, in order to ascertain, they touch the region of the heart (saying), ‘Is there warmth or not?’, and the region of the nostril, ‘Is there breath or not?’. If they do not find the existence of breath and warmth, then concluding ‘He is dead’, they take him to the wood for cremation. But if they detect breath or warmth, then concluding ‘This man is not dead’, they apply medicine for the regaining of consciousness. And, on account of his rising again, he has not gone to his appointed end (death); for none returns from the realm of Yama. Let him then be (one who is) in deep sleep, since he is unconscious and not dead. (We reply:) No, on account of dissimilarity. The swooned man sometimes does not breathe even for a long time; his body is trembling, his face is dreadful, his eyes are wide open. The deep sleeper, on the contrary, has a serene face, breathes again and again at equal intervals, his eyes are closed, and his body does not tremble. They rouse the deep sleeper merely by squeezing his hands; but the swooned man not even by the blow of a hammer. There is also difference of cause between swoon and sleep — swoon is caused by the falling of a club and the like, while sleep is caused by exhaustion and the like. Nor is it customary in the world (to say), ‘the swooned one is asleep’. Hence by exclusion (parisesa) we understand that swoon is half-attainment — by reason of unconsciousness, attained (i.e. like deep sleep); by reason of dissimilarity from the rest, not attained.
BS_C03_S02_V10::block-2: (Pūrvapakṣa:) But how can it be said that swoon is half-attainment? Inasmuch as with reference to deep sleep itself it is declared by the śruti — ‘With Being, dear one, he then becomes united’ (Chā. Up. 6.8.1) (citation), ‘There the thief is no thief’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.22) (citation), ‘Day and night do not cross this bridge, nor old age, nor death, nor sorrow, nor merit, nor demerit’ (Chā. Up. 8.4.1) (citation), and so on. For in the jīva the experience of merit and demerit comes about by the production of the cognitions of being-happy and being-miserable. Neither the cognition of being-happy nor that of being-miserable exists in deep sleep. In the swooned man too those two cognitions do not exist at all. Hence, on account of the cessation of the limiting adjuncts, just as in deep sleep, in the swooned man also there ought to be complete attainment alone, not half-attainment. (Siddhānta:) To this we reply — we do not say that in the swooned man there is half-attainment of the jīva with Brahman. What then? We say that swoon-ness consists half in the side of deep sleep, and half in the side of another state. The similarity and dissimilarity of swoon with sleep have already been shown. And this (swoon) is the door of death. When his (residual) karma still has a remnant, then speech and mind return; but when his karma is wholly exhausted, then breath and warmth depart. Therefore the knowers of Brahman accept ‘half-attainment’. As to what was urged — that no fifth state is established — that is no defect; being occasional, it may not be (popularly) established. But it is established in the world and in āyurveda. Moreover, since half-attainment alone is admitted, it is not counted as a fifth (state); thus there is no fault. ‖ 10 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V11: Even on account of place (i.e. limiting adjunct), the Supreme cannot have a twofold characteristic, because everywhere (it is taught as devoid of attributes). ‖ 11 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V11::block-0: Of that Brahman by which the jīva, in deep sleep and the like, becomes attained through the cessation of limiting adjuncts, the very nature is now ascertained on the strength of śruti. There are śruti-texts of two kinds with reference to Brahman — (texts) such as ‘all-acting, all-desiring, all-fragrant, all-savouring’ (Chā. Up. 3.14.2) (citation), which have marks of attributes (saviśeṣa-liṅga); and (texts) such as ‘not gross, not subtle, not short, not long’ (Bṛ. Up. 3.8.8) (citation), which have marks of being attributeless (nirviśeṣa-liṅga). Is Brahman to be cognised in these śrutis as having a twofold characteristic, or only one of the two? And if (only) one, is it as possessed of attributes (saviśeṣa) or as devoid of attributes (nirviśeṣa)? Thus is the enquiry made. (Pūrvapakṣa:) On the strength of the śrutis of twofold characteristic, Brahman has indeed twofold characteristic. (Siddhānta:) When this position is attained, we reply: in the first place, twofold characteristic of the supreme Brahman is not possible by its very own nature (svataḥ); for it is impossible to determine that one and the same thing is, by its own nature, possessed of distinctions of form etc. and at the same time the opposite of that, on account of contradiction. Let it then be by reason of place (sthānataḥ) — i.e. by the conjunction of limiting adjuncts such as earth and so on. That too is not tenable — for, even by the conjunction of limiting adjuncts, no other-natured property is possible for an other-natured thing. The crystal, while transparent, does not become non-transparent through the conjunction of an adjunct like red lac and the like, since the apprehension of non-transparency is mere illusion (bhrama-mātra). And the limiting adjuncts (upādhis) are themselves brought up by avidyā. Hence, even when (only) one of the two marks is to be accepted, Brahman is to be cognised only as without all distinctions, free of all alternatives (nirvikalpaka), not as the opposite of that. For everywhere — in those passages whose chief import is the establishing of the very nature of Brahman, such as ‘soundless, touchless, formless, undecaying’ (Kaṭha Up. 1.3.15), (Mukti. Up. 2.12) (citation), and so on — Brahman is taught only as that from which all attributes have been removed. ‖ 11 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V12: If it be objected ‘not so, on account of difference (taught in scripture)’, (we say) no, because in each case (the scripture itself) declares that it is not so. ‖ 12 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V12::block-0: (Pūrvapakṣa:) Yet it might be said — what was urged, that Brahman is only nirvikalpa, of one mark, and that it has no twofold characteristic either by itself or by place — that is not tenable. Why? On account of difference (bheda). For different forms of Brahman are taught with reference to each (upāsanā) — Brahman as four-footed, Brahman as having sixteen parts, Brahman characterised by ‘the controller of speech’ etc., Brahman with the three worlds as body and designated by the word ‘Vaiśvānara’, and so on. Hence Brahman’s being possessed of attributes (saviśeṣatva) too is to be admitted. As to what was said — that Brahman cannot have twofold characteristic — there is no contradiction here either, since the difference of form is brought about by the limiting adjuncts. Otherwise the scripture treating of difference would itself become without object — if you say so, (Siddhānta:) we say no. Why? Because in each (passage) there is the declaration that it (the difference) is not real (atad-vacanāt). For with reference to each separate adjunct, the scripture makes one hear only the non-difference of Brahman — ‘And he who is in this earth, made of light, made of the immortal, the puruṣa; and he who is here in the body, the embodied one, made of light, made of the immortal, the puruṣa — this very one, indeed, is he who is this Self’ (Bṛ. Up. 2.5.1) (citation), and so on. Hence it cannot be said that Brahman’s being conjoined with different forms is scriptural — for difference is for the sake of upāsanā, while the import (tātparya) lies in non-difference. ‖ 12 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V13: And likewise some (recensions teach the same view). ‖ 13 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V13::block-0: Moreover, in this very manner, some recensionists hand down only the doctrine of non-difference, prefaced by the censure of the perception of difference — ‘By the mind alone is this to be attained; there is no plurality whatsoever here’ (Kaṭha Up. 2.1.11) (citation), ‘From death to death he goes who sees as if there were plurality here’ (Kaṭha Up. 2.1.10) (citation). Likewise, others (declare) — ‘Knowing the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and the impeller — all this is declared as the threefold Brahman; that is mine’ (Śvet. Up. 1.12) (citation) — declaring that the entire phenomenal world, characterised by enjoyer, enjoyed, and ruler, has Brahman as its sole essential nature. ‖ 13 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V14: (Brahman is) verily formless alone, since that is the principal (purport of the texts). ‖ 14 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V14::block-0: (Leading bhāṣya:) But how is it that, when there are śrutis on Brahman both with form and without form, only formless Brahman is to be ascertained, and not the opposite? Hereto the next answer is read —
