BS_C03_S02_V14::block-1: Brahman is to be ascertained as without form etc. alone, not as possessed of form etc. Why? Because that is the principal (purport) — texts such as ‘not gross, not subtle, not short, not long’ (Bṛ. Up. 3.8.8) (citation), ‘soundless, touchless, formless, undecaying’ (Kaṭha Up. 1.3.15), (Mukti. Up. 2.72) (citation), ‘Verily, ākāśa is the bearer-out of name and form; that within which the two are — that is Brahman’ (Chā. Up. 8.14.1) (citation), ‘Divine, indeed, formless is the puruṣa, with both outer and inner, unborn’ (Muṇḍ. Up. 2.1.2) (citation), ‘This Brahman is without prior, without posterior, without inner, without outer; this Self is Brahman, the all-experiencer’ (Bṛ. Up. 2.5.19) (citation), and so on — these have for their principal (import) the truth of the Self-Brahman free from phenomenal multiplicity (niṣprapañca-brahmātma-tattva), not anything else as their principal import. This has been established in ‘But that, on account of harmonious purport’ (Br. Sū. 1.1.4) (citation). Hence in such passages Brahman is to be ascertained as it is heard (yathāśrutam) — formless alone. The other passages — those that have form-possessing Brahman as their object — are not principal (in their import). They are principal in respect of the injunction of upāsanā. In these (latter) passages, when there is no contradiction, what is heard (yathāśrutam) is to be resorted to. But when there is contradiction, the principal (texts) are stronger than the non-principal — this is the reason for the determination (vinigamanā), by which, even when there are both kinds of śrutis, Brahman is ascertained as formless alone, not as the opposite. ‖ 14 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V15: And like light (which assumes the form of its adjunct without becoming such), since otherwise (the scripture would be) purposeless. ‖ 15 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V15::block-0: (Question:) Then what becomes of the śrutis dealing with the form-possessing (Brahman)? Hereto he says —
BS_C03_S02_V15::block-1: Just as the light of the sun or the moon, pervading the sky and remaining (there), on the conjunction of an adjunct such as a finger and the like, when these (adjuncts) assume forms straight, crooked, etc., appears as if it had assumed those very forms — so Brahman too, on the conjunction of adjuncts such as earth and so on, appears as if it had taken on those forms. The teaching of distinct forms of Brahman, which is based on this (apparent assumption), is for the sake of upāsanā and is not contradictory. Thus, the non-purposelessness (avaiyarthya) of the passages dealing with the form-possessing Brahman is also (secured). For it is not proper to take that some Vedic passages are meaningful and others not, since their authority does not differ. (Pūrvapakṣa:) But even so, what was previously claimed — that Brahman’s twofold characteristic does not exist even by the conjunction of adjuncts — is (now) contradicted. (Siddhānta:) We say no — because what is caused by an adjunct cannot be a property of the substance (vastu-dharmatva-anupapatteḥ). And the limiting adjuncts (upādhis) are themselves brought up by avidyā. And it is precisely while natural avidyā exists that the entire course of worldly and Vedic transaction proceeds — as we have said in various places. ‖ 15 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V16: And (the śruti) declares (Brahman) to be that (Consciousness) only. ‖ 16 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V16::block-0: And the śruti declares Brahman to be Consciousness alone (caitanya-mātra), free of any other distinguishing form, devoid of attributes — ‘As, my dear, a lump of salt is without inner, without outer, wholly a mass of taste alone — even so, indeed, is this Self without inner, without outer, wholly a mass of cognition (prajñāna-ghana) alone’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.5.13) (citation). What is intended is this: of this Self, neither within nor without is there any form other than caitanya; rather, caitanya alone, uninterrupted, is its essential nature — as of a lump of salt, within and without, the salt-taste alone, uninterrupted, exists, not any other taste — just so. ‖ 16 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V17: (The śruti) shows (this), and so too is it remembered (in smṛti). ‖ 17 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V17::block-0: And the śruti shows Brahman by the very negation of all alien forms — on account of its being attributeless — ‘Now, therefore, the instruction is: not thus, not thus’ (Bṛ. Up. 2.3.6) (citation), ‘Other indeed than the known, and beyond the unknown’ (Kena Up. 1.4) (citation), ‘Whence words turn back, together with the mind, not having attained’ (Tait. Up. 2.4.1) (citation), and so on. And it is heard that Bādhva, when questioned by Bāṣkalin, taught Brahman by silence itself — ‘He said, “Sir, teach me”; he remained silent. When the question was put a second and a third time, he said, “We are indeed teaching, but you do not understand. Tranquil is this Self.”’ (citation). Likewise also in the smṛtis, (Brahman) is taught by the negation of the other (paraprātiṣedha) — ‘What is to be known I shall declare, by knowing which one attains immortality. The supreme Brahman, beginningless, is called neither sat nor asat’ (Bhag. Gītā 13.12) (citation), and so on. So also it is recorded that the universe-formed Nārāyaṇa said to Nārada — ‘This is māyā, indeed, fashioned by me, that you see me, O Nārada, as endowed with the qualities of all beings; not thus oughtest thou to know me’ (Mahābhārata 12.339.45–46) (citation). ‖ 17 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V18: And for this very reason (the scriptures employ) the simile, like (the reflection of) the sun (in water) and the like. ‖ 18 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V18::block-0: Precisely because this Self is of the nature of pure consciousness, free from all attributes (nirviśeṣa), beyond speech and mind (vāṅmanasātīta), and to be taught (only) through the negation of (everything) other (parapratiṣedhopadeśya) — for this very reason, having in view its non-real (apāramārthikī) particularisation occasioned by the limiting adjuncts (upādhi-nimittā), the simile of the reflection of the sun in water and the like is adopted in the scriptures of liberation (mokṣaśāstras), as in: ‘Just as this luminous Self, the sun, though one, on becoming associated with the various waters becomes manifold; so too this divine, unborn Self, by reason of the upādhi, is rendered, as it were, of the form of difference in the (several) bodily fields’ (citation), and ‘There is verily one Bhūtātman seated in being after being; he is seen as one and as manifold, like the moon (reflected) in water’ (Brahmabindu 12) (citation), and similar passages. ‖ 18 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V19: But (the cases) are not so alike, since (the Self) is not apprehended (in the manner) of water. ‖ 19 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V19::block-1: Equality with the case of the reflection of the sun in water and the like cannot here hold good, because (the Self) is not apprehended in that manner. For water — being itself corporeal, and distinct from the sun and other corporeal bodies, and located in a remote region — is what is apprehended; in regard to it, the rise of the reflection of the sun and the like is fitting. But the Self is not corporeal (mūrta), nor are the upādhis distinct from it and located in a remote region, since (the Self) is all-pervading and non-different from all. Therefore this illustration is unfitting (ayukta). ‖ 19 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V20: (The Self’s) participation in increase and decrease (of the upādhis), through entering into them, (is established) — owing to the appropriateness of both (the example and that to which it is applied), it is so. ‖ 20 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V20::block-1: On the contrary, this illustration is altogether fitting, since the intended portion (vivakṣitāṃśa) does in fact obtain. For nowhere can total resemblance between the example (dṛṣṭānta) and that which it illustrates (dārṣṭāntika) be shown apart from some particular intended point; were total resemblance to obtain, the very relation of example and exemplified would collapse. Nor is this analogy of the reflection of the sun in water our own private invention; this being a śāstra-given (illustration), only its purpose is set forth (here). What then is the intended likeness? It is stated — ‘participation in increase and decrease’ (vṛddhihrāsabhāktva). For the reflection of the sun in water grows when the water grows, shrinks when the water shrinks, moves when the water moves, becomes divided when the water is divided — thus it conforms to the dharmas of water (jaladharmānuvidhāyī); yet in reality (paramārthatas) the sun is not really thus. Even so Brahman, though in truth unmodified and of one form (paramārthato’vikṛtam ekarūpam api sat), in consequence of (its) entering into the upādhis of the body and the like, partakes, as it were (bhajata iva), of their dharmas — increase, decrease and the rest. Thus, owing to the appropriateness on both sides — that of the illustration and that of the thing illustrated — there is no contradiction. ‖ 20 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V21: And on account of the (scriptural) declaration. ‖ 21 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V21::block-0: And the Śruti declares the entry of the supreme Brahman itself within the upādhis of the body and the like: ‘He made the bodies (cities) of the bipeds, he made the bodies of the quadrupeds; having become a bird, he entered the bodies as the puruṣa’ (Bṛ. Up. 2.5.18) (citation), and ‘Having entered (these) by this living self’ (Chā. Up. 6.3.2) (citation). Therefore that which has been said — ‘And for this very reason (there is) the simile, like (the reflection of) the sun (in water) and the like’ (Br. Sū. 3.2.18) (citation) — is fitting. Hence it is established that Brahman is of one mark only (ekaliṅga), free from determinations (nirvikalpaka), and not of two marks (ubhayaliṅga) nor of the contrary mark (viparītaliṅga).
BS_C03_S02_V21::block-1: Here some (commentators) construct two adhikaraṇas — first, whether Brahman is of one form, with the entire phenomenal world set aside, or whether, like the world, it is endowed with manifold forms; secondly, the phenomenal world having been set aside, whether Brahman is of the nature of Being only (sallakṣaṇa), or of the nature of Consciousness only (bodhalakṣaṇa), or of both natures (ubhayalakṣaṇa). To this we reply — in every way the construction of an additional adhikaraṇa is purposeless. If the labour be for the sake of refuting the manifold-form-ness of the supreme Brahman, that has already been refuted by the previous adhikaraṇa beginning ‘not even by way of place (na sthānato’pi)’ (citation); the latter adhikaraṇa beginning ‘like the light’ (prakāśavac ca) (citation) would then become wholly redundant. Nor can it be said that Brahman is of the nature of Being only and not of the nature of Consciousness, since this would render the Śrutis such as ‘a mass of consciousness alone’ (vijñānaghana eva) (citation) futile. How indeed could a Brahman from which consciousness is excluded be taught as the Self of the conscious individual jīva? Nor can it be said that Brahman is of the nature of Consciousness only and not of the nature of Being, since this would render Śrutis such as ‘He is to be apprehended as “He is” alone’ (Ka. Up. 2.3.13) (citation) futile. How indeed could a consciousness from which Being is excluded be admitted? Nor can it be said that Brahman is of both natures only, since this would contravene what was previously admitted. For one who proclaims Brahman as endowed with a Consciousness exclusive of Being and a Being exclusive of Consciousness, the very state of being-with-the-phenomenal-world (saprapañcatva), which was rejected in the earlier adhikaraṇa, would result. If it be said that, since this is heard from the Śruti, there is no fault — no, since one (Brahman) cannot intelligibly possess many (mutually exclusive) natures. If it be urged that Being itself is Consciousness and Consciousness itself is Being, and there is no mutual exclusion between them — even then, the alternative — whether Brahman is of the nature of Being, or of Consciousness, or of both — would be without basis (nirālambana). The sūtras have been carried by us as constituting one adhikaraṇa. Moreover, since the Śrutis on Brahman, taken as portraying it as having form and as having no form, are conflicting, and since formless Brahman has been (already) accepted, the rest of the Śrutis must necessarily have their import explained. With that purpose, sūtras such as ‘like the light’ (prakāśavac ca) become all the more meaningful.
BS_C03_S02_V21::block-2: And as for what is said — that even the form-affirming Śrutis aim only at the realisation of formless (Brahman) by way of the dissolution of the phenomenal world (prapañca-pravilaya), and have no separate purpose — this too does not appear sound. How? Such phenomenal descriptions as occur in the section of the higher knowledge (paravidyādhikāra), e.g. ‘His horses verily are yoked, a hundred or ten; this verily are the horses, this verily ten thousand and many and infinite’ (Bṛ. Up. 2.5.19) (citation), and the like, are indeed for the purpose of dissolution, since the section concludes with ‘This is that Brahman, without a prior, without a posterior, without inside, without outside’ (Bṛ. Up. 2.5.19) (citation). But descriptions of the phenomenal which occur in the section on meditation (upāsanādhikāra), such as ‘Made of mind, having prāṇa for body, of the form of light’ (Chā. Up. 3.14.2) (citation) — for these the purpose of (mere) dissolution is not just; for they are connected with the very upāsana-injunction in question, as in ‘Let him form a definite resolution’ (Chā. Up. 3.14.1) (citation). Since the primary signification (śruty-avakalpana) of such qualities is upāsana, recourse to secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) for the sake of dissolution is unwarranted. Were dissolution to be the common purport of all (such passages), the statement of the cause for definite restriction in ‘only as formless, since That is principal’ (Br. Sū. 3.2.14) (citation) would have no scope. Their fruit too is understood, in accordance with the upadeśa, to be in some places destruction of demerit, in others attainment of lordship, in others gradual liberation (krama-mukti) — therefore separateness of purport (pārthagarthya) is the right view for upāsana-vākyas and brahma-vākyas, not their being one sentence (eka-vākyatā).
BS_C03_S02_V21::block-3: But how then is the unity of these sentences imagined? — this should be told. If it be said: ‘from the perception of a single nikṣa (injunction), as in the prayāja-darśapūrṇamāsa-vākyas’ — no, since there is no nikṣa in brahma-vākyas. The brahma-vākyas culminate in the bare entity (vastumātra-paryavasāyin) and do not teach an injunction (niyoga). This has been established at length under ‘But that, on account of the harmony (of the texts)’ (Br. Sū. 1.1.4) (citation). And what is the object of the supposed niyoga? — that should be stated. A man being enjoined is enjoined to do something — ‘do thus’ — in some activity of his own. Should it be said: ‘the dissolution of the manifold of duality is the object of the niyoga; for, so long as the manifold of duality is not dissolved, knowledge of Brahman’s reality does not arise; therefore the manifold of duality, which is opposed to the cognition of Brahman, must be dissolved — just as the sacrifice is enjoined upon the heaven-desirer, so the dissolution of the phenomenal upon the liberation-desirer; or just as one wishing to know a pot or other reality lying in darkness dispels the darkness opposed to it, so one wishing to know Brahman’s reality must dissolve the phenomenal opposed to it; for the phenomenal is of the nature of Brahman, not Brahman of the nature of the phenomenal; thus by dissolving the manifold of name and form, the cognition of Brahman’s reality arises’ — to this we ask: what is this so-called dissolution of the phenomenal? Is it like the dissolution of the solidity of ghee on contact with the heat of fire — should the dissolution of the phenomenal be (so) effected? Or is it that the manifold of name and form, superimposed by avidyā upon Brahman, is to be dissolved by knowledge — as the manifold of many moons, produced in one moon by ocular disorder, is dissolved? Now if it be said that the actually existing phenomenal — bodily and other ādhyātmika, and pṛthivī and other bāhya — is to be dissolved, this is impossible for any individual to accomplish; the upadeśa of its dissolution would have an unrealisable object. And were even one of the first liberated to have dissolved earth and the rest, the world would now be devoid of earth and the like. But if it be said that this manifold superimposed by avidyā on the one Brahman is dissolved by knowledge, then Brahman alone is to be intimated by the rejection of the avidyā-superimposed manifold — ‘Brahman, one only without a second’ (citation), ‘That is Truth, that is the Self, That thou art’ (Chā. Up. 6.8.7) (citation); when That is intimated, knowledge arises spontaneously, and by it avidyā is sublated, and thereupon the entire manifold of name and form superimposed by avidyā is dissolved, like the dream-manifold. But if Brahman be not (first) intimated, then even were one to enjoin a hundred times — ‘Have the cognition of Brahman, and the dissolution of the phenomenal’ — neither cognition of Brahman nor dissolution of the phenomenal arises. If it be objected: ‘When Brahman is intimated, the niyoga has its object as that cognition or as the dissolution of the phenomenal’ — no; for both are accomplished merely by the intimation of one’s being identical with Brahman free from the phenomenal. By the very disclosure of the rope’s nature, both the cognition of its nature and the dissolution of the avidyā-superimposed manifold of snake etc. take place; and what has already been done is not done over again.
BS_C03_S02_V21::block-4: Moreover, the supposed enjoinable agent (niyojya) — whom we know in the state of the phenomenal as the jīva — must belong either to the side of the phenomenal or to the side of Brahman. On the first alternative, since by the teaching of phenomenon-free Brahman the jīva, like earth and the rest, is itself dissolved, who is to be enjoined to dissolve the phenomenal? Or for whom would liberation be said to be attained through the niyoga? On the second alternative also, when it has been taught that the unenjoinable Brahman (anniyojyasvabhāva) is the very nature of the jīva, and that jīva-hood is itself a creation of avidyā, then there being no niyojya, there is no niyoga either. The words ‘He is to be seen’ (draṣṭavya) and the rest, recited in the section on supreme knowledge (paravidyādhikāra), are aimed at turning (the mind) towards the truth (tattvābhimukhīkaraṇa-pradhāna), not at being injunctions for cognition of the truth (tattvāvabodhavidhi). In ordinary usage too, in directives such as ‘See this!’, ‘Hear this!’, only attention (praṇidhāna) is enjoined, not cognition itself. For even one whose face is turned towards the object-to-be-known sometimes has cognition, sometimes does not. Therefore the speaker who wishes to make known must show only the object of cognition; and once that is shown, cognition arises by itself, in conformity with the object and the means of knowing. And cognition contrary to what is established by another pramāṇa cannot arise even in one enjoined. If on being enjoined a man should produce a contrary cognition, that would not be cognition (jñāna) at all; rather it would be an act of mind (mānasī kriyā). And were the contrary to arise spontaneously, it would simply be an error (bhrānti). But cognition is born of pramāṇa and has the as-is object; it cannot be produced by even a hundred niyogas, nor warded off by a hundred prohibitions. For it is not subject to the person (puruṣatantra), but subject to the object (vastutantra). For this reason too, niyoga is absent. Furthermore — if the Veda were to terminate in niyoga (alone), then the unenjoinable Brahman-Selfhood of the jīva, which is admitted (in the texts), would itself be without pramāṇa. If, again, the śāstra were itself to declare the unenjoinable Brahman-Selfhood and at the same time enjoin man upon its cognition, then on the single Brahma-śāstra would fall the predicament of being twofold in import (dvyarthapara) and contradictory in import (viruddhārthapara). And on the supposition of niyoga-import, faults such as abandonment of the heard (śrutahāni), construction of the unheard (aśrutakalpanā), liberation having a fruit-like-action’s unseen result (adṛṣṭaphalatva), and impermanence (anityatva) — none of these can be averted by anyone. Therefore the brahma-vākyas terminate in cognition (avagati-niṣṭha), not in niyoga. Hence the inference of one-sentence-ness (eka-vākyatā) from the perception of a single niyoga is unsound.
BS_C03_S02_V21::block-5: Even granting the existence of niyoga in the brahma-vākyas, the unity (between phenomenon-less and phenomenon-full passages) is unestablished. When difference of niyoga is recognised by other means such as differing words, recourse to a single niyoga everywhere cannot be had. In the prayāja-darśapūrṇamāsa-passages oneness is fitting because of identity in the qualifying part (adhikāraṃśa). But here, as between sa-guṇa and nir-guṇa injunctions, there is no such identity in qualifying part. The qualities of being-of-the-form-of-light and the like are not aids to the dissolution of the phenomenal, nor is the dissolution of the phenomenal an aid to the qualities such as being-of-the-form-of-light, since they are mutually contradictory. Total dissolution of the phenomenal and consideration of a portion of the phenomenal cannot rightly be co-ordinated in one substrate. Therefore the division as we have stated, between teachings of the formed and the formless, is the more fitting. ‖ 21 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V22: For (the text) negates only the ‘so-muchness’ that has been mentioned, and thereafter speaks (of Brahman) further. ‖ 22 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V22::block-0: Beginning with ‘Two indeed are the forms of Brahman, the formed and the formless’ (Bṛ. Up. 2.3.1) (citation), and dividing the five great elements into two classes, and showing that the formless essence (amūrtarasa) — designated by the word puruṣa — has the colours of saffron and the rest, (the text) again recites: ‘Now therefore the teaching: not so, not so (neti neti); for there is nothing higher than this “not so” — there is nothing other’ (Bṛ. Up. 2.3.6) (citation). Therein we are eager to know what is the object of this negation. For nothing is here marked out by ‘this’ or ‘that’ as what is to be negated. But by the word iti, something is here intimated as the object of negation, since the use of the negative particle nañ here is connected with iti. The word iti is one whose ground is something proximate, and is seen used in a sense equivalent to evam, ‘thus’, in usages such as ‘Thus indeed the teacher relates’ (iti ha smopādhyāyaḥ kathayati) and the like. And what is proximate here, by the force of the topic, is the twofold form of Brahman together with the phenomenal, and that Brahman whose those two forms are. Hence the doubt arises in us — does this negation negate both, the form and the form-possessor? Or one (only)? And if one only, does it negate Brahman and reserve the forms, or does it negate the forms and reserve Brahman?
BS_C03_S02_V22::block-1: There (with the pūrvapakṣa-view) — owing to the equal proximity (prakṛtatva) of both, we entertain the apprehension that it negates both. And there are two negations here, since the word neti is used twice. By one of them the form of Brahman together with the phenomenal is negated, and by the other the form-possessing Brahman — such is the surmise. Or rather, Brahman as form-possessor is itself negated; for Brahman, being beyond speech and mind, has its existence as inaccessible to imagining, and is therefore fit for negation. But the manifold of forms, being within reach of perception and the rest, is not fit for negation. The repetition is for emphasis. — Such being the prima-facie position, we say (in the siddhānta):
BS_C03_S02_V22::block-2: First, the negation of both is not tenable, since it would entail the doctrine of the void (śūnyavāda) — for indeed, taking some real (paramārtha) as basis, the unreal (aparamārtha) is negated, as the snake and the like in regard to the rope and the like; and that operates only when some entity is left over. In a total negation, what other entity could remain? And if no other remains, that very thing which is undertaken to be negated, being unable to be negated, would attain reality, whereby negation becomes impossible. Nor is the negation of Brahman tenable — it conflicts with the opening text ‘I shall expound to you Brahman’ (Bṛ. Up. 2.1.1) (citation), with the censure ‘He becomes verily as a non-entity, if he knows Brahman as non-being’ (Tai. Up. 2.6.1) (citation), with the affirmative ‘He is to be apprehended as “He is” alone’ (Ka. Up. 2.3.13) (citation), and would result in the disruption of all Vedānta. Brahman’s being beyond speech and mind also is not stated with intent of non-being. For not, after, with great preparatory ardour, having taught Brahman in the Vedānta passages — ‘The knower of Brahman attains the highest’ (Tai. Up. 2.1.1) (citation), ‘Brahman is truth, knowledge, infinite’ (Tai. Up. 2.1.1) (citation) — would the same Brahman’s non-being be then asserted; for the maxim is ‘rather than wash off mud, it is better not to touch it from afar’. The way of (the text’s) exposition is this: ‘That from which words turn back, not having reached, together with the mind’ (Tai. Up. 2.4.1) (citation). What is meant is — Brahman is beyond speech and mind, not contained within (any) object, the inmost Self (pratyagātman), eternally pure, free, and of the nature of mukta. Therefore it must be admitted that (the text) negates the manifold of forms of Brahman and reserves Brahman.
BS_C03_S02_V22::block-3: It is this that is now stated — ‘For (the text) negates the so-muchness that has been mentioned’ (prakṛtaitāvattvaṃ pratiṣedhati). The form of Brahman, having (its) so-muchness — circumscribed extent, marked by the formed and the formless — that has been mentioned in the prior portion of the text, that this expression negates. For that has been the topic, expounded in the prior text both adhidaivata and adhyātma. And the other form, born of that, in the form of vāsanā, the formless essence designated by puruṣa, having for its support the subtle body (liṅgātman), shown by the analogies of saffron and the like — for the formless essence, the puruṣa, cannot be ocularly grasped as having (visible) form. Hence this whole form-bearing form of Brahman is, by the word iti whose ground is what is proximate, brought up before the negative particle (nañ); this is what is understood. But Brahman has been indicated in the prior text by the genitive (rūpasya brahmaṇaḥ) as a qualifier of (the) form, not in its own primary position. After the two forms belonging to Brahman have been expounded, when the inquiry as to the proper nature of the form-possessor is raised, this is begun: ‘Now therefore the teaching: not so, not so’ (Bṛ. Up. 2.3.6) (citation). Therein, by the rejection of the imagined form, the apprehension of Brahman’s own nature is determined as ‘this’. For this entire effect (kārya), having (Brahman) for its substrate, is what is negated by ‘not so, not so’. And it is fitting that the effect, on account of being a creation of speech and so forth, is unreal — hence the negation ‘not so, not so’. But not (the negation) of Brahman, since (Brahman) is the root of all imagination. Nor should this apprehension be entertained — how is it that the śāstra itself, having shown the twofold form of Brahman, itself again negates it? — to which the maxim ‘rather than wash off mud, better not to touch it from afar’ applies; for this śāstra does not indicate Brahman’s twofold form as something to-be-conveyed; rather it adverts to that twofold form which is popularly imagined upon Brahman, in order to negate it and to expound the pure Brahman’s svarūpa — therefore there is no flaw. And these two negations, by the rule of yathāsaṃkhya, negate both the formed (mūrta) and the formless (amūrta). Or, the prior negation negates the heap of beings (bhūtarāśi), the latter the heap of impressions (vāsanārāśi). Or this is a vīpsā (repetition for distributive sense) — ‘not so, not so’: whatever is uttarable, all that is not — for if a number-by-number negation were made, the inquiry ‘if this is not Brahman, what other is Brahman?’ might arise; in vīpsā, all the entire mass of objects being negated, the inquiry ceases — Brahman, the inmost Self (pratyagātman), is non-object. Therefore the determination is: it negates the manifold imagined upon Brahman, reserves Brahman itself.
BS_C03_S02_V22::block-4: And from this also is this the determination — ‘thereafter (it) speaks (of Brahman) further’: ‘there is nothing other than this, supreme’ (anyat param asti) (Bṛ. Up. 2.3.6) (citation). For if the negation terminated in non-being, what could it speak of as ‘there is something other supreme’? Therein this is the construction of the syllables: having designated Brahman by ‘not so, not so’, (the text) further explicates that designation. What is the meaning of ‘not so, not so’? — ‘There is nothing other than this Brahman’: hence ‘not so, not so’; not that (Brahman) itself does not exist — that is the meaning. And it shows: there exists another supreme, unnegated Brahman. When, however, the syllables are construed thus — ‘There is nothing other than this designation in the form of negation of the phenomenal (iti na, iti na), other supreme designation of Brahman is’ — then ‘thereafter speaks further’ must be applied to the topic of the name (nāmadheya): for (the text) says: ‘Now its name is the Truth of truth (satyasya satyam); the prāṇas indeed are truth, the truth of these is He’ (Bṛ. Up. 2.1.20) (citation). And that is samañjasa when the negation terminates in Brahman. But if the negation terminates in non-being, how could it be uttered, ‘the truth of truth’? Therefore we conclude: this negation terminates in Brahman, not in non-being. ‖ 22 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V23: That (Brahman) is unmanifest, for so (the Śruti) declares. ‖ 23 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V23::block-0: If that supreme Brahman, other than the manifold of phenomena negated, exists, why is it not apprehended? — to this it is said: that is unmanifest (avyakta), not apprehensible by sense (anindriyagrāhya), since it is the witness of all that is seen (sarvadṛśya-sākṣitva). For Śruti speaks thus: ‘He is not grasped by the eye, nor by speech, nor by the other deities, nor by tapas, nor by works’ (Mu. Up. 3.1.8) (citation), ‘That Self is “not so, not so”; he is ungraspable, for he is not grasped’ (Bṛ. Up. 3.9.26) (citation), ‘That which is invisible, ungraspable’ (Mu. Up. 1.1.6) (citation), ‘When he becomes (firm) in this invisible, bodiless, indefinable, unsupported (Self)’ (Tai. Up. 2.7.1) (citation), and the like. Smṛti also: ‘This is said to be unmanifest, this unthinkable, this unmodifiable’ (Bh. Gī. 2.25) (citation), and the like. ‖ 23 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V24: And moreover, in absorption (saṃrādhana), (it is seen) by direct perception and inference (i.e. Śruti and Smṛti). ‖ 24 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V24::block-0: Moreover, the yogins, at the time of saṃrādhana (perfect propitiation/absorption), see this very Self — devoid of the entire phenomenal manifold, unmanifest. Saṃrādhana is the practice of devotion (bhakti), meditation (dhyāna), profound concentration (praṇidhāna), and the like. How is it known that they see (Him) at the time of saṃrādhana? By pratyakṣa and anumāna — i.e. by Śruti and Smṛti, that is the meaning. Thus Śruti: ‘The Self-existent pierced the senses outwards; therefore one sees outward, not the inner Self. A certain wise one, longing for immortality, with eyes turned inward, beheld the Inner Self’ (Ka. Up. 2.1.1) (citation), and ‘By tranquillity of knowledge, with the sattva purified, then he, in meditation, sees Him without parts’ (Mu. Up. 3.1.8) (citation), and the like. Smṛti also: ‘To Him, the Yoga-Self, salutations — whom the sleepless, those who have conquered the breath, the contented, the sense-controlled, in absorption behold as Light’ (Mahābhārata 12.47.54) (citation), ‘The yogins behold Him, the Eternal Lord’ (Mahābhārata 5.46.1) (citation), and the like. ‖ 24 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V25: And, like light and the like, (their seeming difference is) non-essential; and there is illumination, owing to the works (or upādhi-functions), as is repeatedly declared. ‖ 25 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V25::block-0: If it be objected — since one admits the relation of saṃrādhya (Him to be propitiated) and saṃrādhaka (the propitiator), there must be otherness between the supreme Self and the other (jīva-self) — to that we say:
BS_C03_S02_V25::block-1: Just as light, ākāśa, the sun and the like, in regard to actions (karmas) such as the finger, the water-pot, the water in it, etc., taken as upādhis, appear as if endowed with particularity, yet do not abandon their natural undifferentiated essence — even so this difference of selves (ātma-bheda) is occasioned by upādhi alone, but in itself there is mere oneness of Self (aikātmya). Thus indeed, in the Vedānta texts, the non-difference (abheda) of the jīva and the prājña is propounded again and again by repetition (abhyāsa). ‖ 25 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V26: Therefore, with the Infinite — for so the indicatory mark shows. (26)
BS_C03_S02_V26::block-0: And therefore, since non-difference is natural and difference is brought about by avidyā, the jīva, having dispelled avidyā by vidyā, attains oneness with the supreme, infinite, omniscient (prājña) Self. So indeed there is an indicatory mark (liṅga) — ‘Verily, he who knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself’ (Muṇḍ. Up. 3.2.9) (citation); ‘Being Brahman alone, he attains Brahman’ (Bṛh. Up. 4.4.6) (citation), and the like. (26)
BS_C03_S02_V27: But on account of the twofold designation (of difference and non-difference, scripture should be understood) like the snake and its coils. (27)
BS_C03_S02_V27::block-0: (Pūrvapakṣa view introduced) — In the very same context of the saṃrādhya–saṃrādhaka (the worshipped and the worshipper), he sets forth another opinion, for the purpose of clarifying his own doctrine. In some places difference between the jīva and the prājña (supreme Self) is declared — ‘Then, meditating, one beholds Him, the partless’ (Muṇḍ. Up. 3.1.8) (citation), thus by the relation of meditator and object of meditation, and seer and seen. ‘He attains the divine Person, higher than the high’ (Muṇḍ. Up. 3.2.8) (citation), thus by the relation of goer and goal. ‘He who, dwelling within all beings, controls (them)’ (citation), thus by the relation of controller and controlled. But in some places the very non-difference of the two is declared — ‘That thou art’ (Chānd. Up. 6.8.7) (citation); ‘I am Brahman’ (Bṛh. Up. 1.4.10) (citation); ‘This is thy Self, the inmost of all’ (Bṛh. Up. 3.4.1) (citation); ‘This is thy Self, the inner controller, the immortal’ (Bṛh. Up. 3.7.3) (citation). Now, when there is such a twofold designation, if non-difference alone were exclusively grasped, the declaration of difference would be without any basis. Hence, owing to the perception of the twofold designation, the truth here ought to be like the snake and its coils — just as ‘snake’ stands for non-difference, while ‘the curve, expanse, length, etc. of the coils’ stand for difference, so it is here also. (27)
BS_C03_S02_V28: Or like light and its source, both being of the nature of luminosity. (28)
BS_C03_S02_V28::block-0: (Pūrvapakṣa continues) — Or this should be understood like light and its substratum — just as the light of the sun and the sun, its substratum, are not absolutely different, since both equally have the nature of tejas (luminous brilliance); yet they admit of the designation of difference — even so here also. (28)
BS_C03_S02_V29::block-0: (Siddhānta) — Or rather, as was previously set forth — ‘And there is non-distinctness, as in the case of light, etc.’ (citation) — even so this should be. For, since bondage is wrought by avidyā, liberation by vidyā stands to reason. But if, on the other hand, some Self were really bound, being either a configuration of the supreme Self by the snake-and-coils analogy, or a part-portion of It by the light-and-substratum analogy, then, since real bondage cannot be removed, the futility of the scriptures of liberation would result. Nor does the śruti here designate both difference and non-difference equally; it teaches non-difference alone as the principal purport, while it merely repeats difference, already established prior, with a view to (conveying) some other purpose. Therefore the established conclusion is just this — ‘And there is non-distinctness, as in the case of light, etc.’ (citation). (29)
BS_C03_S02_V30: And on account of the (scriptural) prohibition. (30)
BS_C03_S02_V30::block-0: And for this reason too the conclusion is just this — because scripture prohibits any other conscious being apart from the supreme Self — ‘There is no other seer than this’ (Bṛh. Up. 3.7.23) (citation), and the like. ‘Now therefore the teaching: Not so, not so’ (Bṛh. Up. 2.3.6) (citation); ‘This Brahman is without a prior, without a posterior, without an inside, without an outside’ (Bṛh. Up. 2.5.19) (citation) — by such (texts) the negation of all the manifold world distinct from Brahman, and the leaving over of Brahman alone, makes it understood that this very (non-dualism) is the established conclusion. (30)
BS_C03_S02_V31: (There is something) higher than this (Brahman), because of the designations of bridge, measure, connection, and difference. (31)
BS_C03_S02_V31::block-0: (Pūrvapakṣa, leading bhāṣya) — There arises a doubt, owing to apparent conflict among śruti texts, as to whether or not, beyond this Brahman in which all manifoldness has been cast off and which has been determined (to be the sole reality), there exists yet another reality. For some passages, on first appearance, seem to teach yet another reality higher than even Brahman. To remove (such doubt) about them this beginning is undertaken —
BS_C03_S02_V31::block-1: (Pūrvapakṣa, main bhāṣya) — There ought to be another reality higher than this Brahman. Whence? From the designation as bridge, the designation as measure, the designation as connection, and the designation as difference. First, the designation as bridge — ‘Now this Self is the bridge, the supporting boundary’ (Chānd. Up. 8.4.1) (citation) — proclaims the bridge-hood of Brahman, denoted by the word ‘ātman’. The word ‘bridge’ in the world is well-known with reference to a structure of earth, wood, and the like that holds back the flow of water. But here the word ‘bridge’ is applied to the Self, hence, like an ordinary bridge, it gives us to understand the existence of yet another thing other than the Self-bridge. And from the use of the verb ‘to cross over’ — ‘having crossed over the bridge’ (Chānd. Up. 8.4.2) (citation) — just as, having crossed over an ordinary bridge, one reaches dry land which is not a bridge, so, having crossed over the Self-bridge, one reaches the non-Self which is not a bridge — so it is understood. There is also the designation as measure — ‘This Brahman is four-footed, eight-hoofed, sixteen-membered’ (citation). Whatever in the world is measured, delimited as ‘this much is this’, like the kārṣāpaṇa coin, with respect to that it is well established that there exists something else (besides). In the same way, from the measuring of Brahman, it is understood that there must be some other thing (apart) from It. So too there is the designation as connection — ‘He becomes united with Being, dear one, at that time’ (Chānd. Up. 6.8.1) (citation); ‘the embodied Self’ (Tait. Up. 2.3.1) (citation); ‘embraced by the all-knowing Self’ (Bṛh. Up. 4.3.21) (citation). And among things measured, connection with another measured thing is observed, as that of men with a city. Now scripture declares the connection of jīvas with Brahman in deep sleep. Hence it is understood that there is some other unmeasured thing higher than that. The designation as difference too conveys this very meaning. Thus — ‘Now He who is seen within the sun, the golden Person’ (Chānd. Up. 1.6.6) (citation) — having designated the Lord with the sun as substratum, He is then designated as a different Lord with the eye as substratum — ‘Now He who is seen within the eye, the Person’ (Chānd. Up. 1.7.5) (citation). And He extends to the latter the (qualities of) form etc. of the former — ‘His form is verily the same as the (other’s) form; whatever are the (other’s) chants are His chants; whatever name is His, that is the (other’s) name’ (Chānd. Up. 1.7.5) (citation). And lordship of both is designated with a fixed limit — ‘Whatever worlds are higher than that one, of those He is lord, and of the gods’ desires’ (Chānd. Up. 1.6.8) (citation), of one; ‘Whatever worlds are lower than this one, of those He is lord, and of the human desires’ (Chānd. Up. 1.7.6) (citation), of the other — like ‘this is the kingdom of the king of Magadha, this is that of the king of Videha’. Thus, by these designations of bridge etc., (it follows that) there is something higher than Brahman. (31)
BS_C03_S02_V32: But (the designation is only) on account of similarity. (32)
BS_C03_S02_V32::block-0: (Siddhānta, leading bhāṣya) — On this being so contended, the response is given —
BS_C03_S02_V32::block-1: (Siddhānta, main bhāṣya) — By the word ‘tu’ (but) the conclusion contended for is set aside. There cannot be anything other than Brahman, since there is no means of valid knowledge for it — for we obtain no pramāṇa whatever for the existence of any other (reality). For it has been determined that the origin etc. of the entire mass of things that come into being belongs to Brahman, and that the effect is non-different from the cause; nor is anything apart from Brahman possibly unborn, owing to the affirmation ‘Being alone, dear one, was this in the beginning, one only, without a second’ (Chānd. Up. 6.2.1) (citation). And from the promise that ‘by the cognition of the One there is the cognition of all’, no existence of any reality apart from Brahman stands to reason. (Objection:) But the designations of bridge etc. were said to indicate a reality apart from Brahman. (Refuted:) ‘No’, we reply — first, the designation as bridge cannot establish the existence of anything outside Brahman. For it says ‘the Self is the bridge’; it does not say ‘there is something higher than that’. Now, when there is no further beyond, bridge-hood would not stand to reason; hence one might fancy some ‘higher’ — but this is not reasonable, for it is forced fancying of what is not established. Moreover, by adducing, on the basis of the designation as bridge, an external reality outside the bridge in the manner of an ordinary bridge, the (consequence of) being made of earth and wood would also follow, which is not reasonable, since it conflicts with the śruti of being unborn etc. (Nirvacana:) Therefore, the word ‘bridge’ is applied to the Self in the sense of similarity to a bridge — by way of fitting (śliṣyate). The holding-apart (vidhāraṇa) of the world and of its boundaries is the bridge-similarity in the Self. Hence ‘bridge as it were’ — thus is the present Self praised. As for ‘having crossed over the bridge’, since (literal) crossing-beyond is impossible, the verb ‘to cross’ stands solely in the sense of ‘to attain (fully)’ — just as ‘he has crossed grammar’ means ‘he has attained (mastery of) it’, not ‘he has gone beyond it’ — so here too. (32)
BS_C03_S02_V33: (The measure-designation is) for the sake of (steadying) understanding, like the (analogy of the) feet (of a coin or of the syllable AUM). (33)
BS_C03_S02_V33::block-0: As to what was urged, that there is something higher (than Brahman) on account of the designation as measure — to that it is replied — even the designation as measure is not for the purpose of conveying the existence of any reality apart from Brahman. Then for what purpose? For the purpose of buddhi — that is, for the sake of upāsanā (meditation). (Reflecting) ‘How indeed may the buddhi (intellect) be made firm in Brahman?’, the very fancying of a measure for Brahman is undertaken, by way of (figurative) modification — of the form ‘four-footed, eight-hoofed, sixteen-membered’. For in unmodified, infinite Brahman, the buddhi is not capable of being steadied by all human beings, since human beings have buddhis of low, middling, and high (capacity). ‘Like the feet’ — just as for the meditational symbols (pratīka) of Brahman, namely manas (mind) at the personal level and ākāśa at the deity level, four feet — speech and the rest, related to the mind — are imagined, and four — fire and the rest, related to ākāśa — are imagined, for the sake of meditation — even so. Or else ‘like the feet’ may mean — just as in a kārṣāpaṇa (coin) the division into ‘pādas’ (quarters) is conceived for the abundance of practical use — for not all people are at all times able to transact (business) with a whole kārṣāpaṇa, since the measure is not fixed in buying and selling — even so is the meaning. (33)
BS_C03_S02_V34: By reason of the particularity of locus, like light and the rest. ‖ 34 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V34::block-0: In this sūtra the refutation of both the designations — the designation of relation and the designation of difference — is set forth. As for what was urged (in the pūrvapakṣa), namely that ‘by reason of the designation of relation and by reason of the designation of difference, [the individual self] would be other than the Supreme,’ that too is unsound; for, even of one and the same [Self], these two designations become intelligible by reference to a particularity of locus (sthāna-viśeṣa-apekṣayā). With regard to the designation of relation, this is the meaning: that quiescence which arises, upon the cessation of the upādhi, of the particular cognition that has sprung up through conjunction with a particular locus consisting of the upādhis such as the buddhi — that quiescence is [spoken of as] ‘relation with the Supreme Self’; thus it is figuratively employed (upacaryate) with reference to the upādhi, not with reference to a [supposed] limitedness [of Brahman]. Likewise the designation of difference also of Brahman is figuratively employed only with reference to the difference of upādhis, not with reference to any difference of intrinsic nature (svarūpa-bheda). The phrase ‘like light and the rest’ (prakāśādivat) is the introduction of an illustration: just as, of one and the same light — solar or lunar — when a particularity has arisen through conjunction with an upādhi, the designation of relation arises upon the cessation of the upādhi, and the designation of difference arises through difference of the upādhis; or just as, in the case of the space within a needle, a noose, etc. (sūcī-pāśa-ākāśādiṣu), these two designations of relation and difference operate solely with reference to the upādhis — even so here. ‖ 34 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V35: And on account of [its] being intelligible. ‖ 35 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V35::block-0: And precisely such a relation, and not any other kind, is intelligible here; for the scripture declares this very relation as a relation of intrinsic identity, in the words ‘he becomes merged in his own [Self]’ (Chā. Up. 6.8.1) (citation); and since the intrinsic nature is imperishable (anapāyitva), no relation on the analogy of ‘man and city’ (nara-nagara-nyāyena) is here possible. But on account of the obscuration of the intrinsic nature brought about by the upādhi, the text ‘he becomes merged in his own [Self]’ (Chā. Up. 6.8.1) (citation) does become intelligible. Likewise, difference too of any other kind is impossible, since it would conflict with the oneness of the Lord (eka-īśvaratva) which is established by very many scriptural texts. And accordingly the śruti renders intelligible a designation of difference based on locus, even of one and the same ākāśa: ‘That ākāśa which is outside of the man’ (Chā. Up. 3.12.7) (citation), ‘That ākāśa which is within the man’ (Chā. Up. 3.12.8) (citation), ‘That ākāśa which is within the heart’ (Chā. Up. 3.12.9) (citation). ‖ 35 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V36: Likewise, because of the negation of any other [reality]. ‖ 36 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V36::block-0: Having thus, by overthrowing the designations such as ‘bridge’ etc. — which are the grounds urged by the opponent — [the Bhāṣyakāra] now closes [the discussion] by reinforcing his own thesis with a further reason. From the negation of any other [reality] also (anya-pratiṣedhāt) it is understood that there is no further entity over and above Brahman. Thus: ‘He himself is below’ (Chā. Up. 7.25.1) (citation), ‘I myself am below’ (Chā. Up. 7.25.1) (citation), ‘The Self alone is below’ (Chā. Up. 7.25.2) (citation), ‘Whosoever knows everything as other than the Self — him does everything forsake’ (Bṛ. Up. 2.4.6) (citation), ‘Brahman alone is all this’, ‘The Self alone is all this’ (Chā. Up. 7.25.2) (citation), ‘There is no plurality whatever here’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.19) (citation), ‘Than which there is nothing higher and nothing lower’ (Śve. Up. 3.9) (citation), ‘That Brahman is without anything before, without anything after, without anything within, without anything outside’ (Bṛ. Up. 2.5.19) (citation) — and other such statements, occurring in their own context and incapable of being construed in any other sense, debar the existence of any further entity distinct from Brahman. And from the śruti regarding [Brahman as] innermost of all (sarva-antara-śruti), it is determined that there is no inner Self other than the Supreme Self. ‖ 36 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V37: By this, [its] all-pervasiveness [is established], from the words denoting extension and the rest. ‖ 37 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V37::block-0: By this — namely, by the refutation of the designations such as ‘bridge’ etc., and by recourse to the negation of any other [reality] — the all-pervasiveness (sarvagatatva) too of the Self is established. For otherwise it could not be established. Indeed, if the designations such as ‘bridge’ and the rest were to be admitted in their primary sense, the Self would be saddled with limitation (paricchedaḥ prasajyeta), since the things of the kind ‘bridge’ etc. are themselves limited. Likewise, were there no negation of any other [reality], then on the principle that ‘an entity is differentiated from another entity,’ limitation alone would attach to the Self. And His all-pervasiveness is known from the words denoting extension and the rest (āyāma-śabda-ādibhyaḥ). The ‘word denoting extension’ (āyāma-śabda) is a word expressive of pervasion (vyāpti-vacanaḥ śabdaḥ). ‘As wide indeed as is this ākāśa, so wide is this ākāśa within the heart’ (Chā. Up. 8.1.3) (citation), ‘Like ākāśa, all-pervading and eternal’ (citation), ‘Greater than the heaven’ (Chā. Up. 3.14.3) (citation), ‘Greater than ākāśa’ (Śat. Br. 10.6.3.2) (citation), ‘Eternal, all-pervading, immovable, unmoving, this primaeval one’ (Bh. Gītā 2.24) (citation) — śrutis, smṛtis and reasonings such as these make known the all-pervasiveness of the Self. ‖ 37 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V38: The fruit [of action proceeds] from Him, on account of [its] being intelligible. ‖ 38 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V38::block-0: Of that very same Brahman, in its empirical condition wherein the distinction of ruler and ruled (īśitr̥-īśitavya-vibhāga) obtains, this further nature is now described. The fruit of action — manifest in the world of saṃsāra, well-known as threefold for living beings, namely as desirable, undesirable, and mixed (iṣṭa-aniṣṭa-vyāmiśra) — is this fruit derived from action itself, or from the Lord? Such is the inquiry. Thereupon it is first propounded — the fruit ought to be from this, [i.e.] from the Lord. Why? On account of [its] being intelligible (upapatteḥ). For He, the surveyor of all, ordaining the manifold creation, sustenance and dissolution, and being knower of the particularities of place and time (deśa-kāla-viśeṣa-abhijñatva), produces for the agents the fruit appropriate to their actions — and so it is intelligible. But action, perishing every moment, cannot produce a fruit that is to come about at a later time — that is unintelligible, because there can be no production of a thing from a non-being. (Pūrvapakṣa) It might be urged: action, while perishing, gives rise at its own time to its appropriate fruit and then perishes; that fruit, intervened by [later] time, will subsequently be enjoyed by the agent. — (Siddhānta) Even that does not stand the test, since fruit-hood (phalatva) is unintelligible apart from antecedent connection with an enjoyer. For in the world that alone is well-known as a ‘fruit’ which, at whatever time, is enjoyed as pleasure or pain by the Self. People in the world do not regard pleasure or pain unconnected with a self as ‘fruit.’ Now if it be said, ‘let there not be the production of fruit immediately after action; the fruit will arise from the apūrva, the after-effect of action’ — that too does not hold, because the apūrva, being non-sentient and on a par with a piece of wood or a clod of earth, cannot, unless set in motion by a sentient being, set itself in motion; and there is also no pramāṇa for its existence. If it be said, ‘arthāpatti (presumption) is the pramāṇa,’ — no; for, the Lord being established [as the giver of fruits], arthāpatti has no further field of operation (arthāpatti-kṣayāt). ‖ 38 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V39: And on account of [its] being declared in śruti. ‖ 39 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V39::block-0: It is not merely from intelligibility (upapatti) alone that we infer the Lord to be the cause of the fruit; but rather — on account of [its] being declared in śruti also (śrutatvāt), we hold the Lord Himself to be the cause of the fruit. And accordingly, the śruti says: ‘He, indeed, is this great unborn Self, the eater of food, the giver of wealth’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.24) (citation) — and other such [texts]. ‖ 39 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V40: Jaimini [holds it to be] dharma, for that very reason. ‖ 40 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V40::block-0: But the ācārya Jaimini holds dharma to be the giver of fruit — for that very reason, namely, śruti and upapatti. (Pūrvapakṣa-of-Jaimini) For this purport is heard in such sentences as ‘He who desires heaven should sacrifice’ and the like. There, since the sacrifice is admitted as the object of the injunctive śruti (vidhi-śruti), the sacrifice is understood to be the producer of heaven. Otherwise the sacrifice would become one without anyone undertaking it, and then the upadeśa (instruction) of it would become purposeless. — Now [the objection], that ‘a fruit is unintelligible from action which perishes every moment,’ is set aside. There is no fault here, because of the authority of śruti — if śruti is pramāṇa, the connection between action and fruit, just as it is heard, must be admitted in such manner as it is intelligible. And action cannot, without producing some apūrva, perish and yet give a fruit intervened by later time. Therefore it is to be inferred that there exists a certain subtle later state of action, or a prior state of fruit, called apūrva. And this purport stands intelligible in the manner stated. But that the Lord gives the fruit is unintelligible — because of the unintelligibility of variegated effects from a non-variegated cause; because of the contingency of partiality and cruelty (vaiṣamya-naighr̥ṇya-prasaṅgāt); and because of the contingency of the futility of [enjoined] performance (anuṣṭhāna-vaiyarthya-āpatti). Therefore the fruit is from dharma alone. ‖ 40 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V41: But the former [view holds]; [thus] Bādarāyaṇa [maintains], on account of [the Lord's] being designated as the cause [even of dharma and adharma]. ‖ 41 ‖
BS_C03_S02_V41::block-0: But the ācārya Bādarāyaṇa holds the previously-stated Lord Himself to be the cause of the fruit. The view that the fruit comes solely from action, or solely from apūrva, is excluded by the word ‘tu’ (‘but’). The siddhānta is — whether dependent upon action or dependent upon apūrva, however that may be, the fruit comes from the Lord. Why? On account of [His] being designated as the cause (hetu-vyapadeśāt). For the Lord is designated as the cause even of dharma and adharma, in that He causes [the agent] to do them, and as the giver of the fruit: ‘He indeed makes him do good action whom He wishes to lead up from these worlds; He alone makes him do evil action whom He wishes to lead downward’ (citation). And this purport is recollected in the Bhagavad-Gītā: ‘Whatever form any devotee desires to worship with faith, that very faith of his I make unwavering’ (Bh. Gītā 7.21) (citation), ‘Endowed with that faith, he engages in the worship of that [form] and obtains therefrom his desires — actually ordained by Me as beneficial’ (Bh. Gītā 7.22) (citation). And in all the Vedānta-texts, creations are designated as caused by the Lord. And this very fact — namely, that He produces creatures conformably to their respective karman (svakarma-anurūpāḥ prajāḥ sr̥jati) — is the Lord's fruit-causality. The faults urged, such as the unintelligibility of variegated effects [from a non-variegated cause] etc., do not attach to the Lord, because of His [acting] in dependence upon the effort already exerted [by the agents] (kr̥ta-prayatna-apekṣatva). ‖ 41 ‖
BS_C03_S03_INTRO1::block-0: The tattva (essential nature) of Brahman, which is to be cognised, has been expounded. Now it is examined whether vijñānāni (modes of knowledge / upāsanās) differ in each separate Vedānta or not. — But surely Brahman, which is to be cognised, has been ascertained to be devoid of distinctions of prior and posterior and the rest, of one taste (eka-rasa), like a homogeneous lump of rock-salt (saindhava-ghana-vat). What occasion is there here for considering difference or non-difference of vijñānas? Nor can it be said that, just as multiplicity of karmas (is taught) so a multiplicity of Brahmans is intended to be expounded in the Vedāntas, since Brahman is one (eka) and of one form (eka-rūpa). And in Brahman which is of one form, vijñānas of many forms cannot arise; for it is not the case that ‘the object is one way and the cognition another way’ — that does not amount to non-erroneous (abhrānta) cognition. If, however, in one Brahman many vijñānas were intended to be expounded in the Vedāntas, then one of them would be non-erroneous, the rest erroneous, and there would arise the contingency of non-trustworthiness (anāśvāsa-prasaṅga) in the Vedāntas. Therefore there is no scope at all to entertain the supposition of a difference of Brahma-vijñāna in each Vedānta. Nor can the non-difference (abheda) of this be asserted on the ground of non-difference of injunction and the like (codanādi-aviśeṣāt), because Brahma-vijñāna is not characterised by injunction (acodanā-lakṣaṇa). For the Ācārya has stated, at ‘But that, on account of harmonious purport (samanvayāt)’ (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.4), that Brahma-vijñāna is generated by Brahma-vākyas which are not principally injunctive but terminate in the (existent) entity (vastu-paryavasāyin). How then does he commence this consideration of difference and non-difference?
BS_C03_S03_INTRO1::block-1: To this we say — this consideration of difference and non-difference of vijñānas pertains to (vidyās) whose object is saguṇa Brahman (Brahman with attributes) and to (vidyās) whose object is prāṇa and the like; hence there is no fault. For here, just as in the case of karmas, difference and non-difference of upāsanās are possible. And like karmas, these upāsanās too are spoken of as having seen (dṛṣṭa) fruits and unseen (adṛṣṭa) fruits, and some of them as having krama-mukti (gradual liberation) as their fruit by way of giving rise to the perfect (samyag) jñāna. Among these, this consideration is possible — is there difference of vijñāna in each Vedānta, or not?
BS_C03_S03_INTRO1::block-2: There, the grounds of the pūrvapakṣa are first set forth — Difference of name (nāma) is, to begin with, a well-known cause for cognising difference, as in the case of jyotis and the like (in the karma-kāṇḍa). And here, in the vijñānas enjoined in different Vedāntas, there is one name and another — Taittirīyaka, Vājasaneyaka, Kauthumaka, Kauṣītaka, Śāṭyāyanaka, and so on. Likewise, difference of form (rūpa-bheda) is well known as conveying difference of karma — as in ‘āmikṣā for the Vaiśvadevī, vājina for the Vājins,’ and the like. And here too there is difference of form. To wit — some śākhins, in the Pañcāgni-vidyā, recite a sixth, further fire; others, however, read just five. Likewise, in the Prāṇa-saṁvāda and the rest, some recite anvāgas (subordinate accompanying members) of fewer (number), some of greater. Likewise, particularity of dharma (dharma-viśeṣa) is also suspected to convey difference of karma in the Kārīrī and the like. And here too there is particularity of dharma — as the Śiro-vrata of the Ātharvaṇikas. So also repetition (punarukti) and the rest, as causes of difference, are to be applied wherever possible to the various Vedāntas. Therefore there is difference of vijñāna in each Vedānta — when this position is reached, we say —
BS_C03_S03_V01: (The vijñānas) (cognised) in all the Vedāntas (are one and the same), because of non-difference of injunction etc. ‖ 1 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V01::block-0: Vijñānas which are cognised in all the Vedāntas (sarva-vedānta-pratyayāni) deserve to be those very same (vijñānas) in this and that Vedānta. Why? Because of non-difference of injunction and the rest (codanādi-aviśeṣāt). By the word ‘ādi’ (and the rest), the grounds of non-difference (abheda-hetus) stated in the Śākhāntarādhikaraṇa-siddhānta-sūtra (of Jaimini) are drawn here — that is, the non-difference of saṁyoga, rūpa, and codanā. Just as, in respect of one and the same Agnihotra, even when there is difference of śākhā, the human effort (puruṣa-prayatna) enjoined is of just that same nature — ‘he should offer’ — so also in ‘he who knows the eldest and the best’ (Chā. Up. 5.1.1), the injunction (codanā) is just the same for the Vājasaneyins and the Chandogas. The conjunction with the goal (prayojana-saṁyoga) too is non-different — ‘he becomes the eldest and the best of his kin’ (Bṛ. Up. 6.1.1). The form (rūpa) of the vijñāna in both places is just the same, namely, prāṇa-tattva qualified by the special attributes ‘eldest,’ ‘best,’ and so on — for, just as substance and deity (dravya-devatā) are the form of a yāga, so the object to be known (vijñeya) is the form of vijñāna; for it is by that that the vijñāna is given form. The designation (samākhyā) too is just the same — Prāṇa-vidyā. Therefore the vijñānas have the character of being cognised throughout all the Vedāntas. So is it to be applied also to the Pañcāgni-vidyā, Vaiśvānara-vidyā, Śāṇḍilya-vidyā, and the rest. As for those apparent grounds of difference, name, form, and the like (nāma-rūpādi-bheda-hetv-ābhāsāḥ), they have been answered in the very first Kāṇḍa (of Pūrva-mīmāṁsā), beginning with ‘not by name (does difference arise), because of its being an unenjoined designation’ (Jaiminī-sūtra 2.4.10). ‖ 1 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V02: If it be said (vidyās are different) on account of difference (of attributes), (we say) no, even within one and the same (vidyā). ‖ 2 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V02::block-0: Here too, having raised some specific (objection), (the bhāṣyakāra) refutes it —
BS_C03_S03_V02::block-1: Let it be — the character of being cognised in all the Vedāntas does not hold for the vijñānas because of difference of attributes (guṇa-bheda). To wit — the Vājasaneyins, having begun the Pañcāgni-vidyā, recite a sixth, further fire by ‘his fire becomes the (sacrificial) fire’ (Bṛ. Up. 6.2.14), and so on. The Chandogas, however, do not recite that, and conclude with the count of just five — ‘Now, he who thus knows these five fires’ (Chā. Up. 5.10.10). Among whom that attribute exists and among whom it does not, how can one and the same vidyā hold of both? Nor here is the supplying of attributes (guṇopasaṁhāra) possible, since it conflicts with the count of five. Likewise, in the Prāṇa-saṁvāda, the Chandogas recite four prāṇas other than the chiefest — speech, eye, ear, mind. The Vājasaneyins, however, recite a fifth too — ‘seed indeed is the source of progeny; he begets progeny, cattle, who thus knows’ (Bṛ. Up. 6.1.6). And, on account of the difference of insertion and removal (āvāpa-udvāpa-bheda), there results difference of the object known; and from difference of the known, difference of vidyā — just as for a yāga (there is difference) due to difference of substance and deity. — If this be said: this is no fault. For, even within one and the same vidyā (ekasyām api vidyāyām), this kind of difference of attributes is intelligible. Even though the supplying of the sixth fire is not possible (in both), still, since the five fires beginning with dyu (heaven) are recognised in both places, there cannot be difference of vidyā. For the Atirātra is not differentiated according as one takes or does not take the Ṣoḍaśin-graha. The Chandogas do read of a sixth fire — ‘Him, departed and assigned, they bear off to the very fire’ (Chā. Up. 5.9.2). The Vājasaneyins recite ‘his fire becomes the (sacrificial) fire, his kindling sticks the kindling sticks’ (Bṛ. Up. 6.2.14) and the rest, in order to put a stop to the imagined sāmpādika (figurative) construal of kindling-sticks, smoke, etc. as continued in (the case of the cremation of the body, regarded as) the five sāmpādika fires. That is a nitya-anuvāda (constant restatement). Even granting that this is a passage meant for upāsana (contemplation), still that attribute can be supplied even by the Chandogas. Nor can the conflict with the count of five be apprehended here, since this count of five, intended for the sāmpādika fires and being a constant restatement, does not inhere in the injunction (na vidhi-samavāyinī) — hence no fault. So too in the Prāṇa-saṁvāda and the rest, the supplying of the additional attribute in the other case is not contradictory. Nor should difference of vedya (object known) and difference of vidyā be apprehended on account of difference of insertion and removal, since, even in respect of insertion and removal of some part of the vedya, non-difference of the much greater mass of the vedya is recognised. Therefore there is just one and the same vidyā. ‖ 2 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V03: (The vow such as the Śiro-vrata) belongs to the (course of) sacred study, because it is so (taught), in the (text on) procedure (samācāra), and because of (specific) eligibility; and like the savas (sacrifices), its restriction (to a particular Veda is established). ‖ 3 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V03::block-0: Now what was said — that, on account of the Ātharvaṇikas’ vidyā requiring the Śiro-vrata and so on, and of others not requiring it, there is difference of vidyā — that is being answered. This dharma belongs to the svādhyāya (sacred study), not to the vidyā. How is this known? Because, ‘as such’ (tathātvena) — namely as a dharma of svādhyāya — in the samācāra (text dealing with the prescriptions for vedic conduct), the Ātharvaṇikas (themselves) record ‘this too has been explained as (a duty) belonging to the Veda-vrata.’ And from ‘one who has not performed the vrata does not study (this)’ (Muṇ. Up. 3.2.11), by the words ‘this’ (etat, with a context of those qualified, adhikṛta-viṣaya) and ‘adhyayana’ (study), it is determined that this is just a dharma pertaining to the study of one’s own Upaniṣad. — But surely from the hearing of (this vow’s) connection with brahma-vidyā in ‘To them alone may one impart this brahma-vidyā — to those by whom the Śiro-vrata has been duly performed’ (Muṇ. Up. 3.2.10), since brahma-vidyā is everywhere one and the same, this dharma would get extended (to all). — No; for there too, by ‘this’ (etām) the reference is to (the brahma-vidyā) under discussion (prakṛta). And the ‘being under discussion’ of brahma-vidyā has reference to the particular text (grantha-viśeṣa) — hence this dharma is connected with that particular text alone. ‘Like the savas, its restriction’ — this is stated by way of illustration. Just as the seven savas, beginning with the Saurya and ending with the Śata-audana, by reason of their non-relation with the Tretāgni taught in other Vedas and their relation with the single fire taught by the Atharvan, are restricted to the Ātharvaṇikas alone, so also this dharma, on account of its connection with a particular svādhyāya, is restricted to that very (Veda). Therefore the unity of vidyā is faultless. ‖ 3 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V04::block-0: And the Veda too shows the oneness of vidyā in all the Vedāntas, by teaching the oneness of the vedya (object to be known) — ‘the seat which all the Vedas declare’ (Kaṭha Up. 1.2.15); likewise, ‘this (Self) the Bahvṛcas inquire into in the great Uktha; this (very Self) the Adhvaryus (inquire into) in the fire; this (very Self) the Chandogas (inquire into) in the Mahāvrata,’ and so on. So too, the ‘great fear (of the Lord), like an upraised thunderbolt’ (Kaṭha Up. 2.3.2), the attribute of the Lord which causes fear, declared in the Kāṭhaka, is referred to in the Taittirīyaka in censure of seeing difference — ‘For when in this (Self) one makes a hollow (gap) within, then there is fear for him; that very thing is fear for the knower who is not (rightly) thinking’ (Tai. Up. 2.7.1). Likewise, in the Vājasaneyaka, the Vaiśvānara is fashioned by sampatti (figurative meditation) as of the size of a span (prādeśa-mātra); in the Chāndogya, this is taken up as already established — ‘But he who worships this Vaiśvānara Self thus, of the size of a span, abhivimāna’ (Chā. Up. 5.18.1). Likewise, on account of the (śruti) referring to the Uktha and the like, enjoined in one (Veda) under the rubric of being cognised in all the Vedāntas, for the sake of enjoining their upāsana in another (Veda), by the maxim of prāya-darśana (preponderance), the upāsanās too are established as cognised in all the Vedāntas. ‖ 4 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V05: (There is) supplying (of attributes), on account of non-difference of purport, like (it is) of (an injunction’s) accessories, in cases that are similar (i.e., one and the same vidyā). ‖ 5 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V05::block-0: This is the prayojana-sūtra (sūtra stating the practical upshot). When it is thus established that all vijñānas have the character of being cognised in all the Vedāntas, the attributes (guṇas) of vijñānas stated in one place are to be supplied (upasaṁhāra) in the same vijñāna (occurring) in another place too. On account of non-difference of purport (artha-abhedāt) — that very purpose of those attributes in one place, namely the rendering of help to the specific vijñāna, is the very same in the other place too. For in both places it is just one and the same vijñāna. Therefore there is supplying. ‘Like (the supplying) of accessories of an injunction’ (vidhi-śeṣa-vat) — just as, in respect of accessories of an injunction such as the Agnihotra and the rest, that very same one Agnihotra-karma being everywhere, there is supplying because of non-difference of purport — so too here. For if there were difference of vijñāna, then, on account of the attributes being bound to a different vijñāna and on account of there being no relation of prakṛti (paradigm) and vikṛti (modification), there would be no supplying. But when there is unity of vijñāna, it is not so. The detailed elaboration of this very prayojana-sūtra will follow, beginning with ‘On account of total non-difference (sarvābhedāt)’. ‖ 5 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V06: If it be said (the vidyā is) different on account of (śruti-) word, (we say) no, on account of non-difference (of the matter generally). ‖ 6 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V06::block-0: In the Vājasaneyaka, having begun with ‘the gods said: come, let us overcome the asuras at the sacrifice by means of the Udgītha’ (Bṛ. Up. 1.3.1), ‘they said to speech: do thou sing the udgītha for us’ (Bṛ. Up. 1.3.2), having censured speech and the other prāṇas as pierced with the evil of the asuras, the apprehension of the chief prāṇa (mukhya-prāṇa) is read — ‘then they said to this prāṇa in the mouth: do thou sing the udgītha for us — so be it; this prāṇa sang for them’ (Bṛ. Up. 1.3.7). So also in the Chāndogya, having begun with ‘the gods took to the udgītha (thinking) by this we shall overcome them’ (Chā. Up. 1.2.1), having censured the other prāṇas as pierced with the evil of the asuras, the apprehension of the chief prāṇa is read in the same way — ‘then this very chief prāṇa, them they meditated upon as the Udgītha’ (Chā. Up. 1.2.7). And in both places, by the praise of prāṇa, the injunction of a Prāṇa-vidyā is determined. There the doubt — is there here difference of vidyā, or is there unity of vidyā? What, then, is obtained (as pūrvapakṣa)? By the previous (line of) reasoning, there is unity of vidyā. — But surely the unity of vidyā is not proper, on account of difference of commencement (prakrama-bheda). For the Vājasaneyins commence in one way, the Chandogas in another. The Vājasaneyins, by ‘do thou sing the udgītha for us’ (Bṛ. Up. 1.3.2), recite prāṇa as the agent (kartṛ) of the udgītha; the Chandogas, however, (recite prāṇa) as the udgītha (itself), in ‘they meditated upon him (the prāṇa) as the udgītha’ (Chā. Up. 1.2.7). How, then, can there be unity of vidyā? — If this be said, this is no fault. By so much specific (difference) the unity of vidyā does not depart, since a much greater non-particularity is being apprehended. To wit — being preceded by the gods’ and asuras’ war, the intention of overcoming the asuras, the introduction of the udgītha, the enumeration of speech and the rest, censuring them and resorting to the chief prāṇa, and through the latter’s vigour the destruction of the asuras illustrated by the example of stone and clod — many such purports are recognised as just the same in both places. In the Vājasaneyaka too, the co-reference (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of prāṇa with the udgītha is heard — ‘this very (prāṇa) indeed is the udgītha’ (Bṛ. Up. 1.3.23). Hence in the Chāndogya too, the agency (of prāṇa) is to be construed by lakṣaṇā. Therefore there is unity of vidyā. ‖ 6 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V07: Or rather not (one and the same), on account of difference of context (prakaraṇa), as in the case of (the meditations on udgītha as) ‘paro-varīyas’ and the like. ‖ 7 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V07::block-0: Or rather, unity of vidyā here is not proper. Difference of vidyā alone is proper here. Why? Because of difference of prakaraṇa (governing context) — that is, difference of commencement (prakrama). For here a difference of commencement is seen — In the Chāndogya, beginning with ‘one should worship this very syllable Om (which is) the Udgītha’ (Chā. Up. 1.1.1), having proposed the worship-worthiness (upāsyatva) of Oṁkāra, an avayava (limb) of the Udgītha, and after explaining there the attributes ‘rasatama’ (most essential) and the rest, having again, by ‘an explanation of this very syllable comes about’ (Chā. Up. 1.1.10), continued with that very Oṁkāra which is the limb of the Udgītha, by way of the legend of the gods and asuras (the śruti) says ‘they meditated upon prāṇa as the udgītha’ (Chā. Up. 1.2.2). There, if by the word udgītha the whole bhakti (the section) were intended, and its agent the udgātṛ-ṛtvik, then the upakrama (the opening) would be obstructed and lakṣaṇā would arise. And by the principle that the upasaṁhāra (conclusion) must be in accord with the upakrama in one and the same passage, here the meditation of prāṇa is taught upon Oṁkāra, a limb of the Udgītha. — In the Vājasaneyaka, however, since there is no reason to take the udgītha-word as designating a limb (only), the bhakti as a whole is conveyed. By ‘do thou sing the udgītha for us’ (Bṛ. Up. 1.3.2) too, its agent the udgātṛ-ṛtvik is determined as prāṇa — this is a different procedure (prasthāna). Even there, the co-reference (sāmānādhikaraṇya) of prāṇa with the udgītha is for the sake of conveying the all-Self-ness of prāṇa, which was sought to be shown precisely as the udgātṛ — hence it does not bring about unity of vidyā. The udgītha-word there is in respect of the bhakti as a whole — that is the disparity. Nor should the agency of prāṇa be given up on the ground of impossibility, since, like the udgītha-bhāva, the udgātṛ-bhāva too is being taught for the purpose of upāsana. And it is by the very vigour of prāṇa that the udgātṛ performs the audgātra (function); hence there is no impossibility. So too there itself is heard — ‘he sang with speech and with prāṇa’ (Bṛ. Up. 1.3.24). And when a difference of intended sense is being apprehended, it is not proper to determine sameness of sense merely by similarity of phrase-structure (vākya-cchāyā-anukāra). To wit — in the abhyudaya passage and in the paśu-kāma passage, despite similarity of expression as in ‘he should divide the rice-grains into three; those that are middling, of these he should make a piece-cake of eight potsherds for Agni Dātṛ,’ on account of difference of upakrama, in the abhyudaya passage the substitution of deities (devatā-apanaya) is determined, but in the paśu-kāma passage a yāga-vidhi (sacrificial injunction) — so here too, on account of difference of upakrama, there is difference of vidyā. ‘Like paro-varīyas and the rest’ — just as, despite the similarity of the superimposition of the Paramātman-view, the udgītha-upāsana qualified by the attributes paro-varīyas and the rest in ‘ākāśa indeed is greater than these, ākāśa is the highest resort’ (Chā. Up. 1.9.1), ‘that itself, the paro-varīyas Udgītha, that itself the endless’ (Chā. Up. 1.9.2), is different from the udgītha-upāsana qualified by attributes such as residing in the eye, the sun, having a golden beard, and the like; and the supplying of one another’s attributes does not occur even within one and the same śākhā — likewise it does not occur in such upāsanās standing in different śākhās. ‖ 7 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V08: ‘If [the unity of meditation be defended] on account of the unity of name — that has [already] been answered; yet that too is [present in cases of admitted difference].’ (8)
BS_C03_S03_V08::block-0: Suppose it be urged (pūrvapakṣa): ‘Since the name is one, it is reasonable here that the vidyā (meditation) be one — for in both places the single designation udgītha-vidyā is current.’ Even that does not stand. For it has [already] been said: ‘Or rather not, on account of difference of context, as in the parovarīyastva and similar [meditations]’ (Brahma-sūtra 3.3.7). And that very [reasoning] is here the more cogent, since it follows the very letter of the śruti, whereas unity of name lies outside the letter of the śruti and is merely the figurative usage of worldly speakers due to the bare employment of the word ‘udgītha.’ Such oneness of name is found even in admittedly distinct upāsanās such as the parovarīyastva-meditation and the rest, [all called] udgītha-vidyā. So too, even though the agnihotra, darśa-pūrṇamāsa and the rest — which are recognised as distinct sacrifices — when read together in one [textual collection] of the Kāṭhakas bear the single name ‘Kāṭhaka,’ this oneness of designation is seen [without entailing oneness of substance]; even so will it be here. But where there is no such ground of difference [as a difference of context], there let oneness of vidyā follow from oneness of name — as in the saṃvarga-vidyā and the like. (8) (siddhānta)
BS_C03_S03_V09: ‘And on account of [its] pervasion, [the option of the qualifier is] proper.’ (9)
