BS_C03_S03_V09::block-0: In the passage ‘Let one meditate upon Om, this akṣara, [as] the udgītha’ (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.1), since the words akṣara and udgītha are heard in samānādhikaraṇya (grammatical co-reference), four alternatives present themselves — adhyāsa (superimposition), apavāda (sublation), aikya (identity), and viśeṣaṇa (qualification). The inquiry is which of these alternatives here is the proper one. Of these, adhyāsa (superimposition) is so called: when, the cognition pertaining to one of two things being not at all set aside, the cognition of the other is superimposed upon it. Where the cognition of the other is superimposed, the cognition of that [substratum] still continues even after the superimposed cognition is established — as the cognition ‘name’ continues even when the cognition ‘brahman’ is being superimposed upon a name, and is not annulled by the cognition of brahman; or, again, as in the superimposition of the cognition of Viṣṇu and the like upon images. So here too, either the cognition of udgītha is superimposed on the akṣara, or the cognition of akṣara on the udgītha. Apavāda (sublation) is so called: when, a false cognition having previously taken hold and become firmly established with regard to some thing, a later, conformant, true cognition arising thereafter sublates that previously established false cognition — as the cognition ‘ātman’ regarding the aggregate of body and senses [is sublated] regarding the ātman alone by the conformant cognition that arises later, namely ‘That thou art’ (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7); or as the cognition of mistaken direction is sublated by the cognition of the true direction. So here too, the cognition of udgītha would be sublated by the cognition of akṣara, or the cognition of akṣara by the cognition of udgītha. Identity (ekatva) means: that the words akṣara and udgītha do not have distinct referents — as in the [coreferential] expressions ‘best of the twice-born,’ ‘brāhmaṇa,’ ‘earthly god.’ Qualification (viśeṣaṇa), again, means: when the akṣara Om, which pervades the entire Veda, is liable to be taken in its full generality, [the word udgītha] hands over [to attention] a particular akṣara, namely the udgātṛ-priest’s [Om] — as in ‘Bring that lotus which is blue,’ so here too, ‘Let one meditate upon that Om-kāra which is the udgītha.’ Thus, when this co-referential sentence is examined, these four alternatives present themselves. Since there is no ground for fixing upon any one of them, when non-determination threatens, this is said —
BS_C03_S03_V09::block-1: ‘And on account of pervasion (vyāpti), [the qualifier-option] is proper.’ The word ca here stands in the place of tu (‘but’) and serves to set aside three of the alternatives. Thus three alternatives are here rejected as flawed; the qualifier-option (viśeṣaṇa-pakṣa) alone, being faultless, is adopted. Now, in the case of adhyāsa, the cognition that is being superimposed on the other [thing] would entail that the word [governing] it must be taken in lakṣaṇā (secondary signification), and a fruit for it would have to be imagined. (objection) ‘But the fruit is heard, viz. ‘He becomes a fulfiller of desires’ (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.7) and so on’ — no; for that fruit pertains to something else. That is the fruit of the dṛṣṭi (vision) of attainment etc., not the fruit of an udgītha-superimposition. In the case of apavāda also, similarly, there is no fruit. (objection) ‘The fruit is the cessation of false knowledge’ — no; for [such cessation] does not bear on any human end (puruṣārtha); nor does the cognition of Om-kāra ever cease through Om-kāra, nor the cognition of udgītha through udgītha. Nor is this sentence aimed at conveying the truth of a thing, since it is aimed at enjoining an upāsanā. Nor again does the identity-option fit. For then the utterance of the two words would serve no purpose, since the intended sense would be conveyed by either alone. And the word ‘udgītha’ is not current as designating Om-kāra in the domain of the hotṛ or the adhvaryu, where Om-kāra goes by [those names]; nor is the word ‘Om-kāra’ current for the entire sāman or for its second [partial portion (bhakti)] which is denoted by the word ‘udgītha’ — so as to make their referents non-distinct. By process of elimination (pariśeṣa), the qualifier-option is taken up — on the strength of vyāpti, viz. that [Om] is common to all the Vedas. ‘Lest the all-pervading akṣara be presented [as the object of upāsanā here],’ for that very purpose the akṣara is qualified by the word ‘udgītha’ — namely, ‘that Om-kāra which is a constituent (avayava) of the udgītha is to be apprehended.’ (objection) ‘But on this option too, lakṣaṇā is equally involved, since the word ‘udgītha’ stands by avayava-lakṣaṇā [for one of its parts].’ True, that is so; yet, even within lakṣaṇā, there is proximity (sannikarṣa) and remoteness (viprakarṣa). On the adhyāsa-option, since the cognition of one thing is cast upon another quite different thing, the lakṣaṇā is remote (viprakṛṣṭā); on the qualifier-option, since by a word denoting the whole the part is handed over, the lakṣaṇā is proximate (sannikṛṣṭā). Words primarily applied to wholes are seen to be applied to parts as well — as in [the words] paṭa (cloth), grāma (village), and so on. Thus by reason of vyāpti, [the word] ‘udgītha’ in ‘Let one meditate upon Om, this akṣara’ is its qualifier — and this is samañjasa, that is, faultless. (9)
BS_C03_S03_V10: ‘On account of non-difference of the whole [meditation], these [qualities are to be carried over] elsewhere [too].’ (10)
BS_C03_S03_V10::block-0: Among the Vājasaneyins and Chāndogas, in the prāṇa-saṃvāda (dialogue of the vital faculties) the upāsyatva (object-of-meditation status) of prāṇa endowed with the quality of supremacy (śraiṣṭhya) is taught. There the speech-faculty and the others too are described as endowed with the qualities of vasiṣṭhatva (being most settled) and the rest. And those qualities are then handed back upon prāṇa: ‘What I am vasiṣṭha by, that thou art vasiṣṭha by’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.14) and so on. But among other branches (śākhins) too — the Kauṣītakins and the rest — in their prāṇa-saṃvādas of the type ‘Now then, the gaining of the highest good: these very deities, disputing among themselves over their [respective] excellence…’ (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 2.14), the supremacy of prāṇa is taught, but these qualities of vasiṣṭhatva and the rest are not stated. Hence the doubt — are these qualities of vasiṣṭhatva etc., taught somewhere, to be carried over (āseran) elsewhere too, or not? (pūrvapakṣa) On this, the prima facie view is that they should not be carried over. Why? On account of the connexion with the word evam. ‘Now he who, knowing thus (evam-vidvān), having known the highest good in prāṇa…’ — by the word evam in each place is conveyed [only] the very thing taught [in that place]. And the word evam, taking its support from what is at hand (sannihita), cannot convey a body of qualities read in another śākhā. Therefore, given fulfilment by the qualities standing in its own context, [the meditation] is without further requirement. — To this prima facie view he replies (siddhānta) —
BS_C03_S03_V10::block-1: These qualities of vasiṣṭhatva etc., taught somewhere, are to be carried over (āseran) elsewhere too. Why? sarva-abhedāt — because in every place the very same single prāṇa-cognition is recognised undivided, by reason of the similarity of the prāṇa-saṃvāda and the rest. And when the cognition is undifferentiated, how should these qualities, taught in one place, fail to be carried over to another? (objection) ‘But it has been said that the word evam in each place hands over only such qualities as are conveyed there for being known.’ To this it is replied — though the body of qualities found in the Vājasaneyi-brāhmaṇa is not co-designated by the evam of the Kauṣītaki-brāhmaṇa, since they are not at hand there, yet that very body of qualities is co-designated by the evam in the Vājasaneyi-brāhmaṇa belonging to the very same cognition; so a body of qualities found in another śākhā, being bound to the same undifferentiated cognition, is not differentiated from those of one’s own śākhā. Nor on this view is there hānī (loss) of what is heard, or kalpanā (assumption) of what is not heard. For qualities heard in even one śākhā are heard everywhere, since there is no difference of the quality-bearer (guṇavat). Devadatta, recognised in his own land for śauryatva (heroism) and the like, does not, when he goes to another country, become bereft of those qualities merely because the people of that country have not noticed his heroism etc. And just as in that other country also, by special acquaintance, the qualities of Devadatta come to be perceived, so by special application (abhiyoga) the qualities to be meditated upon, taught in another śākhā, would be carried over (āseran) here too. Therefore, the dharmas connected with one principal [object], though stated in one place, are to be gathered up everywhere. (10)
BS_C03_S03_V11: ‘[Qualities like] ānanda etc. [belong] to the principal [Brahman, and so are everywhere applicable].’ (11)
BS_C03_S03_V11::block-0: In the śrutis devoted to expounding the very nature of Brahman, dharmas of Brahman of this sort — being of the nature of bliss (ānanda-rūpatva), being a homogeneous mass of consciousness (vijñāna-ghanatva), being all-pervading (sarva-gatatva), being the self of all (sarva-ātmatva) — are heard, some in some places, some in others. Concerning these the doubt: are the dharmas of Brahman beginning with ānanda to be apprehended only as many in number wherever they are heard, or are all to be apprehended everywhere? On the prima facie view, that the dharmas should be received in the divisions in which they are heard, this is said (siddhānta) — the dharmas of Brahman, the principal (pradhāna), beginning with ānanda, are all to be apprehended everywhere. Why? sarva-abhedād eva — for everywhere it is the same one principal, the qualified Brahman, that is unbroken. Therefore the universality of Brahman’s dharmas — by the very illustration of Devadatta’s heroism etc. given in the previous adhikaraṇa. (11)
BS_C03_S03_V12: ‘There is no carrying over of [qualities such as] having the priya as head, since increase and decrease [are possible] only where there is difference.’ (12)
BS_C03_S03_V12::block-0: (leading bhāṣya) (objection) ‘But on this view, dharmas like ‘priya as head’ etc. would all be jumbled together everywhere. For in the Taittirīyaka, beginning with the ānandamaya-ātman, it is recited: ‘Of him the priya itself is the head; the moda is the right wing; the pramoda is the left wing; ānanda is the self; brahman is the tail, the support’ (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.5.1).’ As a reply to this he reads —
BS_C03_S03_V12::block-1: (siddhānta) Of dharmas such as priya-being-head etc. recited in the Taittirīyaka, there is no carrying-over (aprāpti) elsewhere. Why? Because priya, moda, pramoda, ānanda — these — are found, in mutual relation and in relation to a different enjoyer (bhoktṛ), as having the form of upacita (increased) and apacita (decreased). And upacayāpacayau (increase and decrease) are possible only when there is bheda (difference). But Brahman is without difference (nirbheda), as per the śruti ‘One only without a second’ (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1) and the like. Nor are these — priya-as-head etc. — dharmas of Brahman. Rather they are dharmas of the kośa (sheath) — this we have already taught at ‘ānandamayo ’bhyāsāt’ (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.12). Moreover, in the supreme Brahman they are imagined merely as a means for the descent of the mind, not for the sake of being seen [as constituting Brahman]. Even so, all the more is there no carrying over of priya-being-head etc. elsewhere. Treating these as dharmas of Brahman, the ācārya has merely indicated a general nyāya by ‘priya-śirastva-ādy-aprāpti.’ And that nyāya is to be applied to other ascertained dharmas of Brahman taught for upāsanā — such as saṃyad-vāmatva and the rest, satya-kāmatva and the rest. For there, even though the upāsya, namely Brahman, is one, since on account of difference of context (prakrama-bheda) there is difference of upāsanā, the dharmas of one [meditation] are not carried over into the other. Just as two women attend upon one king — one with a parasol, another with a chowrie — there, even with the oneness of the object of attendance, there is difference of attending and a regulation of duties; even so here. The state of having upacita-apacita qualities is intelligible, in the sphere of difference-discourse, in the saguṇa Brahman, not in the supreme nirguṇa Brahman. Hence the [purport] is that of dharmas such as satya-kāmatva, heard in some place, there is no carrying over everywhere. (12)
BS_C03_S03_V13: ‘But the others [viz. ānanda etc.], because of commonness of meaning [are everywhere apprehended].’ (13)
BS_C03_S03_V13::block-0: But the others, namely ānanda and the rest, dharmas, being uttered for the very purpose of expounding the nature of Brahman, would be apprehended everywhere — on account of the sameness of their referent (artha-sāmānya), since the dharmin to be expounded, namely Brahman, is one. Thus the disparity [from the priya-śirastva case]: for those [viz. ānanda etc.] have as their sole purpose [right] apprehension. (13)
BS_C03_S03_V14: ‘[The enumeration is] for the sake of meditation [on the puruṣa], because there is no [other] purpose.’ (14)
BS_C03_S03_V14::block-0: In the Kāṭhaka it is read: ‘Beyond the senses are the objects, beyond the objects is the manas, but beyond manas is the buddhi’ (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.10) — beginning thus, and continuing, ‘Beyond the puruṣa there is nothing whatsoever; that is the goal, that is the supreme path’ (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.11). Concerning this, the doubt — are all these, the objects and the rest, being expounded as severally beyond [what precedes], or is the puruṣa alone being expounded as beyond all these? (pūrvapakṣa) On this, the inclination [first] is that what is being expounded is the beyondness of all of these. For so it is heard — ‘this is beyond that, this is beyond that.’ (objection) ‘But, in expounding beyondness for many objects, there would be vākya-bheda (splitting of the sentence).’ This is no fault, since plurality of sentences is admissible. For these are simply many sentences, capable of expounding many objects as endowed with beyondness. Hence the expounding of beyondness pertains to each of these. — When this prima facie view is reached, we say (siddhānta) —
BS_C03_S03_V14::block-1: It is the puruṣa alone who is fitly being expounded as beyond all these; not the expounding of beyondness for each of these severally. Why? prayojanābhāvāt — because of the absence of [any other] purpose. No purpose is seen or heard in expounding the others as beyond [their predecessors]. But upon the puruṣa being apprehended as beyond the senses and the rest — beyond the entire mass of evils — a purpose is seen, viz. the attainment of mokṣa. So the śruti: ‘Having beheld him, one is released from the mouth of death’ (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.15). Furthermore, by the negation of [anything] beyond and by the word kāṣṭhā [‘goal’], displaying special reverence with regard to the puruṣa, [the Upaniṣad] shows that the entire prior-and-later succession is uttered for the very purpose of apprehending the puruṣa. ‘ādhyānāya’ — i.e., for the sake of full vision (samyag-darśana) preceded by ādhyāna (meditative pondering). It is for the sake of samyag-darśana that ādhyāna is here taught; ādhyāna is not itself principal in its own right. (14)
BS_C03_S03_V15: ‘And on account of the word ātman [also, the puruṣa alone is being expounded].’ (15)
BS_C03_S03_V15::block-0: For this further reason too, this enunciation of the series of senses and the rest is for the sake of apprehending the puruṣa: because [the śruti] ‘He, the gūḍha-ātman (concealed self) in all beings, is not manifest; but he is seen by those who, with subtle vision, see [him] with sharp and subtle buddhi’ (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.12) speaks of the puruṣa, the topic at hand, as ātman. From this it is gathered that the anātmatva (non-self-hood) of the others is intended. And [it] shows the difficulty of his cognition and his accessibility only to a refined intelligence. For the apprehension of him alone too — ‘Let the wise man restrain speech in mind’ (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.13) — is ādhyāna enjoined. That has been explained at ‘ānumānikam apy ekeṣām’ (Brahma-sūtra 1.4.1). Thus is observed in the śruti, in many ways, a special intention with regard to the puruṣa, not with regard to the others. Furthermore, when it has been said ‘He attains the further shore of the path; that is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu’ (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.9), at the natural enquiry ‘what is that further shore of the path, the supreme abode of Viṣṇu?,’ from the enumeration of the senses and the rest [that follows], it is concluded that this entire endeavour is for the very purpose of apprehending the supreme abode. (15)
BS_C03_S03_V16: ātma-gṛhītir itara-vad uttarāt — ‘The Self (the supreme Ātman) is what is taken up (by the word ātman in this passage), as in the other (Upaniṣadic creation accounts), because of what follows.’ ‖ 16 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V16::block-0:
In the Aitareya it is heard: ‘In the beginning, verily, this was the Self alone, one only; there was nothing else whatsoever active. He thought, “Let me now create the worlds.”’ (Ait. Up. 1.1.1) ‘He created these worlds — Ambhas, Marīcis, Mara, and the Waters’ (Ait. Up. 1.1.2), and so on. There a doubt arises — is it the supreme Self alone that is here designated by the word ‘ātman’, or some other (lesser) self? 

[Pūrvapakṣa] What, then, is the prima facie position? It is that the supreme Self does not deserve to be designated here by the word ‘ātman’. Why? Because of what is seen in the connected sense of the passage. 

‘But surely the connected sense of the passage is most readily seen to have the supreme Self as its subject, since (i) the oneness of the Self prior to creation is affirmed and (ii) creatorship preceded by reflection (īkṣaṇa) is spoken of?’ — ‘No,’ we say, ‘because the creation spoken of is a creation of worlds. For if the supreme Self were taken to be the creator, the creation of the great elements (mahābhūta-sṛṣṭi) would have to be spoken of first; but here world-creation is spoken of at the very outset. And worlds are particular configurations of the great elements. Likewise (the text) describes Ambhas and the rest precisely as worlds — ‘That Ambhas is beyond the heaven’ (Ait. Up. 1.1.2), and so on. And world-creation is found, in both śruti and smṛti, to be carried out by some lesser Īśvara presided over by the supreme Īśvara. Thus śruti says: ‘In the beginning this was the Self alone, in the form of Puruṣa’ (Bṛ. Up. 1.4.1), and the like. Smṛti also says: ‘He, indeed, was the first embodied one; he indeed is called Puruṣa; the original maker of beings, Brahmā, came into existence first’ (Mat. P. 45.64). The followers of the Aitareya themselves, in an earlier section beginning ‘Now, then, the creation of seed: the seed of Prajāpati is the gods’, recite a manifold creation whose agent is Prajāpati. The word ‘ātman’ is also seen applied there — ‘In the beginning this was the Self alone, in the form of Puruṣa’ (Bṛ. Up. 1.4.1). The affirmation of oneness prior to creation may also be intelligibly understood with reference to (the lesser self’s) own modifications. ‘Reflection’ (īkṣaṇa) is also intelligible, since (the lesser self) too is admitted to be sentient. Moreover, a great many specific operations of the kind ‘He brought a cow for them’, ‘He brought a horse for them’, ‘He brought a man for them’, ‘They said’, and so on — such as are well established in the case of ordinary, particularised selves — are met with here. Therefore some particularised self should be (the referent) here. 

[Siddhānta] When this is the prima facie position, we reply (in the sūtra above).
BS_C03_S03_V16::block-1: [Siddhānta] Here it is the supreme Self alone that is taken up by the word ‘ātman’. ‘Like the other’ (itara-vat) — just as in other creation-passages such as ‘From that very Self ākāśa came forth’ (Tai. Up. 2.1.1), the supreme Self is what is taken up; and just as in ordinary worldly use of the word ‘ātman’ the inner Self (pratyag-ātman) alone is principally taken up — so it must be here also. Where, however, in passages like ‘In the beginning this was the Self alone’ (Bṛ. Up. 1.4.1), some other qualifier such as ‘in the form of Puruṣa’ (Bṛ. Up. 1.4.1) is heard, there one may take up the qualified (lesser) self. But here, in fact, what follows is precisely a qualifier in conformity with the grasping of the supreme Self — ‘He thought, “Let me now create the worlds”’ (Ait. Up. 1.1.1); ‘He created these worlds’ (Ait. Up. 1.1.2), and so on. Therefore it is just (the supreme Self) alone that is to be taken up. ‖ 16 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V17: anvayād iti cet syād avadhāraṇāt — ‘If it be objected (that the supreme Self is not meant) on the ground of (the connected sense of) the passage — (we reply:) it (i.e., the grasping of the supreme Self) does hold good, because of the (clinching) affirmation.’ ‖ 17 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V17::block-0: What was again said — ‘there is no grasping of the supreme Self because of the connected sense of the passage’ — has to be answered. To this it is said: syād avadhāraṇāt — ‘it is intelligible, because of (the clinching) affirmation’. The grasping of the supreme Self does become intelligible. Why? Because of the (clinching) affirmation. For when the supreme Self is grasped, the affirmation of the oneness of the Self prior to creation comes out straightforward (āñjasa); otherwise it would have to be construed in a roundabout way (anāñjasa). As to the speech about world-creation — I shall construe it as following upon the creation of the great elements established in another śruti. Just as ‘That created fire’ (Chā. Up. 6.2.3) was construed as following upon the creation of ākāśa and vāyu established in another śruti — so here too. For a particular detail well-established in another śruti, on the same topic, is to be incorporated into the (other) śrutis. As for that anugama (continuation) of specific operations such as ‘He brought a cow for them’ etc. — that too should be taken in conformity with the affirmation of the intended import. For it cannot be said that this whole story-narrative is what is intended (vivakṣita), since there would be no human end in cognising it. What is intended here is the identity of the Self with Brahman (brahmātmatva). Thus, having narrated the creation of the worlds beginning with Ambhas and of the world-guardians, the deities Agni and the rest, having taught the sense-organs (karaṇas) and the body (which is their seat), the same Creator, having reflected ‘How could this exist without me?’ (Ait. Up. 1.3.11), shows that He entered into this body — ‘He, having cleft this very crown, entered through that door’ (Ait. Up. 1.3.12). Again, having distinguished the operations of the sense-organs by ‘If by speech I speak, if by breath I breathe’ etc. (Ait. Up. 1.3.11), and reflected ‘Now who am I?’ (Ait. Up. 1.3.11), He clinches the vision of the Self as Brahman: ‘He saw this very Puruṣa as Brahman, the all-pervading’ (Ait. Up. 1.3.13). Likewise later — having enumerated the entire mass of distinctions together with the great elements by ‘This is Brahman, this is Indra’ (Ait. Up. 3.1.3) etc., He clinches once more the vision of the Self as Brahman: ‘All that is led by Prajñāna, established in Prajñāna; the world is led by Prajñāna; Prajñāna is the foundation; Prajñāna is Brahman’ (Ait. Up. 3.1.3). Therefore the grasping of the (supreme) Self here is unassailable.
BS_C03_S03_V17::block-1:
Another construal: ātma-gṛhītir itara-vad uttarāt. In the Vājasaneyaka, beginning with the word ‘ātman’ — ‘Which is the Self? — He who is consisting of consciousness (vijñāna-maya) among the prāṇas, the inner light within the heart, the Puruṣa’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.7) — by establishing his utter freedom from all attachment, the text clinches his identity with Brahman. So it concludes: ‘That is the great unborn Self, ageless, deathless, immortal, fearless, Brahman’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.25). In the Chāndogya, on the other hand, opening without the word ‘ātman’ — ‘Existent alone, my dear, was this in the beginning, one only without a second’ (Chā. Up. 6.2.1) — and concluding ‘That Self thou art’ (Chā. Up. 6.8.7), the text teaches identity (tādātmya). 

[Pūrvapakṣa] There the doubt is — are these two recitations alike in import or unlike? The prima facie view: they are unlike, because the recitations themselves are unlike. For when there is divergence in the recitations, sameness of meaning cannot reasonably be admitted, since the grasp of meaning depends on the recitation. In the Vājasaneyaka, since the opening is by the word ‘ātman’, what is taught is the doctrine of the Self’s reality (ātma-tattva). In the Chāndogya, on the contrary, since the opening is reversed, the teaching too is reversed. — ‘But it has been said that even for the Chāndogas there is a teaching of identity in the conclusion.’ — True, but since the conclusion is governed by the opening, the alleged ‘identity’ in the conclusion is only a contrived achievement (sampatti) of identity, not its real exposition — so the pūrvapakṣin holds. 

[Siddhānta] When this is the prima facie position, it is replied: ātma-gṛhītiḥ — even in ‘Existent alone, my dear, was this in the beginning’ (Chā. Up. 6.2.1), for the Chāndogas too, the grasping of the (supreme) Self is appropriate. ‘Like the other’ (itara-vat) — just as in ‘Which is the Self?’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.7) for the Vājasaneyins there is grasping of the Self, exactly so. Why? ‘From the latter (uttarāt)’ — i.e., from the subsequent teaching of identity (‘That thou art’). ‘If on the ground of the connected sense (it be objected) — it does hold good, because of the (clinching) affirmation.’ — That objection (i.e., that since the opening rules and the word ‘ātman’ is not heard at the opening, there is no grasping of the Self) — what is its reply? It is said: syād avadhāraṇāt — the grasping of the (supreme) Self here does become intelligible because of the (clinching) affirmation. For — having clinched, by ‘that whereby the unheard becomes heard, the unthought thought, the unknown known’ (Chā. Up. 6.1.3), that all-knowledge follows from the knowledge of the One — and wishing to substantiate that, He says ‘sad eva’; and that is established only on the grasping of the (supreme) Self. Otherwise — if that very principal Self were not known — all-knowledge could not be established. Likewise the affirmation of oneness prior to creation, the reference to the jīva by the word ‘ātman’, the description of his attaining that very nature in the state of deep sleep, and again and again the chastening clincher ‘That thou art’ (Chā. Up. 6.8.7) — all this becomes intelligible only when identity is to be expounded, not when identity is to be (artificially) brought about. Nor is it just to urge here the rule that ‘the conclusion follows the opening’. For at the opening there is neither a declaration of selfhood nor a denial of selfhood. And a general opening is not contradicted by a specific (qualifier) found in the rest of the passage, since the general (sāmānya) demands a specifying particular. Even the meaning of the word ‘sat’, when carefully considered, cannot be other than the principal Self, because everything else, since it is a product, is shown to be unreal by the words ‘ārambhaṇa (a mere name from origination)’ and the like. Divergence in recitation does not necessarily entail divergence in meaning, as is seen in ‘Bring the pot’ and ‘The pot bring’ where, despite different wordings, the meaning is the same. Therefore, in such passages, although the modes of exposition differ, there is no difference in the import to be expounded…
BS_C03_S03_V18: kāryākhyānād apūrvam — ‘Because what is being narrated is (already) an established act, what (alone) is novel (to be enjoined here, viz. the conception of waters as the prāṇa’s garment) is what is enjoined.’ ‖ 18 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V18::block-0:
Both the Chāndogas and the Vājasaneyins, in the Prāṇa-saṃvāda, having recited as the prāṇa’s food everything down to dogs and so on, recite the waters as its garment (vāsas). And immediately the Chāndogas recite: ‘Therefore those (knowers), when about to eat, surround (the food/the prāṇa) with water both before and after’ (Chā. Up. 5.2.2). The Vājasaneyins recite: ‘Knowing this, the śrotriyas, when about to eat, sip water; and after eating, sip water; thinking that thereby they make this prāṇa unnaked’ (Bṛ. Up. 6.1.14); ‘Therefore one who knows thus, when about to eat, should sip; and after eating, should sip — thinking that thereby he makes this prāṇa unnaked.’ 

There both an act of sipping (ācamana) and a contemplation of the prāṇa as un-naked are seen. So it is examined: are both enjoined, or only the sipping, or only the un-nakedness contemplation? 

[Pūrvapakṣa] What, then, is the prima facie position? Both are enjoined. Why? Because both are conveyed (by the text), and both, being apūrva (not previously established), deserve to be enjoined. Or else only the sipping is enjoined, for the injunctive form (vidhi-vibhakti) is unmistakable in ‘Therefore one who knows thus, when about to eat, should sip; and after eating, should sip’. The mention of un-nakedness is there merely to praise the sipping itself. 

[Siddhānta] Such being the prima facie view, we say:
BS_C03_S03_V18::block-1:
The being-enjoined of the sipping is not intelligible, because of kārya-ākhyāna — for the sipping, already established as an act for the sake of ritual purity (prāyatya), familiar from smṛti, is here merely being narrated as such (anuvāda). 

‘But may not this śruti be the root (mūla) of that smṛti?’ — No, because the spheres differ. The smṛti has a general scope: it enjoins, with reference to any person whatsoever, sipping for the sake of purity. But the śruti, recited in the context of prāṇa-vidyā, would have to be enjoining a sipping confined to that context. And between śruti and smṛti operating in different spheres, a relation of mūla and mūlin is not intelligible. Nor can it be maintained that this śruti enjoins a novel (apūrva) sipping connected with prāṇa-vidyā, since here the very prior, generally connected sipping is recognised. For the same reason, both cannot be enjoined; otherwise the sentence would split (vākya-bheda). 

Therefore, having referred (anu-vāda) to the sipping that is already established both before and after, in the case of those wishing to eat and those who have eaten, this sentence — ‘thinking that thereby they make this prāṇa un-naked’ (Bṛ. Up. 6.1.14) — newly teaches (apūrva) the conception of the prāṇa being made un-naked, in connection with the prāṇa-vidyā, with respect to the waters used for sipping. Nor is it just to say that this discourse on un-nakedness is for the praise of the sipping, since the sipping is not what is to be enjoined, while the un-nakedness conception is itself perceived as that which is to be enjoined. 

Nor on this view does one have to admit that the single sipping has two purposes — purity and the (prāṇa’s) garment — for they are admitted as different actions: sipping (ācamana) is admitted as a different action serving the purity of the person, while in the waters of that (sipping) the conception of (their being) garment (vāsas) is another action enjoined for the prāṇa’s clothing — and so all is faultless. Moreover, in ‘Whatever there is — even down to dogs, worms, insects, moths — that is your food’ (Bṛ. Up. 6.1.14), the eating of all foods cannot be said to be enjoined, since that is neither in the words nor possible. What is enjoined is the contemplation that all is the prāṇa’s food (anna-dṛṣṭi). By association with that, ‘the waters are the garment’ likewise does not enjoin the sipping of the waters; rather, in the well-known waters used for sipping the conception of (their being) the garment is what is enjoined, as is fitting. For a half-mutilated (ardha-vaiśasa) interpretation is not possible. 

Moreover, since ‘they sip (ācāmanti)’ is a present-tense statement (vartamāna-apadeśin), this expression cannot bear an injunction. — ‘But ‘they think (manyante)’ is likewise present-tense.’ — True; but since one of them must be enjoined, and the prāṇa’s garment-character is what is being narrated as new (apūrva), what is enjoined is the conception of the waters as garment, not the sipping. The sipping is as before — so it has been shown. As for what was said — ‘the injunctive form is unmistakable in the case of sipping’ — that too is answered by the previously-established status of the sipping. Hence, since the sipping is not what is sought to be enjoined, the Kāṇvas conclude with ‘thinking that thereby they make this prāṇa un-naked’ alone, without reciting ‘therefore one who knows thus’ etc. Hence in the Mādhyandina recension as well, by the anuvāda of sipping, what is enjoined is the having-such-knowledge (the knowledge of the prāṇa’s garment-character) — so it is to be understood. The view that ‘in some places the sipping is enjoined, in others the conception of garment’ is also unsound, because the running of the sentence ‘the waters are the garment’ etc. is uniform throughout. Therefore, the conception of the (waters as the prāṇa’s) garment alone is enjoined here, not the sipping — that is the right view. ‖ 18 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V19: samāna evaṃ cābhedāt — ‘And likewise (i.e., as in different recensions, so) when (the recension is) the same, (there is unity of vidyā and consolidation of attributes,) because of the non-difference (of the object of upāsanā).’ ‖ 19 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V19::block-0:
In the Vājasaneyi-śākhā, in the Agni-rahasya, the vidyā stamped with the name Śāṇḍilya is well known. There the qualities are heard: ‘He should meditate upon the Self as consisting of mind, having prāṇa for body, light for form,’ and so on. In the same śākhā, in the Bṛhad-āraṇyaka, again it is recited: ‘This Puruṣa, consisting of mind, of the nature of light, of truth, is within the heart, like a grain of rice or barley. He is the lord of all, the ruler of all; he rules all this — whatever there is’ (Bṛ. Up. 5.6.1). 

[Pūrvapakṣa] There the doubt: is this one and the same vidyā in the Agni-rahasya and the Bṛhad-āraṇyaka, with consolidation of attributes — or are these two distinct vidyās, with the attributes kept apart? The prima facie view: there is difference of vidyā and the attributes are kept severally distributed. Why? Because of the threat of redundancy (paunaruktya). For when the śākhās are different, since the reciters and knowers are different, the avoidance of redundancy was reflected upon, and thus oneness of vidyā was decided, and the additional attributes from one place were consolidated in the other (in cases such as the Prāṇa-saṃvāda) — so it has been said. But in one and the same śākhā, the reciters and knowers being non-different, redundancy being unavoidable, the vidyā situated in distant places cannot be one. Nor here is the division possible whereby ‘one recitation is for enjoining the vidyā, the other for enjoining the attributes’; for then only the additional attributes would be recited each in its place, not the common ones. But common attributes too, like ‘consisting of mind’, are recited in both places. Therefore there is no mutual consolidation of attributes. 

[Siddhānta] When this is the prima facie view, we say:
BS_C03_S03_V19::block-1:
Just as among different śākhās there is unity of vidyā and consolidation of attributes, so it is appropriate even within one and the same śākhā, because of the non-difference (abheda) of the object of meditation. For we recognise the very same Brahman, of attributes such as ‘consisting of mind’, as the object of meditation in both places, undivided. And the form of the vidyā is the upāsya (the object of meditation). When the form is non-different, we cannot decide that the vidyā is different. Nor, when the vidyā is non-different, can the attributes be kept severally distributed. 

‘But because of the threat of redundancy, difference of vidyā is decided.’ — No, we say, because the division of purpose is intelligible: one recitation is for enjoining the vidyā, the other for enjoining the (additional) attributes — there is nothing un-intelligible. ‘But then what was not recited in the Agni-rahasya should alone be recited in the Bṛhad-āraṇyaka — viz. ‘He is the ruler of all’ etc., while what has already been recited — ‘consisting of mind’ etc. — should not be recited.’ — There is no flaw in that, because it is precisely by means of (the repetition of) those that the recognition (pratyabhijñāna) of the vidyā recited elsewhere is brought about. By the repetition of common attributes, the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā situated in a distant place is recognised, and there (i.e., in the recognised vidyā) the attributes such as ‘ruler of all’ are taught. Otherwise, in what other way could this attribute-injunction be made there? Moreover, even when the sentence becomes meaningful through the teaching of the not-yet-attained portion, since the reference to the attained portion can be intelligibly construed as a fixed anuvāda (nityānuvāda), the recognition (yielded by the common attributes) cannot be set aside. Therefore, even in the same śākhā, unity of vidyā and consolidation of attributes is intelligible. ‖ 19 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V20: sambandhād evam anyatrāpi — ‘On account of the connexion (with the same vidyā), so also elsewhere (the two upaniṣad-mantras would apply to both spheres).’ ‖ 20 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V20::block-0:
[Pūrvapakṣa] In the Bṛhad-āraṇyaka, beginning ‘Truth is Brahman’ (Bṛ. Up. 5.5.1) and saying ‘That which is truth — that is yonder Sun, the Puruṣa within yon orb, and the Puruṣa within the right eye’ (Bṛ. Up. 5.5.2), having taught of that very satya-Brahman a particular seat (āyatana) in the adhidaivika and adhyātmika spheres, and having established the body as composed of the vyāhṛtis, two upaniṣads (secret names) are taught: ‘Its upaniṣad is ahaḥ (day)’ — adhidaivika; ‘Its upaniṣad is aham’ — adhyātmika. 

There the doubt: are both upaniṣads to be conjoined indiscriminately in both (spheres), or are they to be applied severally — one in the adhidaivika, the other in the adhyātmika? The sūtra opens (the pūrvapakṣa): just as in the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā, although recited severally, consolidation of attributes was taught, so also elsewhere, in such a topic, it should be — through connection with one and the same vidyā. For this is one satya-vidyā, recited as adhidaivika and adhyātmika together, because of the unity of opening and the interlinked recitation. How can a property obtaining in it not obtain in it (everywhere)? Just as a particular conduct enjoined towards the teacher — such as following — holds equally whether the teacher is in the village or in the forest. Therefore both upaniṣads obtain in both (spheres). ‖ 20 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V21: na vā viśeṣāt — ‘Or rather not, because of the (specific) particularity (of place).’ ‖ 21 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V21::block-0: Such being the prima facie view, (the sūtrakāra) replies —
BS_C03_S03_V21::block-1:
[Siddhānta] Or rather, both do not obtain in both (spheres). Why? Because of the particularity — i.e., because the (upaniṣad-mantras) are tied to specific places of meditation (upāsanā-sthāna-viśeṣa-upanibandha). How are they tied to specific places? It is said: ‘He who is the Puruṣa within yon orb’ (Bṛ. Up. 5.5.3) — having so begun about the adhidaivika Puruṣa, the text says ‘Its upaniṣad is ahaḥ’. ‘He who is the Puruṣa within the right eye’ (Bṛ. Up. 5.5.4) — having so begun about the adhyātmika Puruṣa, the text says ‘Its upaniṣad is aham’. And ‘its (tasya)’ is a pronoun whose support is what is at hand (sannihita-avalambana). Therefore these two upaniṣads are taught with the support of specific seats. How then does both obtain in both? 

‘But this is one and the same Puruṣa, both adhidaivika and adhyātmika — since two seats are taught of one and the same satya-Brahman.’ — True, this is so. But even of the one (Puruṣa), since the specific upaniṣad is taught only by taking up a particular state-aspect (avasthā-viśeṣa), it would belong only to him in that state. There is even an illustration of this: even though the teacher’s essential being does not lapse, the conduct prescribed for following the teacher when he is seated does not apply when he is standing; and what is prescribed for him standing does not apply when he is seated. Whereas in the case of village-and-forest, since the teacher’s essential being does not lapse and the property bound to that essential being does not differ on account of village or forest, the same property holds equally in both — that (the pūrvapakṣin’s example) is a faulty illustration. Therefore there is a (proper) division (vyavasthā) of these two upaniṣads. ‖ 21 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V22: darśayati ca — ‘And (the śruti) shows (this very vyavasthā by an indicatory mark).’ ‖ 22 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V22::block-0: And there is, of such properties, an indicatory mark of vyavasthā (severance) seen — ‘Of this one (the akṣi-puruṣa) the form is precisely the form of yonder one (the āditya-puruṣa); his two joints are the two joints (of the other); his name is the name (of the other)’ (Chā. Up. 1.7.5). How is this an indicator? It is said: seeing that properties bound up with the distinct seats of eye and sun are not to be consolidated in each other, here by an extension (atideśa) the (text) consolidates the form etc. of the āditya-puruṣa onto the akṣi-puruṣa — by ‘Of this one the form is precisely that form’ (Chā. Up. 1.7.5) etc. (The very need for such an atideśa shows that, but for it, properties remain divided.) Therefore the conclusion is: these two upaniṣads are indeed severally distributed. ‖ 22 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V23: sambhṛti-dyu-vyāpty api cātaḥ — ‘And on this same account, (the attributes) of (Brahman’s) holding-together (of powers) and pervading-the-heaven, (recited in the Khilas, are not to be carried over into vidyās such as the Śāṇḍilya).’ ‖ 23 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V23::block-0:
‘Brahman the eldest of forces is gathered together; Brahman first of all stretched out the heaven’ — thus, in the Khilas of the Rāṇāyanīyas, are recited Brahman’s vibhūtis: vīrya-sambhṛti, dyu-niveśa and the rest. And in their (same school’s) Upaniṣad are recited brahma-vidyās such as the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā. 

[Pūrvapakṣa] Now under examination: are those vibhūtis to be consolidated into those brahma-vidyās, or not? When, on account of the connexion with Brahman, consolidation seems to obtain — it (the sūtrakāra) thus speaks: 

[Siddhānta] The vibhūtis — sambhṛti, dyu-vyāpti and the rest — are not to be consolidated in the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā and the like. And precisely on this account: because of the (vidyās’) connection with particular seats. For in the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā Brahman’s seat in the heart is taught — ‘This is my Self within the heart’ (Chā. Up. 3.14.3); likewise in the Dahara-vidyā — ‘A small lotus-house, within it a small ākāśa’ (Chā. Up. 8.1.2). In the Upakosala-vidyā the seat is the eye: ‘That Puruṣa who is seen within the eye’ (Chā. Up. 4.15.1). Thus, in each, some adhyātmika seat is recognised in these vidyās. But these vibhūtis — sambhṛti, dyu-vyāpti and the rest — are adhidaivika. Whence their obtaining in those (vidyās)? 

‘But in those (very vidyās) too, adhidaivika vibhūtis are heard — ‘greater than the heaven, greater than these worlds’ (Chā. Up. 3.14.3); ‘he indeed is bhāmanī, he indeed shines in all the worlds’ (Chā. Up. 4.15.4); ‘as wide as is this ākāśa, so wide is this ākāśa within the heart; in it, indeed, both heaven and earth are placed within’ (Chā. Up. 8.1.3); and the like. There are also other brahma-vidyās without specific seats — the Ṣoḍaśakalā and the rest.’ — True; yet here a particular reason for non-consolidation of sambhṛti etc. is at hand. For in the case of vidyās lying in distant places, when (those) are presented to the mind by the recitation of common attributes, then attributes from a distant place may rightly be consolidated. But sambhṛti and the rest, and the attributes such as ‘consisting of mind’ falling within the scope of the Śāṇḍilya-passage etc., being mutually distinct in nature, are not capable of presenting to the mind a vidyā situated elsewhere. Nor is it fitting to say that, by mere connection with Brahman, a vidyā situated elsewhere is presented; for that would be intelligible even with diversity of vidyā. The settled position is that one and the same Brahman is meditated upon manifold ways through diversity of vibhūtis — as is seen in such graded distinctions as ‘paro-varīyas (higher and higher)’. Therefore vīrya-sambhṛti and the rest are not to be consolidated in the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā and the rest. ‖ 23 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V24: As in the puruṣa-vidyā — because of the non-recital for the others. ‖ 24 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V24::block-0: There exists, in the secret-brāhmaṇa of the Tāṇḍins and the Paiṅgins, a puruṣa-vidyā (meditation on the man as sacrifice). There the puruṣa is figured as the sacrifice (puruṣaḥ yajñaḥ kalpitaḥ); his life-span, divided threefold, is figured as the three savanas (savana-trayam); hunger and the like are figured as the dīkṣā (consecration) and so on; and other dharmas are inculcated there too — the āśīr-mantras (benedictory formulas) and the like. The Taittirīyakas also figure forth a certain puruṣa-yajña, by the anuvāka, ‘Of him, the sacrifice of one who knows thus, the Self is the yajamāna, faith the wife’ (Nā. U. 80). Here the doubt: are those dharmas of the puruṣa-yajña stated in the other (śākhā) to be carried over (upasaṃhartavyāḥ) into the Taittirīyaka also, or are they not? — (Pūrvapakṣa:) Since the character of being a puruṣa-yajña is common to both, carrying over (upasaṃhāra) is in order. (Siddhānta:) We say — they are not to be carried over. Why? Because there is no recognition of that same form (tad-rūpa-pratyabhijñāna-abhāvāt). This the ācārya states by ‘as in the puruṣa-vidyā’: just as among one set of branches — the Tāṇḍins and Paiṅgins — there is the recital of the puruṣa-vidyā, not so is there a recital among the other, the Taittirīyas. For their figuring of the sacrifice is seen to be quite distinct from the other, because of the enumeration of the wife, the yajamāna, the Veda, the vedi, the barhis, the yūpa, the ājya, the paśu, the ṛtvik, etc. The figuring of the savanas too is distinct from the other — ‘What he does in the morning, midday, and evening — those are they’ (Nā. U. 80). Even what little resemblance there is — concerning death-as-avabhṛtha and the like — being slight, is overborne by the much that is dissimilar, and is not capable of grounding recognition. Nor in the Taittirīyaka is the puruṣa heard to be the yajña. ‘Of the knower’ ‘of the sacrifice’ — these two genitives are not in apposition (samānādhikaraṇe), so as to mean ‘of him, who is the sacrifice in the form of the knower’; for the puruṣa has no primary character of being a sacrifice. They are rather two genitives in non-apposition (vyadhikaraṇe) — ‘of the knower, that sacrifice which is his’; for there is a primary connection of the puruṣa with the sacrifice (as its agent). When such a (primary) construal is available, the primary sense alone is to be embraced, not the figurative (na bhāktaḥ). Even ‘the Self is the yajamāna’ — declaring the puruṣa’s being-the-yajamāna — exhibits, by very non-apposition, his connection with the sacrifice. Moreover, since the śruti ‘of him who knows thus’ refers to it as something already established (siddhavad-anuvāda), if one were to set out to teach (now) that the puruṣa is the sacrifice and that the Self etc. are the yajamāna etc., there would be split-of-sentence (vākyabheda). Further, having taught earlier the ātma-vidyā together with renunciation, and seeing that the recital ‘of him who knows thus’ etc. follows immediately afterwards, we apprehend that this passage is a supplement to what precedes (pūrva-śeṣaḥ), not independent (na svatantraḥ). And accordingly we find one and the same fruit for both anuvākas — ‘He attains the greatness of brahman’ (Nā. U. 80); whereas for the others (Tāṇḍins etc.) the recital of the puruṣa-vidyā is not subordinate to anything else (ananya-śeṣaḥ). For there it has length-of-life as its fruit, from the conjunction ‘He lives a hundred-and-sixteen years, who knows thus’ (Chā. U. 3.16.7). Therefore the dharmas of the puruṣa-vidyā studied in another śākhā — the āśīr-mantras and the rest — do not obtain in the Taittirīyaka. ‖ 24 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V25: Because the meanings, viz. piercing etc., differ. ‖ 25 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V25::block-0: (Pūrvapakṣa:) For the Ātharvaṇikas there is, at the beginning of the upaniṣad, a recital of mantras — ‘Piercing all, piercing the heart, having pulled out the arteries, having entirely pulled out the head, threefold severed,’ etc. For the Tāṇḍins — ‘O divine Savitṛ, send forth the sacrifice,’ etc. For the Śāṭyāyanins — ‘White-horsed, green and blue you are,’ etc. For the Kaṭhas and the Taittirīyas — ‘May Mitra be propitious to us, may Varuṇa be propitious’ (Tai. U. 1.1.1), etc. For the Vājasaneyins, however, at the beginning of the upaniṣad, the pravargya-brāhmaṇa is recited — ‘The gods, verily, sat down at a sattra,’ etc. For the Kauṣītakins, too, the agniṣṭoma-brāhmaṇa — ‘Brahman, verily, is the agniṣṭoma; brahman alone is that day; by brahman alone they go to brahman; they attain immortality, who attain that day.’ Are these mantras such as ‘Piercing all’ etc., and the rites such as the pravargya, to be carried over (upasaṃhriyeran) into the meditations (vidyās), or are they not? — Such is our enquiry. What appears to us at first? — Their carrying-over into the vidyās. Why? Because of being read in proximity (sannidhi-pāṭhāt) to the upaniṣadic texts whose principal theme is vidyā. ‘But we do not find injunction of these as being for the sake of vidyā.’ — True; even though we do not find it, we shall infer it from the strength of the proximity. For if proximity is to have any meaning, it is not fitting that, without a cause, it be set aside. ‘But we see no power in these mantras with respect to the topic of vidyā. And how, when the rites such as pravargya are already employed for another purpose, can they also be apprehended as being for vidyā?’ — This is no fault. Some power of the mantras with respect to vidyā can be supposed, because of their mention of the heart and the like; for the heart and the rest are generally taught in upāsanās as seats and so on. And by that route, even mantras such as ‘piercing the heart’ may fittingly be ancillaries of upāsanā; the application of mantras within upāsanās is also seen — ‘I take refuge in bhūḥ, by this, by this, by this’ (Chā. U. 3.15.3) and the like. Likewise the rites such as pravargya, although employed elsewhere too, may also be employed in vidyās without contradiction — as the bṛhaspati-sava in the vājapeya. Such being the prima-facie position, we now state —
BS_C03_S03_V25::block-1: (Siddhānta:) Their carrying-over into the vidyās does not obtain. Why? Because the meanings, viz. piercing etc., differ (vedhādy-artha-bhedāt). For the meanings of mantras such as ‘piercing the heart,’ namely heart-piercings and the rest, are distinct, unconnected (anabhisambaddhāḥ), with the vidyās uttered in the upaniṣads. They have no power to combine with them. ‘But, since the heart is also useful in upāsanās, we have proposed an upāsanā-connection through the heart’ — No, we say. For only the bare mention of the heart could be construed somehow in this way; and the mantra’s meaning here is not the heart alone. The whole of the mantra’s meaning, ‘piercing the heart, having pulled out the arteries,’ does not get connected with the vidyās; for this meaning belongs to ābhicārika (sorcery) usage. Therefore the connection of the mantra ‘Piercing all’ is with an ābhicārika rite. Likewise ‘O divine Savitṛ, send forth the sacrifice’ — being a mark of the impelling of a sacrifice (yajña-prasava-liṅgatvāt) — is connected with a sacrificial rite. Its specific connection should be ascertained from another pramāṇa. So too with the other mantras — some by liṅga, some by direct statement (vacana), some by another pramāṇa — when employed in other meanings, even though read in the rahasya, mere proximity does not establish their being supplements to vidyā. For proximity (sannidhi) is weak in comparison to śruti and the like, as stated in the first tantra — ‘In the conflict of śruti, liṅga, vākya, prakaraṇa, sthāna and samākhyā, the latter are weaker, because of distance from meaning’ (Jai. Sū. 3.3.14). Likewise the rites such as pravargya, employed elsewhere, do not become supplements to vidyās. For they have no unity-of-purpose (aikārthya) with the vidyās. In the case of the vājapeya, however, the bṛhaspati-sava has a clearly other application — ‘Having sacrificed by the vājapeya, one should sacrifice by the bṛhaspati-sava.’ Furthermore this single pravargya, once originated, is employed elsewhere by a stronger pramāṇa, and it does not deserve to be employed elsewhere also by a weaker pramāṇa. For only when the (relative) specifics of the two pramāṇas are not grasped (agṛhyamāṇa-viśeṣatve) could that be so. But between a strong and a weak pramāṇa, the non-apprehension of their distinction is not possible, the very fact of strength-and-weakness being a distinction. Therefore the ancillary-status of such mantras and rites with respect to the vidyās is not to be suspected on the mere ground of proximity. Their proximity-of-recital should be explained as due to a generic similarity-of-dharma — being recited in the forest (araṇyānuvacana) and so on. ‖ 25 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V26: But in (the case of) shaking-off — because of being a complement to the word ‘upayana’ (approaching) — like the kuśa, the metres, the praise, and the upagāna; and that has been declared. ‖ 26 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V26::block-0: (Pūrvapakṣa:) There is the śruti of the Tāṇḍins — ‘As a horse shakes off his hairs, having shaken off evil; as the moon, releasing himself from the mouth of Rāhu; having shaken off the body, with self perfected, I attain (the realm of) brahman, the uncreated’ (Chā. U. 8.13.1). Likewise of the Ātharvaṇikas — ‘Then the wise one, having shaken off merit and demerit, stainless, attains supreme equality’ (Mu. U. 3.1.3). Likewise the Śāṭyāyanins recite — ‘His sons take his inheritance, friends his good deeds, foes his bad deeds.’ Likewise the Kauṣītakins — ‘He shakes off his good and evil deeds; his dear kinsmen take up his good deeds, his unloved take up the evil’ (Kau. U. 1.4). Here, in some places the abandoning (hāna) of merit and demerit is heard; in some places the very same, divided up, with the upayana (taking up) by the dear and the unloved; in some places both — abandoning and taking-up. Where both are heard, nothing need be said. Even where only the taking-up is heard, not the abandoning, the abandoning falls in by implication, since when one’s own merit and demerit are taken up by others, the abandoning is necessary. But where only abandoning is heard, not taking-up — there is doubt: does the taking-up fall in or not? The view is: it does not fall in, because it is not heard, and because the hearing in another śākhā is the domain of another vidyā. Furthermore the abandoning of merit and demerit is done by oneself (ātma-kartṛkam); the taking-up is done by another (para-kartṛkam). When there is no necessary connection between them, how can the taking-up be implied by the abandoning? Therefore the taking-up does not fall in along with the abandoning.
BS_C03_S03_V26::block-1: (Siddhānta:) Against this prima-facie view he says — ‘In abandoning…’. In this very abandoning (hāna) — even when it alone is heard — the taking-up (upayana) deserves to fall in. Because of being a complement to that (tac-cheṣatvāt) — the word ‘upayana’ has been understood, in the Kauṣītaki-rahasya, as a complement of the word ‘hāna’. Therefore, even where the word ‘abandoning’ alone is heard elsewhere, the taking-up persists. As to what was said — that, because of non-hearing, because of being the domain of another vidyā, and because of being unnecessary, it does not fall in — to this we reply: this dictum of restriction would obtain if something to be performed (anuṣṭheyam), heard in one place, were sought to be carried over to another. But here neither abandoning nor taking-up is mentioned as something to be performed. Their mention is only by way of praise of the vidyās — ‘Of such great fortune is this vidyā, by whose power, for him who knows thus, merit and demerit, the cause of saṃsāra, are shaken off; and they take up residence among his friends and foes.’ And in this glorificatory mention (stuty-artha-saṅkīrtana), since the taking-up follows immediately upon the abandoning, where in some place that has been heard, even in another place, when the abandoning is heard, he holds that the taking-up persists, for the sake of obtaining excellence-of-praise (stuti-prakarṣa-lābhāya). Now, recourse to one arthavāda by another arthavāda is well established — in passages such as ‘That sun, verily, is the twenty-first’ (Chā. U. 2.10.5). For how could the twenty-first-ness of the sun be predicated here, without recourse to another arthavāda — ‘The twelve months, the five seasons, these three worlds, that sun is the twenty-first’ (Tai. Saṃ. 5.1.10)? Likewise in passages like ‘There are two triṣṭubh-stotras, for the sake of organs (sa-indriyatva),’ recourse to another arthavāda — ‘The triṣṭubh, verily, is the organ’ — is seen. And since this declaration of upayana is for the sake of praise of vidyā, one need not press too hard the question: how can another’s merit and demerit be taken up by others? And by uttering the word ‘śabda’ in ‘upāyana-śabda-śeṣatvāt’ (the word as supplement of the word) he indicates that the persistence of the upayana in the abandoning is for the sake of praise. For if he meant the carrying over of an attribute (guṇopasaṃhāra), he would have said simply that the meaning of upayana persists in abandoning. Therefore, in the very context of considering attribute-transfer, this sūtra is meant to display the carrying-over of praise. ‘Like the kuśa, the metres, the praise, and the upagāna’ — this is the citation of similes. To wit: among the Bhāllavins, in the verse ‘O kuśas, you are sprung of vanaspati, protect me!’ — when the kuśas are heard generally as having vanaspati for source — by the special statement of the Śāṭyāyanins, ‘The kuśas are of udumbara,’ udumbara-kuśas are taken. Likewise where, in the case of the chants of the gods and the asuras, the order being unspecified generally, by the recital of the Paiṅgya, ‘the chants of the gods are first’ is understood. Likewise in the ṣoḍaśi-stotra, the time being unspecified, by the ārca śruti ‘when the sun has come close-at-hand,’ a particular time is determined. And just as some recite the upagāna without distinction while the Bhāllavins recite it with distinction — as in these cases the speciality from another śruti is appended, so too in the abandoning the persistence of taking-up. For not accepting in one śruti the speciality made in another śruti would result in optionality everywhere; and that is contrary to reasoning when a fixed construal is available. As stated in the Dvādaśa-lakṣaṇī — ‘But, on account of being a sentence-complement, exclusion of the other obtains; in case of negation, optionality would obtain’ (Jai. Sū. 10.8.15).
BS_C03_S03_V26::block-2: Or alternatively, in these very śrutis on shaking-off (vidhūnana), it is by this sūtra that this is to be considered: does this word ‘vidhūnana’ refer to the abandoning (hāna) of merit and demerit, or does it refer to a different meaning? The pūrvapakṣa would be brought to: shaking-off does not denote abandoning, since the dhātu is recited as ‘dhūñ kampane’ (to tremble); and we see the usage ‘the flag-tips quiver (dodhūyante)’ when the flag-tips are agitated by the wind. Therefore vidhūnana denotes agitation. And agitation of merit and demerit makes sense as obstruction of fruit for some time — having brought it to this, the reply: this word vidhūnana ought to operate only in the sense of abandoning (hāna), because of its being a complement to the word ‘upāyana’ (upāyana-śabda-śeṣatvāt). For when others’ merit and demerit are not abandoned (still in their possession), the taking-up of them by others is not possible. Even though the taking-up of others’ merit and demerit by others is not, strictly speaking, intelligible, yet from its very recital, in conformity with that, it can be determined that the abandoning alone is named ‘shaking-off’. And the upayana heard somewhere in the proximity of vidhūnana, like the kuśa, metres, praise, and upagāna, becomes, by the śruti of vidhūnana, expected everywhere, and serves as the universal cause of determination. Nor can agitation, as of flag-tips, primarily belong to merit and demerit, since they are not substances (adravyatvāt). And the horse, when shaking off his hairs, casting off the dust, along with that also makes the worn hairs fall — and the brāhmaṇa says, ‘As a horse shakes off his hairs, having shaken off evil’ (Chā. U. 8.13.1). And since the dhātus are accepted as having many meanings, there is no contradiction with smṛti. ‘That has been declared’ — has been explained. ‖ 26 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V27: At the time of departure, because there is nothing else to be crossed; for thus (do) the others (declare). ‖ 27 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V27::block-0: The Kauṣītakins, in the paryaṅka-vidyā, recite the disjunction from merit and demerit, midway, of one who has set out by the deva-yāna path toward the brahman seated on the couch — beginning ‘He, attaining this deva-yāna path, comes to the agni-loka’ (Kau. U. 1.3), and then ‘He comes to the river Virajā; he crosses it by the mind alone; there he shakes off his merit and demerit’ (Kau. U. 1.4). Now is the disjunction-statement to be taken as the śruti runs — midway on the road — or rather at the very beginning, at the departure from the body? — In this enquiry, since on the strength of śruti the construal as-the-text-runs is at hand, he says — ‘At the time of departure (sāmparāye)’. At the very time of departure, namely going forth from the body (deha-apasarpaṇa), this shaking-off of merit and demerit takes place by the power of the vidyā — so he asserts. And he gives the reason — ‘because there is nothing else to be crossed (tartavyābhāvāt)’. For of the wise one departed, intending by his vidyā to attain brahman, there is nothing in between (antarāle) to be attained by merit and demerit, for the sake of which the two should be supposed to remain unexhausted for some moments. And since the fruit (of those karmas) is contrary to that of the vidyā, by the power of vidyā their destruction occurs. And that should occur precisely at the moment when the vidyā is fruit-facing (vidyā phalābhimukhī). Therefore this destruction of merit and demerit, although already existing earlier, is mentioned later (in the order of recital). Thus also other branch-followers — the Tāṇḍins and the Śāṭyāyanins — recite the abandoning of merit and demerit even in the prior state — ‘As a horse shakes off his hairs, having shaken off evil’ (Chā. U. 8.13.1), and ‘His sons take his inheritance, his friends his good deeds, his foes his bad deeds.’ ‖ 27 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V28: (Performance) at one’s pleasure (chandataḥ); because there is no contradiction either way. ‖ 28 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V28::block-0: And if it were admitted that, for one departed from the body, set forth by the deva-yāna path, the destruction of merit and demerit occurs midway, then, when the body has fallen, since the human effort (puruṣa-yatna) — consisting in yama, niyama, and the practice of vidyā — which is the cause of the destruction of merit and demerit, cannot be undertaken at will (icchātaḥ anuṣṭhāna-anupapatteḥ), the very destruction of merit and demerit caused thereby would not stand. Therefore, it should be seen that the performance, at one’s pleasure (chandataḥ), takes place earlier, in the state of sādhaka (sādhaka-avasthā), and the abandoning of merit and demerit is preceded by that. Thus the relation of cause and effect (nimitta-naimittika) holds good, and the harmony with the śrutis of the Tāṇḍins and Śāṭyāyanins is preserved. ‖ 28 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V29: The (going-) path’s purposefulness is in two ways; otherwise contradiction (would result). ‖ 29 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V29::block-0: In some places, in the proximity of the abandoning of merit and demerit, the deva-yāna path is heard; in some places not. Hence the doubt: should the deva-yāna path fall in indiscriminately wherever there is the abandoning, or by division — in some places it falls in, in some not? Just as it has been stated that the persistence of upayana follows the abandoning indiscriminately, so the persistence of the deva-yāna might also obtain — to this prima-facie position we say: the going-path (gatiḥ) — the deva-yāna path — has its purposefulness (arthavattvam) in two ways (ubhayathā), by division: in some places the going is purposeful, in some not; not indiscriminately. Otherwise — if this going were assumed indiscriminately — there would be contradiction (virodhaḥ). For in the śruti ‘Having shaken off merit and demerit, stainless, he attains supreme equality’ (Mu. U. 3.1.3), a going that conducts to another place would be contradicted. How can the stainless one (nirañjanaḥ), who is no goer (agantā), proceed to another place? And the supreme equality to be attained is not dependent on attaining another place — therefore we hold that here the going is purposeless. ‖ 29 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V30: It is fitting, because the meaning indicated by that (going) is found, as in the world. ‖ 30 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V30::block-0: And this twofold-state — in some places the going is purposeful, in some not — is fitting (upapannaḥ). ‘Because the meaning indicated by that is found (tal-lakṣaṇa-artha-upalabdheḥ)’ — the purpose that is the cause of the going is found in saguṇa upāsanās such as the paryaṅka-vidyā. There the mounting of the couch, the conversation with brahman seated on the couch, the obtaining of distinguished scents and the like — many fruits dependent on the attainment of another place are heard. There the going is purposeful. But in the case of samyag-darśana (the right intuition) there is no finding of any meaning that has the going for its sign (tal-lakṣaṇa-artha-upalabdhi nāsti). For of those who see the oneness of the Self (ātma-aikatva-darśin), whose desires are fulfilled (āpta-kāma), whose seeds of all afflictions have been burnt up here itself (iha eva dagdha-aśeṣa-kleśa-bīja), there is nothing to be expected besides the wearing-out of the karma-deposit that has begun its fruit (ārabdha-bhoga-karma-āśaya-kṣapaṇa). For them the going is purposeless (anarthikā gatiḥ). And this division should be seen as in the world (loka-vat) — just as in the world, for going to a village, a road conducting to another place is needed, but not for the attainment of health; even so here. We shall expound this division more closely in the fourth chapter. ‖ 30 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V31: Non-restriction (applies) to all (vidyās); no contradiction, because of śabda (śruti) and anumāna (smṛti). ‖ 31 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V31::block-0: (Pūrvapakṣa:) It has been stated that in saguṇa vidyās the going is purposeful, not in the nirguṇa Highest-Self vidyā. Even among saguṇa vidyās, in some the going is heard — as in the paryaṅka-vidyā, the upakosala-vidyā, the pañcāgni-vidyā, the dahara-vidyā; not in others — as in the madhu-vidyā, the śāṇḍilya-vidyā, the ṣoḍaśakala-vidyā, the vaiśvānara-vidyā. There the doubt: should this going be restricted to those vidyās in which it is heard, or should it without restriction be associated with all such vidyās? What appears at first? — Restriction (niyamaḥ). It deserves to obtain only where it is heard, since the prakaraṇa is restrictive. If, although heard in one place, the going were to enter another vidyā, the authority of śruti and the rest would be impaired, since everything would have to be (taken as) for the sake of everything. Furthermore, the single arcir-ādi path is recited equally in the upakosala-vidyā and the pañcāgni-vidyā. If it were for all-vidyās, the repetition would be useless. Therefore, restriction obtains. To this he says —
BS_C03_S03_V31::block-1: (Siddhānta:) Non-restriction (aniyamaḥ). For all the saguṇa vidyās, fruits of which are abhyudaya (worldly elevation) and prāpti (attainment), this going called deva-yāna deserves indiscriminately. ‘But in the admission of non-restriction the contradiction with prakaraṇa was urged’ — there is no such contradiction. ‘Because of śabda and anumāna’, that is, śruti and smṛti. Thus the śruti — ‘Those who know thus’ (Chā. U. 5.10.1), introducing the deva-yāna path for the knowers of the pañcāgni-vidyā, with ‘And those who in the forest worship faith and tapas’ (Chā. U. 5.10.1), brings the cultivators of other vidyās also onto the same path with the knowers of the pañcāgni-vidyā. ‘How then is it understood that this going belongs to those of other vidyās? Could it not be only of those devoted to faith and tapas, since only that much is heard?’ — This is no fault. By faith and tapas alone, without the strength of vidyā, this going is not obtained — by the other śruti, ‘By vidyā they ascend it, where desires are gone forth; thither neither the gifts go nor the unlearned ascetics’ (Śat. Br. 10.5.4.6). Therefore here ‘faith and tapas’ is figurative for other vidyās. The Vājasaneyins, in the section of the pañcāgni-vidyā, recite — ‘Those who know thus, and those who in the forest worship faith and the truth’ (Bṛ. U. 6.2.15). There the explanation is: those endowed with faith who worship satya (truth), brahman; for the word ‘satya’ is repeatedly used for brahman. And since the knowers of the pañcāgni-vidyā are taken up by the very ‘know thus’, it is reasonable that here only those devoted to other vidyās are taken up. The śruti ‘And those who do not know these two paths become insects, moths, this whatever bites’ (Bṛ. U. 6.2.16), conducting those fallen from both paths to a wretched downward course (kaṣṭā adho-gatiḥ), includes them within just the deva-yāna and pitṛ-yāna; and there too, by special vidyā, they obtain the deva-yāna. The smṛti also — ‘These bright and dark paths of the world are deemed eternal; by one one goes to non-return, by the other one returns again’ (Bh. Gī. 8.26). As for the twofold recital of the deva-yāna path in the upakosala-vidyā and the pañcāgni-vidyā, that is for the sake of meditative recollection (anucintana) in both. Therefore, non-restriction. ‖ 31 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V32: Those who hold offices [ādhikārikas] continue to abide as long as their office lasts. (32)
BS_C03_S03_V32::block-0: [Pūrvapakṣa:] It is here considered whether, after the falling of the present body of the knower, another body comes into being or not. ‘But surely, when the means — namely vidyā — has been accomplished, the question whether release (kaivalya) issues forth or not is not appropriate. For when the means of cooking are accomplished, there is no doubt whether the rice will become done or not; nor, when one is eating, is it doubted whether one will become satisfied or not.’ Yet this consideration is appropriate, since in the case of some knowers of Brahman, even, the rise of another body is seen in the Itihāsa and Purāṇas. Thus: tradition records that the Vedic teacher named Apāntaratamas, an ancient ṛṣi, by Viṣṇu’s command at the juncture of the Kali and Dvāpara ages came into being as Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana. And Vasiṣṭha, though a mind-born son of Brahmā, having lost his former body through Nimi’s curse, again came into being from Mitra and Varuṇa by the command of Brahmā. The re-arising of Bhṛgu and others — also mind-born sons of Brahmā — at the sacrifice of Varuṇa is heard of as well. Sanatkumāra too, the mind-born son of Brahmā, by his own grant of a boon to Rudra appeared as Skanda. So too of Dakṣa, Nārada, and the rest, repeated taking of new bodies upon various occasions is told in the Smṛti. In the Śruti also, in mantras and arthavādas, this is mostly noticed. Of these, some take a fresh body when the previous body has fallen, while others, by the power of yogic mastery, take other bodies even while the former still stands, on the principle of assuming many bodies. And all these are remembered as having mastered the entire meaning of the Veda. Therefore, from the seeing of their taking of further bodies, it would follow that brahma-vidyā is only sometimes (pākṣikam) the cause of mokṣa, or even no cause at all.
BS_C03_S03_V32::block-1: [Siddhānta:] To this the reply is given: No. For of those — Apāntaratamas and the like — appointed in offices (adhikāras) such as the promulgation of the Veda, which serve as causes of the maintenance of the world, the abiding [in body] is governed by the office (adhikāra-tantratvāt sthiteḥ). Just as the blessed Sun, having exercised authority over the world for a thousand yugas, at the close of that experiences kaivalya devoid of rising and setting — as the Śruti declares: ‘Then thence, having gone upward, he neither rises nor sets — he abides alone in the middle.’ (Ch.U. 3.11.1); and just as living knowers of Brahman, when their commenced enjoyment is exhausted, attain kaivalya — as the Śruti declares: ‘For him there is delay only so long as he is not released; thereupon he becomes one [with Brahman].’ (Ch.U. 6.14.2) — so likewise, Apāntaratamas and the rest, being lords appointed by the Supreme Lord in their respective offices, even though right knowledge — the cause of kaivalya — be present, with their karman not yet exhausted, abide as long as the office endures, and at its close are released. This is not contradictory. For they, having a karmic store that has once set in motion to yield its fruit, pass it through to the end; and out of their own freedom, like one going from house to house, they pass from body to body, with memory unimpaired, by virtue of their mastery over the body, the senses and material nature, fashioning bodies and presiding over them simultaneously or in succession, for the accomplishment of their office. Nor are these called jāti-smaras (those who recall past births), since the Smṛti establishes them as the very same persons. Thus it is remembered: Sulabhā, the female knower of Brahman, wishing to dispute with Janaka, having laid aside her own body and entered Janaka’s body, having disputed through that, afterwards entered her own body again. — If, however, when the once-set karman is being consumed, another karman were to manifest itself as cause for the commencement of yet another body, then any other karman whose seed is not burnt could likewise occur, and so it might be doubted whether brahma-vidyā is only a sometime cause of mokṣa or no cause at all. But this doubt is not proper, for the burning of the seed of karman by knowledge is established by both Śruti and Smṛti. Thus the Śruti: ‘The knot of the heart is sundered, all doubts are cut asunder, and his karmans wear away when That, both higher and lower, is seen.’ (Mu.U. 2.2.9); and ‘On the gaining of memory, all knots are released.’ (Ch.U. 7.26.2) — and others of like kind. The Smṛti also: ‘As a kindled fire, O Arjuna, reduces fuel to ashes, so does the fire of knowledge reduce all karmans to ashes.’ (Bh.G. 4.37); and ‘As seeds burnt by fire do not sprout again, so the self does not arise again through afflictions burnt by knowledge.’ (Mbh. 12.211.17) — and others of like kind. Nor, when the afflictions such as avidyā are burnt, is it possible that the karmic store, which is the seed of the kleśas, should be partly burnt and partly capable of sprouting; for one does not see partial sprouting in the rice-seed burnt by fire. But the karmic store whose fruit has commenced bears nivṛtti, like the spent momentum of an arrow released — for the Śruti ‘For him there is delay only so long’ (Ch.U. 6.14.2) appoints the falling of the body as the limit. Therefore the abiding of the ādhikārikas as long as their office lasts is established. Nor is the fruit of knowledge non-determinative. For the Śruti shows mokṣa from knowledge for all without distinction: ‘Whichever of the gods awoke to It, that very thing he became; so too of the ṛṣis, so too of men.’ (Br.U. 1.4.10). And in other knowledges, namely those whose fruit is lordliness and the like, the great ṛṣis may have remained attached. They, afterwards, on seeing the destruction of lordliness…
BS_C03_S03_V33: But [in the case] of cognitions of the Imperishable, there is comprehensive inclusion, on account of identity (sāmānya) and that being-so (tad-bhāva), as in the case of the upasads — that has been stated. (33)
BS_C03_S03_V33::block-0: In the Vājasaneyaka it is heard: ‘That, O Gārgī, is what the Brāhmaṇas call the Imperishable — neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long, not red, not adhesive…’ (Br.U. 3.8.8) and so on. So too in the Atharva: ‘Then the higher [knowledge], by which That, the Imperishable, is attained’ (Mu.U. 1.1.5); ‘That which is invisible, ungraspable, without family, without color…’ (Mu.U. 1.1.6) and so on. Likewise elsewhere, the Imperishable, the Supreme Brahman, is taught by way of negation of particulars (viśeṣa-nirākaraṇa). And in some places certain additional particulars are denied. The doubt arises whether all these cognitions of the negation of particulars apply everywhere, or whether they are arranged distinctly (vyavasthā) — the latter being the apparent result from the division in the Śruti. [Siddhānta:] To this it is said: All cognitions of the negation of particulars regarding the Akṣara are to be comprehensively included everywhere, on account of identity (sāmānya) and the same being-so (tad-bhāva). For everywhere the mode of teaching Brahman, viz. by negation of particulars, is the same. And the very Brahman to be taught everywhere is recognized as not different. So why should cognitions formed in one place not be valid in another? This has been explained at ‘Bliss and the rest of [Brahman’s qualities] belong to the principal’ (Br.S. 3.3.11). The difference is that there qualifications of an affirmative form were considered, here those of a negative form. The purpose of this divided treatment is detailed exposition (prapañca-artha). The illustration ‘like the upasads’ (aupasadavat). Just as in the Jāmadagnya ahīna sacrifice, when the puroḍāśins and the upasads have been enjoined, the mantras for the offering of the puroḍāśa — ‘O Agni, accept the hotrā, accept the adhvara’ and the like — though originating in the Udgātṛ-veda, are nevertheless connected with the Adhvaryus, since the offering of the puroḍāśa is performed by the Adhvaryu, and since the subordinate elements depend upon the principal — so here too, since the qualifying expressions depend upon the Akṣara (akṣara-tantratva), wherever they may have arisen, they are everywhere connected with the Akṣara. This is the import. This has been stated in the first Kāṇḍa: ‘In the case of conflict between subsidiary and principal, on account of being for the sake of the principal, connection with the Veda is by the principal’ (Jai.S. 3.3.9).
BS_C03_S03_V34: On account of just so much being declared. (34)
BS_C03_S03_V34::block-0: ‘Two birds, fast-bound companions, embrace the self-same tree. Of these two, the one eats the sweet pippala-fruit; the other looks on without eating.’ (Mu.U. 3.1.1) — this mantra the Atharvaṇikas and the Śvetāśvataras read in a context concerning the inner self (adhyātma).
