So too the Kaṭhas read: ‘The two who drink the ṛta in the world of sukṛta, who have entered the cave, in the highest, in the most exalted — they are spoken of as ‘shadow and sunshine’ by knowers of Brahman, by householders of the five fires and those of the threefold Nāciketa.’ (Ka.U. 1.3.1). Here is the doubt — is the vidyā one, or are the vidyās many? [Pūrvapakṣa:] The vidyās are many. Why? On account of the seeing of difference: in ‘Two birds’, of the one being an enjoyer is seen, and of the other, non-enjoyership is seen. In ‘Drinking the ṛta’, both alike are seen as enjoyers. Hence the form to be known, being differentiated, would render the vidyā differentiated. — Such being the prima facie view, [the Sūtrakāra] declares —
BS_C03_S03_V34::block-1: [Siddhānta:] The vidyā is one. Why? Since in both these mantras the form to be known, marked off by ‘so much’ and characterized by twoness, is declared to be not different. ‘But surely a difference of form has been shown!’ — No, we say. For both these mantras teach the Lord with the jīva as second, and not anything else. Now in ‘Two birds’: by ‘the other looks on without eating’, the supreme Self, transcending hunger and the rest, is taught. In the concluding portion too, that very one is seen to be taught: ‘When he sees the other, the Lord, the worshipped, and his greatness…’ (Śv.U. 4.7). In ‘drinking the ṛta’, however, while it is the jīva that drinks, the supreme Self too — though transcending hunger and the rest — is, by association, figuratively spoken of as drinking on the chatrin-nyāya principle (the principle of the umbrella-bearer giving its name to the whole company). For this is a topic on the supreme Self, opening with ‘Other than dharma, other than adharma…’ (Ka.U. 1.2.14). And the concluding portion here too belongs to that very topic: ‘Who is the bridge of those who sacrifice — the Imperishable Brahman that is supreme’ (Ka.U. 1.3.2). And this has been detailed at ‘The two who have entered the cave are the [two] selves’ (Br.S. 1.2.11). Hence there is no difference of object-known. And from this the oneness of vidyā follows. Moreover, on a survey of antecedent and consequent in all three Vedānta passages, only knowledge of the Supreme Self is gathered. The taking up of the jīva is for the express intention of conveying tādātmya (essential identity), not with intent to convey a different entity. And in the knowledge of the Supreme Self there is no occasion for the consideration of identity-in-difference, as has been said. Hence this mention is solely for the sake of detailed exposition (prapañca-artha). And from that, the gathering-up (upasaṃhāra) of additional qualities follows.
BS_C03_S03_V35: [The mention of] the Self [in two places] is not [the indication of two vidyās], like the multitude of beings [that are within one body]. (35)
BS_C03_S03_V35::block-0: ‘That which is directly and immediately Brahman, the Self that is innermost of all’ (Br.U. 3.4.1; 3.5.1) — thus the Vājasaneyins twice declare it without a break, in the questions of Uṣasta and of Kahola. There the doubt arises: is it one vidyā or many vidyās? [Pūrvapakṣa:] The vidyās are many — owing to the force of repetition (abhyāsa-sāmarthya). Otherwise, twofold mention with respect to a non-deficient and non-redundant subject-matter would be purposeless. Hence, just as repetition makes for difference of karman, so also it makes for difference of vidyā. — To this it is replied. [Siddhānta:] The Self is one [in both passages], on account of non-difference of declaration; hence one vidyā. For the Self, innermost of all, is asked about and answered alike in both — and there cannot be in one body two Selves both innermost of all. For if so, of one alone would the innermost-of-all-ness fit straightforwardly, while of the other — like the multitude of beings (bhūta-grāma) — innermost-of-all-ness would not in the primary sense apply. Just as in the body — a collection of the five elements — water is inner to earth, fire is inner to water, etc.; though there is here a relative innerness, there is no primary innermost-of-all-ness — so here too. The meaning is this. Or else, ‘like the multitude of beings’ adduces another Śruti as illustration. Just as in this mantra ‘One God hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner Self of all beings’ (Śv.U. 6.11), in all collections of beings only one Self, innermost of all, is declared — so in these two Brāhmaṇas as well. The meaning is this. Therefore, from the oneness of the object-of-knowing, oneness of vidyā.
BS_C03_S03_V36: If it be argued: ‘Otherwise, the difference [in mention] would not be intelligible’ — we reply: No; as in the case of another teaching [i.e. of Tattvamasi]. (36)
BS_C03_S03_V36::block-0: Now what was urged — that, if difference of vidyā be not admitted, the difference of mention is unintelligible — must be answered. To this it is said: This is no defect, since [the mention] is intelligible like another teaching. Just as in the Upaniṣad of the Tāṇḍins, in the sixth chapter, ‘That Self, that thou art, O Śvetaketu’ (Ch.U. 6.8.7) is taught nine times without there being any difference of vidyā, so it will be here too. And how is it that even with nine teachings there is no difference of vidyā? Because, by the introduction and conclusion (upakrama-upasaṃhāra), the oneness of meaning is grasped — and from ‘May the Lord teach me again’ (Ch.U. 6.5.4) one understands that one and the very same matter is sought to be taught over and over by way of the resolving of further doubts; thus repeated teaching is intelligible. So here too, by the non-difference of the form of question, and by the non-difference of conclusion ‘Other than this is wretched’ (Br.U. 3.4.2), the introduction and conclusion are seen to bear on the same meaning. The use of ‘eva’ (just) in the second question, ‘That alone which is directly and immediately Brahman’ (Br.U. 3.5.1), shows that the very meaning of the prior question is here being drawn through. And in the prior brāhmaṇa is told the existence of a Self distinct from the body and senses (kārya-karaṇa); in the latter, of the very same Self, the transcendence of saṃsāra-attributes such as hunger is told — thus oneness of meaning is intelligible. Hence, one vidyā.
BS_C03_S03_V37: There is mutual exchange [of attributes between meditator and meditated upon], for [the Śruti] particularizes; as in other [meditations]. (37)
BS_C03_S03_V37::block-0: Just as the Aitareyins, with reference to the puruṣa in the sun, declare ‘That which I am is that; that which is that, am I’ (Ai.Ā. 2.2.4.6) and so on, so the Jābālas: ‘Verily I am thou, O divine being; thou indeed art I’. Here is the doubt: should the meditation here be made in the form of mutual exchange (vyatihāra) — bearing both forms — or only of one form? [Pūrvapakṣa:] Only of one form. For here nothing else need be meditated upon save the oneness of the Self with the Lord. If the difference here taught were so envisaged that the saṃsārin acquired Lord-Selfhood, and the Lord saṃsārin-Selfhood, then while the saṃsārin would be exalted by Lord-Selfhood, the Lord would be debased by saṃsārin-Selfhood. Hence the meditation must be of one form only; the mutual-exchange-mention is for confirming oneness — such being the prima facie view, [the Sūtrakāra] replies: [Siddhānta:] This vyatihāra is mentioned for the purpose of meditation (ādhyāna). Like the rest — that is, just as other qualities, sarvātmatva and so on, are mentioned for meditation, so this. For the texts particularize by uttering both: ‘Thou art I, and I am thou’. And that becomes meaningful only when a meditation in both forms is to be made. Otherwise, this special pronouncement of both would be useless, since one alone would suffice. ‘But on supposing that the dual mention has a special meaning, the deity must come to have saṃsārin-Selfhood, hence debasement’ — that has been said. To which we reply: this is no defect, for it is the very oneness of Self that is being meditated upon by this method. ‘But on this view, the very confirmation of oneness results’ — yes, we do not exclude the confirmation of oneness; but [the point is], by force of the [scriptural] declaration, here a dual-form meditation is to be made by way of vyatihāra, not a single-form one — that alone we are establishing. As a fruit (phalataḥ), oneness too becomes confirmed. Just as, even when [qualities such as] satya-kāmatva are taught for the sake of meditation, the Lord becomes proved as endowed with that quality — likewise here. Therefore this vyatihāra is to be meditated upon, and is to be brought together (upasaṃhṛta) wherever the topic is the same.
BS_C03_S03_V38: For this very [Satya-vidyā] is itself the [vidyā with the qualities] satya and the rest. (38)
BS_C03_S03_V38::block-0: ‘He who knows that great Yakṣa, the first-born, as the Satya, the Brahman’ (Br.U. 5.4.1) — having thus enjoined in the Vājasaneyaka the Satya-vidyā as the meditation upon the Akṣara along with the name, immediately afterwards is declared: ‘Now that which is that Satya — yon Sun, that puruṣa who is in this disc, and the puruṣa here in the right eye…’ (Br.U. 5.5.2) and so on. The doubt: are these two Satya-vidyās, or only one? [Pūrvapakṣa:] Two — for the connection with fruit is in two places: ‘he conquers these worlds’ (Br.U. 5.4.1) earlier, and ‘he kills evil and abandons it’ (Br.U. 5.5.4) later. The drawing-in of what is already in context (prakṛta-ākarṣaṇa) is due only to oneness of object of meditation. — Such being the prima facie view, we say:
BS_C03_S03_V38::block-1: [Siddhānta:] The Satya-vidyā is one and the same. Why? On account of the drawing-in of what is already in context — ‘Now that which is that Satya’ (Br.U. 5.5.2). ‘But even where the vidyā is different, the drawing-in is intelligible from oneness of object of meditation’ — we said this. Not so. Where it is grasped from a clear independent cause that the vidyā is different, only then would this be so. But here, where both are possible, by ‘Now that which is that Satya’ — the drawing-in of the prakṛta — only the Satya already connected with the prior vidyā is here drawn in. Hence the determination of one-vidyā-ness. As to what was urged — that the hearing of a different fruit means a different vidyā — we reply: ‘Whose upaniṣad is ahaḥ … aham’ — this hearing of another fruit is praise (stāvaka) for the teaching of another aṅga, not [a fruit-mention]; so no defect. Moreover, when the fruit must be conjectured from arthavāda alone, and the oneness of vidyā is established, the many fruits heard in the parts must be brought together (upasaṃhṛta) in the whole vidyā. Therefore this is one and the very same Satya-vidyā mentioned with this and that particular — hence all the qualities such as satya are to be brought together in one and the same prayoga (application).
BS_C03_S03_V38::block-2: Some, however, with reference to this sūtra, cite this Vājasaneyaka passage on the puruṣa in the eye and in the sun, and in the Chāndogya ‘Now that which is the golden puruṣa within the sun’ (Ch.U. 1.6.6) and ‘Now that puruṣa who is seen within the eye’ (Ch.U. 4.15.1), and holding that this same vidyā concerning the puruṣa-in-eye-and-sun is one in both places, hold that the qualities ‘satya’ etc. are to be transferred from the Vājasaneyins to the Chandogas. This is not seen as proper. For in the Chāndogya, this is a vidyā connected with the udgītha, belonging to the Jyotiṣṭoma rite. There, in the beginning, middle, and end, marks of connection with the rite are present: ‘this Ṛk is the Sāman, this is Agni’ (Ch.U. 1.6.1) at the opening; ‘its Ṛk and Sāman are knot-like joints, hence Udgītha’ (Ch.U. 1.6.8) in the middle; ‘he who, knowing thus, sings the Sāman’ (Ch.U. 1.7.9) at the conclusion. There is no such karma-related mark in the Vājasaneyaka. There, with difference of opening, the vidyās being different, the assignment of the qualities to each in due distribution alone is proper.
BS_C03_S03_V39: ‘Kāma’ (the desires) and the rest [are to be brought in] elsewhere also; [and from the other place, the qualities are to be brought in] there too — on account of the abode (āyatana) and the rest [being common]. (39)
BS_C03_S03_V39::block-0: ‘Now that which is in this Brahma-city, this small lotus-mansion, the small ākāśa within’ (Ch.U. 8.1.1) — beginning thus, the Chandogas read: ‘This Self is free of evil, free of ageing, of death, of grief, of hunger, of thirst — true-desiring, true-resolving’ (Ch.U. 8.1.5) and so on. Likewise the Vājasaneyins: ‘That, indeed, is this great unborn Self that is among the prāṇas, this consisting of vijñāna, the ākāśa within the heart, in which lying It is the controller of all’ (Br.U. 4.4.22) and so on. Here, is there oneness of vidyā and mutual transfer of qualities, or not? — that is the doubt. [Siddhānta:] Oneness of vidyā [holds]. Hence it is said: ‘kāma’ etc., meaning ‘satya-kāma’ etc. — by the same kind of nirvacana as ‘Devadatta’ for ‘Dattaḥ’, ‘Bhāmā’ for ‘Satyabhāmā’. The collection of qualities — satya-kāmatva and so on — that is found in the Chāndogya regarding the heart-ākāśa, that is to be connected elsewhere — in the Vājasaneyaka — at ‘That, verily, is this great unborn Self.’ And what is found in the Vājasaneyaka regarding controllership and the like, that too is to be connected in the other [text], the Chāndogya, at ‘This Self free of evil…’ (Ch.U. 8.1.5). Why? On account of the commonness of abode and the rest. The heart is the same abode in both, the Lord is the same as the object of knowledge, the same is His being a bridge with the purpose of preventing the inter-mingling of worlds — and so much else common is seen. ‘But surely a difference too is seen — in the Chāndogya the qualifying belongs to the heart-ākāśa, while in the Vājasaneyaka to the Brahman that has ākāśa for its abode’ — no, since at ‘“the small”, on account of what follows’ (Br.S. 1.3.14) it has been established that even in the Chāndogya the word ākāśa is Brahman itself. But here this much of difference does obtain: in the Chāndogya saguṇa brahma-vidyā is taught — for from ‘Now those who, having known here this Self, depart [knowing] these true desires too…’ (Ch.U. 8.1.6), the desires likewise are heard of as objects of knowledge along with the Self. In the Vājasaneyaka, however, only the nirguṇa supreme Brahman is seen taught — by the harmony of question and answer, ‘Hence speak [to me] for liberation upward’ (Br.U. 4.3.14), ‘For this puruṣa is unattached’ (Br.U. 4.3.15), and so on. The qualities such as controllership are mentioned in the Vājasaneyaka only for the praise of That. And so further on, with ‘That Self is “not this, not this”’ (Br.U. 3.9.26) and so on, He concludes nirguṇa Brahman alone. But since the saguṇa Brahman is one with the [supreme], the gathering-up of qualities sūtrically given is for the display of His vibhūti, not for upāsana — so it should be seen.
BS_C03_S03_V40: On account of [the scripture's] regard, there is no omission. ‖ 40 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V40::block-0: In the Chāndogya, in connection with the Vaiśvānara-vidyā, it is heard: ‘That food which would come first — that is fit for oblation; the first oblation that he should offer he should offer saying: prāṇāya svāhā’ (Chā. Up. 5.19.1) and so on. There five prāṇa-oblations are enjoined. And subsequently, with reference to them, the word ‘agnihotra’ is employed: ‘He who, knowing thus, offers this agnihotra’ (Chā. Up. 5.24.2), and ‘Just as here hungry children sit around their mother, so do all beings sit around the agnihotra’ (Chā. Up. 5.24.5). On this the following is considered: when there is failure of eating (bhojana-lopa), is there omission (lopa) of the prāṇāgnihotra, or no omission?
BS_C03_S03_V40::block-1: [Pūrvapakṣa:] Since it is heard ‘that food (bhakta) which…’, connecting [the rite] with the arrival of food (bhakta-āgamana-saṃyoga), and since the arrival of food serves the purpose of eating, when eating fails the prāṇāgnihotra too is omitted — thus when this is established [as the prima facie view, the sūtrakāra] first declares: ‘Let it not be omitted.’ Why? ‘Because of regard (ādarāt).’ For thus, in the very Vaiśvānara-vidyā, there is the Jābāla-śruti: ‘He should eat before [serving] guests; for [otherwise], just as one would, without himself offering the agnihotra, offer it for another, so it would be’ — censuring the priority of feeding the guest, and ordaining priority of the householder's own eating, [this passage] shows regard (ādara) for the prāṇāgnihotra. For [the scripture] which does not tolerate even the omission of priority, all the more would not tolerate the omission of the agnihotra which possesses such priority — so it is held.
BS_C03_S03_V40::block-2: [Objection:] But surely, owing to the connection [of this rite] with the arrival of food which is meant for eating, the omission [of the rite] when eating fails has been established. — No; for that [connection] is meant to enjoin a particular substance (dravya-viśeṣa-vidhāna). For, in the standard agnihotra, milk and the like substances are fixed; here too, by the word ‘agnihotra’, like in the Kauṇḍapāyinām-ayana, when its dharmas would [otherwise] be obtained, this passage ‘that food which…’ serves to enjoin food-substance as a special qualifying property (guṇa-viśeṣa). Hence, the omission is only of the qualifying property (guṇa-lopa), not of the principal (mukhya). Thus it is established. Even when eating fails, the prāṇāgnihotra should be performed by the principle of substitution (pratinidhi-nyāya), with water or some other non-contradictory substance. ‖ 40 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V41: When [food] is at hand — from that, because of its mention. ‖ 41 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V41::block-0: [Leading bhāṣya:] To this he gives the reply that follows —
BS_C03_S03_V41::block-1: [Siddhānta:] ‘When food is at hand’, ‘from that’ — that is, from that very food-substance, the one that has first arrived — the prāṇāgnihotra is to be accomplished. Why? ‘Because of its mention (tad-vacanāt).’ For thus: ‘That food which would come first, that is fit for oblation’ (Chā. Up. 5.19.1) — by referring to the arrival of food as something already accomplished (siddha-vat), it ordains that the prāṇa-oblations are to be accomplished by means of a substance meant for another purpose (parārtha-dravya-sādhyatā). When these [prāṇa-oblations] have the character of being non-prompting [as to substance] (aprayojaka-lakṣaṇa-āpanna), how could they cause a substitute substance to be installed when eating fails? Nor is there here the obtaining of the dharmas of the standard agnihotra. For in the Kauṇḍapāyinām-ayana, the agnihotra-word standing in the injunctive statement ‘he offers the agnihotra for a month’ would ordain similarity-of-being (tadvad-bhāva); thus the obtaining of its dharmas is fitting. But here the agnihotra-word, occurring in an arthavāda, is not capable of ordaining similarity-of-being. And were the obtaining of those dharmas to be admitted, even the ‘taking out of the fires’ (agny-uddharaṇa) and the like would be obtained. But this is not possible. The agny-uddharaṇa is for the sake of providing a locus for the homa. But this homa is not in fire — for then the contradiction with its purpose of being eating would arise. And from the connection with the substance brought by eating, this homa is in the mouth (āsye) itself. And so the Jābāla-śruti, ‘He should eat before [serving] guests’, shows that this consummation of the homa has the mouth as its locus (āsya-ādhārā). For this very reason, here too only the mentally-conceived (sāmpādika) limbs of the agnihotra are exhibited: ‘The chest itself is the altar (vedi), the body-hair is the barhis, the heart is the gārhapatya, the mind is the anvāhāryapacana, the mouth is the āhavanīya’ (Chā. Up. 5.18.2). And the mention of ‘altar’ here should be seen as a mere indicator of any plot of ground (sthaṇḍila-mātra-upalakṣaṇa), since in the principal agnihotra there is no ‘altar’, and since here the [agnihotra's] limbs are intended to be brought into mental conception. And from connection with eating — which is itself time-determined — there is no possibility of restriction to the standard agnihotra-time. Thus other dharmas too — like the upasthāna and the rest — somehow contradict in some respects. Therefore, on the eating-side alone these five homas are to be accomplished, by the connection with mantra, substance, and deity. As for the statement that ‘regard is seen’ — that is, on the eating-side, for ordaining priority. There is no excessive burden on the [scriptural] statement. But by this, its perpetuity (nityatā) cannot be shown. Therefore, when eating fails, there is omission of the prāṇāgnihotra itself. ‖ 41 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V42: There is no fixity in the determinations regarding that, since this is seen; for the fruit, namely the non-obstruction [of the rite's fruit], is separate. ‖ 42 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V42::block-0: [Pūrvapakṣa:] There are vijñānas (meditations) which depend on the limbs of [ritual] action — like ‘One should meditate on this syllable Om as the udgītha’ (Chā. Up. 1.1.1) and the rest. Are they perpetual (nitya) in [their] rituals — like being-made-of-parṇa [palāśa wood for the ladle] and the like — or non-perpetual (anitya), like the godohana-vessel and the like? — let us inquire. What, then, is the prima facie view? They are perpetual. Why? Because they are taken up by the prayoga-vacana (statement of performance). For these [meditations], even though learned outside [the ritual context] (anārabhya-adhīta), are touched by the prayoga-vacana of the ritual itself, just like other limbs, through their connection with the ritual via the udgītha and the rest. As for the mention of fruit in their own sentences — ‘He becomes one who fulfils desires’ (Chā. Up. 1.1.7) and so on — that, being of the form of statement-in-the-present (vartamāna-apadeśa-rūpa), is mere arthavāda, like ‘he hears no evil śloka’ and the like; it is not predominantly fruit-stating (phala-pradhāna). Therefore, just as ‘he whose juhū-ladle is made of parṇa hears no evil śloka’ etc., though learned outside the prakaraṇa, are perpetual like things learned within the prakaraṇa because they enter the rite through the juhū and the rest, so too the udgītha-meditations etc. are perpetual — when this is established as the prima facie view, we say:
BS_C03_S03_V42::block-1: [Siddhānta:] ‘There is no fixity in the determinations regarding that.’ Those determinations of the true nature of the qualifying properties of acts like the udgītha — namely ‘rasatama’ (most-essence), ‘āpti’ (attainment), ‘samṛddhi’ (prosperity), ‘mukhya-prāṇa’ (chief vital breath), ‘āditya’ (sun), and the like — are not to be fixed in the rituals like perpetual [limbs]. Why? ‘Because that is seen (tad-dṛṣṭeḥ).’ For the śruti shows the non-fixity of such [meditations]: ‘By that [udgītha] both perform — he who knows it thus and he who does not know’ (Chā. Up. 1.1.10) — since the action is permitted even to one who does not know. And since the prastotṛ and the rest, even when devoid of the knowledge of the deities of the prastāva and the rest, are seen carrying out the sacrifice — ‘O prastotṛ, that deity which follows the prastāva — if, not knowing it, you will sing the prastāva…’ (Chā. Up. 1.10.9), ‘…if, not knowing it, you will sing the udgītha…’ (Chā. Up. 1.10.10), ‘…if, not knowing it, you will perform the pratihāra…’ (Chā. Up. 1.10.11). Moreover, for such a vijñāna depending on the limbs of action, a fruit separate from that of the action is obtained — namely, non-obstruction of the accomplishment of the action's fruit, the prosperity thereof, some special excess: ‘By that both perform — he who knows it thus and he who does not. But the vidyā and the avidyā are different. Whatever one performs with vidyā, with faith, with the upaniṣad — that becomes more potent (vīryavattaram)’ (Chā. Up. 1.1.10). There, by the separation of the performances of the knower and the non-knower indicated by ‘nānā tu’ (‘but they are different’), and by the use of the comparative -tara suffix in ‘vīryavattaram’, it is understood that even action devoid of vidyā is potent (vīryavat). And that is intelligible only on the non-perpetuity of the vidyā. But on its perpetuity, how would action devoid of it be sanctioned as potent? For only when all the limbs are gathered together is action established as potent. Likewise, in the Loka-sāman and so on, definite fruits are taught for each meditation — ‘The worlds, both upward and returning, become arrayed for him’ (Chā. Up. 2.2.3) etc. Nor is it fitting to construe this fruit-statement as mere arthavāda. For thus, secondary-meaning (guṇa-vāda) would result. But on the fruit-instruction, primary-meaning (mukhya-vāda) is intelligible. In the prayājas etc., however, since the ritual that requires the procedural how-to (itikartavyatā) is the topic in question, and they serve that purpose, it is fitting that the fruit-mention be arthavāda. So too in things learned outside the prakaraṇa, like ‘being made of parṇa’; for those that are not action-natured, the connection with fruit is not intelligible without a [ritual] locus (āśraya). For the godohana etc., since they obtain the locus of the apām-praṇayana etc. that are in the prakaraṇa, the fruit-injunction is intelligible. Likewise for the bilva-vessels etc., since they obtain the locus of the standard yūpa etc. that is in the prakaraṇa, the fruit-injunction is intelligible. But for ‘being made of parṇa’ etc., no such locus is in the prakaraṇa; if one were to assume the juhū etc. as locus by mere sentence and intend an injunction also in the fruit, sentence-splitting (vākya-bheda) would result. The upāsanās, however, being action-natured (kriyā-ātmaka), allow for a specific injunction; and for them, having udgītha etc. as locus, the injunction in fruit is not contradicted. Therefore, just as the godohana etc., though belonging to the ritual, are non-perpetual on account of fruit-connection, so too the udgītha-upāsanās etc. should be seen [as non-perpetual]. And for this very reason the kalpasūtra-makers did not arrange such upāsanās in the rituals. ‖ 42 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V43: Like the offerings, that is stated. ‖ 43 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V43::block-0: [Pūrvapakṣa:] In the Vājasaneyaka, in the passage ‘“I shall speak,” said Speech and held herself’ (Bṛ. Up. 1.5.21), in the ādhyātmika [domain] of speech and the rest, the prāṇa is determined to be foremost; in the adhidaivata [domain] of fire and the rest, vāyu. Likewise in the Chāndogya, in ‘Vāyu indeed is the absorber (saṃvarga)’ (Chā. Up. 4.3.1), in the adhidaivata [domain] of fire and the rest, vāyu is determined to be the absorber; in ‘Prāṇa indeed is the absorber’ (Chā. Up. 4.3.3), in the ādhyātmika [domain] of speech and the rest, prāṇa. There the doubt arises: are these vāyu and prāṇa to be approached separately, or non-separately? — Non-separately, on the prima facie view, because the underlying reality is non-different (tattva-abheda). For when the reality is non-different, separate contemplation is not justified. And the śruti does show non-difference of reality between the ādhyātmika and adhidaivata — beginning with ‘Fire, becoming speech, entered the mouth’ (Ai. Up. 1.2.4); and likewise ‘These all indeed are equal, all infinite’ (Bṛ. Up. 1.5.13) — showing the adhidaiva glory of the ādhyātmika prāṇas as one with the self. So too elsewhere, there is in many ways the showing of non-difference of reality between ādhyātmika and adhidaivata. And somewhere ‘That which is prāṇa, that is vāyu’ — clearly making vāyu and prāṇa one. Likewise in the cited Vājasaneya-brāhmaṇa, in the concluding śloka ‘Whence the sun rises’ (Bṛ. Up. 1.5.23), [the śruti] ‘from prāṇa indeed it rises, in prāṇa it sets’ (Bṛ. Up. 1.5.23) — concluding with prāṇa alone, shows oneness. And ‘Therefore one should observe one vow only — one should breathe in and breathe out’ (Bṛ. Up. 1.5.23) — concluding with the single prāṇa-vow, fortifies this very [oneness]. Likewise in the Chāndogya later, ‘Four mighty ones — one god alone, who is he? — has swallowed; he is the protector of the world’ (Chā. Up. 4.3.6) — indicating just one absorber; it does not say one absorber for one set of four and another for another set. Hence, the approach is non-separate. — When this is established as the prima facie view, we say:
BS_C03_S03_V43::block-1: [Siddhānta:] Vāyu and prāṇa are to be approached separately. Why? Because of separate instruction. For this teaching of the division between ādhyātma and adhidaiva is for the sake of meditation. And were there no separateness in meditation, it would be useless. — But it has been said that separate contemplation is not warranted because of non-difference of reality. — There is no fault. Even with non-difference of reality, owing to the difference of states (avasthā-bheda), the difference in contemplation is intelligible by reason of the difference in instruction. The mention of the śloka, even though intelligible with the intention of non-difference of reality, has no power to negate the previously stated meditation-difference. And from ‘As the middle prāṇa among these prāṇas, so vāyu among these deities’ (Bṛ. Up. 1.5.22) — making one a metaphor (upamāna) and the other its subject (upameya). By this also the vow-instruction is explained. The very ‘only one vow’ (Bṛ. Up. 1.5.23), with its ‘only’ (eva), serves to displace the speech etc. vows and to establish the prāṇa-vow. For speech etc. were spoken of as broken-vowed, by the śruti ‘Death seized them, having become weariness’ (Bṛ. Up. 1.5.21). Not for the displacement of the vāyu-vow — for, having proposed ‘Now therefore the vow-inquiry’ (Bṛ. Up. 1.5.21), the unbroken-vow-character of vāyu and prāṇa has been determined equally. Having said ‘He should observe one vow only’ (Bṛ. Up. 1.5.23), and having stated as fruit ‘Therefore he wins union and same-realm with that deity’ (Bṛ. Up. 1.5.23) — by promising the attainment of vāyu, [the śruti] shows the vāyu-vow as not displaced. The deity here would be vāyu, since the unbounded nature is what is intended, and from its earlier use — ‘That deity which has not set, namely vāyu’ (Bṛ. Up. 1.5.22). Likewise ‘These two indeed are the two absorbers — vāyu among the gods, prāṇa among the prāṇas’ (Chā. Up. 4.3.4) — designating them as different. And ‘These five and those other five, being ten, are what is brought about by them’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.8) — concluding with difference itself. Hence the approach is separate. ‘Like the offerings (pradāna-vat)’ — just as in the three-puroḍāśa-iṣṭi: ‘[a puroḍāśa] of eleven cups for Indra-as-king, for Indra-as-overlord, for Indra-as-self-king’, and from the statement ‘Bringing all together, he cuts portions in the manner of acchambaṭkāra’, and from non-difference of Indra, when there might be a doubt about [a single] joint offering — yet on account of difference of guṇas (king etc.) and the prescribed non-interchange of the yājyā and anuvākyā, just as in the prescribed order, separate offering arises from separate deities; so too, even with non-difference of reality, owing to separateness of the contemplated aspect (ādhyeya-aṃśa), there is separateness of contemplation. As stated in the Saṅkarṣa: ‘The deity is multiple because of separate knowledge.’ But there, on account of difference of substance and deity, there is difference of yāga. There is no such difference of vidyā here, since by the upakrama and upasaṃhāra in the ādhyātma and adhidaiva instructions, a single vidyā is intelligibly enjoined. Yet even with the unity of vidyā, owing to difference of ādhyātma and adhidaiva, there is difference of pravṛtti — as in the agnihotra by the difference of evening and morning times. Intending only this much, ‘like the offerings’ has been said. ‖ 43 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V44: Because of the abundance of marks (liṅga); for that is stronger; that too [has been stated]. ‖ 44 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V44::block-0: [Pūrvapakṣa:] In the Vājasaneyins' Agnirahasya, in the brāhmaṇa beginning ‘Indeed this in the beginning was non-existent (asat)’, with reference to the mind, [the śruti] reads: ‘He saw thirty-six thousand fires of his own self, the arkas, made of mind, mind-piled (manaścit)’ etc. Likewise it speaks of separate fires that are mentally-conceived (sāmpādika): ‘speech-piled (vāk-cit), prāṇa-piled, eye-piled, ear-piled, action-piled, fire-piled.’ Concerning these the doubt is: are these manaścit etc. action-entering and subordinate to that, or independent and of the nature of pure vidyā? When prima facie, by the prakaraṇa, action-entry is established, [the sūtrakāra] declares independence: ‘Because of the abundance of marks (liṅga-bhūyastva).’ For many marks are seen in this brāhmaṇa fortifying their pure-vidyā nature: ‘That whatever beings the mind constructs through mind, that very [construction] is theirs’; ‘For one who knows thus, all beings always pile these for him, even when he sleeps’; and similar [statements]. That liṅga is stronger than the prakaraṇa. That too has been stated in the prior section [of the Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā]: ‘When śruti, liṅga, vākya, prakaraṇa, sthāna, and samākhyā occur together, the latter are weaker because of remoteness of meaning’ (Jaim. Sū. 3.3.14). ‖ 44 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V45: [There is] alternative-with-the-prior because of the prakaraṇa; [this would be] action, like the mental [grahaṇa]. ‖ 45 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V45::block-0: [Siddhānta:] This is not right — that these fires are independent and not subordinate to anything else. Owing to the prakaraṇa of the prior fire, which is action-natured (kriyā-maya), this teaching of a special alternative would be with regard to that very [fire], not independent. — But the liṅga is stronger than the prakaraṇa? — True, this is so. But a liṅga of this kind is not stronger than the prakaraṇa. For this is statement-meant-for-another-purpose (anyārtha-darśana), being of the form of praise of the mentally-conceived fires (sāmpādika-agni-praśaṃsā-rūpa). And anyārtha-darśana, when there is no other obtainment, intelligible even by secondary-meaning (guṇa-vāda), is not capable of overriding the prakaraṇa. Therefore, even these mentally-conceived fires would be action-entering on account of the prakaraṇa. ‘Like the mental [grahaṇa]’ — just as on the tenth day of the daśarātra, the avivākya day, the grahaṇa, āsādana, havana, āharaṇa, upahvāna, and bhakṣaṇa of the soma — taken with the earth as vessel for the deity Prajāpati — are taught as purely mental (mānasa); and that mental grahaṇa-procedure, owing to the kriyā-prakaraṇa, is itself a remainder of the action (kriyā-śeṣa) — so too is this fire-procedure. This is the meaning. ‖ 45 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V46::block-0: And the atideśa fortifies the action-entry of these fires: ‘Of these thirty-six thousand fires-arkas, each one alone is as great as that prior one.’ For an atideśa proceeds when there is a common feature (sāmānya). And by extending the mentally-conceived fires by means of the prior brick-piled (iṣṭakā-cita) action-entering fire, [the śruti] indicates the action-entry of these. ‖ 46 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V47: [They are] vidyā alone, however, because of the determination [in the text]. ‖ 47 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V47::block-0: [Final Siddhānta:] The word ‘tu’ (however) sets aside the [previous] view. These manaścit etc. fires are independent and of the nature of vidyā alone, not subordinate to action. For [the śruti] determines this: ‘These indeed are piled by vidyā alone’; and ‘By vidyā alone are these piled for one who knows thus.’ ‖ 47 ‖
BS_C03_S03_V48: And on account of being seen [in śruti]. (48)
BS_C03_S03_V48::block-0: And the indication (liṅga) of the independence (svātantrya) of these [mind-built fires, etc.] is also seen [in the Śruti itself]. That has been shown earlier — at ‘Liṅgabhūyastvāt’ (Br.S. 3.3.44).
BS_C03_S03_V49: And there is no contradiction [of the prakaraṇa-doctrine], because of the greater strength of śruti and the rest. (49)
BS_C03_S03_V49::block-0: [Pūrvapakṣa lead-in:] ‘But surely, even the liṅga, in the absence of any other obtainment, is not capable of establishing any [particular] meaning; setting that aside, by the force of context (prakaraṇa) the being-a-subordinate-element-of-action (kriyā-śeṣatva) has been settled.’ — To this the reply is given:
BS_C03_S03_V49::block-1: [Siddhānta:] Not so. The position of independence is not to be set aside on the strength of context fixing them as subordinate elements of action, since śruti and the rest are stronger. For it has been settled in the śruti-liṅga sūtra (Jai.S. 3.3.14) that, in comparison with prakaraṇa, śruti, liṅga and vākya are stronger. And here those very [stronger means of proof] are seen establishing the position of independence. How? First, śruti — ‘These [fires] are verily built up of vidyā [alone]’. Then, liṅga — ‘Always do all beings build all [these fires], even of one who is asleep’. Then, vākya as well — ‘By vidyā alone these fires are built up for the one who knows thus’. Now, ‘vidyā-citaḥ eva’ — this śruti is uttered with restrictive avadhāraṇa (‘only’), and would be impaired (pīḍitā) if their entry into action (kriyā-anupraveśa) were admitted. — ‘But surely the avadhāraṇa might be intended in the sense that they are accomplished by no external means (abāhya-sādhanatva)’ — No, it is replied. For if that were intended, the very mention ‘vidyā-citaḥ’ would, by simply naming their svarūpa, have already accomplished it; the avadhāraṇa would then become purposeless — for the very svarūpa of these is the being-without-external-means. But on supposing that, even granted abāhya-sādhanatva, [there is yet] a doubt of entry into action — as in the case of the mānasa-graha — the avadhāraṇa, by yielding the fruit of removing that [doubt], will be meaningful. — Likewise, the seeing of constancy (sātatya-darśana) — ‘For the one who knows thus, both for him asleep and awake, all beings always build up all these fires’ — is intelligible only when these are independent (svātantrya). Just as in the case of the saṃpādika vāk-prāṇamaya agnihotra, having said ‘At that time he offers prāṇa into vāk … At that time he offers vāk into prāṇa’ (Kau.U. 2.5), it is then said: ‘These two are unending, immortal oblations — both while waking and asleep one offers them constantly’ — so here. But on entry into action, since the application of an action is of brief duration, application by way of constancy of these would not be tenable. Nor is it proper [to say] that this is mere arthavāda. For where a perspicuous injunctive form (liṅ-ādi) is found, it is right that mere mention be treated as arthavāda. But here, in the absence of any other perspicuous injunction, the prescription of vijñāna must be supposed (kalpanīya) on the basis of the very mention. And since that [prescription] can be conceived only just as the mention has it, the seeing of constancy [forces it to be] conceived in that very form. From that, by force of meaning (sāmarthyāt), the establishment of their independence. By this it is also explained: ‘Whatever these beings will (saṃkalpayanti) by mind, that itself is their kṛti (work)’ (Śat.Br. 10.5.3.3) and so forth. Likewise the vākya too — ‘for the one who knows thus’ (evaṃvide) — declaring of these only the relation to a particular man (puruṣa-viśeṣa-saṃbandha) and not the relation to a sacrifice (kratu-saṃbandha), does not tolerate [the kratu-connection]. Therefore the position of independence (svātantrya-pakṣa) alone is preferable.
BS_C03_S03_V50: And on account of [their] connection [with the action] and the rest, [their independence is] like the separateness of another cognition [from karman]; and [this] is also seen; and that has been said. (50)
BS_C03_S03_V50::block-0: And from this also [must one conclude] that, setting aside the prakaraṇa, the independence of the mind-built fires and the rest is to be acknowledged: that [the Śruti] connects (anubadhnāti) the limbs of the action (kriyā-avayavān) with the operations of mind etc. — ‘They were placed [as fires] by the mind alone, by the mind they were piled up, by the mind alone the grahas were taken, by the mind they sang, by the mind they recited; whatever rite is performed in the sacrifice, whatever sacrificial work is done, by the mind alone is it [done] in those mind-made, mind-fashioned [fires], and only by the mind is it done in those that are mind-built (manaścit)’ (Śat.Br. 10.5.3.3) — and so on. For this connection has saṃpat (figurative correspondence) as its fruit. And the actually-perceptible limbs of the action are not such as need be sought after by saṃpat. Nor here, as in the case of the udgītha-meditations and the like, is it to be apprehended that — owing to connection with a limb of action — these have entered into action (kriyā-anupraveśitva); for there is divergence of śruti (śruti-vairūpyāt). For here [the Śruti] does not say: ‘taking up some limb of the action, in it that name (such-and-such) is to be settled’. Rather, it takes up the thirty-six thousand modifications of the mind (manovṛtti-bheda), and on them it conceives agni-hood and the grahas etc. — like the puruṣa-yajña and the like. And this number — seen as belonging to the days of a man’s life-span — is to be regarded as transferred upon the modes of his mind connected therewith. Thus, by anubandha, independence of the mind-built [fires] etc. By the word ‘ādi’ (and the rest), atideśa (extension) and so on are also to be applied as appropriate. Thus: ‘Of these, each single one is as great as that former one’ (Śat.Br. 10.5.3.3) — extending the greatness of the action-built (kriyāmaya) agni to each one of the knowledge-built (jñānamaya) ones, [the Śruti] shows non-respect (anādara) for the action. Nor can it be said: ‘Even when there is connection with action, alternation (vikalpa) of former and latter [i.e. between kriyāmaya and jñānamaya agni] is possible’. For with the operation by which the former assists in the action — namely, the holding of the āhavanīya, etc. — the latter [knowledge-built] cannot assist. As for what was said [in the pūrvapakṣa] — that even on the prima facie view, the atideśa is corroborative, since extension proceeds when there is some commonality (sāmānya) — that is rebutted (pratyukta), for on our view also extension is possible by the commonality of agni-hood; for even the saṃpādika fires possess agni-hood. And the causes [of independence] — śruti and the rest — have been shown. Thus from anubandha and the rest, the independence of the mind-built [fires] etc. ‘Like the separateness of another cognition (prajñāntara-pṛthaktva-vat)’: just as other cognitions, like the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā etc., being attended each by its own anubandha, become separately independent both from karman and from other cognitions — so here also. ‘And [this] is seen’ — namely, the lifting (utkarṣa) of the aveṣṭi from its prakaraṇa, though read in the rājasūya-prakaraṇa, on the ground of its connection with the three varṇas (varṇa-traya-anubandha), and on the ground that the rājasūya is a king’s sacrifice (rāja-yajña). ‘That has been said’ in the first kāṇḍa — ‘If it be said that it is for the sake of the rite (kratu-artha), no — on account of its connection with the three varṇas’ (Jai.S. 3.4.9, here cited as ‘11.4.9’).
BS_C03_S03_V51: Not [are they kriyā-śeṣa] from [mere] commonality, since the [otherwise] understanding [of independence remains, as is shown]; like ‘mṛtyu’ [death] — for there is no occurrence of [the same] world. (51)
BS_C03_S03_V51::block-0: [Refutation of mānasa-graha analogy:] What was said — ‘like the mānasa-graha (mental cup-offering)’ — is rebutted. The kriyā-śeṣatva (subordinate-ness to action) of the mind-built [fires] etc. is not to be conceived even from commonality with the mānasa-graha, since by the previously given grounds — śruti and the rest — their being for the mere puruṣa (kevala-puruṣārthatva) is gathered. For nothing has every [conceivable] commonality with everything; nor does that [bare commonality] do away with the diversity (vaiṣamya) belonging to each as such. — Like ‘mṛtyu’: just as in ‘That, verily, is mṛtyu — that puruṣa in this [sun-]disc’ and ‘Agni is verily mṛtyu’ (Br.U. 3.2.10), even though the same word ‘mṛtyu’ is used of the puruṣas of agni and of āditya, there is no consequence of absolute identity. And just as in ‘Yonder world, O Gautama, is agni; the sun itself is its kindling-stick’ (Ch.U. 5.4.1), there is no consequence that the world becomes agni from the commonality [of having] kindling-stick and the rest — even so here.
BS_C03_S03_V52: And by [the passage] further on, the word [kriyā etc.] has the character [of being purely-vidyā-injunctive] of that kind; but the connection [with agni] is on account of the multiplicity [of agni-features to be saṃpādita]. (52)
BS_C03_S03_V52::block-0: Further on too, in the brāhmaṇa just following — ‘This very world is that agni built up’ — the purpose of the word (śabdasya prayojanam) is recognized as taddhitya (taddhi-ness, that-quality), namely the being-an-injunction-of-pure-vidyā (kevala-vidyā-vidhitvam), and not the being-an-injunction-of-a-mere-action-limb (śuddha-karma-aṅga-vidhitvam). For there, with the verse — ‘By vidyā they ascend that [region] from which all desires have departed; thither dakṣiṇās do not go, nor the unwise austere’ (Śat.Br. 10.5.4.16) — censuring mere karman and praising vidyā, this is conveyed. Likewise in the brāhmaṇa preceding — ‘That which is this disc that gives heat’ — the predominance of vidyā alone (vidyā-prādhānya) is recognized: from the conclusion by the very fruit of vidyā — ‘He becomes immortal, for mṛtyu becomes his ātman’ — and not karma-prādhānya. From commonality with that, here too the same character. But many limbs of agni (agni-avayavāḥ) are to be saṃpādita-ed (figuratively integrated) in the vidyā — for this very cause is vidyā connected with agni (anubadhyate), not because of being a karma-aṅga. Therefore, the mind-built [fires] etc. are established as of the nature of pure vidyā (kevala-vidyātmakatva).
BS_C03_S03_V53: Some [hold non-difference of the Self from the body, as Self] — on account of [Its] presence only in the body. (53)
BS_C03_S03_V53::block-0: [Introductory:] Here, in support of the [scriptural] qualification for bondage and liberation (bandha-mokṣa-adhikāra-siddhi), the existence of an Ātman distinct from the body is being established. For if there were no Ātman distinct from the body, the codanās promising fruits in the next world (paraloka-phalāḥ codanāḥ) would not be intelligible; and to whom would brahma-ātmatva be taught? — ‘But surely, at the very beginning of the śāstra, in the first pāda, the existence of an Ātman distinct from the body, fit to enjoy the fruit of the śāstra, has been said.’ — True, it has been said by the Bhāṣyakāra; but there is there no sūtra on the existence of the Ātman. Here, however, by the Sūtrakāra himself, the existence of [the Ātman] is established preceded by the [pūrvapakṣa] objection. From this very [fact] indeed, the ācārya Śabarasvāmin, taking it up, has expounded it under the chapter on the marks of pramāṇa (Pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa). And likewise the blessed Upavarṣa, in the first tantra, on the occasion of speaking of the existence of the Ātman, made the reservation: ‘We shall speak [of it] in the Śārīraka’. And here, while the codanā-marked upāsanās are being deliberated upon, the existence of the Ātman is considered, in order to show that [this consideration] is corollary to the entire śāstra (kṛtsna-śāstra-śeṣatva). Moreover, in the previous adhikaraṇa, having admitted the lifting [of the mind-built fires] from their prakaraṇa, their being for the puruṣa (puruṣa-arthatva) was set forth. Who is that puruṣa for whom these mind-built [fires] etc. exist? — on this prasakti, this existence of the Ātman distinct from the body is being said. And this opening sūtra is for the express purpose of the [pūrvapakṣa] objection (ākṣepa-artha) to that [existence]. For an answer-statement (parihāra-ukti) preceded by the objection makes for, in the matter intended to be conveyed, a firm conviction by the analogy of the post-driving (sthūṇā-nikhanana-nyāya).
BS_C03_S03_V53::block-1: [Pūrvapakṣa — Lokāyatika:] Here certain Lokāyatikas, who see the Self as the body alone (deha-mātra-ātma-darśinaḥ), denying the existence of an Ātman distinct from the body, supposing that consciousness — though not seen in the external earth and the rest, whether in their aggregate or severally — should be there in the elements transformed into the form of body, declare that consciousness arises from those [elements], like the inebriating power [from fermented ingredients]: ‘the body, characterized by consciousness, is the puruṣa’ (caitanya-viśiṣṭaḥ kāyaḥ puruṣaḥ). There is no Ātman distinct from the body, capable of going to heaven or to liberation, by reason of which consciousness might exist in the body. Rather, the body itself is both the conscious and the Self — they affirm. They give as reason: ‘On account of [Its] presence in the body’ (śarīre bhāvāt). For whatever exists when something is and not when it is not, that is concluded to be a property of that thing — as heat and light are properties of fire. The activities of life-breath, exertion, consciousness, memory and the rest, regarded as ātma-dharmas by the ātma-vādins — those too, being apprehended only within the body, and not apprehended outside, would, in the absence of an established possessor (dharmin) distinct from the body, deserve to be only properties of the body. Therefore there is no distinction (vyatireka) between the Ātman and the body.
BS_C03_S03_V54: [There is] distinction [of the Self from the body], on account of [the Self’s] not being [present] when that [body] is — yet not in the manner of perceptibility. (54)
BS_C03_S03_V54::block-0: [Lead-in:] Such being the [pūrvapakṣa] obtained, we say —
BS_C03_S03_V54::block-1: [Siddhānta:] Not so — what was urged, namely, that there is no distinction of the Ātman from the body. Distinction (vyatireka) of It from the body alone is what is fitting, ‘on account of [the body-properties’] not being even when that [body] is’ (tad-bhāva-abhāvitvāt). If, because [the Ātma-dharmas] are present when the body is, one were to think them body-properties, then why not, on the same logic, think them not body-properties at all, since even when the body is they are not [always] present? — From the unlikeness of body-properties (deha-dharma-vailakṣaṇyāt). For body-properties — colour and the rest — are present so long as the body is. But prāṇa-cheṣṭā etc., even when the body is — at the time of death (mṛta-avasthā) — are not. Body-properties such as colour are also apprehended by others; not so the Self’s properties — consciousness, memory, etc. Moreover, while the body is, in the living-state (jīvad-avasthāyām), the presence of these can be ascertained; but their absence cannot. Even after this body has fallen, by transmigration to another body, the Self’s properties might continue. Even by mere doubt, the opponent’s position is set aside. — Furthermore, ‘What is the nature of this consciousness, of which he wishes [to claim] arising from the elements?’ — the opponent should be questioned. For the Lokāyatika does not admit any reality apart from the four elements. ‘If [you say] the experiencing of the elemental and the elemental-products is consciousness’ — then, since [the elements] are its objects (viṣaya), it would not have the character of being their property, since action upon one’s own self is contradictory (sva-ātmani kriyā-virodhāt). For agni, though hot, does not burn its own self; nor does a trained acrobat mount his own shoulder. Nor would the elements and elemental-products be objectified by consciousness, were it a property of the elements and elemental-products. For one’s own form (svarūpa) or another’s form is not objectified by colour and the rest. But the elements and elemental-products, both external (bāhya) and internal (ādhyātmika), are objectified by consciousness. And so, just as the existence of upalabdhi (apprehension), having for its object the elemental and elemental-products, is granted, so too is its distinction (vyatireka) from those [elements] to be granted. The Ātman is the very svarūpa of upalabdhi (upalabdhi-svarūpa eva ātmā), [and so] the distinction of the Ātman from the body [follows]. — And the eternity (nityatva) of upalabdhi follows from oneness of form (aikarūpyāt), and from the recognition (pratyabhijñāna) ‘I have seen this’ — recognized as the same upalabdhṛ (apprehender) even amid different states (avasthā-antara-yoga); and from memory etc. being explainable [only thus]. — As to what was said — that being-in-the-body shows upalabdhi to be a body-property — that has been replied to in the manner stated. Furthermore, when there are auxiliaries (upakaraṇa) such as a lamp etc., upalabdhi takes place; in their absence it does not — but on this account upalabdhi does not become a property of the lamp etc. Similarly, when there is the body, upalabdhi takes place, and in its absence it does not — [therefore] it does not deserve to be a body-property. Mere body-instrumentality, like that of lamp etc., is enough to account for body-employment. Nor is the body’s usefulness for upalabdhi exclusive (atyantam), since even in this body, when motionless [in sleep], various upalabdhis are seen in dream. Therefore the existence of an Ātman distinct from the body is unimpeachable.
BS_C03_S03_V55: But [meditations] bound to a limb [of action] are not [confined] to [their own] śākhās — for [they are enjoined] in each Veda. (55)
BS_C03_S03_V55::block-0: The digressive discussion (prāsaṅgikī kathā) is concluded; now we resume the topic at hand. ‘One should meditate on this syllable Om as the udgītha’ (Ch.U. 1.1.1); ‘Among the worlds one should meditate on the fivefold sāman’ (Ch.U. 2.2.1); ‘“Uktham, uktham” thus indeed do the people speak; this very thing is the uktha — this very earth’; ‘This very world’; ‘This is the agni built up’ (Śat.Br. 10.1.2.2) — and so on: those cognitions [upāsanās] enjoined in different śākhās in each Veda, attached to limbs of action such as the udgītha — should they obtain (bhaveyuḥ) only with regard to the udgīthas etc. occurring in their respective śākhās, or with regard to those of all śākhās? — such is the doubt. And this presentation is given by taking up differences of udgītha etc. arising from differences of svara etc. in each śākhā. What then is the prima facie position? [Pūrvapakṣa:] They would be enjoined only with regard to the udgīthas etc. occurring in one’s own śākhā. Why? On account of proximity (sannidhāna). For ‘One should meditate on the udgītha’ — being a general injunction, when its expectancy as to a particular [udgītha] arises, is satisfied by the proximate particular found in one’s own śākhā; transcending that and taking up a particular enjoined in another śākhā has no cause. Therefore there must be the arrangement śākhā by śākhā (prati-śākhaṃ vyavasthā). — On the prima facie view thus established, [the Sūtrakāra] declares: ‘aṅga-avabaddhāstu’. The word ‘tu’ (but) excludes [that] view. These do not stand confined to one’s own śākhā in each Veda; rather, they extend to all śākhās. Why? On account of the non-distinction (aviśeṣa) of śruti as to udgītha etc. For if there were arrangement by one’s own śākhā, then ‘One should meditate on the udgītha’ (Ch.U. 1.1.1) — being a general śruti, set forth without distinction (aviśeṣa-pravṛttā), and being constrained to a particular by force of proximity — would be impaired (pīḍitā). And this is not proper, since śruti is stronger than proximity (saṃnidhānāt śrutir balīyasī). Nor is a cognition resting on the general inadmissible. Therefore, even granted differences of svara etc., yet because of non-distinction with respect to udgītha-hood etc., upāsanās of this kind would obtain with regard to the udgīthas etc. of all śākhās.
BS_C03_S03_V56: Or, like mantras and the rest, there is no contradiction. (56)
BS_C03_S03_V56::block-0: Or rather, no contradiction at all need be apprehended here — namely, the doubt: ‘How can the meditations enjoined in one śākhā (recension) apply to the udgītha and the rest occurring in another śākhā?’ For non-contradiction is established just as in the case of mantras and the like (mantrādivat). To explain: it is observed that mantras, rites, and qualities (mantra-karma-guṇa) which originate in one śākhā are nonetheless taken up (upasaṅgraha) in another śākhā. Thus, even though for some Vedic schools the mantra ‘kuṭarur asi’ (‘thou art kuṭaru’) — the mantra used while taking up the stone (aśmādāna-mantra) — is not recited (na-āmnāta), still its application is found among them too: ‘With ‘kukkuṭo ’si’ (‘thou art the cock’) one takes up the stone, or with ‘kuṭarur asi’’ (citation). Similarly, even for those for whom the prayājas beginning with ‘samidhā’ are not recited, the qualifying injunction (guṇa-vidhi) regarding them is found in their āmnāya: ‘The prayājas are verily the seasons; they are to be offered in one place’ (citation). Likewise, even for those who do not have the specific class-instruction ‘the goat is for Agnī-ṣomīya’, a mantra-passage referring to that subject is met with: ‘Recite the anuvākyā for the omentum-fat of the goat’ (citation). So too, mantras such as ‘O Agni, take up the priestly office, take up the sacrifice’ (Tā. Br. 21.10.11) (citation) and the rest, though originating in one Veda, are seen to be received (parigraha) in another Veda; and the hymn read by the Bahvr̥cas — ‘Who, even when just born, was the first endowed with mind’ (R̥. Saṃ. 2.12.1) (citation) — is seen to be appropriated for the Adhvaryu in the place ‘the Sajanīya hymn is to be recited’ (citation). Therefore, just as the supports — the auxiliaries of the rite (karmāṅgas) — recur (anuvr̥tti) everywhere, even so do the meditations (pratyayas) that rest on them — hence there is no contradiction. (56)
BS_C03_S03_V57: On account of plenitude, the superiority belongs (to the comprehensive worship) like the (sacrificial) krat u; for thus indeed (scripture) shows. (57)
BS_C03_S03_V57::block-0: [pūrvapakṣa] In the legend ‘Prācīnaśāla Aupamanyava…’ (Chā. Up. 5.11.1) (citation) the worship of Vaiśvānara is heard — both as divided (vyasta, member-by-member) and as undivided/whole (samasta). The vyasta-upāsana runs thus: ‘O Aupamanyava, what self do you worship? Heaven indeed, O revered king, said he. — That is the well-luminous (sutejas) self, the Vaiśvānara, whom you worship as self’ (Chā. Up. 5.12.1) (citation), and so on. And the samasta-upāsana likewise: ‘Of this self, the Vaiśvānara, the head indeed is sutejas, the eye is viśvarūpa, the breath is pr̥thag-vartman, the trunk is bahula, the bladder is rayi, the two feet are this very earth’ (Chā. Up. 5.18.2) (citation), and so on. Thereon arises the doubt: is the worship to be done here in both ways — as vyasta and as samasta — or only as samasta? What presents itself first? Because, member by member, in the case of sutejas etc., the verbal form ‘upāsse’ (‘thou worshippest’) is heard, and because diversity of fruit is heard — ‘Therefore in your line are seen the soma-pressing, the squeezing-out, and the steeping’ (Chā. Up. 5.12.1) (citation) — the divided worships (vyasta-upāsanas) too should obtain. Such is the prima facie view.
BS_C03_S03_V57::block-1: [siddhānta] Thereupon it is declared: of the plenum (bhūmnaḥ) — that is, of the comprehensive Vaiśvānara-worship which has the form of an aggregation of meanings (padārtha-upacayātmaka) — the superiority, the principality (jyāyastva = prādhānya), is what is meant to be expressed in this passage; not also of the worships of single members taken severally; ‘like the kratu’ (kratuvat) — that is, just as in the kratus such as the Darśa-pūrṇamāsa, only one performance with all auxiliaries and principals taken together (sāṅga-pradhāna-prayoga) is intended, and not the performance of the prayājas etc. severed (vyasta), nor again the performance of the principal joined with only one member — even so here. Whence is this — that the plenum alone is superior? Because the śruti shows the superiority of the plenum, since unity of statement (eka-vākyatā) is grasped. For this is one single passage on the topic of vaiśvānara-vidyā, as is understood from a survey of antecedent and consequent (paurvāparya-ālocana). Thus, the six r̥ṣis beginning with Prācīnaśāla and ending with Uddālaka, not having attained finality in vaiśvānara-vidyā — opening with this, ‘they approached king Aśvapati Kaikeya’; then, having heard from each r̥ṣi the object of his worship — heaven and the rest — one by one, he establishes them as the head and the rest of (the cosmic Self), saying ‘this is the head of the self’ (Chā. Up. 5.12.2) (citation), etc. By words such as ‘your head would have fallen, had you not come to me’ (Chā. Up. 5.12.2) (citation) he censures (apavadati) the divided worship. Then, again turning aside the divided worship and continuing only the comprehensive worship, he shows the fruit as resting on the plenum: ‘He eats food in all the worlds, in all beings, in all selves’ (Chā. Up. 5.18.1) (citation). And as for what is heard regarding diversity of fruit member by member, in the case of sutejas and the rest — it is to be seen that, this being so, the fruits of the auxiliaries are conceded to the principal alone (aṅga-phalāni pradhāna eva). Likewise the verbal form ‘upāsse’ being heard member by member is for the purpose of restating the opponent’s purport (parābhiprāya-anuvāda), not for the purpose of enjoining a divided worship (na vyasta-upāsana-vidhāna). Therefore the position of comprehensive worship alone is preferable.
BS_C03_S03_V57::block-2: Some, however, after establishing the position of comprehensive worship as superior here, fancy that, by the very statement of ‘superiority’, the sūtrakāra is also approving of the position of divided worship. That is unwarranted (ayuktam): because, when unity-of-statement has been grasped, to imagine division of the passage is improper; because it conflicts with such censures as ‘your head would have fallen’ (Chā. Up. 5.12.2) (citation); because, when the comprehension of comprehensive worship is plain in the upasaṃhāra (concluding portion), its absence cannot be asserted in the pūrva-pakṣa; and because the sūtra’s expression ‘superiority’ (jyāyastva-vacana) can well be made out in the sense of an indication of authoritativeness (pramāṇavattva-abhiprāya) too. (57)
BS_C03_S03_V58: (The vidyās are) various (nānā) on account of the difference of words (śabda) and the rest. (58)
BS_C03_S03_V58::block-0: [pūrvapakṣa] In the previous adhikaraṇa it was said that, even though there is the śruti of diversity of fruit in the case of sutejas and the rest, the comprehensive worship is superior. Hence the following thought arises: even other mutually different śrutis of worships should be combined and worshipped. Moreover, when there is no difference of the object-of-knowledge (vedya), no difference of vidyā can be ascertained. For the vedya is the form of the vidyā, just as substance and deity are the form of the yāga (sacrifice). And the vedya is one and the same Īśvara, even though there is plurality of śrutis, as is to be understood from passages such as ‘mind-formed, prāṇa-bodied’ (Chā. Up. 3.14.2) (citation), ‘bliss is brahman, ether is brahman’ (Chā. Up. 4.10.5) (citation), ‘of true desire, of true resolve’ (Chā. Up. 8.1.5) (citation), and the like. Likewise prāṇa is one and the same in ‘Prāṇa indeed is the absorber (saṃvarga)’ (Chā. Up. 4.3.3) (citation), ‘Prāṇa indeed is the eldest and best’ (Chā. Up. 5.1.1) (citation), ‘Prāṇa is verily the father, prāṇa the mother’ (Chā. Up. 7.15.1) (citation) and the like. From the unity of the vedya follows unity of the vidyā. The diversity of śrutis too, on this view, is not unmeaning, since it serves to convey other qualities (guṇāntara-paratva). Therefore the totality of qualities (guṇa-jāta) enjoined in one’s own and others’ śākhās, resting on a single vedya, is to be drawn together (upasaṃhartavya) for the completeness of the vidyā. — When such is presented, the answer is propounded:
BS_C03_S03_V58::block-1: [siddhānta] ‘Various’ (nānā). Even when there is no difference in the vedya, vidyās of this kind may very well be different. How? On account of difference of word (śabda-bheda) and the rest. There is indeed difference of word: ‘he knows’ (veda), ‘let him meditate’ (upāsīta), ‘let him form the resolve’ (sa kratuṃ kurvīta) (Chā. Up. 3.14.1) (citation), and the like. And difference of word as cause of difference of action (karma-bheda) has already been settled before in the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā: ‘where there is difference of word, there is difference of karma, owing to the having-been-applied-to (kr̥tānubandhatva)’ (citation). By the word ‘ādi’ (‘etc.’), qualities (guṇa) and the rest are also to be employed as causes of difference, as may be possible. — But surely, in ‘veda’ etc. only difference of word is grasped, not difference of meaning, as in ‘yajati’ etc., since for all of these the meaning ‘mental operation’ is the same and any other meaning is impossible. How, then, can there be difference of vidyā from difference of word? — That is no fault. Even though the meaning of being a mental operation is one, since by difference of association (anubandha-bheda) there results difference of vedya, difference of vidyā is established. For of one and the same Īśvara, the worshippable, distinct qualities are taught topic by topic (prati-prakaraṇa). And of one and the same prāṇa as worshippable here and there, even though it is one, a quality of one kind is to be worshipped in one place and a quality of another kind in another. Thus, by difference of association entailing difference of vedya, difference of vidyā is ascertained. Nor is it possible to say that here there is one injunction of vidyā and the rest are injunctions of qualities — because there is no determining ground (vinigamanā-hetu-abhāva) to single one out, and because, the qualities being many topic by topic, the (other) injunctions cannot be made out as restating an already-established vidyā. Nor on this view need such common qualities as ‘satya-kāma’ etc. be heard repeatedly. Topic by topic — ‘by him who desires this, this is to be worshipped; and by him who desires this, this’ — there is grasped a complete absence of expectancy (nairākāṅkṣya), so unity-of-statement does not arise. Nor is there here, as in the vaiśvānara-vidyā, another, comprehensive, injunction (samasta-codanā) by whose force the worships of members in each topic might unite into one statement. And if unity of vidyā on the ground of unity of vedya were to be promised everywhere unrestrictedly, the comprehensive drawing-together of all qualities could not be promised. Therefore it is well said: ‘various, on account of difference of word and the rest’. And, this adhikaraṇa being thus settled, ‘the conception in all Vedānta-passages’, etc., is to be understood (in this light). (58)
BS_C03_S03_V59: Option (vikalpa, alternative use), since the fruit is undifferentiated. (59)
BS_C03_S03_V59::block-0: Now that the difference of vidyās is settled, it is considered: should there, at the worshipper’s wish, be combination (samuccaya) of these, or option (vikalpa); or rather, only option as a fixed rule? Now, since difference of vidyā is established, there is no ground for a fixed rule of samuccaya. — But surely, even for distinct rites such as the agnihotra, the darśa-pūrṇamāsa, etc., a fixed rule of samuccaya is observed. — That is no fault: in those cases the cause is the śruti of perpetuity (nityatā-śruti); but for the vidyās there is no such śruti of perpetuity. Hence there is no fixed rule of samuccaya. Nor is there a fixed rule of option, since there is no prohibition of one vidyā by one qualified for another. By exclusion, then, optionality-at-will (yāthākāmya) results. — But surely, since the fruit is undifferentiated, an option among them is reasonable. To explain: ‘mind-formed, prāṇa-bodied’ (Chā. Up. 3.14.2) (citation), ‘bliss is brahman, ether is brahman’ (Chā. Up. 4.10.5) (citation), ‘of true desire, of true resolve’ (Chā. Up. 8.1.5) (citation), and the like, are seen to have, in equal measure, attainment of Īśvara as their fruit. — That is no fault, since in actions productive of svarga and the like, even though the fruits are alike, optionality-at-will is observed. — Therefore, even though optionality-at-will obtains, it is now stated: there should be option (vikalpa) among them, not combination (samuccaya). Why? Because the fruit is undifferentiated. Their fruit, undifferentiated, is the direct realization (sākṣāt-karaṇa) of the object of worship. And once the worshippable object — Īśvara and the rest — has been directly realized by a single worship, a second is purposeless. Moreover, on the position of samuccaya, direct realization is itself impossible, since (combination) is a cause of distraction of mind (citta-vikṣepa-hetutva). And the śrutis show that the fruit of vidyā is to be effected by direct realization: ‘of one for whom there is, indeed, no doubt’ (Chā. Up. 3.14.4) (citation), ‘having become a god, he goes to the gods’ (Br̥. Up. 4.1.2) (citation) and the like. The smr̥tis too: ‘ever filled with the thought of That’ (Bh. Gītā 8.6) (citation) and the like. Therefore, taking up one of the vidyās of undifferentiated fruit, one should be devoted to it until, by direct realization of its worshippable object, the fruit thereof is attained. (59)
BS_C03_S03_V60: But the kāmya (desire-prompted) ones may be combined according to wish, or not, since the previous reason is absent. (60)
BS_C03_S03_V60::block-0: This is the counter-instance to ‘because the fruit is undifferentiated’. But where, on the contrary, in such desire-prompted (kāmya) vidyās as ‘he who knows this Vāyu as the calf of the quarters does not weep for the death of his son’ (Chā. Up. 3.15.2) (citation), and ‘he who worships nāman as brahman, his desire moves freely as far as nāman reaches’ (Chā. Up. 7.1.5) (citation), and the like — which, like an action (kriyā-vat), produce one’s own fruit through an unseen agency (adr̥ṣṭena ātmanā) — there is no need for direct realization. Those may be combined according to wish (yathākāmaṃ samuccīyeran), or they may not be combined — because the previous reason is absent: that is, the reason for option, namely, ‘undifferentiated fruit’, does not apply. (60)
BS_C03_S03_V61: In the case of (rite-)limbs, (the conduct of the meditations) is according to the (conduct of the) supports. (61)
BS_C03_S03_V61::block-0: On the doubt — concerning the meditations (pratyayas) which rest upon karmāṅgas like the udgītha and the rest, and which are enjoined in (all) the three Vedas: are they to be combined (samuccīyeran), or are they at one’s wish (yathākāmaṃ syuḥ)? — it is said: ‘according to the supports’ (yathāśraya-bhāva). Just as their supports — the stotras and the rest — occur jointly, so too do the meditations occur jointly, since the meditations are dependent on the supports (āśraya-tantratva). (61)
BS_C03_S03_V62::block-0: Or rather, just as the supports — the stotras and the rest — are taught (śiṣyante) in the three Vedas, so too are the meditations resting upon them. The meaning is: there is no peculiarity even with respect to instruction (upadeśa-kr̥ta) between the (rite-)limbs and the meditations resting upon them. (62)
BS_C03_S03_V63::block-0: ‘From the seat of the hotr̥ even the badly-sung is, indeed, brought back into order’ (Chā. Up. 1.5.5) (citation) — this passage, by stating that, through the greatness of the knowledge of the unity of praṇava and udgītha, the udgātr̥ repairs (pratisamādhāti) the defect arisen in his own duty by means of an act belonging to the hotr̥’s function — indicates that, since the meditation expressed in one Veda has a generic connection with what is expressed in another Veda, there is a drawing-together (upasaṃhāra) of meditations declared in all the Vedas. Thus this is an inferential mark (liṅga-darśana). (63)
BS_C03_S03_V64: And on account of the Śruti [declaring] generality of the qualities (guṇa-sādhāraṇya-śruti). (64)
BS_C03_S03_V64::block-0: [Continuing the support for combination:] The Śruti, indeed, makes it heard that Oṃkāra — being a quality of the vidyā (vidyā-guṇa) and resting upon the vidyā (vidyā-āśraya) — is common to all three Vedas: ‘By that this triple knowledge proceeds — with “Oṃ” one calls forth, with “Oṃ” one praises, with “Oṃ” one chants the Udgītha’ (Ch.U. 1.1.9). And from that, by reason of the commonness of the substratum, the commonness of what rests upon that substratum [follows] — this is itself an indicatory mark (liṅga-darśana). Or else [the sūtra is to be construed as]: ‘And on account of the Śruti [declaring] generality of the qualities’ (guṇa-sādhāraṇya-śruteḥ ca). If these qualities of action — Udgītha and the rest — were not all common to every performance, then the cognitions resting upon them would not have co-existence. But these Udgītha and the rest are heard, by injunctions of performance which take in all the limbs (sarva-aṅga-grāhī prayoga-vacana), to be all common to every performance. And therefore, from the co-existence of the substrate (āśraya-saha-bhāva), there follows the co-existence of the cognitions (pratyaya-saha-bhāva).
BS_C03_S03_V65: Or rather not, since their co-existence is not heard of [in Śruti]. (65)
BS_C03_S03_V65::block-0: [The siddhānta now refutes the prima facie position:] ‘Or rather not’ — this is the turning aside of the [previous] view. The upāsanās, which rest [upon the limbs], cannot necessarily be co-existent in the manner of their substrate. Why? Because their co-existence is not heard of (tat-saha-bhāva-aśruteḥ). For just as the co-existence of the limbs enjoined in the three Vedas — the stotras and the rest — is heard: ‘Having drawn out the graha, or having drawn the camasa, he begins the stotra; he praises what has been chanted; he says, “O Prastotṛ, sing the sāman; O hotṛ, recite this”’ — and so on; there is no such Śruti of the co-existence of the upāsanās. ‘But surely the injunction of performance (prayoga-vacana) would bring about their co-existence!’ — We say no, because the upāsanās are for the sake of the person (puruṣārthatva). The injunction of performance can bring about the co-existence only of those Udgītha and the rest that are for the sake of the sacrificial rite (kratv-artha). The Udgītha and other upāsanās, although having for their substrate things that are for the sake of the rite, are themselves for the sake of the person (puruṣārthāni), like the godohana and the like — as we have said at ‘Separately, indeed, [the fruit] is on account of being unobstructed [by other elements]’ (Br.S. 3.3.42). And this is the very distinction between the limbs [of the rite] and the upāsanās that take their stand upon them — that the former are for the sake of the rite, and the latter for the sake of the person. Moreover, the two indicatory marks [adduced in V.64] cannot be the cause of the co-existence of the upāsanās, in the absence of Śruti and reasoning [to that effect]. Nor can the inclusiveness in respect of every performance — i.e., the comprehensive bringing-together of the entire substrate — be known to apply to the cognitions which rest thereon, since the upāsanās are not so prompted (a-tat-prayuktatva); for the upāsanās, even though dependent upon the substrate (āśraya-tantra), let them indeed not be in the absence of the substrate. But they cannot, on the strength of the co-existence of the substrate, claim a rule of co-existence — precisely because their own co-existence is not heard. Therefore the upāsanās are to be performed just as desired (yathā-kāmam).
BS_C03_S03_V66: And because [it is] seen [thus in Śruti]. (66)
BS_C03_S03_V66::block-0: The Śruti also shows the non-co-existence of the cognitions: ‘The brahman who knows thus, indeed, protects the sacrifice, the sacrificer, and all the ṛtvijs’ (Ch.U. 4.17.10). For if there were comprehensive bringing-together of all the cognitions, all would be all-knowers, and then it would not be celebrated that the others are protected by the brahman who is endowed with vijñāna. Therefore the upāsanās admit either combination (samuccaya) or option (vikalpa) just as one desires (yathā-kāmam).
BS_C03_S04_INTRO1::block-0: [Introduction to the fourth pāda:] Now, at this point, inquiring whether the upaniṣadic knowledge of the Self enters into action only by means of [its] qualifying-the-agent (adhikāri-dvāreṇa anupraviśati), or whether it is independent and is itself a means of the puruṣārtha — [the Sūtrakāra] commences first with the siddhānta itself —
BS_C03_S04_V01: [The Self-knowledge] is for the sake of man (puruṣārtha), thence [i.e., independently], [as is known] from the [Vedic] word — thus says Bādarāyaṇa. (1)
BS_C03_S04_V01::block-0: [Siddhānta:] ‘It is for the sake of man, thence’ — that is, from this Self-knowledge enjoined in the Vedānta, taken as independent (svatantra), the puruṣārtha is accomplished — so the ācārya Bādarāyaṇa holds. Whence is this known? He says: ‘from the [Vedic] word (śabdāt)’. Thus: ‘The knower of the Self crosses sorrow’ (Ch.U. 7.1.3); ‘He, indeed, who knows that supreme Brahman, becomes Brahman itself’ (Mu.U. 3.2.9); ‘The knower of Brahman attains the supreme’ (Tai.U. 2.1.1); ‘The man having a teacher knows; for him there is delay only so long as he is not released; thereupon he becomes one [with Brahman]’ (Ch.U. 6.14.2); beginning ‘The Self that is free from evil…’ (Ch.U. 8.7.1) — ‘He attains all the worlds and all desires, who, having known that Self, comprehends [It]’ (Ch.U. 8.7.1); beginning ‘Verily, O dear, the Self is to be seen’ (Br.U. 4.5.6) — ‘This much, indeed, is immortality’ (Br.U. 4.5.15) — Śruti of this kind makes it heard that vidyā alone (kevalāyāḥ vidyāyāḥ) is the cause of the puruṣārtha.
BS_C03_S04_V02: [Self-knowledge] is a subordinate part [of action]; therefore [the talk of its giving] the puruṣārtha is mere arthavāda (eulogy), as in other [cases] — thus says Jaimini. (2)
BS_C03_S04_V02::block-0: [Leading bhāṣya:] Now here [Jaimini] sets up an opposition —
BS_C03_S04_V02::block-1: [Pūrvapakṣa (Jaimini’s view as opponent):] Since the Self is a subordinate part of action through agency (kartṛtva), the knowledge of It also, like the sprinkling of paddy and the like, is connected with action only by way of its object (viṣaya-dvāreṇa) — therefore, the Śruti regarding the fruit [given for] the Self-knowledge whose purpose is [thus] already understood is only an arthavāda — so the ācārya Jaimini holds. Just as in the case of other dravya-saṃskāra-karmans (acts purifying the substance), the Śruti of the fruit, such as ‘He whose juhū is made of palāśa-leaf hears no evil śloka’ (Tai.S. 3.5.7), ‘When he anoints, he wipes out the eye of his rival’ (Tai.S. 6.1.1), ‘When the prayājas and anuyājas are offered, this is made the armor of the sacrifice, the armor of the sacrificer, for the overthrow of the rival’ (Tai.S. 2.6.1) — these are arthavādas. Just so here. ‘But how can it be suspected that this Self-knowledge, taught without commencement [of any specific context] (anārabhya-adhīta), enters into the rite without any of the means such as prakaraṇa and the like?’ — If you say, ‘Because of the sentence (vākya), through the door of the agent, that knowledge has connection with the rite,’ — no, because the application (viniyoga) cannot be established by sentence. For only by some non-deviating (avyabhicāri) door is the connection of even anārabhya-adhīta [matters] with the rite, on the basis of sentence, possible.
