But the agent is a deviating door (vyabhicāri-dvāra), since [agency] is common to both worldly and Vedic action. Therefore, through that door, the establishment of the connection of Self-knowledge with the rite is not possible. — No [we reply, on the pūrvapakṣa view], because the knowledge of distinction [of Self from body] (vyatireka-vijñāna) has no use anywhere except in the Vedic rites. For knowledge of the Self distinct from the body has no use in worldly actions, since pravṛtti towards a seen object is in every way possible [without it]. But in Vedic rites — those whose fruits come after the falling of the body — pravṛtti is not possible without knowledge of the Self distinct from the body, and so the knowledge of distinction is useful [there]. — ‘But surely, the upaniṣadic vision, having for its object the non-saṃsārī Self characterized by being apahata-pāpman and the like, cannot be a limb of pravṛtti [of action]?’ — No, since the saṃsārī Self itself, indicated by [its possessing] dear ones and the like, is taught as the seer (draṣṭavya). The qualifications such as ‘apahata-pāpman’ are for the sake of eulogy (stuty-artham). — ‘But surely, it has been established here and there that Brahman, the cause of the world, is non-saṃsārī and superior; and that very Brahman is taught in the Upaniṣads to be the highest reality of the saṃsārī Self?’ — True, that has been established. But for the very same [point], for firm setting (dārḍhya), like the planting of a post (sthūṇā-nikhanana-vat), objection and resolution by way of the fruit are made [here again].
BS_C03_S04_V03: On account of [their] practice being seen [as performing rites]. (3)
BS_C03_S04_V03::block-0: [Pūrvapakṣa continues:] ‘Janaka of Videha sacrificed with a sacrifice of many gifts’ (Br.U. 3.1.1); ‘Verily, O sirs, I am about to sacrifice’ (Ch.U. 5.11.5) — and the like — even of the knowers of Brahman, in passages that are intended for other things, the connection [of those knowers] with action is seen. So too, of Uddālaka and the rest, from the seeing of [their] instruction to sons and the like, connection with the gārhasthya [i.e., the householder’s life of rites] is understood. If the puruṣārtha were established from knowledge alone (kevalāt jñānāt), why would they perform the actions accompanied by manifold exertion? On the maxim, ‘If one would obtain honey at hand (in the arka-flower), why should one go to the mountain?’
BS_C03_S04_V04: On account of the Śruti to that [effect]. (4)
BS_C03_S04_V04::block-0: [Pūrvapakṣa concludes:] ‘That very [act] which one performs with knowledge, with faith, with the upaniṣad — that itself becomes more potent’ (Ch.U. 1.1.10) — from the Śruti of [its] being a subordinate part of action (karma-śeṣatva-śravaṇāt), the puruṣārtha-hetutva does not pertain to vidyā taken alone (kevalāyāḥ na puruṣārtha-hetutvam).
BS_C03_S04_V05::block-0: And from the text ‘Knowledge and works (vidyākarmaṇī) take hold of him together — samanvārabhete’ (Bṛ. U. 4.4.2), since knowledge and works are seen to be conjoint (sāhitya-darśanāt) in originating their fruit, knowledge has no autonomy (svātantrya). ‖ 5 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V06: Because of injunction for the one possessed of that (tadvataḥ). ‖ 6 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V06::block-0: And a śruti of this kind — ‘Having studied the Veda from the family of the teacher in accordance with the rule, having returned home in the residue of time left over from the teacher’s works, in his own household, in a clean place, reciting his own portion of the Veda…’ (Chā. U. 8.15.1) — shows the eligibility for works (karmādhikāra) for one who has the cognition of the entire Vedic meaning (samasta-vedārtha-vijñānavataḥ). Therefore too, knowledge (vijñāna) is not a cause of fruit by way of autonomy (svātantryeṇa). ‘But here, by ‘adhītya’ (having studied), only mere recitation (adhyayana-mātra) of the Veda is heard of, not the cognition of meaning (artha-vijñāna)’ — this is no fault. Since the study of the Veda has a visible purpose (dṛṣṭārthatvāt), it has been settled that Vedic study extends up to comprehension of meaning (arthāvabodha-paryantam). ‖ 6 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V07: And on account of restrictive injunction (niyamāt). ‖ 7 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V07::block-0: ‘Performing works alone here let one wish to live a hundred years; thus alone, and not otherwise, in you (does it stand) — work does not cling to (such) a man’ (Īśā U. 2) — likewise, ‘This indeed is the life-long session (jarāmaryaṃ satram), namely the agnihotra; for one is freed from this (bondage) only by old age or by death’ — from a restrictive injunction (niyama) of this kind too, knowledge is merely a subordinate adjunct of works (karma-śeṣatvam eva vidyāyāḥ). ‖ 7 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V08: But because of the teaching of (something) higher (adhikopadeśāt), it is, according to Bādarāyaṇa, just so (evaṃ); for that is seen (taddarśanāt). ‖ 8 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V08::block-0: [Leading bhāṣya — transition from pūrvapakṣa to siddhānta:] When such (a pūrvapakṣa) is established, (the Sūtrakāra) replies —
BS_C03_S04_V08::block-1: By the word ‘tu’ (but), the (pūrvapakṣa) thesis is reversed. What was said — ‘because of being subordinate (śeṣatvāt), the statement (regarding the fruit being) human-end is a mere arthavāda’ (Br. Sū. 3.4.2) — that does not stand. Why? ‘Because of the teaching of (something) higher (adhikopadeśāt).’ If only the transmigrating self (saṃsārī ātman), the embodied (śārīraḥ), the doer and enjoyer, were taught in the Vedānta-texts as nothing more than the body, then in the manner described (above) the śruti about the fruit could be (treated as) arthavāda. But what is taught is something higher (adhikam) than the embodied self — viz. the non-transmigrating Lord (asaṃsārī īśvaraḥ), the Supreme Self (paramātman) free from the saṃsāric attributes such as agency etc., qualified by ‘free from sin’ (apahatapāpmatva) and so forth, who is taught in the Vedānta as the object to be known (vedyatvena). And the cognition of That is not a promoter of works; on the contrary, it cuts off works — as will be said in ‘And destruction (upamarda)…’ (Br. Sū. 3.4.16). Therefore the position of the venerable Bādarāyaṇa, ‘The human end (results) from this, on the strength of scripture (śabdāt)’ (Br. Sū. 3.4.1), stands just as it is; it cannot be shaken by fallacious reasonings (hetv-ābhāsa) such as ‘subordinacy’ etc. So indeed do the śrutis show that Self, the Lord, who is higher than the embodied (śārīrāt) — ‘He who is omniscient, all-knowing’ (Mu. U. 1.1.9), ‘Out of fear of Him the wind blows’ (Tai. U. 2.8.1), ‘A great terror, a thunderbolt held aloft’ (Ka. U. 2.3.2), ‘Under the rule of this Imperishable, O Gārgī’ (Bṛ. U. 3.8.9), ‘He thought, ‘May I be many, may I procreate’; He emitted fire’ (Chā. U. 6.2.3), and so on. As to the apparent drawing-in (anukarṣaṇa) — as the object to be known (vedyatayā) — of the very transmigrating self indicated by ‘dear’ etc., as in ‘Verily, all is dear for the sake of the Self. Verily, the Self, my dear, is to be seen’ (Bṛ. U. 2.4.5), ‘He who breathes by the prāṇa, He is your Self, the inmost of all’ (Bṛ. U. 3.4.1), ‘That puruṣa who is seen in the eye’ (Chā. U. 8.7.4) and the closing ‘I shall expound this to you yet again’ (Chā. U. 8.9.3) and the like — even that, by the concluding statements (vākya-śeṣa) such as ‘This which is the Ṛgveda is but the breath of this Great Being’ (Bṛ. U. 2.4.10), ‘He who transcends hunger and thirst, sorrow, delusion, old age and death’ (Bṛ. U. 3.5.1), ‘Having reached the Supreme Light he is realized in his own form — He is the Highest Person’ (Chā. U. 8.12.3), and the like, when the intention of teaching something higher (adhikopadidikṣā) is in fact present, has the import of absolute non-difference (atyantābheda) — and so there is no contradiction. For the Lordly itself is the supreme reality (pāramārthikam) of the embodied self’s own nature; embodiedness (śārīratva) is brought about by the limiting adjuncts (upādhi-kṛtam) — from the śrutis ‘That thou art’ (Chā. U. 6.8.7), ‘There is no other seer than this’ (Bṛ. U. 3.8.11), and so on. All this we have set forth at length earlier in the appropriate places. ‖ 8 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V09: But the (cited) instance is (equally) capable of (the opposite interpretation) — tulyaṃ tu darśanam. ‖ 9 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V09::block-0: As for what was said — that ‘from the observed conduct (ācāra-darśana) (of knowers performing rites) knowledge is a subordinate adjunct of works’ — to that we reply: equally is conduct seen (tulyam ācāra-darśanam) (of knowers as renouncers of works), establishing that knowledge is not a subordinate of works (akarma-śeṣatva) (as well). For the śruti runs thus — ‘This indeed, knowing this, the Ṛṣis, the descendants of Kavaṣa, said, ‘For what purpose shall we study? for what purpose shall we sacrifice?’’; ‘Verily, the men of old, knowing this, did not perform the agnihotra’; ‘Verily, having known this Self, the Brāhmaṇas, having risen above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, lead the life of mendicancy’ (Bṛ. U. 3.5.1) — and so forth. The non-engagement-in-works (akarmaniṣṭhatva) of Brahman-knowers such as Yājñavalkya is also seen, from śrutis like ‘‘So much indeed, my dear, is immortality,’ saying which Yājñavalkya wandered forth (i.e. renounced)’ (Bṛ. U. 4.5.15) and the like. Moreover, the indicatory token (liṅga-darśana) ‘Sirs, I am about to perform a sacrifice’ (Chā. U. 5.11.5) belongs to the topic of the Vaiśvānara-vidyā. And it is possible that in a Brahma-vidyā with adjuncts (sopādhikāyāṃ), works are seen accompanying it. Yet not even there is there subordinacy to works (karma-aṅgatva), since the prerequisites such as prakaraṇa etc. are absent. ‖ 9 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V10: (That śruti is) not of universal application — asārvatrikī. ‖ 10 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V10::block-0: [Leading bhāṣya:] As to what was further said — ‘from that very śruti (tac-chruteḥ)’ (Br. Sū. 3.4.4) — to that we reply —
BS_C03_S04_V10::block-1: ‘What one does with knowledge…’ (Chā. U. 1.1.10) — this śruti is not concerned with all knowledge (sarva-vidyā-viṣayā), because of its connection with the vidyā under discussion (prakṛta-vidyābhisambandhāt). And the topic in hand is the Udgītha-vidyā — as in ‘One should meditate upon this syllable Om as the udgītha’ (Chā. U. 1.1.1). ‖ 10 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V11: There is a division (vibhāgaḥ), as in (the division of) ‘a hundred’ — śatavat. ‖ 11 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V11::block-0: As to what was said — ‘Knowledge and works take hold of him together — samanvārabhete’ (Bṛ. U. 4.4.2) — that this statement of joint commencement (samanvārambha-vacana) is the indicatory mark (liṅga) of knowledge being non-autonomous — to that we answer: a division (vibhāga) is to be seen here — knowledge takes hold of one (kind of) man, works of another. Like (the division of) ‘a hundred’ (śatavat) — just as, when one says ‘Let a hundred be given to these two,’ it is given by dividing — fifty to one, fifty to the other — so here. Nor is this statement of joint commencement (samanvārambha-vacana) directed at the seeker of release (mumukṣu-viṣayam) — because of its conclusion ‘So indeed (does it fare with) one who desires’ (Bṛ. U. 4.4.6), confining its scope to the transmigrator (saṃsāri-viṣayatva), and because of the separate beginning ‘Now (concerning) the one who does not desire’ (Bṛ. U. 4.4.6) for the seeker of release. There, in the topic of the transmigrator (saṃsāri-viṣaye), knowledge — both that which is enjoined and that which is prohibited — is intended, since no distinction is made; works too, both enjoined and prohibited, (are intended), since this is a re-statement of what is otherwise obtained (yathā-prāpta-anuvāditvāt). This being so, this statement of joint commencement is intelligible even without (the present) division. ‖ 11 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V12: (The injunction is) for one possessed of mere study (adhyayana-mātravataḥ). ‖ 12 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V12::block-0: [Leading bhāṣya:] And as to what (was urged) — ‘from the injunction for one possessed of that (tadvataḥ)’ (Br. Sū. 3.4.6) — the answer is given —
BS_C03_S04_V12::block-1: In ‘Having studied the Veda from the family of the teacher…’ (Chā. U. 8.15.1), since only mere study (adhyayana-mātra) is heard of, we conclude that the injunction of works is for one possessed of mere study alone (adhyayana-mātravata eva). ‘But in that case, owing to non-knowledge (avidyatvāt), there would arise non-eligibility (anadhikāra) for works’ — this is no fault. We do not deny that the cognition of works arising from study (adhyayana-prabhavaṃ karmāvabodhanam) is the cause of eligibility. Then what? — only this much do we maintain: that the Upaniṣadic knowledge of the Self (aupaniṣadam ātma-jñānam), being known to be purposive autonomously by itself (svātantryeṇaiva prayojanavat), does not assume the role of being a cause of eligibility for works. And just as the cognition of one sacrifice is not required for eligibility in another sacrifice (kratv-antara), so this too is to be regarded. ‖ 12 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V13: Not so, because of the absence of any specifying difference. ‖ 13 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V13::block-0: And as for what was said — ‘And on account of the injunction’ (Brahma-sūtra 3.4.7) — to that this is the reply —
BS_C03_S04_V13::block-1: In such injunctive passages as ‘Performing works alone here let one wish to live’ (Īśa Up. 2), there is no specification that ‘this applies to one who knows’; for the regulation is laid down without any such distinction. ‖ 13 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V14: Or rather, the permission (to perform works) is for the eulogy (of knowledge). ‖ 14 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V14::block-0: Concerning ‘Performing works alone here…’ (Īśa Up. 2), a further special consideration is now stated. Although in that passage, by the force of the context, it is the knower alone who is connected with the word ‘performing’, even so this permission to perform works is to be regarded as serving the eulogy of knowledge. For the same text will go on to declare ‘Work does not cling to a man’ (Īśa Up. 2). The purport is this — even when the knower performs works as long as life lasts, work does not bring about bondage in him, by virtue of the power of knowledge; and thus knowledge is being eulogised. ‖ 14 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V15: And some, by free choice (set works aside). ‖ 15 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V15::block-0: Moreover, some knowers, having directly realised the fruit of knowledge, supported by that very realisation, reflect — out of free choice — upon the absence of any purpose in the means to other fruits, namely progeny and the like. Thus there is the Vājasaneyin śruti — ‘This indeed it is that the knowers of yore, knowing it, did not desire offspring, saying: What shall we do with offspring, we whose is this Self, this world?’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.22). And we have said again and again that the fruit of knowledge is something that has already mounted to direct experience, and is not, like the fruit of action, something that comes into being at a later time. For this reason too it is impossible to maintain either that knowledge is subordinate to action, or that the śruti speaking of its fruit is non-literal. ‖ 15 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V16: And (knowledge involves) the destruction (of the qualification for works). ‖ 16 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V16::block-0: Moreover, the entire complex — characterised by action, agent and fruit — which is the very ground of qualification for works, and which is created by ignorance, is declared by the śruti to undergo destruction in its very nature through the power of knowledge — ‘But where for him all has become the very Self, by what should one then see whom, by what should one smell whom’ (Bṛ. Up. 2.4.14) and so on. But for one who looks for the establishment of qualification for works as following upon the realisation of the Self taught in the Vedānta, the very uprooting of qualification for works would result. Therefore on this ground too the independence of knowledge (from action) stands established. ‖ 16 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V17: And (knowledge is found) in those of upward-flowing seed (the celibate orders) too; for there is scriptural evidence. ‖ 17 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V17::block-0: And knowledge is heard of in the orders of those whose seed flows upward (i.e., the lifelong celibate, the forest-dweller, and the wandering monk). And there knowledge cannot stand as a limb of works, because of the absence of works — for they have no Vedic works such as the Agnihotra and the rest. It might be said: ‘But the orders of upward-flowing seed are not heard of in the Veda.’ This too is not so. For these orders too are made known in Vedic words — ‘There are three branches of dharma’ (Ch. Up. 2.23.1); ‘And those who in the forest practise faith and austerity as their worship’ (Ch. Up. 5.10.1); ‘Those who, dwelling in the forest, observe austerity and faith’ (Mu. Up. 1.2.11); ‘Wishing for this very world, wandering ascetics renounce’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.22); ‘He should renounce straight from studentship’ (Jābāla Up. 4); and so on. And it is well known both in śruti and in smṛti that the state of upward-flowing seed belongs both to those who have entered the householder’s life and to those who have not, and to those who have discharged the three debts as well as to those who have not. Therefore on this ground too the independence of knowledge stands established. ‖ 17 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V18: Jaimini holds (these passages) to be (mere) reference, not injunction; for (śruti even) condemns (the other orders). ‖ 18 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V18::block-0: Pūrvapakṣa (Jaimini): Those words ‘There are three branches of dharma’ (Ch. Up. 2.23.1) and the rest, which were quoted in support of the existence of the orders of upward-flowing seed, are not competent to establish them. For Jaimini the Ācārya holds that in these words there is only a reference (parāmarśa) to the other orders, not an injunction (vidhi). Why? Because here there is no injunctive word, no liṅ-suffix and the like. And in each of these passages a different intention is in fact found. Thus in ‘There are three branches of dharma’ — ‘Sacrifice, study, and gift, this is the first; austerity is just the second; the brahmacārin dwelling in the teacher’s house, ending his self utterly in the teacher’s house, is the third — all these become possessors of meritorious worlds’ — after first referring to the orders and stating the non-ultimate character of their fruit, the state of being established in Brahman is being eulogised as bearing ultimate fruit — ‘He who is established in Brahman attains immortality’ (Ch. Up. 2.23.1). ‘But surely the orders are understood even in such reference?’ True, they are understood; but their existence is established only by smṛti and by usage, not by direct śruti. And therefore, when there is conflict with direct śruti, they will either be set aside, or be confined to those not qualified (for Vedic works). ‘But the householder’s order too is referred to along with those of upward-flowing seed — ‘‘Sacrifice, study, and gift, this is the first’’.’ True, it is so; yet because the Agnihotra and the other works are enjoined precisely upon the householder, his existence is already well established by śruti. Therefore this reference is meant only for eulogy, not as an injunction. Moreover, direct śruti even condemns the other order — ‘Verily he is a slayer of the heroes of the gods who lets the (sacred) fire die out’; ‘Bringing dear wealth to the teacher, do not cut off the line of progeny’ (Tai. Up. 1.11.1); ‘There is no world for one without a son — thus do all the beasts know.’ Likewise ‘And those who in the forest practise faith and austerity as their worship’ (Ch. Up. 5.10.1) and ‘Those who, dwelling in the forest, observe austerity and faith’ (Mu. Up. 1.2.11) are teachings about the deva-yāna path, not about another order. And the indication of another order in such passages as ‘Austerity is just the second’ (Ch. Up. 2.23.1) is doubtful. Likewise ‘Wishing for this very world, the wandering ascetics renounce’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.22) is mere praise of the world (of the Self), not an injunction of the wandering life. ‘But surely ‘‘He should renounce straight from studentship’’ (Jābāla) is a perfectly direct, explicit injunction of the wandering life.’ True, it is so; but the present discussion is to be regarded as proceeding without taking that śruti into account. ‖ 18 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V19: Bādarāyaṇa (holds them) to be (positively) to be observed; because of the equality of the scriptural statement. ‖ 19 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V19::block-0: Siddhānta (Bādarāyaṇa): Bādarāyaṇa the Ācārya holds that the other order is to be observed. The view that, because the other orders are not heard of in the Veda and because the Agnihotra and the rest are obligatory, the other order — being in conflict with these — is to be observed only by the unqualified — this view he rejects, holding that, just like the householder’s state, the other order also must be entered upon, even by one who has no inclination towards it. Why? Because of the equality of scriptural statement. The reference-śruti to the other order is found to be on a par with that of the householder’s state, in such passages as ‘There are three branches of dharma’ (Ch. Up. 2.23.1). Just as here the householder’s state, which is enjoined by other śrutis, is referred to, so too the other order is to be understood — just as in the sentence enjoining the wearing of the sacred thread, there is reference to nivīta and prācīnāvīta which are obtained from other scriptures. Therefore, the other order is on a par with the householder’s state in being something to be observed. So too ‘Wishing for this very world, the wandering ascetics renounce’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.22) stands in the company of ‘Veda recitation’ and the rest. And ‘And those who in the forest practise faith and austerity as their worship’ (Ch. Up. 5.10.1) stands in the company of the Pañcāgni-vidyā. As to what was said — that the indication of another order in ‘Austerity is just the second’ and the rest is doubtful — that is no fault, since there are grounds of certainty. For ‘There are three branches of dharma’ (Ch. Up. 2.23.1) declares the triplicity of branches of dharma. And the manifold dharmas such as sacrifice, etc., being distinct in their origination, cannot, except through connection with an order, be brought within the threefold count. There, the household order, marked by sacrifice and the rest, is pointed out as one branch of dharma; ‘brahmacārin’ is an explicit naming of an order; and as for ‘austerity’ — what other branch of dharma can be admitted under that head save the order in which austerity predominates (i.e., the forest-dweller)? And in ‘And those who in the forest…’ (Ch. Up. 5.10.1), from the indication ‘in the forest’ together with ‘faith’ and ‘austerity’, the order (of the wandering monk) is grasped. Therefore, even on (the assumption of) reference, the other order is to be observed. ‖ 19 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V20: Or rather it is an injunction, like (the injunction of) holding (the kindling-stick upward). ‖ 20 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V20::block-0: Siddhānta (continued): Or rather, this passage is an injunction (vidhi) of the other order, not a mere reference. ‘But if injunctiveness be admitted, the apprehension of unity of sentence (with the praise of brahma-saṃsthatā) would be obstructed; and unity of sentence is in fact apprehended here — that the three branches of dharma have meritorious worlds as their fruit, while the state of being established in Brahman has immortality as its fruit.’ This is true; yet, even though such an apprehension of unity of sentence does present itself, that must be set aside and an injunction must be admitted; because (the injunction is) something not before known (apūrva); because no other injunction is to be seen; and because, given the perfectly clear cognition of another order, the connection of unity of sentence by way of resorting to a secondary or figurative sense (guṇavāda) cannot be made out. Like the holding (of the kindling-stick): just as in ‘He should hold the kindling-stick from below and not run after; for from above one holds it for the gods’ — even though, with the holding-from-below, an apprehension of unity of sentence does arise, the holding-from-above is in fact enjoined, because it is something not before known; and accordingly it has been said in the section on Śeṣa-lakṣaṇa: ‘But it is an injunction in the case of holding, because of being apūrva’ (Jaiminīya-sūtra 3.4.15). In the same way, here too, the reference-śruti to the orders is to be construed as an injunction.
BS_C03_S04_V20::block-1: Even on the alternative that this is mere reference to the other orders, the state of being established in Brahman, by force of being eulogised, must in any case be admitted as something to be enjoined. And it must be discerned whether that (state) is to belong to anyone in any of the four orders, or only to the wandering monk (parivrāḍ). If, when the orders ending with the brahmacārin are referred to, the parivrāḍ also is referred to, then since all four orders are equally referred to, and since the state of being out of the orders altogether (anāśramin) is not tenable, anyone in any of the four orders may become brahma-saṃstha. But if (the parivrāḍ) is not referred to, then he, being left over, will turn out to be the brahma-saṃstha alone. Now some say that by the word ‘austerity’, which is taken (here) to denote the vaikhānasa (forest-dweller), the parivrāḍ also is referred to. That is improper; for when an alternative course is open, the parivrāḍ does not deserve to be taken in by the qualifier proper to the vānaprastha. Just as here the brahmacārin and the gṛhamedhin are each marked by their own non-overlapping qualifiers, so too it is fitting that the bhikṣu and the vaikhānasa should be similarly marked. And austerity is the proper, distinguishing dharma of the forest-dwellers, since they have bodily mortification as their main feature, and the word ‘austerity’ is by convention (rūḍhi) used for that. The dharma of the bhikṣu, however, marked by sense-restraint and the like, is not at all expressed by the word ‘austerity’. And to refer to the orders as three when they are well known to be four is improper. Moreover, here a distinction is expressly drawn — ‘these three are partakers of meritorious worlds; (one) is partaker of immortality.’ This statement of distinction is intelligible only on the basis of separateness. For one does not say ‘Devadatta and Yajñadatta are dull-witted; one of these two is keenly intelligent’; one does, however, say ‘Devadatta and Yajñadatta are dull-witted; but Viṣṇumitra is keenly intelligent.’ Therefore, the former three orders are partakers of meritorious worlds, and the parivrāḍ, who is left over, is alone partaker of immortality. ‘But how can the word ‘‘brahma-saṃstha’’, which by etymology (yoga) is applicable everywhere, be made to rest on the parivrāḍ alone?’ ‘And if rūḍhi (conventional sense) be admitted, then immortality being attained from the order alone, it would follow that knowledge becomes purposeless.’ To this we reply: by ‘brahma-saṃstha’ is meant complete merging in Brahman — fixity in That having no other activity as its form. And that is not possible for those in the (other) three orders, since the non-performance of the works enjoined upon their respective orders is heard of as bringing about transgression. But for the parivrāḍ, since all works are renounced, no transgression arising from non-performance is possible. Śama (control of mind), dama (control of senses) and the rest, which are his proper dharma, are supports of the state of being established in Brahman, not opposed to it. For his very fixity in Brahman, supported by śama, dama and the rest, is the work enjoined upon his own order. And sacrifice and the rest are (the works) of the others. And in their transgression there is for him too a transgression. Thus also do śrutis declare — ‘Renunciation is Brahmā, Brahmā indeed is the Supreme, the Supreme indeed is Brahmā; truly all these austerities are inferior; renunciation alone exceeded’ (Nārāyaṇa Up. 78); ‘Ascetics whose meaning has been fully ascertained by Vedānta-knowledge, who are pure in being through the yoga of renunciation’ (Mu. Up. 3.2.6; Nā. Up. 12.3; Kai. Up. 3); and so on. And smṛtis likewise — ‘With minds set on That, with selves set on That, with That as their basis, with That as their final goal’ (Bhagavadgītā 5.17), and so on — show the absence of works for one established in Brahman. Therefore, the supposed defect — that, since immortality is attained merely from the order, knowledge becomes purposeless — does not arise for the parivrāḍ. Thus, even on (the supposition of) reference to the other orders, the wandering life characterised by the state of being established in Brahman is at any rate obtained. (And this stands) without depending (on other śruti)…
BS_C03_S04_V21: If it be objected that (such passages) are merely eulogistic because of (their) taking up (sacrificial accessories), we say no, on account of (their) novelty (apūrvatva). ‖ 21 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V21::block-0: Such Śruti-passages as ‘That very one which is the most savoury of savours, supreme, the highest, the eighth — namely, the udgītha’ (Chā. Up. 1.1.3) (citation), ‘This (earth) itself is the Ṛk; fire is the Sāman’ (Chā. Up. 1.6.1) (citation), ‘This very world (earth) is that fire which has been piled up’ (Śat. Br. 10.1.2.2) (citation), ‘This same (earth) is indeed the Uktha; this very (earth) is the earth’ (Ait. Ār. 2.1.2) (citation) — concerning these the doubt arises: are they meant for the eulogy of the udgītha and the like, or are they intended for enjoining upāsanā (meditation)? — (Pūrvapakṣa:) It is fitting that they are eulogistic, because they are heard while taking up the udgītha and other limbs of sacrificial action. Just as ‘This (earth) itself is the juhū (oblation-ladle); the sun is the tortoise; heaven is the world (called) Āhavanīya’ and similar (statements) are meant for eulogising the juhū etc., so also (here). — If this be (urged), (the Sūtra) says: No. For mere eulogy cannot rightly be the purpose of these Śrutis, on account of (their) apūrvatva (novelty — i.e., conveying something not already known). For when (a passage) has the purpose of vidhi (injunction), some apūrva (hitherto-unknown) matter is enjoined; whereas in the case of (its) being for eulogy, sheer purposelessness alone would result. For it has been said — at the place ‘But on account of (eulogy's) forming one syntactical whole with the injunction, eulogies are subordinate to injunctions on account of their (eulogising) purpose’ (Jai. Sū. 1.2.7) (citation) — that a eulogy serves a purpose only by attaining the status of being a complementary part (vākyaśeṣa) of an injunctive word. But of the udgītha and the rest, which are (already) enjoined elsewhere, this eulogy that is recited at another place, not attaining the status of a complementary sentence-portion, would be quite purposeless. As for ‘This (earth) itself is the juhū’ etc., it is recited in the very vicinity of the (sacrificial) injunction — there lies the difference. Therefore Śrutis of this class are meant solely for vidhi (injunction of upāsanā). ‖ 21 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V22: And (this is so) because of the (occurrence of) words denoting injunction. ‖ 22 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V22::block-0: ‘One should meditate upon the udgītha’ (Chā. Up. 1.1.1) (citation), ‘One should meditate upon the Sāman’ (Chā. Up. 2.2.1) (citation), ‘He should know thus: I am the Uktha’ — and similar very explicit injunctive words are heard. And these would stand contradicted if (such passages) had mere eulogy as their purpose. Likewise there is the recollection of (those expert in) the methods (of Mīmāṁsā): ‘kuryāt (one should do), kriyeta (let it be done), kartavyam (it is to be done), bhavet (let it be), syāt (it should be) — these five (forms) — this everywhere in all the Vedas is the settled mark of vidhi.’ Those who hold that the meaning of the liṅ-suffix and the like is vidhi remember it thus. And in each topical context, fruits are made to be heard — ‘He becomes a fulfiller of desires’ (Chā. Up. 1.1.7) (citation), ‘He indeed becomes lord of singing-out-desires’ (Chā. Up. 1.7.9) (citation), ‘The worlds, both the higher and the returning ones, become fit for him’ (Chā. Up. 2.2.3) (citation), and so forth. Therefore also the Śrutis concerning the udgītha and the rest are meant for the enjoining of upāsanā. ‖ 22 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V23: If it be said that (the narratives) are meant for the pāriplava (recitation), we say no, on account of (the texts') having specified (only certain narratives). ‖ 23 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V23::block-0: ‘Now, Yājñavalkya had two wives, Maitreyī and Kātyāyanī’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.5.1) (citation); ‘Pratardana, son of Divodāsa, by valour and manliness, reached the beloved abode of Indra’ (Kau. Up. 3.1) (citation); ‘Jānaśruti the great-grandson was a giver of food in faith, a great donor, one in whose house much was cooked’ (Chā. Up. 4.1.1) (citation) — concerning such narratives recited in the Upaniṣads, the doubt arises: are they meant for use in the pāriplava (the cyclical recitation in the aśvamedha sacrifice), or are they meant for the apprehension of the vidyā that is in the immediate context (sannihita-vidyā)? — (Pūrvapakṣa:) These narrative-Śrutis are meant for the pāriplava, since they have the general character of narrative (ākhyāna-sāmānya), and since the use of narrative is enjoined in the pāriplava. Consequently the Vedānta-texts would not have vidyā as their primary import; like mantras, they would be subordinate to (sacrificial) employment. — If (this be urged), no. Why? On account of (the texts') having specified (particular narratives only — viśeṣitatva). Indeed, having taken up (the topic), ‘He should narrate the pāriplava,’ certain narratives only — ‘Manu Vaivasvata is king’ and the like — are particularly specified there. If (the basis were) the mere general character of narrative, there would be the inclusion of all (narratives), and this specification would itself be purposeless. Therefore these narrative-Śrutis are not meant for the pāriplava. ‖ 23 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V24: And so, on account of (their) connection in one syntactical whole (with the vidyās). ‖ 24 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V24::block-0: (Siddhānta:) When the (narratives) are not meant for the pāriplava, it is fitting that the narratives should serve the apprehension of the vidyā that stands in the immediate context (sannihita-vidyā), since they are bound up with it as one syntactical whole (eka-vākyatā-upabandha). For at each place a oneness-of-sentence (eka-vākyatā) with the proximate vidyās is observed — serving the purpose of allurement (prarocana) and of facilitating apprehension. In the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa, for instance, oneness-of-sentence is seen with the vidyā ‘O dear, the Self is to be seen’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.5.6) (citation) and so forth. In the Pratardana also, with ‘I am prāṇa, the prajñātman’ and the like. In ‘Jānaśruti’ too, with ‘Vāyu indeed is the saṁvarga’ (Chā. Up. 4.3.1) (citation) and so forth. Just as the narratives occurring in the karma-Śrutis, such as ‘He scooped out the omentum from himself’ (citation) and the like, serve as eulogies of the proximate injunction — so it is here also. Hence (these narratives) are not meant for the pāriplava. ‖ 24 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V25: And for this very reason (the vidyā) does not require the kindling of fires and so forth. ‖ 25 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V25::block-0: (The clause) ‘there is human aim from this — from the (Upaniṣadic) word’ (Br. Sū. 3.4.1) (citation), though intervened by other (sūtras), is yet referred back to by ‘from this’ (ataḥ) since (such reference) is possible. And precisely for this reason — namely, that vidyā is itself the cause of the human aim (puruṣārtha) — the āśrama-karmas such as the kindling of fires (agnīndhana) need not be looked to by the vidyā for the accomplishment of its own end. Thus, with a view to saying something further, (the Sūtra) winds up the result of the very first adhikaraṇa. ‖ 25 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V26: And (vidyā) requires all (the āśrama-karmas), because of Śruti speaking of sacrifice etc., as in the case of the horse. ‖ 26 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V26::block-0: Now this is what is to be considered — is the vidyā absolutely without need of the āśrama-karmas, or is there some need (of them)? — There, by force of (the previous declaration that) ‘for this very reason the āśrama-karmas such as kindling of fires are not required by the vidyā for the accomplishment of its own end,’ when the (conclusion of) absolute non-requirement is obtained, this is now stated: ‘And requirement of all’ (sarvāpekṣā ca). The vidyā does require all the āśrama-karmas; it is not (a case of) absolute non-requirement. — But this statement is contradictory: ‘the vidyā requires the āśrama-karmas’ and ‘it does not require (them)’! — We say: not so. For an arisen (utpannā) vidyā does not require anything else for the accomplishment of its fruit; but as regards (its own) arising it does require (them). Why? Because of the Śruti about sacrifice and so on. Thus the Śruti — ‘That very (Self) the brāhmaṇas seek to know by the recitation of the Vedas, by sacrifice, by gift, by penance, by fasting’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.22) (citation) — shows that sacrifice and the rest are means of vidyā. And from the connection (of yajñas etc.) with the desire to know (vividiṣā), it is ascertained that they are means for (vidyā's) arising. And in ‘Now, what they call sacrifice, that itself is brahmacarya’ (Chā. Up. 8.5.1) (citation), since brahmacarya — which is itself a means of vidyā — is praised together with sacrifice and the rest, the means-character of sacrifice and so on too is hinted at. The Śruti — ‘That state which all the Vedas declare, which all penances speak of, desiring which they practise brahmacarya — that state I tell thee in brief’ (Ka. Up. 1.2.15) (citation) and the like — also hints at the means-character of the āśrama-karmas with respect to vidyā. Smṛti likewise: ‘Karmans (ripen) the maturing of impurity (kaṣāya); knowledge, however, is the supreme goal. When impurity is matured by karmans, then knowledge proceeds’ — and the like. ‘As in the case of the horse’ (aśvavat) is the showing of suitability (yogyatā): just as a horse, by force of its suitability, is not yoked to the drawing of a plough but is yoked to the drawing of a chariot, so the āśrama-karmas are not required for the accomplishment of vidyā's fruit but are required at (its) arising. ‖ 26 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V27: (The aspirant) should also be endowed with calmness, control and the rest, since these too, being subordinate to it (vidyā), are necessarily to be undertaken on account of the injunction (regarding) them. ‖ 27 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V27::block-0: If someone should think — ‘the means-character of sacrifice etc. with respect to vidyā is not justified, since there is no injunction (about it). For Śrutis of the type ‘they seek to know by sacrifice’ are of the nature of an anuvāda (re-statement) aiming at the eulogy of vidyā, not at the injunction of sacrifice etc. — (the meaning being:) so highly fortunate is vidyā, that men desire to attain it by sacrifices and the like’ — even so (tathāpi tu), the seeker of vidyā must be endowed with calmness (śama), control (dama) and the like, since calmness, control and the rest are enjoined as means of vidyā in (the passage) ‘Therefore he who knows thus, having become calm, controlled, withdrawn, forbearing, collected, sees the Self in the Self alone’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.23) (citation), and what is enjoined is necessarily to be undertaken. — But here too one might find a designation in the present tense: ‘having become endowed with calmness etc., he sees’ — not an injunction. — We say: no; the sense of injunction is apprehended on account of (the word) ‘therefore’ (tasmāt) signifying the taking up by way of praise of the topic in hand. And the Mādhyandinas read it very explicitly as a vidhi: ‘paśyet’ (he should see). Therefore, even if there be no need of sacrifice and so on, calmness etc. must be relied upon. But sacrifices and the like also must be relied upon, on the very ground of the Śruti about sacrifice etc. — But it has been said that in ‘they seek to know by sacrifices etc.’ no vidhi is to be found! — True, that has been said; but even so, on account of the apūrvatva (newness) of the connection (of yajñas with vividiṣā), an injunction is presumed. For this connection of sacrifice and the rest with the desire to know (vividiṣā) is not previously obtained, so that it could be merely re-stated. In sentences such as ‘therefore Pūṣan has the share of pounded grain, since he is toothless’ — though no vidhi is heard there — yet, presuming a vidhi on account of apūrvatva, the inquiry ‘the pounding for Pūṣan is to be taken in the modification’ (Śābara-bhāṣya 3.3.34) (citation) and so forth has been pursued in the First Tantra (i.e., the Pūrva Mīmāṁsā). And so it has been said: ‘Or it is an injunction, like dhāraṇa’ (Br. Sū. 3.4.20) (citation). In the smṛtis too, in the Bhagavad-Gītā and the rest, it has been elaborated that yajñas and the like, performed without aiming at fruit, become for the seeker of liberation means of knowledge. Therefore yajñas and the like, and śama and dama and the rest, all the āśrama-karmas as suited to (each) āśrama, should be looked to at the arising of vidyā. There also, śama and the rest, by their connection through ‘knowing thus’ (evaṁvit), are the means of vidyā that are very near; while yajñas and the rest, being connected through vividiṣā (desire-to-know), are more external — thus is the discrimination to be made. ‖ 27 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V28: And (there is) the permission of all (kinds of) food (only) when life is in danger; this is seen. ‖ 28 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V28::block-0: (Pūrvapakṣa:) In the Prāṇa-saṁvāda of the Chāndogas, it is heard — ‘For one who knows thus, nothing whatever becomes non-food’ (Chā. Up. 5.2.1) (citation). Likewise of the Vājasaneyins — ‘For him no food is uneaten, nothing is unaccepted’ (Bṛ. Up. 6.1.14) (citation). The meaning is: everything becomes for him verily edible. Now is this permission of all food enjoined as a limb of vidyā, like śama and the rest, or is it celebrated by way of eulogy? — In this doubt, the position obtained at first is: it is a vidhi (injunction). For an instructive teaching produces a particular activity (pravṛtti-viśeṣa-kara). Hence, on account of (its) being in the proximity of the prāṇa-vidyā, this absence-of-restriction (niyama-nivṛtti) is enjoined as a limb thereof. — But in that case there would be a contradiction with the śāstras dividing edibles and inedibles (bhakṣya-abhakṣya-vibhāga)! — This is no fault, since cancellation can be by virtue of the relation of the general and the particular (sāmānya-viśeṣa-bhāva). Just as the prohibition of injuring living beings is set aside by the injunction of the slaying of the (sacrificial) animal; and just as ‘He should avoid no woman; this is his vow’ (Chā. Up. 2.13.2) (citation), pertaining to the Vāmadevya-vidyā, by enjoining non-avoidance of any woman, sets aside the general śāstra dividing women approachable and unapproachable — so this injunction of eating all food, pertaining to the prāṇa-vidyā, would set aside the (general) śāstra dividing edibles and inedibles. — When (this) is obtained, we say (the siddhānta):
BS_C03_S04_V28::block-1: (Siddhānta:) This permission of all food is not enjoined. For no injunctive word is found here, since (the passage) ‘For one who knows thus, nothing whatever becomes non-food’ (Chā. Up. 5.2.1) (citation) is by way of designation in the present tense. Nor, even when there is no apprehension of vidhi, can a vidhi be assumed merely out of the desire to make it ‘productive of a particular activity.’ Moreover, having said that the food of prāṇa is bounded only by the dog and the like, this is then said: ‘to him who knows thus, nothing is non-food.’ Now food bounded by the dog and the like cannot be enjoyed by a human body. But it can be reflected upon, that ‘all this is the food of prāṇa.’ Therefore this is an arthavāda for the eulogy of the prāṇa-anna-vijñāna (knowledge of prāṇa as the eater of all food); it is not an injunction permitting all food. (The Sūtra) shows this by ‘And the permission of all food (is only) at the time of danger to life’ (sarvānnānumatiś ca prāṇātyaye). The meaning is: only at the time of danger to life, in extreme distress, is all food sanctioned as edible — tad-darśanāt (this being seen). Thus the Śruti, in the brāhmaṇa beginning ‘Among the Kurus stricken by hailstones’ (Chā. Up. 1.10.1) (citation), shows the engaging in the eating of forbidden food on the part of the sage Cākrāyaṇa in (his) wretched state. The sage Cākrāyaṇa, fallen on hard times, ate the half-eaten beans (kulmāṣa) of a wealthy man (ibhya). The drink offered with them, however, he refused on account of the defect of being leavings (ucchiṣṭa). And he gave the reason there: ‘Truly I would not have lived had I not eaten these’ (Chā. Up. 1.10.4) (citation), and ‘drink-water is at my pleasure’ (Chā. Up. 1.10.4) (citation). Again, the next day, he ate those very beans, leavings of his own and others', and stale (paryuṣita). Now, from this Śruti showing the eating of leavings-of-leavings and stale (food), an over-and-above intention is observed: at the contingency of danger to life, for the preservation of life, even the inedible may be eaten; but in (one's) normal state it is not to be done, even by one possessed of vidyā — this is gathered from his refusal of the drink-water. Therefore (the passage) ‘For one who knows thus, nothing’ (Chā. Up. 5.2.1) (citation) and the like is an arthavāda. ‖ 28 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V29: And because (the rule about food) is not contradicted. (29)
BS_C03_S04_V29::block-0: And it being thus (i.e., when the maxim ‘food may be eaten without restriction at the time of distress to life’ is taken as referring only to such an emergency), the scriptural rule distinguishing between what may and may not be eaten — ‘When food is pure, the inner being becomes pure’ (āhāra-śuddhau sattva-śuddhiḥ) and so forth — will remain unviolated (abādhita). (29)
BS_C03_S04_V30::block-0: Moreover, even the eating of any kind of food in a state of distress (āpadi sarvānna-bhakṣaṇam) is recorded by smṛti without distinction between the knower and the non-knower (viduṣaḥ aviduṣaḥ ca aviśeṣeṇa) — ‘He who, when reduced to peril of life, eats food from any source whatever, is not tainted by sin, just as the lotus-leaf is not tainted by water’ (Manu-smṛti 10.104) (citation). Likewise, ‘Liquor (madya) is forever (forbidden) to the brāhmaṇa’ (Gautama-dharma-sūtra 1.2.25) (citation), ‘On the brāhmaṇa who has drunk liquor they should pour (the liquor) hot’ (Gautama-dharma-sūtra 3.5.1) (citation), and ‘From eating what is not to be eaten (abhakṣya-bhakṣaṇāt), liquor-drinkers become worms’ — thus is the avoidance of what is not food (anannasya varjanam) recorded. (30)
BS_C03_S04_V31: And there is a (scriptural) word from this (Upaniṣad) prohibiting (it) where there is no compulsion. (31)
BS_C03_S04_V31::block-0: And a scriptural word (śabda) prohibiting what is not food (anannasya pratiṣedhakaḥ), having for its purpose the cessation of wilful behaviour (kāmakāra-nivṛtti-prayojanaḥ), is heard in the saṁhitā of the Kaṭhas — ‘Therefore the brāhmaṇa shall not drink liquor’ (citation). And that very (text), in view of the passage ‘Verily, in one who knows thus (no harm clings)’ (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.2.1) (citation) being an arthavāda, becomes all the more cogent (upapanna-tara). Hence arthavādas of this class are not injunctions (vidhi). (31)
BS_C03_S04_V32: And the duties of the (other) āśramas also (are to be performed), because they are enjoined. (32)
BS_C03_S04_V32::block-0: Under ‘And there is the requirement of all (works)’ (Brahma-sūtra 3.4.26) (citation), the āśrama-works were ascertained to be means of knowledge (vidyā-sādhanatva). Now, however, the question is considered: For one who is not a seeker of liberation (amumukṣoḥ) but is rooted in mere āśrama-life (āśrama-mātra-niṣṭha) and does not desire knowledge (vidyām akāmayamāna), are these (works) to be performed, or not? On this, the pūrvapakṣa: From the injunction (under the text) ‘Him the brāhmaṇas seek to know through Veda-recitation…’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22) (citation) and so forth, where the āśrama-works are enjoined as means of knowledge, the nityas are not to be performed by one who does not desire knowledge but desires some other fruit. If, on the other hand, they are to be performed by him too, then they cannot be means of knowledge — for there is contradiction in being conjoined both with the perpetually-required (nitya) and with the occasional (anitya). To this (suggested) conclusion (the ācārya) replies: Even for the non-seeker-of-liberation who stands in mere āśrama-life, the nitya works are still obligatory, because of the injunction ‘He shall offer the agnihotra so long as he lives’ and the like; for there is no such thing as an over-burden (atibhāra) in (Vedic) statement. (32)
BS_C03_S04_V33: And as auxiliaries (to knowledge also they are required). (33)
BS_C03_S04_V33::block-0: Now, to what was urged — that, this being so, these (works) cannot be means of knowledge — he gives this reply:
BS_C03_S04_V33::block-1: And these may also be auxiliaries (sahakārī) to knowledge, on the very strength of the injunction ‘Him the brāhmaṇas seek to know through Veda-recitation…’ (citation) and so on; this has already been stated — ‘And there is the requirement of all (works), because the śruti speaks of yajña and the rest, like the horse’ (Brahma-sūtra 3.4.26) (citation). Nor is this statement of the auxiliary-status of the āśrama-works to be regarded as having for its scope the fruit of knowledge in the manner of the prayājas (subsidiary oblations) — because knowledge is not characterized by injunction (avidhi-lakṣaṇatva) and because the fruit of knowledge is not something to be brought about (asādhyatva). For a means whose nature is injunction, like the darśa-pūrṇamāsa, requires another auxiliary means in order to accomplish its fruit, heaven; not so knowledge. So too has it been said — ‘For this very reason there is no requirement of kindling fires and the rest’ (Brahma-sūtra 3.4.25) (citation). Hence the predication of auxiliary-status to these (works) is solely as regards the production (utpatti-sādhanatva) (of knowledge). Nor here need the contradiction of being conjoined both with the nitya and the anitya be apprehended; for, even though the work is one, the conjunctions (saṁyoga) are different. The one (saṁyoga) — perpetual — is constructed by sentences such as ‘so long as one lives’; this has not the fruit of knowledge. The other — non-perpetual — is constructed by sentences such as ‘Him the brāhmaṇas (seek to know) by Veda-recitation’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22) (citation); this has the fruit of knowledge — just as the one and the same khādiratva (the use of khadira-wood) has, by perpetual conjunction, kratvarthatva (subservience to the rite), and, by non-perpetual conjunction, puruṣārthatva (subservience to the human end). (33)
BS_C03_S04_V34: In every way (the works) are the very same, on the strength of both indications (of śruti and smṛti). (34)
BS_C03_S04_V34::block-0: In every way — whether on the view of (their being) āśrama-works or on the view of (their being) auxiliaries to knowledge — the same dharmas, the agnihotra and the rest, are to be performed. By the emphasizing word ‘the very same’ (ta eva), what does the ācārya exclude? We say: the suspicion of a difference of work (karma-bheda). For, just as in the Kuṇḍapāyināmayana, by the text ‘they offer the agnihotra for a month’, a work other than the perpetual agnihotra is enjoined, here there is no such difference of work — that is the meaning. Whence (is this established)? From the twofold indication (ubhaya-liṅga) — the śruti-liṅga and the smṛti-liṅga. As for the śruti-liṅga: ‘Him the brāhmaṇas seek to know through Veda-recitation…’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22) (citation) — here yajñas and the rest, in their already accomplished form (siddha-vat utpanna-rūpāṇi), are simply employed (viniyukta) in the desire-to-know (vividiṣā); the (śruti) does not, like ‘they offer’, generate for them a fresh form (apūrva rūpa). And the smṛti-liṅga too — ‘He who, without depending on the fruit of work, performs the work that ought to be done’ (Bhagavad-gītā 6.1) (citation) — shows that it is the work whose ‘ought-to-be-done-ness’ is already known (vijñāta-kartavyatāka) that is for the production of knowledge. And the well-known designation as saṁskāra — ‘He who has these forty-eight saṁskāras…’ (Gautama-dharma-sūtra 1.8.25) (citation) and the like — applied to the Vedic works in smṛti, is with reference to the production of knowledge in him who has been refined (saṁskṛta) by them. Hence this affirmation of non-difference (abheda-avadhāraṇa) is sound. (34)
BS_C03_S04_V35: And (the śruti) also shows non-overpowering (of the knower by afflictions). (35)
BS_C03_S04_V35::block-0: This indication is supportive (upodbalaka) of the very (doctrine of) auxiliary-status. Śruti shows the non-overpowering (anabhibhava) by afflictions such as attachment of one endowed with the means beginning with brahmacarya — ‘This Self does not perish, whom one obtains through brahmacarya’ (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.5.3) (citation), and the like. Hence it is determined that yajñas and the rest are both āśrama-works and auxiliaries to knowledge. (35)
BS_C03_S04_V36: And also one in between (the āśramas is qualified), because that is seen. (36)
BS_C03_S04_V36::block-0: Of widowers and the like, and of those who lack wealth and other (means), and of those who, having failed to enter any one of the āśramas, stand in the interval (antarāla-vartin) — does qualification for knowledge (vidyāyām adhikāraḥ) belong (to them) or not? — such is the doubt. The pūrvapakṣa: It does not, since āśrama-works have been ascertained as the cause of knowledge, and since for these (people) the āśrama-works are not possible. — When this is the prima facie conclusion, (the sūtrakāra) says: ‘And also one in between’ (antarā cāpi tu) — even one existing in the state of being outside an āśrama (anāśramitvena vartamānaḥ) is qualified for knowledge. Whence? From its being seen (tad-dṛṣṭeḥ) — because the śruti reports the brahma-knowership of Raikva, Vācaknavī (Gārgī) and the like, who were of just such (status). (36)
BS_C03_S04_V37::block-0: It is recorded in the Itihāsa that of Saṃvarta and others, who, by reason of their resorting to nakedness and the like, were not bound to the duties of any āśrama (anapekṣita-āśrama-karman), there nevertheless was great yogic mastery (mahā-yogitva). (37)
BS_C03_S04_V38: And there is special favouring [of vidyā by other dharmas]. (38)
BS_C03_S04_V38::block-0: [Leading bhāṣya:] But surely this presentation of Śruti, Smṛti, and observation has been adduced merely as an indicative ground (liṅga). What now is the actual obtainment? — That is now stated:
BS_C03_S04_V38::block-1: Even of those — the widowers and the rest (vidhura-ādi) — there is possible a favouring (anugraha) of vidyā by means of dharma-particulars unopposed [to their state] and pertaining to one merely as a person (puruṣa-mātra-sambandhin), such as japa, fasting, the worship of deities and the like. So says Smṛti: ‘By japa alone the Brāhmaṇa would attain accomplishment — there is no doubt about this. Whether he performs other [karma] or does not perform it, he is called a Brāhmaṇa friendly [to all] (maitra)’ (Manu-smṛ. 2.87) — thus showing the eligibility for japa even of one for whom āśrama-karma has become impossible. And by āśrama-karmas performed in another birth too, the favouring of vidyā is indeed possible. So Smṛti says: ‘Then, perfected through many births, he attains the supreme goal’ (Bh.G. 6.45) — thus showing that vidyā is favoured even by impressions (saṃskāra-viśeṣa) accumulated in other births. Moreover, vidyā, being of seen purpose (dṛṣṭa-arthā), qualifies the seeker for śravaṇa and the rest by the mere absence of prohibition. Therefore, the eligibility of widowers and the like is not contradicted. (38)
BS_C03_S04_V39: But the other [— viz. abiding in an āśrama —] is superior to that [— viz. the in-between state —], on account of the indicatory mark [in Śruti and Smṛti]. (39)
BS_C03_S04_V39::block-0: ‘But than that’ — i.e. than the in-between state (antarāla-vartitva) — ‘the other’, namely abiding within an āśrama (āśrama-vartitva), is the superior means of vidyā, since it is well-attested by both Śruti and Smṛti. From the Śruti-liṅga: ‘By that the knower of Brahman, the doer of meritorious deeds, and the radiant (taijasa) one go forth’ (Br.U. 4.4.9). And from the Smṛti-liṅga: ‘A twice-born should not remain even for a single day outside an āśrama (anāśramī); having stayed without an āśrama for a year, he should perform one kṛcchra’ (Dakṣa-smṛ. 1.10). (39)
BS_C03_S04_V40: But of one who has become that [— ūrdhva-retas —], there is no becoming-otherwise; thus Jaimini also [holds]; on account of injunction, the absence of that-form, and the [absence of any down-going usages]. (40)
BS_C03_S04_V40::block-0: [Pūrvapakṣa:] It has been established that there exist āśramas of those who hold up the seed (ūrdhva-retas). But, having attained those, is there or is there not the possibility of one’s falling back from them somehow? It is doubtful. One who has fallen back, whether out of a desire to perform actions of the prior [āśramas] or under the sway of attachment and the rest, may [still] be permissible — for there is no special bar. — Such being the prima facie view, [the Sūtrakāra] declares: [Siddhānta:] But of one who has become that — that is, of one who has attained the state of being ūrdhva-retas — there is in no way at all (na kathañcid api) any becoming-otherwise (atad-bhāva): there can be no falling back from that. Why? — Because of injunction, the absence of any such [reverse] form, and the [absence of corresponding usages of the wise]. Thus: ‘Settling the self utterly in the household of the teacher’ (Ch.U. 2.23.1); ‘That he should go to the forest is the [ultimate] step (padam); thence he should not return — that is the upaniṣad’; ‘Permitted by the teacher, of the four [āśramas] he should follow one according to rule, until the release of the body’ (Mbh. 12.234.4) — such injunctions of this kind show the absence of falling back. And just as one finds passages of an ascending form (āroha-rūpa) such as ‘Having completed brahmacarya, let him become a householder’ (Jābāla-U. 4); ‘From brahmacarya itself let him go forth [as a wandering ascetic]’ (Jābāla-U. 4) and the like, one does not find passages of a descending form (pratyavaroha-rūpa). Nor are observances of that kind known among the cultured (śiṣṭas). As to the suggestion that there might be a descent owing to the wish to perform the duties of the prior [stages] — that is wrong; for it is remembered: ‘Better is one’s own dharma, [though] devoid of merit, than another’s dharma well-performed’ (Bh.G. 3.35); and reasoning [confirms it] — for that which is enjoined upon someone is dharma for him, not [merely] that which one is able to perform; for dharma is characterized by injunction (codanā-lakṣaṇatva). Nor [can there be] falling back through the sway of attachment and the rest, since the rule-scripture (niyama-śāstra) is more authoritative. ‘Of Jaimini also’ — by the word ‘also’ [the Sūtra] declares the agreement (sampratipatti) of Jaimini and Bādarāyaṇa here, for the firmness of the conclusion. (40)
BS_C03_S04_V41: And there is no [prāyaścitta] of the kind [prescribed] for the [office-holding upakurvāṇa-brahmacārī], on account of the inference of [his] fall, and the unfitness [of any expiation] for that. (41)
BS_C03_S04_V41::block-0: [Pūrvapakṣa:] If a naiṣṭhika brahmacārin should, through inadvertence, become avakīrṇin (one who has spilt his seed), is the prāyaścitta — ‘the brahmacārin who has fallen should offer a donkey to Nairṛti’ — applicable to him or not? [Siddhānta:] It is not, we reply. Even that prāyaścitta which has been settled in the section on adhikāra: ‘And the avakīrṇi-paśu likewise, since the time for ādhāna has not yet arrived’ (Jai.S. 6.8.22) — that too cannot be applicable to the naiṣṭhika. Why? Because there is the Smṛti recording an irremediable fall: ‘Of one who, having ascended (āruḍha) the dharma of a naiṣṭhika, again falls — I see no expiation by which the slayer of the self might be purified’ (Agni-P. 165.23, 24). [The case is] like the impossibility of remedy for one whose head has been severed. But of the upakurvāṇa, [the eligible candidate], since there is no record of such a fall [as irremediable], that prāyaścitta does become applicable. (41)
BS_C03_S04_V42: But some [hold] that [the fall of a naiṣṭhika] is also a minor sin (upapātaka); [hence they hold] the existence [of a prāyaścitta], like in the case of [eating prohibited] food; that has [already] been stated. (42)
BS_C03_S04_V42::block-0: But certain teachers (eke ācāryāḥ) hold that this is a minor sin only (upapātaka). What — namely, that the brahmacarya of a naiṣṭhika should be broken with one other than the teacher’s wife and the like — that does not become a great sin (mahāpātaka), since it is not enumerated among the great sins such as defiling the teacher’s bed (guru-talpa) and the rest. Therefore, just as in the case of the upakurvāṇa, they wish for the existence of a prāyaścitta in the case of the naiṣṭhika as well — since the brahmacāri-state is alike, and the avakīrṇi-state is alike. ‘Like in the case of food (aśanavat)’: just as for a brahmacārin there is, on the eating of honey or meat, breaking of the vow and re-initiation (punaḥ-saṃskāra), so here. For those who hold the non-existence of any prāyaścitta there is no scriptural foundation found. But for those who hold its existence, the foundation is the undifferentiated mention ‘the brahmacārin who is avakīrṇin’. Therefore the [view holding] existence is the more reasonable. This has been declared in the Pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa: ‘There would be equal divergence’ (Jai.S. 1.3.8); ‘Or rather [the rule] is in the scripture, since it depends on that’ (Jai.S. 1.3.9). The Smṛti recording the absence of prāyaścitta is, in such a case, to be explained as intended for the production of greater effort (yatna-gaurava). Likewise also for the bhikṣu and the vaikhānasa: ‘The vānaprastha, in the case of breach of his consecration (dīkṣā-bheda), having performed the kṛcchra of twelve nights, should let his hair grow long’; ‘the bhikṣu, like the vānaprastha, but excluding [the use of] the soma-creeper, [is to undergo] re-initiation according to his own scripture’ (Vasiṣṭha-dh. 21.35, 36) — and other Smṛtis recording prāyaścitta of this kind are to be followed. (42)
BS_C03_S04_V43: But [such fallen ones] are [to be regarded] as outside [society], in either case, on account of Smṛti and on account of [śiṣṭa-]usage. (43)
BS_C03_S04_V43::block-0: Whether the falling away of the ūrdhva-retas from their respective āśramas is a great sin (mahā-pātaka) or a minor sin (upapātaka), in either case (ubhayathāpi) such persons are to be cast out (bahiṣ-kartavya) by the cultured. [So] from such Smṛtis of supreme censure as: ‘Of one who, having ascended the dharma of a naiṣṭhika, again falls away — I see no expiation by which the slayer of the self could be purified’ (Agni-P. 165.23, 24); and ‘Having touched a Brāhmaṇa who has been a fallen one from the heights, who has gone forth from the maṇḍala, who has hanged himself, or who has been worm-eaten, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa’ — and the like. And from the conduct of the cultured (śiṣṭa-ācāra) — for the cultured do not associate with such persons in sacrifice, study, marriage, and so on. (43)
BS_C03_S04_V44: [The agency in upāsanas pertains] to the master [of the sacrifice], on account of the declaration of the fruit [as accruing to him]; thus [holds] Ātreya. (44)
BS_C03_S04_V44::block-0: [Pūrvapakṣa:] Concerning the upāsanas which are subsidiary to limbs [of sacrifice] (aṅgeṣu upāsaneṣu), there is doubt: are they actions of the yajamāna (sacrificer) or actions of the ṛtvik (priest)? What, then, is the prima facie position? — That they are actions of the yajamāna. Why? — On account of the declaration of the fruit (phala-śruti). For the fruit is heard of: ‘It rains for him, he causes it to rain — he who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman in the rain’ (Ch.U. 2.3.2) and so forth. And it stands to reason that [the fruit] should accrue to the master, since he is the one qualified for the [sacrifice] together with its limbs (sāṅge prayoge), and since one who is qualified for [a thing] is qualified for [its kind] — viz. for what is of this sort. And the fruit is heard as accruing to the doer of upāsanas: ‘He upon whom it rains who meditates’ and the like. ‘But surely, of the ṛtvik also a fruit is seen — “Whatever desire he desires either for himself or for the yajamāna, that he sings forth” (Br.U. 1.3.28)’ — No, for that is by special textual statement (vācanika). Therefore, in upāsanas accompanied by fruit, agency belongs to the master alone — thus the ācārya Ātreya holds. (44)
BS_C03_S04_V45: ‘It is the office of the ṛtvik’ — so holds Auḍulomi; for it is to that end that he (the ṛtvik) is engaged. ‖ 45 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V45::block-0: (Siddhānta resumed against the previous view): This is not so — namely, that the upāsanās (such as that of the udgītha) are kāryāṇi (acts) of the master, the yajamāna. Rather, these are the duties of the ṛtviks — so the teacher Auḍulomi opines. What is the reason? ‘For to that end’ — i.e. for the sake of the sacrifice taken together with all its limbs (sāṅgāya karmaṇe) — ‘the ṛtvik is engaged’ (parikrīyate) by the yajamāna. And the upāsanās of the udgītha and the rest, falling within the performance of that very (sacrifice), belong to him (the ṛtvik) by virtue of his being the qualified agent in respect of those (acts to which they are accessory). Therefore, just like the rule about the godohana vessel and the like (which is enjoined for the priest to use), they ought to be carried out by the ṛtviks (themselves). And accordingly the śruti shows that the agency of this (upāsana-) cognition belongs to the udgātṛ: ‘Baka Dālbhya knew this; and he became the udgātṛ of the Naimiṣīyas’ (Chā. U. 1.2.13). As for the objection raised, that the fruit is heard of as resorting to the agent — that is no flaw; for since the ṛtvik functions for another’s sake, in the absence of a separate scriptural injunction the connection of the fruit (with himself) is unwarranted. ‖ 45 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V46: And from the śruti (also it is established). ‖ 46 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V46::block-0: ‘“Whatever blessing the ṛtviks invoke at the sacrifice, they invoke it for the yajamāna” — thus indeed he said,’ and ‘therefore one who knows thus, being the udgātṛ, should say: “For what (boon) shall I sing forth?”’ (Chā. U. 1.7.8) and ‘“…that thou mayest sing the desire (of the yajamāna)”’ (Chā. U. 1.7.9) — by these (passages) the śruti shows that the fruit of the cognition of which the ṛtvik is the agent goes to the yajamāna. Therefore, the establishment of the upāsanās (which are) limbs (of sacrifice) as belonging to the kārya of the ṛtvik (is settled). ‖ 46 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V47: (In the passage about bālya etc.) there is the injunction of an additional accessory (mauna) — optionally, as the third (item, this being enjoined) for one who possesses that (vidyā) — like the (ordinary) injunction (of accessories) and so forth. ‖ 47 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V47::block-0: (Pūrvapakṣa): ‘Therefore, having well-known scholarship (pāṇḍitya), let the brāhmaṇa wish to abide in childlike-state (bālya); and having well-known childlike-state and scholarship, then (let him become) a muni; and having well-known non-silence and silence (amauna and mauna), then (he is) a brāhmaṇa’ (Bṛ. U. 3.5.1) — so it is heard in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka. Here arises a doubt — is mauna being enjoined, or not? It first appears that it is not enjoined, because the injunction has already exhausted itself in ‘let him wish to abide by bālya’; for in ‘atha muniḥ’ no vidhi-marking inflection is found. Therefore this (statement about muni) is fitly an anuvāda (a re-statement of what is already established). ‘How is it (mauna) then already obtained?’ — (we answer:) since the words muni and paṇḍita signify (the same thing, namely) jñāna, mauna is already obtained by the very phrase ‘pāṇḍityaṃ nirvidya.’ Moreover, in ‘having well-known non-silence and silence, then a brāhmaṇa’ — there brāhmaṇatva is not being enjoined (for that is already established prior); hence ‘atha brāhmaṇaḥ’ is a praśaṃsāvāda (declaration of praise). In the same way ‘atha muniḥ’ may also be such, by parity of mention (samāna-nirdeśatvāt). To this prima-facie position we reply —
BS_C03_S04_V47::block-1: (Siddhānta): ‘sahakāry-antara-vidhi’ — i.e. the injunction of an additional accessory. The injunction of mauna, as a co-operative accessory of vidyā, on a par with bālya and pāṇḍitya, must be accepted, because it is something not previously known (apūrvatvāt). ‘But it has been said that mauna is already obtained by the very word pāṇḍitya?’ — That is no flaw, because the word muni signifies a special excellence of jñāna, since the nirvacana ‘mananān muniḥ’ (a muni is so called from manana) is possible, and since usage shows it: ‘Among munis I am Vyāsa’ (Bh. Gītā 10.37). ‘But the word muni is also heard as denoting the highest āśrama, in “gārhasthyam, ācāryakulam, maunaṃ vānaprastham”?’ — No, since deviation is seen in such (uses) as ‘Vālmīki, the foremost of munis,’ etc. There, by reason of the proximity of the other āśramas, by elimination (pāriśeṣya) muni is taken for the highest āśrama, since the highest āśrama is jñāna-pradhāna. Therefore, in relation to bālya and pāṇḍitya, this third item — mauna in the form of an excellence of jñāna — is being enjoined. As for (the objection) that the injunction terminates in bālya alone — even so, on account of muni-tva being apūrva, its enjoinedness is to be accepted: ‘let him be a muni.’ Also, from the very fact that mauna is mentioned as something to be ‘well-known’ (nirvedanīya), it is to be accepted as enjoined like bālya and pāṇḍitya. ‘Tadvataḥ’ — of one possessing that, i.e. of the saṃnyāsin who possesses vidyā. ‘How is the saṃnyāsin who possesses vidyā ascertained (here)?’ — From the context (tadadhikārāt): ‘having known the Self, having risen from the desire for sons and the rest, then they go forth as mendicants.’ ‘But when there already exists possession of vidyā, that very excellence is obtained — what need of an injunction of mauna?’ — To this he says: ‘pakṣeṇa.’ The meaning is — in that pakṣa wherein, owing to the strength of dualistic perception (bheda-darśana), it is not (spontaneously) obtained, this injunction (applies). ‘Vidhy-ādivat’ — just as in injunctions like ‘by the darśa-pūrṇamāsa let one desirous of heaven sacrifice,’ accessories such as agny-anvādhāna are enjoined as cooperative; in the same way, even in this vidyā-statement which is not primarily a vidhi, the injunction of mauna (is to be accepted). ‖ 47 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V48: But because of (his) entirety (of duties), the (final) summation is by way of the householder. ‖ 48 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V48::block-0: (Leading): When thus the kaivalya-āśrama (of the renunciate), distinguished by bālya and the rest, exists with śruti-support, why in the Chāndogya is the summation made through the householder, in ‘abhisamāvṛtya kuṭumbe’ (Chā. U. 8.15.1)? For by summing up therewith, (the śruti) shows respect (ādara) for that (gārhasthya). To this is given the answer:
BS_C03_S04_V48::block-1: The word ‘tu’ (‘but’) serves to mark off the special point. The kṛtsna-bhāva (entirety) here pertains to him (the gṛhastha) — that is what is being distinguished. For laborious are the many āśrama-duties of yajña etc. enjoined upon him as obligatory; and the duties of the other āśramas — non-injury, sense-restraint and so on — also exist for him to the extent feasible. Therefore the summation by way of the householder is not in conflict (with the doctrine that saṃnyāsa is the prescribed āśrama for the vidvān). ‖ 48 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V49: Like mauna, so also of the others (āśramas) — because of (their) being (alike) upadiṣṭa (taught). ‖ 49 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V49::block-0: Just as mauna (saṃnyāsa) and gārhasthya are two āśramas śruti-supported, so too are the other two — vānaprastha and gurukulavāsa (brahmacarya). For the śruti has been shown earlier — ‘tapas (austerity) indeed is the second; the brahmacārin dwelling in the ācārya’s house is the third’ (Chā. U. 2.23.1) and the like. Therefore, of all four āśramas, since the upadeśa is undifferentiated, the recourse (to them) is to be alike, by way of vikalpa (option) and samuccaya (combination, as appropriate). The plural ‘itareṣām’ (of the others) — for the two āśramas — should be understood either with reference to the difference of mode of life (vṛtti-bheda) or to the difference of practitioners (anuṣṭhātṛ-bheda). ‖ 49 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V50: Without manifesting (himself) — by reason of consistency (with the principal sense). ‖ 50 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V50::block-0: (Pūrvapakṣa): ‘Therefore, having well-known scholarship, let the brāhmaṇa wish to abide in bālya’ (Bṛ. U. 3.5.1) — thus bālya is heard of as something to be practised. Now, taking ‘bālya’ as ‘the state of a child’ or ‘the conduct of a child’ by the taddhita (suffix) — since the state of a child, being a particular age, cannot be brought about at will — a doubt arises: should bālya be the conduct of a child such as urinating and defecating just as it happens (yathopapāda), or should it be an inner purity of disposition, such as the non-prominence of the senses, or freedom from hypocrisy and arrogance? What appears first? — Acting at will, eating anything, urinating-defecating yathopapāda — these are more widely known in the world as bālya; hence to take it as such is fitting. ‘But on account of incurring the faults of patita-hood (degradation), it is not fitting to resort to wantonness etc.?’ — Not so; for the vidvān saṃnyāsin, by the force of the (śruti-)injunction, those faults stand removed, just as in the killing of animals (in sacrifice) etc. Thus on the prima facie view, we reply —
BS_C03_S04_V50::block-1: (Siddhānta): No (this view is not right), because there is the possibility of an alternative interpretation of the injunction. For when something not in conflict (with the principal aim), denoted by the word ‘bālya,’ is (already) available, it is not fitting to imagine the violation of (other) injunctions. An accessory is enjoined for the support of the primary thing. And here for the yatis, the primary thing to be practised is jñāna-abhyāsa. The practice of knowledge is not possible if the entire conduct of a child is admitted. Therefore, the inner state proper to a child — the non-prominence of the senses etc. — is here taken as bālya. That is what (the sūtra) says — ‘anāviṣkurvan’ — not making oneself known by displaying jñāna, learning, righteousness etc., but being free from hypocrisy, arrogance and the like. Just as a child, by reason of the non-prominence of the senses, does not strive to manifest himself to others, so too (let the vidvān be). For thus the conformity with the meaning of the support to the primary purpose of this passage is intelligible. So too the smṛti-authors have said: ‘Whom no one knows, neither as existing nor as non-existing, neither as unlearned nor as much-learned, neither as well-conducted nor as ill-conducted — he is a brāhmaṇa. The wise one, abiding in concealed dharma, should walk a path that none knows; like a blind man, like a dull man, like a mute, let him roam the earth’ (Vasiṣṭha-smṛti 6.40-41), and ‘with insignia unmanifest, with conduct unmanifest’ (Vas. Sm. 10.12) and so on. ‖ 50 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V51: (The arising of vidyā may be) even in this very life — when there is no obstructing (karma) lying in wait; for that is seen. ‖ 51 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V51::block-0: (Pūrvapakṣa): Beginning from ‘And the dependence on all (the means) is on account of the śruti about yajña etc., as in the case of the horse’ (Bra. Sū. 3.4.26), various (means) — high and low — have been determined as means to vidyā. (Now,) does its fruit, the vidyā as it arises, arise in this very birth, or sometimes also in another (birth)? It is here being considered. What appears first? In this very (birth). What is the reason? Vidyā is preceded by śravaṇa etc. And no one engages in śravaṇa etc. with the resolve, ‘Let vidyā arise for me in another (life)’; rather, one is seen engaging therein with the resolve that the arising of vidyā occur in the same birth. Yajñas etc. also generate vidyā only through the door of śravaṇa etc., since vidyā is born of pramāṇa. Therefore the arising of vidyā is right in this life — thus prima facie. We reply —
BS_C03_S04_V51::block-1: (Siddhānta): The arising of vidyā is in this very life when there is no obstruction lying in wait. The meaning is — when there is no obstruction created against the means of vidyā in operation by some other karma whose fruition is at hand, then in this very (birth) vidyā arises. But when there is such obstruction, then in another (birth). The being-on-the-verge-of-fruition of a karma comes about by the conjunction of the appropriate place, time and instrumental conditions. The very places-times-conditions which ripen one karma cannot be regulated to ripen another also; for there are karmas with mutually contrary fruits. Even śāstra terminates only at saying, ‘Of this karma the fruit is this’ — it does not also enumerate the particular places, times and conditions. Owing to the special potency of the means, in some person an extraordinary śakti (capacity) becomes manifest, while in another it is held in check by the obstruction (of contrary karma). Nor is it the case that without distinction (in a generic way) there can be no resolve regarding vidyā, ‘Let vidyā arise for me here or hereafter’ — for resolve is unrestricted (nirańkuśa). Even when it arises through śravaṇa etc., vidyā arises only with reference to the destruction of the obstacle. Thus the śruti shows the difficulty of cognising the Self: ‘He whom many do not even obtain to hear of, and whom many, even hearing of, do not know — wonderful is the speaker (of him), skilled is the obtainer (of him); wonderful is the knower of him, instructed by a skilled (teacher)’ (Kaṭha U. 1.2.7). And the (śruti) saying that Vāmadeva even while in the womb attained brahma-bhāva, shows the arising of vidyā in another birth from means accumulated in another birth; for of one (still) in the womb no this-life means can be conceived. In smṛti also, when Arjuna asked, ‘Without attaining yoga-perfection, what state, O Kṛṣṇa, does (such a one) reach?’ (Bh. Gītā 6.37), the Lord Vāsudeva replied, ‘For no doer of good, dear one, comes to a bad state’ (Bh. Gītā 6.40), and after declaring his attainment of holy worlds and his birth in a virtuous family, he then says, ‘There he obtains the union with the (yogic) intellect of his former body’ (Bh. Gītā 6.43) and so on, up to ‘perfected through many births, then he reaches the supreme goal’ (Bh. Gītā 6.45) — by this very (sequence) showing the same. Therefore it stands established that the arising of vidyā, whether in this life or hereafter, depends on the destruction of the obstacle. ‖ 51 ‖
BS_C03_S04_V52: Likewise, with regard to the fruit (which is) liberation, there is no such regulation (of differential variation), since that state (mukti-state) is determinately ascertained (as one) — since that state is so determinately ascertained. ‖ 52 ‖
