BS_C03_S04_V52::block-0: Just as in the case of one desirous of liberation, holding fast to the means of vidyā, owing to the special potency of the means, a regulated distinction was seen in the fruit characterised as vidyā — the distinction made by being a fruit of this life or of the next — even so, in the fruit characterised as mukti, there might be some regulated distinction made by superiority and inferiority. Anticipating this objection, he says: ‘evaṃ muktiphala-aniyamaḥ’ (thus there is no regulation of the fruit which is liberation). Indeed in the case of the fruit mukti, no such regulated distinction need be entertained. Why? ‘Tad-avasthā-avadhṛteḥ’ — for the mukti-state is determined as of one form alone in all the Vedāntas. The mukti-state is verily Brahman itself. And Brahman cannot be associated with multiple forms, since it is determined as having a single mark (eka-liṅgatva-avadhāraṇāt) — from such śrutis as: ‘not gross, not subtle’ (Bṛ. U. 3.8.8); ‘that Self (is described) as “not this, not this”’ (Bṛ. U. 3.9.26 / 4.2.4 / 4.4.22); ‘where one sees nothing else’ (Chā. U. 7.24.1); ‘this immortal Brahman is in front’ (Muṇḍ. U. 2.2.12); ‘this all is what this Self (is)’ (Bṛ. U. 2.4.6); ‘that great unborn Self, ageless, undying, immortal, fearless, is Brahman’ (Bṛ. U. 4.4.25); ‘where for him all has become the very Self, by what should one see what?’ (Bṛ. U. 4.5.15) and so on. Moreover, the means of vidyā, by special potency, may attach some excellence to its own fruit — namely, vidyā — but not to the fruit of vidyā, namely mukti. For that (mukti), being unaccomplishable (asādhya), is by its very nature ever-accomplished (nitya-siddha-svabhāva), and is only known by means of vidyā — as we have said again and again. Nor does any excellence of the form of superiority or inferiority pertain to vidyā either, because what is inferior could not be vidyā at all — vidyā is verily superior (alone). Therefore, in vidyā an excellence in the form of swift or delayed arising might exist; but in mukti no excellence at all can be admitted. Even from the absence of distinction in vidyā, there is absence of regulation in distinction of its fruit — unlike the fruits of karma. For unlike karmas, vidyā which is the means of mukti has no internal distinction. But in saguṇa-vidyās such as ‘consisting of mind, with prāṇa for body’ (Chā. U. 3.14.2) etc., there is distinction by way of insertion or omission of attributes, and accordingly there can be regulation of the fruit each according to its own — like fruit of karma. Indicatory evidence (liṅga-darśana) for that: ‘As they meditate on him, that very he becomes.’ Not so in nirguṇa-vidyā, since there are no attributes (gunas). Likewise the smṛti: ‘There is indeed no higher gati for any one; only when there is a guṇa do they speak of inequality’ (Mahābhārata 12.194.60). The repetition ‘tad-avasthā-avadhṛteḥ tad-avasthā-avadhṛteḥ’ marks the conclusion of the adhyāya. ‖ 52 ‖
BS_C04_S01_INTRO1::block-0: In the third chapter, the inquiry concerning the means (sādhana-āśraya-vicāra) in respect of both the higher and lower vidyās has been, for the most part, completed. Now, in this fourth chapter, what concerns the fruit (phala-āśraya) will follow. Other matters too, as they arise incidentally (prasaṅga-āgata), will be considered. First, then, in a few adhikaraṇas, we will follow up the residue of the inquiry concerning the means itself —
BS_C04_S01_V01: Repetition (āvṛtti) is to be performed, because the instruction is more than once (asakṛd-upadeśāt). ‖ 1 ‖
BS_C04_S01_V01::block-0: In such passages of śruti as ‘The Self, verily, O Maitreyī, is to be seen, to be heard of, to be reflected on, to be meditated on’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.5.6), ‘Knowing Him alone, the wise one should attain insight (prajñā)’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.21), and ‘He is to be sought after, He is to be desired to be known’ (Chā. Up. 8.7.1) — there arises a doubt: should the cognition (pratyaya) be made once only, or by way of repetition (āvṛtti)? What position prevails first (pūrvapakṣa)? — That the cognition should be performed once only, just as in the case of the prayājas and the like, since the śāstra's purpose is fulfilled thereby. For if a repetition not enjoined by the śruti were to be performed, that would be doing what is not enjoined by the śāstra. — But have not instructions repeated more than once been cited — ‘to be heard of, to be reflected on, to be meditated on’ and so forth? — Even so, one should repeat (only) as far as the verbal indication extends — once hearing, once reflecting, once meditating — and not beyond. But where the instruction occurs only once — as in ‘he knows’ (veda), ‘he should meditate upon’ (upāsīta) and the like — there is no repetition. When this view (pūrvapakṣa) has been thus reached, we say (siddhānta): repetition of the cognition is to be performed. Why? Because of the instruction being more than once. For an instruction occurring more than once, of the type ‘to be heard of, to be reflected on, to be meditated on’, indicates the repetition of the cognition. — But it has been said: one should repeat only as much as the verbal indication, not more. — No, because these (śravaṇa etc.) culminate in (direct) seeing (darśana-paryavasānatva). For śravaṇa and the rest, since they culminate in seeing, when repeatedly performed have a perceptible (dṛṣṭa) result, just as pounding and the like culminate in producing rice and so on. Moreover, ‘upāsana’ (worship) and ‘nididhyāsana’ (meditation) are themselves activities that have repetition built into them as their inherent quality. Thus, in the world, when one says ‘he serves (upāste) the teacher’, ‘he serves the king’ — it is one who attends upon the teacher etc. with sustained intentness who is so spoken of. Similarly, in ‘the wife, whose lord is gone abroad, meditates upon (dhyāyati) her husband’ — that uninterrupted longing remembrance of the husband is what is so denoted. And in the Upaniṣads, ‘knowing’ (vid) and ‘worshipping’ (upās) are seen used without distinction; in some places one begins with vid and concludes with upās, as in ‘Whoever knows that, what he knows is told by me’ (Chā. Up. 4.1.4), where (later it is said) ‘teach me, sir, that deity which you worship (upāsse)’ (Chā. Up. 4.2.2). And in some places one begins with upās and concludes with vid, as in ‘Let one worship the mind as Brahman’ (Chā. Up. 3.18.1), where (later it is said) ‘He who knows thus shines and burns with fame, glory and the splendour of Brahman’ (Chā. Up. 3.18.3). Therefore, even where the instruction is only once given, the establishment of repetition holds. Where it is given more than once, that is itself an indicator (sūcaka) of repetition. ‖ 1 ‖
BS_C04_S01_V02::block-0: An indicatory mark (liṅga) too proves the repetition of the cognition. Thus, having introduced the meditation on the udgītha — ‘the sun is the udgītha’ (Chā. Up. 1.5.1) — and having set that aside on the ground of the defect of (granting) only one son, the śruti enjoins, in ‘Convert the rays’ (Chā. Up. 1.5.2), the meditation on the multiplicity of rays for the sake of (obtaining) many sons, and thereby shows the repetition of the cognition as a settled matter (siddhavat). By parity of reasoning, repetition is established in all cognitions. ‖
BS_C04_S01_V02::block-1: Here someone (a pūrvapakṣin) says: Let there be repetition in those cognitions whose fruit is to be accomplished (sādhya-phala), since in them an excellence (atiśaya) attainable through repetition is possible. But that cognition which has the supreme Brahman for its object — Brahman which presents itself as the very Self, eternally pure, awakened and free by nature — what purpose can repetition serve there? — If it be said that repetition is admitted because at a single hearing the cognition of one's identity with Brahman does not arise, then no — for even on repetition that does not arise. For if a sentence such as ‘That thou art’ (Tat tvam asi), heard once, does not produce the cognition of one's identity with Brahman, what hope is there that the same, when repeated, will produce it? — If it be said: a sentence by itself cannot make any object directly known (sākṣātkartum); therefore the sentence, depending on (auxiliary) reasoning (yukti), will cause one to experience identity with Brahman — even so, repetition is purposeless. For that reasoning too, when applied once, will cause one to experience its object. — If, again, it be said: by reasoning and the sentence only a generic (sāmānya-viṣaya) cognition is produced, not a specific (viśeṣa-viṣaya) one — just as from the statement ‘there is a pain in my heart’ and the indicatory mark of trembling of limbs etc., another person comes only to a generic apprehension of the existence of pain, but does not experience the particular as the very sufferer does. The experience of the particular is what removes ignorance; for that purpose repetition is needed — no. For even if performed many times, in respect of just that much (the same generic content), the arising of a specific cognition is impossible. For a specific feature not grasped through the śāstra and reasoning when applied once cannot be grasped even by their being applied a hundred times. Therefore, whether the śāstra and reasoning convey a specific feature or only a generic one, in either case they accomplish their function on a single application — hence the uselessness of repetition. Nor can it be laid down as a rule that the śāstra and reasoning, when applied once, do not produce experience in anyone, since the cognising agents have manifold capacities. Moreover, with respect to a worldly object that has many parts and is endowed with the generic and the specific, one can grasp one part by one act of attention and another by another — so there is some use for repetition (abhyāsa), as in apprehending a long passage and the like. But in respect of Brahman, which is partless, devoid of generic and specific (features), and is the very nature of pure consciousness, the supposition that the arising of valid cognition (pramā) requires repetition is not tenable. ‖
BS_C04_S01_V02::block-2: To this we (the siddhāntin) reply: Yes, repetition would be useless for him who is able, on hearing once ‘That thou art’ (Chā. Up. 6.8.7), to experience identity with Brahman. But for him who is not able, repetition is indeed useful. Thus in the Chāndogya, after instructing ‘That thou art, O Śvetaketu’ (Chā. Up. 6.8.7), in response to the repeated solicitation ‘May the venerable one instruct me again’ (Chā. Up. 6.8.7), removing one by one the causes of doubt, the teacher repeats again and again ‘That thou art’; and similarly, ‘to be heard of, to be reflected on, to be meditated on’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.5.6) and the like has been pointed out. — But it has been said: if the sentence ‘Tat tvam asi’ heard once does not enable one to experience its meaning, then even when repeated it will not. — That is no fault. For there is nothing impossible in what is observed. We do see people who, on hearing a sentence once, have only a faint apprehension of its meaning, then by repeated reflection on it, dispelling the various semblances (ābhāsas) of meaning, come to apprehend it correctly. Moreover, the sentence ‘That thou art’ declares that the referent of the word ‘thou’ is the same as the referent of the word ‘that’. By the word ‘that’ (tat) is denoted Brahman, the contextually established Being, the seer (īkṣitṛ), the cause of the origin etc. of the world — well-known from the śāstra by ‘Brahman is truth, knowledge, infinite’ (Tai. Up. 2.1.1), ‘Brahman is consciousness, bliss’ (Bṛ. Up. 3.9.28), ‘unseen but seer’ (Bṛ. Up. 3.8.11), ‘unknown but knower’ (Bṛ. Up. 3.8.11), ‘unborn, unageing, deathless’, ‘not gross, not subtle, not short, not long’, and so forth. There, by ‘unborn’ etc. the modifications of being — birth and the rest — are negated; by ‘not gross’ etc. the qualities of substances — grossness etc. — are negated; by ‘knowledge’ etc. its nature as the very light of consciousness is stated. This referent of ‘that’, of the nature of pure experience, designated ‘Brahman’, with all attributes of saṃsāra excluded, is well known to those versed in Vedānta. So too the referent of ‘thou’, the inner Self, the hearer, beginning with the body and provisionally taken as the inner Self — is determined to be (in its true nature) consciousness itself. There, those for whom these two referents are obstructed by ignorance (ajñāna), doubt (saṃśaya), and contrary apprehension (viparyaya) — for them the sentence ‘That thou art’ cannot produce valid cognition of its own purport, since cognition of a sentence's purport presupposes cognition of the referents of its words; therefore, for such persons, repeated practice of the śāstra and reasoning, having for its purpose the discrimination of the referents of the words, is desirable. And though the Self to be known is partless, yet there is superimposed on it many parts characterised by body, sense-organs, mind, intellect, objects, sensations and so forth. There, one removes one part by one act of attention, another by another — so a graded (kramavatī) cognition is appropriate there. That, however, is only the preliminary stage of the apprehension of the Self. But for those of subtle intellect who do not have any obstruction in the form of ignorance, doubt or contrary apprehension regarding the referents of the words, they are able to experience the meaning of ‘That thou art’ as soon as it is uttered once; for them the uselessness of repetition is indeed admitted. For the Self-realisation that arises once removes ignorance — no graded process is admitted here at all. — That would be true if anyone actually had such an apprehension. Strong is the apprehension that the Self is the sufferer etc.; therefore no one apprehends the absence of suffering and so forth — if it be so objected, no — because, just like the misidentification with the body and the like, the misidentification of the Self as the sufferer is itself fit to be a false (mithyā) identification. (Direct…)
BS_C04_S01_V03: But (the śrutis) approach (Brahman) as ‘the Self’ and (so) cause (others) to apprehend (It). ‖ 3 ‖
BS_C04_S01_V03::block-0: Should the supreme Self, possessed of the qualifications stated in the śāstra, be apprehended as ‘I’ (aham), or as ‘other than me’? — this is what is being inquired into. — But how can there be a doubt when the word ‘ātman’, which has its primary reference to the inner Self, is heard? — It is replied: this word ‘ātman’ can be admitted in its primary sense (mukhya) only if there is the possibility of non-difference between the jīva and the Īśvara; otherwise it must be admitted only in a secondary sense (gauṇa). What position prevails first (pūrvapakṣa)? — He should not be apprehended as ‘I’. For one possessed of qualities such as freedom from sin (apahata-pāpmatva) cannot be apprehended as one possessed of the contrary qualities, nor one of contrary qualities as possessed of freedom from sin etc. The supreme Lord has freedom from sin etc.; the embodied (śārīra) jīva has the contrary qualities. If the Īśvara were to be the very self of the saṃsārin, there would follow the absence of an Īśvara, and consequently the śāstra would become purposeless. If on the other hand the saṃsārin were to be of the nature of Īśvara, there would be an absence of any qualified person (adhikārin), and again the śāstra would become purposeless, and there would be conflict with perception and the rest. — If it be said: even though they are different, an identification (tādātmya) is to be performed in accordance with the śāstra, as in the case of the seeing of Viṣṇu and the like in images — let it be so. But it is not to be made out for us that the saṃsārin's primary Self is the Īśvara. ‖
BS_C04_S01_V03::block-1: When this view is reached (siddhāntin replies), we say: the supreme Lord is to be apprehended only as ‘the Self’ (ātman). For thus, in the procedure dealing with the supreme Lord, the Jābālas approach Him as the very Self — ‘Thou indeed am I, O divine deity, and I indeed am Thou, O divine deity’; similarly, others — ‘I am Brahman’ (Aham Brahmāsmi) and the like — should be regarded as approaches identifying Him with the Self. The Vedānta-sentences too cause the apprehension of Īśvara as the Self only — ‘He is your Self, the inner controller of all’ (Bṛ. Up. 3.4.1), ‘He is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal’ (Bṛ. Up. 3.7.3), ‘That is the truth, that is the Self, that thou art’ (Chā. Up. 6.8.7) and the like. As to what was said — that this is a (mere) symbol-meditation (pratīka-darśana) on the analogy of (worshipping) an image of Viṣṇu — that is improper. For (1) it would entail (only) a secondary (gauṇa) sense, and (2) there is dissimilarity in the form of the sentences. Where the apprehension of a symbol (pratīka) is intended, the statement is made only once, as in ‘the mind is Brahman’ (Chā. Up. 3.18.1), ‘the sun is Brahman’ (Chā. Up. 3.19.1) and so on. But here it is said both ‘thou art I’ and ‘I am thou’. Hence, from the dissimilarity from the pratīka-statements, the apprehension is of non-difference (abheda). And from the depreciation (apavāda) of the apprehension of difference also; thus, ‘Now, he who worships another deity (thinking) ‘He is one, I am another’, does not know’ (Bṛ. Up. 1.4.10), ‘He who sees (anything as) manifold here goes from death to death’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.19), ‘All forsakes him who sees all elsewhere than in the Self’ (Bṛ. Up. 2.4.6) — and many such śrutis depreciate the seeing of difference. As to what was said — that there can be no mutual identity of two whose qualities are contradictory — this is no fault, since the contradictoriness of qualities is itself fit to be (taken as) false (mithyā). And as to what was said — that there would follow the absence of an Īśvara — that is wrong, both on the authority of the śāstra and because no such thing is admitted. For we do not admit that the Īśvara becomes the very self of the saṃsārin. What then? — That what is intended to be conveyed is that the saṃsārin, by removal of his being a saṃsārin, has the Īśvara as his Self. So, in the (advaita) Īśvara, the qualities of freedom from sin etc. are settled (as real); the contrary qualities of the other are settled as false (mithyā). As to what was said — about absence of qualified persons and conflict with perception etc. — that too is wrong, because saṃsārin-hood is admitted prior to awakening (prāk-prabodhāt), and the empirical use (vyavahāra) of perception etc. has that as its province. For ‘But where to him all has become the very Self, then by what could he see what?’ (Bṛ. Up. 2.4.14) and the like indeed shows the absence of perception etc. on awakening. — If the absence of perception etc. is admitted, then the absence of the śruti too would follow — no, because that is itself acceptable. Beginning with ‘There the father is no father’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.22) and (continuing with) ‘the Vedas are non-Vedas’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.22), the absence of the śruti also on awakening is admitted by us. — Whose then is this non-awakening? — Whoever you are who asks, it is yours, we reply. — But the śruti has said, ‘I am Īśvara himself’! — If you are thus awakened, then there is no non-awakening of anyone. The fault that some object — that, since the Self has another (avidyā) along with it, non-duality is not established — that too is hereby answered. Therefore one should fix the mind on the Īśvara as ‘the Self’ alone. ‖ 3 ‖
BS_C04_S01_V04: Not in a symbol (pratīka), for he (the meditator) is not That. ‖ 4 ‖
BS_C04_S01_V04::block-0: In ‘Let one worship the mind as Brahman, that is in the individual (adhyātma); now in the cosmic (adhidaivata), let space be worshipped as Brahman’ (Chā. Up. 3.18.1), and likewise in ‘the sun is Brahman, this is the teaching’ (Chā. Up. 3.19.1), ‘he who worships ‘name’ as Brahman’ (Chā. Up. 7.1.5) and so forth — in such symbol-worships (pratīka-upāsana) the doubt arises: should the apprehension as Self (ātma-graha) be performed in those too, or not? What position prevails first (pūrvapakṣa)? — In those too the apprehension as Self alone is fit to be performed. Why? Because Brahman is well known in the śrutis as the Self; and since the symbols too, being modifications of Brahman, are themselves Brahman, the apprehension as Self is appropriate — when this view is reached, we say (siddhānta): one should not fasten the apprehension of Self upon the symbols. For that worshipper does not apprehend the symbols, severally, as the Self. As to (the argument) that the symbols, being modifications of Brahman, are Brahman, and hence Self — that is wrong, since this would entail the absence of the symbol. For (only) by abolishing the modification's own form would the names and the rest be reduced to Brahman. And on abolishing their own form, whence the symbol-hood of the names etc., or the apprehension as Self? Nor, simply because Brahman is the Self, can the seeing of Self be imagined in the instructions of seeing as Brahman, since agency etc. are not negated (in those instructions). For only by negating all the dharmas of saṃsāra such as agency etc. is Brahman taught as the Self. But here, without that negation, the worship is enjoined. Hence, since the worshipper is on a par with the symbols (in being qualified by saṃsāra-dharmas), the apprehension as Self does not fit. There is no mutual identity between the rucaka and the svastika (two ornaments of gold). Only as gold (suvarṇa-ātmana) would there be unity (in them); just so we have said that on identity through the form of Brahman, the absence of the symbol would follow. Hence the apprehension as Self is not made in symbols. ‖ 4 ‖
BS_C04_S01_V05: (Let there be) the apprehension as Brahman (in the symbols), because of the elevation. ‖ 5 ‖
BS_C04_S01_V05::block-0: In those very examples, another doubt arises: should the apprehensions as ‘the sun’ etc. be superimposed on Brahman, or should the apprehension as Brahman be superimposed on ‘the sun’ and the rest? Whence the doubt? — Because in the co-reference (sāmānādhikaraṇya) the cause is not determined. For here a co-reference between the word ‘brahman’ and the words ‘sun’ etc. is observed — ‘the sun is Brahman’, ‘prāṇa is Brahman’, ‘lightning is Brahman’ and the like — by the use of the same case-ending. But a straightforward (āñjasa) co-reference is not possible here, because the words ‘brahman’, ‘sun’ etc. denote different objects. There is no co-reference like ‘a cow is a horse’. — But might it not be a co-reference based on the relation of cause and effect (prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva), as in ‘potsherd is a clay-vessel (mṛc-charāva)’ — No; for thereby there would be a dissolving of the modification (vikāra) into the cause (prakṛti), and we have already said that this entails the absence of the symbol. Then this would (have to) be a sentence on the supreme Self, and that would set aside the eligibility for upāsana, and the inclusion of the limited (pariṇāma) modification (in the sentence) would be in vain. Therefore, as in ‘the brāhmaṇa is the Vaiśvānara fire’, since one (cognition) is superimposed on another, the doubt is: where is which apprehension to be superimposed? On this there is indeterminateness, since there is no determining śāstra — when this view is reached. Or rather, the apprehensions as ‘the sun’ etc. alone are to be performed in Brahman; for thus, by the apprehensions as ‘the sun’ etc., Brahman becomes worshipped (upāsita), and the worship of Brahman has fruit — such is the rule of the śāstra. Hence, no apprehension as Brahman is to be made in ‘the sun’ etc. — when this position is reached, we say (siddhānta):
BS_C04_S01_V05::block-1: Let the apprehension as Brahman alone be (superimposed) on ‘the sun’ etc. Why? Because of the elevation (utkarṣa). For thus, ‘the sun’ etc. become regarded with elevation, since the apprehension of the more elevated (utkṛṣṭa) is superimposed on them. So the worldly maxim is also followed. The worldly maxim is that the apprehension of the more elevated should be superimposed on the less elevated, as the apprehension of the king on the charioteer (kṣattṛ). And that should be followed; in the contrary case, there would be the contingency of harmful consequence (pratyavāya). For if the king were apprehended as a charioteer and were thereby brought down, that would not be for one's good. — But because of the authority of the śāstra, no contingency of harmful consequence need be feared here, and a śāstric apprehension cannot be regulated by a worldly maxim — to this we reply: That would be so if the meaning of the śāstra were already determined. But while it is doubtful, the worldly maxim, when applied to its determination, is not in conflict (with it). And by it, when the meaning of the śāstra — that the apprehension of the more elevated should be superimposed — is fixed, then if one were to superimpose the apprehension of the less elevated, harmful consequence would follow — that is consistent. Also, because of the priority (prāthamya) of the words ‘sun’ etc., they should be taken in their primary sense, since there is no contradiction. When the cognition is occupied by them in their own (primary) functions, since the word ‘brahman’, coming later, cannot have its primary function in co-reference, only the purpose of enjoining the apprehension as Brahman remains. Even from the fact that the word ‘brahman’ is followed by ‘iti’ (the quotative particle), this very meaning is the proper one. For — ‘brahmeti ādeśaḥ’, ‘brahmeti upāsīta’, ‘brahmeti upāste’ — everywhere the word ‘brahman’ is uttered followed by ‘iti’, while ‘sun’ etc. are uttered without it. Hence, just as in ‘one apprehends the mother-of-pearl as silver’, the word ‘mother-of-pearl’ denotes mother-of-pearl, while the word ‘silver’ refers (only) to the apprehension of silver — for one merely apprehends ‘silver’; there is no silver there — even so here it is understood that one apprehends ‘the sun’ etc. as Brahman. The remainder of the sentence too, by the use of the second case-ending, shows that ‘the sun’ etc. are pervaded by the act of worship — ‘He who, knowing thus, worships the sun as Brahman’ (Chā. Up. 3.19.4), ‘He who worships speech as Brahman’ (Chā. Up. 7.2.2), ‘He who worships saṅkalpa as Brahman’ (Chā. Up. 7.4.3) and the like. As to what was said — that here the worship of Brahman should be honoured for the sake of fruit — that is improper, since by the maxim already stated, only ‘the sun’ etc. are understood as objects of worship. The fruit, however, will be granted in the worship of ‘the sun’ etc. by Brahman alone, just as in the worship of a guest etc. (the fruit comes from Brahman), since He is the overseer of all. This has been described in ‘The fruit (comes) from Him, on the ground of fitness’ (Br. Sū. 3.2.38). Such, here, is the (mode of) worship of Brahman — namely, the superimposition of the apprehension of It on the symbols — like (the worship) of Viṣṇu and the rest in images. ‖ 5 ‖
BS_C04_S01_V06: And the apprehensions as ‘the sun’ etc. (are to be superimposed) on the (sacrificial) limb (aṅga), because of fitness. ‖ 6 ‖
BS_C04_S01_V06::block-0: In ‘He who burns yonder, that one let one worship as the udgītha’ (Chā. Up. 1.3.1), ‘Let one worship the fivefold sāman in the worlds’ (Chā. Up. 2.2.1), ‘Let one worship the sevenfold sāman in speech’ (Chā. Up. 2.8.1), ‘This indeed is the ṛc; fire is the sāman’ (Chā. Up. 1.6.1) and the like — in worships connected with sacrificial limbs (aṅga-avabaddha) — there is a doubt: are the apprehensions as ‘udgītha’ etc. enjoined upon ‘the sun’ etc., or are the apprehensions as ‘the sun’ etc. enjoined upon ‘the udgītha’ etc.? There is indeterminateness, since there is no determining cause — when this view is reached. For here, unlike in the case of Brahman, no special elevation can be ascertained for any one (of the two). Brahman, being the cause of the entire universe and possessed of qualities like freedom from sin etc., can be ascertained as superior to ‘the sun’ etc. But there is no cause to ascertain any special elevation in the case of ‘the sun’ and ‘the udgītha’ etc., since both are uniformly modifications. Or rather, by rule, the apprehensions as ‘udgītha’ etc. should be superimposed upon ‘the sun’ etc. Why? Because the udgītha etc. are of the nature of (Vedic) action (karma), and action is well known to bring fruit. ‘The sun’ etc., when worshipped with apprehensions as ‘udgītha’ etc., become of the nature of action and thus causes of fruit. Likewise in ‘this indeed is the ṛc, fire is the sāman’ (Chā. Up. 1.6.1), in ‘that very (sāman) is set on this very ṛc’ (Chā. Up. 1.6.1), the word ‘ṛc’ is used to indicate the earth, and ‘sāman’ to indicate fire. And that fits the wish to make the apprehensions of ṛc and sāman in the earth and fire (respectively), not the wish to make the apprehensions of earth and fire in the ṛc and sāman. For in the charioteer (kṣattṛ), since the apprehension of the king is to be made, the word ‘king’ is figuratively used for him; the word ‘charioteer’ is not so used for the king. Moreover, ‘Let one worship the fivefold sāman in the worlds’ (Chā. Up. 2.2.1), by the locative-use, indicates that the sāman is to be superimposed in the worlds. ‘That gāyatra is woven in the prāṇas’ (Chā. Up. 2.11.1) shows the same. And in ‘the sun is Brahman, this is the teaching’ (Chā. Up. 3.19.1) and the like, Brahman, mentioned later, is superimposed on ‘the sun’ etc., mentioned first. And the earth etc., mentioned first, are (the locus); the hiṅkāra etc., mentioned later — as in ‘the earth is the hiṅkāra’ (Chā. Up. 2.2.1) and the like — (are superimposed). Hence, the limb-apprehensions are superimposed on non-limbs ‘the sun’ etc. — when this view is reached, we say (siddhānta):
BS_C04_S01_V06::block-1: The apprehensions as ‘the sun’ etc. should be superimposed on the limbs ‘udgītha’ etc. Why? Because of fitness (upapatti). For thus, the udgīthas etc., refined by the apprehensions as ‘the sun’ etc., having the proximity of the apūrva (the unseen result), bring about fullness (samṛddhi) of the action. ‘What one performs with knowledge, faith, and the upaniṣad — that becomes more potent’ (Chā. Up. 1.1.10) shows that knowledge is a cause of the action's fullness. — Let it be so in (vidyās) whose fruit is the fullness of action; but how (is it) in (vidyās) of independent fruit, as in ‘He who, knowing thus, worships the fivefold sāman in the worlds’ (Chā. Up. 2.2.3) etc.? In those too, since the qualified person's qualification carries over (adhikṛta-adhikāra), the imagining of fruit through the proximity of the contextual apūrva is fitting, like the rule of milking the cow (godohana-niyama). And from the fact that ‘the sun’ etc. are themselves of the nature of fruit, their elevation over the udgītha etc., which are of the nature of action, is established. The śrutis enumerate the attainment of the sun etc. as the fruit of action. Moreover, in ‘Let one worship the syllable Oṃ as the udgītha’ (Chā. Up. 1.1.1), having begun with the udgītha as the object of worship, ‘Now there will be an exposition of just this syllable’ (Chā. Up. 1.1.10), the apprehensions as ‘the sun’ etc. are enjoined. As to what was said — that ‘the sun’ etc., when worshipped through the apprehensions as ‘udgītha’ etc., would, becoming of the nature of action, give the fruit — that is wrong. Worship itself, being action, can give fruit. And even though seen in the form of ‘the sun’ etc., the udgīthas etc. do not lose their nature as action. ‘That very (sāman) is set on this very ṛc’ (Chā. Up. 1.6.1) — there the use of the words ‘ṛc’ and ‘sāman’ for earth and fire is metaphorical (lākṣaṇika). And metaphor (lakṣaṇā) operates by a near or remote relation to its own meaning, as far as is possible. There, even though the wish were to apprehend earth and fire in the ṛc and sāman, since the well-known ṛc and sāman are mentioned by their distinctness, and since the earth and fire are in proximity, it is determined that this use of the words ‘ṛc’ and ‘sāman’ is for them (earth and fire), through the relation with ṛc and sāman. For the word ‘charioteer’ also, on some ground, when used for the king, cannot be excluded. ‘This indeed is the ṛc’ (Chā. Up. 1.6.1) — by the order of the words, ascertains the ṛc-hood of the (earth herself); for if the ṛc-hood were to be ascertained of the earth, the order of the words would have been ‘this earth itself is the ṛc’. ‘He who, knowing thus, sings the sāman’ (Chā. Up. 1.7.9) too concludes the cognition with reference to the limb (sāman) only, not to the earth etc. Likewise in ‘Let one worship the fivefold sāman in the worlds’ (Chā. Up. 2.2.1), although the worlds are mentioned in the locative case, even so they should be superimposed on the sāman, since by the use of the second case-ending the object of worship is understood to be the sāman. For when worlds are superimposed on the sāman, the sāman is worshipped with the form of the worlds; otherwise, the worlds would be worshipped with the form of the sāman. By this, ‘That gāyatra is woven in the prāṇas’ (Chā. Up. 2.11.1) etc. is also explained. Where there is similarly the use of the second case-ending — ‘Now indeed, let one worship the sevenfold sāman as yonder sun’ (Chā. Up. 2.9.1) — there too, since ‘the worship of the entire sāman is good’ (Chā. Up. 2.1.1), ‘so of the fivefold (sāman)’ (Chā. Up. 2.7.2), ‘now of the sevenfold’ (Chā. Up. 2.8.1) — having begun with the sāman as the object of worship, the superimposition of ‘the sun’ etc. is upon that very sāman. And from this very ascertainment of the sāman as the object of worship, ‘the earth is the hiṅkāra’ (Chā. Up. 2.…)
BS_C04_S01_V07::block-0: In worships connected with the limbs of (ritual) action, since they are dependent on the action (karma-tantratva), there is no consideration of posture (āsana) etc. Nor in the right vision (samyag-darśana), since cognition depends on its object (vastu-tantra). But in the other worships, the question is: should one engage in them indeterminately — standing, seated, or lying down — or by the rule (only) seated? There, since worship is mental, indeterminacy (with regard to bodily posture) holds — when this view is reached (pūrvapakṣa), (the siddhāntin) declares: one should worship seated only (āsīna eva). Why? Because of fitness (sambhava). Worship is the production of an unbroken stream of similar cognitions. And that is not possible for one going or running, since motion etc. cause distraction of the mind. For one standing too, the mind, being engaged in supporting the body, becomes incapable of looking at a subtle object. The lying-down person too is suddenly overcome by sleep. But for the seated, this kind of considerable defect is easily avoided. Hence the worship is fitting for him. ‖ 7 ‖
BS_C04_S01_V08::block-0: Furthermore, this is the meaning of ‘dhyāyati’ (meditates) — that which makes a continuous flow of homogeneous cognitions (samāna-pratyaya-pravāha-karaṇam). The verb ‘dhyāyati’ is observed to be employed with reference to those whose limbs are completely relaxed, whose gaze is fixed, and whose mind is engrossed in a single object — as in ‘the crane meditates’ (dhyāyati bakaḥ) and ‘one whose kinsman has gone abroad meditates’ (dhyāyati proṣita-bandhuḥ). And one who is seated is free from exertion (anāyāsa). Therefore on this ground also upāsana is an act-to-be-performed-while-seated (āsīna-karman). (8)
BS_C04_S01_V09: And by reason of (the consideration of) immobility. (9)
BS_C04_S01_V09::block-0: Moreover, in the passage ‘the earth, as it were, meditates’ (dhyāyatīva pṛthivī) (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.6.1) (citation), the use of the verb ‘dhyāyati’ with regard to the earth and the like is made having regard to their very immobility (acalatva). And that is an indicatory mark (liṅga) for upāsana being an act-to-be-performed-while-seated. (9)
BS_C04_S01_V10::block-0: And the venerable (śiṣṭāḥ) also record sitting (āsana) as an ancillary (aṅga) of upāsana — by such (statements) as ‘having established a firm seat for oneself in a clean place’ (śucau deśe pratiṣṭhāpya sthiram āsanam ātmanaḥ) (Bhagavad-gītā 6.11) (citation). For this very reason, the special postures such as the lotus-posture (padmaka) and the rest are taught in the science of yoga. (10)
BS_C04_S01_V11: Wherever there is one-pointedness (of mind), there (one may meditate), since there is no special rule. (11)
BS_C04_S01_V11::block-0: There is a doubt regarding direction, place, and time — is there any rule, or not? Since in Vedic undertakings rules concerning direction and the rest are generally seen, one might form the opinion that here also there must be some rule. To such a one (as pūrvapakṣa) it is replied — in respect of direction, place, and time the rule is determined merely by the (pragmatic) end (artha-lakṣaṇa). In whatever direction, place, or time one’s mind easily attains one-pointedness, just there one should worship; for no specifying scriptural injunction is heard, such as in the rules ‘the eastern direction’, ‘the forenoon’, ‘ground sloping eastward’, etc.; because the desired one-pointedness is uniformly available everywhere. — But (objects pūrvapakṣin) some do indeed teach a special (rule), as ‘On a level, clean (place), free from gravel, fire, and sand, with sounds and water-resorts and the like, agreeable to the mind, not painful to the eyes, in a hidden recess sheltered from wind, one should engage (in yoga)’ (same śucau śarkarā-vahni-vālukā-vivarjite śabda-jalāśrayādibhiḥ; manonukūle na tu cakṣu-pīḍane guhā-nivātāśrayaṇe prayojayet) (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.10) (citation). — It is replied (siddhānta): True, such a rule does exist. But this being granted, the ācārya, becoming kindly disposed (suhṛd-bhūtvā), declares that within the matters mentioned therein there is no fixed rule. The very śruti, by saying ‘mano-anukūle’ (agreeable to the mind), shows just this — namely, ‘wherever there is one-pointedness, just there’. (11)
BS_C04_S01_V12: Up to (the moment of) death; for there too it is seen (in scripture). (12)
BS_C04_S01_V12::block-0: It was settled in the first adhikaraṇa that repetition (āvṛtti) is to be observed in all upāsanas. Now, of those upāsanas which serve the purpose of right knowledge (samyag-darśana), since they (like the act of pounding etc.) culminate in their own effect (kārya-paryavasāyin), the limit of repetition is already known. For when the effect, viz. samyag-darśana, has been accomplished, no further effort can be enjoined; because the realisation that one is Brahman, who is not subject to injunctions (an-iyojya-brahmātmatva-pratipatti), is no province of scripture (śāstrasya aviṣayatva). But of those (upāsanas) which yield prosperity (abhyudaya) as their fruit, this enquiry arises — should one repeat the cognition for some span of time and desist, or should one repeat it lifelong? — What then is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa)? — One should repeat the cognition for some time and then leave off, since the meaning of the word upāsana, characterised by repetition, has been fulfilled. — When this has been thus prima facie urged, we say (siddhānta): One should repeat the cognition right up to death (āprāyaṇāt); because the unseen fruit (adṛṣṭa-phala) is attained through the last cognition. For karmas too, when initiating a fruit to be experienced in another birth, project at the time of dying a state of bhāvanā-vijñāna (a meditative cognition) suited to that fruit — as is shown by such śrutis as ‘he becomes possessed of (such-and-such) cognition; with cognition alone he passes on’ (sa-vijñāno bhavati sa-vijñānam evānvavakrāmati) (citation), ‘whatever is one’s thought, by that does this (jīva) reach the prāṇa’ (yac-cittas tenaiṣa prāṇam āyāti) (citation), ‘the prāṇa, conjoined with the fire and accompanied by the self, leads (him) to whatever world he has resolved upon’ (prāṇas tejasā yuktaḥ sahātmanā yathāsaṅkalpitaṁ lokaṁ nayati) (citation). And from the analogy of the leech in the grass (tṛṇa-jalūkā-nidarśana). What other death-time bhāvanā-vijñāna would these cognitions presuppose, save the continuance of their own form? Therefore, in the case of those cognitions which consist of the meditation upon the fruit to be attained, repetition (āvṛtti) is up to death. So says the śruti: ‘Of whatever resolve he is, with that he passes from this world’ (sa yāvat-kratur ayam asmāl lokāt praiti) (citation), thereby showing the continuance of the cognition even at the time of death. The smṛti also: ‘Whatever object a man, leaving the body at the end, calls to mind, that alone, O son of Kuntī, he attains, ever moulded by that thought’ (yaṁ yaṁ vāpi smaran bhāvaṁ tyajaty ante kalebaram; taṁ tam evaiti kaunteya sadā tad-bhāva-bhāvitaḥ) (Bhagavad-gītā 8.6) (citation), and ‘at the time of departure, with unwavering mind…’ (prayāṇa-kāle manasācalena) (Bhagavad-gītā 8.10) (citation). And ‘at the moment of departure he should resort to this triad’ (so’nta-velāyām etat trayaṁ pratipadyeta) (citation) declares the duty remaining to be done even at the moment of dying. (12)
BS_C04_S01_V13: On the attainment of That (Brahman), there is non-clinging (of future) and destruction (of past sins) — because that is so declared. (13)
BS_C04_S01_V13::block-0: The third (pāda’s) remainder is now over. Now begins the enquiry concerning the fruit of brahma-vidyā. — The doubt is: when Brahman is attained, does sin (durita), being its opposite-fruit, perish, or does it not perish? — What then is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa)? — Since karma exists for the sake of fruit, its destruction without yielding its fruit is not credible. Its fruit-bestowing power is well established by śruti. If it were to be cancelled apart from the experiencing of its fruit, the śruti would be flouted. The smṛti also says, ‘karma is not destroyed (without being experienced)’ (na hi karma kṣīyate) (Gautama Dharma-sūtra 3.1.5) (citation). — But if so, the prescription of expiations (prāyaścitta) would become meaningless. — This is no flaw, since the expiations may be naimittika (occasional) like the iṣṭi for a burnt house. — Moreover, expiations being prescribed in connection with sin, dosha-removal can be their purpose. But there is no such prescription in brahma-vidyā. — But if karma-destruction is not admitted for the brahmavid, his liberation would be impossible, since the fruit (of accumulated karma) must necessarily be experienced. — Not so; mokṣa, like the fruit of karma, will depend upon (specific) place, time, and (occasional) cause. — Therefore, on the attainment of Brahman, sin is not destroyed. — On this prima facie view being thus presented, we say (siddhānta): —
BS_C04_S01_V13::block-1: On its attainment, that is, on the attainment of Brahman, there occurs the non-clinging (aśleṣa) of the latter (uttara, future) and the destruction (vināśa) of the former (pūrva, past) sins — non-clinging of what is to come, and destruction of what is past. Why? Because of that very declaration (tad-vyapadeśa). For thus, in the brahma-vidyā section, the absence of any connection between the knower and possible coming sin is declared — ‘As water does not cling to the lotus-leaf, so does sinful action not cling to one who knows thus’ (yathā puṣkara-palāśa āpo na śliṣyante evam evaṁ-vidi pāpaṁ karma na śliṣyate) (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.14.3) (citation). And likewise the destruction of the previously accumulated sin is also declared — ‘As the cotton-tip of an iṣīkā-reed, when laid in fire, is consumed, even so are all his sins consumed’ (tad yatheṣīkātūlam agnau protaṁ pradūyetaivaṁ hāsya sarve pāpmānaḥ pradūyante) (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.24.3) (citation). And there is yet this other declaration of karma-destruction — ‘The knot of the heart is rent asunder, all doubts are cleft, and his karmas are destroyed when That is seen which is both higher and lower’ (bhidyate hṛdaya-granthiś chidyante sarva-saṁśayāḥ; kṣīyante cāsya karmāṇi tasmin dṛṣṭe parāvare) (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.9) (citation). As to what was said — that to suppose the destruction of karma whose fruit has not been experienced is to flout śruti — this is no flaw. We do not deny the fruit-bestowing power of karma. It does indeed exist. But we say it is obstructed (pratibadhyate) by another cause, namely vidyā and the like. Śruti is concerned only with the existence of that power, not with its obstruction or non-obstruction. The (smṛti) ‘karma is not destroyed’ (na hi karma kṣīyate) (Gautama Dharma-sūtra 3.1.5) (citation) is also a general statement (autsargika) — namely, ‘karma, being meant for it (i.e. its fruit), is not destroyed save by experiencing the fruit’. But its destruction by prāyaścitta and the like is admitted — by śrutis and smṛtis like ‘he conquers all sin, he conquers even brahma-hatyā, who performs the aśvamedha, and so does he who knows it thus’ (sarvaṁ pāpmānaṁ tarati, tarati brahma-hatyām, yo’śvamedhena yajate, ya u cainam evaṁ veda) (citation). As for what was said, that the expiations may be naimittika — that is unsound, since when these are enjoined upon the contingency of sin, and the destruction of the doṣa (sin) is a possible fruit for them, it is unwarranted to imagine some other fruit. As to what was further said — that, unlike prāyaścitta, there is no prescription of vidyā for the purpose of destroying sin — to that we reply: in the saguṇa vidyās, prescription does indeed exist; and there, in the supplementary portions (vākya-śeṣa), the attainment of īśvarya (lordship) and the cessation of pāpa are stated to belong to the knower; and there is no reason to suppose that these are not intended; hence it is settled that the attainment of īśvarya, preceded by the destruction of sin, is their fruit. In the nirguṇa vidyā, although there is no (such) prescription, still, by the realisation of the akartṛ-ātmatva (the non-agency of the Self), the consumption of karmas is established. By saying ‘aśleṣa’ (non-clinging), it is shown that with regard to coming karmas the brahma-vid does not assume agency at all. As for the past, although owing to mithyā-jñāna it appeared as if he had been an agent, yet by the power of vidyā mithyā-jñāna is removed, and so they too dissolve away — hence ‘vināśa’ (destruction). For, contrary to the previously established sense of agency and enjoyership, the brahma-vid realises ‘I am Brahman, of the very nature of non-agency and non-enjoyership in all three times — neither before this was I an agent or enjoyer, nor now, nor in the future shall I be’. Only thus can mokṣa stand. Otherwise, since beginningless karmas could not perish, there could be no liberation. And mokṣa cannot, like the fruit of karma, depend upon place, time, and occasion; for then it would be non-eternal, and the fruit of jñāna (which is direct) could not be remote. Therefore it stands established that on the attainment of Brahman, durita perishes. (13)
BS_C04_S01_V14: Of the other (puṇya) too there is similar non-clinging; but at (the body’s) fall (mokṣa is reached). (14)
BS_C04_S01_V14::block-0: In the previous adhikaraṇa it was determined, on the strength of the scriptural declaration, that the natural sin (svābhāvika agha) which is the cause of bondage is non-clinging and destroyed by knowledge. But dharma (puṇya), being scriptural in its origin, might be supposed not to conflict with scriptural knowledge. To remove that doubt, the maxim of the previous adhikaraṇa is extended to it (atideśa). — Of the other also, namely puṇya-karma, just as of agha (sin), there occurs non-clinging (asaṁśleṣa) and destruction (vināśa) for the man of knowledge. — Why? — Because it too, being a cause of its own fruit, is liable to obstruct the fruit of jñāna; and because in śrutis like ‘this one verily crosses both these’ (ubhe u haivaiṣa ete tarati) (Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣat 4.4.22) (citation) the destruction of sukṛta is declared along with that of duṣkṛta; and because the destruction of karma, having as its cause the realisation of the akartṛ-ātmatva, is the same in both sukṛta and duṣkṛta; and the śruti ‘his karmas are destroyed’ (kṣīyante cāsya karmāṇi) (Muṇḍakopaniṣat 2.2.9) (citation) is unspecific. Even where the word ‘pāpman’ alone is read, by it puṇya too should be understood as included, since (compared with jñāna) it is of inferior fruit. And in śruti the word ‘pāpman’ is used even of puṇya — as in ‘these (day and night) do not cross this dam’ (nainaṁ setum aho-rātre tarataḥ) (Chāndogyopaniṣat 8.4.1) (citation), where, after enumerating both duṣkṛta and sukṛta, the word ‘pāpman’ is used in ‘all sins (pāpmānaḥ) turn back from this’ — applied without distinction to the very puṇya in context. The particle ‘tu’ in ‘pāte tu’ has the force of emphasis (avadhāraṇārtha). Thus, since by the power of vidyā the non-clinging and destruction of dharma and adharma — both bondage-causes — is established, the muktī of the knower is unfailing at the fall of the body — this is what is emphasised. (14)
BS_C04_S01_V15: But (this destruction belongs) only to those (karmas) whose effect (this body) has not begun; that being the limit (i.e. up to the body’s fall). (15)
BS_C04_S01_V15::block-0: In the two preceding adhikaraṇas it has been settled that there is destruction, occasioned by knowledge, of sukṛta and duṣkṛta. Now is it considered: does this take place indifferently (aviśeṣeṇa) of those (karmas) whose effect has begun (ārabdha-kārya) and those whose effect has not begun (anārabdha-kārya), or only of those whose effect has not begun? — On this, since śrutis like ‘this one crosses both’ (ubhe u haivaiṣa ete tarati) (Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣat 4.4.22) (citation) speak without specification, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that the destruction is indifferent. — In reply (siddhānta) it is said: ‘only those whose effect has not begun (anārabdha-kārye eva tu)’. The previous (karmas, both sukṛta and duṣkṛta), accumulated in former births and also accumulated in this birth before the rise of knowledge, whose fruit has not yet started, perish on the dawning of knowledge — but not those whose effect has begun, whose fruit is already half-experienced (sāmi-bhukta-phala), by which this body, the locus of brahma-jñāna, has been formed. — Whence is this? — From the śruti ‘For him only so long is the delay as until I shall be released; then I shall reach (Brahman)’ (tasya tāvad eva ciraṁ yāvan na vimokṣye’tha sampatsye) (Chāndogyopaniṣat 6.14.2) (citation), wherein the attainment of kṣema is shown to wait until the fall of the body. Otherwise, when by jñāna all karmas are destroyed, no cause of (bodily) continuance remaining, the man would attain kṣema (release) immediately upon the rise of jñāna, and would not have to wait for the body’s fall. — But (objection): granted that this realisation of the akartṛ-ātman is, by its very vastu-bala (power of the real fact), itself the consumer of karmas — how then can it consume some and pass over others? For when fire and seeds are equally in contact, surely it cannot be admitted that the seed-power of some perishes and of some does not. — It is replied: the rise of jñāna does not occur at all without taking shelter in the karma-deposit whose effect has begun (āśritya ārabdha-kāryam karmāśayam). Once it has so taken shelter, since obstruction in the midst of motion already imparted is impossible (as in the case of a potter’s wheel, kulāla-cakra-vat pravṛtta-vegasya), one waits for the exhaustion of that motion. The realisation of the akartṛ-ātman too cuts away karmas through cancellation of mithyā-jñāna. But mithyā-jñāna, even when sublated, persists for some time by the force of saṁskāra, like the perception of two moons (dvi-candra-jñāna-vat saṁskāra-vaśāt). Moreover, this is no point for dispute — whether the body of the brahma-vit is held for some time or is not held; for how can one (an outsider) deny another’s self-felt cognition of Brahman (sva-hṛdaya-pratyaya) and the upholding of the body? Śruti and smṛti, by the description of the marks of the sthita-prajña, expound this very thing. Therefore the conclusion is: by the power of vidyā only those sukṛtas and duṣkṛtas whose effect has not begun are destroyed. (15)
BS_C04_S01_V16: But the agnihotra and the like (serve) only for that same purpose, because that is seen. (16)
BS_C04_S01_V16::block-0: The maxim of ‘agha’ (sin) — namely non-adhesion (to the knower) and destruction (at his death) — was extended (in the previous sūtra) to puṇya (merit) as well. The pūrvapakṣin apprehends that this extension applies to all puṇya whatsoever; the siddhānta replies — ‘But the agnihotra and the like.’ The word ‘tu’ (but) dispels the apprehension. Whatever is the nitya (obligatory daily) Vedic ritual — agnihotra and the rest — that serves for that very effect (tatkāryāya); the meaning is: whatever is the effect of jñāna (knowledge), that itself is the effect of this (nitya-karma) too. How so? From the seeing (in scripture) — ‘Him, indeed, the Brāhmaṇas seek to know by recitation of the Vedas, by sacrifice, by gift’ (Bṛ.U. 4.4.22) and so on. Objection: Since the effects of jñāna and karma are dissimilar, oneness of effect is not tenable. — This is no defect; for though curd and poison have the effects of fever and death (respectively), when conjoined with jaggery and mantras they are seen to produce the effects of satisfaction and nourishment; likewise karma too, when conjoined with jñāna, may produce the effect of mokṣa. Objection: Mokṣa is non-originable; how then can it be called an effect of karma? — This is no defect, since karma is an ‘ārād-upakāraka’ (remote auxiliary). For karma, by being a procurer of jñāna itself, is figuratively called the cause of mokṣa through that channel. And precisely for this reason, this assertion of oneness of effect refers to the past (karmas, before knowledge arose). For the knower of Brahman has no future agnihotra and the like, since śāstra has no scope (over him) on account of his realisation of his being the non-commandable Brahman-Self. But in the saguṇa-vidyās, since agency is not transcended, future agnihotra and the like are possible; and that too, when free from desire (nirabhisandhi), having no other effect, is consistent with being conjoined to vidyā. (16)
BS_C04_S01_V17: For (such karma) other than this also (is mentioned by) some, of both. (17)
BS_C04_S01_V17::block-0: (leading) But what then is the scope of this statement of non-adhesion and destruction, and what is the scope of this declaration of allotment among certain śākhins (recensionists) — ‘His sons inherit his property, his friends his good deeds, his enemies his evil deeds’? In reply, he recites:
BS_C04_S01_V17::block-1: Other than this — i.e., other than the agnihotra and the like which is nitya-karma — there does indeed exist sādhu-kṛtyā (good action), namely that which is performed with reference to a fruit (kāmya); of that this allotment is stated by some śākhins — ‘his friends inherit his good deeds.’ And it is of that very (kāmya-karma) that this exposition like that of agha (evil) — viz. non-adhesion and destruction — applies: that the other (kāmya-puṇya) too has no contact (with the knower) in this way. With regard to such kāmya-karma, both ācāryas — Jaimini and Bādarāyaṇa — agree that it does not contribute to vidyā. (17)
BS_C04_S01_V18: ‘What one does with knowledge’ etc. — for (so the śruti says). (18)
BS_C04_S01_V18::block-0: It was ascertained in the previous adhikaraṇa that the nitya agnihotra and the like, performed by a mumukṣu (aspirant for liberation) with the aim of mokṣa, becomes — through being a cause of the destruction of the accumulated demerits and thereby a cause of purity of mind (sattva-śuddhi) — the cause of the attainment of Brahman, which has mokṣa as its purpose; and thus comes to share one effect with brahma-vidyā. Now agnihotra and the like exists in two forms: conjoined with the vidyā which leans on the limbs of karma, and unconjoined (kevala). From statements like ‘He who, knowing thus, sacrifices,’ ‘He who, knowing thus, offers oblations,’ ‘He who, knowing thus, recites,’ ‘He who, knowing thus, sings,’ ‘Therefore one should make only such a knower one’s brahmā-priest, not a non-knower’ (Ch.U. 4.17.10), ‘Both perform with it — he who knows thus and he who does not know’ (Ch.U. 1.1.10) — there is agnihotra and the like that is vidyā-conjoined, and also that which is kevala (alone). Here is examined: Does only vidyā-conjoined agnihotra etc., as cause of vidyā in the mumukṣu, attain oneness of effect with vidyā, not the kevala; or does both vidyā-conjoined and kevala, without distinction (do so)? Why the doubt? Because in ‘They seek to know that very Self by sacrifice,’ etc., yajña and so on are heard of without distinction as auxiliaries to ātma-jñāna; yet vidyā-conjoined agnihotra etc. is understood as superior. (Pūrvapakṣa) What is to begin with established? Only vidyā-conjoined agnihotra-etc. attains the status of auxiliary to ātma-vidyā, not that devoid of vidyā, since the vidyā-endowed is understood as superior to the vidyā-devoid; from śrutis such as ‘On the very day on which he offers, on that day he conquers death again — he who knows thus’ (Bṛ.U. 1.5.2); and from smṛtis such as ‘Endowed with that buddhi, O Pārtha, by which thou shalt cast off karma-bondage’ (Gītā 2.39), ‘For karma is far inferior to buddhi-yoga, O Dhanañjaya’ (Gītā 2.49). — On this prima facie position being granted, (the siddhānta) is established —
BS_C04_S01_V18::block-1: ‘What one does with knowledge’ — for (so śruti says). True, vidyā-conjoined agnihotra etc. is superior to vidyā-devoid agnihotra etc., just as a learned brāhmaṇa is superior to a brāhmaṇa devoid of learning. Even so, vidyā-devoid agnihotra etc. is not utterly without relevance. Why? Because in ‘They seek to know that very Self by sacrifice,’ agnihotra etc. is heard of as cause of vidyā without distinction. Objection: Since vidyā-conjoined agnihotra etc. is understood as superior to that devoid of vidyā, it is proper that the latter, as cause of ātma-vidyā, be entirely set aside — Not so; vidyā-aided agnihotra etc., on account of its connection with an excess of capacity due to vidyā, may have some excess of causal-power towards ātma-jñāna, but not so the vidyā-devoid — that much is right to suppose. But it cannot be admitted that agnihotra etc., heard of in ‘they seek to know by sacrifice’ as auxiliary to ātma-jñāna without distinction, is not an auxiliary at all. So śruti says — ‘Whatever one does with knowledge, with faith, with the upaniṣad — that very thing becomes more potent’ (Ch.U. 1.1.10) — by speaking of greater potency of the karma conjoined with vidyā with respect to its own effect, it shows that the same karma devoid of vidyā has (some) potency with respect to that purpose. And the potency of karma is precisely this — its capacity to accomplish its proper purpose. Therefore both nitya agnihotra etc., conjoined with vidyā and devoid of it — whatever has been performed by the mumukṣu with mokṣa as the aim, in this birth or in another, prior to the arising of jñāna — that, according to its capacity, becoming a cause of attaining Brahman through being the cause of the destruction of the accumulated demerit which is the obstructing cause of brahmādhigama, awaiting the inner causes such as śravaṇa, manana, śraddhā and earnest application — comes to share one effect with brahma-vidyā. Thus is it established. (18)
BS_C04_S01_V19: But the others (the prārabdha karmas), having exhausted them through enjoyment, he attains (Brahman). (19)
BS_C04_S01_V19::block-0: It was stated that, by the power of vidyā, the unbegun puṇya and pāpa are destroyed. But the others — the puṇya and pāpa whose effects have begun (ārabdha-kārya, i.e. prārabdha) — having exhausted them through enjoyment, he attains Brahman; from śrutis such as ‘For him there is delay only so long as I am not freed; then I shall attain’ (Ch.U. 6.14.2) and ‘Being Brahman alone, he merges into Brahman.’ Objection: Even when samyag-darśana exists, just as before the fall of the body the perception of difference continues by the analogy of seeing two moons (dvi-candra-darśana), so it might continue afterwards too — No, owing to absence of cause. Exhaustion of the residue of enjoyment is the cause of its continuance there; and no such (cause) exists here. Objection: Some other karmāśaya may begin a fresh enjoyment — No; for its seed is burnt. For another karma, leaning on mithyā-jñāna, begins another enjoyment at the fall of the body; and that mithyā-jñāna has been burnt by samyag-jñāna. — Therefore it stands well established that, on the destruction of the begun effects, kaivalya for the knower necessarily follows. (19)
BS_C04_S02_INTRO1::block-0: Now, intending to introduce the devayāna path for the obtaining of fruits in the apara-vidyās (lower meditations), he first describes, in accordance with śāstra, the order of utkrānti (departure of the soul). For he will say (later) that the utkrānti of the knower and the non-knower is identical (up to a certain stage) —
BS_C04_S02_V01: Speech (merges) into mind, on account of the seeing (of this in śruti) and on account of the (later) word. (1)
BS_C04_S02_V01::block-0: There is a śruti regarding the time of departure — ‘Of this man, dear one, when he is departing, speech (vāk) merges into mind, mind into prāṇa, prāṇa into tejas (fire), tejas into the supreme deity’ (Ch.U. 6.8.6). Now, is it speech itself, along with its possessor (vṛttimattvena), that is here said to merge into mind, or only the function (vṛtti) of speech? — herein the doubt. (Pūrvapakṣa) First, it is established that speech itself merges into mind. For thus the śruti is upheld in its primary sense; otherwise, lakṣaṇā (figurative interpretation) would have to be resorted to. And in a doubt between śruti and lakṣaṇā, śruti is preferable, not lakṣaṇā. Therefore the merger of speech itself into mind here.
BS_C04_S02_V01::block-1: (Siddhānta) On this position, we say: it is the function (vṛtti) of speech that merges into mind. How is it explained as ‘function of speech’, when the ācārya simply states ‘vāk into mind’? True; but he will state later — ‘Non-distinction, on account of the (later) statement’ (B.S. 4.2.16). Therefore here only cessation of vṛtti is intended; that is understood. If essence-dissolution were intended, since non-distinction holds equally in all (stages), why specify only later — ‘Non-distinction’? Therefore here cessation of vṛtti is intended. The vṛtti of speech is first absorbed when the vṛtti of mind is still operative — that is the meaning. Why? On account of the seeing (darśana) — for the prior absorption of speech-vṛtti is seen while mind-vṛtti is still functioning. But the merging of speech itself, along with its substance, into mind cannot be seen by anyone. Objection: It was said that, by the force of śruti, the merging of speech itself into mind is proper — Not so, says he, on account of (mind) not being its prakṛti (material cause). For of that which has its origin in something, the merging in that is proper — like a clay-dish in clay. And there is no proof that vāk arises from manas. But arising and absorbing of a vṛtti are seen also when their support is not the prakṛti. For the vṛtti of fire (tejas), which is fiery in nature, arises from earthy fuel and is extinguished in water. How then, on this view, the word ‘speech merges into mind’? Hence (the sūtra) says — and on account of the (later) word. The word also is consistent on this view, by figurative non-distinction (abheda-upacāra) between vṛtti and the possessor of vṛtti — that is the meaning. (1)
BS_C04_S02_V02: And for this very reason, all (the senses) follow (similarly). (2)
BS_C04_S02_V02::block-0: ‘Hence with quiescent tejas (warmth), he goes to rebirth with the senses merging into mind’ (Pra.U. 3.9) — here the merging of all the senses into mind is heard of without distinction. There also, for this very reason, just as in the case of speech, so also in the case of the eye etc., when mind with its function is still established, since cessation of (their) vṛtti is seen, since dissolution of essence is impossible, and since the word (in śruti) is consistent (only thus) — all the senses follow (i.e. merge into) the mind by way of their vṛtti alone. Although merging of all instruments into mind is uniform, the separate mention of speech is in conformity with the example-citation ‘speech merges into mind.’ (2)
BS_C04_S02_V03: That mind (merges) into prāṇa, from the subsequent (passage). (3)
BS_C04_S02_V03::block-0: It has been ascertained that in ‘speech merges into mind’ (Ch.U. 6.8.6) the intended meaning is the merging of vṛtti. Now, in the next sentence — ‘mind into prāṇa’ (Ch.U. 6.8.6) — is the merging of vṛtti alone intended, or merging of the substance possessing the vṛtti? In this doubt, (Pūrvapakṣa) merging of the substance itself is what is established here, by virtue of the support of śruti and on account of (prāṇa) being the prakṛti (material cause of mind). For thus — ‘Mind, dear one, is composed of food; prāṇa is composed of waters’ (Ch.U. 6.5.4) — they declare mind as having food for its source, and prāṇa as having water for its source. ‘And the waters created food’ — so śruti. Therefore, when mind merges into prāṇa, it is food merging into water; mind being food and prāṇa being water, on the principle of non-difference between effect and cause (prakṛti-vikāra-abheda). — On this position, we say: even that, having absorbed the external sense-vṛttis, mind merges into prāṇa only by way of vṛtti — this is to be understood from the subsequent passage. For thus, when one is about to sleep or about to die, when prāṇa-vṛtti, of the form of throbbing motion, is established, the cessation of mind-vṛttis is seen. And essence-dissolution of mind into prāṇa is not possible, on account of (prāṇa) not being its prakṛti. Objection: But the prāṇa-prakṛti-nature of mind has been shown — this has no substance. For with such a (remote) prakṛtitva mediated by prāṇāḍika (the channel of prāṇa), mind is not fit to merge into prāṇa as such. For even thus, mind would merge into food, food into waters, and prāṇa itself into waters. For even on this view, there is no proof that mind is born from the waters when transformed into prāṇa-state. Therefore there is no essence-dissolution of mind into prāṇa. Even on the merging of vṛtti, the word (śruti) is consistent, by figurative non-distinction between vṛtti and possessor of vṛtti — as has been shown. (3)
BS_C04_S02_V04: That (prāṇa, at the time of departure) abides in the presiding (jīva), because of (the scripture's) approaching him, etc. ‖ 4 ‖
BS_C04_S02_V04::block-0: It has been established — that of which (one entity) does not have its origin from another, in that (other) the former undergoes only a dissolution of its function (vṛtti-pralaya), not a dissolution of its very nature (svarūpa-pralaya). Now this is examined here, with regard to ‘prāṇa (merges) into tejas’ (Chā. Up. 6.8.6) — is the merging of prāṇa's function literally into tejas alone, as the śruti reads, or is it into the jīva, who is the presiding lord (adhyakṣa) over the cage of body and senses? On this, the pūrvapakṣa would be: since śruti is not to be doubted, the merger of prāṇa should be into tejas alone; for postulating something not heard (in the text) is improper. — When this is the prima facie view, (the sūtrakāra) replies: ‘so'dhyakṣe’ (he abides in the presiding one). The said prāṇa abides in the adhyakṣa, namely in the vijñānātman conditioned by the upādhis of avidyā, karma, and prior cognitions; the import is that prāṇa's function (at that time) has him as its principal locus. Why? ‘tad-upagamādibhyaḥ’ — from (texts speaking of) approaching him and so on. For another śruti, ‘In just this way do all the prāṇas, at the time of the end, gather into this Self, around whom one breathes upward’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.2 — paraphrase), shows without distinction that all the prāṇas approach the adhyakṣa. And specifically, ‘When he is departing, prāṇa departs after him’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.2) shows the five-fold prāṇa's following of the adhyakṣa, and ‘When prāṇa is departing, all the prāṇas depart after it’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.2) shows the others' following of that (prāṇa). And ‘He becomes endowed with consciousness (savijñāna)’ — by displaying the inner-knowledge nature of the adhyakṣa, this conveys that the prāṇa, with the band of senses absorbed (into it), abides in him. — Objection: But ‘prāṇa (merges) into tejas’ is what is heard; how can an additional clause, ‘prāṇa (abides) in the adhyakṣa,’ be made? — This is no fault, since the matter of departure and so on principally pertains to the adhyakṣa, and since the specification given in the other śruti is to be taken into account. ‖ 4 ‖
BS_C04_S02_V05: (He abides) in the elements, since śruti so declares ‖ 5 ‖
BS_C04_S02_V05::block-0: How then is the śruti ‘prāṇa (merges) into tejas’? On this he says —
BS_C04_S02_V05::block-1: That adhyakṣa, conjoined with prāṇa, is to be understood as abiding in the subtle elements that accompany tejas — those subtle elements which serve as the seed of the (next) body — for so declares the śruti ‘prāṇa (abides) in tejas.’ — Objection: But this śruti shows the abiding of prāṇa in tejas, not of the adhyakṣa conjoined with prāṇa. — This is no fault, because by ‘so'dhyakṣe’ the adhyakṣa too has been included as an intermediate (locus). For one who, having gone from Srughna to Mathurā, then proceeds from Mathurā to Pāṭaliputra, can equally well be said to be going from Srughna to Pāṭaliputra. Therefore (the text) ‘prāṇa (abides) in tejas’ means precisely the abiding of the adhyakṣa, conjoined with prāṇa, in the elements that accompany tejas. ‖ 5 ‖
BS_C04_S02_V06: Not in one alone, for both (śruti and smṛti) so declare ‖ 6 ‖
BS_C04_S02_V06::block-0: How is it said ‘in the elements that accompany tejas,’ when only one — tejas alone — is heard (in) ‘prāṇa (merges) in tejas’? On this he says —
BS_C04_S02_V06::block-1: Not in one tejas alone does the jīva, at the time of seeking another body, abide; because the body, the effect, is seen to be made up of many (elements). And the question and answer — ‘the waters speak as the puruṣa’ (Chā. Up. 5.3.3) — display this very point. This was explained at ‘tryātmakatvāt tu bhūyastvāt’ (Br. Sū. 3.1.2). And both śruti and smṛti show this. Śruti: ‘consisting of earth, of water, of air, of ether, of tejas,’ and the like; smṛti likewise: ‘the indestructible subtle parts (mātrās) of the five (elements) which are recorded — together with these this whole (body) comes into being in due succession’ (Manu Smṛ. 1.27), and the like. — Objection: But when the senses such as speech are absorbed, at the time of seeking another body, beginning ‘where then is this person?’ (Bṛ. Up. 3.2.13), another śruti establishes karma as the locus: ‘What those two said, that they spoke as karma; and what they praised, that they praised as karma’ (Bṛ. Up. 3.2.13). — Here it is replied: There the operation of the bondage called grahas and atigrahas, which is karma-prompted and consists of senses-and-objects, is meant; thus karma's being the locus is spoken of (with respect to that bondage). Here, on the other hand, what is stated is the elements' being the locus, in the sense that the next body is produced by taking up the (subtle) elements as material. By the word ‘praised,’ moreover, only the predominance of karma (in that context) is shown — no other locus is excluded. Therefore there is no contradiction. ‖ 6 ‖
BS_C04_S02_V07: And (this departure) is identical (for both knower and non-knower) up to the commencement of the path; and immortality (is gained by the knower) without burning up (the kleśas) ‖ 7 ‖
BS_C04_S02_V07::block-0: Is this departure the same for the knower and the non-knower, or different? — The pūrvapakṣa for those who doubt is that it is different. For this departure is qualified by having (subtle) elements as its locus. Elements are taken up only for re-birth. And re-birth is not possible for the knower; for the knower attains immortality — such is the established teaching. Therefore this departure belongs to the non-knower alone. — Objection: But since it is mentioned in a vidyā-section (a chapter on knowledge), it must belong to the knower. — No, just as in the case of sleep and so on, it is recounted as it is generally known. For just as ‘where this person is said to sleep’ (Chā. Up. 6.8.1), ‘is said to be hungry’ (Chā. Up. 6.8.3), ‘is said to thirst’ (Chā. Up. 6.8.5) — these states (sleep etc.) are common to all living beings, yet are mentioned in the vidyā-section in conformity with the matter sought to be conveyed, and are not enjoined as something special of the knower; in the same way, this departure too is being recounted only as common to the multitude (mahājana), in order to convey: ‘that supreme deity in which the tejas of the well-purified person merges — that is the Self, that art thou.’ And this (departure) has been forbidden of the knower: ‘the prāṇas of him do not depart’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.6). Therefore it belongs to the non-knower alone.
BS_C04_S02_V07::block-1: When this is the (pūrva)pakṣa, we reply (the siddhānta): This departure beginning ‘speech (merges) in mind’ etc. is the same for both knower and non-knower up to the commencement of the path (āsṛty-upakramāt), since no distinction is heard (in the texts). The non-knower, having taken up the subtle elements that form the seed of the body, prompted by karma, transmigrates to undergo the assumption of (another) body; the knower, however, takes recourse to the doorway of the mokṣa-nāḍī illumined by knowledge — that is what is meant by ‘up to the commencement of the path.’ — Objection: But immortality is what is to be attained by the knower, and it is not dependent upon any other location; whence then any locus of elements or a commencement of a path? — Here it is replied: ‘anupoṣya ca’ — without burning up entirely the kleśas such as avidyā, by virtue of the apara-vidyā (lower knowledge) one seeks a relative (āpekṣika) immortality; in that (case) a commencement of the path and a locus of elements are possible — for prāṇas without a locus cannot have any going. Therefore there is no fault. ‖ 7 ‖
BS_C04_S02_V08: (The merging into the supreme Deity is) up to (the rise of right knowledge) — for (scripture) speaks of (continued) saṁsāra ‖ 8 ‖
BS_C04_S02_V08::block-0: By the force of the context, the meaning of ‘tejas (merges) in the supreme Deity’ (Chā. Up. 6.8.6) is this: that very tejas in question, together with the adhyakṣa, with prāṇa, with the band of senses, and accompanied by the other (subtle) elements, of the well-purified person, merges into the supreme Deity. Now what is the nature of this merger? — On this it is examined. The pūrvapakṣa is that there is utter dissolution of the very nature (svarūpa-praviḷaya), since (the supreme Deity) has been established as the prakṛti (material cause) of all. For it has been laid down that of every born thing the supreme Deity is the prakṛti. Therefore this attainment of non-distinction is final (ātyantikī). — When this is the prima facie view, we reply (the siddhānta): That tejas etc., the subtle elements which form the locus of the senses such as ear, abide ‘āpīteḥ’ — until the dissolution of saṁsāra brought about by right knowledge — for (scripture) speaks of saṁsāra (continuing): ‘some embodied beings approach a womb for embodiment; others go to (motionless) stationary forms — according to their works, according to their learning’ (Kaṭha Up. 2.2.7). Otherwise, every person at the very time of death, by the dropping away of the upādhis, would attain Brahman utterly; in which case the scripture of injunction would be useless, as also the scripture of vidyā. And bondage, caused by mithyā-jñāna, cannot be unloosened except by samyag-jñāna. Therefore, even though (Brahman) is the prakṛti, this merging into Sat is — like the dissolution in deep sleep — only the residue in seed-form (bīja-bhāvāvaśeṣā). ‖ 8 ‖
BS_C04_S02_V09: Subtle (it is), in nature and in measure, since it is so apprehended ‖ 9 ‖
BS_C04_S02_V09::block-0: And that tejas, accompanied by the other elements, which serves as the locus of the jīva departing from this body, must be subtle both in nature (svarūpa) and in measure (parimāṇa). For its subtleness is apprehended from such (texts as) speak of its issuing forth through the nāḍīs. There, by reason of (its) being attenuated, motion is feasible; and by reason of (its) translucence, non-obstruction is feasible. Hence too, when departing from the body, it is not perceived by those standing nearby. ‖ 9 ‖
BS_C04_S02_V10: Not by destruction (of the gross body) (is the subtle destroyed), because of this (subtleness) ‖ 10 ‖
BS_C04_S02_V10::block-0: Hence too, by virtue of (its) subtleness, the other — the subtle body — is not destroyed by the destruction of this gross body brought about by burning and the like. ‖ 10 ‖
BS_C04_S02_V11: And this warmth (in the body) belongs to this (subtle body) alone, since this is reasonable ‖ 11 ‖
BS_C04_S02_V11::block-0: And this warmth, which one knows by touch in this body, belongs to this very subtle body. For in the state of death, even though the body remains and even though the body's qualities such as form (rūpa) are present, warmth is not apprehended; only in the living state is it apprehended — hence it stands to reason —
BS_C04_S02_V11::block-1: that this warmth has its locus in something other than the well-known (gross) body. So too the śruti: ‘warm indeed when about to live, cold when about to die.’ ‖ 11 ‖
BS_C04_S02_V12: ‘If on account of the prohibition (it be argued that there is no departure for the knower of Brahman), (we say) no, (the prohibition is) from the embodied self.’ ‖ 12 ‖
BS_C04_S02_V12::block-0: (Pūrvapakṣa:) From the qualifying clause ‘And immortality (is obtained) without (the body) being burnt up’ (citation), the absence of going (gati) and departure (utkrānti) has been admitted in the case of absolute immortality. Even there, suspecting that for some reason there might still be a departure, the śruti negates it: ‘But of him who does not desire — who is desireless, freed from desire, whose desire is fulfilled, whose desire is the Self — the prāṇas do not depart; being Brahman itself, he merges in Brahman’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.6) (citation). Hence, on account of this prohibition pertaining to the higher knowledge (para-vidyā-viṣayāt pratiṣedhāt), there is no departure of the prāṇas from the body for the knower of the supreme Brahman — if this be urged, (the Sūtrakāra) replies: No. For this prohibition of the departure of the prāṇas is from the embodied self (śārīrāt — the jīva), not from the body (na śarīrāt). How is this known? Because in another recension the ablative (pañcamī) is used: ‘the prāṇas do not depart from him (na tasmāt prāṇā utkrāmanti)’. The genitive (ṣaṣṭhī), which has only a general relational sense, is restricted to a specific relation by the ablative found in the other recension. And by ‘from him’ (tasmāt), it is the embodied being qualified for prosperity (abhyudaya) and supreme good (niḥśreyasa) that is referred to by virtue of principality, not the body. The meaning is: from the jīva who is intent on departing, the prāṇas do not depart away — rather they remain together with him. And the departure from the body indeed belongs to one (a jīva) who is travelling forth along with the prāṇas (saprāṇasya pravasataḥ). ‖ 12 ‖
BS_C04_S02_V13: ‘For (the meaning) is clear in (the recension of) some.’ ‖ 13 ‖
BS_C04_S02_V13::block-0: (Leading bhāṣya — transition to siddhānta:) Such being the prima facie position, the reply is given —
