BS_C04_S02_V13::block-1: (Siddhānta:) What was urged — that even for the knower of supreme Brahman there is departure from the body, since the prohibition of departure has the embodied self as its ablative point of origin (dehy-apādānatva) — that is not so. For in the recension of some teachers (ekeṣāṃ samāmnātṝṇām) the prohibition of departure with the body itself as its point of origin (deha-apādāna) is clearly seen. Thus, in the questioning by Ārtabhāga: ‘When this person dies, do the prāṇas depart out from him or not?’ (Bṛ. Up. 3.2.11) (citation), and the response ‘ “No,” said Yājñavalkya’ (Bṛ. Up. 3.2.11) (citation), the position of non-departure is accepted. Then, in the apprehension ‘Has he then died with the prāṇas not having departed?’, the dissolution of the prāṇas is declared by ‘they are gathered together right here (atraiva samavanīyante)’; and to establish this, the puffing up etc. — ‘he swells, gets bloated, and the bloated one lies dead’ (Bṛ. Up. 3.2.11) (citation) — are stated as the limit (avadhi) of the departure of that one referred to by ‘sa’ (he). And these (swelling etc.) belong to the body, not to the embodied self. By that very analogy, even in ‘the prāṇas do not depart from him; they are gathered together right here’, it is by the figurative non-distinction (abheda-upacāra) the prohibition is of the departure that has the body as its point of origin — though the principal meaning belongs to the embodied being. Thus must it be explained for those who have the ablative reading. As for those who have the genitive reading (ṣaṣṭhī-pāṭha), it is the departure pertaining to the knower (vidvat-sambandhinī utkrānti) that is being prohibited; since the very purpose of this sentence is the prohibition of a departure that would otherwise have been obtained — and the departure obtained is from the body, not from the embodied self — the prohibition is of the departure with the body as its point of origin. Furthermore, having shown elaborately departure and saṃsāric going (utkramaṇa and saṃsāra-gamana) in the case of the unenlightened — ‘when he departs from the eye, or from the head, or from other regions of the body, the prāṇa departs after him; the prāṇa being the departure, all the prāṇas depart after him’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.2) (citation) — and concluding the discourse on the unenlightened with ‘so does the desiring one (kāmayamānaḥ)’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.6) (citation), and then designating the enlightened with ‘but the desireless one (akāmayamānaḥ)’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.6) (citation) — if even in his case (śruti) were to lead to departure alone, the very designation (vyapadeśa) would be incongruous (asamañjasa). Therefore, the prohibition is of the going and departure obtained in the case of the unenlightened, in the case of the enlightened — only thus must it be explained, in order that the designation (vyapadeśa) may have meaning (vyapadeśārthavattva). Nor is departure or going possible for the knower of Brahman — who has become identical with the all-pervading Brahman and whose desires and karmas are exhausted — there being no occasioning cause (nimitta-abhāva). And śruti texts of this kind such as ‘here he attains Brahman’ (citation) indicate the absence of going and departure. ‖ 13 ‖
BS_C04_S02_V14::block-0: The absence of going and departure is also recorded in smṛti, in the Mahābhārata: ‘For one who has become the Self of all beings, who sees all beings rightly, even the gods are bewildered on his path — they who seek the footprint of one who has no footprint (apadasya pada-eṣiṇaḥ)’ (M.Bh. 12.239.23) (citation). (Pūrvapakṣa objection:) But going too is recorded in smṛti for the knower of Brahman who has become identical with the all-pervading Brahman: ‘Śuka, the son of Vyāsa, desirous of liberation, is said to have set forth toward the orb of the sun; and being followed and called out to by his father, he responded with “bho!”’ — (so going is also recorded in smṛti). (Reply:) No; this should be understood as the casting off of the body preceded by the attainment of a particular region through the power of yoga, by one still endowed with body — because the account speaks of his being seen by all beings etc. For all beings cannot see one going forth bodiless. And accordingly it is concluded there itself: ‘Then Śuka, having made his pace swifter than the wind, traversed the sky’ (M.Bh. 12.333.19) (citation), ‘and having displayed his power, became one who is in all beings’ (M.Bh. 12.333.20) (citation). Therefore, for the knower of supreme Brahman there is the absence of going and departure. As for the śrutis that mention going (gati-śruti), we shall later explain their (proper) sphere of application. ‖ 14 ‖
BS_C04_S02_V15: ‘Those (merge) in the supreme; for thus does (śruti) declare.’ ‖ 15 ‖
BS_C04_S02_V15::block-0: Those (tāni) — namely the indriyas (sense-organs) and the bhūtas (elements) referred to by the word ‘prāṇa’ — in the case of the knower of supreme Brahman, dissolve in that very supreme Self (parasmin ātmani). How (is this known)? Because thus does the śruti say: ‘Even so do these sixteen kalās of this perceiver, having the puruṣa as their refuge, attaining the puruṣa, come to setting (asta)’ (Pra. Up. 6.5) (citation). (Pūrvapakṣa objection:) But ‘the fifteen kalās go to their resting-places’ (Mu. Up. 3.2.7) (citation) — this other śruti, pertaining to the knower, declares the dissolution of the kalās elsewhere than in the supreme Self. (Reply:) No. That śruti pertains to vyavahāra (empirical perspective) — the earthly etc. kalās return to earth etc., their respective material causes (sva-prakṛti). But the other (Praśna text) pertains to the cognitive realisation (pratipatti) of the knower — the entire collection of kalās of the knower of supreme Brahman becomes Brahman alone. Therefore there is no fault. ‖ 15 ‖
BS_C04_S02_V16: ‘(There is) non-distinction; on account of (scriptural) statement.’ ‖ 16 ‖
BS_C04_S02_V16::block-0: Now, is this dissolution of the kalās of the knower a partial one with a residue (sa-avaśeṣa), as in the case of others, or is it without remainder (niravaśeṣa)? Where, by reason of the general nature of the dissolution, the persistence of (the kalās in) potential form (śakty-avaśeṣatā) might be apprehended, (the Sūtrakāra) declares: it is verily the attainment of non-distinction (avibhāga-āpattir eva). Whence? On account of (scriptural) statement (vacanāt). For having stated the dissolution of the kalās, (the śruti) says: ‘Their name and form are dissolved, and one speaks merely thus: “puruṣa”; he becomes that one without parts, immortal’ (Pra. Up. 6.5) (citation). And of the kalās which are caused by avidyā, persistence with residue is not possible at the time of the dissolution caused by vidyā. Therefore it is non-distinction alone. ‖ 16 ‖
BS_C04_S02_V17: ‘(For him), there is the lighting up of the tip of his abode (the heart); through the door thus illumined, by virtue of the power of vidyā and through the constant remembering of the path which is an ancillary of that vidyā, favoured by the Lord seated in the heart, (he departs) by the one (nāḍī) which exceeds a hundred.’ ‖ 17 ‖
BS_C04_S02_V17::block-0: The incidental discussion concerning para-vidyā is concluded; now (the Sūtrakāra) resumes the discussion which is the proper subject — that of apara-vidyā. It has been said that, up to the entry into the path (ā-sṛty-upakramāt), the departure of the knower and the unknower is the same. (The Sūtrakāra) now points out that very entry into the path. Of that vijñāna-ātman (the cognitive self) — who has gathered together his vāc and other kalās and is about to depart — the okas (abode) is the heart (hṛdaya); for the śruti says: ‘That self, gathering up these portions of light, descends right into the heart’ (citation). And the departure is heard of as preceded by the lighting up of its tip and as having the eye and other stations as its place of egress (apādāna): ‘The tip of his heart shines forth; lit by that light, this self departs through the eye, or through the head, or through other regions of the body’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.2) (citation). Now, does this happen indiscriminately for the knower and the unknower (vidvad-aviduṣor anyatameṇa eva), or is there some special restriction (viśeṣa-niyama) for the knower? In this doubt — śruti being non-specific, indiscrimination might at first be supposed; but the Sūtrakāra declares: even when the lighting up of the tip of the heart and the entry through the door thus illumined are common to both, it is from the station of the head alone (mūrdha-sthānāt eva) that the knower departs, while the others depart from other stations. Whence? On account of the power of vidyā (vidyā-sāmarthyāt). If even the knower were to depart, like the rest, from any region of the body whatsoever, he would not attain the highest world, and his vidyā would be useless (anarthikā). And on account of the conjunction with the constant remembering (anusmṛti-yogāt) of the path which is an ancillary (śeṣa-bhūtā) of that vidyā: in particular vidyās, the path connected with the nāḍī of the head (mūrdhanya-nāḍī-sambaddhā gatiḥ) is enjoined as an ancillary of vidyā to be steadily contemplated. It is fitting that one practising it should set forth by that very path. Therefore, the knower — being favoured (anugṛhīta) by Brahman seated in the heart (hārda) when properly meditated upon, having attained identity with that Brahman — departs by the very head-going one which is the one in excess of a hundred (śatādhikā), the one hundred-and-first nāḍī (eka-śatatamī nāḍī); the others depart by the other (nāḍīs). For thus do (the texts) record with reference to the hārda-vidyā: ‘A hundred and one are the nāḍīs of the heart; of these one goes out toward the head; ascending by it one attains immortality; the others, in their various directions, serve for departure (in saṃsāra)’ (Chā. Up. 8.6.6) (citation). ‖ 17 ‖
BS_C04_S02_V18::block-0: There is a hārda-vidyā that is enjoined beginning with ‘Now, in this Brahman-city there is a small lotus-like dwelling’ (Chā. Up. 8.1.1) (citation). In its course, beginning with ‘Now these are the nāḍīs of the heart’ (Chā. Up. 8.6.1) (citation), having elaborately declared the conjunction of the nāḍīs and the rays, it has been said: ‘Then, when this (self) departs from this body, then by these very rays it ascends upward’ (Chā. Up. 8.6.5) (citation). Again it is said: ‘Ascending by it (the head-nāḍī) one attains immortality’ (Chā. Up. 8.6.6) (citation). Therefore it is understood that one departing by the nāḍī in excess of a hundred departs as a follower of a ray (raśmy-anusārī). Now, is the following of a ray (something that holds) without distinction (aviśeṣeṇa) for one who dies by day or by night, or only by day? In this doubt, since śruti speaks without distinction (aviśeṣa-śravaṇāt), it is first laid down that the soul follows a ray without distinction. ‖ 18 ‖
BS_C04_S02_V19: ‘ “Not at night,” if it be said, (we say) no; for the connection lasts as long as the body; and (śruti) shows (this).’ ‖ 19 ‖
BS_C04_S02_V19::block-0: (Pūrvapakṣa:) The connection of the nāḍīs and the rays exists by day; therefore for one dying by day there might be the following of a ray. But for one departing by night there could not be — because the connection of the nāḍīs and the rays is broken — if this be said, (we say) no; because the connection of the nāḍīs and the rays lasts as long as the body lasts (yāvad-deha-bhāvitvāt). For the connection of the veins and the rays is co-extensive with the body. And the śruti shows this very meaning: ‘From that yonder sun (these rays) extend; they are spread out into these nāḍīs; and from these nāḍīs they extend, they are spread out into that yonder sun’ (Chā. Up. 8.6.2) (citation). Even in the season of summer, the persistence of the rays even at night is observed, from the perception of the effects such as warmth etc. The slight persistence is hard to perceive in the nights of other seasons — as in cloudy days in winter. And ‘this very day-time it deposits in the night’ (citation) shows the same. Moreover, if one dying at night could ascend upward without dependence on a ray, the dependence on a ray would become useless (anarthakya). For it is not specifically taught that one who dies by day, depending on the rays, ascends upward, but the one who dies at night ascends without depending on them. Now, if even the knower, by the mere fault of dying at night, were not to ascend upward, vidyā would have its fruit only contingently (pākṣika-phalā), and there would be a non-engagement (apravṛtti) with it — because the time of death is not fixed. Even were he, dying at night, to wait for the coming of dawn — even at the coming of dawn his body might sometimes be unfit for connection with the rays, owing to its contact with fire (cremation) etc. And the śruti — ‘In the time it takes the mind to be flung, in that time he reaches the sun’ (Chā. Up. 8.6.5) (citation) — shows the absence of any waiting. Therefore, this following of a ray applies indiscriminately, both by night and by day. ‖ 19 ‖
BS_C04_S02_V20: And for this very reason, even when [death occurs] in the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) [the knower attains the fruit of knowledge]. ‖ 20 ‖
BS_C04_S02_V20::block-0: For these very reasons — because waiting (until uttarāyaṇa) is not feasible, because the fruit of vidyā is not dependent on a fortnight (apākṣika-phalatva), and because the time of death is not predetermined (aniyata-kālatva) — the knower (vidvān), even while dying in the dakṣiṇāyana (southern course), assuredly attains the fruit of vidyā. By this sūtra, the Ācārya removes the following doubt: ‘Because the prevalence of the praise of dying in the uttarāyaṇa is well-known, because Bhīṣma is seen to have waited (for the uttarāyaṇa), and because of the śruti — ‘the six (months) during which (the sun) goes north from the waxing fortnight onwards’ (Chā. Up. 4.15.5) — the uttarāvayaṇa must be awaited.’ The renown of the praise (of dying in uttarāyaṇa) pertains to the non-knower (avidvad-viṣayā). Bhīṣma's awaiting of the uttarāyaṇa was for the sake of upholding (worldly) custom (ācāra-paripālana) and to make known the fact that he had obtained from his father the boon of dying at will (svacchanda-mṛtyutā). The meaning of the śruti, however, the Ācārya will state in ‘ātivāhikāstalliṅgāt’ (Br. Sū. 4.3.4). ‖ 20 ‖
BS_C04_S02_V21: And [the time of going] is mentioned with reference to yogins; and these two (paths) belong to smṛti. ‖ 21 ‖
BS_C04_S02_V21::block-0: [Pūrvapakṣa]: But surely, having begun by giving primacy to time — ‘O bull of the Bharatas, I shall declare to you that time at which yogins, departing, attain non-return and (also) return’ (Bha. Gī. 8.23) — particular times such as day and so on are laid down in smṛti for non-return. How, then, can one departing in the night or in the dakṣiṇāyana attain non-return? — to this it is replied:
BS_C04_S02_V21::block-1: [Siddhānta]: With reference to yogins this assignment of times — day, etc. — for non-return is mentioned in smṛti (smaryate). And these two — yoga and sāṅkhya — are smārta (belonging to smṛti), not śrauta. Therefore, owing to the difference of subject-matter (viṣaya-bheda) and the difference of pramāṇa (pramāṇa-viśeṣa), this smārta assignment of times has no entry into the cognitions taught in śruti (śrauteṣu vijñāneṣu). [Pūrvapakṣa]: But ‘fire, light, day, the bright (fortnight), the six months of the northern course’ (Bha. Gī. 8.24); ‘smoke, night, the dark (fortnight), the six months of the southern course’ (Bha. Gī. 8.25) — these very śrauta deva-yāna and pitṛ-yāna are also recognised (pratyabhijñāyete) in the smṛti. [Reply]: It is said — since in the smṛti, by the declaration ‘I shall declare to you that time’ (Bha. Gī. 8.23) there is a promise of (instruction about) time, suspecting a contradiction (with what is stated in śruti), this rebuttal has been given. But when, in smṛti also, fire and the rest are taken (gṛhyante) as the very deities that are conductors (ātivāhikyaḥ), then there is no contradiction whatever. ‖ 21 ‖
BS_C04_S03_INTRO1::block-0: It has been stated up to (the topic of) the path (āsṛtyupakramāt) that there is identity of utkrānti (departure for both knower and non-knower). The path (sṛti), however, is described in various ways in different śrutis — one (path) connected with nāḍī and rays: ‘Then by these very rays he ascends upward’ (Chā. Up. 8.6.5); another beginning with arcis: ‘They reach the flame, from the flame the day’ (Bṛ. Up. 6.2.15); another: ‘Having attained that path of the gods, he reaches the world of fire’ (Kau. Up. 1.3); yet another: ‘When a person departs from this world, he reaches the wind’ (Bṛ. Up. 5.10.1); and another: ‘Through the door of the sun they go free of dust’ (Mu. Up. 1.2.11). Here arises the doubt — are these paths different from one another, or is there but one (path) qualified by many specifications? [Pūrvapakṣa]: There it is concluded — these paths are different, because of the difference of contexts (bhinna-prakaraṇatva) and because they are subsidiary to different upāsanās (bhinna-upāsanā-śeṣatva). Moreover, the restriction (avadhāraṇa) ‘Then by these very rays’ (Chā. Up. 8.6.5) would be obstructed if arcis and the rest were also expected, and the statement of swiftness — ‘In the time it takes to throw the mind, he goes to the sun’ (Chā. Up. 8.6.5) — would also be impeded. Therefore these are paths mutually different. This being so attained, we declare —
BS_C04_S03_V01: By the (path) beginning with arcis, on account of its being well-known. ‖ 1 ‖
BS_C04_S03_V01::block-0: ‘Arcirādinā’ (by the path of arcis etc.) — we maintain that every aspirant for Brahman travels by the very path beginning with arcis. Why? ‘Tat-prathiteḥ’ — because that path is well-known (prathita). Indeed this path is well-known for all knowers. Thus, in the section on the pañcāgni-vidyā, ‘And those who in the forest worship faith and truth’ (Bṛ. Up. 6.2.15) — even of those given to other vidyās, the arcirādi path is heard of. [Pūrvapakṣa]: Let it be so — in those vidyās in which no path is mentioned, let the arcirādi path obtain. But where another (path) is heard, why should the arcirādi be resorted to? [Siddhānta]: It is replied — this would be so if these paths were utterly different from one another. But we say that there is but one path, qualified by many specifications, leading to brahmaloka, characterised in different places by different specifications, since one part is recognised in all (sarvatraikadeśa-pratyabhijñāna) and the relation of mutual qualifier-qualified is feasible. Even when the contexts (prakaraṇa) differ, since the vidyā is one, just as the mutual specifications are gathered together (itaretara-viśeṣaṇopasaṃhāra), so too are the path-specifications gathered. And even when the vidyās differ, on account of the recognition of one part of the path and the non-difference of the goal (gantavyābheda), there is non-difference of the path itself. Thus — ‘In those brahma-worlds they dwell for vast eons’ (Bṛ. Up. 6.2.15), ‘There they dwell for everlasting years’ (Bṛ. Up. 5.10.1), ‘That conquest which is brahman's, that prosperity — that conquest he conquers, that prosperity he attains’ (Kau. Up. 1.7), ‘He who through brahmacarya finds out this brahmaloka’ (Chā. Up. 8.4.3) — in all these, the very same one fruit, namely attainment of brahmaloka (brahmaloka-prāpti-lakṣaṇa), is shown. As to the objection that the restriction ‘by these very’ would not stand if arcis-etc. were resorted to — that is no fault, since this (statement) aims at attainment of the rays (raśmi-prāpti-paratvāt). For one and the same word cannot both effect attainment of the rays and exclude arcis etc. Therefore it should be understood that only the connection with the rays is being affirmed by this restriction. The mention of swiftness, even when arcis-etc. are presupposed, is not obstructed, because it is intended to express speediness in comparison with other (longer) paths to be traversed — as when it is said ‘he reaches there in the time of a wink.’ Moreover, the passage ‘then by neither of these two paths’ (Chā. Up. 5.10.8), declaring the painful third place for those fallen from both paths, makes known apart from the pitṛyāna only one deva-yāna path, namely the one with arcis as its first stage. The stages on the arcirādi path are many; on the others, fewer. Since it is reasonable to lead the few in conformity with the many, hence too it is said ‘arcirādinā tatprathiteḥ.’ ‖ 1 ‖
BS_C04_S03_V02: (They reach) the wind, from (after) the year (saṃvatsara), on account of non-specification and specification. ‖ 2 ‖
BS_C04_S03_V02::block-0: By what specific arrangement, then, is the relation of mutual qualifier-qualified among the path-specifications? — this the Ācārya, taking on the role of friend, weaves together. ‘Having attained that path of the gods, he reaches the world of fire, then the world of wind, then the world of Varuṇa, then the world of the sun, then the world of Indra, then the world of Prajāpati, then the world of Brahman’ (Kau. Up. 1.3) — thus the Kauṣītakins recite the deva-yāna path. There, the words ‘arcis’ and ‘fire-world’ have one meaning, since both denote flame (jvalana-vacanatva); hence no order of placement need be sought there. But the wind, being unmentioned in the arcirādi path, in which place is it to be inserted? — it is replied: ‘They reach the flame; from the flame, the day; from the day, the waxing fortnight; from the waxing fortnight, those six months in which the (sun) goes northward’ (Chā. Up. 5.10.1); ‘from the months, the year; from the year, the sun’ (Chā. Up. 5.10.2) — here, beyond the year and before the sun, they reach the wind. Why? On account of avi-śeṣa and viśeṣa (non-specification and specification). For at ‘sa vāyulokam’ (Kau. Up. 1.3), wind is taught without specification (aviśeṣopadiṣṭa), while in another śruti specification is seen — ‘When a person departs from this world, he reaches the wind. There it (the wind) makes for him an opening as wide as the hub of a chariot-wheel; through that he ascends upward and reaches the sun’ (Bṛ. Up. 5.10.1). From this seeing of the wind's priority to the sun (the specification), wind is to be placed between the year and the sun. Why, then, is the wind not placed immediately after arcis, on the strength of seeing it after fire (in the Kau. Up.)? We say there is no such specification (in that passage). [Pūrvapakṣa]: But the cited śruti says — ‘Having attained that path of the gods, he reaches the agniloka, the vāyuloka, the varuṇaloka’ (Kau. Up. 1.3). [Reply]: It is said — there it is mere recital placed in sequence (paurvāparyeṇāvasthitaḥ pāṭhaḥ); there is no word indicative of order (krama-vacana). Only an enumeration of items is being made there — ‘he reaches this and this.’ But in the other (passage) the order is grasped: ‘ascending upward through an opening as wide as a chariot-wheel given by the wind, he reaches the sun.’ Therefore it is rightly said ‘aviśeṣa-viśeṣābhyām.’ The Vājasaneyins, however, recite ‘from the months, the deva-loka; from the deva-loka, the sun’ (Bṛ. Up. 6.2.15). There, for the sake of immediacy with the sun, they should reach the wind from the deva-loka. ‘From the cloud (or year), the wind’ (vāyumabdāt) is, however, stated with reference to the Chāndogya śruti. In the Chāndogya and Vājasaneyaka, in one the deva-loka is absent, in the other the saṃvatsara. There, by accepting the testimony of both śrutis, both should be threaded into both. Even there, by virtue of the connection with the months, the saṃvatsara comes first, the deva-loka after — thus it should be discriminated. ‖ 2 ‖
BS_C04_S03_V03: Above the lightning, Varuṇa, on account of the connection. ‖ 3 ‖
BS_C04_S03_V03::block-0: ‘From the sun the moon, from the moon the lightning’ (Chā. Up. 4.15.5) — above this lightning, ‘sa varuṇalokam’ — this Varuṇa is connected. For there is a connection between lightning and Varuṇa. When vast lightnings, with the resounding crashes of intense thunder, dance in the bellies of clouds, then the waters fall. And there is the brāhmaṇa: ‘It lightens, it thunders, it will rain’ (Chā. Up. 7.11.1). And the lordship of waters belonging to Varuṇa is well-known in śruti and smṛti. Above Varuṇa come Indra and Prajāpati, since there is no other place (for them) and by virtue of the recital. Also, since Varuṇa and the rest are adventitious (āgantukatva), their placement is at the very end, there being no special station (for them). And lightning is the last on the arcirādi path. ‖ 3 ‖
BS_C04_S03_V04: (They are) conductors (ātivāhikas), on account of the indicatory mark of that. ‖ 4 ‖
BS_C04_S03_V04::block-0: Now in those very (entities) — arcis and the rest — there is a doubt: are these mere mile-marks of the path (mārga-cihnāni), or scenes of enjoyment (bhoga-bhūmayaḥ), or conductors of the travellers (netāraḥ)? [Pūrvapakṣa]: There it is first established that arcis and the rest are characteristics of the path (mārga-lakṣaṇa-bhūtāḥ), since the teaching is of that very form. Just as in the world someone setting out for a village or town is instructed — ‘Go from here; (you will reach) such-and-such mountain, then a banyan, then a river, then you will reach the village or town’ — so here too: ‘from arcis the day, from the day the waxing fortnight,’ etc. Or, alternatively, it is established that they are scenes of enjoyment. Thus the word ‘loka’ is appended to fire and the rest — ‘he reaches the agniloka’ (Kau. Up. 1.3), etc. And the word ‘loka’ is used for the abodes of enjoyment of beings: ‘the manuṣya-loka, pitṛ-loka, deva-loka’ (Bṛ. Up. 1.5.16). And the brāhmaṇa: ‘In those days-and-nights they are attached to those worlds,’ etc. Therefore arcis and the rest are not ātivāhikas. Owing to their unconsciousness (acetanatva) too, their being ātivāhikas is not feasible. For in the world, conscious men appointed by the king conduct travellers across forts and roads. [Siddhānta]: This being so attained, we say — these (arcis and the rest) must be ātivāhikas alone. Why? On account of the indicatory mark (talliṅgāt). Thus — ‘from the moon to the lightning; from the lightning a non-human person — he leads them to brahman’ (Chā. Up. 4.15.5) — here the conducting (gamayitṛtva) is shown as established. [Objection]: That statement is exhausted in that very topic. [Reply]: No — for the qualification (amānava) aims at excluding (the implication of) being human, which would otherwise be obtained. If men were obtained as conductors among arcis and the rest, and they were human, then it is appropriate that for the sake of excluding that, the qualification ‘amānava’ (non-human) be given to ‘puruṣa.’ ‖ 4 ‖
BS_C04_S03_V05: Because of the bewilderment of both, that (conductorship) is established. ‖ 5 ‖
BS_C04_S03_V05::block-0: [Pūrvapakṣa]: But that liṅga alone is not conclusive (agamaka), there being no logical ground (nyāyābhāva). [Reply]: This is no fault —
BS_C04_S03_V05::block-1: Those who travel by the arcirādi path, having separated from the body, have their group of organs withdrawn (sampiṇḍita-karaṇa-grāma) and so are not independent (asvatantra); arcis and the rest, being unconscious, are also not independent — therefore conscious deities, presiding over arcis and the rest, are appointed for the journeying-across (atiyātrāyāṃ niyuktāḥ). For in the world too, the intoxicated, the swooning, etc., having their organs withdrawn, are made to travel by the impulse of others (parapra-yukta-vartmāno bhavanti). Owing to their unsteadiness (anavasthitatva) too, arcis and the rest cannot serve as path-marks. For of one who has died at night, encountering the very form of day is not feasible, and there is no waiting (pratipālana), as has been stated previously. But owing to the permanence (dhruvatvāt) of the deity-selves, this fault does not arise. And their being denoted by the words ‘arcis’ etc. is feasible because of their presiding over arcis and the rest (arcir-ādy-abhimāna). The expression ‘from arcis the day’ (Chā. Up. 4.15.5) is not contradicted even when (they are) ātivāhikas — through arcis as cause one reaches the day, through the day as cause the waxing fortnight, etc. Likewise, in the world too, with regard to well-known ātivāhikas (conducting officers), this kind of teaching is seen — ‘Go from here to Balavarman, then to Jayasiṃha, then to Kṛṣṇagupta.’ Moreover, in the introduction (upakrama) ‘they reach arcis’ (Bṛ. Up. 6.2.15) only mere connection (sambandha-mātra) is mentioned, not any specific connection. But in the conclusion (upasaṃhāra) ‘he leads them to brahman’ (Chā. Up. 4.15.5), a specific connection — namely that of conducted-and-conductor (ativāhya-ativāhakatva) — is stated. By this, that very same (relation) is determined for the upakrama too. And precisely on account of the withdrawal of the organs of the travellers, there is no possibility of enjoyment (bhoga-sambhava) there. The word ‘loka,’ even when the travellers are not enjoying, can be applied (because of) the others, the dwellers in those lokas, who use them as scenes of enjoyment. Hence the connection should be made: having reached the loka of which fire is the master, he is conducted across by fire; having reached that of which wind is the master, by wind. ‖ 5 ‖
BS_C04_S03_V06: By the lightning itself, thereafter (does the soul reach Brahman); for so the scripture declares. ‘vaidyutenaiva tatas tac-chruteḥ’ (4.3.6).
BS_C04_S03_V06::block-0: [Leading bhāṣya — anticipation of objection] But how, on the view that (the deities Varuṇa and the rest) are conductors-along-the-way (ātivāhika), is their inclusion at all possible here? For Varuṇa and the others have been mentioned as superintending stations above the lightning (vidyut); whereas, after the lightning, all the way up to the attainment of Brahman, scripture declares the leading-onward to be carried out by the non-human Person (amānava-puruṣa) alone. — Hence the answer is given in the next sūtra:
BS_C04_S03_V06::block-1: [Bhāṣya — siddhānta] After ascending into (or being met by) the lightning — that is, beyond the lightning — it is by the non-human Person (amānava-puruṣa), who comes immediately after the lightning, that they (the upāsakas) are conducted onward through the world of Varuṇa and the rest, and reach Brahmaloka. So it is to be understood. For the scripture declares precisely this Person to be the conductor: ‘Then a Person who is non-human comes from the lightning; he, having come, leads them to the world of Brahman’ (Br̥hadāraṇyaka 6.2.15 / Chāndogya 4.15.5) — (citation). As for Varuṇa and the others, they are merely auxiliaries, helping along by not putting up obstruction (a-pratibandha-karaṇa) or by performing some assistance (sāhāya-anuṣṭhāna). Therefore it has been well stated that the conductors-along-the-way (ātivāhika) are deity-souls beginning with Arcis (the flame). ‖ 6 ‖
BS_C04_S03_V07: (That to which the soul is conducted is) the effected (kārya, i.e. lower / saguṇa) Brahman — so holds Bādari, because going (gati) is logically possible (only with respect to it). ‘kāryaṁ bādarir asya gaty-upapatteḥ’ (4.3.7).
BS_C04_S03_V07::block-0: [Bhāṣya — pūrvapakṣa of Bādari, beginning the new adhikaraṇa] Concerning the passage ‘He leads them to Brahman’ (Chāndogya 4.15.5) — (citation), an inquiry is raised: is it the effected (kārya), the lower (apara) Brahman that he leads them to, or is it the supreme (para), unmodified (avikr̥ta), principal (mukhya) Brahman? Whence the doubt? From the use of the very word ‘brahman’ (which is shared by both), and from the scriptural mention of ‘going’ (gati). Thereon, the ācārya Bādari holds: it is the effected, qualified (saguṇa), lower Brahman alone that the non-human Person leads them to. Why? ‘Because going is intelligible (only) with respect to it’ — for the effected Brahman, possessing locality (pradeśavattva), can intelligibly be ‘that which is to be reached.’ But with respect to the supreme Brahman, neither the status of goer, nor that of goal, nor going itself, can stand — since (the supreme) is all-pervading (sarva-gata) and is the inmost Self (pratyag-ātman) of those who would do the going. ‖ 7 ‖
BS_C04_S03_V08: And because of (the goal’s) being qualified (specified by particularising features in another text). ‘viśeṣitatvāc ca’ (4.3.8).
BS_C04_S03_V08::block-0: [Bhāṣya — pūrvapakṣa continued] In another scripture also — ‘He leads them to the Brahmā-worlds (in the plural); in those Brahmā-worlds they dwell as the highest, far away’ (Br̥hadāraṇyaka 6.2.15) — (citation), the goal is qualified (viśeṣita), and from this it is understood that the going pertains only to the effected (kārya) Brahman. For specification by the plural (bahuvacana) is not intelligible with regard to the supreme Brahman; whereas in the case of the effected (Brahman) the plural is possible, since differentiation by stages/states (avasthā-bheda) is admissible there. The śruti-word ‘loka’ (world) too applies in its primary (āñjasī) sense only to a place of enjoyment (bhoga-bhūmi) endowed with arrangement (sannivesa-viśiṣṭā), and that lies within the domain of the modified (vikāra-gocara). It applies only secondarily (gauṇī) elsewhere, as in ‘Brahman alone is the world (loka), O emperor’ — (citation). Likewise, the designation of (the world as) substratum (adhikaraṇa) and of (the soul as) one to be placed there (adhikartavya) would not be straight-forward (anāñjasaḥ) in the supreme Brahman. Hence this leading-onward (nayana) has only the effected (Brahman) for its sphere. ‖ 8 ‖
BS_C04_S03_V09: But (the use of the word ‘Brahman’ for the lower Brahman is) on account of nearness (sāmīpya) (to the supreme Brahman) — hence that designation. ‘sāmīpyāt tu tad-vyapadeśaḥ’ (4.3.9).
BS_C04_S03_V09::block-0: [Leading bhāṣya — objection] But (it may be objected): even with regard to the effected (kārya), the word ‘brahman’ is not justified, for in the Samanvaya (sūtras) it has been established that ‘Brahman is the cause of the birth, etc., of the entire universe.’ — To this it is replied:
BS_C04_S03_V09::block-1: [Bhāṣya — siddhānta within the pūrvapakṣa-stretch] The word ‘tu’ (‘but’) is for setting aside the doubt. By reason of the lower Brahman’s nearness (sāmīpya) to the supreme Brahman, the application of the word ‘brahman’ even to it is not contradicted. For the established position (sthiti) is this: the very same supreme Brahman, when, in connection with a pure limiting adjunct (viśuddha-upādhi-sambandha), is taught here and there for the purpose of upāsanā by means of certain attributes belonging to the modification — such as ‘consisting of mind’ (mano-mayatva) and so forth — is (then designated) ‘the lower’ (apara). ‖ 9 ‖
BS_C04_S03_V10: On the dissolution of the effected (Brahmaloka), they (the upāsakas), along with the ruler thereof (Hiraṇyagarbha), reach what is higher than that — for so the scripture declares. ‘kāryātyaye tad-adhyakṣeṇa sahātaḥ param abhidhānāt’ (4.3.10).
BS_C04_S03_V10::block-0: [Leading bhāṣya — objection] But (it may again be objected): on the attainment of the effected (Brahmaloka), the scriptural statement of ‘non-return’ (anāvr̥tti) does not fit. For nowhere outside the supreme Brahman is eternality even imagined. And scripture does declare non-return for those who have set out by the path of the gods (devayāna): ‘Those who proceed by this (path) do not return to this human cycle’ (Chāndogya 4.15.5) — (citation); and ‘For them there is here no return’ — (citation); and ‘Going upwards by them, one attains immortality’ (Chāndogya 8.6.6 / Kaṭha 2.3.16) — (citation). — To this we reply:
BS_C04_S03_V10::block-1: [Bhāṣya — siddhānta] When the dissolution (pralaya) of the effected Brahmaloka comes upon them, those who have, while there, attained perfect knowledge (utpanna-samyag-darśana), together with its ruler, Hiraṇyagarbha, attain thereafter the supremely pure highest state of Viṣṇu (viṣṇoḥ paramaṁ padam) — thus a gradual liberation (krama-mukti) is to be admitted, on the strength of the texts speaking of non-return and so forth. For (as has already been shown in this very pāda), the attainment of the supreme, preceded by literal going, is simply impossible. ‖ 10 ‖
BS_C04_S03_V11: And from smr̥ti (the same is established). ‘smr̥teś ca’ (4.3.11).
BS_C04_S03_V11::block-0: [Bhāṣya — siddhānta concluded (Bādari’s view ratified)] Smr̥ti also concedes this very point: ‘Together with Brahmā (Hiraṇyagarbha), all of them, when the (Brahma-)reabsorption (pratisañcara) has come on, those of perfected souls, at the end of the supreme (Brahmā), enter the supreme state (paraṁ padam)’ — (citation). Therefore, the conclusion (siddhānta) is: the śrutis speaking of going (gati-śrutayaḥ) have only the effected Brahman for their sphere. ‖ 11 ‖
BS_C04_S03_V12: (They reach) the supreme (Brahman), says Jaimini — because of (its) primary (sense). ‘paraṁ jaiminir mukhyatvāt’ (4.3.12).
BS_C04_S03_V12::block-0: [Leading bhāṣya — pūrvapakṣa now displayed via sūtras] Now, anticipating which view as pūrvapakṣa was the present siddhānta established by ‘kāryaṁ bādariḥ’ (4.3.7) etc.? — that very (anticipated view) is now exhibited by the sūtras themselves:
BS_C04_S03_V12::block-1: [Bhāṣya — Jaimini’s view, here functioning as the displayed pūrvapakṣa] But the ācārya Jaimini holds that, in the passage ‘He leads them to Brahman’ (Chāndogya 4.15.5) — (citation), it is the supreme Brahman alone to which (the non-human Person) leads them. Why? ‘Mukhyatvāt’ — because of (its being the) principal (sense). For the supreme Brahman is the principal (mukhya) referent of the word ‘brahman’; the lower (apara) is its secondary (gauṇa) referent; and between the principal and the secondary, the (correct) understanding settles on the principal. ‖ 12 ‖
BS_C04_S03_V13: And from observation (in scripture, this is established). ‘darśanāc ca’ (4.3.13).
BS_C04_S03_V13::block-0: [Bhāṣya — pūrvapakṣa (Jaimini’s side) continues] ‘Going upwards by them, one attains immortality’ (Chāndogya 8.6.6 / Kaṭha 2.3.16) — (citation): here, scripture shows immortality preceded by going (gati-pūrvakam amr̥tatvam). And immortality is intelligible only in the supreme Brahman, not in the effected, since the effected is perishable (vināśitvāt) — ‘Now, where one sees something else… that is small… that is mortal’ (Chāndogya 7.24.1) — (citation). Moreover, in the Kaṭhavallī this very going is read as having only the supreme for its object; for there, no separate vidyā is being introduced, since by ‘that which is other than dharma, other than adharma…’ (Kaṭha 1.2.14) — (citation), it is the supreme Brahman itself that is under discussion (prakrāntatva). ‖ 13 ‖
BS_C04_S03_V14: And the resolve to attain (the abode) is not with reference to the Effect (Hiraṇyagarbha-Brahman). (14)
BS_C04_S03_V14::block-0: Moreover, the text ‘I take refuge in the assembly-hall, the abode of Prajāpati’ (Chā. Up. 8.14.1) does not have the Effect (kārya-Brahman) as its object of resolve. For the Supreme Brahman alone, distinct from the Effect, is the topic under consideration, as is shown by ‘That which is the Sustainer (nirvahitā) of name and form, that which is between (yad antarā), that is Brahman’ (Chā. Up. 8.14.1). And by the opening declaration of all-Self-hood, ‘I become the glory (yaśas) of brāhmaṇas’ (Chā. Up. 8.14.1). Moreover, the having of glory as a name belongs to the Supreme Brahman alone, as established by ‘There is no likeness of Him whose name is great glory (mahad yaśaḥ)’ (Śve. Up. 4.19). And this very ‘taking-refuge in the abode’ has been already mentioned in the Dahara-vidyā (Hārda-vidyā) as preceded by going (gati-pūrvikā) — ‘That unconquered citadel of Brahman, the golden mansion measured by the Lord (prabhu-vimitam hiraṇmayam)’ (Chā. Up. 8.5.3). And since the root √pad too has the sense of going, dependence on a path is determined. Therefore, the gati-śrutis (texts of going) have the Supreme Brahman as their object — this is an alternative position. Thus the Ācārya has formulated two views in the sūtras — one based on the appropriateness of going etc. (gati-upapatti-ādi), the other based on primary sense etc. (mukhyatva-ādi). Of these, the appropriateness-of-going considerations are competent to make the primary-sense considerations appear as merely apparent (ābhāsayitum), but the primary-sense considerations cannot do likewise to the appropriateness-of-going considerations. Therefore the first itself has been expounded as the siddhānta, while the second is the pūrvapakṣa. There is indeed no commander to enjoin: ‘Take only the primary sense even when (a non-primary sense) is possible.’ Even in a section dealing with the Supreme-Knowledge (para-vidyā), the recital of the going (gati) which belongs to other vidyās is fitting for the sake of praising it (tat-stuty-artham) — just as ‘In the case of others, (the prāṇas) depart in different directions at the time of leaving’ (Chā. Up. 8.6.6). And ‘I take refuge in the assembly of Prajāpati’ (Chā. Up. 8.14.1), being severed from the previous sentence, is not inconsistent with a resolve relating even to the Effect. And in saguṇa-Brahman too, the proclamation of all-Self-hood is acceptable, just like ‘all-action, all-desire’ etc. Therefore, the gati-śrutis pertain only to the Lower (Brahman). (pūrvapakṣa)
BS_C04_S03_V14::block-1: But some, adhering to the rule that the prior sūtras are pūrvapakṣa-sūtras and the latter are siddhānta-sūtras, establish that the gati-śrutis pertain only to the Supreme (para-Brahman). That is untenable, because Brahman cannot stand as ‘that which is to be reached’ (gantavyatva). For that Supreme Brahman which is all-pervading, innermost of all, and the Self of all — whose distinguishing features are ascertained by śrutis like ‘Like ākāśa, all-pervading and eternal’; ‘That which is Brahman directly, not indirect’ (Bṛ. Up. 3.4.1); ‘the Self that is innermost of all’ (Bṛ. Up. 3.4.1); ‘All this is verily the Self’ (Chā. Up. 7.25.2); ‘Brahman alone is this universe, the most excellent’ (Mu. Up. 2.2.12) — for that, never can the status of being-reached be appropriate. For that which is already attained is not (further) reached. ‘One thing reaches another’ — this is well-known in the world. (Objection): But in the world, even what is already attained is seen to be a thing-to-be-reached when distinguished by another locus — as one standing on earth goes to (another part of) the earth via different regions; just so, even though there is non-difference, for a child the old age associated with another time, though one’s own self, is seen as a thing-to-be-reached; in the same way for Brahman too, since it possesses all powers, somehow being-reached may obtain. (Reply): No, because all distinctions are negated of Brahman. By śrutis, smṛtis and reasoning such as ‘partless, actionless, tranquil, faultless, taintless’ (Śve. Up. 6.19); ‘not gross, not minute, not short, not long’ (Bṛ. Up. 3.8.8); ‘unborn, both inside and outside’ (Mu. Up. 2.1.2); ‘That, indeed, is the great unborn Self, undecaying, immortal, deathless, fearless, Brahman’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.25); ‘That Self is — “Not thus, not thus”’ (Bṛ. Up. 3.9.26) — no association with distinctions of place, time, etc. can be imagined in the Supreme Self, by which, on the analogy of regions of the earth or stages of life, it could be a thing-to-be-reached. For the earth and (life-) age, the being-reached qualified by space and time is fitting because of association with distinctions of region, condition and so on. (Objection): From the śruti regarding (Brahman’s) being the cause of the universe’s origin, sustenance and dissolution, Brahman has manifold powers. (Reply): No, because the śrutis negating distinctions are not directed to anything else (ananyārtha — they have no further purpose). (Objection): The same holds equally of śrutis on origination etc. — they too are non-secondary in import. (Reply): No, because those (origination śrutis) are directed to teaching Oneness (ekatva-pratipādana-paratvāt). For the śāstra, by examples like clay etc., teaches the reality (satyatva) of the One existent Brahman and the unreality (anṛtatva) of the modification — it cannot be intent on origination etc.
BS_C04_S03_V14::block-2: (Objection): Why then are the śrutis of origination etc. supplementary (śeṣa) to the śrutis of negation-of-distinctions, and not the latter to the former? — Reply: Because the śrutis of negation-of-distinctions have a self-complete, expectation-free meaning (nirākāṅkṣa-arthatva). For when there is the cognition of the Self’s oneness, eternity, purity etc., no further expectation arises, since the consummation of human ends (puruṣārtha-samāpti) is grasped — as per ‘What delusion, what sorrow, for one who sees Oneness?’ (Īśa Up. 7); ‘Janaka, you have attained fearlessness’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.2.4); ‘The knower fears nothing whatever. This very (fearless one) is not afflicted (by the thought) — “Why did I not do good? Why did I do evil?”’ (Tai. Up. 2.9.1). And likewise it is observed that the wise experience contentment etc.; and there is also condemnation of resolves regarding modification and the unreal — ‘He goes from death to death, who sees here as if there were many’ (Kaṭha 2.1.10 / Bṛ. Up. 4.4.19). Therefore, the śrutis negating distinctions cannot be understood as supplementary to anything else. The śrutis of origination etc., on the other hand, do not have the capacity to teach an expectation-free meaning. Their being directed to another purpose (anyārthatva) is plainly observed. Thus: ‘There, dear, recognize this sprout that has come up — it will not be without a root’ (Chā. Up. 6.8.3) — having proposed thus, the text shows that subsequently the One existent root of the world alone is to be cognized; and ‘That from which these beings are born, by which when born they live, into which on departing they enter — That seek to know. That is Brahman’ (Tai. Up. 3.1.1). Thus, since the śrutis of origination etc. are directed at the cognition of one-Selfhood (aikātmya-avagama), Brahman is not to be associated with manifold powers. And hence the unfittingness of being-reached. ‘His prāṇas do not depart’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.6) and ‘Being Brahman alone, he attains Brahman’ — these too negate going in respect of the Supreme Brahman. This has been explained at ‘It is clear (in the texts) of some’ (Br. Sū. 4.2.13). (siddhānta begins)
BS_C04_S03_V14::block-3: Further, in the postulation of going, the goer would be the jīva, and the to-be-reached Brahman would either be a part, a modification, or wholly other than him — for in absolute identity (atyanta-tādātmya), going is impossible. (Objection): If so, what then? (Reply): It is said — if (the jīva is) a part (eka-deśa), then since the part-possessor is eternally attained by the part, no further reaching of Brahman is possible. The conception of part and part-possessor is moreover impossible in Brahman, since its being partless (niravayava) is well established. The same holds in the modification view, for the modifier (vikārin) is eternally attained by its modification too. The pot does not abide having abandoned its clay-nature; on abandoning it, non-existence would result. And in the part-view and modification-view, since their possessor is fixed, even saṃsāric going of Brahman would be inadmissible. Now, if the jīva is altogether other than Brahman, he must be either atomic, all-pervading, or of medium size. If all-pervading, going is impossible. If of medium size, impermanence would follow. If atomic, the cognition of the entire body would be impossible. Both atomicity and medium-size have been refuted in detail earlier. And on (the view of) the jīva’s being other than the Supreme, scriptures like ‘That thou art’ (Chā. Up. 6.8.7) would be contradicted. The same defect applies in the part-view and modification-view too. (Objection): Since a modification or part is non-different from its possessor, this is not a defect. (Reply): No, for the primary sense of oneness (mukhya-ekatva) cannot be sustained. In all these alternatives there results the un-deliverance of the soul, since transmigratory selfhood is not nullified; and if it is nullified, the destruction of (the jīva’s) own nature would follow, since (in this view) Brahman-Selfhood is not admitted.
BS_C04_S03_V14::block-4: As to what is uttered by some — ‘The nitya (regular) and naimittika (occasional) rites are performed for the non-arising of pratyavāya (sin of omission); the kāmya (desire-prompted) and pratiṣiddha (forbidden) actions are abandoned for the non-attainment of heaven and hell; and the rites whose fruits are enjoyable in the present body are exhausted by enjoyment itself — therefore, after the fall of the present body, in the absence of any cause for connecting to a further body, even apart from Self-being-Brahman, kaivalya as abiding in one’s own form will be accomplished merely by such conduct’ — that is incorrect, due to absence of any pramāṇa. For no scripture has propounded this — ‘The seeker after liberation should conduct himself thus.’ This is merely speculation by their own intellect — ‘since saṃsāra is caused by karma, in absence of the cause it will not arise.’ But even this cannot be reasoned, for the absence of a cause is hard to know. For many karmas accumulated in other births, with desirable and undesirable fruits, are conceivable for each being. Since their contradictory fruits cannot be enjoyed simultaneously, some, having gained their occasion, fashion this birth, while others wait for their place, time and instrumental conditions — hence, since the remaining ones cannot be exhausted by present enjoyment, even of one whose conduct is as described, on the fall of the present body the absence of a cause for another body cannot be settled. And the existence of karma-residue is established by śrutis and smṛtis like ‘There those whose conduct here is pleasant…’; ‘then by the residue’ etc. (Objection): The nityas and naimittikas will exhaust them. (Reply): No, since there is no opposition. For there is the relation of expungeable-and-expunger only when there is opposition. And there is no opposition between meritorious deeds accumulated from previous births and the nitya-naimittikas, since both are alike of the form of purification (śuddhi-rūpatva). For demerits, however, since they are of the form of impurity (aśuddhi-rūpatva), there being opposition, let there be expunging. Yet from that mere fact, the absence-of-cause for another body cannot be established, because the cause-hood of meritorious deeds (sukṛta) is intact, and because complete expunging even of demerits is not perceived. Nor is there any pramāṇa that from the performance of nitya-naimittika rites there is only the non-arising of sin, and not also the rise of some other fruit — for the rise of another fruit too as a concomitant is possible. Indeed Āpastamba recalls — ‘Just as on a mango that is intended for fruit, shade and fragrance arise as concomitants, so on the practice of dharma, worldly goods arise as concomitants’ (Āp. Dh. Sū. 1.7.20.3). Nor, in the absence of right-vision (samyag-darśana), can it be guaranteed by anyone that, between birth and death, kāmya and pratiṣiddha (acts) will be wholly avoided, since even very accomplished persons are seen to commit subtle transgressions. It can only be doubted. Even so, the absence of a cause is hard to know. And, without admitting Self-being-Brahman accessible through knowledge, kaivalya cannot be desired for the Self whose nature (svabhāva) is doership and enjoyer-hood, since svabhāva, like fire’s heat, is unavoidable. (Objection): The effects of doership and enjoyer-hood are the calamity (anartha), not the power (śakti) for them; hence, even if the power abides, by avoiding the effects, mokṣa is consistent. (Reply): That too is wrong, for the production of effects is hard to ward off when the power exists. (Objection): The power alone, without depending on other causes, does not initiate effects; hence even if it stands alone, it does not transgress. (Reply): That too is wrong, for the (auxiliary) causes too are eternally connected by the relation called śakti-lakṣaṇa. Therefore, the Self being of the nature of doer-and-enjoyer …
BS_C04_S03_V14::block-5: (Objection): Even on the non-difference of the jīva from the Supreme, the consequence is that all worldly transactions (vyavahāra) would be lost, since the means of valid cognition such as perception (pratyakṣa) etc. would not function. (Reply): No, this stands consistent like the dream-vyavahāra prior to awakening (prāk-prabodhāt). And the śāstra, having stated worldly transactions of perception etc. with reference to the un-awakened, by ‘For where there is, as it were, duality, there one sees another’ (Bṛ. Up. 2.4.14) etc., shows the absence thereof again with reference to the awakened — ‘But where for him all has become the Self, then by what should he see whom?’ (Bṛ. Up. 2.4.14). Thus, since the cognition of a thing-to-be-reached etc. is sublated for the knower of Supreme Brahman, going (gati) cannot in any way be established. (Question): What then is the object of the gati-śrutis? It is replied — they will pertain to saguṇa-vidyās. Thus, somewhere going is mentioned in connection with the Pañcāgni-vidyā, somewhere with the Paryaṅka-vidyā, somewhere with the Vaiśvānara-vidyā. Even where going is mentioned in connection with Brahman — as ‘Prāṇa is Brahman, kha is Brahman, the spatial Brahman’ (Chā. Up. 4.10.4); and ‘Now in this city of Brahman, there is the small lotus, the abode’ (Chā. Up. 8.1.1) — there too, since saguṇa-Brahman alone is to be worshipped through such qualities as vāmanītva (leadership of the dear), satyakāmatva (true-desires) etc., going is possible. Nowhere is going heard with respect to the Supreme Brahman. Likewise the prohibition of going is heard — ‘His prāṇas do not depart’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.6). In passages such as ‘The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme’ (Tai. Up. 2.1.1), although √āp has the sense of reaching, since reaching of another locus is impossible by the reasoning explained, this is stated only as recovery of one’s own form (svarūpa-pratipatti) with reference to the dissolution of names-and-forms superimposed by avidyā — to be understood like ‘Being Brahman alone, he attains Brahman’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.6). Furthermore, going to the Supreme, when expounded, would be either for the sake of allurement (prarocanā) or for the sake of contemplation (anucintana). Of these, allurement is not produced for the knower of Brahman by the mention of going, since that is accomplished by the self-evident, immediate well-being conferred by knowledge itself. Nor for that knowledge — which conveys the eternally attained Highest-good and is not such as has a fruit yet to be effected — is there any need for the contemplation of going. Therefore the going pertains to the Lower Brahman. There, due to non-discrimination between Supreme and Lower, the gati-śrutis abiding in the Lower Brahman are superimposed upon the Supreme. (Question): Are there then two Brahmans, the higher and the lower? Reply: Yes, two indeed — as seen from ‘O Satyakāma, this very (Oṃkāra) is both the higher and the lower Brahman’ (Pra. Up. 5.2). (Question): What then is the higher Brahman, and what the lower? Reply: Where Brahman is taught by such words as ‘not gross’ etc., by negating distinctions of name-and-form etc. created by avidyā, that is the higher (para). The same Brahman, when taught for upāsanā as qualified by some specific name-and-form-distinction — by words like ‘mind-made, prāṇa-bodied, light-formed’ (Chā. Up. 3.14.2) etc. — is the lower (apara). (Objection): Then would not the śruti of non-duality be obstructed? (Reply): No, since (the lower) is laid aside as having name-and-form upādhis fashioned by avidyā. And of that worship of the lower Brahman, the fruit heard in its proximity — ‘Should he wish for the world of fathers’ (Chā. Up. 8.2.1) etc. — being characterized as world-lordship, falls within the saṃsāric domain itself, since avidyā is not removed. And since that (lower Brahman) is bound to a particular locus, going for its attainment is not contradictory. Even in (Brahman’s) all-pervadingness …
BS_C04_S03_V15: Bādarāyaṇa (holds): (the amānava-puruṣa) leads (only) those whose support is non-symbolic (apratīka), since either way is faultless and according to (the rule of) ‘as is the meditation’. (15)
BS_C04_S03_V15::block-0: It is settled that the gati pertains to the Effect (kārya-Brahman), not to the Supreme. Now this doubt arises — does the amānava-puruṣa lead to Brahmaloka all the meditators on modifications without distinction (sarvān avikār-ālambanān aviśeṣeṇa), or only some of them? (Pūrvapakṣa): For all these knowers, going to a place other than the Supreme Brahman would obtain. For at ‘There is no rule (of restriction) regarding all (such vidyās)’ (Br. Sū. 3.3.31), this (going) was extended without distinction to other vidyās. To this view obtained, he replies — ‘apratīkālambanāt’ (only of those whose support is non-symbolic). The Ācārya Bādarāyaṇa holds that, having excluded those whose support is a symbol (pratīka), (the amānava-puruṣa) leads all other meditators on modifications to Brahmaloka. There is no fault in admitting both modes thus, since the rule of non-restriction (aniyama-nyāya) applies to upāsanās other than those of symbols. ‘And tat-kratu’ (and accordingly as is the meditation) — this should be seen as the supportive reason for this two-fold mode. He who has Brahman as his determined contemplation (brahma-kratu) attains Brahman’s lordship — this is well-fitted (śliṣyate) by the śruti ‘As one meditates upon Him, so he becomes’; but in symbols there is no Brahman-as-determined-contemplation, since the worship there has the symbol as primary (pratīka-pradhānatva). (Objection): But even one whose contemplation is not Brahman is heard to go to Brahman, as in the Pañcāgni-vidyā — ‘He leads them to Brahman’ (Chā. Up. 4.15.5). (Reply): Be it so where such a directly-stated text (āhatya-vāda) is found. In its absence, by the general rule of tat-kratu-nyāya, only those of brahma-kratu attain Him, not others — thus is gathered. (15)
BS_C04_S03_V16: And (the śruti) shows a distinction (in fruits of pratīka-upāsanās). (16)
BS_C04_S03_V16::block-0: In symbol-meditations on Name etc., the (śruti) shows for each successive upāsanā a distinction in fruit superior to the prior — ‘As far as Name reaches, there one has free movement at will’ (Chā. Up. 7.1.5); ‘Speech, indeed, is greater than Name’ (Chā. Up. 7.2.1); ‘As far as Speech reaches, there one has free movement at will’ (Chā. Up. 7.2.2); ‘Mind, indeed, is greater than Speech’ (Chā. Up. 7.3.1) and so on. This distinction in fruits is consistent because such upāsanās have the symbol as their dependence (pratīka-tantratva). But if they had Brahman as their dependence, since Brahman is undifferentiated, how could there be a distinction in fruit? Therefore, those whose support is a symbol do not have a fruit equal to that of others. (16)
BS_C04_S04_INTRO1::block-0: It is heard — ‘In just this way this Sam-prasāda (the deep-sleep Self), having risen from this body and reached the Supreme Light, becomes manifest in his own form (svena rūpeṇa abhiniṣpadyate)’ (Chā. Up. 8.12.3). Here the doubt arises: does he become manifest with some adventitious feature (āgantukena viśeṣeṇa), as in places of enjoyment such as the world of devas, or by his own Self alone (ātma-mātreṇa)? (Pūrvapakṣa): The manifestation should be by some adventitious form, as in other realms — for mokṣa too is well-known to be a fruit, and ‘abhiniṣpadyate’ is a synonym for ‘arising’ (utpatti). If the manifestation were by mere own form, then since one’s own form is not lost in the prior states, it would already have been recognizable. Therefore (the manifestation) is by some specific feature. To this view obtained, we say —
BS_C04_S04_V01: On (Brahma-) sampatti, the manifestation (is by his own Self), from the word ‘svena’ (his own). (1)
BS_C04_S04_V01::block-0: He becomes manifest by the Self alone (kevalena ātmanā), not by any other attribute. Why? — From the word ‘svena’ (own) in ‘He becomes manifest in his own form.’ Otherwise, the qualifier ‘svena’ would be unjustified. (Objection): The word ‘sva’ may be in the sense of ‘one’s own’ (ātmīya). (Reply): No, that is unstateable here. For whatever form he becomes manifest in, that itself would be ‘his own’ — so the qualifier ‘svena’ would be purposeless. But on construing ‘sva’ as referring to the Self (ātma-vacanatā), it is purposeful — he becomes manifest by the Self-form alone, not by some adventitious other-form. (1)
BS_C04_S04_V02: (He is) liberated, (it being) from the (initial) declaration. (2)
BS_C04_S04_V02::block-0: (Leading bhāṣya): What then is the difference between the prior states and this, when the non-loss of own-form is equally true? — (Reply):
BS_C04_S04_V02::block-1: He who is said to ‘become manifest’ here, abides freed of all bondage, by the pure Self alone. In the prior states, on the contrary, the Self was clouded by the three states — ‘he becomes blind,’ ‘he as if cries,’ ‘he goes to utter loss’ — this is the distinction. (Objection): How is it known that he is now liberated? — (Reply): From the (initial) declaration (pratijñāna). For the text, having declared as the topic the Self free from the defects of the three states by ‘But this very (Self), I shall expound to you again’ (Chā. Up. 8.9.3), and having proposed ‘being bodiless, pleasure and pain do not touch (him)’ (Chā. Up. 8.12.1), concludes ‘he becomes manifest in his own form — that is the Highest Person’ (Chā. Up. 8.12.3). And in the opening of the narrative also, the declaration is concerning the liberated Self alone — ‘That Self which is sinless, etc.’ (Chā. Up. 8.7.1). The well-known fruit-hood of mokṣa is only with reference to the cessation of bondage, not with reference to the production of something previously non-existing. As for the synonymity of ‘abhiniṣpadyate’ with ‘arising,’ that is also with reference to the prior state — as one who is now free from disease is said to ‘arise’ on the cessation of disease; just so. Therefore there is no fault. (2)
BS_C04_S04_V03: (The ‘Light’ is) the Self, from the context. (3)
BS_C04_S04_V03::block-0: (Objection): How is he called ‘liberated’ when ‘having reached the Supreme Light’ (Chā. Up. 8.12.3) brings him within the domain of the modification (kārya), since the word ‘jyotis’ (light) is conventionally established in the elemental light? And one who has not transcended the domain of modification cannot be liberated, since modification is well-known to be afflicted (ārta). — (Reply): No fault. Here the word ‘jyotis’ refers to the Self alone, from the context (prakaraṇa). For in a context where the topic is the Supreme Self ‘sinless, ageless, deathless’ (Chā. Up. 8.7.1), the elemental light cannot suddenly be taken — it would entail abandoning what is being treated and proceeding with what is irrelevant (prakṛta-hāna and aprakṛta-prakriyā). The word ‘jyotis’ is also seen in the sense of the Self — ‘the devas (worship) Him as the Light of lights’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.4.16). This has been elaborated at ‘Light, on account of the seeing’ (Br. Sū. 1.3.40). (3)
BS_C04_S04_V04: (He abides) in non-difference (avibhāga), since (this) is (so) seen (in the śruti). (4)
BS_C04_S04_V04::block-0: When inquiring whether he who, having reached the Supreme Light, becomes manifest in his own form, becomes separate from the Supreme Self, or abides in non-difference — to one whose view is that, from ‘He moves about there’ (Chā. Up. 8.12.3) indicating locus and located, and from ‘having reached the Light’ (Chā. Up. 8.12.3) indicating agent and object, abiding is by separation alone — to him this is being expounded: the liberated abides in non-division with the Supreme Self alone. Why? — Because this is (so) seen. Thus — ‘That thou art’ (Chā. Up. 6.8.7); ‘I am Brahman’ (Bṛ. Up. 1.4.10); ‘where one sees nothing else’ (Chā. Up. 7.24.1); ‘there is not a second other than that, distinct, that he might see’ (Bṛ. Up. 4.3.23) — such passages show the Supreme Self in non-division alone. The fruit must be in accordance with one’s seeing (yathā-darśanam), by the rule of tat-kratu. And ‘As pure water poured into pure (water) becomes just like that — so, O Gautama, becomes the Self of the discerning sage who knows’ (Kaṭha 2.1.15) and similar passages, intent on portraying the form of the liberated, show non-division alone. So too the analogies of rivers and the ocean. The mention of difference is figuratively used even in non-difference, as seen from ‘In what is he, sir, established? In his own greatness’ (Chā. Up. 7.24.1); ‘delighting in the Self, sporting in the Self’ (Chā. Up. 7.25.2) and so on. (4)
BS_C04_S04_V05: ‘By (his) Brahman-(nature he becomes manifest)’ — so Jaimini, on the strength of the introduction (upanyāsa) and the rest. ‖ 5 ‖
BS_C04_S04_V05::block-0: It has been settled that in ‘svena rūpeṇa’ (Chā. U. 8.3.4) (the meaning is) — he becomes manifest (abhiniṣpadyate) by his own self-form alone, not by any adventitious other-form. Now, however, when one wishes to know the particularity of that (own form), it is being declared — his own form is the brāhma-form, terminating in apahata-pāpmatva and the rest down to satya-saṅkalpatva, and likewise sarva-jñatva and sarva-īśvaratva; by that own (form), he becomes manifest — so the teacher Jaimini holds. Whence (this view)? Because such a nature is ascertained from the upanyāsa (introductory exposition) and the rest. Thus, by the introduction running ‘ya ātmā apahata-pāpmā’ (Chā. U. 8.7.1) and ending in ‘satya-kāmaḥ satya-saṅkalpaḥ’ (Chā. U. 8.7.1), (the śruti) makes known that the Self is of such a nature. So too, ‘he there moves about, eating, playing, taking delight’ (Chā. U. 8.12.3) — by this it makes known the lordly form (aiśvarya-rūpa); and ‘his free movement (kāma-cāra) is in all the worlds’ (Chā. U. 7.25.2). And expressions such as ‘omniscient, all-lord’ (sarva-jñaḥ sarva-īśvaraḥ) and the like will become coherent in this way. ‖ 5 ‖
BS_C04_S04_V06: ‘By mere consciousness (citi-tan-mātra), since (the Self) is of that essence’ — thus says Auḍulomi. ‖ 6 ‖
BS_C04_S04_V06::block-0: (Siddhānta of Auḍulomi against Jaimini): Although apahata-pāpmatva and the rest are stated separately as (so many) attributes, yet these are merely born of verbal alternatives (śabda-vikalpa-jāḥ); for therein only the (mere) cessation of evil and the rest is conveyed. But pure caitanya alone is the very own form (svarūpa) of this Ātman; hence it is fitting that the manifestation be by that essence (tan-mātra) alone as svarūpa. And in this way the śruti also, of the kind ‘Verily, my dear, this Self is without inside, without outside, entire, a homogeneous mass of pure cognition (prajñāna-ghana)’ (Bṛ. U. 4.5.13), will receive its proper accommodation. As for satya-kāmatva and the rest — although they are spoken of as attributes by way of vastu-svarūpa, namely ‘his desires are real,’ yet, since they depend upon a relation with upādhis, there is no possibility of their being svarūpa like caitanya, since manifoldness (aneka-ākāratva) of Brahman has been refuted. For Brahman’s aneka-ākāratva has been refuted under ‘not even by way of place is the Supreme of two-fold mark’ (Br. Sū. 3.2.11). And for this very reason the mention of jakṣaṇa (eating) and the like is also intended for nothing but the absence of suffering, by way of stuti, like ‘ātma-ratiḥ’ and so on. For erotic delight, sportive play, and pairings cannot be described as primary in the Self (mukhya), since they presuppose a second object (dvitīya-viṣayatva). Therefore, He becomes manifest as that whose entire prapañca is utterly negated, as serene (prasanna), beyond all designation (avyapadeśya), as the very Self of cognition — so the teacher Auḍulomi holds. ‖ 6 ‖
BS_C04_S04_V07: Even so, on account of (the lordly form’s) being mentioned earlier (in the upanyāsa) and not being abolished, Bādarāyaṇa (holds) that there is no contradiction. ‖ 7 ‖
BS_C04_S04_V07::block-0: (Bādarāyaṇa’s reconciliation): Even so — that is, even granting that the pāramārthika (absolute) (form) is mere caitanya as svarūpa — yet from the standpoint of vyavahāra, the brāhma aiśvarya-rūpa, which had earlier been ascertained from the upanyāsa and the rest, is not repudiated; hence there is no contradiction — so the teacher Bādarāyaṇa holds. ‖ 7 ‖
BS_C04_S04_V08: But (the things desired arise) from (his) saṅkalpa alone, since the śruti (says) so. ‖ 8 ‖
BS_C04_S04_V08::block-0: (Context — the Hārda-vidyā): In the Hārda-vidyā it is heard — ‘If he becomes desirous of the world of fathers, by his very saṅkalpa his fathers rise up (to him)’ (Chā. U. 8.2.1) and so on. There a doubt arises — is mere saṅkalpa alone the cause of the rising up of the fathers and the rest, or is it accompanied by other instrumentalities (nimitta-antara)?
BS_C04_S04_V08::block-1: (Pūrvapakṣa): Even though ‘saṅkalpād eva’ is heard, dependence on other instrumentalities is fitting, on the analogy of the world. Just as in the world for ourselves the obtaining of fathers etc. follows from saṅkalpa together with the other causes, viz. going (to them) etc., so also for the mukta. In this way no contradiction with what is seen will arise (dṛṣṭa-viparītam na kalpitam). The expression ‘from saṅkalpa alone’ is uttered with reference to the easy availability of all the other ancillary means that bring about the resolved object — as for a king. Moreover, (fathers and the rest) arising from mere saṅkalpa, like the unfoldings of fancy (mano-ratha-vijṛmbhita-vat), being unstable (cañcala), would not suffice to provide ample enjoyment.
BS_C04_S04_V08::block-2: (Siddhānta): When this prima-facie position is established, we say — the rising up of fathers and the rest is from mere saṅkalpa alone. Whence? Because the śruti (says) so (tac-chruteḥ). The śruti ‘by his very saṅkalpa his fathers rise up’ (Chā. U. 8.2.1) and the like would be straitened (pīḍyeta) if dependence on other instrumentalities were posited. If indeed an additional instrumentality were one which itself only follows the saṅkalpa, let it be so; but no instrumentality requiring a separate effort (prayatna-antara-sampādyam) is desired, since prior to its accomplishment the saṅkalpa would be rendered futile (vandhya-saṅkalpatva-prasaṅgāt). Nor does the maxim ‘as in the world,’ being a sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa, prevail in respect of a matter ascertained from the śruti. And the persistence of these (fathers etc.) for as long as the purpose lasts is achieved by the very strength of saṅkalpa, since the mukta’s saṅkalpa is of a nature distinct from the natural (prākṛta) saṅkalpa. ‖ 8 ‖
BS_C04_S04_V09: And for this very reason (he is) one having no other lord. ‖ 9 ‖
BS_C04_S04_V09::block-0: And for this very reason — namely, because his saṅkalpa is unfailing (avandhya) — the knower (vidvān) is anan-yādhipati: there is no other lord over him. That is the meaning. For not even an ordinary person, while willing, would, when free movement is open, will himself to be under another’s mastery. The śruti also shows this — ‘Now, those who, having known the Self here, depart together with these real desires (satya-kāmas) — for them there is free movement (kāma-cāra) in all the worlds’ (Chā. U. 8.1.6). ‖ 9 ‖
BS_C04_S04_V10: (There is) absence (of body and senses for the released), says Bādari, for thus indeed (the śruti) says. ‖ 10 ‖
BS_C04_S04_V10::block-0: (Context — extent of bodily/sense apparatus for the released): From the śruti ‘by his saṅkalpa alone his fathers rise up’ (Chā. U. 8.2.1) it is established at any rate that the manas is the instrument of saṅkalpa. But whether the body and sense-organs exist or do not exist for the knower who has attained lordship — this is now examined.
BS_C04_S04_V10::block-1: (Bādari’s view): To begin with, the teacher Bādari holds the absence of body and senses for the knower, who is being magnified (mahīyamāna). Why? Because the āmnāya speaks thus: ‘by the manas he sees these desires, he sports’ (Chā. U. 8.12.5), ‘these (desires) which are in the brahma-loka’ (Chā. U. 8.12.5). If he were to disport with the manas together with body and senses, the qualifier ‘by the manas’ (manasā iti) would not occur. Therefore (there is) absence of body and senses in mokṣa. ‖ 10 ‖
BS_C04_S04_V11: (There is) presence (of body and senses), says Jaimini, on account of the recital of (manifold) alternatives. ‖ 11 ‖
BS_C04_S04_V11::block-0: (Jaimini’s view): The teacher Jaimini, however, holds with respect to the released (mukta) the existence (bhāva) of the body too along with the senses, just as of the manas. For (the śruti) recites the alternative of his being manifold, in ‘he becomes one, he becomes threefold’ (Chā. U. 7.26.2) and the like. For there cannot be straightforward (āñjasī) manifoldness apart from a multiplicity of bodies. Although this alternative of manifoldness is read in the nirguṇa Bhūma-vidyā, yet this lordship (aiśvarya), already existing in the saguṇa stage, is celebrated for the praise of the Bhūma-vidyā; hence it is said to be present as the fruit of saguṇa-vidyā. ‖ 11 ‖
BS_C04_S04_V12: Bādarāyaṇa (holds it to be) of both kinds, like the dvādaśāha (sacrifice), and from this (very reason). ‖ 12 ‖
BS_C04_S04_V12::block-0: (Bādarāyaṇa’s reconciliation): The teacher Bādarāyaṇa, however, on this very ground — namely, on the strength of the seeing of śrutis of both marks (ubhaya-liṅga-śruti-darśana) — properly holds the case to be of both kinds. When (the released) wills having a body, he becomes embodied; and when (he wills) having no body, he becomes disembodied; for he is satya-saṅkalpa, and saṅkalpa is variously diverse (saṅkalpa-vaicitryāt). Like the dvādaśāha — just as the dvādaśāha is (both) a sattra and an ahīna, on account of the seeing of śrutis of both marks — even so is this (case) too. ‖ 12 ‖
BS_C04_S04_V13: When there is no body, (the desires are fulfilled) as in the intermediate state (of dream), since that is intelligible. ‖ 13 ‖
BS_C04_S04_V13::block-0: When there is the absence (abhāva) of the body (tanu) endowed with the senses (sa-indriya), then — just as in the intermediate state (sandhya-sthāna, i.e., dream) the desired objects such as fathers and the like (pitr-ādi-kāmāḥ) come into being merely as cognitions (upalabdhi-mātrāḥ), even though body, senses and objects are non-existent — so too in liberation they would arise. For only thus is this (i.e., the prior śruti about fulfilled desires) intelligible. ‖ 13 ‖
BS_C04_S04_V14: When the body exists, (it is) as in the waking state. ‖ 14 ‖
BS_C04_S04_V14::block-0: When, on the other hand, the body exists (bhāve tanoḥ), then — just as in the waking state (jāgarita) the desired objects such as fathers, etc., come about as actually existent — so likewise it is intelligible for the liberated one. ‖ 14 ‖
BS_C04_S04_V15: (His) entry (into many bodies is) like (that of) a lamp, for thus does (śruti) declare. ‖ 15 ‖
BS_C04_S04_V15::block-0: In ‘Jaimini (holds) the existence (of body for the liberated), since (the śruti) recounts (it) by way of alternatives’ (Br. Sū. 4.4.11) (citation), the embodiedness (sa-śarīratva) of the liberated has been stated. There, in the case of the multiple-body creation in (states like) ‘he becomes threefold’ etc., this enquiry arises (siddhāntic enquiry framed as pūrvapakṣa): are the many bodies created without selves (nirātmaka), like wooden puppets (dāru-yantra-vat), or are they ensouled (sātmaka), like our own bodies?  Now, since differentiation between the (single) self and (single) mind is not intelligible, the conjunction (of the liberated) is with one body (alone), and the rest of the bodies are without selves — when (the pūrvapakṣa) is thus established, (the siddhānta) is set forth: ‘like a lamp is the entry’ (pradīpa-vad āveśaḥ). Just as one lamp assumes the form of many lamps through its capacity for transformation (vikāra-śakti-yoga), so too the wise one (vidvān), though one, by reason of (his) lordliness (aiśvarya-yoga) assumes manifoldness and enters into all the bodies. How (is this known)? Because thus does scripture (śāstra) show the manifoldness of the one — ‘he becomes one, becomes threefold, fivefold, sevenfold, ninefold’ (Chā. U. 7.26.2) (citation), and so on. This is not consonant with the assumption of the wooden-puppet analogy, nor with the entry of another jīva. And bodies without selves cannot have any activity (pravṛtti). As for (the objection) that, because differentiation between self and mind is not intelligible, the conjunction with many bodies is impossible — this is no fault; (the liberated one) being of true resolve (satya-saṅkalpatva), will create the other bodies as also possessed of mind (samanaska), each following the one (master) mind. And once they are created, owing to the difference of adjuncts (upādhi-bheda), the self too will fittingly preside (adhiṣṭhātṛtva) by way of (apparent) difference. This very procedure of yogins’ conjunction with many bodies (is taught) in the yoga-śāstras. ‖ 15 ‖
BS_C04_S04_V16: (The denial of particular cognition) refers to either of the two — merging-into-self or attainment (of Brahman); for it has been (so) declared. ‖ 16 ‖
BS_C04_S04_V16::block-0: But how can the lordliness characterized by entry into many bodies, etc., be conceded for the liberated (mukta), when such śruti as ‘by what should one know what?’ (Br. U. 4.5.15) (citation), ‘there is not that second thing distinct from him which he might know’ (Br. U. 4.3.30) (citation), and ‘he becomes the one seer, the non-dual, like water’ (Br. U. 4.3.32) (citation) prohibits particular cognition (viśeṣa-vijñāna)? — to (this objection from the pūrvapakṣin), (the siddhāntin) replies (the next sūtra is read).
BS_C04_S04_V16::block-1: Svāpyaya (merging-into-self) is deep sleep (suṣupta), per the śruti ‘he is merged into his own; therefore they say of him “he sleeps”’ (Chā. U. 6.8.1) (citation) — nirvacana of svapiti as svam apītaḥ. Sampatti is absolute isolation (kaivalya), per the śruti ‘being Brahman alone, he attains Brahman’ (Br. U. 4.4.6) (citation). It is in reference to one or the other of these two states (avasthā) that this declaration of the absence of particular designation (viśeṣa-saṁjñā-abhāva-vacanam) is made — somewhere with reference to the deep-sleep state, somewhere with reference to the kaivalya state. How is this ascertained? Because in the very (passages) under that very topic, this has been declared (āviṣkṛtam) — ‘arising out of these elements, it perishes along with them; after death there is no consciousness’ (Br. U. 2.4.12) (citation), ‘when, for him, all becomes the very Self’ (Br. U. 2.4.14) (citation), ‘where (the man) asleep desires no desire whatsoever and sees no dream whatsoever’ (Br. U. 4.3.19) (citation), and the like. But the dwelling that is the fruition of the saguṇa-vidyā is another state, like svarga and the like, where this lordliness (aiśvarya) is described. Therefore there is no defect. ‖ 16 ‖
BS_C04_S04_V17: Excepting the world-operation (jagad-vyāpāra); because (Brahman alone) is the topic and because the others are not relevant. ‖ 17 ‖
BS_C04_S04_V17::block-0: Of those who, by upāsana of the saguṇa-Brahman, attain communion (sāyujya) with Īśvara along with their mind itself, is the lordliness unrestricted (niravagraha) or restricted (sāvagraha)? — this is the doubt. What, first, is established (pūrva-pakṣa)? — Their lordliness must be unconditioned (niraṅkuśa), per such śrutis as ‘he attains autonomous sovereignty (svārājya)’ (Tai.
