U. 1.6.2) (citation), ‘all the gods bring tribute to him’ (Tai. U. 1.5.3) (citation), ‘they have free movement (kāma-cāra) in all the worlds’ (Chā. U. 7.25.2) (citation). When this is established, (the siddhāntin) says — ‘excepting the world-operation’ (jagad-vyāpāra-varjam). Excepting the operation consisting of the origination, etc., of the world (jagad-utpatty-ādi-vyāpāra), the rest — the lordliness consisting of (powers like) aṇimā etc. — may be befitting for the liberated; but the world-operation belongs to the eternally established (nitya-siddha) Īśvara alone. Why? Because He is the topic prakṛta (in the world-operation passages); and because the others are not on hand (asannihita). For it is the supreme Īśvara alone who is qualified for the world-operation, since the teaching of origination, etc., proceeds with reference to Him alone, and because (the relevant) words denote eternality. Whereas the lordliness consisting of aṇimā, etc., of the others (i.e., of the liberated upāsakas) is heard of as being preceded by enquiry and search. Hence they are not on hand for the world-operation. Moreover, because they are still possessed of mind (samanaska), there could at times even be conflict among them due to disagreement — the intent of one being preservation, of another, dissolution. If, on the other hand, it is maintained that the resolve of the others follows the resolve of (one of them), so that there is no conflict — then it stands established that (the resolves of) the others are entirely subordinate (ākūta-tantra) to the supreme Īśvara. ‖ 17 ‖
BS_C04_S04_V18: If it be said (the lordliness of the liberated is unconditioned) on account of the direct teaching, (we say) no — for (such teaching) refers to (Brahman) abiding in the official sphere (adhikārika-maṇḍala). ‖ 18 ‖
BS_C04_S04_V18::block-0: Now, what was said (by the pūrvapakṣin) — that, owing to direct teaching such as ‘he attains autonomous sovereignty (svārājya)’ (Tai. U. 1.6.2) (citation), the unrestricted lordliness is appropriate for the wise — that is to be refuted. Here it is said: this is no defect, because of the statement (uktiḥ) about (the supreme Īśvara) abiding in the sphere of office (adhikārika-maṇḍala). The official (ādhikārika) supreme Īśvara who abides in special seats such as the orb of the sun and the like — it is upon Him that this attainment of svārājya depends, as is here being stated. The reason: immediately afterwards (the text) says ‘he attains the lord of the mind (manasaspati)’ (Tai. U. 1.6.2) (citation). For the meaning is: he attains that pre-established (pūrva-siddha) Īśvara who is the lord of all minds. In accordance with this, immediately afterwards it says he becomes ‘lord of speech, lord of the eye, lord of the ear, lord of cognition’ (citation). Likewise, in other places too, the lordliness of the others (the liberated upāsakas) is to be construed, as far as possible, as dependent upon the eternally established Īśvara alone. ‖ 18 ‖
BS_C04_S04_V19: And (there is also Brahman) untouched by transformation; for thus does (śruti) declare its (twofold) standing. ‖ 19 ‖
BS_C04_S04_V19::block-0: And (there is also) the eternally liberated, supreme-lordly form (pārameśvaraṁ rūpam) which is untouched by transformation (vikāra-avartin) — not merely the form located in adjuncts such as the orb of the sun, which falls within the realm of transformation (vikāra-mātra-gocara). For thus does the Veda (āmnāya) declare His twofold (dvi-rūpa) standing — ‘so great is His glory; greater than that is the Puruṣa. One foot of His is all beings; three feet of His are immortal in the heaven’ (Chā. U. 3.12.6) (citation), and the like. Nor can it be said that those who depend upon the other (i.e., the saguṇa form) attain that nirvikāra (transformation-free) form — because they are not of that intent (a-tat-kratutva). Therefore, just as in the dvi-rūpa supreme Īśvara they remain in the saguṇa alone without attaining the nirguṇa form, so too within the saguṇa itself they remain in the restricted (sāvagraha) (lordliness) alone, without attaining the unrestricted (niravagraha) lordliness — thus is it to be understood. ‖ 19 ‖
BS_C04_S04_V20: And both (śruti and smṛti) show this (transformation-free nature of the supreme light). ‖ 20 ‖
BS_C04_S04_V20::block-0: Śruti and smṛti both show the transformation-untouched nature (vikāra-avartitva) of the supreme light (paraṁ jyotis) — ‘there the sun does not shine, nor moon and stars, nor do these lightnings shine — whence this fire?’ (Mu. U. 2.2.11; Ka. U. 2.2.15) (citation), and ‘that the sun illumines not, nor moon, nor fire’ (Bh. Gītā 15.6) (citation). Thus, the transformation-untouched nature of the supreme light is well-established — this is the import. ‖ 20 ‖
BS_C04_S04_V21: And from the liṅga (indicatory mark) of (mere) parity in bhoga (enjoyment) only. ‖ 21 ‖
BS_C04_S04_V21::block-0: (Siddhānta continued): For this further reason too, the aiśvarya (lordly power) of those who take their stand on the (effected) vikāra (i.e., the saguṇa-brahmaloka attainers) is not unimpeded (niraṅkuśa), since śruti declares that theirs is bhoga-mātra (mere enjoyment) parity with the anādi-siddha (beginninglessly established) Īśvara — and not parity in the work of creation, sustenance, and dissolution. So it is heard: ‘The waters indeed are measured by him; that yonder world (is his domain)’ and ‘As all beings serve that very deity, so do all beings serve one who knows thus,’ ‘Through that he wins sāyujya (union) and salokatā (co-residence) with that very deity’ (Bṛ. U. 1.5.23) — and from such other liṅgas (indicatory marks) which mention bheda (difference) (between the upāsaka and the upāsya, between the muktāvasthā jīva and Īśvara), it is established that their aiśvarya is bounded. ‖ 21 ‖
BS_C04_S04_V22: Non-return — from the śabda (śruti); non-return — from the śabda. ‖ 22 ‖
BS_C04_S04_V22::block-0: (Leading bhāṣya — pūrvapakṣa): But, this being so, the aiśvarya (of these saguṇa-brahmaloka attainers), being sātiśaya (admitting of degrees, i.e., limited), would be antavat (terminating, finite); and from that it would follow that there is āvṛtti (return) of these (mukta-jīvas, back into saṃsāra) — to this objection, the venerable teacher Bādarāyaṇa furnishes the (concluding) reply (which is the very last sūtra of the śāstra):
BS_C04_S04_V22::block-1: (Siddhānta): Those who, by the deva-yāna path — endowed with the nāḍī (subtle channel) and (sun-)raśmi (rays), parvan-ed (segmented) by the arcir-ādi (flame-and-the-rest stations) — go to the brahmaloka qualified by the śāstra (as in ‘yasmin Aro and Ṇyo, the two oceans, in brahmaloka in the third heaven from here, in which the lake Airaṃ Madīyam, in which the aśvattha-tree Soma-savana, in which the unconquered citadel of Brahman, in which the lordly-measured golden mansion,’ which is detailed manifoldly in the mantra-, arthavāda-, and other passages) — they, having attained that, do not return like those who have come from candraloka after their bhoga is exhausted (bhukta-bhogāḥ). Why? — From the śabdas (scriptural words): ‘Going upward through that, he attains immortality’ (Chā. U. 8.6.6 / Ka. U. 2.3.16), ‘For them there is no return’ (Bṛ. U. 6.2.15), ‘Those who proceed by this (path) do not return to this human cycle’ (Chā. U. 4.15.5), ‘He attains the brahmaloka’ (Chā. U. 8.15.1), ‘And he does not return again’ — and the like. Even though the aiśvarya is antavat (finite), how nevertheless there is anāvṛtti (non-return) — that has been described earlier in ‘Upon the dissolution of the kārya (the saguṇa-brahmaloka), along with its presider (Hiraṇyagarbha), to that supreme (akṣara is the going)’ (Br. Sū. 4.3.10). For those whose tamas (ignorance) is wholly demolished by samyag-darśana (right vision) — those who are devoted to the eternally-established nirvāṇa — anāvṛtti is established as a matter of course. Indeed, it is by recourse to that (samyag-darśana / liberation in the Supreme) alone that even those who have taken refuge in the saguṇa attain the siddhi of anāvṛtti. ‘anāvṛttiḥ śabdāt, anāvṛttiḥ śabdāt’ — the repetition of the sūtra signifies the conclusion of the śāstra. ‖ 22 ‖
